stem: A 72-year-old woman tripped at home and landed on her outstretched left arm. An X-ray in the emergency department shows a fracture through the surgical neck of the humerus. Pinprick sensation is reduced over a small patch on the outer aspect of the upper arm just below the point of the shoulder. Sensation in the forearm and hand is normal, and she can extend her wrist and fingers. Which nerve has most likely been injured?
why_correct: The axillary nerve winds around the surgical neck of the humerus, so it is vulnerable in fractures here and in anterior shoulder dislocation. It supplies deltoid and teres minor and gives sensation to the regimental badge area over the lateral upper arm. Reduced sensation in exactly this patch after a surgical neck fracture points to axillary nerve injury.
why_wrong: A. Radial nerve injury follows mid-shaft fractures and causes wrist drop, but her wrist extension is intact. B. The suprascapular nerve supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus and has no cutaneous area on the lateral arm. C. Long thoracic nerve injury causes winging of the scapula without arm numbness. D. Musculocutaneous nerve injury weakens elbow flexion and numbs the lateral forearm, not the shoulder.
pearl: Always test and document regimental badge sensation in surgical neck fractures and shoulder dislocations, both before and after any manipulation.
thinking: Fall onto outstretched arm ↓ Fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus ↓ Nerve that wraps around the surgical neck ↓ Numb patch over lateral upper arm: regimental badge area ↓ Axillary nerve
exam_trap: A, radial nerve — the best-known nerve injury with humeral fractures, but it follows mid-shaft fractures and causes wrist drop; her wrist extension is normal.
takeaway: Surgical neck fracture with a numb regimental badge area: axillary nerve injury.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 9 Oct 2026 (held pack H01). Do not return to the live bank.

presentation: Peak flow variability and reversibility — asthma
stem: A 23-year-old woman sees her GP with several months of night-time cough, chest tightness and wheeze, worse in cold air. Her twice-daily home peak flow diary shows wide swings, with the lowest readings on waking. Spirometry shows a reduced FEV1/FVC ratio, and repeat spirometry 15 minutes after inhaled salbutamol shows a substantial rise in FEV1. What do these findings indicate?
why_correct: Marked variability in peak flow, worst in the morning, together with obstructive spirometry that improves substantially after a bronchodilator, shows airflow obstruction that varies and reverses. This is the physiological hallmark of asthma and, with a typical history, supports the diagnosis. UK guidance confirms asthma with objective tests such as FeNO, spirometry with bronchodilator reversibility and peak flow variability, rather than relying on symptoms alone.
why_wrong: A. Fixed obstruction, as in established COPD, shows little change after a bronchodilator and little day-to-day variation. B. A restrictive defect reduces FVC with a normal or high FEV1/FVC ratio. D. Upper airway obstruction produces a flattened flow–volume loop and stridor rather than bronchodilator reversibility. E. Normal diurnal variation is small and does not produce obstructive spirometry.
pearl: Asthma is variable and reversible; COPD is persistent and largely fixed. A reduced FEV1/FVC that improves significantly with salbutamol, with early-morning dips in peak flow, points to asthma.
thinking: Nocturnal cough and wheeze, cold-air trigger ↓ Peak flow swings, lowest on waking ↓ Obstructive spirometry ↓ Large improvement after salbutamol ↓ Variable, reversible airflow obstruction
exam_trap: A, fixed airflow obstruction — the reduced FEV1/FVC ratio shows obstruction, which tempts this answer, but the substantial bronchodilator response and diurnal swings show it is reversible, not fixed.
takeaway: Morning peak flow dips plus bronchodilator reversibility mean reversible obstruction, the signature of asthma.

presentation: Dyspepsia with alarm features — urgent endoscopy
stem: A 64-year-old man sees his GP with 6 weeks of gnawing upper abdominal discomfort after meals. He has never had indigestion before. He has had to tighten his belt by two notches without trying, and his wife thinks he looks pale. He takes no regular medicines. Abdominal examination is unremarkable. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Carbon-13 urea breath test for H. pylori
options.B: Full-dose proton pump inhibitor for 4 weeks, then review
options.D: Routine referral to the gastroenterology clinic

correct_answer: E. Urgent direct-access upper gastrointestinal endoscopy
why_correct: New dyspepsia in an older man with unexplained weight loss raises concern about oesophageal or gastric cancer. NICE suspected cancer guidance recommends urgent direct-access upper gastrointestinal endoscopy in this situation, so that any lesion can be seen and biopsied. Starting empirical treatment or testing for H. pylori first would delay the diagnosis.
why_wrong: A. Test-and-treat for H. pylori is for uncomplicated dyspepsia without alarm features. B. An empirical PPI trial may mask symptoms and delay the diagnosis of a cancer. C. Ultrasound does not assess the gastric or oesophageal mucosa. D. A routine referral is too slow when cancer is suspected.
pearl: Upper GI red flags: dysphagia at any age, or age 55 and over with weight loss plus upper abdominal pain, reflux or dyspepsia. These need urgent direct-access endoscopy, not a PPI trial.
thinking: New-onset dyspepsia in an older adult ↓ Unexplained weight loss and pallor ↓ Alarm features for upper GI cancer ↓ Tissue diagnosis needed quickly ↓ Urgent direct-access endoscopy
exam_trap: B, full-dose PPI for 4 weeks — it is the usual first step for dyspepsia, but alarm features change the pathway, and a PPI may heal the surface of a cancer and delay its diagnosis.
takeaway: New dyspepsia with weight loss in an older adult needs urgent endoscopy, not a PPI trial.

stem: A 47-year-old woman who has had several admissions with alcohol-related pancreatitis attends clinic. Over the last few months her stools have become pale, bulky and oily; they are difficult to flush and smell very offensive. She has lost weight despite a good appetite and has recently been diagnosed with diabetes. She is not jaundiced. What is the most likely cause of the change in her stools?

options.C: Obstruction of the common bile duct

why_correct: Repeated pancreatitis has progressed to chronic pancreatitis, destroying acinar tissue and reducing lipase secretion. Undigested fat then reaches the colon, producing pale, bulky, oily, offensive stools that are hard to flush, with weight loss. New diabetes reflects loss of islet tissue as well. Treatment is pancreatic enzyme replacement taken with meals, alongside stopping alcohol.
why_wrong: B. Coeliac disease can cause steatorrhoea but does not fit the history of recurrent alcohol-related pancreatitis. C. Bile duct obstruction causes pale stools with jaundice and dark urine, which she does not have. D. Bacterial overgrowth can coexist with chronic pancreatitis but is not the primary explanation. E. Bile acid diarrhoea causes watery stools, typically after ileal disease or resection, rather than fatty ones.
pearl: Chronic pancreatitis gives pain, steatorrhoea and diabetes as exocrine and endocrine tissue are lost. Treat malabsorption with pancreatic enzyme replacement taken with food, and check fat-soluble vitamins.
thinking: Recurrent alcohol-related pancreatitis ↓ Pale, bulky, oily stools that are hard to flush ↓ Weight loss and new diabetes ↓ Loss of acinar and islet tissue ↓ Pancreatic exocrine insufficiency
exam_trap: C, common bile duct obstruction — pale stools tempt this answer, but obstruction comes with jaundice and dark urine, whereas oily, hard-to-flush stools point to fat maldigestion.
takeaway: Steatorrhoea after recurrent pancreatitis means exocrine insufficiency; treat with enzyme replacement.

stem: A 51-year-old man presents to the emergency department after a weekend of heavy drinking with 12 hours of constant, severe upper abdominal pain boring through to his back, and repeated vomiting. His heart rate is 108/min and blood pressure 128/80 mmHg. His epigastrium is tender with guarding and bowel sounds are reduced. An erect chest X-ray shows no free air under the diaphragm. Serum lipase is many times the upper limit of normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Acute pancreatitis is diagnosed from typical pain (constant, severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, often with vomiting) together with a markedly raised serum lipase or amylase. Alcohol and gallstones are the commonest causes in the UK. Management is supportive with IV fluids, analgesia and severity assessment, with ultrasound to look for gallstones.
why_wrong: A. A perforated ulcer usually causes sudden generalised peritonitis with free air under the diaphragm, which is absent here. B. Cholecystitis causes right upper quadrant pain with fever and a positive Murphy's sign, without a markedly raised lipase. C. An inferior myocardial infarction can cause epigastric pain, so an ECG is essential, but it does not raise lipase. E. Biliary colic is self-limiting pain with normal pancreatic enzymes.
pearl: Acute pancreatitis is diagnosed with two of three: typical pain, lipase or amylase at least three times normal, and imaging features. Gallstones and alcohol are the leading UK causes; always perform an ECG in epigastric pain.
thinking: Constant epigastric pain radiating to the back ↓ Vomiting after heavy alcohol intake ↓ No free air on erect film ↓ Lipase markedly raised ↓ Acute pancreatitis
exam_trap: A, perforated duodenal ulcer — epigastric pain with guarding fits, and amylase can rise modestly in perforation, but the absence of free air and a markedly raised lipase point to pancreatitis.
takeaway: Back-radiating epigastric pain with a markedly raised lipase is acute pancreatitis.

presentation: Stable upper GI bleed — timing of endoscopy
stem: A 72-year-old woman who takes aspirin and has been buying ibuprofen for knee pain presents to the emergency department after passing two black, tarry stools. She feels a little light-headed on standing but is alert. Her heart rate is 88/min and blood pressure 132/78 mmHg. Her haemoglobin is lower than on her previous blood test. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Immediate endoscopy before IV access or blood tests
options.B: Admit, resuscitate as needed, calculate a risk score and arrange endoscopy within 24 hours
options.C: Discharge with an oral PPI and an outpatient endoscopy
options.D: Start an IV PPI infusion and defer endoscopy for a week

correct_answer: B. Admit, resuscitate as needed, calculate a risk score and arrange endoscopy within 24 hours
why_correct: This is an acute upper GI bleed from a probable aspirin- and NSAID-related ulcer in a patient who is currently haemodynamically stable. NICE advises resuscitation as needed, formal risk assessment with the Glasgow–Blatchford score before endoscopy, and endoscopy within 24 hours of admission for stable patients. Endoscopy immediately after resuscitation is reserved for unstable patients with severe bleeding.
why_wrong: A. Endoscopy never precedes basic assessment and resuscitation, and immediate endoscopy is for unstable patients. C. Melaena with a falling haemoglobin in an older patient on aspirin is not a low-risk bleed suitable for discharge. D. NICE advises against starting acid suppression before endoscopy in non-variceal bleeding, and delaying endoscopy is unsafe. E. Terlipressin and antibiotics are for suspected variceal bleeding, for which there are no features here.
pearl: Upper GI bleed: unstable means resuscitate then endoscope immediately; stable means risk-score and endoscope within 24 hours. Only very low-risk patients (Glasgow–Blatchford score of 0) may be considered for early discharge.
thinking: Melaena on aspirin and an NSAID ↓ Probable peptic ulcer bleed ↓ Currently haemodynamically stable ↓ Resuscitate as needed and risk-score ↓ Endoscopy within 24 hours
exam_trap: A, immediate endoscopy — urgency feels right in any GI bleed, but immediate endoscopy is for unstable patients after resuscitation; a stable patient needs endoscopy within 24 hours.
takeaway: Stable upper GI bleed: resuscitate as needed, risk-score and endoscope within 24 hours.

stem: A 31-year-old man with terminal ileal Crohn's disease, treated with azathioprine, is seen in the emergency department with 5 days of worsening right lower abdominal pain and swinging fevers. His bowels are opening normally and there is no blood in his stool. His temperature is 38.9°C. There is a tender, fixed fullness in the right iliac fossa without generalised peritonism. CRP and white cell count are raised. What is the most likely complication?

options.B: Small bowel obstruction from a stricture

why_correct: Crohn's disease is transmural, so inflamed bowel can penetrate and form a contained collection. Swinging fevers, focal pain and a tender mass in the right iliac fossa with raised inflammatory markers point to an ileocaecal abscess. Contrast CT or MRI confirms it, and treatment is antibiotics with percutaneous drainage where feasible; immunosuppression should not be escalated until sepsis is controlled.
why_wrong: A. Toxic megacolon involves colonic dilatation with systemic toxicity, usually in severe colitis. B. Obstruction would cause colicky pain, vomiting and distension, and his bowels are working normally. D. A perianal abscess causes perianal pain and swelling, not a right iliac fossa mass. E. Carcinoma would not explain swinging fevers and a tender mass developing over days.
pearl: Swinging fever plus a tender right iliac fossa mass in Crohn's disease is an abscess until proven otherwise. Image first, drain and give antibiotics, and avoid escalating immunosuppression until sepsis is controlled.
thinking: Known ileal Crohn's on immunosuppression ↓ Swinging fevers and raised inflammatory markers ↓ Tender fixed right iliac fossa mass ↓ Transmural penetrating disease ↓ Intra-abdominal abscess
exam_trap: B, small bowel obstruction from a stricture — strictures are common in ileal Crohn's disease, but obstruction causes vomiting and distension, not swinging fevers with a tender mass.
takeaway: Crohn's disease with swinging fever and a tender RIF mass: think abscess, image and drain.

stem: A 27-year-old man with stricturing terminal ileal Crohn's disease presents with 24 hours of colicky central abdominal pain, green vomiting and abdominal distension. He has not passed flatus since the morning. He is afebrile and his observations are stable. The abdomen is distended and mildly tender without guarding. CT shows dilated small bowel loops down to a narrowed segment of terminal ileum, with no perforation, abscess or features of ischaemia. What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.B: Nil by mouth, nasogastric decompression, IV fluids and close monitoring
options.C: Oral budesonide and a low-residue diet at home
options.D: A stimulant laxative to relieve the obstruction

correct_answer: B. Nil by mouth, nasogastric decompression, IV fluids and close monitoring
why_correct: Small bowel obstruction from a Crohn's stricture, without signs of strangulation, perforation or sepsis, is managed conservatively first: nil by mouth, nasogastric decompression, IV fluids with electrolyte correction and regular reassessment. Many episodes settle, particularly when there is an inflammatory component, after which the IBD and surgical teams plan definitive treatment. Surgery is reserved for failure to settle or signs of bowel compromise.
why_wrong: A. Emergency surgery is reserved for peritonitis, ischaemia or failure of conservative management. C. Oral treatment at home is unsafe in a patient who is vomiting and obstructed. D. Stimulant laxatives are contraindicated in mechanical obstruction. E. Endoscopic dilatation is a planned procedure for selected short strictures, not an emergency treatment for acute obstruction.
pearl: Bowel obstruction without peritonism, sepsis or ischaemia: drip and suck first. Features of strangulation, such as constant pain, fever, tachycardia or peritonism, demand urgent surgical review.
thinking: Known stricturing ileal Crohn's disease ↓ Colicky pain, bilious vomiting, distension ↓ CT: obstruction at the stricture ↓ No perforation, abscess or ischaemia ↓ Conservative drip and suck first
exam_trap: A, emergency laparotomy — obstruction feels surgical, but without strangulation or peritonism, Crohn's-related obstruction is first managed conservatively and bowel is preserved where possible.
takeaway: Uncomplicated Crohn's stricture obstruction: nil by mouth, NG tube, IV fluids and review.

presentation: Lower GI symptoms — FIT to guide referral
stem: A 56-year-old woman sees her GP with 2 months of looser, more frequent stools, with occasional dark blood mixed in. She has no abdominal pain and her weight is stable. Abdominal examination is normal and digital rectal examination reveals no mass. Her full blood count is normal. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Urgent suspected cancer referral for colonoscopy without further testing
options.D: Routine referral to the gastroenterology clinic

why_correct: NICE suspected cancer guidance uses a quantitative faecal immunochemical test to guide referral for most adults with lower GI symptoms, including a change in bowel habit or unexplained rectal bleeding. A result above the referral threshold triggers a suspected cancer pathway referral. If the result is negative but symptoms persist or concern remains, she should still be safety-netted and reassessed. Direct referral without FIT is kept for findings such as a rectal or anal mass.
why_wrong: A. Referral without FIT is not the standard route when examination is normal. B. Calprotectin helps separate inflammatory bowel disease from functional symptoms in younger adults and is not used for cancer triage at this age. D. A routine referral would be too slow if this is cancer. E. Treating symptoms without investigation risks missing colorectal cancer.
pearl: Lower GI symptoms in primary care: FIT first to guide referral, and a positive result means a suspected cancer pathway referral. A rectal or anal mass needs referral regardless, and a negative FIT never overrides ongoing clinical concern.
thinking: Woman in her fifties with a change in bowel habit ↓ Blood mixed with the stool ↓ Normal abdominal and rectal examination ↓ NICE uses FIT to guide referral ↓ Quantitative FIT
exam_trap: A, urgent referral without testing — red-flag symptoms make immediate referral feel safest, but current UK guidance uses FIT to guide referral unless there is a rectal or anal mass.
takeaway: Change in bowel habit with a normal rectal examination: request a FIT to guide urgent referral.

stem: A 17-year-old girl is brought to her GP by her mother with 3 months of intermittent crampy right-sided abdominal pain and loose stools without visible blood. She has lost weight and keeps getting painful mouth ulcers. For the past week she has had tender, raised, dusky red lumps on both shins. There is a fleshy skin tag at the anal margin. Faecal calprotectin is raised. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Chronic right-sided pain, non-bloody diarrhoea and weight loss in a teenager, with mouth ulcers, a perianal skin tag and erythema nodosum, point to Crohn's disease. Crohn's can affect any part of the gut from mouth to anus, and erythema nodosum often parallels disease activity. The raised faecal calprotectin confirms intestinal inflammation, and she needs specialist referral for endoscopy and imaging.
why_wrong: A. Coeliac disease causes diarrhoea and weight loss but not erythema nodosum, perianal tags or a raised calprotectin. B. Irritable bowel syndrome does not cause weight loss, raised inflammatory markers or extra-intestinal signs. C. Ulcerative colitis typically causes bloody diarrhoea and does not involve the mouth or cause perianal skin tags. D. Sarcoidosis causes erythema nodosum but not chronic diarrhoea with perianal disease.
pearl: Crohn's disease: mouth to anus, skip lesions, transmural inflammation, often non-bloody diarrhoea and perianal disease. Erythema nodosum, mouth ulcers and peripheral arthritis tend to flare with bowel activity.
thinking: Teenager with weight loss and non-bloody diarrhoea ↓ Right-sided pain, mouth ulcers, perianal skin tag ↓ Erythema nodosum on the shins ↓ Raised faecal calprotectin ↓ Crohn's disease
exam_trap: C, ulcerative colitis — it can also cause erythema nodosum and a raised calprotectin, but the absence of blood, right-sided pain, mouth ulcers and perianal disease point to Crohn's.
takeaway: Non-bloody diarrhoea with mouth ulcers, perianal tags and erythema nodosum suggests Crohn's disease.

presentation: Painless obstructive jaundice — pancreatic head cancer
stem: A 70-year-old man sees his GP because his wife noticed that his eyes have turned yellow. He has had generalised itching for 3 weeks, with dark urine and pale stools. He has no abdominal pain but has lost weight, and he was diagnosed with diabetes 4 months ago. He is jaundiced, and there is a smooth, non-tender mass below the right costal margin that moves with respiration. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Gallstone in the common bile duct
options.B: Carcinoma of the head of the pancreas

correct_answer: B. Carcinoma of the head of the pancreas
why_correct: Painless obstructive jaundice with a palpable, non-tender gallbladder suggests malignant obstruction of the distal common bile duct, most often from a carcinoma of the head of the pancreas (Courvoisier's law). Weight loss and new-onset diabetes in later life add to the suspicion. NICE advises an urgent suspected cancer pathway referral for older adults with jaundice, and urgent pancreatic imaging.
why_wrong: A. Gallstone obstruction is usually painful, and chronic inflammation leaves a fibrosed gallbladder that rarely distends. C. Viral hepatitis gives a hepatitic picture without a palpable gallbladder or progressive weight loss. D. An empyema is acutely tender with fever and systemic upset. E. Primary sclerosing cholangitis is usually associated with ulcerative colitis and does not cause a distended gallbladder.
pearl: Courvoisier's law: in a jaundiced patient, a palpable non-tender gallbladder is unlikely to be due to stones. Painless jaundice, weight loss and new diabetes in an older adult should prompt urgent pancreatic imaging.
thinking: Painless obstructive jaundice: itch, dark urine, pale stools ↓ Weight loss and new diabetes ↓ Palpable non-tender gallbladder ↓ Malignant distal bile duct obstruction ↓ Pancreatic head carcinoma
exam_trap: A, common bile duct stone — it is the commonest cause of obstructive jaundice, but stones usually cause pain and a shrunken fibrotic gallbladder, so a painless palpable gallbladder points to cancer.
takeaway: Painless jaundice with a palpable non-tender gallbladder suggests carcinoma of the pancreatic head.

stem: A 33-year-old woman sees her GP with 10 days of loose stools containing blood and mucus. She is opening her bowels several times a day with urgency and crampy lower abdominal pain. She has never had bowel problems before. She is eating and drinking, her temperature is 37.6°C and she is otherwise well. What is the most appropriate initial investigation?

options.C: Stool microscopy and culture with C. difficile testing
options.D: CT of the abdomen and pelvis

correct_answer: C. Stool microscopy and culture with C. difficile testing
why_correct: New bloody diarrhoea may be infective or the first presentation of inflammatory bowel disease, and the two can look identical. Stool microscopy and culture (for organisms such as Campylobacter, Salmonella, Shigella and E. coli O157) with C. difficile testing should be sent first, because infection must be excluded before a diagnosis of colitis is made. Endoscopy and further tests follow if stool tests are negative and symptoms persist.
why_wrong: A. Calprotectin is raised in both infective and inflammatory colitis, so it cannot separate them. B. Endoscopy is used once infection has been excluded, unless she is acutely unwell. D. CT is not a first-line test in a clinically stable patient. E. Coeliac disease does not cause bloody diarrhoea.
pearl: Bloody diarrhoea: send stool culture and C. difficile testing before labelling it inflammatory bowel disease. Remember E. coli O157 and haemolytic uraemic syndrome, and avoid antimotility drugs in suspected infective colitis.
thinking: First episode of bloody diarrhoea with urgency ↓ Infection and new IBD can look identical ↓ Infection must be excluded first ↓ Stool tests are quick and non-invasive ↓ Stool culture with C. difficile testing
exam_trap: B, flexible sigmoidoscopy with biopsies — it is the key test for suspected colitis, but infection must be excluded first, as infective colitis can mimic IBD endoscopically.
takeaway: New bloody diarrhoea: send stool culture and C. difficile testing before investigating for IBD.

presentation: Unstable upper GI bleed — resuscitation and endoscopy
stem: A 58-year-old woman with a known duodenal ulcer collapses at home after vomiting a large amount of fresh blood. In the emergency department she is pale and clammy, with a heart rate of 128/min and blood pressure of 82/48 mmHg. She has no history of liver disease and rarely drinks alcohol. Two large-bore cannulas are in place. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Resuscitate, including blood transfusion, then endoscopy immediately after resuscitation
options.B: IV PPI infusion and endoscopy on the next day's list
options.C: CT angiography before any fluid or blood is given
options.D: Terlipressin and antibiotics with endoscopy within 24 hours

correct_answer: A. Resuscitate, including blood transfusion, then endoscopy immediately after resuscitation
why_correct: She has a severe upper GI bleed with shock. Resuscitation comes first, including blood transfusion and activation of the major haemorrhage protocol if needed, with blood tests, crossmatch and senior and critical care involvement. NICE advises endoscopy immediately after resuscitation for unstable patients with severe acute upper GI bleeding, so that the bleeding ulcer can be treated endoscopically. Interventional radiology or surgery is used if endoscopic treatment fails.
why_wrong: B. Waiting until the next day is unsafe in a shocked patient, and acid suppression does not replace endoscopic haemostasis. C. Imaging before resuscitation delays life-saving treatment. D. Terlipressin and antibiotics are for suspected variceal bleeding, and a 24-hour window is for stable patients. E. Surgery is reserved for failure of endoscopic and radiological control.
pearl: Unstable upper GI bleed: ABCDE, two large-bore cannulas, transfuse blood (major haemorrhage protocol if needed), then endoscopy immediately after resuscitation; interventional radiology or surgery if endoscopy fails.
thinking: Large haematemesis with shock ↓ Known ulcer, no liver disease ↓ Resuscitate with blood first ↓ Unstable severe bleed ↓ Endoscopy immediately after resuscitation
exam_trap: D, terlipressin and antibiotics — they are often reached for in haematemesis, but without features of liver disease this is a peptic ulcer bleed, and a 24-hour endoscopy window is too slow for an unstable patient.
takeaway: Unstable upper GI bleed: resuscitate with blood, then endoscope immediately after resuscitation.

presentation: Rheumatoid arthritis — escalation to biological therapy
stem: A 49-year-old man with seropositive rheumatoid arthritis attends the rheumatology clinic. Despite 6 months of combination treatment with methotrexate, sulfasalazine and hydroxychloroquine at optimal doses, he has multiple swollen, tender joints, persistently raised inflammatory markers and new erosions on hand X-rays. His disease activity score remains in the severe range. Tuberculosis screening is negative and he has no history of cancer or heart failure. What is the most appropriate next step?
correct_answer: D. A TNF inhibitor with methotrexate
why_correct: Severe active rheumatoid arthritis that has not responded to intensive combination conventional DMARDs is an indication for advanced therapy under NICE technology appraisal guidance. In a patient who has not previously had a biological drug, a TNF inhibitor such as adalimumab or etanercept, given with methotrexate, is the usual first choice. Screening for tuberculosis and other infections is completed beforehand, as here.
why_wrong: A. Rituximab is generally used after an inadequate response to, or intolerance of, a TNF inhibitor, or when TNF inhibitors cannot be used. B. Long-term steroids cause significant harm and do not adequately control erosive disease. C. Swapping one conventional DMARD for another is unlikely to help once combination therapy has failed. E. Joint injections relieve individual joints but do not control systemic erosive disease.
pearl: RA ladder: conventional DMARD (usually methotrexate) started early, short-term steroid bridging, then combination therapy, then a biological or targeted synthetic DMARD if disease stays active. Screen for TB and hepatitis before biologics.
thinking: Seropositive erosive rheumatoid arthritis ↓ Failed intensive combination conventional DMARDs ↓ Disease remains severely active ↓ Eligible for advanced therapy, TB screen negative ↓ TNF inhibitor with methotrexate
exam_trap: A, rituximab — it is a licensed biological drug for rheumatoid arthritis, so it tempts, but it is usually reserved for after a TNF inhibitor has failed or cannot be used.
takeaway: RA still severe after combination DMARDs: add a TNF inhibitor to methotrexate.

stem: A 13-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department at 5 am with severe pain in the right lower abdomen and groin that woke him 2 hours ago, and he has vomited twice. He was reluctant to mention any scrotal symptoms. On examination the right testis is very tender, lies higher than the left with a horizontal lie, and the right cremasteric reflex is absent. What is the most appropriate management?

options.B: Urgent scrotal exploration by the surgical team
options.D: Observe for appendicitis with serial abdominal examination
options.E: Analgesia, scrotal support and review later in the day

correct_answer: B. Urgent scrotal exploration by the surgical team
why_correct: A suddenly painful, high-riding testis with a horizontal lie and an absent cremasteric reflex is testicular torsion until proven otherwise. It is a surgical emergency because testicular viability falls rapidly over hours, so urgent scrotal exploration with detorsion and bilateral fixation is needed. Imaging should not delay surgery when the clinical picture is typical.
why_wrong: A. Doppler ultrasound can be falsely reassuring and delays definitive treatment. C. Epididymo-orchitis has a more gradual onset and is unusual at this age without sexual activity or urinary symptoms. D. Testicular pain is often referred to the lower abdomen, and the scrotal findings make torsion the diagnosis. E. Any delay risks loss of the testis.
pearl: Always examine the testes in a boy with lower abdominal pain. Suspected torsion means urgent exploration; salvage rates are highest within about 6 hours, and both testes are fixed at surgery.
thinking: Adolescent with sudden pain and vomiting ↓ Pain felt in the groin and lower abdomen ↓ Tender high-riding testis with a horizontal lie ↓ Absent cremasteric reflex ↓ Torsion: urgent exploration
exam_trap: A, Doppler ultrasound — imaging feels like a safe confirmatory step, but it delays surgery and can show apparently preserved flow in partial torsion.
takeaway: Suspected testicular torsion: urgent surgical exploration without waiting for imaging.

stem: A 26-year-old woman is admitted with a closed fracture of both forearm bones, now in an above-elbow backslab. Six hours later she is distressed by increasing forearm pain despite IV morphine. Passive extension of her fingers causes severe pain. The forearm feels tense, the radial pulse is palpable and capillary refill in the fingers is normal. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Elevate the arm high on pillows and review in 4 hours
options.B: Split the backslab and dressings down to skin and arrange urgent fasciotomy
options.C: Doppler the radial artery and reassure if flow is normal
options.D: Increase the opioid dose and reassess in the morning
options.E: Repeat the forearm X-ray to check the fracture position

correct_answer: B. Split the backslab and dressings down to skin and arrange urgent fasciotomy
why_correct: Pain out of proportion to the injury, escalating despite strong opioids and severe on passive stretch of the muscles in a tense compartment, is acute compartment syndrome. All circumferential dressings and casts should be released down to skin, the limb kept at heart level, and the orthopaedic team should perform urgent fasciotomy once the diagnosis is made. A palpable pulse and normal capillary refill do not exclude it, because raised compartment pressure compromises muscle perfusion long before it occludes large arteries.
why_wrong: A. High elevation reduces arterial inflow and can worsen compartment ischaemia; the limb should be kept at heart level. C. Normal arterial flow does not exclude compartment syndrome. D. Escalating analgesia masks the key symptom and delays surgery. E. Fracture position does not explain the clinical picture, and delay risks muscle necrosis.
pearl: Compartment syndrome: pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch are the earliest signs; pulses are often present until late. Split casts to skin, keep the limb at heart level and proceed to urgent fasciotomy.
thinking: Forearm fracture in a backslab ↓ Escalating pain despite opioids ↓ Severe pain on passive finger extension, tense forearm ↓ Palpable pulse does not reassure ↓ Release dressings and urgent fasciotomy
exam_trap: C, Doppler and reassure — a normal pulse feels reassuring, but compartment syndrome is a tissue perfusion problem and arterial flow is usually preserved until it is too late.
takeaway: Pain on passive stretch after a fracture: release dressings to skin and arrange urgent fasciotomy.

stem: A 23-year-old woman is on the trauma ward after a motorcycle collision in which she fractured her left femur and tibia; she is awaiting fixation. About 36 hours after admission she becomes restless and confused and is breathing rapidly, with an oxygen saturation of 86% on air. There are fine petechiae in her axillae and on the conjunctivae. Her temperature is 38.0°C. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Pulmonary embolism from deep vein thrombosis

why_correct: Respiratory distress, neurological dysfunction and a petechial rash appearing 1 to 3 days after long-bone fractures is fat embolism syndrome. Fat globules from the marrow reach the lungs and systemic circulation, causing hypoxaemia, confusion and petechiae, typically in the axillae, upper trunk and conjunctivae. Management is supportive with oxygen and organ support, and early fracture stabilisation reduces the risk.
why_wrong: A. Pulmonary embolism causes hypoxia but not a petechial rash, and typically occurs later. C. Pneumonia would not explain petechiae and confusion this early. D. Meningococcal sepsis causes a non-blanching rash and confusion, but the timing after long-bone fractures and the axillary and conjunctival petechiae point to fat embolism. E. Opioid toxicity causes slow breathing and pinpoint pupils, not tachypnoea and petechiae.
pearl: Fat embolism triad: hypoxia, confusion and petechiae (axillae, upper chest, conjunctivae), 24–72 hours after long-bone or pelvic fractures. Early fixation reduces the risk; treatment is supportive.
thinking: Long-bone fractures awaiting fixation ↓ Onset after 1 to 2 days ↓ Hypoxia and tachypnoea ↓ Confusion with axillary and conjunctival petechiae ↓ Fat embolism syndrome
exam_trap: A, pulmonary embolism — trauma and immobility raise the risk of VTE and hypoxia fits, but PE does not produce petechiae or such early confusion; the triad points to fat embolism.
takeaway: Hypoxia, confusion and petechiae a day or two after long-bone fractures is fat embolism syndrome.

stem: A 34-year-old woman with an anxiety disorder is brought to the emergency department three hours after swallowing a large quantity of her propranolol tablets. She is drowsy and cool peripherally. Her pulse is 38/min and blood pressure 74/40 mmHg, and her capillary glucose is at the lower limit of normal. Two doses of IV atropine have produced no change in her heart rate. In addition to seeking poisons-service advice, which is the most appropriate next drug?
why_correct: Bradycardia, hypotension and borderline hypoglycaemia after propranolol overdose is beta-blocker poisoning. Glucagon acts on its own receptor to raise intracellular cAMP, bypassing the blocked beta-receptor and improving heart rate and contractility when atropine has failed. Further measures such as high-dose insulin with glucose, inotropes or pacing follow specialist advice if she remains shocked.
why_wrong: A. Calcium is the classic therapy for calcium-channel blocker poisoning and has a limited role in pure beta-blockade. B. Atropine has already failed and repeating it is unlikely to help. C. Digoxin-specific antibody fragments treat digoxin toxicity, not beta-blocker poisoning. D. Sodium bicarbonate is for sodium-channel toxicity such as tricyclic poisoning, not bradycardia from beta-blockade.
pearl: Beta-blocker poisoning: bradycardia, hypotension and hypoglycaemia. Calcium-channel blocker poisoning: bradycardia, hypotension and hyperglycaemia. The glucose helps tell them apart.
thinking: Propranolol overdose ↓ Bradycardia, hypotension and low glucose ↓ Atropine has failed ↓ Need to raise cAMP without beta-receptors ↓ IV glucagon
exam_trap: A, IV calcium chloride — calcium is the reflex antidote for cardiotoxic overdoses, but it is the specific therapy for calcium-channel blockers rather than beta-blockers.
takeaway: Atropine-resistant bradycardia and hypotension after beta-blocker overdose: give IV glucagon.

stem: An 82-year-old man with a fractured neck of femur receives a fascia iliaca block with levobupivacaine in the emergency department. Ten minutes later he complains of tingling around his mouth and ringing in his ears, becomes agitated, and then has a generalised tonic-clonic seizure. The monitor now shows a slow, broad-complex rhythm and his blood pressure is falling. Help has been called and his airway is being managed. What is the most appropriate specific treatment?
why_correct: Perioral tingling, tinnitus and agitation progressing to seizures and cardiovascular collapse shortly after a regional block is local anaesthetic systemic toxicity. IV lipid emulsion 20% binds the lipophilic local anaesthetic and draws it away from the heart and brain, and is the specific treatment alongside stopping the injection, airway management, seizure control and standard resuscitation.
why_wrong: B. Naloxone reverses opioids and has no effect on local anaesthetic toxicity. C. Calcium gluconate is used for hyperkalaemia or calcium-channel blocker toxicity. D. Magnesium is used for torsades de pointes and eclampsia, not local anaesthetic toxicity. E. Bicarbonate treats tricyclic sodium-channel blockade; lipid emulsion is the specific reversal here.
pearl: Local anaesthetic toxicity runs from neurological warning signs (perioral numbness, tinnitus, agitation) to seizures and then arrhythmia or arrest. Lipid emulsion should be immediately available wherever blocks are done.
thinking: Recent regional block with levobupivacaine ↓ Perioral tingling, tinnitus, agitation, then seizure ↓ Bradycardia and broad complexes with falling blood pressure ↓ Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity ↓ IV lipid emulsion 20%
exam_trap: E, IV sodium bicarbonate — both local anaesthetics and tricyclics block sodium channels, so bicarbonate seems logical, but lipid emulsion is the specific antidote for local anaesthetic toxicity.
takeaway: Seizures or cardiovascular collapse after a local anaesthetic block: give IV lipid emulsion 20%.

stem: A 74-year-old man under surveillance for an abdominal aortic aneurysm calls 999 after sudden severe pain in his left flank radiating to his groin, followed by a brief faint. In the emergency department he is grey and sweaty, with a pulse of 128/min and blood pressure of 78/44 mmHg. A tender, pulsatile mass is felt above the umbilicus. Two large-bore cannulae are in place and blood has been sent for crossmatch. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Urgent CT angiogram of the aorta before contacting the vascular team
options.B: IV fluids to restore a normal blood pressure
options.C: Admit to the surgical ward for analgesia and observation
options.D: Immediate transfer to theatre under the vascular surgeons
options.E: CT of the kidneys, ureters and bladder for suspected renal colic

correct_answer: D. Immediate transfer to theatre under the vascular surgeons
why_correct: Sudden flank or back pain, collapse, shock and a pulsatile mass in a man with a known aneurysm is a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm until proven otherwise. In a shocked patient this is a clinical diagnosis, and the priority is immediate surgical control of the bleeding with the vascular team, using permissive hypotension rather than restoring a normal blood pressure. Imaging is reserved for patients stable enough to tolerate the delay.
why_wrong: A. Sending a shocked patient to CT before involving the vascular team delays haemorrhage control. B. Raising the blood pressure to normal increases bleeding from the rupture; permissive hypotension is used until the aorta is controlled. C. Ward observation of a ruptured aneurysm is fatal. E. Flank pain radiating to the groin mimics renal colic, but shock and a pulsatile mass make rupture the diagnosis.
pearl: In an older man, a first presentation of renal colic should prompt you to think of the aorta. Shock plus a pulsatile mass means theatre, not the scanner.
thinking: Known aneurysm with sudden flank pain and collapse ↓ Shocked with a tender pulsatile mass ↓ Ruptured aneurysm is a clinical diagnosis ↓ Imaging delays bleeding control ↓ Immediate transfer to theatre under the vascular team
exam_trap: A, urgent CT angiogram — CT feels like the safe confirmation step, but in a shocked patient it costs time that the patient does not have; imaging is for those who are haemodynamically stable.
takeaway: Shocked patient with suspected ruptured aortic aneurysm: straight to theatre with the vascular team.

stem: A 16-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department by her mother four hours after swallowing a large number of her mother's ferrous sulfate tablets following an argument. She has vomited several times, has profuse diarrhoea and colicky abdominal pain, and is becoming drowsy. A venous gas shows a metabolic acidosis, an abdominal X-ray shows multiple radio-opaque tablets, and her serum iron is markedly raised. What is the most appropriate specific treatment?
why_correct: Gastrointestinal symptoms, drowsiness, metabolic acidosis and a high serum iron after a large ingestion indicate significant iron poisoning. IV desferrioxamine chelates free iron, which is then excreted in the urine, and is the specific treatment in severe toxicity, given with supportive care and poisons-service advice. Her self-harm also needs a psychosocial assessment once she is medically stable.
why_wrong: A. Activated charcoal does not bind iron. B. Acetylcysteine is the antidote for paracetamol, not iron. D. Bicarbonate may be used for acidosis but does not remove iron or treat the toxicity. E. Penicillamine chelates copper in Wilson disease and is not used for iron poisoning.
pearl: Iron tablets are radio-opaque, so an abdominal X-ray can show the tablet load. Charcoal does not bind iron, lithium or alcohols.
thinking: Large ingestion of ferrous sulfate ↓ Vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain and drowsiness ↓ Acidosis and high serum iron: severe toxicity ↓ Needs an iron chelator ↓ IV desferrioxamine
exam_trap: A, oral activated charcoal — charcoal is the default decontamination step for many overdoses, but it does not adsorb iron and adds nothing here.
takeaway: Severe iron poisoning is treated with IV desferrioxamine; activated charcoal does not bind iron.

stem: A 63-year-old woman had a myocardial infarction treated with a coronary stent two years ago. She has now been diagnosed with type 2 diabetes, and despite three months of dietary changes and increased activity her HbA1c remains above target. Her BMI is 29 kg/m2 and her renal function is normal. What is the most appropriate drug treatment?

options.B: Metformin alone, reviewing in three months

correct_answer: A. Metformin plus an SGLT2 inhibitor
why_correct: Metformin remains the foundation of drug treatment for type 2 diabetes. In a person with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, NICE recommends adding an SGLT2 inhibitor with proven cardiovascular benefit to metformin. Of the options, metformin plus an SGLT2 inhibitor gives the best protection against further cardiovascular events as well as lowering glucose.
why_wrong: B. Metformin alone misses the cardiovascular benefit recommended for patients with established cardiovascular disease. C. Gliclazide lowers glucose but adds hypoglycaemia and weight gain without cardiovascular benefit. D. DPP-4 inhibitors lower glucose but are cardiovascular-neutral. E. Insulin is not first-line in a newly diagnosed patient without symptomatic hyperglycaemia.
pearl: Type 2 diabetes plus established cardiovascular disease: metformin plus an SGLT2 inhibitor with proven cardiovascular benefit. Counsel about genital infections and sick-day rules for ketoacidosis.
thinking: New type 2 diabetes above target after lifestyle measures ↓ Metformin is first-line ↓ Previous MI = established cardiovascular disease ↓ Add an agent with proven cardiovascular benefit ↓ Metformin plus an SGLT2 inhibitor
exam_trap: B, Metformin alone, reviewing in three months — classic stepwise teaching suggests one drug first, but established cardiovascular disease changes the plan to include an SGLT2 inhibitor.
takeaway: In type 2 diabetes with cardiovascular disease, combine metformin with an SGLT2 inhibitor.

stem: A 72-year-old woman has an X-ray for back pain that began after lifting a bag of shopping. It shows a new wedge compression fracture of a thoracic vertebra, and a DXA scan confirms osteoporosis. Her calcium and renal function are normal, she has no swallowing difficulty and she can sit upright after taking tablets. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.C: Weekly oral alendronic acid with calcium and vitamin D

correct_answer: C. Weekly oral alendronic acid with calcium and vitamin D
why_correct: A vertebral fragility fracture with osteoporosis on DXA needs bone-protective treatment to reduce further fractures. An oral bisphosphonate such as weekly alendronic acid is first-line, provided she can follow the administration instructions (taken fasting with a full glass of water, staying upright for 30 minutes). Calcium and vitamin D are given alongside unless dietary intake and vitamin D status are adequate.
why_wrong: A. Denosumab is an option when bisphosphonates are unsuitable or not tolerated. B. Raloxifene is not first-line and increases the risk of venous thromboembolism. D. Teriparatide is a specialist treatment for severe osteoporosis, for example with multiple vertebral fractures. E. Calcium and vitamin D alone do not adequately reduce fracture risk after a fragility fracture.
pearl: Fragility fracture plus osteoporosis: oral bisphosphonate first, with calcium and vitamin D. Check the patient can take it fasting and upright, and consider dental health before starting.
thinking: Low-trauma vertebral fracture ↓ DXA confirms osteoporosis ↓ Needs drug treatment to cut future fracture risk ↓ No barriers to oral therapy ↓ Weekly alendronic acid with calcium and vitamin D
exam_trap: A, Six-monthly subcutaneous denosumab — it is effective and convenient, but it is used when oral bisphosphonates cannot be taken or tolerated.
takeaway: First-line treatment after a fragility fracture with osteoporosis is an oral bisphosphonate.

stem: A 29-year-old woman with antiphospholipid syndrome, diagnosed after two late miscarriages, stopped her warfarin a month ago. Over three days she develops abdominal pain, falling urine output with a rapidly rising creatinine, mottled skin over her legs, painful dusky fingertips and new weakness of her right arm. Imaging shows renal infarcts and a small cerebral infarct. Her platelet count is mildly low, her clotting screen and fibrinogen are normal, and the blood film shows no significant red-cell fragmentation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Thrombosis developing in three or more organs over a few days, in a patient with known antiphospholipid syndrome (here after stopping anticoagulation), is catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome. It is a rare but frequently fatal emergency caused by widespread small-vessel occlusion. Management is in critical care with anticoagulation, high-dose corticosteroids and often plasma exchange or intravenous immunoglobulin.
why_wrong: A. TTP causes a microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia with many red-cell fragments on the film, which are absent. B. DIC prolongs clotting times and consumes fibrinogen, but these are normal. C. HUS is usually diarrhoea-associated and features fragmentation haemolysis with renal failure. E. Vasculitis inflames rather than thromboses vessels and does not fit known antiphospholipid syndrome with multiple infarcts.
pearl: Antiphospholipid syndrome plus multi-organ thrombosis evolving over days = catastrophic APS. Treat aggressively in critical care: anticoagulation, steroids, and plasma exchange or IVIG.
thinking: Known antiphospholipid syndrome, anticoagulation stopped ↓ Rapid thrombosis in kidney, brain, skin and digits ↓ Normal clotting and no film fragments ↓ Not DIC or TTP ↓ Catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome
exam_trap: A, Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura — low platelets, renal impairment and neurological signs fit, but TTP requires a haemolytic anaemia with red-cell fragments, which this film lacks.
takeaway: Multi-organ thrombosis over days in antiphospholipid syndrome is catastrophic APS, a medical emergency.

stem: A 52-year-old woman who has taken prednisolone 10 mg daily for over a year for sarcoidosis telephones her GP surgery. She has had a fever, aching and a cough for two days but is eating and drinking and has had no vomiting or diarrhoea. She asks what she should do about her steroid tablets. What is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: Stop prednisolone until she has recovered
options.C: Temporarily double her daily dose while she has a fever, and seek urgent help if she vomits or cannot take tablets
options.D: Halve her dose to reduce the risk of the infection worsening
options.E: Switch to alternate-day dosing until she recovers

correct_answer: C. Temporarily double her daily dose while she has a fever, and seek urgent help if she vomits or cannot take tablets
why_correct: Long-term glucocorticoids at this dose suppress the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis, so she cannot mount the normal rise in cortisol during illness. Sick-day rules advise doubling the usual daily oral dose during an intercurrent illness with fever until recovered, and seeking urgent medical help, with injected hydrocortisone, if vomiting or diarrhoea prevents her taking or absorbing tablets. Steroids must never be stopped abruptly in such patients because of the risk of adrenal crisis.
why_wrong: A. Stopping long-term steroids abruptly, especially during illness, can cause an adrenal crisis. B. Her usual dose may not meet the extra demand of a febrile illness. D. Reducing the dose raises the risk of adrenal crisis, which is more dangerous than the infection risk. E. Alternate-day dosing leaves days with inadequate steroid cover during the illness.
pearl: Sick-day rules for steroid-dependent patients: double the oral dose with fever or illness, use injectable hydrocortisone and seek urgent care if vomiting, and carry a steroid emergency card.
thinking: Long-term prednisolone = suppressed adrenal axis ↓ Febrile illness increases cortisol demand ↓ She cannot generate her own stress response ↓ Under-replacement risks adrenal crisis ↓ Double the dose; urgent help if vomiting
exam_trap: A, Stop prednisolone until she has recovered — steroids are immunosuppressive, so stopping them during infection seems logical, but abrupt withdrawal with a suppressed axis can cause an adrenal crisis.
takeaway: Patients on long-term steroids should double their dose during febrile illness and never stop abruptly.

stem: A 64-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation has been stable on warfarin for years. A week ago she was prescribed a course of fluconazole for oral thrush. At her anticoagulation clinic visit today her INR is 11. She has no bleeding, bruising or black stools, and her observations are normal. What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Continue warfarin at the same dose and recheck the INR in a week
options.B: Give IV vitamin K and prothrombin complex concentrate urgently
options.C: Increase the warfarin dose to compensate for the antifungal
options.D: Stop warfarin permanently and switch straight to a direct oral anticoagulant
options.E: Withhold warfarin, give oral vitamin K, restart once the INR has fallen sufficiently, and review the interacting drug

correct_answer: E. Withhold warfarin, give oral vitamin K, restart once the INR has fallen sufficiently, and review the interacting drug
why_correct: Fluconazole inhibits the liver enzymes that metabolise warfarin, so the INR rises. For a very high INR without bleeding, the BNF advises stopping warfarin and giving oral vitamin K (phytomenadione), then restarting warfarin once the INR has fallen to a safer level, with close INR monitoring. The interacting drug should be stopped if possible and the interaction documented to prevent a recurrence.
why_wrong: A. Continuing warfarin at a very high INR exposes her to a serious risk of bleeding. B. Intravenous vitamin K with prothrombin complex concentrate is reserved for major bleeding. C. Increasing the dose would raise the INR further, because the interaction potentiates warfarin. D. Changing anticoagulant is not the immediate priority, and starting another anticoagulant while the INR is high would add to bleeding risk.
pearl: Enzyme inhibitors (clarithromycin, erythromycin, fluconazole, metronidazole) raise the INR. Very high INR without bleeding: withhold warfarin and give oral vitamin K; major bleeding: IV vitamin K plus PCC.
thinking: Stable on warfarin, new azole antifungal ↓ Enzyme inhibition, INR very high ↓ No bleeding ↓ Lower the INR without full reversal ↓ Withhold warfarin, oral vitamin K, review the interacting drug
exam_trap: B, Give IV vitamin K and prothrombin complex concentrate urgently — the number is alarming, but full rapid reversal is for major bleeding, and she is not bleeding.
takeaway: A very high INR without bleeding: withhold warfarin, give oral vitamin K and review interacting drugs.

stem: A 61-year-old man with severe plaque psoriasis is started on methotrexate by the dermatology team, and his GP is asked to take over prescribing. When the GP goes through the plan with him, which instruction about taking methotrexate is correct?

options.A: Take it once a week on the same day, and take folic acid on a different day of the week
options.B: Take it every day, with folic acid on the same day
options.C: Take it once a week, and avoid folic acid as it stops methotrexate working
options.D: Take it every day, stopping it if mouth ulcers appear
options.E: Take it twice a week, with daily folic acid

correct_answer: A. Take it once a week on the same day, and take folic acid on a different day of the week
why_correct: Methotrexate for psoriasis or inflammatory arthritis is taken once weekly on the same day each week; accidental daily dosing has caused fatal marrow suppression, so the day should be stated on the prescription and the patient counselled. Folic acid is co-prescribed, usually on a different day, to reduce adverse effects such as mouth ulcers, nausea and marrow toxicity. Regular full blood count, liver and renal function monitoring is required.
why_wrong: B. Daily dosing is a potentially fatal error. C. Folic acid is recommended to reduce toxicity, not avoided. D. Daily dosing is dangerous, and mouth ulcers are a warning sign of toxicity needing an urgent blood count rather than simply stopping. E. Twice-weekly methotrexate is not a standard regimen and risks overdose.
pearl: Methotrexate: once weekly, same day, day named on the prescription; folic acid on another day; monitor FBC, LFTs and U&Es. Sore throat, mouth ulcers or bruising need an urgent FBC.
thinking: Methotrexate for psoriasis ↓ Narrow safety margin with marrow toxicity ↓ Weekly dosing; daily dosing is a known fatal error ↓ Folic acid reduces side effects ↓ Once weekly with folic acid on a different day
exam_trap: C, Take it once a week, and avoid folic acid as it stops methotrexate working — methotrexate is a folate antagonist, so this sounds logical, but folic acid is routinely given to reduce toxicity.
takeaway: Methotrexate is taken once weekly, with folic acid on a different day.

stem: An 82-year-old woman is admitted with urosepsis and started on IV gentamicin alongside other antibiotics. Her eGFR was reduced on admission. On day 3 she complains of ringing in her ears and feels unsteady when she stands, and her creatinine has risen since admission. Her regular furosemide was restarted yesterday. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Continue gentamicin and increase her furosemide to protect her kidneys
options.B: Check a gentamicin level and renal function urgently, withhold further doses pending the result, and review the need for gentamicin with microbiology
options.C: Check liver function tests for drug-induced hepatitis
options.D: Start betahistine and continue the same antibiotic regimen
options.E: Increase the gentamicin dose to ensure the sepsis is adequately treated

correct_answer: B. Check a gentamicin level and renal function urgently, withhold further doses pending the result, and review the need for gentamicin with microbiology
why_correct: Gentamicin is an aminoglycoside with a narrow therapeutic index that is cleared by the kidneys and is both nephrotoxic and ototoxic. Older age, pre-existing renal impairment and loop diuretics all increase the risk. Tinnitus, unsteadiness and a rising creatinine suggest toxicity, so levels and renal function should be checked, further doses withheld until results are available, and an alternative antibiotic considered with microbiology advice.
why_wrong: A. Furosemide increases aminoglycoside ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity, and continuing gentamicin unchecked risks permanent harm. C. Gentamicin is not significantly hepatotoxic. D. Betahistine treats Ménière's disease and would mask, not address, vestibular toxicity. E. Increasing the dose in worsening renal function would worsen toxicity.
pearl: Gentamicin: dose by weight and renal function, monitor levels and creatinine, and stop if tinnitus, hearing loss or unsteadiness appear. Vestibular damage can be permanent; avoid combining with loop diuretics where possible.
thinking: Older patient with reduced eGFR on gentamicin ↓ Tinnitus and unsteadiness = ototoxicity ↓ Rising creatinine = nephrotoxicity; furosemide adds risk ↓ Narrow therapeutic index, renally cleared ↓ Check level and renal function, withhold and review
exam_trap: A, Continue gentamicin and increase her furosemide to protect her kidneys — diuresis sounds protective, but loop diuretics increase aminoglycoside ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity.
takeaway: Gentamicin is nephrotoxic and ototoxic; monitor levels and renal function and stop when toxicity appears.

stem: A 58-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes, hypertension and albuminuria was started on lisinopril by her GP. Her blood tests two weeks later show that her creatinine has risen slightly from her pre-treatment value and her potassium remains within the normal range. She feels well and her blood pressure has improved. What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Stop lisinopril and switch to amlodipine
options.B: Stop lisinopril and refer urgently for renal artery imaging
options.D: Continue lisinopril, as this small rise is expected, and monitor renal function as planned
options.E: Halve the lisinopril dose and recheck in one week

correct_answer: D. Continue lisinopril, as this small rise is expected, and monitor renal function as planned
why_correct: ACE inhibitors reduce efferent arteriolar tone in the glomerulus, so a small rise in creatinine and potassium is expected after starting and reflects the change in glomerular pressure that underlies their kidney-protective effect. A modest rise with a potassium still within the normal range needs no change in treatment; the ACE inhibitor should be continued and renal function monitored. A large or progressive rise would prompt review, including consideration of renal artery stenosis.
why_wrong: A. Stopping would lose the renal and cardiovascular protection of ACE inhibition in diabetic albuminuria without good reason. B. A small, expected rise does not suggest renal artery stenosis. C. Adding spironolactone would push the potassium up further and is not indicated. E. Reducing the dose is unnecessary for a small, expected change.
pearl: After starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB, recheck U&Es within a couple of weeks. A small creatinine rise is expected; a large rise or hyperkalaemia needs review and consideration of renal artery stenosis.
thinking: Diabetic albuminuria, ACE inhibitor started ↓ Creatinine up modestly, potassium normal ↓ Expected haemodynamic effect ↓ Benefit outweighs a small change ↓ Continue and monitor
exam_trap: A, Stop lisinopril and switch to amlodipine — any creatinine rise can look like drug-induced kidney injury, but a small rise is expected and stopping loses the protective benefit in albuminuria.
takeaway: A small creatinine rise after starting an ACE inhibitor is expected; continue and monitor.

stem: A 44-year-old man with bipolar disorder who has taken lithium for many years was started on bendroflumethiazide for hypertension two weeks ago. During a heatwave he has become drowsy, with slurred speech, a coarse tremor of both hands, unsteady walking and diarrhoea. His reflexes are brisk. His sodium and glucose are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Lithium has a narrow therapeutic range and is excreted by the kidneys. Thiazide diuretics reduce its clearance, and dehydration from hot weather and diarrhoea raises levels further, pushing them into the toxic range. Coarse tremor, ataxia, slurred speech, hyperreflexia, drowsiness and gastrointestinal upset are typical. An urgent lithium level and renal function are needed; lithium and the thiazide are stopped and the patient rehydrated, with haemodialysis for severe toxicity.
why_wrong: A. Serotonin syndrome follows serotonergic drugs and causes clonus, agitation, sweating and hyperthermia. B. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome follows antipsychotics, with rigidity, hyperthermia and a raised CK. D. A stroke would not explain a bilateral tremor and diarrhoea after starting an interacting drug. E. Wernicke's encephalopathy causes confusion, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia from thiamine deficiency, usually with alcohol excess.
pearl: Lithium levels rise with dehydration, thiazides, ACE inhibitors, ARBs and NSAIDs. A fine tremor is a side effect; a coarse tremor, ataxia and confusion suggest toxicity.
thinking: Long-term lithium ↓ New thiazide plus dehydration from heat and diarrhoea ↓ Reduced renal lithium clearance ↓ Coarse tremor, ataxia, dysarthria, drowsiness ↓ Lithium toxicity
exam_trap: A, Serotonin syndrome — tremor, hyperreflexia and diarrhoea overlap, but there is no new serotonergic drug, and a thiazide with dehydration points to lithium accumulation.
takeaway: Thiazides and dehydration can tip lithium into toxicity: coarse tremor, ataxia and confusion.

stem: A 47-year-old man with bipolar disorder and type 2 diabetes attends his GP for an annual medication review. His regular medicines are atorvastatin, omeprazole, amlodipine, lithium carbonate and metformin. Which of his medicines needs regular blood level measurement because its toxic dose lies close to its therapeutic dose?
why_correct: Lithium has a narrow therapeutic index, so toxic levels lie close to the effective range. Plasma lithium levels are measured regularly on a sample taken about 12 hours after the dose, alongside renal and thyroid function, because lithium can cause renal impairment and hypothyroidism. Patients should carry a lithium record book and know the symptoms of toxicity.
why_wrong: A. Atorvastatin is monitored with lipid and liver tests, not plasma drug levels. B. Omeprazole has a wide safety margin and needs no level monitoring. C. Amlodipine is monitored by its effect on blood pressure. E. Metformin is monitored through renal function and HbA1c, not drug levels.
pearl: Drugs commonly monitored by plasma level: lithium, phenytoin, gentamicin, vancomycin, theophylline, ciclosporin, and digoxin when toxicity is suspected. Lithium also needs renal, thyroid and calcium checks.
thinking: List of common long-term medicines ↓ Which has toxicity close to the therapeutic range ↓ Lithium is renally cleared with a narrow margin ↓ Needs regular levels about 12 hours post-dose ↓ Lithium carbonate
exam_trap: E, Metformin — it needs renal monitoring because of the risk of lactic acidosis, but this is done through renal function, not by measuring its plasma concentration.
takeaway: Lithium has a narrow therapeutic index and needs regular plasma level, renal and thyroid monitoring.

stem: A 68-year-old woman has a colonoscopy in the endoscopy unit under intravenous midazolam; no opioid or other sedative was given. Ten minutes after the procedure she is difficult to rouse, her breathing is slow and shallow, and her oxygen saturation is falling despite airway manoeuvres and supplemental oxygen. Her pupils are normal in size. Which drug is most appropriate to reverse the cause of her deterioration?
why_correct: Midazolam is a benzodiazepine, and over-sedation with respiratory depression after procedural sedation is reversed with flumazenil, a competitive benzodiazepine antagonist, alongside airway support. Its action is shorter than that of many benzodiazepines, so the patient must be observed for re-sedation. It is avoided in mixed overdoses and in chronic benzodiazepine users because it can provoke seizures.
why_wrong: A. Naloxone reverses opioids, and no opioid was given. B. Acetylcysteine is the antidote for paracetamol poisoning. C. Glucagon is used in beta-blocker toxicity and hypoglycaemia. E. Sugammadex reverses the neuromuscular blockers rocuronium and vecuronium, not sedatives.
pearl: Flumazenil's safest use is reversing benzodiazepine sedation given in hospital; it is short-acting, so watch for re-sedation, and avoid it in mixed overdose or long-term benzodiazepine users because of seizure risk.
thinking: Respiratory depression after procedural sedation ↓ Only a benzodiazepine (midazolam) was given, pupils normal ↓ Opioid reversal will not help ↓ Benzodiazepine antagonist needed ↓ Flumazenil
exam_trap: A, Naloxone — it is the reflex reversal drug for a sedated patient with slow breathing, especially after endoscopy where opioids are often co-administered. But this patient received midazolam alone, and naloxone has no effect on benzodiazepines.
takeaway: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines; naloxone reverses opioids. Match the antidote to the drug actually given.

stem: A 79-year-old woman with hypertension and chronic kidney disease takes ramipril and furosemide. Two weeks ago she began taking ibuprofen bought from a pharmacy for hip pain. She now feels tired and is passing less urine. Her creatinine has roughly doubled from her baseline and her potassium is raised. A bladder scan shows a small residual volume, and she has had no recent contrast, vomiting or diarrhoea. What is the most likely explanation?

options.A: Natural progression of her chronic kidney disease
options.C: Reduced kidney perfusion from ibuprofen combined with ramipril and furosemide

correct_answer: C. Reduced kidney perfusion from ibuprofen combined with ramipril and furosemide
why_correct: NSAIDs block prostaglandin-mediated dilatation of the afferent arteriole, ACE inhibitors remove angiotensin II-mediated constriction of the efferent arteriole, and diuretics reduce circulating volume. Together, this 'triple whammy' can sharply reduce glomerular filtration and cause acute kidney injury with hyperkalaemia, especially in older people and those with CKD. The NSAID should be stopped and the ACE inhibitor and diuretic withheld while kidney function recovers.
why_wrong: A. CKD progresses slowly and would not double the creatinine within two weeks of a new drug. B. A small post-void residual excludes significant outflow obstruction. D. Nothing suggests a statin, muscle pain or muscle injury. E. She has had no recent iodinated contrast.
pearl: Avoid NSAIDs in older people taking an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker together with a diuretic, particularly in CKD, heart failure or dehydration. Always ask about medicines bought over the counter.
thinking: Sudden rise in creatinine and potassium ↓ New drug: pharmacy ibuprofen ↓ Already on ACE inhibitor and loop diuretic ↓ Obstruction and contrast excluded ↓ Triple-whammy prerenal AKI
exam_trap: A, Natural progression of her chronic kidney disease — she has known CKD, so a worse creatinine seems expected. But the rise is abrupt and follows a new NSAID, which points to an acute, reversible drug cause.
takeaway: NSAID plus ACE inhibitor plus diuretic is a recipe for AKI; ask about over-the-counter painkillers.

stem: A 32-year-old woman with asthma, controlled on a regular inhaled corticosteroid, saw a locum GP and was started on propranolol for anxiety before job interviews. Three days later she attends the surgery with chest tightness and audible wheeze, and she is using her reliever much more often. She has had no recent infection or new allergen exposure. What is the most likely explanation for her worsening asthma?

options.B: Bronchoconstriction from beta-2 receptor blockade by propranolol
options.C: Propranolol reducing the absorption of her inhaled corticosteroid

correct_answer: B. Bronchoconstriction from beta-2 receptor blockade by propranolol
why_correct: Propranolol is a non-selective beta-blocker; blocking beta-2 receptors in bronchial smooth muscle causes bronchoconstriction and can precipitate severe bronchospasm in people with asthma. It also blunts the response to beta-2 agonist relievers. Beta-blockers should be avoided in asthma, and propranolol should be stopped and an alternative found for her anxiety.
why_wrong: A. Hyperventilation does not produce wheeze and an increasing need for a reliever. C. Beta-blockers do not affect inhaled corticosteroid absorption or action. D. Nothing suggests allergy, such as rash, urticaria or angioedema. E. Beta-blockers tend to raise potassium rather than lower it.
pearl: Beta-blockers, especially non-selective ones such as propranolol, can trigger bronchospasm and blunt the response to salbutamol. Avoid them in asthma and check for asthma before prescribing them for anxiety or migraine.
thinking: Known asthma ↓ New propranolol, then wheeze within days ↓ Propranolol is non-selective and blocks beta-2 ↓ Airway smooth muscle constricts ↓ Beta-2 blockade causing bronchoconstriction
exam_trap: A, Hyperventilation caused by uncontrolled anxiety — she is an anxious patient, so it is tempting to blame the anxiety. But hyperventilation does not cause wheeze, and the timing points to the new beta-blocker.
takeaway: Beta-blockers can precipitate bronchospasm in asthma; avoid them, particularly non-selective agents.

stem: A 41-year-old woman with two children attends her GP because of heavy periods. She floods through protection and has to change it at night, and she now has iron deficiency. Her periods are regular, and she has no intermenstrual or post-coital bleeding. Pelvic examination is normal, and a pelvic ultrasound shows no fibroids or polyps. She needs reliable contraception and is unsure whether she may want another child in a few years. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
why_correct: For heavy menstrual bleeding with no structural or histological abnormality, the levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system is the first-line treatment in NICE guidance. It greatly reduces menstrual blood loss, provides highly effective contraception for several years and is fully reversible, which suits a woman who may want a future pregnancy.
why_wrong: B. Tranexamic acid reduces bleeding but provides no contraception and is used when the intrauterine system is declined or unsuitable. C. Mefenamic acid helps less and provides no contraception. D. Endometrial ablation is not suitable for a woman who may want to become pregnant again. E. Cyclical norethisterone is not effective as a contraceptive or as long-term first-line treatment.
pearl: In heavy menstrual bleeding with a normal pelvis, offer the levonorgestrel intrauterine system first; tranexamic acid or NSAIDs are for women who decline it or want non-hormonal treatment.
thinking: Heavy, regular periods with iron deficiency ↓ No structural cause on examination or scan ↓ Needs contraception and may want fertility later ↓ Treatment that reduces bleeding, contracepts and is reversible ↓ Levonorgestrel intrauterine system
exam_trap: B, Tranexamic acid during menstruation — it is effective, quick to start and commonly prescribed in primary care. But it gives no contraception, and NICE places the intrauterine system first when there is no structural cause.
takeaway: Heavy periods with no structural cause: the levonorgestrel intrauterine system is first-line and also contraceptive.

stem: A 22-year-old woman in her first pregnancy attends the maternity day assessment unit at 37 weeks with a severe frontal headache and pain under the ribs. Her blood pressure is in the severe range on repeated readings, urine dipstick shows heavy proteinuria, and she has three beats of ankle clonus. The CTG is reassuring. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Oral nifedipine and home blood pressure monitoring with review in two days
options.B: Labetalol to control blood pressure and intravenous magnesium sulfate, then plan birth once stable
options.C: Enalapril to control blood pressure and diazepam for seizure prevention
options.D: Oral methyldopa and admission for bed rest with weekly review
options.E: Immediate category 1 caesarean section before treating the blood pressure

correct_answer: B. Labetalol to control blood pressure and intravenous magnesium sulfate, then plan birth once stable
why_correct: Severe hypertension with proteinuria, headache, epigastric or right upper quadrant pain and clonus is severe pre-eclampsia. Management is admission, blood pressure control (labetalol is first-line), intravenous magnesium sulfate to prevent eclamptic seizures, and planned birth, which is the definitive treatment, once the mother is stabilised. At term, birth should not be delayed.
why_wrong: A. Severe features need admission and seizure prophylaxis, not outpatient monitoring. C. ACE inhibitors are contraindicated in pregnancy, and magnesium sulfate, not diazepam, prevents eclampsia. D. Methyldopa is slow-acting, and expectant management is wrong with severe features at term. E. The mother must be stabilised before birth, as operating with uncontrolled blood pressure risks stroke.
pearl: Severe pre-eclampsia: control blood pressure first (labetalol, or nifedipine or hydralazine), give magnesium sulfate to prevent fits, then plan birth. Stabilise the mother before delivering the baby.
thinking: Pregnant with severe hypertension and proteinuria ↓ Headache, epigastric pain, clonus: severe features ↓ Risks are stroke and eclampsia ↓ Antihypertensive plus magnesium sulfate, then birth ↓ Labetalol and magnesium sulfate
exam_trap: E, Immediate category 1 caesarean section before treating the blood pressure — birth is the cure, so rushing to theatre feels decisive. But the fetus is not compromised, and operating before blood pressure is controlled and seizures are prevented puts the mother at risk.
takeaway: Severe pre-eclampsia: labetalol plus magnesium sulfate, stabilise the mother, then plan birth.

stem: A 34-year-old woman who has had three previous births has just had a vaginal twin delivery. Twenty minutes after the placenta was delivered and checked as complete, she has brisk, heavy vaginal bleeding. On abdominal palpation the fundus is above the umbilicus and feels soft and poorly contracted. Help has been called and intravenous access secured. What is the most appropriate next step to control the bleeding?

options.A: Transfuse fresh frozen plasma and cryoprecipitate
options.B: Transfer to theatre to look for a cervical tear
options.C: Manual removal of the placenta under anaesthesia
options.D: Rub up a contraction with uterine massage and give oxytocin

correct_answer: D. Rub up a contraction with uterine massage and give oxytocin
why_correct: A soft, high, poorly contracted uterus after an overdistended (twin) pregnancy points to uterine atony, the commonest cause of primary postpartum haemorrhage. Alongside resuscitation, first-line measures are uterine massage (rubbing up a contraction) and a uterotonic such as oxytocin, escalating through other uterotonics and then surgical measures if bleeding continues.
why_wrong: A. Blood products are part of resuscitation but do not treat atony, and coagulopathy is not the likely cause. B. Genital tract trauma usually causes bleeding with a well-contracted uterus. C. The placenta was delivered and checked as complete. E. Balloon tamponade is used only if massage and uterotonics fail.
pearl: The four Ts of postpartum haemorrhage are tone, trauma, tissue and thrombin. A boggy uterus means tone: rub up a contraction and give uterotonics while you resuscitate.
thinking: Heavy bleeding soon after birth ↓ Uterus soft and high, twin pregnancy ↓ Placenta complete ↓ Tone problem: atony ↓ Uterine massage and oxytocin
exam_trap: E, Insert an intrauterine balloon tamponade — it is a recognised and effective treatment for atonic bleeding. But it is a second-line step after massage and uterotonics have failed, not the first action.
takeaway: A soft, boggy uterus after birth is atony: massage and oxytocin first, escalating if bleeding continues.

stem: A 34-year-old woman of South Asian origin was diagnosed with gestational diabetes at 28 weeks on a glucose tolerance test. At the joint diabetes antenatal clinic two weeks later, her home capillary glucose readings remain above target despite consistent changes to her diet and daily walking. A growth scan shows normal fetal growth and liquor volume, and she has no other medical problems. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.D: Continue diet alone and recheck glucose at 36 weeks
