why_correct: When diet and exercise do not achieve glucose targets in gestational diabetes, metformin is offered next, with insulin added or substituted if targets are still not met or metformin is unsuitable. Metformin and insulin are the agents recommended in pregnancy. Persistent hyperglycaemia increases the risk of macrosomia, shoulder dystocia and neonatal hypoglycaemia, so treatment should not be delayed.
why_wrong: A. DPP-4 inhibitors are not recommended in pregnancy. C. SGLT2 inhibitors are not recommended in pregnancy. D. Uncontrolled glucose cannot be left for weeks because of the risks to the baby. E. GLP-1 receptor agonists are not used in pregnancy.
pearl: Gestational diabetes steps: diet and exercise, then metformin, then insulin. Very high glucose at diagnosis or signs of fetal complications call for insulin straight away.
thinking: Gestational diabetes ↓ Diet and exercise tried ↓ Readings still above target ↓ Need a drug that is safe in pregnancy ↓ Metformin
exam_trap: D, Continue diet alone and recheck glucose at 36 weeks — the scan is normal, so watching seems reasonable. But glucose that stays above target needs treatment now to reduce macrosomia and neonatal hypoglycaemia.
takeaway: Gestational diabetes not controlled by diet and exercise: add metformin, then insulin if needed.

stem: A 67-year-old woman tells her GP that for the past two months she has felt full after small meals, her skirts have become tight around the waist, and she needs to pass urine more often. Her bowel habit is unchanged and she has no rectal bleeding. On examination her abdomen is mildly distended, with no palpable mass and no shifting dullness. What is the most appropriate initial investigation?

options.E: No test; manage as irritable bowel syndrome

why_correct: Persistent abdominal distension, early satiety and urinary frequency in a woman over 50 are possible features of ovarian cancer, and NICE recommends measuring serum CA125 as the first test in primary care. If the CA125 is raised, an urgent ultrasound of the abdomen and pelvis follows, with a suspected cancer referral if it is abnormal. A palpable mass or ascites would prompt direct urgent referral.
why_wrong: A. A faecal immunochemical test looks for colorectal cancer, and she has no change in bowel habit or bleeding. B. Coeliac serology does not address the main concern in a woman of this age with these symptoms. C. Urinary frequency here is part of a pattern pointing to a pelvic mass, not an isolated urinary infection. E. A new irritable bowel picture in a woman over 50 should prompt CA125 testing.
pearl: Bloating, early satiety, pelvic pain and urinary urgency that persist in a woman over 50 are ovarian cancer warning signs; new irritable bowel-type symptoms at this age need a CA125.
thinking: Woman over 50 ↓ Persistent bloating, early satiety, urinary frequency ↓ Pattern of possible ovarian cancer ↓ No mass or ascites to prompt direct referral ↓ Serum CA125 first
exam_trap: E, No test; manage as irritable bowel syndrome — the symptoms resemble IBS and are common. But IBS rarely starts after 50, and these symptoms in an older woman should be investigated for ovarian cancer first.
takeaway: Persistent bloating and early satiety in a woman over 50: check CA125, then ultrasound if raised.

stem: A 31-year-old woman telephones her GP surgery after receiving her routine cervical screening result letter, which says that high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) was not found. She asks whether her cells have also been examined under the microscope and what happens next. What is the correct explanation?

options.A: Her cells were examined as well, and she will be recalled for repeat testing in 12 months
options.B: Her cells were not examined because HPV was not found, and she returns to routine recall
options.C: She needs a repeat test in three months to confirm the negative result
options.D: She should be referred for colposcopy to complete her screening
options.E: She needs a blood test to complete her screening

correct_answer: B. Her cells were not examined because HPV was not found, and she returns to routine recall
why_correct: The NHS cervical screening programme uses primary high-risk HPV testing. Cytology is examined only on samples that are HPV-positive, because women without high-risk HPV are at very low risk of significant cervical disease. An HPV-negative result therefore means she returns to routine recall for her age.
why_wrong: A. Cytology is not examined on HPV-negative samples, and early recall at 12 months is for HPV-positive results with normal cytology. C. A negative HPV result does not need confirming. D. Colposcopy is for HPV-positive results with abnormal cytology or persistent HPV. E. Cervical screening does not involve a blood test.
pearl: Cervical screening starts with a high-risk HPV test. HPV-negative samples go straight back to routine recall; only HPV-positive samples have cytology, which decides between colposcopy and early repeat testing.
thinking: Routine cervical screening ↓ First test is for high-risk HPV ↓ HPV not found ↓ No cytology needed ↓ Routine recall
exam_trap: A, Her cells were examined as well, and she will be recalled for repeat testing in 12 months — this reflects the older cytology-first model, which many people still assume. Under primary HPV testing, cytology is done only if HPV is detected.
takeaway: Cervical screening tests HPV first; cytology is examined only on HPV-positive samples.

stem: A 37-year-old woman attends the early pregnancy unit after slight brown spotting. By her dates she is 10 weeks pregnant. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an intrauterine pregnancy with a fetal pole measuring about 7 weeks and no cardiac activity, which a second experienced sonographer confirms. Her observations are normal, she is afebrile, and she is upset but wants to know her options. What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Intramuscular methotrexate with serial hCG monitoring
options.B: Vaginal progesterone and a repeat scan in two weeks
options.C: Discuss expectant, medical and surgical management and support her choice
options.D: Surgical management is required because tissue remains in the uterus
options.E: Admission for an intravenous oxytocin infusion

correct_answer: C. Discuss expectant, medical and surgical management and support her choice
why_correct: This is a confirmed missed miscarriage in a woman who is clinically stable with no infection. Expectant, medical (mifepristone followed by misoprostol) and surgical management (including manual vacuum aspiration under local anaesthetic) are all appropriate, and the choice is made with her after discussing the benefits and risks of each. Surgery is advised if there is heavy bleeding, infection or a clinical preference.
why_wrong: A. Methotrexate is used for selected ectopic pregnancies, not miscarriage. B. Progesterone is for threatened miscarriage with a history of previous miscarriage, not a pregnancy that has already failed. D. Retained tissue alone does not make surgery mandatory in a stable woman. E. Oxytocin infusion is not used to manage first-trimester miscarriage.
pearl: Missed miscarriage in a stable woman: expectant, medical or surgical management are all valid. Shared decision-making decides, and surgery is favoured for heavy bleeding or infection.
thinking: No cardiac activity, confirmed by a second sonographer ↓ Missed miscarriage ↓ Stable and not infected ↓ All three routes acceptable ↓ Discuss options and support her choice
exam_trap: D, Surgical management is required because tissue remains in the uterus — surgery feels definitive and quick. But in a stable woman without infection, expectant and medical management are equally valid, and she should choose.
takeaway: Stable missed miscarriage: offer expectant, medical or surgical management and let her choose.

stem: A 24-year-old woman who is 10 weeks pregnant is seen in the emergency department. For three days she has been unable to keep down food or fluids despite oral cyclizine prescribed by her GP. She has lost weight, feels dizzy on standing, and has a dry mouth and a fast pulse. Urine dipstick shows heavy ketonuria. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Advise ginger and small frequent meals, with GP review next week
options.B: Stop all antiemetics because they may harm the fetus
options.C: Offer termination of pregnancy as first-line treatment
options.D: Admit for intravenous fluids with potassium, parenteral antiemetics and thiamine
options.E: Prescribe oral ondansetron and discharge home

correct_answer: D. Admit for intravenous fluids with potassium, parenteral antiemetics and thiamine
why_correct: Severe vomiting in early pregnancy with weight loss, dehydration and ketonuria, despite oral antiemetics, is hyperemesis gravidarum needing admission. Treatment is intravenous fluid (normal saline with potassium as needed), parenteral antiemetics, thiamine to prevent Wernicke's encephalopathy, and thromboprophylaxis. Electrolytes and kidney function should also be checked.
why_wrong: A. Simple measures are for mild nausea, not dehydration with ketonuria. B. First-line antiemetics are considered safe in pregnancy and withholding them is harmful. C. Termination is considered only after all treatment has failed and at the woman's request. E. She cannot keep fluids down, so oral treatment at home will fail.
pearl: Hyperemesis gravidarum: weight loss, dehydration and electrolyte disturbance. Rehydrate with saline plus potassium, use parenteral antiemetics, give thiamine, and consider thromboprophylaxis.
thinking: Early pregnancy with persistent vomiting ↓ Weight loss, postural dizziness, ketonuria ↓ Oral treatment already failed ↓ Hyperemesis gravidarum needing admission ↓ IV fluids, antiemetics and thiamine
exam_trap: E, Prescribe oral ondansetron and discharge home — ondansetron is an effective second-line antiemetic. But she is dehydrated and cannot keep anything down, so she needs admission and intravenous treatment.
takeaway: Hyperemesis with dehydration and ketonuria: admit for IV fluids, parenteral antiemetics and thiamine.

stem: A 53-year-old woman whose last menstrual period was 14 months ago sees her GP about frequent hot flushes and drenching night sweats that disturb her sleep. She has not had a hysterectomy. She has migraine without aura and a body mass index in the obese range, so the GP recommends transdermal oestrogen. She has no other contraindications to HRT. Which regimen is most appropriate?
correct_answer: C. Transdermal oestradiol with a progestogen
why_correct: A woman with a uterus who takes systemic oestrogen must also have a progestogen, given orally, transdermally or through a levonorgestrel intrauterine system, to protect the endometrium from hyperplasia and cancer. A transdermal route is preferred here because it carries less risk of venous thromboembolism than oral oestrogen in women with a raised BMI.
why_wrong: A. Unopposed oestrogen in a woman with a uterus increases the risk of endometrial hyperplasia and cancer. B. Vaginal oestrogen treats urogenital symptoms, not vasomotor symptoms. D. Testosterone may be considered for low sexual desire, not hot flushes. E. The combined pill is not appropriate for a postmenopausal woman over 50 with obesity.
pearl: Has a uterus? Add a progestogen to any systemic oestrogen. The route of oestrogen (patch, gel or tablet) does not change this; transdermal oestrogen lowers clot risk.
thinking: Postmenopausal with vasomotor symptoms ↓ HRT appropriate, transdermal preferred ↓ Uterus present ↓ Endometrium needs protecting ↓ Transdermal oestrogen plus progestogen
exam_trap: A, Transdermal oestradiol alone — the patch is the right route for her, so it feels complete. But she still has a uterus, and oestrogen without a progestogen raises the risk of endometrial cancer whatever the route.
takeaway: Systemic oestrogen in a woman with a uterus always needs a progestogen, whatever the route.

stem: A 58-year-old woman tells her GP she has had two episodes of light vaginal spotting in the past month. Her last period was seven years ago, and she is not taking HRT. Her cervical screening is up to date and was normal. Speculum examination shows thin, pale vaginal walls but no visible lesion. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Prescribe vaginal oestrogen and review if spotting recurs
options.B: Take a cervical screening sample today
options.C: Reassure and refer routinely if a further episode occurs
options.D: Prescribe tranexamic acid and review in three months
options.E: Make a suspected cancer referral for transvaginal ultrasound

correct_answer: E. Make a suspected cancer referral for transvaginal ultrasound
why_correct: Postmenopausal bleeding in a woman aged 55 or over must be treated as possible endometrial cancer and needs a suspected cancer pathway referral. Transvaginal ultrasound assesses endometrial thickness, and a thickened endometrium leads to endometrial sampling or hysteroscopy. Visible atrophic changes do not explain away the bleeding until cancer has been excluded.
why_wrong: A. Atrophy may coexist with cancer, so bleeding must not be attributed to it before investigation. B. Cervical screening is a screening test for symptom-free women and her screening is up to date. C. A single episode of postmenopausal bleeding needs urgent investigation, not a wait for a second one. D. Tranexamic acid masks bleeding without diagnosing its cause.
pearl: Any postmenopausal bleeding is endometrial cancer until proven otherwise. Atrophic changes on examination are common and do not remove the need for urgent ultrasound.
thinking: Bleeding more than a year after the last period ↓ Postmenopausal bleeding at age 58 ↓ Endometrial cancer must be excluded ↓ Suspected cancer pathway ↓ Urgent referral for transvaginal ultrasound
exam_trap: A, Prescribe vaginal oestrogen and review if spotting recurs — the examination shows atrophy, which can cause spotting. But atrophy is a diagnosis of exclusion here, and treating it first could delay the diagnosis of endometrial cancer.
takeaway: Postmenopausal bleeding needs urgent referral for ultrasound, even when atrophy is visible.

stem: A 28-year-old woman in her second pregnancy attends maternity triage at 24 weeks after tripping and landing on her abdomen. She is RhD-negative, and her booking bloods showed no red cell antibodies. She has no pain or bleeding, fetal movements are normal and the fetal heart is heard. Her routine antenatal anti-D is planned for later in pregnancy. What is the most appropriate action to prevent rhesus sensitisation?

options.A: Anti-D immunoglobulin within 72 hours, with a test to measure fetomaternal haemorrhage
options.B: No action, as her planned routine antenatal anti-D will protect her
options.E: Give anti-D only if she develops vaginal bleeding

correct_answer: A. Anti-D immunoglobulin within 72 hours, with a test to measure fetomaternal haemorrhage
why_correct: Abdominal trauma is a potentially sensitising event in an RhD-negative woman, even without bleeding. Anti-D immunoglobulin should be given within 72 hours to prevent her forming anti-D antibodies that could cause haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn. After 20 weeks, a test of the size of fetomaternal haemorrhage (such as a Kleihauer test) shows whether more anti-D is needed. Routine antenatal prophylaxis is still given as planned.
why_wrong: B. Routine antenatal prophylaxis does not replace anti-D for a sensitising event that happens before it. C. Intravenous immunoglobulin is not used to prevent rhesus sensitisation. D. Intrauterine transfusion treats established fetal anaemia, which there is no sign of. E. Abdominal trauma is sensitising even without bleeding.
pearl: In an RhD-negative woman, give anti-D within 72 hours of any sensitising event, including abdominal trauma, bleeding, procedures and external cephalic version. Check fetomaternal haemorrhage after 20 weeks.
thinking: RhD-negative and not sensitised ↓ Abdominal trauma at 24 weeks ↓ Possible fetal red cells entering her circulation ↓ Prevent antibody formation ↓ Anti-D within 72 hours plus a fetomaternal haemorrhage test
exam_trap: B, No action, as her planned routine antenatal anti-D will protect her — routine prophylaxis is designed to prevent sensitisation. But it does not cover an event that happens weeks earlier, so she needs anti-D now as well.
takeaway: Sensitising event in an RhD-negative woman: anti-D within 72 hours, plus routine prophylaxis as planned.

stem: A 36-year-old woman who has had three previous caesarean sections has a scan at 32 weeks showing an anterior placenta covering the internal os. On MRI the normal boundary between placenta and uterine wall is lost and there are abnormal blood vessels extending into the myometrium. She has had no bleeding so far. What is the most likely diagnosis and the key principle of management?

options.A: Vasa praevia — elective caesarean at 39 weeks in her local unit
options.B: Placental abruption — induction of labour at 37 weeks
options.C: Uncomplicated placenta praevia — routine elective caesarean by the on-call team
options.D: Placental insufficiency — serial growth scans and early induction
options.E: Placenta accreta spectrum — planned birth in a specialist centre with a multidisciplinary team

correct_answer: E. Placenta accreta spectrum — planned birth in a specialist centre with a multidisciplinary team
why_correct: A low-lying placenta over a previous caesarean scar, together with loss of the placental-myometrial interface and abnormal vessels, indicates placenta accreta spectrum, where the placenta invades the uterine wall. It carries a risk of massive haemorrhage and often hysterectomy at birth. Birth should be planned in a specialist centre with senior obstetricians, anaesthetists, interventional radiology, blood products and access to critical care.
why_wrong: A. Vasa praevia involves fetal vessels over the cervix and needs earlier delivery, not this imaging picture. B. Abruption is premature separation of the placenta, the opposite of abnormal adherence. C. The abnormal invasion makes this far from routine, and an unplanned caesarean risks catastrophic bleeding. D. Nothing suggests fetal growth restriction.
pearl: Placenta praevia plus previous caesarean section is the major risk combination for placenta accreta spectrum. Plan birth with a specialist multidisciplinary team, cross-matched blood and critical care.
thinking: Multiple previous caesareans ↓ Placenta lying over the scar ↓ Imaging shows invasion into myometrium ↓ Placenta accreta spectrum with haemorrhage risk ↓ Planned specialist multidisciplinary birth
exam_trap: C, Uncomplicated placenta praevia — routine elective caesarean by the on-call team — praevia alone is managed by elective caesarean, so this looks familiar. But the invasion on MRI changes everything: the bleeding risk needs a planned specialist team, not a routine list.
takeaway: Placenta praevia over a caesarean scar: think accreta and plan birth with a specialist multidisciplinary team.

stem: A 33-year-old woman at 35 weeks in a twin pregnancy presents with a week of malaise, poor appetite, vomiting and excessive thirst. She now looks jaundiced. Her blood pressure is 128/80 and urine shows no protein. Blood tests show raised transaminases and bilirubin, a low blood glucose, a prolonged prothrombin time, a raised creatinine and a normal platelet count. What is the most likely diagnosis?
correct_answer: D. Acute fatty liver of pregnancy
why_correct: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy is a third-trimester emergency causing acute liver failure; it is more common in twin pregnancies. Vomiting, malaise and jaundice with hypoglycaemia, coagulopathy and kidney impairment are typical, and polydipsia can occur. Management is maternal stabilisation, correction of glucose and clotting, and prompt delivery.
why_wrong: A. HELLP usually occurs with hypertension and is defined by low platelets and haemolysis, which are absent. B. Cholestasis presents with itching and does not cause liver failure, hypoglycaemia or coagulopathy. C. Viral hepatitis is possible but the pregnancy stage, twins and hypoglycaemia make this specific obstetric emergency far more likely. E. Hyperemesis occurs in the first trimester and does not cause liver failure.
pearl: Third-trimester jaundice with hypoglycaemia and coagulopathy suggests acute fatty liver of pregnancy. Low platelets with haemolysis and hypertension point instead to HELLP. Both are treated by delivery.
thinking: Third trimester, twin pregnancy ↓ Vomiting and jaundice ↓ Low glucose, prolonged clotting, kidney injury ↓ Normal blood pressure and platelets argue against HELLP ↓ Acute fatty liver of pregnancy
exam_trap: A, HELLP syndrome — both cause abnormal liver tests and vomiting in late pregnancy and both need delivery. But HELLP is defined by haemolysis and low platelets, usually with hypertension, whereas hypoglycaemia and liver failure are the hallmarks of fatty liver.
takeaway: Late-pregnancy jaundice with hypoglycaemia and coagulopathy: acute fatty liver of pregnancy until proven otherwise.

stem: A 33-year-old woman attends the antenatal clinic at 34 weeks. Her first baby was born by caesarean section at 26 weeks, and the operation note confirms a vertical incision in the upper segment of the uterus. She very much wants a vaginal birth this time. The pregnancy has been uncomplicated, and the baby is cephalic. What is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: Planned vaginal birth with continuous CTG monitoring in labour
options.B: Planned vaginal birth, provided labour starts spontaneously
options.C: Induction of labour with prostaglandins at 39 weeks
options.D: Planned repeat caesarean section, as vaginal birth is contraindicated
options.E: Vaginal birth is safe because more than two years have passed since her caesarean

correct_answer: D. Planned repeat caesarean section, as vaginal birth is contraindicated
why_correct: A previous classical (vertical upper-segment) caesarean carries a high risk of uterine rupture in labour and is a contraindication to vaginal birth after caesarean. She should be offered a planned repeat caesarean, usually earlier than for a lower-segment scar. Classical incisions are more common after very preterm caesareans, when the lower segment has not yet formed.
why_wrong: A. Monitoring does not make labour safe with a classical scar, which is a contraindication. B. Spontaneous labour still carries an unacceptable risk of rupture. C. Induction with prostaglandins further increases the risk of rupture. E. The interval between births does not offset the risk from an upper-segment scar.
pearl: Contraindications to vaginal birth after caesarean include a previous classical uterine incision, previous uterine rupture and the usual contraindications to vaginal birth such as placenta praevia.
thinking: Previous caesarean ↓ Check the type of uterine incision ↓ Vertical upper-segment (classical) scar ↓ High risk of rupture in labour ↓ Planned repeat caesarean
exam_trap: A, Planned vaginal birth with continuous CTG monitoring in labour — this is the standard plan for vaginal birth after a lower-segment caesarean. But a classical scar is a contraindication, and monitoring cannot prevent rupture.
takeaway: A previous classical caesarean scar rules out vaginal birth; plan a repeat caesarean.

stem: A 29-year-old woman has been trying to conceive for 18 months. She describes pelvic pain that starts a few days before each period and lasts throughout it, pain on opening her bowels during periods, and deep pain during intercourse. Her periods are regular and not heavy. On bimanual examination the uterus is retroverted and fixed, and there is tenderness behind the cervix. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Cyclical pelvic pain, painful bowel movements during periods, deep dyspareunia and subfertility, with a fixed retroverted uterus and tenderness in the pouch of Douglas, are classic features of endometriosis. Laparoscopy is the definitive diagnostic test, although ultrasound or MRI can identify endometriomas and deep disease. Treatment depends on symptoms and fertility wishes.
why_wrong: B. Chronic pelvic inflammatory disease can cause pain and subfertility but the pain is not usually cyclical, and there is no infection history. C. IBS does not explain the cyclical pattern, fixed uterus or subfertility. D. Adenomyosis typically causes heavy painful periods with a bulky, tender uterus in older women who have had children. E. Fibroids more often cause heavy bleeding and an enlarged, irregular uterus.
pearl: The endometriosis cluster is dysmenorrhoea, deep dyspareunia, painful bowel movements during periods and subfertility. A normal examination does not exclude it, and laparoscopy is the definitive test.
thinking: Cyclical pelvic pain ↓ Pain on opening bowels during periods and deep dyspareunia ↓ Subfertility ↓ Fixed retroverted uterus with posterior tenderness ↓ Endometriosis
exam_trap: D, Adenomyosis — it also causes painful periods and is caused by ectopic endometrial tissue. But adenomyosis usually causes heavy periods and a bulky uterus in older women, whereas pain on opening the bowels, a fixed uterus and subfertility point to endometriosis.
takeaway: Cyclical pain, painful bowel movements during periods, deep dyspareunia and subfertility: think endometriosis.

stem: During a spontaneous vaginal birth on the labour ward, the baby's head delivers but the chin is pulled back tightly against the perineum. Gentle axial traction during the next contraction does not deliver the anterior shoulder. The emergency bell has been pressed and the team has arrived. What is the most appropriate first manoeuvre?

options.A: Fundal pressure with continued maternal pushing
options.B: Internal rotation with Woods' screw manoeuvre
options.C: Firm downward traction on the baby's head
options.D: Replacement of the head into the vagina (Zavanelli manoeuvre) and caesarean section

correct_answer: E. McRoberts' position with suprapubic pressure
why_correct: Retraction of the head (the turtle sign) and failure of the shoulders to deliver with gentle axial traction is shoulder dystocia. First-line measures are McRoberts' position (flexing and abducting the mother's hips onto her abdomen) and suprapubic pressure behind the anterior shoulder; these resolve most cases. If they fail, internal manoeuvres or delivery of the posterior arm follow.
why_wrong: A. Fundal pressure worsens impaction and risks uterine rupture. B. Internal rotation is a second-line manoeuvre if McRoberts' and suprapubic pressure fail. C. Excessive or downward traction causes brachial plexus injury. D. The Zavanelli manoeuvre is a last resort.
pearl: Shoulder dystocia: call for help, McRoberts' position plus suprapubic pressure first, then internal manoeuvres or posterior arm, with no fundal pressure and no excessive traction. Document the timing.
thinking: Head delivers then retracts ↓ Shoulders do not deliver with gentle traction ↓ Shoulder dystocia ↓ Simplest effective manoeuvres first ↓ McRoberts' position with suprapubic pressure
exam_trap: C, Firm downward traction on the baby's head — it feels natural to pull harder when the shoulder is stuck. But excessive traction on an impacted shoulder causes brachial plexus injury and does not free it.
takeaway: Shoulder dystocia: McRoberts' position and suprapubic pressure first; never fundal pressure or excessive traction.

stem: A 38-year-old woman is telephoned by the antenatal screening midwife after her 13-week combined screening test (nuchal translucency with blood markers) returns a higher-chance result for Down's syndrome. She is distressed and asks whether this means her baby definitely has Down's syndrome. What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Explain it is a screening result, not a diagnosis, and offer further testing such as NIPT or an invasive diagnostic test
options.B: Explain that the baby has Down's syndrome and discuss her options for the pregnancy
options.C: Advise repeating the combined test in two weeks
options.D: Advise waiting for the 20-week anomaly scan to confirm
options.E: Offer the quadruple test to confirm the result

correct_answer: A. Explain it is a screening result, not a diagnosis, and offer further testing such as NIPT or an invasive diagnostic test
why_correct: The combined test estimates the chance of a trisomy; a higher-chance result is not a diagnosis, and many such pregnancies are unaffected. She should be offered, with informed choice, either non-invasive prenatal testing (a more accurate screening test with no miscarriage risk) or a diagnostic test (chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis), or she may choose no further testing.
why_wrong: B. A screening test cannot confirm the diagnosis. C. Repeating the same screening test adds nothing. D. The anomaly scan is not a diagnostic test for Down's syndrome and delays her choices. E. The quadruple test is a less accurate screening alternative used when the combined test was missed.
pearl: Combined, quadruple and NIPT tests are screening tests; only CVS or amniocentesis is diagnostic. After a higher-chance result, offer the choice of NIPT, invasive testing or no further testing.
thinking: Higher-chance combined test result ↓ Screening estimates chance, it does not diagnose ↓ Many such pregnancies are unaffected ↓ Further testing offered with informed choice ↓ NIPT or CVS or amniocentesis
exam_trap: B, Explain that the baby has Down's syndrome and discuss her options for the pregnancy — the result sounds definitive and she is asking for certainty. But a screening result only gives a chance; diagnosis needs CVS or amniocentesis.
takeaway: A higher-chance screening result is not a diagnosis; offer NIPT or diagnostic testing as her choice.

stem: A 27-year-old woman who is breastfeeding her three-week-old baby has a painful, hot, red area in the upper outer part of her left breast. She feels achy and shivery and her temperature is 38.3°C. She has a cracked left nipple. There is no fluctuant swelling. She has stopped feeding from the left side because she is worried the milk will harm her baby. What is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: Avoid feeding from the left breast until the redness settles
options.B: Take cabergoline to suppress milk production
options.D: Continue feeding or expressing from both breasts, take analgesia and start flucloxacillin
options.E: Be admitted for intravenous antibiotics and stop breastfeeding

correct_answer: D. Continue feeding or expressing from both breasts, take analgesia and start flucloxacillin
why_correct: This is lactational mastitis. Effective milk removal from the affected breast is the most important treatment, and the milk is safe for the baby. With systemic symptoms and an infected nipple fissure, an oral antibiotic is indicated: flucloxacillin, or erythromycin or clarithromycin if penicillin-allergic. Analgesia, rest and help with positioning and attachment also matter.
why_wrong: A. Stopping feeding from the affected breast causes milk stasis and increases the risk of abscess. B. Suppressing lactation is unnecessary and removes a treatment that works. C. There is no fluctuant collection to suggest an abscess needing drainage. E. She is not severely unwell, and breastfeeding should continue.
pearl: Mastitis: keep the milk flowing from the affected breast. Antibiotics (flucloxacillin) are for an infected nipple fissure, systemic illness or failure to improve; a fluctuant lump suggests abscess needing drainage.
thinking: Breastfeeding with a red, painful breast segment ↓ Fever and cracked nipple ↓ No fluctuant collection: mastitis, not abscess ↓ Milk removal plus antibiotic ↓ Keep feeding and start flucloxacillin
exam_trap: A, Avoid feeding from the left breast until the redness settles — resting an inflamed area seems sensible and matches her own worry. But stopping feeding causes milk stasis, prolongs mastitis and can lead to abscess.
takeaway: Mastitis: keep feeding from the affected breast and add flucloxacillin if infection is likely.

stem: A 61-year-old woman sees her GP with burning and itching around the vaginal entrance and pain during sex for the past year. She has had no vaginal bleeding or discharge. On examination the vaginal walls are pale, smooth and dry, with loss of the normal folds, and the vulval skin is of normal colour without white patches. What is the most likely diagnosis and appropriate treatment?

options.A: Lichen sclerosus — potent topical corticosteroid ointment
options.B: Atrophic vaginitis — vaginal oestrogen with moisturisers and lubricants
options.E: Trichomoniasis — oral metronidazole and partner treatment

correct_answer: B. Atrophic vaginitis — vaginal oestrogen with moisturisers and lubricants
why_correct: Vaginal dryness, irritation and dyspareunia after the menopause with pale, smooth, dry vaginal walls is atrophic vaginitis (genitourinary syndrome of menopause), caused by oestrogen deficiency. Low-dose vaginal oestrogen is effective and can be used long term, with vaginal moisturisers and lubricants. Any postmenopausal bleeding would still need separate investigation.
why_wrong: A. Lichen sclerosus causes white, thickened or shiny vulval plaques, which are absent. C. Candidiasis causes a thick white discharge and red, inflamed mucosa. D. Bacterial vaginosis causes a thin, fishy-smelling discharge without these atrophic findings. E. Trichomoniasis causes a frothy discharge and inflamed mucosa.
pearl: Postmenopausal dryness, irritation and dyspareunia with pale, thin mucosa is atrophy: treat with vaginal oestrogen and moisturisers. White vulval plaques suggest lichen sclerosus instead.
thinking: Postmenopausal woman ↓ Dryness, burning and dyspareunia, no discharge ↓ Pale, smooth, dry vaginal walls ↓ No white vulval plaques ↓ Atrophic vaginitis treated with vaginal oestrogen
exam_trap: A, Lichen sclerosus — potent topical corticosteroid ointment — it is common in postmenopausal women and also causes itching and dyspareunia. But it produces white, shiny vulval skin changes, which this patient does not have.
takeaway: Postmenopausal dryness and dyspareunia with pale, thin mucosa: vaginal oestrogen plus moisturisers.

stem: A 34-year-old woman tells her GP her periods stopped eight months ago. She has vaginal dryness, poor sleep and episodes of feeling hot and sweaty. Pregnancy test is negative. Her follicle-stimulating hormone is raised on two samples taken several weeks apart, and her oestradiol is low. Prolactin and thyroid function are normal. She exercises moderately and her weight is stable. What is the most likely diagnosis and management?

options.A: Hypothalamic amenorrhoea — reduce exercise and increase calorie intake
options.B: Polycystic ovary syndrome — weight loss and cyclical progestogen
options.C: Hyperprolactinaemia — dopamine agonist after pituitary imaging
options.D: Normal early menopause — no treatment needed unless symptoms become severe
options.E: Premature ovarian insufficiency — hormone replacement until at least the average age of menopause

correct_answer: E. Premature ovarian insufficiency — hormone replacement until at least the average age of menopause
why_correct: Menopausal symptoms with amenorrhoea and a raised FSH on two occasions in a woman under 40 is premature ovarian insufficiency. Hormone replacement, with HRT or a combined hormonal contraceptive, is recommended until at least the average age of natural menopause, to relieve symptoms and protect against osteoporosis and cardiovascular disease. Specialist referral and support for fertility and emotional effects are also appropriate.
why_wrong: A. Hypothalamic amenorrhoea causes low or normal FSH, not a raised one. B. Polycystic ovary syndrome does not cause a raised FSH with low oestradiol and menopausal symptoms. C. Her prolactin is normal. D. Menopause under 40 is not a normal variant, and hormone replacement is advised to protect bone and heart health, not just for symptoms.
pearl: Under 40 with amenorrhoea and a raised FSH on two samples is premature ovarian insufficiency. Replace hormones until at least the average age of menopause; the benefit is long-term protection, not only symptom relief.
thinking: Amenorrhoea and vasomotor symptoms at 34 ↓ Pregnancy excluded ↓ FSH raised twice, oestradiol low ↓ Ovarian failure before 40 ↓ Premature ovarian insufficiency treated with hormone replacement
exam_trap: D, Normal early menopause — no treatment needed unless symptoms become severe — it treats HRT as optional symptom relief, as it would be at the usual age. But before 40, oestrogen deficiency threatens bone and cardiovascular health, so replacement is recommended regardless of symptom severity.
takeaway: Premature ovarian insufficiency: offer HRT or combined contraception until at least the age of natural menopause.

stem: A 26-year-old woman taking the combined oral contraceptive pill attends a sexual health clinic with occasional light bleeding after intercourse for two months. Her cervical screening a year ago was normal. On speculum examination there is a smooth, velvety red area surrounding the external os that bleeds slightly when touched with a swab; there is no mass or ulceration. What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Urgent suspected cancer referral for colposcopy
options.B: Likely cervical ectropion — test for chlamydia and gonorrhoea, and reassure if negative
options.D: Refer for large loop excision of the transformation zone
options.E: Treat empirically for pelvic inflammatory disease

correct_answer: B. Likely cervical ectropion — test for chlamydia and gonorrhoea, and reassure if negative
why_correct: A smooth, red, velvety area around the os in a young woman taking oestrogen-containing contraception is a cervical ectropion, where columnar epithelium lies on the ectocervix; it is benign and can bleed on contact. Infection, particularly chlamydia, should be excluded, and her screening is up to date with a normal cervix that does not look suspicious. If bleeding persists or is troublesome, she can be referred to gynaecology, and cautery is an option.
why_wrong: A. The cervix does not look suspicious for cancer, and her screening is up to date. C. Stopping the pill without discussion risks unintended pregnancy; it can be considered later if bleeding persists. D. LLETZ treats confirmed cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, not ectropion. E. There is no pelvic pain, cervical motion tenderness or other sign of PID.
pearl: Post-coital bleeding with a smooth red ring around the os in a young woman on the pill suggests ectropion. Exclude infection, check screening is up to date, and refer if the cervix looks suspicious or bleeding persists.
thinking: Post-coital bleeding in a young woman on the pill ↓ Smooth, velvety red area around the os, no mass ↓ Screening up to date ↓ Benign ectropion likely ↓ Exclude infection, then reassure
exam_trap: A, Urgent suspected cancer referral for colposcopy — post-coital bleeding is a recognised symptom of cervical cancer. But NICE bases urgent referral on a cervix that looks suspicious, and a smooth ectropion in a screened young woman does not.
takeaway: Smooth red area around the os on the pill is ectropion: exclude infection and check screening before reassuring.

stem: A 15-year-old girl attends her GP with her mother because of cramping lower abdominal pain on the first two days of each period, causing her to miss school. Her periods started two years ago, the pain has been present since then, and her cycles are regular with normal flow. She is not sexually active and has no pain between periods. Abdominal examination is normal. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.D: An NSAID such as ibuprofen or mefenamic acid

correct_answer: D. An NSAID such as ibuprofen or mefenamic acid
why_correct: Painful periods beginning soon after menarche, with regular cycles, no other symptoms and a normal examination, are primary dysmenorrhoea, caused by prostaglandin-driven uterine contractions. First-line treatment is an NSAID taken at the start of the period or just before it; paracetamol is an alternative if NSAIDs are unsuitable. A hormonal contraceptive can be added if needed.
why_wrong: A. Paracetamol is less effective and is used when NSAIDs are contraindicated. B. Laparoscopy is not indicated for typical primary dysmenorrhoea. C. Imaging is not needed when the history and examination are typical. E. Codeine is not recommended for dysmenorrhoea and is less effective than an NSAID.
pearl: Primary dysmenorrhoea starts within a couple of years of menarche and responds to NSAIDs. Pain starting later, between periods, or with dyspareunia or abnormal bleeding suggests a secondary cause.
thinking: Teenager with period pain since menarche ↓ Regular cycles, no other symptoms ↓ Normal examination ↓ Primary dysmenorrhoea from prostaglandins ↓ NSAID first-line
exam_trap: A, Paracetamol alone — it is the gentlest, most familiar option for a teenager. But NSAIDs target the prostaglandins that cause the pain and work better, so they are first-line unless contraindicated.
takeaway: Primary dysmenorrhoea is treated first with an NSAID; investigate only if features are atypical.

stem: A 27-year-old woman asks her GP about starting contraception. She mentions headaches that are preceded by flashing zigzag lines spreading across her vision for about 20 minutes. She is a non-smoker with normal blood pressure and BMI. She wants a reliable method that she does not have to remember daily. Which method is most appropriate?

options.A: A low-dose combined oral contraceptive pill
options.C: Avoid all hormonal methods and use condoms only
options.E: A combined pill taken continuously without a hormone-free interval

why_correct: Visual symptoms that precede the headache are migraine with aura, which is an absolute contraindication to combined hormonal contraception because oestrogen increases the risk of ischaemic stroke. Progestogen-only methods do not carry this risk and can be used. The implant is long-acting, highly effective and needs no daily action, so it fits her wishes.
why_wrong: A. Any oestrogen-containing pill is contraindicated in migraine with aura, whatever the dose. B. The ring contains oestrogen, so the same contraindication applies. C. Progestogen-only methods are safe, so avoiding all hormonal methods is unnecessary. E. Changing how the combined pill is taken does not remove the stroke risk from oestrogen.
pearl: Migraine with aura means no oestrogen: no combined pill, patch or ring. Progestogen-only methods and intrauterine devices are suitable, and long-acting methods are the most effective.
thinking: Visual aura before headaches ↓ Migraine with aura ↓ Oestrogen increases stroke risk ↓ Combined methods excluded; progestogen-only safe ↓ Long-acting implant fits her wish
exam_trap: B, The combined vaginal ring — it is not a pill and needs no daily action, so it seems to avoid the problem. But it still delivers oestrogen, and any combined method is contraindicated in migraine with aura.
takeaway: Migraine with aura rules out all combined hormonal contraception; offer progestogen-only or intrauterine methods.

stem: A 33-year-old woman attends her GP with a symptom diary she has kept over three cycles. For about a week before each period she becomes tearful and short-tempered, feels bloated and has sore breasts. The symptoms clear within two days of her period starting, and she feels completely well in the first half of each cycle. Her periods are regular. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Psychological and physical symptoms that recur in the luteal phase, settle soon after menstruation starts and are absent in the first half of the cycle are the defining pattern of premenstrual syndrome. A prospective symptom diary over at least two cycles supports the diagnosis. Management ranges from lifestyle changes and cognitive behavioural therapy to a combined pill or an SSRI for more severe symptoms.
why_wrong: A. Depression persists throughout the cycle and does not disappear in the follicular phase. B. Bipolar disorder causes distinct episodes of mood elevation and depression not tied to the cycle. D. Hypothyroidism causes persistent symptoms, not cyclical ones. E. Generalised anxiety is persistent rather than limited to the days before each period.
pearl: The key to premenstrual syndrome is timing: luteal phase symptoms that resolve soon after bleeding starts, with a symptom-free week. A prospective diary over two cycles confirms the pattern.
thinking: Mood and physical symptoms ↓ Appear the week before periods ↓ Resolve soon after bleeding starts ↓ Symptom-free first half of cycle ↓ Premenstrual syndrome
exam_trap: A, Depressive disorder — tearfulness and low mood are prominent, so depression comes to mind. But depression does not switch off for half of each cycle; the strict cyclical pattern is diagnostic of PMS.
takeaway: Symptoms confined to the luteal phase that resolve with menstruation define premenstrual syndrome.

stem: A 30-year-old woman at 33 weeks attends maternity triage because of itching that has been keeping her awake for a week. It is worst on her hands and feet. Apart from scratch marks, her skin looks normal. Her blood pressure is normal and her urine shows no protein. Blood tests show raised bile acids and a mildly raised ALT, with normal platelets and glucose. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Itching in later pregnancy, worst on the palms and soles, with no primary rash and raised bile acids is intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy. The main concern is an increased risk of stillbirth, which rises with higher bile acid levels. Management involves monitoring bile acids and liver function and planning the timing of birth; ursodeoxycholic acid may ease itch but does not reduce stillbirth risk.
why_wrong: A. Polymorphic eruption causes an itchy rash, often starting in abdominal striae, and does not raise bile acids. C. Pemphigoid gestationis causes blistering lesions, often starting around the umbilicus. D. Acute fatty liver causes a systemically unwell woman with hypoglycaemia and coagulopathy. E. HELLP causes hypertension, haemolysis and low platelets.
pearl: Itching on the palms and soles without a rash in the third trimester: check bile acids. Cholestasis of pregnancy is mostly a risk to the fetus, and the timing of birth depends on the bile acid level.
thinking: Third-trimester itch ↓ Worst on hands and feet ↓ No primary rash ↓ Raised bile acids, normal platelets and glucose ↓ Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy
exam_trap: A, Polymorphic eruption of pregnancy — it is the commonest itchy condition of late pregnancy. But it causes a visible rash, whereas cholestasis causes itch with normal skin and raised bile acids.
takeaway: Itchy palms and soles with no rash and raised bile acids in late pregnancy: obstetric cholestasis.

stem: A 19-year-old woman attends the early pregnancy unit at 11 weeks with dark brown vaginal spotting and frequent vomiting. Her uterus is palpable well above the pubic symphysis, larger than expected for her dates. Her blood pressure is raised, and her serum hCG is far higher than expected for her gestation. Ultrasound shows a heterogeneous intrauterine mass with many small cystic spaces and no fetal pole. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Bleeding, exaggerated vomiting, a uterus large for dates, very high hCG and early hypertension, with an intrauterine mass of multiple cystic spaces and no fetus, indicate a molar pregnancy (gestational trophoblastic disease). Management is surgical evacuation with histology, followed by registration with a specialist trophoblastic screening centre for hCG follow-up, because a minority develop persistent disease.
why_wrong: A. Twins can raise hCG and enlarge the uterus but would show two gestational sacs or fetuses on ultrasound. B. A missed miscarriage does not produce very high hCG or a cystic mass. C. Hyperemesis does not explain the ultrasound appearance or the large uterus. D. The pregnancy is intrauterine.
pearl: Molar pregnancy: very high hCG, large-for-dates uterus, severe vomiting and sometimes early hypertension or hyperthyroidism, with a snowstorm-like cystic mass on scan. Evacuate, then follow up hCG.
thinking: Early pregnancy bleeding and severe vomiting ↓ Uterus larger than dates ↓ hCG far above expected, early hypertension ↓ Cystic intrauterine mass, no fetus ↓ Molar pregnancy
exam_trap: A, Twin pregnancy — it also gives a large uterus, high hCG and more severe vomiting. But ultrasound would show two sacs or fetuses, not a cystic mass with no fetal pole.
takeaway: Very high hCG, large-for-dates uterus and a cystic mass without a fetus mean molar pregnancy.

stem: A 44-year-old woman tells her GP about two months of bleeding after intercourse and an offensive, bloodstained vaginal discharge. She has not attended her last two cervical screening invitations. On speculum examination there is an irregular, ulcerated area on the cervix that bleeds readily on contact. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Take a cervical screening sample today and act on the result
options.B: Make an urgent suspected cancer referral to gynaecology
options.C: Take swabs and start doxycycline for presumed cervicitis
options.E: Treat as ectropion and review in three months

correct_answer: B. Make an urgent suspected cancer referral to gynaecology
why_correct: An irregular, ulcerated cervix that bleeds on contact, with post-coital bleeding and offensive discharge, is suspicious for cervical cancer. NICE recommends a suspected cancer pathway referral when the appearance of the cervix is consistent with cancer, for colposcopy and biopsy. A screening test is not appropriate for a woman with symptoms and a visible lesion.
why_wrong: A. Screening is for women without symptoms, and a result could falsely reassure and delay diagnosis. C. Infection does not explain an ulcerated, irregular lesion and treating it would delay referral. D. A suspicious cervix needs the urgent pathway, not a routine appointment. E. An ectropion is smooth and regular, not ulcerated and irregular.
pearl: A visibly abnormal cervix needs urgent referral, whatever the screening history. Never use a screening test to investigate symptoms or a visible lesion.
thinking: Post-coital bleeding and offensive discharge ↓ Missed screening ↓ Irregular, ulcerated, contact-bleeding cervix ↓ Appearance consistent with cancer ↓ Urgent suspected cancer referral
exam_trap: A, Take a cervical screening sample today and act on the result — she is overdue for screening, so catching up seems efficient. But screening is designed for well women, and a visible suspicious lesion needs urgent referral regardless of any sample.
takeaway: A cervix that looks suspicious for cancer needs urgent referral, not a screening test.

presentation: Tubal ectopic pregnancy suitable for methotrexate
stem: A 27-year-old woman attends the early pregnancy unit at six weeks of amenorrhoea with light spotting and only mild, intermittent pelvic discomfort. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus and a small adnexal mass consistent with a tubal ectopic pregnancy, with no fetal heartbeat and no free fluid. Her serum hCG is modestly raised and has risen on a repeat sample 48 hours later. She is haemodynamically stable, can attend follow-up reliably, and would prefer to avoid an operation. What is the most appropriate treatment?
why_correct: A stable woman with a small, unruptured tubal ectopic, no heartbeat, no significant pain and a modest hCG is suitable for medical management with a single dose of intramuscular methotrexate, provided she can attend follow-up for serial hCG. This avoids surgery, which matches her preference. Expectant management is suitable only when hCG is low and falling.
why_wrong: B. Her hCG is rising, which shows the pregnancy is still active and makes expectant management unsuitable. C. Salpingectomy is appropriate for rupture, significant pain, a larger mass or a visible heartbeat, or if she chooses it, but she prefers to avoid surgery and is a good candidate for medical treatment. D. Mifepristone with misoprostol is used for miscarriage and termination, not ectopic pregnancy. E. Salpingotomy is a surgical option mainly for women with fertility risk factors, and she wishes to avoid surgery.
pearl: Methotrexate suits a stable, pain-free woman with a small unruptured tubal ectopic, no heartbeat, a modest hCG and reliable follow-up. A rising hCG rules out expectant management.
thinking: Tubal ectopic, haemodynamically stable ↓ Small mass, no heartbeat, no free fluid, minimal pain ↓ hCG modest but rising, so not expectant ↓ Wants to avoid surgery and can attend follow-up ↓ Intramuscular methotrexate
exam_trap: B, Expectant management with repeat hCG — she is well with a small ectopic, so a watch-and-wait approach seems least invasive. But a rising hCG shows active trophoblast, and expectant management is reserved for a low and falling hCG.
takeaway: Small unruptured ectopic, stable, rising but modest hCG and wants no surgery: single-dose methotrexate.

stem: A 36-year-old woman at 32 weeks attends maternity triage with severe epigastric pain going through to her back, vomiting and feeling generally unwell. Her blood pressure is raised and urine dipstick shows proteinuria. Blood tests show a low platelet count, a markedly raised ALT, a raised LDH and fragmented red cells on the blood film. Amylase, glucose and clotting are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Haemolysis (fragmented red cells, raised LDH), elevated liver enzymes and low platelets in a hypertensive woman with proteinuria in the third trimester is HELLP syndrome, a severe form of pre-eclampsia. Epigastric or right upper quadrant pain is typical and can be mistaken for gastrointestinal disease. It is an obstetric emergency requiring stabilisation, magnesium sulfate, blood pressure control and delivery.
why_wrong: A. Pancreatitis is unlikely with a normal amylase and does not explain haemolysis or low platelets. B. Biliary colic does not cause haemolysis, thrombocytopenia or hypertension. C. Fatty liver of pregnancy typically causes hypoglycaemia and coagulopathy, which are absent. D. Reflux does not cause abnormal blood tests or hypertension.
pearl: Epigastric pain in late pregnancy is pre-eclampsia or HELLP until proven otherwise. Check blood pressure, urine, platelets, liver enzymes and a blood film before calling it reflux or gallstones.
thinking: Third trimester epigastric pain ↓ Hypertension and proteinuria ↓ Low platelets, raised ALT, haemolysis ↓ Normal glucose and clotting argue against fatty liver ↓ HELLP syndrome
exam_trap: A, Acute pancreatitis — severe epigastric pain radiating to the back with vomiting is its textbook description. But the amylase is normal, and haemolysis with low platelets in a hypertensive woman points to HELLP.
takeaway: Late-pregnancy epigastric pain with hypertension, haemolysis, high liver enzymes and low platelets is HELLP.

stem: A 16-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department after waking with sudden, severe right lower abdominal pain that comes in waves. She has vomited three times. She is afebrile. There is marked tenderness in the right iliac fossa and right adnexa. A urine pregnancy test is negative and urine dipstick is normal. Ultrasound shows an enlarged right ovary containing a large cyst. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Sudden onset of severe unilateral pelvic pain with vomiting, in a girl with an enlarged ovary containing a cyst, is ovarian torsion until proven otherwise. A cyst or mass makes the ovary prone to twisting on its pedicle, cutting off its blood supply. It needs urgent gynaecological review and laparoscopy to untwist and preserve the ovary; a normal Doppler flow does not exclude torsion.
why_wrong: A. Appendicitis usually develops gradually, with central pain moving to the right iliac fossa and fever, not sudden onset on waking. B. PID causes gradual bilateral pain with fever and discharge, usually in sexually active women. C. The pregnancy test is negative. E. A normal urine dipstick and the ovarian cyst make ureteric colic unlikely.
pearl: Sudden unilateral pelvic pain with vomiting and an ovarian cyst is torsion. Go to laparoscopy on clinical suspicion; Doppler flow can be normal, and delay costs the ovary.
thinking: Sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain ↓ Vomiting, afebrile ↓ Pregnancy test negative, urine normal ↓ Enlarged ovary with a cyst ↓ Ovarian torsion
exam_trap: A, Acute appendicitis — right iliac fossa pain and vomiting in a teenager is the classic appendicitis presentation. But the sudden onset, lack of fever and the ovarian cyst point to torsion.
takeaway: Sudden pelvic pain with vomiting and an ovarian cyst is torsion: urgent laparoscopy to save the ovary.

stem: A 78-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation stopped taking apixaban a month ago because of nosebleeds. Four hours ago her right foot and calf suddenly became painful. On examination the leg is pale and cold below the knee, with no popliteal or foot pulses; the femoral pulse is present. She has reduced sensation in her toes but can move them. The calf is soft. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.A: Restart apixaban and arrange an outpatient arterial duplex scan
options.B: Aspirin and clopidogrel with a vascular clinic appointment
options.C: Intravenous unfractionated heparin and urgent vascular surgical review
options.E: Elevate the leg and apply compression bandaging

correct_answer: C. Intravenous unfractionated heparin and urgent vascular surgical review
why_correct: Sudden pain, pallor, coldness and pulselessness in a patient with atrial fibrillation off anticoagulation is acute limb ischaemia, most likely embolic. The limb is threatened but salvageable, with sensory loss but preserved movement and a soft calf. Immediate intravenous heparin limits clot propagation while urgent vascular surgical assessment arranges revascularisation, such as embolectomy.
why_wrong: A. This is a limb-threatening emergency that cannot wait for outpatient tests. B. Antiplatelets do not treat an acute embolus, and a clinic appointment is far too slow. D. Movement is preserved and the calf is soft, so the limb is salvageable. E. Elevation and compression reduce arterial flow further and worsen ischaemia.
pearl: The six Ps of acute limb ischaemia are pain, pallor, pulselessness, perishingly cold, paraesthesia and paralysis. Sensory or motor loss means a threatened limb: heparin and urgent revascularisation.
thinking: Sudden painful, pale, cold, pulseless leg ↓ AF off anticoagulation: embolus ↓ Sensory loss, movement preserved ↓ Threatened but salvageable limb ↓ IV heparin and urgent vascular review
exam_trap: A, Restart apixaban and arrange an outpatient arterial duplex scan — she clearly needs anticoagulation for her AF, so restarting it looks logical. But an acutely ischaemic limb needs immediate heparin and revascularisation, not outpatient care.
takeaway: Acute limb ischaemia: immediate IV heparin and urgent vascular surgery to save the limb.

stem: A 58-year-old man who smokes sees his GP with three months of tiredness, night sweats and weight loss. He mentions one episode of blood in his urine that he did not report. On examination there is a left-sided scrotal swelling feeling like a bag of worms, which does not empty when he lies down. His full blood count shows a raised haemoglobin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Visible haematuria, systemic symptoms and a new left varicocele that does not empty on lying down suggest renal cell carcinoma: a left renal tumour can obstruct the left renal vein, into which the left testicular vein drains. Some kidney cancers secrete erythropoietin, causing a raised haemoglobin. Smoking is a risk factor, and he needs an urgent suspected cancer referral.
why_wrong: A. The swelling is a varicocele of the veins, not a testicular mass, and testicular tumours do not cause haematuria or polycythaemia. B. Bladder cancer causes haematuria but would not explain the varicocele or raised haemoglobin. C. Polycythaemia vera does not cause haematuria or a varicocele. E. Stones cause pain, not systemic symptoms, polycythaemia or a varicocele.
pearl: A new left varicocele that does not empty on lying down suggests renal vein obstruction, so examine and image the left kidney. Kidney cancer can also cause polycythaemia, fever and hypercalcaemia.
thinking: Haematuria in a smoker with systemic symptoms ↓ Left varicocele that stays full when lying down ↓ Left renal vein obstruction ↓ Raised haemoglobin from erythropoietin ↓ Renal cell carcinoma
exam_trap: B, Bladder cancer — visible haematuria in a smoker is its classic presentation. But bladder cancer cannot explain a non-emptying left varicocele or a raised haemoglobin, which both point to the kidney.
takeaway: Haematuria plus a new non-emptying left varicocele suggests a left renal cell carcinoma.

stem: A 30-year-old man attends the emergency department with 18 hours of abdominal pain that started around his umbilicus and has settled in the right lower abdomen. He has no appetite, his temperature is 37.9°C, and he winced at every bump on the drive in. Pressing in the left iliac fossa causes pain in the right iliac fossa, and there is guarding over the right iliac fossa. Urine dipstick is normal. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Discharge with oral antibiotics and safety-netting advice
options.B: Surgical review for appendicectomy, with IV fluids, analgesia and antibiotics
options.E: Analgesia and discharge with GP follow-up

correct_answer: B. Surgical review for appendicectomy, with IV fluids, analgesia and antibiotics
why_correct: Pain moving from the umbilicus to the right iliac fossa, anorexia, low-grade fever, pain on movement, Rovsing's sign and localised guarding make acute appendicitis highly likely. It is a clinical diagnosis in a young man and needs urgent surgical review, keeping him nil by mouth with IV fluids, analgesia and antibiotics, and laparoscopic appendicectomy to prevent perforation.
why_wrong: A. Antibiotic-only treatment is not the standard of care for a man with peritonism and needs specialist decision, not discharge. C. Colonoscopy has no role and could risk perforation. D. Delaying assessment for a week risks perforation. E. Discharging a patient with localised peritonism is unsafe.
pearl: Pain moving from the umbilicus to the right iliac fossa, anorexia and localised peritonism make appendicitis a clinical diagnosis in young men. Imaging is more useful in women, children and older adults.
thinking: Periumbilical pain moving to the right iliac fossa ↓ Anorexia, low-grade fever ↓ Rovsing's sign and guarding ↓ Acute appendicitis ↓ Surgical review for appendicectomy
exam_trap: A, Discharge with oral antibiotics and safety-netting advice — antibiotic treatment of uncomplicated appendicitis is discussed widely. But it is not standard care in UK practice, and a patient with peritonism should be assessed by surgeons, not sent home.
takeaway: Migratory right iliac fossa pain with peritonism: urgent surgical review for appendicectomy.

stem: A 48-year-old woman was admitted two days ago with constant right upper quadrant pain, fever and a positive Murphy's sign. Ultrasound showed gallstones with a thickened gallbladder wall and no bile duct dilatation. She is improving on intravenous antibiotics, her liver tests are normal, and she is otherwise fit and well. On the ward round, she asks when she should have her gallbladder removed. What is the most appropriate plan?

options.A: Discharge and add her to the waiting list for surgery in 6 to 8 weeks
options.B: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy during this admission, within a week of diagnosis
options.C: Percutaneous cholecystostomy now, with surgery later
options.D: No surgery unless she has another attack

correct_answer: B. Laparoscopic cholecystectomy during this admission, within a week of diagnosis
why_correct: NICE recommends early laparoscopic cholecystectomy, within a week of diagnosis, for people with acute cholecystitis who are fit for surgery. Early surgery is as safe as delayed surgery, shortens the total length of illness and hospital stay, and avoids readmissions with recurrent attacks while waiting.
why_wrong: A. Delayed interval surgery was traditional practice but leads to more recurrent attacks and readmissions. C. Cholecystostomy is for patients too unwell or frail for surgery. D. Gallstone cholecystitis commonly recurs, so surgery is advised in fit patients. E. ERCP treats bile duct stones, and her liver tests and bile duct are normal.
pearl: Acute cholecystitis in a fit patient: laparoscopic cholecystectomy within a week of diagnosis. Cholecystostomy is for patients too unwell for surgery.
thinking: Acute calculous cholecystitis ↓ Responding to antibiotics ↓ Fit for surgery ↓ Early surgery shortens illness and avoids readmission ↓ Laparoscopic cholecystectomy within a week
exam_trap: A, Discharge and add her to the waiting list for surgery in 6 to 8 weeks — this cooling-off approach was standard teaching for years. But current evidence and NICE favour early surgery, which reduces recurrent attacks and overall time in hospital.
takeaway: Fit patient with acute cholecystitis: early laparoscopic cholecystectomy within a week of diagnosis.

stem: A 67-year-old man with a right inguinoscrotal hernia that he has always been able to push back attends the emergency department. For eight hours the lump has been painful and he has been unable to reduce it. He has vomited several times and has not passed wind since the morning. The lump is tense, very tender and the overlying skin is red and warm. He is tachycardic. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Attempt manual reduction and discharge if successful
options.B: Refer to the routine hernia clinic
options.C: Fit a truss and review in six weeks
options.E: Admit for analgesia and observation overnight

correct_answer: D. Resuscitate and arrange emergency surgery
why_correct: A previously reducible hernia that has become painful, tense and irreducible, with vomiting, absent flatus, red overlying skin and tachycardia, is obstructed and strangulated, meaning the blood supply to its contents is compromised. He needs resuscitation with IV fluids, analgesia, a nasogastric tube and emergency surgery to assess bowel viability, resect any dead bowel and repair the hernia.
why_wrong: A. Forcing reduction of a strangulated hernia can push dead bowel back into the abdomen. B. A routine clinic is far too slow for a surgical emergency. C. A truss has no role in an irreducible or strangulated hernia. E. Observation delays surgery and allows bowel to infarct and perforate.
pearl: Painful, tense, irreducible hernia with obstruction or skin changes means strangulation: no forceful reduction, but resuscitation and emergency surgery. Red skin and tachycardia suggest ischaemic bowel.
thinking: Known hernia, now irreducible and painful ↓ Vomiting and no flatus: obstruction ↓ Tender, red overlying skin and tachycardia ↓ Strangulation with threatened bowel ↓ Resuscitation and emergency surgery
exam_trap: A, Attempt manual reduction and discharge if successful — reduction can work for a recently incarcerated hernia without obstruction. But with red skin, obstruction and tachycardia the bowel may be ischaemic, and reducing it hides the problem.
takeaway: Irreducible, tender hernia with obstruction or skin changes: resuscitate and operate urgently.

stem: A 54-year-old woman tells her GP that over the past two months her right nipple has become pulled inwards, and she can feel a firm area beneath it. On examination there is a hard, irregular mass behind the right nipple, fixed to the overlying tissue, and a firm node in the right axilla. She had a normal screening mammogram two years ago. What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Wait for her next screening mammogram
options.B: Review after her next period to see whether it changes
options.C: Urgent suspected cancer referral to a breast clinic for triple assessment
options.D: Prescribe antibiotics for presumed duct ectasia
options.E: Request a breast ultrasound from primary care and act on the result

correct_answer: C. Urgent suspected cancer referral to a breast clinic for triple assessment
why_correct: A new hard, irregular, fixed breast mass with nipple retraction and an axillary node is highly suspicious for breast cancer. NICE recommends a suspected cancer pathway referral for women aged 30 and over with an unexplained breast lump. The breast clinic performs triple assessment: clinical examination, imaging (mammography and ultrasound) and core biopsy.
why_wrong: A. Screening is for women without symptoms, and waiting would delay diagnosis. B. A hard, fixed lump with nipple retraction should not be observed through a cycle. D. Duct ectasia does not explain a hard, fixed mass with an axillary node, and antibiotics delay diagnosis. E. Imaging is arranged as part of triple assessment at the breast clinic, not by the GP.
pearl: Hard, fixed, irregular breast lump with skin or nipple changes or an axillary node needs urgent referral for triple assessment. A recent normal mammogram does not exclude cancer.
thinking: New breast mass in a woman over 30 ↓ Hard, irregular and fixed ↓ Nipple retraction and axillary node ↓ Highly suspicious for cancer ↓ Urgent referral for triple assessment
exam_trap: A, Wait for her next screening mammogram — she is within the screening programme and had a normal mammogram recently. But screening is for women without symptoms; a symptomatic lump needs urgent referral regardless.
takeaway: Suspicious breast lump: urgent referral for triple assessment, regardless of recent screening.

stem: A 34-year-old woman who tends to be constipated has had two months of tearing pain when she opens her bowels, followed by a burning ache lasting about an hour. She has noticed streaks of bright red blood on the toilet paper. When the buttocks are gently parted, there is a linear split at the posterior midline of the anal verge with a small skin tag at its outer end. Digital rectal examination is deferred because of pain. What is the most appropriate first-line management?

options.A: Topical glyceryl trinitrate with dietary fibre, fluids and a bulk-forming laxative
options.E: Oral metronidazole and referral to exclude a fistula

correct_answer: A. Topical glyceryl trinitrate with dietary fibre, fluids and a bulk-forming laxative
why_correct: Severe pain on defecation with bright red bleeding and a posterior midline tear is an anal fissure; symptoms for more than six weeks and a sentinel skin tag show it is chronic. First-line treatment is softening the stool (fibre, fluids, laxatives) with a topical agent that relaxes the internal sphincter, such as glyceryl trinitrate ointment, or diltiazem as an alternative. Surgery is considered only if this fails.
why_wrong: B. Sphincterotomy is reserved for fissures that do not heal with medical treatment, because of the risk of incontinence. C. Banding treats internal haemorrhoids, which are painless. D. Topical steroids do not help a fissure to heal. E. There is no abscess or fistula, and metronidazole is not standard treatment.
pearl: Anal fissure: pain on defecation with bright red blood, usually posterior midline. Off-midline or multiple fissures should prompt a search for Crohn's disease, infection or malignancy.
thinking: Tearing pain on defecation and bright red blood ↓ Posterior midline split ↓ Over six weeks with a sentinel tag: chronic fissure ↓ Relax the sphincter and soften the stool ↓ Topical GTN with fibre and laxatives
exam_trap: B, Referral for lateral internal sphincterotomy — it heals most chronic fissures and the fissure here is chronic. But medical treatment comes first, and surgery carries a risk of incontinence.
takeaway: Chronic anal fissure: topical GTN or diltiazem with stool softening first; surgery only if it fails.

stem: A 21-year-old woman found a lump in her left breast while showering three weeks ago. It has not changed through her menstrual cycle. On examination there is a 2 cm smooth, rubbery, well-defined lump that moves freely under the fingers and is not tender. There are no skin or nipple changes and no axillary nodes. What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Reassure that it is a fibroadenoma and discharge without referral
options.B: Prescribe antibiotics and review in two weeks
options.C: Probable fibroadenoma — refer to a breast clinic for triple assessment
options.D: Aspirate the lump in the surgery

correct_answer: C. Probable fibroadenoma — refer to a breast clinic for triple assessment
why_correct: A smooth, rubbery, well-defined and highly mobile painless lump in a young woman is most likely a fibroadenoma. However, a new discrete lump should still be assessed in a breast clinic, where triple assessment (examination, ultrasound and biopsy if needed) confirms the diagnosis. Once confirmed, most fibroadenomas can be left alone, with excision offered if large, growing or troublesome.
why_wrong: A. A clinical diagnosis alone is not enough; a discrete lump needs specialist assessment to confirm it. B. There are no signs of infection. D. Aspiration in primary care is not appropriate for a solid lump and is not part of GP management. E. Wide excision is for phyllodes tumours or cancer, not a presumed fibroadenoma.
pearl: A smooth, mobile, rubbery lump in a young woman is usually a fibroadenoma, but it should be confirmed by triple assessment before reassurance. Most can then be left alone.
thinking: Young woman with a discrete breast lump ↓ Smooth, rubbery, very mobile, painless ↓ Probable fibroadenoma ↓ Diagnosis still needs confirming ↓ Breast clinic for triple assessment
exam_trap: A, Reassure that it is a fibroadenoma and discharge without referral — the features are classic, and cancer is rare at 21. But a new discrete lump still needs triple assessment to confirm the diagnosis before she is reassured.
takeaway: Probable fibroadenoma still needs triple assessment; once confirmed, it can usually be observed.

stem: An 82-year-old man with Parkinson's disease and long-standing constipation is on a medical ward. Over two days his abdomen has become hugely distended and drum-like, he has passed no stool or wind, and he has started to vomit. His abdomen is not peritonitic, his lactate is normal and he is haemodynamically stable. An abdominal X-ray shows a massively dilated loop of bowel arising from the left side of the pelvis and extending towards the right upper quadrant, shaped like a coffee bean. What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.A: Phosphate enema and regular oral laxatives
options.E: Endoscopic decompression with a flexible sigmoidoscope and a flatus tube

correct_answer: E. Endoscopic decompression with a flexible sigmoidoscope and a flatus tube
why_correct: A massively dilated, coffee bean-shaped loop arising from the pelvis in an elderly, constipated man with neurological disease is sigmoid volvulus. Without peritonitis or signs of ischaemia, first-line management is endoscopic decompression with a flexible sigmoidoscope, leaving a flatus tube in place. Emergency surgery is needed if decompression fails or bowel ischaemia or perforation is suspected, and recurrence is common.
why_wrong: A. Enemas and laxatives do not untwist a volvulus and laxatives can worsen obstruction. B. Right hemicolectomy is for caecal volvulus, which arises on the right. C. Neostigmine treats colonic pseudo-obstruction, where there is no twist. D. This is an acute obstruction that needs decompression now, not elective investigation.
pearl: Sigmoid volvulus: elderly, constipated, often with neurological or psychiatric illness; coffee bean sign from the pelvis. Decompress with a flexible sigmoidoscope unless there is peritonitis.
thinking: Elderly, constipated, Parkinson's disease ↓ Massive distension with no stool or flatus ↓ Coffee bean loop from the left pelvis ↓ No peritonitis or ischaemia ↓ Endoscopic decompression
exam_trap: C, Intravenous neostigmine — colonic pseudo-obstruction also causes massive distension in frail elderly inpatients. But the coffee bean loop shows a twist, which neostigmine cannot correct and which needs decompression.
takeaway: Sigmoid volvulus without peritonitis: endoscopic decompression with a flatus tube first.

stem: A 68-year-old woman tells her GP about a small, painless swelling in her right groin that she noticed three weeks ago. On examination there is a soft, non-tender lump below the inguinal ligament, inferior and lateral to the pubic tubercle. It does not disappear when she lies down and is not reducible. There is no thrill on coughing and no varicose veins. What is the most likely diagnosis and appropriate management?

options.A: Direct inguinal hernia — watchful waiting as it is painless
options.C: Femoral hernia — prompt surgical referral for repair
options.D: Inguinal lymph node — observe and review in six weeks
options.E: Indirect inguinal hernia — fit a truss

correct_answer: C. Femoral hernia — prompt surgical referral for repair
why_correct: A groin lump below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, in an older woman, is a femoral hernia; inguinal hernias lie above and medial to the tubercle. Femoral hernias pass through a narrow, rigid femoral canal, are often irreducible and carry a high risk of strangulation. They should be referred promptly for repair even when painless.
why_wrong: A. An inguinal hernia lies above and medial to the pubic tubercle, and watchful waiting is unsafe for a femoral hernia. B. A saphena varix disappears on lying down, has a cough thrill and usually accompanies varicose veins. D. A lymph node is usually firm and may be multiple; this is a hernia in a typical position and should not be observed. E. The lump is not inguinal, and trusses have no role.
pearl: Femoral hernia: below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, commonest in older women, often irreducible and at high risk of strangulation. Refer for repair even if painless.
thinking: Groin lump in an older woman ↓ Below and lateral to the pubic tubercle ↓ Irreducible, no thrill, no varicose veins ↓ Femoral hernia with high strangulation risk ↓ Prompt surgical repair
exam_trap: A, Direct inguinal hernia — watchful waiting as it is painless — watchful waiting is acceptable for small, painless inguinal hernias. But the position below and lateral to the pubic tubercle makes this femoral, where strangulation risk makes repair essential.
takeaway: Lump below and lateral to the pubic tubercle is femoral: refer for repair even if painless.

stem: A 42-year-old woman attends the emergency department with sudden, severe right loin pain that comes in waves and spreads to her groin. She cannot keep still and has vomited. She is afebrile, her urine dipstick shows blood, and a pregnancy test is negative. Her kidney function is normal and she has no history of peptic ulcer, asthma or heart disease. What is the most appropriate analgesia and imaging?

options.A: Intravenous morphine and a renal ultrasound
options.C: Oral paracetamol and a plain KUB X-ray
options.D: Intravenous paracetamol and contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen
options.E: Intramuscular or rectal diclofenac and non-contrast CT of the kidneys, ureters and bladder

correct_answer: E. Intramuscular or rectal diclofenac and non-contrast CT of the kidneys, ureters and bladder
