What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Same-day eye referral for steroid drops
options.B: Urgent intraocular pressure measurement in the eye unit
options.C: Corneal scraping in the eye unit
options.D: Hygiene advice and lid cleaning, considering chloramphenicol if not settling
options.E: Chloramphenicol drops and exclusion from work until the discharge stops

correct_answer: D. Hygiene advice and lid cleaning, considering chloramphenicol if not settling
why_correct: A gritty red eye with purulent discharge, normal acuity, no photophobia, no real pain and a normal pupil is infective conjunctivitis. It is usually self-limiting, so management is lid cleaning and hygiene advice to prevent spread, with topical chloramphenicol considered for severe or persistent cases.
why_wrong: A. Steroid drops are for uveitis under specialist care and could worsen infection. B. Angle closure causes severe pain, haloes, a hazy cornea and a fixed mid-dilated pupil. C. Corneal scrapes are for suspected keratitis with pain, photophobia and reduced vision. E. Antibiotics are not routinely needed, and exclusion from work or school is not required for conjunctivitis.
pearl: Pain, photophobia, reduced acuity or an abnormal pupil should prompt a search for a more serious cause of a red eye; take extra care in contact lens wearers.
thinking: Red gritty eye with sticky discharge ↓ Normal acuity, no photophobia, no real pain ↓ Normal pupil, no lens wear ↓ Infective conjunctivitis ↓ Hygiene advice; antibiotic drops only if needed
exam_trap: E, chloramphenicol with exclusion from work — purulent discharge seems to demand an antibiotic, and she works with children. But most cases settle without treatment, and exclusion is not recommended for conjunctivitis.
takeaway: Red eye with discharge but normal vision, normal pupil and no pain: conjunctivitis; self-care first.

stem: A 46-year-old man attends the emergency department with a week of headache and blurred vision. He has not seen a doctor for many years. His blood pressure is 232/138 mmHg. Fundoscopy shows narrowed arterioles, flame-shaped haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots and blurring of both optic disc margins. Urine dipstick shows blood and protein. What do the fundal findings indicate?

options.D: Chronic hypertensive changes needing routine treatment

correct_answer: E. Malignant (accelerated) hypertension needing emergency treatment
why_correct: Severe hypertension with retinal haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots and bilateral optic disc swelling is accelerated (malignant) hypertension, a hypertensive emergency often accompanied by acute kidney involvement. He needs admission and specialist-supervised, controlled blood pressure reduction, avoiding too rapid a fall, which can cause cerebral, renal or retinal ischaemia.
why_wrong: A. Idiopathic intracranial hypertension causes papilloedema, typically in young women, without severe hypertensive retinal changes. B. Retinal vein occlusion is usually unilateral, with widespread haemorrhages in one eye. C. Diabetic maculopathy causes exudates near the macula rather than disc swelling. D. Disc swelling with severe hypertension is an emergency, not a routine finding.
pearl: Severe hypertension with retinal haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots or papilloedema needs same-day specialist assessment.
thinking: Severely raised blood pressure ↓ Headache, blurred vision, haematuria and proteinuria ↓ Haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots and bilateral disc swelling ↓ Accelerated (malignant) hypertension ↓ Emergency: admit for controlled reduction
exam_trap: A, idiopathic intracranial hypertension — headache with papilloedema fits. But the extreme blood pressure with haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots and renal involvement points to malignant hypertension.
takeaway: Papilloedema with severe hypertension means malignant hypertension: an emergency.

stem: An 82-year-old man attends his annual review with his GP. Over the past two years he has found reading the newspaper and recognising faces increasingly difficult, although he gets around his flat without trouble. He has not noticed straight lines looking bent. A letter from his optometrist reports scattered yellow deposits and patchy pigment changes at both maculae, with no fluid or bleeding. What is the most likely diagnosis and appropriate management?

options.A: Wet AMD — urgent referral for anti-VEGF injections
options.C: Dry AMD — low-vision support, smoking advice and monitoring for new distortion
options.D: Chronic open-angle glaucoma — prostaglandin eye drops

correct_answer: C. Dry AMD — low-vision support, smoking advice and monitoring for new distortion
why_correct: Slowly progressive bilateral central visual loss with drusen and pigmentary change, but no fluid, haemorrhage or distortion, is dry (atrophic) age-related macular degeneration. There is no curative treatment; management is low-vision aids and support, stopping smoking, and safety-netting to seek urgent review if distortion or sudden worsening suggests conversion to the wet form.
why_wrong: A. Anti-VEGF treats wet AMD with fluid or haemorrhage, which is absent here. B. Cataract causes generalised blur and glare rather than macular drusen. D. Glaucoma causes peripheral field loss with central vision preserved until late. E. Diabetic maculopathy causes exudates, haemorrhages or macular oedema in a person with diabetes; drusen with pigment change are the hallmark of AMD.
pearl: Smoking is the main modifiable risk factor for AMD; cessation advice is part of management for both forms.
thinking: Elderly patient with gradual central visual loss over years ↓ Reading and faces affected, peripheral vision intact ↓ Drusen and pigment change, no fluid, bleeding or distortion ↓ Dry AMD ↓ Supportive care and monitoring for wet change
exam_trap: A, urgent anti-VEGF — AMD is the diagnosis and anti-VEGF is its best-known treatment. But it only helps the wet form; dry AMD has no fluid or bleeding to treat.
takeaway: Gradual central visual loss with drusen: dry AMD; support, stop smoking and watch for distortion.

stem: A 71-year-old man with hypertension and type 2 diabetes sees his GP the day after an episode in which the vision in his right eye went completely dark, as if a blind had been pulled across it, for about five minutes before returning to normal. He has no headache, jaw pain on chewing or scalp tenderness, and eye examination is now normal. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Aspirin and urgent specialist TIA assessment with carotid imaging
options.B: Reassure that this was a retinal migraine

correct_answer: A. Aspirin and urgent specialist TIA assessment with carotid imaging
why_correct: Sudden painless transient monocular blindness resolving within minutes is amaurosis fugax, a retinal transient ischaemic attack usually caused by carotid or cardiac emboli. It carries a high early stroke risk, so it is managed as a TIA: start antiplatelet treatment unless contraindicated and refer for urgent specialist assessment including carotid imaging, with carotid endarterectomy considered for significant symptomatic stenosis.
why_wrong: B. Retinal migraine is a diagnosis of exclusion in younger people; in an older man with vascular risk factors this must be treated as a TIA. C. Retinal detachment causes a persistent progressive shadow, not a brief blackout that fully resolves. D. A routine optician review ignores the high early stroke risk. E. Steroids are for suspected giant cell arteritis, and he has none of its features.
pearl: In older patients with transient visual loss, always ask about headache, jaw claudication and scalp tenderness to exclude giant cell arteritis.
thinking: Older patient with vascular risk factors ↓ Sudden painless monocular blackout, fully resolved in minutes ↓ No features of giant cell arteritis ↓ Amaurosis fugax: a retinal TIA ↓ Antiplatelet and urgent TIA assessment with carotid imaging
exam_trap: D, routine optician review — his vision is back to normal and the eye looks normal, so it may seem non-urgent. But this is a TIA with a high early stroke risk.
takeaway: Transient monocular blindness: treat as a TIA, with antiplatelet and urgent carotid assessment.

stem: A 49-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes, who has missed her last two retinal screening appointments, wakes to find the vision in her left eye hazy, with dark cobweb-like shapes that drift as she moves her eye. There is no pain and the eye is white. On examination the left red reflex is dull and the retina cannot be seen clearly. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Sudden painless visual loss with new dark floaters, a reduced red reflex and an obscured fundal view in a diabetic patient with probable untreated proliferative retinopathy indicates vitreous haemorrhage from fragile new vessels. She needs prompt ophthalmology referral to identify and treat the cause, such as with laser, and to exclude an associated retinal detachment.
why_wrong: A. Artery occlusion causes profound sudden loss with a pale retina and cherry-red spot that remains visible, without floaters. B. Angle closure is painful, with a red eye and hazy cornea. C. Optic neuritis causes pain on eye movement and colour desaturation with a normal red reflex. D. Cataract develops over months rather than overnight with floaters.
pearl: In a diabetic patient, missed screening plus sudden floaters and a dull red reflex should suggest bleeding from proliferative retinopathy.
thinking: Diabetes with missed screening ↓ Sudden painless blurring with dark drifting floaters ↓ Dull red reflex, retina obscured ↓ Bleeding into the vitreous from new vessels ↓ Vitreous haemorrhage
exam_trap: A, central retinal artery occlusion — sudden painless monocular loss fits. But artery occlusion causes no floaters and the pale retina remains visible; a dull reflex with an obscured view means blood in the vitreous.
takeaway: Sudden floaters, dull red reflex and a hidden retina in diabetes: vitreous haemorrhage.

stem: A 35-year-old builder attends a minor injuries unit after something blew into his right eye while he was sweeping a dusty site an hour ago. The eye is watering, red and painful, and he feels there is still something under the lid. Visual acuity is normal, and he was not using any power tools or hammering. After a topical anaesthetic is instilled for examination, what is the most important next step?

options.A: Fluorescein staining and eversion of the upper eyelid
options.B: Prescribe topical anaesthetic drops for home use

correct_answer: A. Fluorescein staining and eversion of the upper eyelid
why_correct: A foreign-body sensation after low-velocity debris enters the eye calls for fluorescein staining under blue light to show any corneal abrasion or embedded particle, together with eversion of the upper lid to find a subtarsal foreign body. Any foreign body is then removed, and a topical antibiotic and analgesia are given for an abrasion.
why_wrong: B. Repeated topical anaesthetic delays epithelial healing and masks further injury. C. Routine padding does not improve healing and is not recommended. D. Steroids impair healing and increase infection risk in an abrasion. E. Imaging is for high-velocity injuries such as hammering or grinding, where penetration is possible.
pearl: Vertical linear abrasions on fluorescein suggest a particle trapped under the upper lid; always evert it.
thinking: Debris blown into the eye at low velocity ↓ Pain, watering, persistent foreign-body sensation ↓ Need to find an abrasion or retained particle ↓ Fluorescein shows epithelial defects; lid eversion finds subtarsal particles ↓ Fluorescein staining and upper lid eversion
exam_trap: B, topical anaesthetic for home — it relieves the pain dramatically in the department. But repeated use delays healing and can damage the cornea, so it is never prescribed to take home.
takeaway: Foreign-body sensation: fluorescein and evert the upper lid before anything else.

stem: A 68-year-old long-sighted woman is brought to the emergency department in the evening, having left a dimly lit cinema. She has a severe ache in her left eye and forehead, is vomiting, and describes rainbow-coloured rings around lights. The left eye is red, the cornea looks cloudy, the pupil is mid-dilated, oval and unreactive to light, and the globe feels firm on gentle palpation. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.B: Urgent pressure-lowering treatment and immediate ophthalmology referral
options.C: Intensive topical antibiotic drops for keratitis
options.E: Antiemetic, analgesia and a CT head

correct_answer: B. Urgent pressure-lowering treatment and immediate ophthalmology referral
why_correct: A painful red eye with haloes, a hazy cornea, a fixed mid-dilated pupil, a hard globe and vomiting, triggered by dim light in an older hypermetropic woman, is acute angle-closure glaucoma. It is a sight-threatening emergency: pressure-lowering treatment such as acetazolamide and topical agents is started immediately according to local protocol, with immediate ophthalmology referral for definitive laser iridotomy.
why_wrong: A. Steroid and cycloplegic drops treat uveitis, and dilating the pupil could worsen angle closure. C. Keratitis causes a corneal infiltrate, not a fixed pupil and a hard globe. D. A routine referral would allow permanent optic nerve damage within hours. E. Treating this as migraine or intracranial disease misses the eye as the source.
pearl: Pupil dilation in dim light or after mydriatic drops can precipitate angle closure in older, long-sighted people with shallow anterior chambers.
thinking: Older long-sighted woman, onset in dim light ↓ Severe eye pain, haloes, vomiting ↓ Hazy cornea, fixed mid-dilated pupil, hard globe ↓ Acute angle-closure glaucoma ↓ Immediate pressure lowering and ophthalmology referral
exam_trap: E, antiemetic and CT head — headache and vomiting dominate and suggest an intracranial cause. But the red eye, hazy cornea, fixed pupil and hard globe locate the problem in the eye.
takeaway: Painful red eye, haloes and a fixed mid-dilated pupil: angle closure; lower the pressure and refer now.

stem: A 19-year-old woman attends the emergency department on day five of a sore throat that had been improving but is now much worse on the left. She cannot open her mouth fully, is spitting out her saliva because swallowing hurts, and her voice sounds thick and muffled. Examination shows a bulging swelling above the left tonsil, pushing the uvula to the right. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Worsening one-sided throat pain after tonsillitis, with trismus, a muffled 'hot potato' voice, drooling and a swelling above the tonsil displacing the uvula to the opposite side, is a peritonsillar abscess (quinsy). It needs same-day ENT referral for needle aspiration or incision and drainage, with intravenous antibiotics.
why_wrong: A. Ludwig's angina is a floor-of-mouth infection, usually dental, with submandibular swelling and a raised tongue. B. Glandular fever causes bilateral tonsillar enlargement with widespread lymphadenopathy, not a one-sided bulge with uvular deviation. D. Epiglottitis causes stridor and toxicity with a relatively normal-looking oropharynx. E. Simple tonsillitis is bilateral and does not displace the uvula or cause trismus.
pearl: Uvular deviation away from the affected side, with trismus, is the key finding that separates quinsy from severe tonsillitis.
thinking: Tonsillitis that worsens on one side ↓ Trismus, drooling, muffled voice ↓ Swelling above one tonsil, uvula pushed away ↓ Pus collection beside the tonsil ↓ Peritonsillar abscess
exam_trap: E, bacterial tonsillitis — she has a typical sore throat history. But one-sided bulging, uvular deviation and trismus indicate a collection that needs drainage.
takeaway: One-sided sore throat with trismus and uvular deviation: quinsy; same-day ENT.

stem: A 46-year-old man telephones his GP surgery and is seen that afternoon. He woke this morning unable to hear properly in his left ear, with a ringing noise in it; there was no preceding cold, ear pain or discharge. Otoscopy shows normal ear canals and eardrums. A 512 Hz tuning fork placed on his forehead sounds louder in the right ear, and air conduction is better than bone conduction on both sides. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Olive oil drops for presumed wax
options.B: Immediate ENT referral for assessment and corticosteroid treatment
options.C: Routine audiology referral for a hearing aid
options.D: Intranasal steroid for Eustachian tube dysfunction
options.E: Review in a month if not improved

correct_answer: B. Immediate ENT referral for assessment and corticosteroid treatment
why_correct: Weber lateralising to the good ear with air conduction better than bone conduction on the affected side indicates a sensorineural loss. Sudden unexplained sensorineural hearing loss is an otological emergency needing immediate ENT referral, where early corticosteroid treatment gives the best chance of recovery and investigation, including MRI to exclude a vestibular schwannoma, is arranged.
why_wrong: A. The canals are clear and the pattern is sensorineural, not conductive. C. A routine audiology route loses the short window for steroid treatment. D. Eustachian tube dysfunction gives a conductive pattern, usually after a cold. E. Waiting a month removes the benefit of early treatment.
pearl: Weber lateralises to the better ear in sensorineural loss and to the worse ear in conductive loss; Rinne stays positive in sensorineural loss.
thinking: Sudden one-sided hearing loss with tinnitus ↓ Normal otoscopy ↓ Weber to the good ear, Rinne positive on both sides ↓ Sudden sensorineural hearing loss ↓ Immediate ENT referral for steroids
exam_trap: E, review in a month — hearing often returns after a cold, so waiting seems reasonable. But sudden sensorineural loss needs treatment within days, and delay worsens the outcome.
takeaway: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss: immediate ENT referral for steroid treatment.

stem: A 52-year-old woman tells her GP that over the past year she has had several attacks in which the room suddenly spins violently, lasting most of an afternoon, with vomiting. Before each attack her right ear feels blocked and the roaring noise in it gets louder, and her hearing on that side dips during attacks before partly recovering. Between attacks she is well. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Recurrent spontaneous attacks of rotatory vertigo lasting hours, with fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus and aural fullness in one ear, are typical of Ménière's disease (endolymphatic hydrops). The diagnosis is confirmed by ENT with audiometry; acute attacks are treated with a vestibular sedative such as prochlorperazine, and betahistine may be tried to reduce attacks.
why_wrong: A. BPPV causes brief vertigo lasting seconds on head movement, without hearing symptoms. B. A vestibular schwannoma causes progressive one-sided hearing loss and tinnitus rather than discrete hours-long vertigo attacks. C. Labyrinthitis is a single prolonged episode lasting days, usually after a viral illness. E. Vestibular neuronitis causes a single attack lasting days without hearing loss.
pearl: Classify vertigo by duration: seconds suggests BPPV, hours suggests Ménière's or vestibular migraine, days suggests vestibular neuronitis or labyrinthitis.
thinking: Recurrent spontaneous spinning attacks lasting hours ↓ Preceding aural fullness and louder tinnitus ↓ Fluctuating one-sided hearing loss ↓ Well between attacks ↓ Ménière's disease
exam_trap: C, labyrinthitis — vertigo with hearing loss suggests it. But labyrinthitis is a single episode lasting days, not recurrent hours-long attacks with fluctuating hearing.
takeaway: Recurrent hours-long vertigo with fluctuating hearing, tinnitus and fullness: Ménière's disease.

stem: A 5-year-old girl is seen in a GP out-of-hours clinic with right ear pain that started last night after a cold. Her temperature is 38.1°C. She is alert, playing in the waiting room and drinking well. Otoscopy shows a red, bulging right eardrum with no perforation or discharge; the left ear is normal. She has no significant past medical history. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Paracetamol or ibuprofen, with no antibiotic or a back-up prescription

correct_answer: A. Paracetamol or ibuprofen, with no antibiotic or a back-up prescription
why_correct: She has acute otitis media but is systemically well, with one ear affected and no discharge. Most episodes resolve within a few days without antibiotics, so management is regular analgesia and antipyretics with a no-antibiotic or back-up antibiotic strategy, plus safety-netting advice to return if she worsens.
why_wrong: B. Immediate antibiotics are for children who are systemically very unwell or at high risk of complications, and are considered in younger children with both ears affected or those with discharge. C. Ear drops are not effective for middle-ear infection behind an intact drum. D. ENT referral is not needed for an uncomplicated episode. E. Decongestants and antihistamines do not help acute otitis media.
pearl: Pain relief is the most useful treatment in acute otitis media; antibiotics shorten symptoms only slightly and cause side effects.
thinking: Ear pain and fever after a cold ↓ Red, bulging, intact drum on one side ↓ Child well, eating and drinking ↓ Uncomplicated acute otitis media ↓ Analgesia with no or back-up antibiotic
exam_trap: B, immediate amoxicillin — a red bulging drum with fever looks bacterial. But most well children recover without it, and immediate antibiotics are reserved for specific higher-risk situations.
takeaway: Well child with acute otitis media: analgesia, with no antibiotic or a back-up prescription.

stem: A 16-year-old boy attends the emergency department with a nosebleed from his left nostril that started 20 minutes ago after picking his nose. His pulse and blood pressure are normal and he has no history of bleeding problems. His father has been holding a tissue against the bridge of the nose with the boy's head tipped back. What should he be advised to do first?

options.A: Lie flat with an ice pack on the forehead
options.B: Keep the head tilted back and press on the bony bridge
options.C: Sit up, lean forward and firmly pinch the soft part of the nose for 10–15 minutes
options.D: Have silver nitrate cautery straight away
options.E: Have an anterior nasal pack inserted straight away

correct_answer: C. Sit up, lean forward and firmly pinch the soft part of the nose for 10–15 minutes
why_correct: Most nosebleeds arise from Little's area on the anterior septum. First aid is to sit up, lean forward, breathe through the mouth and pinch the soft lower part of the nose firmly and continuously for 10–15 minutes without releasing; cautery or packing is used only if bleeding continues.
why_wrong: A. Lying flat lets blood run down the throat, risking swallowing, vomiting and aspiration. B. Tipping the head back has the same problem, and pressing the bony bridge does not compress the bleeding vessels. D. Cautery is for a visible bleeding point once first aid has failed or the bleeding has slowed. E. Packing is reserved for bleeding not controlled by pressure or cautery.
pearl: Sucking ice or an ice pack may help, but continuous pressure on the soft part of the nose is what stops most anterior bleeds.
thinking: Stable patient, anterior nosebleed after nose-picking ↓ Bleeding from Little's area ↓ Direct pressure over the cartilaginous septum ↓ Lean forward to avoid swallowing blood ↓ Sit forward and pinch the soft nose for 10–15 minutes
exam_trap: B, head back with pressure on the bridge — it is common lay advice and what his father was doing. But blood runs into the throat, and the bony bridge is not where the bleeding vessels are.
takeaway: Anterior nosebleed: sit forward and pinch the soft nose firmly for 10–15 minutes.

stem: A 27-year-old woman has a video consultation with her GP about a sore throat that started three days ago. She feels feverish, and on camera her tonsils look swollen with some white spots. She has no cough or runny nose. She asks whether she needs antibiotics. What is the most appropriate way to make this decision?

options.A: Send a throat swab and decide when the culture result returns
options.B: Apply a clinical score such as FeverPAIN or Centor
options.C: Prescribe antibiotics because the tonsils have white spots
options.D: Measure CRP and treat if it is raised
options.E: Wait until symptoms have lasted more than two weeks

correct_answer: B. Apply a clinical score such as FeverPAIN or Centor
why_correct: Most sore throats are viral and settle within about a week. A validated clinical score such as FeverPAIN (fever, purulence, attending rapidly, inflamed tonsils, no cough or coryza) or Centor estimates the likelihood of streptococcal infection and guides a no-antibiotic, back-up or immediate antibiotic strategy, with phenoxymethylpenicillin first choice when antibiotics are needed.
why_wrong: A. Routine throat swabs are not recommended; they delay decisions and cannot distinguish carriage from infection. C. Tonsillar exudate alone does not reliably separate bacterial from viral infection. D. CRP testing is not part of the recommended assessment of acute sore throat. E. Symptom duration alone is not the basis for the antibiotic decision.
pearl: Penicillin V is first-line for streptococcal sore throat; avoid amoxicillin if glandular fever is possible, because it can cause a widespread rash.
thinking: Acute sore throat ↓ Most are viral and self-limiting ↓ Need to estimate streptococcal likelihood ↓ Validated clinical scoring system ↓ FeverPAIN or Centor guides the antibiotic strategy
exam_trap: A, throat swab — it seems an objective way to confirm bacteria. But swabs are not routinely recommended, delay decisions and detect carriage; the clinical score is the recommended tool.
takeaway: Sore throat: use FeverPAIN or Centor to guide the antibiotic decision.

stem: A 38-year-old man is seen in the emergency department with continuous severe spinning dizziness since waking yesterday, worse with any head movement, and repeated vomiting. He had a flu-like illness the previous week. His hearing is unchanged and he has no tinnitus. There is horizontal nystagmus beating to the left and an abnormal head impulse test when his head is turned to the right. He can walk with support and has no headache, weakness, numbness, slurred speech or double vision. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Acute continuous vertigo lasting days after a viral illness, with one-directional horizontal nystagmus, an abnormal head impulse test and no hearing loss, tinnitus or central neurological signs, is vestibular neuronitis. It is managed with a short course of a vestibular sedative such as prochlorperazine and early vestibular rehabilitation exercises.
why_wrong: A. Ménière's causes recurrent attacks lasting hours with fluctuating hearing loss and tinnitus. B. BPPV causes brief episodes lasting seconds triggered by head position, not continuous vertigo. C. Labyrinthitis has the same picture but with hearing loss or tinnitus. E. A central cause is less likely with an abnormal head impulse test and no neurological signs, although it must be considered if these are present or he cannot stand.
pearl: Labyrinthitis is vestibular neuronitis plus hearing loss; both follow viral illness and both cause days of continuous vertigo.
thinking: Continuous vertigo for days after a viral illness ↓ Vomiting, horizontal nystagmus, abnormal head impulse test ↓ No hearing loss or tinnitus ↓ No central neurological features ↓ Vestibular neuronitis
exam_trap: C, labyrinthitis — the timing and viral trigger are identical. But labyrinthitis involves the cochlea too, giving hearing loss or tinnitus, which he does not have.
takeaway: Days of vertigo after a viral illness with hearing intact: vestibular neuronitis.

stem: A 63-year-old man who has smoked 20 cigarettes a day since his teens sees his GP because his wife says his voice has become rough and croaky. It began about two months ago with a cold and has not improved since. He has no difficulty swallowing and has not noticed any lumps. Examination of the mouth and neck is normal. What is the most appropriate action?

options.B: Voice rest and review in three months
options.D: Chest X-ray first, referring only if it is abnormal
options.E: Suspected cancer pathway referral to ENT

correct_answer: E. Suspected cancer pathway referral to ENT
why_correct: Persistent unexplained hoarseness in an older smoker raises suspicion of laryngeal cancer and warrants a suspected cancer pathway referral to ENT for laryngoscopy. The referral should not wait for other tests, although a chest X-ray may also be arranged because hoarseness can reflect lung cancer affecting the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
why_wrong: A. Antibiotics have no role in persistent hoarseness without infection. B. Further delay risks missing a laryngeal cancer at an early, treatable stage. C. A routine referral is too slow for a red-flag symptom. D. A normal chest X-ray does not exclude laryngeal cancer, so referral must not depend on it.
pearl: Hoarseness may arise from the larynx itself or from recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy due to lung or thyroid cancer; both need urgent assessment.
thinking: Older long-term smoker ↓ Persistent hoarseness not settling after a cold ↓ No benign explanation ↓ Possible laryngeal cancer ↓ Suspected cancer pathway referral to ENT
exam_trap: D, chest X-ray first — hoarseness can come from lung cancer and an X-ray is quick. But a normal film does not exclude laryngeal cancer, so the ENT referral must not wait for it.
takeaway: Persistent unexplained hoarseness in an older smoker: suspected cancer referral to ENT.

stem: A 4-year-old girl was diagnosed with a left ear infection by her GP a week ago and managed with analgesia. She is brought to the emergency department because she is now feverish and irritable, with a painful red swelling behind the left ear. The left ear sticks out more than the right, and the swelling is boggy and very tender. What is the most appropriate management?

options.B: Oral amoxicillin and GP review in 48 hours
options.C: Incision and drainage in the emergency department
options.D: Admission for intravenous antibiotics and urgent ENT assessment

correct_answer: D. Admission for intravenous antibiotics and urgent ENT assessment
why_correct: Fever with a tender, red, boggy swelling behind the ear that pushes the pinna outwards and forwards after otitis media is acute mastoiditis. It can lead to subperiosteal abscess, meningitis, venous sinus thrombosis and brain abscess, so she needs admission, intravenous antibiotics and urgent ENT assessment, with imaging and surgery if indicated.
why_wrong: A. Ear drops treat otitis externa and cannot reach infected mastoid air cells. B. Oral antibiotics at home are inadequate for an infection that can spread intracranially. C. Drainage in the emergency department is inappropriate; any surgery is planned by ENT after imaging. E. Conservative measures leave a serious bacterial infection untreated.
pearl: A protruding ear with swelling behind it after otitis media is mastoiditis until proved otherwise; check for neurological signs.
thinking: Recent acute otitis media ↓ Fever and irritability ↓ Tender boggy swelling behind the ear, pinna pushed out ↓ Acute mastoiditis ↓ Admit, IV antibiotics, urgent ENT
exam_trap: B, oral amoxicillin — it is the right drug for the preceding ear infection. But spread to the mastoid needs intravenous treatment and ENT input because of intracranial complications.
takeaway: Swelling behind the ear with a protruding pinna after otitis media: admit for IV antibiotics and ENT.

stem: A 19-year-old apprentice electrician sees his GP in early June. For the past three summers he has had weeks of a blocked and streaming nose, bouts of sneezing and red, itchy, watering eyes, worse on dry, windy days. He is otherwise well and has mild asthma controlled with an inhaler. What is the most appropriate management?

options.B: Xylometazoline nasal spray throughout the season
options.C: Allergen-avoidance advice with an intranasal corticosteroid and/or a non-sedating antihistamine
options.E: Oral prednisolone for the whole season

correct_answer: C. Allergen-avoidance advice with an intranasal corticosteroid and/or a non-sedating antihistamine
why_correct: Recurrent summer sneezing, rhinorrhoea, nasal blockage and itchy watery eyes are seasonal allergic rhinitis (hay fever). Management is allergen-avoidance advice, with a non-sedating oral antihistamine for mild intermittent symptoms and an intranasal corticosteroid for persistent or more troublesome symptoms; good rhinitis control may also help his asthma.
why_wrong: A. This is an allergic, not bacterial, process, so antibiotics are not indicated. B. Prolonged decongestant use causes rebound congestion (rhinitis medicamentosa). D. Depot steroid injections are not recommended because of systemic adverse effects. E. Systemic steroids are only for short courses in exceptional circumstances, not for a whole season.
pearl: Intranasal steroids work best when started a couple of weeks before the pollen season and used regularly rather than as needed.
thinking: Recurrent symptoms each summer ↓ Sneezing, rhinorrhoea, blockage and itchy watery eyes ↓ Atopic background with asthma ↓ Seasonal allergic rhinitis ↓ Allergen avoidance, intranasal steroid and/or antihistamine
exam_trap: D, a depot steroid injection — some patients request it as a one-off fix for the season. But it carries systemic steroid risks and is not recommended when topical treatment works.
takeaway: Hay fever: allergen avoidance, intranasal steroid and/or a non-sedating antihistamine.

stem: A 34-year-old woman telephones her GP surgery four days into a head cold. She now has a throbbing ache across her cheeks and above her eyes that worsens when she bends forward, with a blocked nose and thick discoloured nasal discharge. She feels tired but is eating and drinking, and has no swelling around her eyes, no change in her vision and no severe headache. What is the most appropriate management?

options.B: Self-care with analgesia and fluids, with no antibiotic

correct_answer: B. Self-care with analgesia and fluids, with no antibiotic
why_correct: Facial pain, nasal blockage and discoloured discharge a few days into a cold are typical of acute sinusitis, which is usually viral and self-limiting. With symptoms of only a few days and no red flags, she should be offered self-care such as paracetamol or ibuprofen and fluids, with no antibiotic, and advised to seek review if symptoms persist for more than about 10 days or worsen.
why_wrong: A. Discoloured discharge does not indicate bacterial infection, and antibiotics offer little benefit early on. C. Imaging is not needed for uncomplicated acute sinusitis. D. Oral steroids are not recommended for acute sinusitis. E. ENT referral is for red flags such as swelling around the eye, visual change or severe headache.
pearl: Periorbital swelling, double vision, reduced acuity, severe frontal headache or neurological signs in sinusitis need same-day hospital referral.
thinking: A few days into a viral cold ↓ Facial pain, blockage, discoloured discharge ↓ Systemically well, no red flags ↓ Early acute sinusitis, usually viral ↓ Self-care without antibiotics
exam_trap: A, amoxicillin — thick coloured discharge is often taken as a sign of bacterial infection. But colour does not distinguish bacterial from viral infection, and early sinusitis settles without antibiotics.
takeaway: Early acute sinusitis in a well patient: self-care, no antibiotic.

stem: A 50-year-old man with asthma that began in adulthood and flares when he takes ibuprofen sees his GP with a year of gradually worsening blockage of both nostrils, a constant watery nasal drip and loss of his sense of smell and taste. Anterior rhinoscopy shows smooth, glistening, greyish swellings in both nostrils that are not tender to touch. What is the most likely diagnosis, and which additional finding would be a red flag needing urgent referral?

options.A: Nasal polyps — a polyp confined to one side
options.B: Allergic rhinitis — sneezing on exposure to pollen
options.D: Inverted papilloma — swellings in both nostrils

correct_answer: A. Nasal polyps — a polyp confined to one side
why_correct: Gradual bilateral nasal obstruction, rhinorrhoea and loss of smell with pale, grey, insensate swellings, especially with asthma and aspirin or NSAID sensitivity, indicate nasal polyps, which are usually treated with intranasal corticosteroids. A unilateral polyp in an adult, or associated bleeding, crusting or facial pain or swelling, is a red flag for malignancy needing urgent ENT referral; any nasal polyp in a child should raise the possibility of cystic fibrosis.
why_wrong: B. Allergic rhinitis does not produce grey insensate swellings, and sneezing is not a red flag. C. Aspirin-sensitive asthma is a recognised benign association of polyps, not a sign of malignancy. D. Inverted papilloma is typically one-sided, and bilateral swellings are the expected benign pattern. E. Turbinates are pink and sensitive to touch, and snoring is not a red flag.
pearl: Asthma, nasal polyps and aspirin sensitivity form Samter's triad (aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease); advise these patients to avoid NSAIDs.
thinking: Bilateral blockage and loss of smell ↓ Pale grey insensate swellings ↓ Asthma with NSAID sensitivity ↓ Bilateral nasal polyps, usually benign ↓ A one-sided polyp would be the red flag
exam_trap: C, aspirin-sensitive asthma — it is a striking association and might seem sinister. But it is a recognised benign pattern; it is a one-sided polyp that raises concern about malignancy.
takeaway: Bilateral nasal polyps are usually benign; a one-sided polyp needs urgent ENT referral.

stem: A 26-year-old woman who swims several times a week sees the practice nurse with three days of right ear pain, itch and a scanty discharge. Pulling on the ear makes the pain worse. The ear canal is red, swollen and contains moist debris, and the eardrum is visible and intact. She is otherwise well, is not diabetic and has no spreading redness. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.B: Topical antibiotic–steroid ear drops, with cleaning of the canal if needed

correct_answer: B. Topical antibiotic–steroid ear drops, with cleaning of the canal if needed
why_correct: An itchy, painful, discharging ear with a red, swollen canal and pain on moving the pinna, in a swimmer with an intact drum, is acute otitis externa. Treatment is a topical antibiotic, usually combined with a steroid, plus removal of debris where possible and advice to keep the ear dry; oral antibiotics are kept for spreading infection or immunocompromised patients.
why_wrong: A. Amoxicillin treats middle-ear infection, and systemic treatment is not needed for localised canal infection. C. Oral flucloxacillin is only for infection spreading beyond the canal. D. Antifungal drops are for fungal otitis externa, not first-line treatment of acute bacterial infection. E. Olive oil softens wax but does not treat infection.
pearl: In a diabetic or immunocompromised patient with severe ear pain and granulation tissue in the canal, consider necrotising (malignant) otitis externa and refer urgently.
thinking: Swimmer with itch, pain and discharge ↓ Pain on moving the pinna ↓ Red swollen canal with debris, intact drum ↓ Acute otitis externa ↓ Topical antibiotic–steroid drops with canal cleaning
exam_trap: A, oral amoxicillin — earache with discharge suggests a standard ear infection. But the infection is in the canal, not the middle ear, so topical treatment is effective and appropriate.
takeaway: Otitis externa: topical antibiotic–steroid drops and canal cleaning; oral antibiotics rarely needed.

stem: A 66-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer is reviewed at home by the community palliative care nurse. His bone pain is controlled on modified-release oral morphine 45 mg twice daily, but he has occasional episodes of pain when he moves. He has no immediate-release morphine prescribed. What is the most appropriate as-required dose of immediate-release oral morphine?
why_correct: His regular dose totals 90 mg of oral morphine in 24 hours. The breakthrough dose of immediate-release oral morphine is usually one-tenth to one-sixth of the total daily dose, so 10–15 mg, rounded to a practical dose, is appropriate as required, with frequent use prompting review of the background dose.
why_wrong: A. 5 mg is below one-tenth of his daily dose and is unlikely to control breakthrough pain. B. 45 mg is a full twelve-hour dose and risks opioid toxicity. C. 30 mg is a third of the daily dose, well above the recommended range. E. 90 mg is his entire daily dose and would be dangerous as a single extra dose.
pearl: If more than two or three breakthrough doses are needed each day, review and increase the regular background opioid rather than relying on repeated rescue doses.
thinking: Modified-release morphine 45 mg twice daily ↓ Total daily dose 90 mg ↓ Breakthrough dose is one-tenth to one-sixth of the daily total ↓ Range roughly 9–15 mg ↓ 10–15 mg immediate-release morphine as required
exam_trap: B, 45 mg — it matches the dose on his prescription. But that is a twelve-hour dose; breakthrough doses are a fraction of the 24-hour total.
takeaway: Breakthrough opioid dose: one-tenth to one-sixth of the total 24-hour dose.

stem: A 72-year-old woman with advanced pancreatic cancer under the community palliative care team has worsening nausea. She feels full after a few mouthfuls, is bloated, and some time after meals vomits large volumes of undigested food, which briefly relieves the nausea. She is passing wind and opening her bowels, and has no colicky abdominal pain. Her calcium and renal function are normal. Which antiemetic is the most appropriate?
why_correct: Early satiety, bloating and large-volume vomiting that relieves nausea suggest gastric stasis (delayed gastric emptying), which is common with pancreatic cancer. Antiemetic choice in palliative care should match the likely mechanism, and a prokinetic such as metoclopramide is first-line for gastric stasis, provided there is no complete bowel obstruction or colic.
why_wrong: A. Cyclizine suits raised intracranial pressure, vestibular causes or bowel obstruction, and its anticholinergic effect can slow gastric emptying. B. Haloperidol is best for chemical or metabolic causes such as opioids, hypercalcaemia or renal failure. C. Ondansetron is mainly used for chemotherapy- or radiotherapy-related nausea and can slow gut transit. D. Lorazepam is for anticipatory or anxiety-related nausea, not gastric stasis.
pearl: Avoid giving metoclopramide and cyclizine together, as cyclizine's anticholinergic action opposes the prokinetic effect of metoclopramide.
thinking: Advanced pancreatic cancer ↓ Early satiety, bloating, large undigested vomits that relieve nausea ↓ Bowels working, no colic, normal biochemistry ↓ Gastric stasis ↓ Prokinetic: metoclopramide
exam_trap: A, cyclizine — it is a widely used first-choice antiemetic in palliative care. But its anticholinergic effect slows gastric emptying and worsens stasis; this cause calls for a prokinetic.
takeaway: Palliative nausea: match the antiemetic to the cause; gastric stasis needs metoclopramide.

stem: A 42-year-old woman attends the emergency department 10 days after a knee arthroscopy. Her right calf has become swollen and sore over 2 days. There is tenderness along the line of the deep veins and the right calf is noticeably larger in circumference than the left. There is no alternative explanation more likely than venous thrombosis. Her two-level Wells score is 3. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: D-dimer, arranging a leg ultrasound only if the result is raised
options.B: Proximal leg vein ultrasound, with interim anticoagulation if the scan is delayed
options.C: CT pulmonary angiogram to look for embolism
options.D: Start a direct oral anticoagulant for 3 months without imaging
options.E: Below-knee compression stockings and review in 1 week

correct_answer: B. Proximal leg vein ultrasound, with interim anticoagulation if the scan is delayed
why_correct: A Wells score of 2 or more makes DVT 'likely', and NICE advises a proximal leg vein ultrasound, ideally with the result available within 4 hours. If the scan cannot be done in time, take a D-dimer, start interim therapeutic anticoagulation and arrange the scan within 24 hours. A D-dimer-first approach is reserved for patients in whom DVT is 'unlikely'.
why_wrong: A. A negative D-dimer cannot safely exclude DVT when the pre-test probability is high. C. She has no chest symptoms; CTPA investigates pulmonary embolism, not a leg clot. D. Committing to months of anticoagulation without confirming the diagnosis exposes her to unnecessary bleeding risk. E. Stockings neither diagnose nor treat a suspected DVT and delay risks propagation.
pearl: Wells score sets the order of tests: in the 'likely' group image first, because a normal D-dimer cannot reassure when pre-test probability is high.
thinking: Recent surgery, calf swelling and deep vein tenderness ↓ Wells score of 3 places her in the 'DVT likely' group ↓ D-dimer is not reliable for exclusion at this probability ↓ Answer: proximal leg vein ultrasound, with interim anticoagulation if delayed
exam_trap: A, D-dimer first — it is the familiar opening test for suspected DVT, so it feels routine. But it is only used first when DVT is 'unlikely'; with a likely score, imaging comes first.
takeaway: DVT likely on Wells: ultrasound first, interim anticoagulation if the scan is delayed.

stem: A 52-year-old hairdresser sees her GP about bulging, twisted veins on both lower legs. By the end of each working day her legs feel heavy and itchy, and her ankles are slightly puffy. On examination there is no eczema, pigmentation, lipodermatosclerosis or ulceration, and she has never had bleeding from the veins. She would like help. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Reassure her that the veins are cosmetic and no treatment is available
options.B: Prescribe compression stockings as definitive treatment without referral
options.C: Refer her to a vascular service for assessment and treatment
options.D: Request a D-dimer to exclude deep vein thrombosis
options.E: Refer urgently for surgical stripping within 2 weeks

correct_answer: C. Refer her to a vascular service for assessment and treatment
why_correct: Her varicose veins are symptomatic (heaviness, itching, swelling), so NICE recommends referral to a vascular service. There, duplex ultrasound confirms reflux and endothermal ablation is usually offered first, followed by foam sclerotherapy and then surgery if unsuitable. Compression hosiery is only offered as treatment if interventional treatment is unsuitable.
why_wrong: A. Symptoms such as heaviness and itching make these veins more than cosmetic. B. Compression is not first-line treatment for symptomatic varicose veins when intervention is possible. D. Nothing suggests an acute DVT; the problem is chronic superficial venous disease. E. Uncomplicated varicose veins do not need urgent surgery, and stripping is no longer first-line.
pearl: Symptomatic varicose veins (aching, heaviness, itching, swelling) qualify for vascular referral even without skin changes; ablation, not stockings, is first-line treatment.
thinking: Bilateral tortuous superficial veins ↓ Troublesome symptoms: heaviness, itching, ankle swelling ↓ Symptomatic varicose veins meet the threshold for specialist assessment ↓ Answer: refer to a vascular service
exam_trap: B, compression stockings — they are cheap, safe and widely used, so they seem a sensible first step. But NICE does not offer compression as treatment unless interventional treatment is unsuitable.
takeaway: Symptomatic varicose veins: refer to vascular services; stockings only if intervention is unsuitable.

stem: A 63-year-old man asks his GP whether a new tablet is worth taking. In the trial he has read about, 8% of people on placebo had a stroke over 5 years, compared with 4% of those taking the tablet. How many people need to take the tablet for 5 years to prevent one stroke?
why_correct: The absolute risk reduction is the difference in event rates: 8% minus 4% = 4%, or 0.04. The number needed to treat is the reciprocal of the absolute risk reduction: 1 divided by 0.04 = 25. So 25 people must take the tablet for 5 years to prevent one stroke.
why_wrong: A. This is the absolute risk reduction as a percentage, not the NNT. B. This would follow from an absolute reduction of 2%. C. This comes from wrongly using the 50% relative risk reduction instead of the absolute reduction. E. This would follow from an absolute reduction of 1%.
pearl: NNT = 1 divided by the absolute risk reduction (as a decimal). Always state the time period, because NNT applies over the trial duration.
thinking: Control risk 8%, treated risk 4% ↓ Absolute risk reduction = 4% = 0.04 ↓ NNT = 1/0.04 ↓ Answer: 25
exam_trap: C, 2 — the risk halves, so dividing by the relative reduction is tempting. But NNT uses the absolute difference, not the relative one.
takeaway: NNT is the reciprocal of the absolute risk reduction, over a stated time period.

stem: Researchers compare mothers of babies born with congenital heart disease with mothers of healthy babies. All mothers complete the same structured questionnaire, given by interviewers who do not know which group each mother belongs to, about medicines taken in early pregnancy. Mothers of affected babies report over-the-counter medicine use much more often, partly because they have spent months searching for a reason. What type of error is most likely?
why_correct: Recall bias occurs when cases and controls remember or report past exposures differently. Mothers of affected babies have searched their memories more thoroughly, so they report exposures more completely than controls. This systematic error is a typical problem of retrospective case-control studies and can create a false association.
why_wrong: A. Confounding needs a third factor linked to both exposure and outcome, which is not described. B. The problem is in how exposure is reported, not how participants were chosen. C. Interviewers were unaware of group status and used a structured questionnaire. D. Lead-time bias relates to screening and apparent survival, not exposure recall.
pearl: Recall bias is a case-control hazard: people with a disease, or their parents, search their memory harder for possible causes than controls do.
thinking: Case-control design asking about past exposure ↓ Cases report exposure more thoroughly ↓ Difference arises from memory and motivation, not true exposure ↓ Answer: recall bias
exam_trap: C, interviewer bias — questionnaires given by interviewers make this tempting. But the interviewers were blinded and used a fixed script; the difference comes from the mothers' recall.
takeaway: Cases remembering exposures differently from controls is recall bias — a case-control weakness.

stem: A cross-sectional survey of adults attending a health check finds that people with grey hair have a much higher rate of previous myocardial infarction than people without grey hair. A local newspaper reports that grey hair may damage the heart. Which concept best explains this association?
why_correct: A confounder is associated with both the exposure and the outcome and is not on the causal pathway. Age is linked to grey hair and independently to myocardial infarction, producing a spurious association between the two. Confounding can be handled by design (randomisation, matching, restriction) or analysis (stratification, adjustment).
why_wrong: A. A heart attack does not cause grey hair, so reverse causation does not explain this. B. Hair colour is observed, not recalled, so recall bias is unlikely. D. Nothing suggests the sample was unrepresentative in a way that creates the link. E. Effect modification describes an effect that differs between subgroups, not a spurious association.
pearl: A confounder links to both exposure and outcome and is not on the causal pathway. Age, sex and smoking are the classic culprits.
thinking: Grey hair associated with heart attacks ↓ No biological reason for grey hair to cause MI ↓ Age is linked to both grey hair and MI ↓ Answer: confounding by age
exam_trap: A, reverse causation — when an association looks implausible, reversing the direction is a tempting explanation. But a heart attack does not cause grey hair; a third factor, age, drives both.
takeaway: A third factor linked to both exposure and outcome that distorts the association is a confounder.

stem: A GP practice with 10,000 registered patients reviews its records for the year 2025. The practice manager counts the number of patients who were given a first-ever diagnosis of type 2 diabetes during that year. Which measure is being calculated?
why_correct: Incidence is the number of new cases arising in a defined population over a specified time period. Counting first-ever diagnoses over 1 year among registered patients measures incidence. Prevalence, in contrast, counts all existing cases, old and new.
why_wrong: B. Point prevalence counts all existing cases at a single moment, not new ones over time. C. Period prevalence counts all cases present at any time in the period, including long-standing ones. D. Attributable risk compares risk between exposed and unexposed groups. E. The standardised mortality ratio compares observed with expected deaths.
pearl: Incidence counts new cases over a period; prevalence counts everyone who has the condition. Prevalence roughly equals incidence multiplied by duration.
thinking: Defined population: registered patients ↓ Only first-ever diagnoses counted ↓ Over a set period of 1 year ↓ Answer: incidence
exam_trap: C, period prevalence — the measure covers a year, so 'period' sounds right. But period prevalence includes existing cases; only new cases define incidence.
takeaway: New cases in a population over a set time is incidence; all existing cases is prevalence.

stem: A 68-year-old woman tells her GP she has read that a new tablet 'cuts the risk of hip fracture by a third'. In the trial, 3% of women on placebo and 2% of women on the tablet had a hip fracture over 3 years. Which explanation of the benefit is most useful for her?

options.A: One in three women who take the tablet will avoid a hip fracture
options.B: About 3 women need to take it for 3 years to prevent one fracture
options.C: Her risk of hip fracture falls by 33 percentage points
options.D: Her risk falls by about 1 percentage point, so about 100 women need treating for 3 years
options.E: The one-third relative reduction is the best guide to her personal benefit

correct_answer: D. Her risk falls by about 1 percentage point, so about 100 women need treating for 3 years
why_correct: The relative risk reduction is one-third, but the absolute risk reduction is only 3% minus 2% = 1%. The number needed to treat is 1 divided by 0.01 = 100 over 3 years. Absolute figures convey the real benefit for an individual and support shared decision-making.
why_wrong: A. This misreads a relative reduction as the proportion of women who benefit. B. This uses the relative reduction to calculate NNT, which is incorrect. C. The fall is 1 percentage point, not 33. E. Relative figures exaggerate benefit when the baseline risk is low.
pearl: Relative risk reductions sound impressive when baseline risk is low. Convert to absolute risk reduction and NNT before advising a patient.
thinking: Risk 3% falls to 2% ↓ Relative reduction one-third, absolute reduction 1% ↓ NNT = 1/0.01 = 100 over 3 years ↓ Answer: absolute fall of about 1 point, NNT about 100
exam_trap: E, the relative reduction — it is the headline figure and is technically correct. But it overstates individual benefit when the starting risk is small.
takeaway: Explain benefit to patients in absolute terms and NNT, not relative risk reduction.

stem: At a journal club, an FY2 doctor presents a trial of a new anticoagulant. For major bleeding, the hazard ratio compared with warfarin is 1.12, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.94 to 1.33. How should this result be interpreted?

options.A: There is significantly more bleeding, because the hazard ratio is above 1
options.B: The result is significant, because the interval does not include 0
options.C: There is significantly more bleeding, because most of the interval lies above 1
options.D: The trial proves the two drugs have identical bleeding risk
options.E: The result is not statistically significant, because the interval includes 1

correct_answer: E. The result is not statistically significant, because the interval includes 1
why_correct: For ratio measures such as hazard ratio, relative risk or odds ratio, the value of no effect is 1. A 95% confidence interval that includes 1 means the result is not statistically significant at the 5% level. The width of the interval reflects the precision of the estimate.
why_wrong: A. A point estimate above 1 is not significant if the interval crosses 1. B. Zero is the line of no effect for differences, not ratios. C. Where most of the interval lies does not make it significant. D. A non-significant result does not prove equivalence; the trial cannot exclude a real difference.
pearl: Line of no effect: 1 for ratios (RR, OR, HR), 0 for differences. An interval crossing that line means not significant at the chosen level.
thinking: Ratio measure: hazard ratio ↓ Value of no effect is 1 ↓ Interval 0.94 to 1.33 includes 1 ↓ Answer: not statistically significant
exam_trap: D, identical bleeding risk — a non-significant result tempts candidates to conclude no difference exists. But absence of evidence is not evidence of absence; the interval still allows a real increase.
takeaway: For ratio measures, a 95% CI including 1 means not significant — not proof of no effect.

stem: A hospital guideline group is deciding whether to recommend a new antiemetic for preventing post-operative nausea and vomiting. Several types of evidence are available. Which should carry the most weight in judging whether the drug works?

options.A: A single large, well-conducted randomised controlled trial
options.B: A systematic review and meta-analysis of high-quality randomised controlled trials
options.C: A large prospective cohort study from several hospitals
options.D: A consensus statement from senior consultant anaesthetists
options.E: A detailed case series from a specialist centre

correct_answer: B. A systematic review and meta-analysis of high-quality randomised controlled trials
why_correct: For questions about treatment effectiveness, a systematic review and meta-analysis of well-conducted randomised controlled trials is the highest level of evidence. It pools data from several trials, increasing precision and reducing the influence of any single study. Individual trials come next, followed by observational studies, case series and expert opinion.
why_wrong: A. A single RCT is strong but ranks below a systematic review of several good RCTs. C. Cohort studies are observational and prone to confounding. D. Expert opinion is the lowest level of evidence. E. Case series have no control group and cannot establish effectiveness.
pearl: For treatment questions: systematic review of RCTs, then RCT, then cohort, then case-control, then case series, then expert opinion.
thinking: Question about whether a treatment works ↓ Randomised evidence minimises confounding ↓ Pooling several good RCTs adds precision ↓ Answer: systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs
exam_trap: A, a single large RCT — the RCT is the gold-standard design, so it feels like the top answer. But a systematic review of several good RCTs sits above any single trial.
takeaway: Systematic reviews of good-quality RCTs give the strongest evidence of treatment effect.

stem: A randomised trial compares a structured physiotherapy programme with usual care for chronic low back pain. A fifth of the physiotherapy group attended no sessions, and several people in the usual-care group paid privately for similar physiotherapy. The investigators want an analysis that keeps the benefit of randomisation. Which approach should they use?

options.A: Analyse everyone in the group to which they were randomised
options.B: Analyse only those who completed their allocated treatment
options.C: Analyse participants by the treatment they actually received
options.D: Exclude participants who crossed over and analyse the rest
options.E: Analyse only participants with complete outcome data

correct_answer: A. Analyse everyone in the group to which they were randomised
why_correct: Intention-to-treat analysis keeps participants in their originally allocated groups regardless of adherence or crossover. This preserves the balance of known and unknown confounders achieved by randomisation. It gives a realistic, usually conservative estimate of effect in real-world use.
why_wrong: B. Per-protocol analysis loses the balance created by randomisation and can overestimate benefit. C. As-treated analysis reorganises groups by choice, reintroducing confounding. D. Excluding crossovers removes non-random subgroups and biases the result. E. Complete-case analysis can introduce attrition bias.
pearl: Intention-to-treat: once randomised, always analysed in that group. It protects randomisation and reflects real-world effectiveness.
thinking: RCT with non-adherence and crossover ↓ Reorganising groups breaks randomisation ↓ Keep everyone in their allocated group ↓ Answer: intention-to-treat analysis
exam_trap: B, per-protocol analysis — analysing those who actually had the treatment sounds like a purer test of the drug. But it undermines randomisation and tends to overstate benefit.
takeaway: Intention-to-treat analysis preserves randomisation by analysing people as allocated.

stem: A trial comparing two antihypertensive drugs reports that one lowers systolic blood pressure more than the other, with p = 0.03. A colleague asks what the p-value means. What is the correct interpretation?

options.A: There is a 97% probability that the first drug is truly better
options.B: If there were no true difference, a result at least this extreme would occur about 3% of the time
options.C: There is a 3% probability that the null hypothesis is true
options.D: The difference is large enough to be clinically important
options.E: There is a 3% chance that the trial results are wrong

correct_answer: B. If there were no true difference, a result at least this extreme would occur about 3% of the time
why_correct: A p-value is the probability of obtaining the observed result, or one more extreme, if the null hypothesis were true. A value below 0.05 is conventionally called statistically significant. It does not tell you the size or clinical importance of the effect, nor the probability that any hypothesis is true.
why_wrong: A. The p-value is not the probability that the alternative hypothesis is true. C. The p-value assumes the null is true; it cannot give the probability that it is true. D. Statistical significance says nothing about clinical importance. E. The p-value does not measure the chance that results are wrong overall.
pearl: The p-value assumes the null hypothesis is true and asks how surprising the data are. It does not measure effect size or clinical importance.
thinking: p = 0.03 ↓ Assume no true difference between drugs ↓ Probability of a result this extreme by chance alone is 3% ↓ Answer: chance of such a result if the null were true
exam_trap: C, 3% probability the null is true — this is the most common misreading of p-values. But the p-value is calculated assuming the null is true, so it cannot give that probability.
takeaway: p-value: chance of a result this extreme if the null were true — not effect size.

stem: To estimate how much alcohol adults in a town drink, a team surveys patients on the hospital's medical wards. The results suggest much higher alcohol intake than national figures. What is the main problem with this study?
why_correct: Selection bias is a systematic error arising from how participants are chosen, making the sample unrepresentative of the target population. Hospital inpatients are more likely to have alcohol-related illness than the general adult population. The results therefore cannot be generalised to the town.
why_wrong: A. Recall bias concerns inaccurate memory of exposures, not who is sampled. B. Confounding distorts an association between an exposure and an outcome; this is an estimate of frequency. C. Publication bias concerns which studies get published. E. Observer bias arises from how investigators measure or record outcomes.
pearl: Selection bias is about who gets into the study. Hospital samples over-represent illness and its causes, so they rarely reflect the general population.
thinking: Aim: estimate alcohol intake in a whole town ↓ Sample drawn only from hospital inpatients ↓ Inpatients differ systematically from the general population ↓ Answer: selection bias
exam_trap: A, recall bias — self-reported drinking is notoriously inaccurate, so recall seems likely. But that would usually underestimate intake; the main problem is that the sample is unrepresentative.
takeaway: An unrepresentative sample caused by how participants are chosen is selection bias.

stem: Researchers identify 200 people with a rare cancer of the bladder and 400 people without it, matched for age and sex, and ask about previous occupational exposure to industrial dyes. Which measure of association should be reported?

options.A: The relative risk, calculated directly from the exposure groups
options.B: The incidence of bladder cancer among exposed workers
options.C: The hazard ratio from time-to-event analysis
options.E: The odds ratio, which approximates relative risk because the cancer is rare

correct_answer: E. The odds ratio, which approximates relative risk because the cancer is rare
why_correct: In a case-control study participants are selected by outcome, so the true population at risk and incidence cannot be measured. The odds ratio of exposure is therefore reported. When the outcome is rare, the odds ratio is a good approximation of the relative risk; when it is common, the odds ratio overstates it.
why_wrong: A. Relative risk needs incidence in exposed and unexposed groups, which a case-control design cannot provide. B. Incidence cannot be calculated because the number of cases was fixed by the researchers. C. Hazard ratios come from cohort or trial data with follow-up over time. D. The number needed to harm requires absolute risks, which are not available.
pearl: Case-control studies give odds ratios, because the researcher chooses how many cases to include. With a rare outcome, the OR approximates the RR.
thinking: Participants chosen by disease status ↓ Design is case-control ↓ Incidence and RR cannot be measured ↓ Answer: odds ratio, approximating RR for a rare disease
exam_trap: A, relative risk — it is the most intuitive measure of association. But it needs incidence data that a case-control study cannot supply.
takeaway: Case-control studies report odds ratios; these approximate relative risk only for rare outcomes.

stem: A cross-sectional survey of 5,000 adults shows that people with depression are much more likely to be physically inactive. A health campaign claims that inactivity causes depression. Which is the most important consideration before accepting this claim?

options.A: Whether the p-value is below 0.05, which would confirm a causal link
options.B: Whether the association is strong, which would prove causation
options.C: Excluding chance, bias and confounding, and showing inactivity came before the depression
options.D: Whether the sample size is large enough to remove confounding
options.E: Whether a biological mechanism exists, which alone would establish cause

correct_answer: C. Excluding chance, bias and confounding, and showing inactivity came before the depression
why_correct: An association does not establish causation. Chance, bias and confounding must first be excluded, and criteria such as temporality, dose-response, consistency and plausibility considered (the Bradford Hill considerations). A cross-sectional design cannot show which came first, and depression could itself cause inactivity.
why_wrong: A. Statistical significance only addresses chance, not bias, confounding or direction. B. Strength supports causation but cannot prove it alone. D. Large samples reduce random error but do not remove confounding or bias. E. Plausibility is supportive but not sufficient on its own.
pearl: Temporality is the one essential Bradford Hill criterion: the cause must come before the effect. Cross-sectional data cannot show which came first.
thinking: Association found in a cross-sectional survey ↓ Exposure and outcome measured at the same time ↓ Reverse causation, bias and confounding all possible ↓ Answer: exclude chance, bias, confounding and establish temporality
exam_trap: B, a strong association — strength is a genuine Bradford Hill consideration, so it feels convincing. But a strong association can still be caused by confounding or reverse causation.
takeaway: Before inferring cause, exclude chance, bias and confounding and confirm the exposure came first.

stem: A team carries out a meta-analysis of a new antidepressant using published trials and finds a large benefit. A regulator later reveals several registered trials that were completed but never published; most showed no benefit. What is this problem, and how is it usually looked for in a meta-analysis?

options.A: Selection bias, looked for by comparing baseline characteristics
options.B: Confounding, looked for by stratified analysis
options.C: Recall bias, looked for using validated questionnaires
options.D: Publication bias, looked for using a funnel plot
options.E: Attrition bias, looked for by intention-to-treat analysis

correct_answer: D. Publication bias, looked for using a funnel plot
why_correct: Publication bias occurs when studies with positive or significant results are more likely to be published than those with negative results. Meta-analyses based only on published studies then overstate the effect. Asymmetry on a funnel plot suggests it, and trial registration helps prevent it.
why_wrong: A. Selection bias concerns how participants enter a study, not which studies are published. B. Confounding distorts an association within a study. C. Recall bias affects how participants remember exposures. E. Attrition bias arises from losses to follow-up within a trial.
pearl: Negative trials that stay unpublished make treatments look better than they are. Funnel plot asymmetry suggests the problem; trial registration helps prevent it.
thinking: Meta-analysis shows large benefit ↓ Unpublished trials were mostly negative ↓ Positive results were preferentially published ↓ Answer: publication bias, detected with a funnel plot
exam_trap: A, selection bias — the meta-analysis did 'select' only published trials, so the term seems to fit. But the specific term for preferential publication of positive studies is publication bias.
takeaway: Preferential publication of positive trials is publication bias; look for funnel plot asymmetry.

stem: In the emergency department, a 29-year-old woman with pleuritic chest pain is judged to have a low clinical probability of pulmonary embolism. A blood test known to have very high sensitivity but low specificity for venous thromboembolism comes back negative. Why is this result useful?

options.A: Most people without the disease test negative, so a positive result confirms it
options.B: A positive result would make the disease very likely
options.C: Most people with the disease test positive, so a negative result makes it unlikely
options.D: The test gives few false positives, so it is good for confirming disease
options.E: High sensitivity guarantees a high positive predictive value

correct_answer: C. Most people with the disease test positive, so a negative result makes it unlikely
why_correct: Sensitivity is the proportion of people with the disease who test positive. A highly sensitive test has few false negatives, so a negative result helps rule the disease out (SnNout), especially when pre-test probability is low. Specificity is the proportion without the disease who test negative; highly specific tests help rule disease in (SpPin).
why_wrong: A. This describes specificity, not sensitivity. B. With low specificity, a positive result is often a false positive. D. Few false positives describes high specificity. E. Positive predictive value depends on specificity and prevalence, not sensitivity alone.
pearl: SnNout: a highly Sensitive test, when Negative, rules disease out. SpPin: a highly Specific test, when Positive, rules disease in.
thinking: Low pre-test probability ↓ Highly sensitive test is negative ↓ Few false negatives mean disease is unlikely ↓ Answer: negative result helps rule it out
exam_trap: B, a positive result makes the disease very likely — a 'good' test seems to work both ways. But with low specificity, many positives are false, so a positive result rules nothing in.
takeaway: High sensitivity means few false negatives: a negative result helps rule disease out.

stem: A team designs a trial comparing a new analgesic with placebo after knee replacement. Participants are allocated by a computer-generated random sequence, and both tablets look identical so that patients, ward staff and the pain assessors do not know who received which. What are the main purposes of these two features?

options.A: Random allocation balances known and unknown confounders; blinding reduces bias in care and outcome assessment
options.B: Random allocation increases statistical power; blinding improves adherence
options.C: Random allocation ensures a representative sample; blinding removes confounding
options.D: Random allocation reduces losses to follow-up; blinding improves generalisability
options.E: Random allocation conceals the next assignment; blinding balances baseline characteristics

correct_answer: A. Random allocation balances known and unknown confounders; blinding reduces bias in care and outcome assessment
why_correct: Randomisation allocates participants by chance, so known and unknown confounders are distributed evenly between groups. Blinding of participants, clinicians and assessors reduces performance bias and detection bias. Allocation concealment is a separate safeguard that stops recruiters predicting the next allocation.
why_wrong: B. Power depends mainly on sample size and effect size, not randomisation. C. Representativeness depends on who is recruited, and confounding is addressed by randomisation, not blinding. D. Randomisation does not prevent drop-out and blinding does not improve generalisability. E. Concealment is a separate step, and baseline balance comes from randomisation, not blinding.
pearl: Randomisation tackles confounding, including factors nobody has measured. Blinding tackles bias in how people are treated and how outcomes are judged.
thinking: Random allocation by computer ↓ Balances confounders, known and unknown ↓ Identical tablets hide treatment from patients, staff and assessors ↓ Answer: randomisation balances confounders; blinding reduces performance and detection bias
exam_trap: C, representative sample — random selection and random allocation are easily confused. Representativeness depends on recruitment, whereas randomisation in a trial is about comparable groups.
takeaway: Randomisation balances confounders; blinding prevents bias in care and outcome assessment.

stem: A committee assessing a new cancer drug is told it extends survival but that patients spend much of the extra time with significant side effects. The committee's decision will be based on the cost per quality-adjusted life year (QALY) gained. What does a QALY represent?

options.A: The number of years of life gained, without adjustment for quality
options.B: A quality-of-life score, without reference to survival
options.C: The cost of the treatment for each hospital admission avoided
options.D: Years of healthy life lost to disease across the population
options.E: Length of life weighted by its quality, combined in a single measure

correct_answer: E. Length of life weighted by its quality, combined in a single measure
why_correct: A QALY combines quantity of life with quality of life, weighting each year by a utility value between 0 (death) and 1 (full health). One year in full health equals one QALY. Cost per QALY lets interventions be compared and funding decisions made against a willingness-to-pay threshold.
why_wrong: A. Life-years alone ignore quality, which a QALY adjusts for. B. Utility scores are one ingredient; a QALY also includes duration. C. This is a cost-consequence measure, not a QALY. D. This describes a disability-adjusted life year (DALY).
pearl: QALY = years of life multiplied by a quality weight (0 to 1). One year in perfect health equals one QALY; NICE uses cost per QALY to judge value.
thinking: Drug extends life but with reduced quality ↓ Need a measure that captures both ↓ Each year weighted by a utility from 0 to 1 ↓ Answer: length of life weighted by quality
exam_trap: D, healthy years lost — DALYs sound very similar. But DALYs measure disease burden lost, whereas QALYs measure health gained from an intervention.
takeaway: A QALY combines length and quality of life into one measure used for cost-effectiveness.

stem: A health board plans a two-stage programme for a cancer. Everyone invited will first have a simple blood test, and anyone with a positive result will then have a definitive biopsy. The planners are most worried about people with early cancer being falsely reassured by the first test. Which property is most important for the first-stage blood test?

options.D: Low prevalence of disease in the screened group

why_correct: A first-stage screening test should be highly sensitive so that few true cases are missed. The extra false positives are acceptable because a more specific confirmatory test, here a biopsy, follows. This balance avoids false reassurance in people who have the disease.
why_wrong: A. High specificity reduces false positives but is the priority of the confirmatory test. C. Positive predictive value depends on specificity and prevalence and does not stop cases being missed. D. Prevalence is a feature of the population, not of the test. E. Screening aims to detect early disease, not advanced disease.
pearl: Screening first, confirm second: a sensitive first test catches nearly all cases, and a specific second test sorts out the false positives.
thinking: Two-stage programme with biopsy to confirm ↓ Main concern is missing true cases ↓ Few false negatives needed ↓ Answer: high sensitivity
exam_trap: A, high specificity — avoiding unnecessary biopsies matters, so specificity seems important. But the planners' main concern is missed cases, which sensitivity addresses.
takeaway: First-line screening tests prioritise sensitivity; confirmatory tests provide specificity.

stem: An FY1 doctor and a ward pharmacist check whether patients admitted to their surgical ward have a venous thromboembolism risk assessment completed within the time set by the trust policy.
