Only 60% meet the standard. They add a prompt to the admission proforma and repeat the same check 3 months later. What best describes this project?
why_correct: Clinical audit measures current practice against an agreed standard, makes changes, and re-measures to see whether practice has improved, closing the loop. It is a quality-improvement process rather than research. Here a trust standard was used, a change was introduced and the same measurement repeated.
why_wrong: A. Research generates new knowledge, often testing a hypothesis, rather than checking practice against a standard. B. Service evaluation describes a service without comparing it to a set standard. C. A cohort study follows groups over time to study exposures and outcomes. E. Significant event analysis reviews a single incident in depth.
pearl: Audit asks 'are we doing what we should?' against a standard; research asks 'what should we be doing?'. Re-auditing closes the loop.
thinking: Practice measured against a trust standard ↓ Gap identified and change introduced ↓ Same measure repeated afterwards ↓ Answer: clinical audit
exam_trap: B, service evaluation — both look at current local practice, so they are easily confused. Audit is defined by comparison against an explicit standard, which is present here.
takeaway: Measuring practice against a standard, changing it and re-measuring is clinical audit.

stem: A GP sees a 6-year-old unvaccinated boy with 4 days of fever, cough, red eyes and a blotchy maculopapular rash that started behind his ears. Measles is suspected and an oral fluid sample is sent for testing. What should the GP do about notification?

options.A: Notify only once the laboratory confirms measles
options.B: Notify only after obtaining written consent from his parents
options.C: Leave notification to the laboratory that processes the sample
options.D: Notify only if he needs hospital admission
options.E: Notify the local health protection team now, on clinical suspicion

correct_answer: E. Notify the local health protection team now, on clinical suspicion
why_correct: Registered medical practitioners have a statutory duty to notify suspected cases of notifiable diseases, including measles, without waiting for laboratory confirmation. In England this is to the local UKHSA health protection team. Prompt notification allows contact tracing, protection of vulnerable contacts and outbreak control.
why_wrong: A. Waiting for results delays public health action against a highly infectious disease. B. Notification is a legal duty and does not require consent. C. Laboratories have their own duty, but this does not replace the clinician's duty. D. Notification depends on suspicion of the disease, not its severity.
pearl: Notify on suspicion, not confirmation. The clinician's duty is statutory and does not need consent; the laboratory has a separate duty.
thinking: Fever, coryza, conjunctivitis, rash in an unvaccinated child ↓ Clinical suspicion of measles, a notifiable disease ↓ Duty to notify arises on suspicion ↓ Answer: notify the health protection team now
exam_trap: A, waiting for confirmation — confirming the diagnosis before acting seems careful. But for notifiable diseases the duty is triggered by suspicion so that public health action is not delayed.
takeaway: Notifiable diseases are reported on clinical suspicion, without waiting for lab confirmation.

stem: A 45-year-old man is seen in the pre-operative assessment clinic before a hernia repair. He smokes 20 cigarettes a day and wants to stop. He tried once before using willpower alone and relapsed within a week. Which approach offers him the best chance of stopping?

options.A: Referral to a stop smoking service for behavioural support combined with stop-smoking medication
options.B: Brief advice and a leaflet, with no further follow-up
options.C: Gradually cutting down over a year without setting a quit date
options.D: A short course of a benzodiazepine to manage withdrawal anxiety
options.E: Stopping abruptly on the day of surgery without any support

correct_answer: A. Referral to a stop smoking service for behavioural support combined with stop-smoking medication
why_correct: NICE advises that the most effective way to stop smoking is behavioural support combined with medication. Options include nicotine replacement therapy (particularly combining long- and short-acting forms), varenicline or bupropion, and nicotine-containing e-cigarettes can also be discussed. Stop smoking services offer this combination and substantially improve quit rates compared with willpower alone.
why_wrong: B. Brief advice alone helps some people but is much less effective than structured support with medication. C. Cutting down without a quit date is less effective than a planned quit with support. D. Benzodiazepines are not a smoking cessation treatment. E. Unsupported abrupt quitting is the approach that has already failed for him.
pearl: Behavioural support plus medication beats willpower alone. Surgery is a 'teachable moment', and stopping smoking reduces wound and chest complications.
thinking: Motivated smoker, previous unsupported attempt failed ↓ Combined support and pharmacotherapy is most effective ↓ Stop smoking services provide both ↓ Answer: behavioural support plus medication
exam_trap: B, brief advice — very brief advice is recommended at every opportunity, so it sounds like the expected answer. But for a motivated smoker the most effective approach is referral for support with medication.
takeaway: Best quit rates come from behavioural support combined with stop-smoking medication.

stem: A public health registrar is classifying local health programmes. One of them invites men in their 65th year for a single abdominal ultrasound to detect aortic aneurysms before they cause symptoms. Which level of prevention does this programme represent?
why_correct: Screening is secondary prevention: it detects disease at an early, asymptomatic stage so that intervention can prevent complications. The aneurysm already exists; screening aims to find it before rupture. Primary prevention stops disease arising, and tertiary prevention limits the impact of established disease.
why_wrong: A. Primary prevention stops disease developing, such as smoking cessation or vaccination. B. Tertiary prevention reduces complications of established, symptomatic disease, such as rehabilitation. D. Primordial prevention tackles underlying social and environmental conditions that lead to risk factors. E. Quaternary prevention protects patients from overmedicalisation and unnecessary intervention.
pearl: Primary stops disease starting; secondary finds it early (screening); tertiary limits the damage of established disease.
thinking: Programme targets an asymptomatic population ↓ Aim is to detect existing disease early ↓ Early detection is screening ↓ Answer: secondary prevention
exam_trap: A, primary prevention — preventing rupture sounds like preventing disease. But the aneurysm is already present; finding it early is secondary prevention.
takeaway: Screening to detect existing disease before symptoms is secondary prevention.

stem: A 9-year-old boy is receiving chemotherapy for acute lymphoblastic leukaemia and cannot have live vaccines. His mother is reassured to learn that almost all the children in his class are fully immunised against measles. Which concept explains why this lowers his risk of catching measles?

options.C: Active immunity from his earlier vaccinations

why_correct: Herd immunity occurs when a high enough proportion of a population is immune that transmission is interrupted. This indirectly protects people who cannot be vaccinated or who respond poorly, such as immunosuppressed children. The proportion needed depends on how transmissible the infection is and is very high for measles.
why_wrong: A. Maternal antibodies wane in the first year of life and would not protect a 9-year-old. C. Chemotherapy can impair his own vaccine-induced immunity, and the question concerns protection from others' immunity. D. Antigenic shift describes major changes in influenza viruses. E. Other vaccines do not protect against measles.
pearl: Herd immunity protects those who cannot be vaccinated. Highly transmissible infections such as measles need very high uptake to maintain it.
thinking: Immunosuppressed child unable to have live vaccines ↓ Classmates are highly immunised ↓ Transmission around him is reduced ↓ Answer: herd immunity
exam_trap: C, his own active immunity — he may have had vaccines before his illness. But chemotherapy can impair that protection, and the scenario stresses his classmates' immunity.
takeaway: High vaccine uptake reduces transmission and indirectly protects the non-immune: herd immunity.

stem: A director of public health reports that life expectancy differs by several years between two neighbourhoods a short bus ride apart. The neighbourhood with lower life expectancy has higher unemployment, poorer housing and lower educational attainment. What does this difference best illustrate?

options.A: Random variation expected between small areas
options.B: Genetic differences between the two populations
options.C: Lead-time bias in how deaths are recorded
options.E: Health inequalities arising from the social determinants of health

correct_answer: E. Health inequalities arising from the social determinants of health
why_correct: Systematic, avoidable differences in health between groups linked to social and economic conditions are health inequalities. They arise from the social determinants of health, such as income, employment, housing, education and environment. They are tackled by upstream policy and proportionate universalism rather than by blaming individuals.
why_wrong: A. A consistent gap linked to deprivation is systematic, not random. B. Neighbouring populations rarely differ genetically enough to explain this. C. Lead-time bias concerns screening and apparent survival, not life expectancy. D. Behaviours are shaped by social conditions and do not fully explain the gradient.
pearl: Health follows a social gradient: the more deprived the area, the worse the outcomes. These differences are systematic and avoidable, which makes them inequalities.
thinking: Large gap in life expectancy between nearby areas ↓ Linked to unemployment, housing and education ↓ Systematic and avoidable differences driven by social conditions ↓ Answer: health inequalities from social determinants
exam_trap: D, lifestyle choices — smoking and diet do differ between areas. But these behaviours are themselves shaped by social circumstances and do not account for the whole gradient.
takeaway: Avoidable health gaps linked to social conditions are health inequalities from social determinants.

stem: A 56-year-old man is admitted with 2 days of constant right upper quadrant pain, fever and vomiting. He has marked tenderness under the right costal margin that stops him breathing in on palpation. His white cell count and CRP are raised, and liver function tests are normal. Ultrasound shows gallstones, a thick-walled gallbladder and a normal-calibre common bile duct. He is otherwise fit and well. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: IV antibiotics, then elective cholecystectomy in 2 to 3 months
options.D: IV antibiotics and laparoscopic cholecystectomy within 1 week of diagnosis
options.E: Oral antibiotics and discharge with an outpatient surgical appointment

correct_answer: D. IV antibiotics and laparoscopic cholecystectomy within 1 week of diagnosis
why_correct: NICE recommends laparoscopic cholecystectomy within 1 week of diagnosis for people with acute cholecystitis who are fit for surgery. Early surgery reduces recurrent attacks, complications such as empyema and perforation, and total hospital stay compared with delayed surgery. It has similar complication rates to interval surgery.
why_wrong: A. Delayed surgery risks recurrent attacks and complications while waiting. B. ERCP treats bile duct stones; his duct is normal and LFTs are normal. C. Cholecystostomy is for patients too unwell or frail for surgery. E. He is systemically unwell and needs admission, IV treatment and early surgery.
pearl: Fit patients with acute cholecystitis should have laparoscopic cholecystectomy in the same admission or within a week; drainage is for those unfit for surgery.
thinking: RUQ pain, fever, positive Murphy's sign ↓ Ultrasound: gallstones and thickened wall, normal duct ↓ Fit for surgery ↓ Answer: antibiotics and early laparoscopic cholecystectomy
exam_trap: A, interval cholecystectomy — 'cool it down then operate' was standard practice for years. Current NICE guidance favours early surgery within a week for fit patients.
takeaway: Acute cholecystitis in a fit patient: early laparoscopic cholecystectomy within a week.

stem: A 74-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department with a day of colicky abdominal pain, repeated vomiting and no flatus. There is a hard, very tender, irreducible lump in her right groin, below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, with red overlying skin. Her pulse is 112 beats per minute and temperature is 38.1°C. Her abdomen is distended. What is the most appropriate definitive management?

options.A: Attempt manual reduction after IV opioid analgesia
options.B: Nasogastric decompression and IV fluids, reviewing in 24 hours
options.C: Urgent outpatient referral to the surgical clinic
options.D: Plain abdominal X-ray to confirm obstruction before referral
options.E: Emergency surgery to explore and repair the hernia

correct_answer: E. Emergency surgery to explore and repair the hernia
why_correct: A tender, irreducible femoral hernia with overlying erythema, fever, tachycardia and bowel obstruction indicates strangulation. She needs resuscitation followed by emergency surgery to assess bowel viability, resect any dead bowel and repair the hernia. Femoral hernias have a high risk of strangulation because of their narrow neck.
why_wrong: A. Reducing a strangulated hernia can return dead bowel to the abdomen and cause peritonitis. B. Conservative management suits adhesional obstruction, not a strangulated hernia. C. Outpatient referral is far too slow for strangulation. D. Imaging should not delay surgery when the clinical diagnosis is clear.
pearl: Femoral hernias lie below and lateral to the pubic tubercle and often strangulate. Tender, red, irreducible lump with systemic upset means theatre, not reduction.
thinking: Irreducible groin lump below and lateral to the pubic tubercle: femoral hernia ↓ Tenderness, red skin, fever, tachycardia and obstruction ↓ Features of strangulation ↓ Answer: emergency surgery
exam_trap: A, manual reduction — reducing a hernia relieves obstruction and seems to buy time. But with strangulation it risks returning ischaemic bowel to the abdomen.
takeaway: Strangulated hernia: do not reduce; resuscitate and take to theatre urgently.

stem: A 76-year-old woman with advanced pulmonary fibrosis is brought to the emergency department with severe pneumonia. She is drowsy and hypoxic despite high-flow oxygen, and the intensive care team is considering intubation. She cannot take part in discussion. Her husband hands over a document she wrote a year ago after talking with her respiratory consultant. It refuses intubation and mechanical ventilation, states that this applies even if her life is at risk, and is signed by her and witnessed. He does not hold a lasting power of attorney. What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Intubate under the doctrine of necessity because this is an emergency
options.B: Intubate because she now lacks capacity to confirm her wishes
options.C: Intubate while an urgent Court of Protection ruling is sought
options.D: Ask her husband to decide whether she should be intubated
options.E: Respect the advance decision, do not intubate and continue other treatment and symptom control

correct_answer: E. Respect the advance decision, do not intubate and continue other treatment and symptom control
why_correct: A valid and applicable advance decision has the same force as a refusal made with capacity. For life-sustaining treatment it must be written, signed, witnessed and state that it applies even if life is at risk, which this does. Intubation must not be given, but treatments not refused, such as antibiotics, oxygen and symptom control, continue in her best interests.
why_wrong: A. The emergency exception does not apply to treatment validly refused in advance. B. Loss of capacity is exactly when an advance decision takes effect. C. Court involvement is for genuine doubt about validity, and treating meanwhile would override her refusal. D. Without a lasting power of attorney, her husband cannot make the decision for her.
pearl: Advance decisions are designed for when capacity is lost. A valid one refusing ventilation must be followed even in an emergency; other care continues.
thinking: Life-threatening illness, intubation considered ↓ Written, signed, witnessed refusal stating it applies even if life is at risk ↓ Valid and applicable now she lacks capacity ↓ Answer: respect it, withhold intubation, continue other care
exam_trap: A, doctrine of necessity — emergencies usually justify treatment without consent. But necessity cannot override a valid, applicable advance refusal of that specific treatment.
takeaway: A valid advance decision refusing ventilation binds clinicians, even in an emergency.

stem: A 27-year-old woman at 37 weeks in her first pregnancy, being monitored for pre-eclampsia, suddenly develops severe continuous abdominal pain on the antenatal ward. There is only a small amount of dark vaginal bleeding. She is pale and sweaty, with a pulse of 118 beats per minute and a blood pressure of 92/58 mmHg, much lower than her usual readings. Her uterus is rigid and very tender. The fetal heart rate is persistently around 80 beats per minute. Her cervix is closed. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Resuscitate and proceed to category 1 caesarean section
options.B: Give nifedipine to relax the uterus
options.C: Arrange an ultrasound to locate the placenta before deciding
options.D: Give corticosteroids and continue fetal monitoring

correct_answer: A. Resuscitate and proceed to category 1 caesarean section
why_correct: Sudden severe pain, a rigid tender uterus and shock out of proportion to visible bleeding indicate a concealed placental abruption. With maternal compromise and fetal bradycardia in a term pregnancy, the mother is resuscitated and the baby delivered immediately by category 1 caesarean section. Major haemorrhage protocols should be activated as abruption can cause coagulopathy.
why_wrong: B. Tocolysis is contraindicated in abruption with fetal compromise. C. Ultrasound is unreliable for abruption and delays delivery. D. Steroids are not indicated at term and monitoring wastes time with fetal bradycardia. E. Induction is far too slow with a closed cervix and an acutely compromised fetus.
pearl: Concealed abruption: maternal shock can exceed the visible blood loss. A woody uterus with fetal distress means resuscitate and deliver.
thinking: Pre-eclampsia, sudden constant pain, woody tender uterus ↓ Shock out of proportion to visible bleeding: concealed abruption ↓ Fetal bradycardia, term, closed cervix ↓ Answer: resuscitate and category 1 caesarean section
exam_trap: C, ultrasound first — imaging feels like a sensible confirmation step. But ultrasound often misses abruption and delaying delivery risks fetal death.
takeaway: Abruption with maternal shock and fetal distress: resuscitate and deliver by category 1 caesarean.

stem: A 33-year-old woman has a vaginal delivery of twins. She had an oxytocic drug at delivery and the placenta is complete. An hour later she has a sudden heavy loss of blood. Her uterus is soft and well above the umbilicus, and becomes firmer briefly with fundal massage before relaxing again. Her bladder has been emptied and there is no tear. Her pulse is 124 beats per minute and her blood pressure is 90/52 mmHg. Help has been called and resuscitation started. She does not have asthma or hypertension. Which treatment best addresses the cause of the bleeding at this stage?

options.D: A further uterotonic such as oxytocin, ergometrine or carboprost

correct_answer: D. A further uterotonic such as oxytocin, ergometrine or carboprost
why_correct: A soft, high uterus that relaxes after massage indicates uterine atony, the commonest cause of postpartum haemorrhage, and twin pregnancy is a risk factor. The cause is treated with further uterotonics: oxytocin, ergometrine (avoided in hypertension), carboprost (avoided in asthma) and misoprostol. Resuscitation and tranexamic acid continue alongside, and surgical measures follow if drugs fail.
why_wrong: A. Tranexamic acid reduces bleeding but does not make the atonic uterus contract. B. Fluids support circulation but do not treat the cause. C. Balloon tamponade is a mechanical step used if uterotonics fail. E. Vitamin K does not treat uterine atony.
pearl: Four Ts of PPH: tone, trauma, tissue, thrombin. Atony (tone) is the commonest; treat with massage and uterotonics while resuscitating.
thinking: Heavy bleeding after twin delivery ↓ Soft, high uterus that relaxes after massage, no tear, placenta complete ↓ Cause is uterine atony ↓ Answer: further uterotonic drug
exam_trap: A, tranexamic acid — it is part of PPH management and reduces bleeding. But it does not correct uterine atony, which is the cause here.
takeaway: PPH from atony: further uterotonics treat the cause, alongside resuscitation.

stem: A 30-year-old woman at 33 weeks' gestation is on the antenatal ward with severe pre-eclampsia. Her blood tests show haemolysis, markedly raised transaminases and a low platelet count. She suddenly complains of severe epigastric and right upper quadrant pain spreading to her right shoulder, then collapses. Her pulse is 136 beats per minute and her blood pressure 78/42 mmHg. Her abdomen is distending, but the uterus is soft and not tender. She has never had uterine surgery. What is the most likely diagnosis and the most appropriate management?

options.B: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy — supportive care and planned delivery
options.C: Rupture of a subcapsular liver haematoma — resuscitation, delivery and laparotomy

correct_answer: C. Rupture of a subcapsular liver haematoma — resuscitation, delivery and laparotomy
why_correct: Haemolysis, raised liver enzymes and low platelets in pre-eclampsia indicate HELLP syndrome. Sudden severe right upper quadrant pain radiating to the shoulder, collapse and abdominal distension suggest a ruptured subcapsular liver haematoma. Management is resuscitation with activation of the major haemorrhage protocol, urgent delivery and laparotomy with liver packing or embolisation, involving hepatobiliary surgeons.
why_wrong: A. A soft, non-tender uterus makes abruption unlikely. B. Acute fatty liver of pregnancy causes liver failure but not sudden collapse with haemoperitoneum. D. Pulmonary embolism does not cause right upper quadrant pain with abdominal distension in this setting. E. Uterine rupture is very unlikely in an unscarred uterus that is not in labour.
pearl: HELLP with sudden RUQ pain, shoulder-tip pain and shock: think ruptured liver haematoma, a catastrophic haemorrhage needing surgery.
thinking: Pre-eclampsia with haemolysis, raised liver enzymes, low platelets: HELLP ↓ Sudden RUQ and shoulder-tip pain with shock ↓ Soft uterus argues against abruption ↓ Answer: ruptured liver haematoma — resuscitate, deliver, laparotomy
exam_trap: A, placental abruption — it is the classic cause of pain and shock in pre-eclampsia. But the uterus is soft and non-tender, and the pain is in the liver area.
takeaway: HELLP plus sudden RUQ pain and shock: suspect liver capsule rupture; resuscitate, deliver, operate.

stem: A 34-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his flatmate, who found several empty blister packs in his room. He says that at about 10 pm last night he swallowed around forty 500 mg paracetamol tablets in one go and took nothing else. It is now 10 am. He feels a little queasy but otherwise says he is fine. His observations are normal and his abdomen is soft. Blood samples, including a paracetamol level and liver function tests, have just been sent to the laboratory. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Wait for the paracetamol level and plot it on the treatment graph before deciding on treatment
options.B: Give activated charcoal and repeat the paracetamol level in 4 hours
options.C: Discharge with community mental health follow-up, as he is clinically well
options.D: Start intravenous acetylcysteine now, before the blood results are available
options.E: Give oral methionine and repeat liver function tests the next morning

correct_answer: D. Start intravenous acetylcysteine now, before the blood results are available
why_correct: He has taken a large, potentially hepatotoxic single overdose and is presenting around 12 hours later. When a patient with a potentially toxic ingestion presents more than 8 hours after the overdose, intravenous acetylcysteine is started immediately rather than waiting for the paracetamol level, because its protective effect falls the longer treatment is delayed. The level, liver function, INR and renal function are still measured and used to decide whether treatment should continue. Feeling well does not exclude liver injury, which usually becomes apparent later.
why_wrong: A. Waiting for the level delays treatment in a late presentation after a potentially toxic dose. B. Activated charcoal is only useful within about an hour of ingestion and has no role 12 hours later. C. Medical fitness cannot be judged before toxicity is excluded, and early symptoms of hepatotoxicity are often mild. E. Methionine is not used in UK practice and delaying effective treatment risks liver failure.
pearl: In paracetamol overdose, time since ingestion drives the plan: beyond 8 hours after a potentially toxic dose, start acetylcysteine first and let the bloods decide whether to stop.
thinking: Large single paracetamol overdose ↓ Presenting about 12 hours after ingestion ↓ Acetylcysteine efficacy falls with delay beyond 8 hours ↓ Do not wait for the level in late presenters ↓ Start IV acetylcysteine now
exam_trap: A, Wait for the paracetamol level — the treatment graph is familiar and feels like the evidence-based step, but in a late presentation after a potentially toxic dose waiting for the result wastes protective time; the level is used to decide whether to continue, not whether to start.
takeaway: Late presentation after a potentially toxic paracetamol overdose: start IV acetylcysteine without waiting for bloods.

stem: A 27-year-old woman fell from a horse and sustained displaced fractures of the radius and ulna shafts. After closed reduction she was placed in an above-elbow plaster backslab secured with a crepe bandage and admitted to the orthopaedic ward. Four hours later the nurse asks you to see her because she is distressed with forearm pain that has not eased despite intravenous morphine. She describes tingling in her fingertips, and the pain becomes much worse when the nurse gently straightens her fingers. Her hand is warm and the radial pulse is palpable. What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.A: Release the bandage and split the backslab and padding down to skin
options.B: Elevate the arm high in a sling and review in one hour
options.C: Increase the morphine dose and reassess at the next observation round
options.D: Request an urgent arterial duplex scan of the arm
options.E: Reassure her, as a palpable radial pulse excludes compartment syndrome

correct_answer: A. Release the bandage and split the backslab and padding down to skin
why_correct: Escalating pain out of proportion to the injury, pain on passive stretch of the forearm flexors and paraesthesia point to acute compartment syndrome. The first action is to remove all circumferential constriction by releasing the bandage and splitting the cast and padding right down to skin, keeping the limb at heart level, and calling the senior orthopaedic surgeon urgently. If symptoms do not settle promptly she needs emergency fasciotomy.
why_wrong: B. Elevating the limb high lowers arterial inflow pressure and can worsen compartment ischaemia; keep it at heart level. C. Escalating analgesia masks the key symptom and delays decompression. D. This is not an arterial occlusion problem, and imaging delays treatment. E. Distal pulses are usually preserved in compartment syndrome until very late.
pearl: Compartment syndrome is a clinical diagnosis: pain out of proportion plus pain on passive stretch. Pulses and warmth are usually preserved until the limb is already lost.
thinking: Forearm fracture in a circumferential cast ↓ Pain unresponsive to opioids ↓ Pain on passive finger extension and paraesthesia ↓ Suspect compartment syndrome; remove constriction first ↓ Split bandage, cast and padding to skin
exam_trap: B, Elevate the arm high — swelling instinctively prompts elevation, but raising the limb above the heart reduces perfusion pressure into a tight compartment and worsens ischaemia.
takeaway: Suspected compartment syndrome: split everything to skin, limb at heart level, urgent orthopaedic review.

stem: A 13-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his father. He was woken at 5 am by severe pain in his left groin and lower abdomen and has vomited twice. Two hours later he is pale and lying still. The left side of his scrotum is exquisitely tender, the left testis sits higher than the right, and the cremasteric reflex cannot be elicited on the left. Urinalysis is normal. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Doppler ultrasound of the scrotum before contacting urology
options.B: Oral antibiotics for epididymo-orchitis and review in 48 hours
options.C: Analgesia and reassessment once the pain has settled
options.D: Send a first-void urine for chlamydia and gonorrhoea testing
options.E: Urgent surgical exploration of the scrotum in theatre

correct_answer: E. Urgent surgical exploration of the scrotum in theatre
why_correct: Sudden severe testicular pain waking an adolescent, vomiting, a high-riding testis and an absent cremasteric reflex make testicular torsion the working diagnosis. Testicular viability falls rapidly within hours, so when the clinical picture is convincing he should go straight to theatre for exploration, detorsion and fixation of both testes. Imaging must not delay surgery.
why_wrong: A. Doppler ultrasound can be falsely reassuring and costs time when the clinical diagnosis is clear. B. Epididymo-orchitis is usually gradual with urinary symptoms, and treating it here risks losing the testis. C. Waiting for pain to settle wastes the salvage window. D. STI testing is irrelevant to a surgical emergency in this presentation.
pearl: Torsion pain can be referred to the groin or lower abdomen, so always examine the scrotum of a boy with abdominal pain and vomiting.
thinking: Adolescent with sudden severe pain waking him ↓ Vomiting, high-riding tender testis ↓ Absent cremasteric reflex ↓ Clinical torsion; time-critical ↓ Urgent scrotal exploration
exam_trap: A, Doppler ultrasound first — it seems sensible to confirm the diagnosis, but in a clear clinical torsion it delays surgery and a normal scan does not exclude torsion.
takeaway: Clinically likely testicular torsion goes straight to theatre; do not wait for imaging.

stem: A 31-year-old woman is under general anaesthesia for an elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy, maintained with sevoflurane. Forty minutes into the operation the end-tidal carbon dioxide keeps climbing even though the anaesthetist has increased ventilation. Her heart rate rises to 135 beats per minute, her jaw and limbs become rigid, her temperature is rising and an arterial gas shows a mixed respiratory and metabolic acidosis. What is the most important specific treatment, alongside stopping the sevoflurane?

options.B: Intravenous atracurium to relax the muscles

why_correct: A rising end-tidal carbon dioxide despite increased ventilation, tachycardia, muscle rigidity, rising temperature and acidosis during a volatile anaesthetic is malignant hyperthermia. Triggering agents are stopped, the patient is hyperventilated with 100% oxygen and actively cooled, but the only specific treatment is intravenous dantrolene, which reduces calcium release from the muscle sarcoplasmic reticulum. Without it, rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalaemia and cardiac arrest can follow.
why_wrong: A. Cooling is supportive only and paracetamol does not treat this hypermetabolic muscle process. B. A non-depolarising relaxant does not act on the muscle cell defect driving the hypermetabolism. D. Bicarbonate may be used for severe acidosis but does not stop the underlying reaction. E. There is no rash, bronchospasm or hypotension pattern of anaphylaxis, and adrenaline would worsen the tachycardia.
pearl: An unexplained rise in end-tidal CO2 is often the earliest sign of malignant hyperthermia; volatile agents and suxamethonium are the triggers, and first-degree relatives need testing.
thinking: Volatile anaesthetic in progress ↓ Rising ETCO2 despite more ventilation ↓ Tachycardia, rigidity, rising temperature, acidosis ↓ Malignant hyperthermia ↓ Stop trigger and give IV dantrolene
exam_trap: B, Intravenous atracurium — rigidity tempts a muscle relaxant, but the defect lies within the muscle cell, not at the neuromuscular junction, so a non-depolarising blocker does not stop the hypermetabolism.
takeaway: Malignant hyperthermia: stop the trigger, cool, ventilate with oxygen, and give IV dantrolene.

stem: A 52-year-old man attends the emergency department with a sore throat that has become much worse over the course of the day. He cannot swallow his saliva and is spitting into a bowl. His voice is muffled and he is sitting forward with his hands on his knees. There is a soft inspiratory noise on breathing. His temperature is 38.8°C and his heart rate is 116 beats per minute. What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.A: Examine his throat with a tongue depressor to look for a quinsy
options.B: Call a senior anaesthetist and ENT surgeon urgently to secure the airway
options.C: Send him for a lateral soft-tissue neck X-ray
options.D: Lie him flat and give oxygen via a non-rebreathe mask
options.E: Start oral penicillin and arrange ENT clinic review tomorrow

correct_answer: B. Call a senior anaesthetist and ENT surgeon urgently to secure the airway
why_correct: Drooling, a muffled voice, tripod positioning and stridor with fever indicate acute epiglottitis with impending airway obstruction. The priority is immediate senior airway expertise, with the airway examined and secured in a controlled setting such as theatre with surgical airway equipment ready. He should be kept upright and calm; antibiotics and steroids follow once the airway plan is in place.
why_wrong: A. Instrumenting the throat can trigger laryngospasm and complete airway obstruction. C. Sending a patient with stridor away for an X-ray removes him from airway support and delays definitive care. D. Lying him flat can precipitate complete obstruction; let him adopt the position he finds easiest. E. This is an airway emergency, not an outpatient sore throat.
pearl: In suspected epiglottitis, do not instrument or examine the throat outside a controlled airway setting; keep the patient upright and call for help early.
thinking: Rapidly worsening sore throat ↓ Drooling, muffled voice, sitting forward ↓ Stridor with fever ↓ Epiglottitis threatening the airway ↓ Urgent senior anaesthetic and ENT airway management
exam_trap: A, Examine the throat with a tongue depressor — looking for a quinsy feels like routine sore-throat assessment, but instrumenting the oropharynx can trigger laryngospasm and complete obstruction.
takeaway: Drooling, muffled voice and stridor: leave the throat alone, keep upright, call senior airway help now.

stem: A 74-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation, who stopped her anticoagulant a month ago because of nosebleeds, presents with 3 hours of sudden severe pain in her right leg. Below the knee the leg is white and cold. There are no palpable pulses below the femoral and no Doppler signals in the foot. She cannot move her toes, her calf is tender to squeeze and she has reduced light-touch sensation over the foot. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Catheter-directed thrombolysis and reassessment the following day
options.B: Referral to the vascular outpatient clinic within two weeks
options.C: Aspirin and a high-intensity statin, with reassessment in 6 hours
options.D: Arterial duplex scan on the next routine vascular laboratory list
options.E: Immediate referral to the vascular surgeons for emergency revascularisation

correct_answer: E. Immediate referral to the vascular surgeons for emergency revascularisation
why_correct: Sudden onset in a patient with atrial fibrillation off anticoagulation suggests an embolus. Loss of motor function, sensory loss and calf tenderness mean the limb is immediately threatened and needs emergency revascularisation, usually embolectomy, within hours. Unfractionated heparin is started while the vascular team is mobilised, but it is an adjunct and must not delay referral.
why_wrong: A. Thrombolysis is too slow for a limb with motor and sensory loss. B. An outpatient referral would result in limb loss. C. Antiplatelets and statins do not restore flow in an acutely occluded artery. D. Routine imaging delays treatment of a limb with neurological deficit.
pearl: In acute limb ischaemia, sensory loss and paralysis mark a limb that is immediately threatened; this is a surgical emergency measured in hours.
thinking: Sudden painful, pale, pulseless leg ↓ AF off anticoagulation suggests embolus ↓ Motor and sensory loss with tender calf ↓ Immediately threatened limb ↓ Emergency vascular revascularisation
exam_trap: A, Catheter-directed thrombolysis — it is a recognised treatment for acute ischaemia, but it acts over hours and is not appropriate when motor and sensory deficits show the limb cannot wait.
takeaway: Pale, pulseless leg with paralysis or sensory loss needs emergency vascular surgery, with heparin as a bridge.

stem: A 61-year-old woman attends her GP surgery three weeks after she fractured her proximal humerus when she tripped on a kerb while walking. Her menopause was at 50 and she takes no regular medicines. She asks whether her bones should be checked. What is the most appropriate next step in assessing her?

options.A: Plain radiographs of the thoracic and lumbar spine
options.B: Calculate her FRAX score and arrange DXA only if she is at intermediate risk
options.C: Heel quantitative ultrasound in the surgery
options.D: Arrange a DXA scan of the hip and lumbar spine

correct_answer: D. Arrange a DXA scan of the hip and lumbar spine
why_correct: A fracture after a fall from standing height or less is a fragility fracture, and the proximal humerus is one of the major osteoporotic fracture sites. In a postmenopausal woman with a recent fragility fracture, UK guidance supports proceeding to a DXA scan of the hip and lumbar spine to measure bone mineral density; the result confirms osteoporosis, guides the choice of treatment and provides a baseline for monitoring.
why_wrong: A. Spinal films may show fractures but do not measure bone density. B. A risk tool is optional after a recent major fragility fracture and should not gate DXA. C. Heel ultrasound is not used for diagnosing osteoporosis or guiding treatment. E. Bone turnover markers do not diagnose osteoporosis or replace bone density measurement.
pearl: Hip, spine, wrist and humerus are the major osteoporotic fracture sites; a recent fragility fracture at any of them is a direct route to DXA.
thinking: Fall from standing height ↓ Proximal humerus fracture = major osteoporotic fragility fracture ↓ Postmenopausal woman, recent fracture ↓ Risk score should not gate assessment ↓ DXA scan
exam_trap: B, FRAX first and DXA only if intermediate risk — a risk calculator is useful for people without a fracture, but a recent fragility fracture already places her at raised risk, so a risk score should not act as a gateway to bone density measurement.
takeaway: Recent major osteoporotic fragility fracture: offer DXA directly; a risk score is optional.

stem: A 46-year-old woman attends her GP surgery for a contraceptive pill review. A friend has just had her first screening mammogram, and she asks when she will be invited for routine NHS breast screening and for how long it continues. She has no family history of breast or ovarian cancer and examination of her breasts is normal. Which statement best describes the routine programme in England?

options.A: Mammography every 3 years from age 50 up to her 71st birthday, after which she can self-refer
options.B: Annual mammography from age 40 to 50, then every 3 years until 70
options.C: Mammography every 2 years from age 45 to 70
options.D: Mammography every 3 years from age 50 to 74
options.E: Mammography every 3 years from age 47 to 65

correct_answer: A. Mammography every 3 years from age 50 up to her 71st birthday, after which she can self-refer
why_correct: The NHS Breast Screening Programme invites women for mammography every 3 years from age 50 up to their 71st birthday; the first invitation arrives some time after the 50th birthday. Women over this age are not routinely invited but can request screening every 3 years. Women at higher familial risk follow a separate surveillance pathway, which does not apply to her.
why_wrong: B. Annual screening in the 40s is for women at increased familial risk, not routine screening. C. The programme is three-yearly, not two-yearly. D. Screening to 74 describes bowel screening in England, not breast screening. E. Routine screening neither starts at 47 nor stops at 65.
pearl: UK screening ages are commonly tested together: cervical 25 to 64, breast 50 to 70, and bowel screening in England from 50 to 74.
thinking: Average-risk woman asking about breast screening ↓ No family history, so routine programme ↓ Starts at 50, three-yearly ↓ Invitations stop at the 71st birthday, then self-referral ↓ 50 to 70, every 3 years
exam_trap: D, Every 3 years from 50 to 74 — the upper age is borrowed from the bowel screening programme in England; routine breast screening invitations stop at the 71st birthday.
takeaway: NHS breast screening: three-yearly mammography from 50 to 70, with self-referral after that.

stem: A health visitor asks a GP to see a 5-week-old breastfed girl who is still jaundiced. Her mother says the stools have become pale and putty-coloured over the last two weeks and the urine is leaving yellow stains on the nappy. On examination she is alert, her liver edge is palpable 3 cm below the costal margin, and her weight has dropped from the 25th to the 9th centile. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Same-day referral to the paediatric team for assessment
options.B: Reassure that jaundice is common in breastfed babies and review in 2 weeks
options.C: Advise changing to formula feeds and recheck in a week
options.D: Arrange a split bilirubin through the practice and review the result
options.E: Advise exposing the baby to indirect sunlight at home

correct_answer: A. Same-day referral to the paediatric team for assessment
why_correct: Jaundice persisting beyond the first weeks of life with pale stools, dark urine and hepatomegaly suggests conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and possible biliary atresia. Outcomes depend on early surgery (the Kasai procedure), ideally in the first two months of life, so she needs same-day paediatric assessment for urgent bloods and imaging rather than investigation in primary care.
why_wrong: B. Breast milk jaundice does not cause pale stools or dark urine. C. Stopping breastfeeding is unnecessary and does not address possible obstruction. D. Testing in primary care delays the urgent hospital work-up that pale stools and dark urine demand. E. Sunlight is ineffective and unsafe, and conjugated jaundice does not respond to light treatment.
pearl: Pale stools and dark urine in a jaundiced baby mean conjugated jaundice until proven otherwise; ask about stool colour in every case of prolonged jaundice.
thinking: Jaundice persisting at 5 weeks ↓ Pale stools and dark urine ↓ Hepatomegaly and falling weight ↓ Possible biliary atresia, time-critical surgery ↓ Same-day paediatric referral
exam_trap: D, Split bilirubin through the practice — measuring conjugated bilirubin is the right test for prolonged jaundice, but with pale stools and dark urine waiting for a primary care result delays an urgent hospital work-up.
takeaway: Prolonged jaundice with pale stools and dark urine needs same-day paediatric assessment.

stem: A 79-year-old man with heart failure takes lisinopril and furosemide. He attended an out-of-hours walk-in centre with acute gout in his right big toe and was prescribed naproxen. Ten days later his routine blood tests show that his creatinine has doubled from baseline and his potassium is mildly raised. What is the most likely cause of this change?

options.B: Naproxen added to his ACE inhibitor and diuretic
options.D: Urate nephropathy from the gout flare

correct_answer: B. Naproxen added to his ACE inhibitor and diuretic
why_correct: The new event is the NSAID. An ACE inhibitor, a diuretic and an NSAID together form the triple whammy: the NSAID constricts the afferent arteriole by blocking prostaglandins, the ACE inhibitor removes efferent constriction, and the diuretic reduces circulating volume, so glomerular filtration falls. Naproxen should be stopped, the other drugs reviewed during the AKI, and an alternative gout treatment chosen.
why_wrong: A. Lisinopril is long-standing; the new NSAID completed the triple whammy. C. He has been on furosemide long term and the timing points to the new drug. D. A single gout flare does not cause acute urate nephropathy. E. Age-related decline is gradual and would not double creatinine in ten days.
pearl: Before prescribing an NSAID, check for an ACE inhibitor or ARB plus a diuretic; the combination is a common cause of community-acquired AKI in older people.
thinking: AKI 10 days after a new prescription ↓ Already on ACE inhibitor and loop diuretic ↓ NSAID added for gout ↓ Triple whammy reduces glomerular perfusion ↓ Naproxen with ACE inhibitor and diuretic
exam_trap: A, Lisinopril — ACE inhibitors are well known to raise creatinine, but he has taken it for a long time; the trigger is the newly added NSAID completing the triple whammy.
takeaway: ACE inhibitor plus diuretic plus NSAID is the triple whammy: a common, avoidable cause of AKI.

stem: A 22-year-old woman had an uncomplicated vaginal delivery of her first baby three days ago and is still on the postnatal ward. She complains of a pounding headache and flashing lights. Her blood pressure is 166/110 mmHg and urinalysis shows proteinuria. While being assessed she has a generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting about a minute. Her airway is maintained and she is given oxygen. What is the most appropriate drug treatment?
why_correct: A seizure with hypertension, headache, visual symptoms and proteinuria after delivery is eclampsia, which can occur postpartum. Intravenous magnesium sulfate is the treatment of choice to control and prevent further eclamptic seizures, with a loading dose followed by an infusion and monitoring of reflexes, respiratory rate and urine output. Severe hypertension is treated in parallel, and senior obstetric and anaesthetic help is called.
why_wrong: B. Benzodiazepines are less effective than magnesium sulfate for eclamptic seizures. C. Levetiracetam is an epilepsy treatment and is less effective than magnesium for eclampsia. D. Blood pressure control is essential but does not treat or prevent the seizures. E. Phenytoin is inferior to magnesium sulfate in eclampsia.
pearl: Eclampsia can occur in the days after delivery; new headache, visual disturbance and raised blood pressure postpartum need urgent review.
thinking: Recently delivered woman ↓ Severe hypertension, headache, visual symptoms, proteinuria ↓ Generalised seizure ↓ Postpartum eclampsia ↓ IV magnesium sulfate
exam_trap: B, Intravenous lorazepam — benzodiazepines are first-line for most seizures, but in eclampsia magnesium sulfate is the specific and more effective treatment.
takeaway: Eclampsia, before or after delivery, is treated with IV magnesium sulfate plus BP control.

stem: A 33-year-old woman attends the early pregnancy assessment unit with two days of brown vaginal spotting and cramping pain in her right lower abdomen. Her last period was 7 weeks ago and a home pregnancy test was positive. She was treated for chlamydia some years ago. Her pulse is 78 beats per minute and blood pressure 122/76 mmHg. There is mild tenderness in the right iliac fossa without guarding. What is the most appropriate initial investigation?

options.C: CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis

why_correct: In a haemodynamically stable woman with a positive pregnancy test and pain or bleeding, transvaginal ultrasound is the first-line investigation to locate the pregnancy and look for an adnexal mass or free fluid suggesting ectopic pregnancy. Serum hCG levels complement the scan, particularly when the pregnancy location is unknown.
why_wrong: A. Serial hCG supports the scan but does not replace it as the first-line test. B. A plain X-ray has no role in diagnosing ectopic pregnancy and involves radiation. C. CT exposes a possible pregnancy to radiation and is not the test of choice. E. Laparoscopy is for unstable patients or where the diagnosis remains uncertain after imaging.
pearl: Any woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain or bleeding needs a pregnancy test; if it is positive, consider ectopic pregnancy until the pregnancy is located.
thinking: Positive pregnancy test ↓ Lower abdominal pain and spotting ↓ Previous pelvic infection raises ectopic risk ↓ Haemodynamically stable ↓ Transvaginal ultrasound first
exam_trap: A, Serial serum hCG — hCG trends are useful, but only as an adjunct; the scan is the first-line test to locate the pregnancy.
takeaway: Stable woman with suspected ectopic: transvaginal ultrasound first, hCG as an adjunct.

presentation: Giant cell arteritis with visual symptoms
stem: A 77-year-old man is seen urgently at his GP surgery. For two weeks he has had a new headache over both temples, tenderness when combing his hair and aching in his jaw after chewing meat. This morning the vision in his left eye went dark for a few minutes and then recovered. His temporal arteries feel thickened and tender. What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.A: Refer to the rheumatology clinic within two weeks
options.B: Arrange a temporal artery biopsy and start treatment if it is positive
options.C: Prescribe aspirin and review in one week
options.D: Arrange an urgent MRI scan of the brain
options.E: Start high-dose glucocorticoid immediately and refer the same day for specialist assessment

correct_answer: E. Start high-dose glucocorticoid immediately and refer the same day for specialist assessment
why_correct: New temporal headache, scalp tenderness and jaw claudication in an older person strongly suggest giant cell arteritis, and transient visual loss shows that sight is under threat. High-dose glucocorticoids should be started immediately on clinical suspicion, with same-day assessment by ophthalmology or the specialist GCA service. Biopsy or ultrasound can still confirm the diagnosis after steroids have been started.
why_wrong: A. A two-week wait risks permanent blindness. B. Steroids must not wait for biopsy when sight is threatened. C. Aspirin does not prevent visual loss in GCA. D. Brain imaging is not the priority and delays treatment.
pearl: Transient visual loss in GCA is a warning sign of impending permanent blindness; treat the same day and involve ophthalmology.
thinking: Older patient with new temporal headache ↓ Scalp tenderness and jaw claudication ↓ Transient monocular visual loss ↓ GCA threatening sight ↓ High-dose steroids now, same-day specialist review
exam_trap: B, Biopsy first — confirming the diagnosis feels rigorous, but steroids should never wait for biopsy; diagnostic findings persist for some time after treatment starts.
takeaway: Suspected GCA with visual symptoms: high-dose steroids immediately and same-day specialist review.

stem: A 58-year-old man who is very short-sighted attends the emergency department. Two days ago he noticed a shower of black dots and flickering lights at the edge of the vision in his right eye. Today a dark shadow has started spreading down from the top of his vision in that eye. The eye is painless and not red. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Flashes and new floaters followed by a progressive shadow or curtain across the visual field in a painless, white eye are typical of rhegmatogenous retinal detachment, and high myopia is a risk factor. He needs same-day ophthalmology referral, particularly as the macula may still be attached and saving it preserves central vision.
why_wrong: A. Posterior vitreous detachment alone does not cause a spreading field shadow. C. Central retinal artery occlusion causes sudden, profound painless loss of vision, without preceding flashes and floaters. D. Migraine aura is usually bilateral visual disturbance that resolves within an hour. E. Acute angle-closure glaucoma causes a painful red eye with haloes.
pearl: Flashes and floaters with any field loss, reduced acuity or a shadow need same-day ophthalmology review to exclude retinal detachment.
thinking: Painless, white eye ↓ Flashes and new floaters ↓ Progressive shadow across the field ↓ High myopia as risk factor ↓ Retinal detachment
exam_trap: A, Posterior vitreous detachment alone — it causes flashes and floaters, but it does not cause a spreading shadow; field loss means the retina has detached.
takeaway: Flashes and floaters followed by a spreading shadow: retinal detachment until proven otherwise.

presentation: Anal mass on straining: rectal prolapse
stem: A 69-year-old woman who has had four children and lifelong constipation attends the colorectal clinic. She says something comes out of her back passage after she opens her bowels, which she has to push back, and her underwear is often soiled with mucus. When she is asked to strain while squatting, a 5 cm reddish mass extrudes from the anus, with mucosa arranged in circumferential rings. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A large protrusion on straining with concentric, circumferential mucosal rings is full-thickness rectal prolapse. It is commonest in older women, particularly with multiparity, chronic straining and pelvic floor weakness, and causes mucus discharge, soiling and sometimes bleeding.
why_wrong: A. Haemorrhoids show radial folds in separate cushions, not concentric rings. B. A perianal haematoma is a small, painful, bluish lump at the anal margin. D. A polyp is a discrete mass on a stalk, not a circumferential protrusion. E. Anal carcinoma is usually a fixed, ulcerated or indurated lesion rather than a reducible protrusion.
pearl: Concentric folds mean full-thickness rectal prolapse; radial folds separated by grooves mean prolapsing haemorrhoids or mucosal prolapse.
thinking: Older multiparous woman with chronic straining ↓ Protrusion after defecation needing manual reduction ↓ Mucus soiling ↓ Concentric circumferential mucosal rings ↓ Full-thickness rectal prolapse
exam_trap: A, Prolapsed internal haemorrhoids — they also prolapse and cause mucus and bleeding, but they show radial folds in separate cushions, not concentric rings.
takeaway: Anal protrusion with concentric mucosal rings is full-thickness rectal prolapse.

stem: A 58-year-old woman, who is fit and active, has a confirmed full-thickness rectal prolapse that now comes down when she walks and causes mucus leakage and soiling. Fibre supplements, stool softeners and pelvic floor physiotherapy have not helped. She is keen for a long-term solution. What is the most appropriate definitive treatment?
why_correct: Full-thickness rectal prolapse that persists despite conservative measures needs surgical repair. In a fit patient an abdominal rectopexy, often performed laparoscopically, is usually preferred because recurrence is lower. Perineal procedures are generally reserved for frailer patients who are less able to tolerate abdominal surgery.
why_wrong: B. Banding treats haemorrhoids, not full-thickness prolapse. C. Sphincterotomy treats anal fissure and would worsen continence. D. Topical GTN treats anal fissure, not prolapse. E. Laxatives reduce straining but cannot correct a full-thickness prolapse.
pearl: Fitness for surgery guides the operation for rectal prolapse: abdominal rectopexy for fit patients, a perineal approach for frail patients.
thinking: Full-thickness rectal prolapse ↓ Symptomatic despite conservative measures ↓ Definitive treatment is surgical ↓ Fit patient tolerates abdominal surgery ↓ Abdominal rectopexy
exam_trap: B, Rubber band ligation — it is a familiar outpatient anal procedure, but it treats haemorrhoids and cannot fix a full-thickness prolapse.
takeaway: Symptomatic full-thickness rectal prolapse in a fit patient: surgical repair, usually abdominal rectopexy.

stem: An 18-month-old boy, who moved to the UK from abroad with his family at the age of one, is brought to the GP surgery. Twice this month his parents have seen a red, tube-like swelling come out of his bottom after a bowel motion; each time it went back by itself. He passes large, oily, foul-smelling stools that are hard to flush, and he has dropped across weight centiles despite eating hungrily. Which underlying condition is most important to exclude?
why_correct: Rectal prolapse in a young child with steatorrhoea and faltering growth despite a large appetite strongly suggests pancreatic insufficiency from cystic fibrosis. As he was born outside the UK he may not have had newborn screening, so he needs referral for a sweat test. Bulky stools and malnutrition weaken the supporting tissues, predisposing to prolapse.
why_wrong: A. Hirschsprung's disease causes constipation, not oily stools. C. Coeliac disease causes malabsorption but is not the classic association of childhood rectal prolapse. D. Intussusception is an acute illness with colicky pain, vomiting and redcurrant stool, and only rarely prolapses through the anus. E. Children with toddler's diarrhoea grow normally and their stools are not fatty.
pearl: Rectal prolapse in a young child should prompt a sweat test, especially if there is steatorrhoea, faltering growth or chest symptoms, or no record of newborn screening.
thinking: Young child with recurrent rectal prolapse ↓ Oily, offensive, hard-to-flush stools ↓ Faltering growth despite good appetite ↓ Pancreatic insufficiency; may not have had newborn screening ↓ Exclude cystic fibrosis
exam_trap: C, Coeliac disease — it also causes malabsorption and faltering growth, but children with coeliac disease are often irritable with poor appetite, and rectal prolapse is classically linked to cystic fibrosis.
takeaway: Rectal prolapse with steatorrhoea and faltering growth in a child: exclude cystic fibrosis.

stem: A 69-year-old man who smokes collapsed at home with sudden severe pain in his left flank radiating to the groin. The paramedics suspected renal colic. In the emergency department he is grey and sweaty, with a heart rate of 124 beats per minute and blood pressure of 82/48 mmHg. There is a tender, expansile mass above the umbilicus. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Immediate referral to the on-call vascular team for emergency repair
options.B: CT of the kidneys, ureters and bladder to look for a stone
options.C: CT angiogram to confirm the diagnosis before contacting the vascular team
options.D: Rapid IV fluids until his blood pressure is normal

correct_answer: A. Immediate referral to the on-call vascular team for emergency repair
why_correct: Sudden flank or back pain, collapse, shock and an expansile abdominal mass in an older male smoker indicate a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm. This is a time-critical surgical emergency: the vascular team must be contacted immediately and the patient taken for repair, with imaging only if the vascular team judges him stable enough. Blood is cross-matched and massive transfusion support prepared meanwhile.
why_wrong: B. Renal colic is a common misdiagnosis of AAA rupture, and a stone does not explain shock with a pulsatile mass. C. CT delays surgery in a shocked patient with a clinical diagnosis of rupture. D. Restoring a normal blood pressure can worsen bleeding; permissive hypotension is used until the bleeding is controlled. E. Urology is the wrong team and delay is fatal.
pearl: In an older patient with presumed first presentation of renal colic, always examine for an AAA; rupture can mimic a stone.
thinking: Older male smoker with sudden flank pain ↓ Collapse and shock ↓ Expansile abdominal mass ↓ Ruptured AAA, unstable ↓ Immediate vascular referral for repair
exam_trap: C, CT angiogram first — imaging is useful in stable patients, but in a shocked patient with a clinical diagnosis of rupture it delays surgery and risks death in the scanner.
takeaway: Shock with an expansile abdominal mass: call vascular surgery immediately; do not delay for CT.

stem: A 31-year-old man with asthma is brought to the emergency department by ambulance. The paramedics gave one salbutamol nebuliser with little effect. He is speaking in single words, his respiratory rate is 28 per minute and his pulse is 118 beats per minute. He is alert, his chest is wheezy throughout with good air entry, and oxygen saturation is 94% on air. His peak flow is about 45% of his best. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Repeated oxygen-driven salbutamol nebulisers with ipratropium, and oral prednisolone
options.B: IV aminophylline loading dose and infusion
options.C: Discharge with a 5-day course of prednisolone and GP review
options.D: Immediate rapid sequence induction and ventilation
options.E: IV magnesium sulfate as the next treatment instead of steroids

correct_answer: A. Repeated oxygen-driven salbutamol nebulisers with ipratropium, and oral prednisolone
why_correct: Inability to complete sentences, tachycardia, tachypnoea and a markedly reduced peak flow indicate acute severe asthma without life-threatening features. UK guidance is to give oxygen-driven high-dose salbutamol nebulisers, repeated or back-to-back if response is poor, add nebulised ipratropium, and give systemic steroids promptly, usually oral prednisolone.
why_wrong: B. IV aminophylline is a later, senior-led option after first-line treatment has failed. C. Discharge is unsafe while he still has features of acute severe asthma. D. Intubation is for life-threatening or near-fatal asthma, such as exhaustion, confusion or a rising carbon dioxide. E. Magnesium may be added if response is poor, but it does not replace steroids and repeated bronchodilators.
pearl: Steroids are given in every acute asthma attack needing hospital assessment. Oral prednisolone works as well as IV hydrocortisone when the patient can swallow.
thinking: Single words, tachycardia, low peak flow ↓ Acute severe asthma ↓ No silent chest, confusion or exhaustion ↓ Not yet life-threatening ↓ Repeated nebulisers, ipratropium and prednisolone
exam_trap: E, IV magnesium sulfate — it is a real treatment for poor response, so it tempts, but it is an add-on after steroids and bronchodilators, never a replacement for them.
takeaway: Acute severe asthma: oxygen-driven salbutamol, ipratropium and prompt steroids, then escalate if no response.

stem: A 74-year-old woman with long-standing COPD is reviewed on the respiratory ward because she has become more drowsy since admission with an infective exacerbation. An arterial blood gas on room air shows: pH 7.30, PaO2 7.2 kPa, PaCO2 8.6 kPa, bicarbonate 31 mmol/L. How should this result be interpreted?

options.B: Chronic type 2 respiratory failure with full compensation
options.C: Primary metabolic alkalosis with respiratory compensation
options.E: Acute type 2 respiratory failure with no chronic component

why_correct: She is hypoxaemic with a raised PaCO2, which is type 2 respiratory failure. The raised bicarbonate shows longstanding renal compensation for chronic carbon dioxide retention, but the pH is still low, so there has been an acute rise in carbon dioxide on top of chronic retention. This pattern is typical of an exacerbation in COPD and is a common indication to consider non-invasive ventilation.
why_wrong: A. Type 1 failure has a normal or low PaCO2. B. Full compensation would bring the pH back into the normal range. C. In a primary metabolic alkalosis the pH would be high, not low. E. A purely acute rise in carbon dioxide would not yet have produced a raised bicarbonate.
pearl: Read the gas in order: pH, then PaCO2, then bicarbonate. Low pH plus high PaCO2 plus high bicarbonate means chronic retention with a fresh acute rise.
thinking: Low PaO2 and high PaCO2 ↓ Type 2 respiratory failure ↓ Raised bicarbonate means chronic retention ↓ pH still acidaemic ↓ Acute-on-chronic type 2 failure
exam_trap: B, chronic compensated type 2 failure — the raised bicarbonate draws you to chronicity, but compensation is only complete when the pH is normal; this pH is still acidaemic.
takeaway: High CO2, high bicarbonate and low pH means acute-on-chronic type 2 respiratory failure.

stem: A 21-year-old man presents to the emergency department with sharp left-sided chest pain that started suddenly while he was sitting at his desk this morning. He becomes slightly breathless only on climbing stairs. He has no previous lung disease. Pulse is 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 124/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute and oxygen saturation 98% on air. Chest X-ray shows a left pneumothorax with a visible rim of about 2.5 cm at the level of the hilum. He would prefer to go home. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Needle aspiration in the emergency department
options.B: Insertion of a small-bore chest drain and admission
options.C: Admission for high-flow oxygen and repeat chest X-ray
options.D: Conservative management with safety-net advice and outpatient review
options.E: Referral for surgical pleurodesis during this admission

correct_answer: D. Conservative management with safety-net advice and outpatient review
why_correct: This is a primary spontaneous pneumothorax in a young man who is stable and has minimal symptoms. Current British Thoracic Society guidance bases management on symptoms, high-risk features and patient preference rather than size alone, so conservative management with clear return advice and planned follow-up is appropriate. He should avoid flying until resolution is confirmed and should be advised never to scuba dive unless he has had definitive surgery.
why_wrong: A. Aspiration is for patients who are significantly breathless, have high-risk features or choose intervention. B. A chest drain is not needed in a stable patient with minimal symptoms. C. Admission for oxygen is unnecessary when he is suitable for ambulatory management. E. Surgery is reserved for recurrence, persistent air leak or failure of other measures.
pearl: In a stable primary spontaneous pneumothorax, ask how the patient is rather than how big the rim is. Breathlessness, instability and high-risk features drive intervention.
thinking: Young, no lung disease ↓ Primary spontaneous pneumothorax ↓ Stable, minimal breathlessness, no high-risk features ↓ Symptoms guide treatment, not size ↓ Conservative with follow-up
exam_trap: A, needle aspiration — older algorithms tied a rim of 2 cm or more to aspiration, but current guidance lets a stable, minimally breathless patient be managed conservatively.
takeaway: Stable, minimally symptomatic primary pneumothorax can be managed conservatively whatever the rim size.

stem: A 55-year-old man develops pleuritic right-sided chest pain and breathlessness 10 days after an open inguinal hernia repair. Pulse is 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 132/80 mmHg and oxygen saturation 94% on air. CT pulmonary angiography shows segmental pulmonary emboli in the right lower lobe. Renal and liver function are normal and he has no history of cancer or bleeding. What is the most appropriate treatment?
why_correct: He has a confirmed pulmonary embolism with stable blood pressure. NICE recommends a direct oral anticoagulant, apixaban or rivaroxaban, as first-line treatment, and these can be started without initial parenteral anticoagulation. As the clot was provoked by surgery, around 3 months of treatment is usually enough.
why_wrong: A. Thrombolysis is for pulmonary embolism with haemodynamic instability. B. Unfractionated heparin is reserved for situations such as instability, possible thrombolysis or severe renal impairment. C. Aspirin is not adequate treatment for venous thromboembolism. D. Warfarin needs parenteral anticoagulant cover until the INR is in range and is no longer first-line.
pearl: Apixaban and rivaroxaban need no heparin lead-in; dabigatran and edoxaban do need at least 5 days of parenteral anticoagulation first.
thinking: Post-operative pleuritic pain and breathlessness ↓ CTPA confirms PE ↓ Blood pressure stable ↓ No renal or cancer issues ↓ DOAC such as apixaban
exam_trap: B, unfractionated heparin — tachycardia and hypoxia make him seem sick, but he is normotensive, so the DOAC pathway applies and heparin infusion adds nothing.
takeaway: Stable pulmonary embolism: start a DOAC such as apixaban; save thrombolysis for instability.

stem: A 71-year-old woman who smoked for 40 years is seen in the respiratory clinic. She has had a cough for 2 months, has lost 6 kg and has new finger clubbing. Her GP arranged a chest X-ray, which shows a left hilar mass with widening of the mediastinum. What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.C: Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest including the liver and adrenal glands
options.E: A course of antibiotics and repeat chest X-ray in 6 weeks

correct_answer: C. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest including the liver and adrenal glands
why_correct: NICE advises a contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, extending to include the liver and adrenal glands, for people whose chest X-ray suggests lung cancer. This both stages the disease and shows the safest and most informative site for tissue sampling, so it comes before bronchoscopy or PET-CT.
why_wrong: A. PET-CT is used after CT to stage patients who may be suitable for curative treatment. B. Bronchoscopy follows CT, which guides the choice of biopsy route. D. Sputum cytology is insensitive and gives no staging information. E. Waiting and repeating the film delays diagnosis in a high-risk woman with a suspicious mass.
pearl: In suspected lung cancer the order is chest X-ray, contrast CT chest and upper abdomen, then the biopsy that gives both diagnosis and the highest stage.
thinking: Heavy smoker with weight loss and clubbing ↓ Chest X-ray shows hilar mass ↓ Suspected lung cancer ↓ Stage first to plan biopsy ↓ Contrast CT chest with liver and adrenals
exam_trap: B, bronchoscopy with biopsy — getting tissue feels like the priority, but CT first shows whether a lymph node or metastasis gives a better, single diagnostic and staging biopsy.
takeaway: Chest X-ray suggesting lung cancer: next is contrast CT of chest including liver and adrenals.

presentation: Pleural fluid analysis using Light's criteria
stem: A 63-year-old woman is seen on the medical ward with a moderate left pleural effusion. A diagnostic tap produces straw-coloured fluid. Results: pleural fluid protein 28 g/L, serum protein 50 g/L, pleural fluid LDH 260 U/L, serum LDH 300 U/L. How should this fluid be classified?
why_correct: When pleural protein is borderline, Light's criteria are applied. The fluid is an exudate if the pleural to serum protein ratio is above 0.5, the pleural to serum LDH ratio is above 0.6, or pleural LDH is more than two-thirds of the upper limit of normal for serum. Here the protein ratio is 0.56 and the LDH ratio is 0.87, so this is an exudate despite the low absolute protein.
why_wrong: A. The protein looks low, but both ratios meet Light's criteria for an exudate. C. Empyema is frankly purulent or turbid fluid, often with a low pH. D. Chylothorax is milky fluid with high triglycerides. E. Haemothorax is blood-stained fluid with a high haematocrit.
pearl: An absolute protein under 30 g/L does not guarantee a transudate. If protein is borderline, calculate Light's ratios; meeting any one criterion means exudate.
thinking: Borderline pleural protein ↓ Apply Light's criteria ↓ Protein ratio 0.56, LDH ratio 0.87 ↓ At least one criterion met ↓ Exudate
exam_trap: A, transudate — a protein below 30 g/L looks transudative at first glance, but the ratios to serum values decide and both point to an exudate.
takeaway: Light's criteria: meeting any one ratio criterion makes the fluid an exudate.

stem: A 34-year-old man presents to his GP with a 10-day history of fever, painful swollen ankles and tender red lumps on both shins. A chest X-ray shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with clear lung fields. He has no cough, eye symptoms or weight loss. Serum calcium, renal function and liver tests are normal, and respiratory review finds normal lung function. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Oral prednisolone with a slow taper
options.B: NSAIDs for symptoms and clinical review; spontaneous resolution is expected
options.C: Endobronchial ultrasound-guided biopsy of a hilar lymph node
options.D: Start methotrexate as a steroid-sparing agent

correct_answer: B. NSAIDs for symptoms and clinical review; spontaneous resolution is expected
why_correct: Fever, ankle periarthritis, erythema nodosum and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy form Löfgren syndrome, an acute form of sarcoidosis. It has an excellent prognosis and usually resolves without specific treatment, so management is symptom relief with NSAIDs and monitoring. The classic combination is specific enough that tissue diagnosis is not usually required.
why_wrong: A. Steroids are kept for significant organ involvement such as hypercalcaemia or impaired lung function. C. A biopsy is unnecessary in the typical Löfgren picture. D. Methotrexate is for chronic sarcoidosis needing long-term treatment. E. There are no features of tuberculosis.
pearl: Löfgren syndrome carries the best prognosis of all sarcoidosis presentations; most patients recover fully within months to 2 years.
thinking: Erythema nodosum plus ankle arthritis plus fever ↓ Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy ↓ Löfgren syndrome ↓ No organ-threatening disease ↓ NSAIDs and observe
exam_trap: A, oral prednisolone — sarcoidosis is classically steroid-responsive, but Löfgren syndrome is self-limiting and steroids are only for significant organ involvement.
takeaway: Löfgren syndrome usually settles on its own: NSAIDs and observation.

stem: A 69-year-old woman with COPD confirmed on spirometry attends her annual review at the GP surgery. She stopped smoking last year, has completed pulmonary rehabilitation and is up to date with vaccinations. She uses a salbutamol inhaler several times a day and is still breathless when walking to the shops. She has had no exacerbations in the past year. There is no history of atopy, no variation in symptoms during the day and her blood eosinophil count is normal. What is the most appropriate change to her treatment?

options.A: Add a long-acting muscarinic antagonist with a long-acting beta-2 agonist
options.B: Add a long-acting beta-2 agonist with an inhaled corticosteroid
options.C: Start triple therapy with an inhaled corticosteroid, LABA and LAMA

correct_answer: A. Add a long-acting muscarinic antagonist with a long-acting beta-2 agonist
why_correct: NICE advises that people with COPD who remain limited by breathlessness despite non-drug measures and a short-acting bronchodilator, and who have no asthmatic features or features suggesting steroid responsiveness, are offered a LAMA plus a LABA. Dual long-acting bronchodilation improves breathlessness without the pneumonia risk of inhaled steroids.
why_wrong: B. LABA with an inhaled corticosteroid is for patients with asthmatic features or features suggesting steroid responsiveness. C. Triple therapy is for continued exacerbations or symptoms despite dual therapy. D. Theophylline is used only after inhaled therapy has been optimised. E. Long-term oral steroids are rarely used and are not a routine step.
pearl: In COPD, the presence or absence of asthmatic or steroid-responsive features (atopy, raised eosinophils, diurnal or marked variability) decides between LAMA plus LABA and LABA plus ICS.
thinking: COPD, still breathless on short-acting bronchodilator ↓ Non-drug measures done ↓ No asthmatic or steroid-responsive features ↓ No inhaled steroid needed ↓ LAMA plus LABA
exam_trap: B, LABA with inhaled corticosteroid — many patients are on this combination, but without asthmatic features an inhaled steroid adds pneumonia risk without benefit at this stage.
takeaway: COPD without asthmatic features, still breathless: add LAMA plus LABA.

stem: A 34-year-old woman recently recruited from a country with a high incidence of tuberculosis attends occupational health before starting work as a nurse on a UK ward. She feels well, with no cough, fever, night sweats or weight loss. An interferon-gamma release assay is positive and her chest X-ray is normal. HIV test and liver function tests are normal. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Three months of isoniazid (with pyridoxine) and rifampicin
options.B: Six months of rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol
options.D: No treatment and discharge from follow-up
options.E: Repeat interferon-gamma release assay in 12 months

correct_answer: A. Three months of isoniazid (with pyridoxine) and rifampicin
why_correct: A positive IGRA with a normal chest X-ray and no symptoms indicates latent tuberculosis infection. NICE recommends treating latent infection in eligible adults, including recent arrivals from high-incidence countries, with either 3 months of isoniazid plus rifampicin or 6 months of isoniazid, both given with pyridoxine. Treatment greatly reduces the lifetime risk of reactivation.
why_wrong: B. Four-drug therapy is for active tuberculosis, which has been excluded here. C. BCG does not treat existing infection and offers little benefit to infected adults. D. Leaving latent infection untreated leaves a lifetime risk of reactivation. E. A repeat test does not change the diagnosis or reduce the risk.
pearl: Rifampicin induces liver enzymes and makes hormonal contraception unreliable; advise women of reproductive age to use another method during treatment. It also turns urine and tears orange.
thinking: Positive IGRA ↓ No symptoms and normal chest X-ray ↓ Latent TB, not active disease ↓ Eligible adult from high-incidence country ↓ 3 months isoniazid plus rifampicin
exam_trap: B, standard four-drug therapy — a positive TB test prompts thoughts of full treatment, but with no symptoms and a normal X-ray this is latent infection, which needs a shorter, simpler regimen.
takeaway: Latent TB in an eligible adult: treat with 3 months isoniazid plus rifampicin or 6 months isoniazid.
