stem: A 47-year-old man is reviewed in the sleep clinic. His wife reports loud snoring and pauses in his breathing at night, and he has fallen asleep in afternoon meetings at work. He has a BMI of 36 kg/m2 and treated hypertension. An overnight sleep study confirms moderate obstructive sleep apnoea. He has already been referred to a weight management service. What is the most appropriate treatment?
why_correct: NICE recommends continuous positive airway pressure for adults with moderate or severe obstructive sleep apnoea. CPAP splints the upper airway open during sleep, abolishing obstructive events and improving daytime sleepiness. Weight loss is encouraged alongside, and he should be advised about his duty to inform the DVLA if sleepiness affects his driving.
why_wrong: A. A mandibular advancement device is an option for mild disease or for people who cannot tolerate CPAP. C. Oxygen does not prevent the airway collapse that causes the apnoeas. D. Modafinil does not treat the airway obstruction and is not a primary treatment. E. Upper airway surgery is not a first-line treatment for obstructive sleep apnoea in adults.
pearl: Excessive sleepiness from OSA that affects driving must be reported to the DVLA; drivers can usually resume once symptoms are controlled on treatment.
thinking: Snoring, witnessed apnoeas, daytime sleepiness ↓ Sleep study confirms moderate OSA ↓ Airway collapses during sleep ↓ Keep it open mechanically ↓ CPAP
exam_trap: A, mandibular advancement device — it is less intrusive and does treat OSA, but it is for mild disease or CPAP intolerance, not first choice in moderate disease.
takeaway: Moderate or severe obstructive sleep apnoea: CPAP is first-line, with weight loss alongside.

stem: A 76-year-old man who spent 30 years fitting pipe lagging in power stations sees his GP with 3 months of a dull, constant right chest ache, worsening breathlessness and a 7 kg weight loss. Chest X-ray shows a large right pleural effusion. CT shows nodular, irregular pleural thickening encasing the right lung and extending onto the mediastinal pleura. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Pipe lagging is a classic source of asbestos exposure. Decades later, persistent chest wall pain, breathlessness, weight loss and a unilateral effusion with nodular, circumferential pleural thickening are typical of malignant pleural mesothelioma. Diagnosis is confirmed by pleural biopsy, and the patient may be entitled to industrial injuries compensation.
why_wrong: B. Tuberculous pleurisy usually presents with fever and night sweats and lacks this encasing nodular thickening. C. Heart failure typically causes bilateral effusions without pleural thickening or chest pain. D. Pleural plaques are asymptomatic, discrete and calcified, and do not cause effusions or weight loss. E. A parapneumonic effusion follows a pneumonia with fever and productive cough.
pearl: Mesothelioma usually appears 30 to 40 or more years after asbestos exposure. Chest wall pain and weight loss with nodular pleural thickening should raise concern.
thinking: Occupational asbestos exposure ↓ Chest pain, breathlessness and weight loss ↓ Unilateral effusion ↓ Nodular pleural thickening encasing the lung ↓ Mesothelioma
exam_trap: D, benign pleural plaques — they are the commonest asbestos-related finding, but they are asymptomatic and never cause a large effusion or weight loss.
takeaway: Asbestos exposure plus chest pain, effusion and nodular pleural thickening suggests mesothelioma.

stem: A 71-year-old retired accountant who has never smoked and has no occupational dust exposure sees his GP with 9 months of gradually worsening breathlessness on exertion and a persistent dry cough. He has finger clubbing and fine, velcro-like crackles at both lung bases. There is no ankle swelling and his JVP is not raised. Spirometry shows a reduced FVC with a normal FEV1/FVC ratio, and his gas transfer is reduced. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Progressive exertional breathlessness, dry cough, clubbing and fine bibasal inspiratory crackles in an older adult, with a restrictive pattern and reduced gas transfer, are typical of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. With no relevant exposure, an idiopathic cause is most likely. High-resolution CT is the key next test and usually shows basal, subpleural reticulation and honeycombing.
why_wrong: A. COPD gives an obstructive pattern and is usually smoking-related. C. Asbestosis would look similar but needs significant asbestos exposure, which he does not have. D. Bronchiectasis causes a chronic productive cough with coarse crackles. E. Heart failure can cause basal crackles, but not clubbing, and there are no signs of fluid overload.
pearl: Fine end-inspiratory velcro crackles plus clubbing in an older patient with a restrictive pattern should prompt high-resolution CT for pulmonary fibrosis.
thinking: Slowly progressive breathlessness and dry cough ↓ Clubbing and fine bibasal crackles ↓ Restrictive spirometry, low gas transfer ↓ No exposure to explain it ↓ Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
exam_trap: C, asbestosis — it gives an identical clinical picture, but the question deliberately removes any occupational exposure, leaving an idiopathic cause.
takeaway: Clubbing, fine bibasal crackles and restrictive spirometry without exposure suggest IPF.

stem: A 74-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her daughter after 3 days of cough, fever and increasing drowsiness. She is newly confused about the date and place. Respiratory rate is 32 per minute, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, pulse 112 beats per minute and oxygen saturation 90% on air. Urea is raised. Chest X-ray shows left lower lobe consolidation. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Oral amoxicillin and discharge home with her daughter
options.B: Oral doxycycline at home with GP review in 48 hours
options.D: Admission, withholding antibiotics until sputum culture results are available
options.E: Admission, oxygen and IV antibiotics for high-severity pneumonia

correct_answer: E. Admission, oxygen and IV antibiotics for high-severity pneumonia
why_correct: New confusion, raised urea, tachypnoea, low blood pressure and age over 65 give a high CURB-65 score, indicating high-severity community-acquired pneumonia with a high risk of death. She needs admission, controlled oxygen, fluids and prompt antibiotics for high-severity pneumonia, usually a beta-lactam such as co-amoxiclav with a macrolide, given IV because of the severity, following local policy.
why_wrong: A. Oral amoxicillin at home is only for low-severity pneumonia. B. Home treatment is unsafe for a confused, hypotensive, hypoxic patient. C. Amoxicillin alone does not give the broader cover needed for high-severity disease. D. Antibiotics should start promptly; delay worsens outcomes.
pearl: CURB-65 = Confusion, Urea raised, Respiratory rate 30 or more, Blood pressure low, age 65 or over. Use it alongside clinical judgement, not instead of it.
thinking: Cough, fever and consolidation ↓ Confusion, raised urea, tachypnoea, low BP, age over 65 ↓ High-severity pneumonia ↓ Needs hospital care ↓ Admit, oxygen and IV antibiotics
exam_trap: C, admission with oral amoxicillin — admitting feels like the key decision, but high-severity pneumonia needs broader cover, given IV in a patient this unwell.
takeaway: High-severity pneumonia: admit, give oxygen and start broad IV antibiotics promptly.

stem: A 52-year-old man on the surgical ward becomes acutely breathless 20 minutes after a right subclavian central venous catheter was inserted. He is agitated, oxygen saturation is 84% on high-flow oxygen, pulse 138 beats per minute and blood pressure 76/40 mmHg. His neck veins are distended, the trachea is deviated to the left, and the right chest is hyper-resonant with absent breath sounds. What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.A: Immediate needle decompression of the right hemithorax
options.B: Urgent portable chest X-ray to confirm the diagnosis
options.C: Formal insertion of a right-sided chest drain as the first step
options.D: Rapid IV fluid bolus and reassess

correct_answer: A. Immediate needle decompression of the right hemithorax
why_correct: A pneumothorax after central line insertion, with hypotension, distended neck veins, tracheal deviation away from the affected side and a silent, hyper-resonant hemithorax is a tension pneumothorax. This is a clinical diagnosis and needs immediate decompression on the affected side without waiting for imaging, followed by a chest drain.
why_wrong: B. Waiting for an X-ray delays life-saving treatment in obstructive shock. C. A chest drain follows decompression and takes too long as the first step in a peri-arrest patient. D. Fluids do not relieve the obstruction to venous return. E. CT is unsafe in an unstable patient, and pulmonary embolism does not explain the chest signs.
pearl: Tension pneumothorax pushes the trachea away from the affected side. Hypotension plus a silent, hyper-resonant hemithorax means decompress first, image later.
thinking: Sudden collapse after subclavian line ↓ Hypotension, raised JVP, tracheal deviation away ↓ Hyper-resonant silent right chest ↓ Tension pneumothorax ↓ Immediate decompression
exam_trap: B, urgent portable chest X-ray — confirmation feels responsible, but tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis and the patient may arrest while waiting for the film.
takeaway: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis: decompress immediately, image afterwards.

presentation: Suspected subarachnoid haemorrhage with normal CT
stem: A 38-year-old man was lifting weights at the gym when he felt a sudden, severe pain at the back of his head, reaching its worst within a few seconds. He vomited and went home to rest, coming to the emergency department the following morning. A non-contrast CT head performed 14 hours after the onset of the headache is normal. Neurological examination is normal. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Discharge with analgesia and GP follow-up
options.C: Lumbar puncture to look for xanthochromia
options.E: Start IV antibiotics for possible meningitis

correct_answer: C. Lumbar puncture to look for xanthochromia
why_correct: A thunderclap headache reaching maximum intensity within seconds must be investigated for subarachnoid haemorrhage. CT is less sensitive when it is performed more than 6 hours after onset, so a normal scan does not exclude bleeding. NICE advises considering lumbar puncture at least 12 hours after onset to look for xanthochromia, so it can be done now.
why_wrong: A. Discharge before subarachnoid haemorrhage has been excluded is unsafe. B. MRI is not the standard next test for suspected subarachnoid haemorrhage after a normal CT. D. Repeating the CT does not improve sensitivity as blood is cleared and becomes harder to see. E. There is no fever or other feature to suggest meningitis.
pearl: Xanthochromia takes about 12 hours to develop, so lumbar puncture is timed for at least 12 hours after headache onset; earlier samples can be falsely reassuring.
thinking: Sudden severe headache peaking in seconds ↓ Suspected subarachnoid haemorrhage ↓ CT done late is normal ↓ Late CT can miss blood ↓ Lumbar puncture for xanthochromia
exam_trap: A, discharge — a normal CT and normal examination feel reassuring, but a late CT can miss subarachnoid haemorrhage and a missed bleed can be fatal.
takeaway: Thunderclap headache with a normal late CT: lumbar puncture for xanthochromia.
review_note: answer hinges on movable time thresholds; needs reframing or confirmation against NICE NG228 (dropped from pack 09, 17 Oct 2026)

stem: A 24-year-old man with type 1 diabetes attends the emergency department with a day of vomiting and abdominal pain. He has not taken his insulin since the vomiting began. He is breathing deeply and rapidly. Capillary glucose is 17 mmol/L and blood ketones are 5.2 mmol/L. Venous pH is 7.14 and bicarbonate is 9 mmol/L. Lactate is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Diabetic ketoacidosis is defined by the combination of diabetes or hyperglycaemia, a high blood ketone level and a metabolic acidosis (low pH or low bicarbonate). He meets all three, and missed insulin during illness is a common trigger. The glucose does not have to be very high: ketoacidosis can occur with only moderately raised or even normal glucose.
why_wrong: A. Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state usually has very high glucose and osmolality without significant ketosis or acidosis. C. Alcoholic ketoacidosis occurs after heavy drinking, usually with normal or low glucose. D. Starvation ketosis causes mild ketosis without significant acidosis. E. A normal lactate makes lactic acidosis unlikely.
pearl: Never rule out DKA because the glucose is only moderately raised; check ketones and blood gases in any unwell person with diabetes, particularly those taking SGLT2 inhibitors.
thinking: Type 1 diabetes, missed insulin, vomiting ↓ Raised glucose ↓ High ketones ↓ Acidosis with low bicarbonate ↓ Diabetic ketoacidosis
exam_trap: A, hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state — any hyperglycaemic emergency may come to mind, but HHS lacks marked ketosis and acidosis, and this glucose is too low for it.
takeaway: DKA = diabetes or hyperglycaemia plus ketonaemia plus acidosis; glucose need not be very high.

stem: A 38-year-old woman sees her GP with 4 months of tiredness, dry skin, constipation, weight gain and heavier periods. She has no heart disease and is not pregnant. Blood tests show a markedly raised TSH, a low free T4 and positive thyroid peroxidase antibodies. What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.D: No treatment, with repeat thyroid function tests in 6 months

why_correct: A raised TSH with a low free T4 and positive peroxidase antibodies indicates overt primary hypothyroidism due to autoimmune (Hashimoto's) thyroiditis. NICE recommends levothyroxine. In adults under 65 without cardiovascular disease, a full replacement dose based on body weight can be considered from the start, and TSH is checked after a few weeks to adjust the dose.
why_wrong: B. Liothyronine is not recommended for routine treatment of primary hypothyroidism. C. Carbimazole treats hyperthyroidism. D. Watching and waiting is for some cases of subclinical hypothyroidism, not overt disease with symptoms. E. Hydrocortisone is for adrenal insufficiency, not thyroid hormone deficiency.
pearl: Start levothyroxine at a low dose and increase slowly in older people and those with heart disease, to avoid provoking angina or arrhythmia.
thinking: Tiredness, weight gain, constipation, menorrhagia ↓ High TSH, low free T4 ↓ Overt primary hypothyroidism ↓ Autoimmune cause ↓ Levothyroxine
exam_trap: D, repeat tests in 6 months — this is used for mild subclinical hypothyroidism, but a low free T4 with symptoms is overt disease that needs treatment.
takeaway: Overt primary hypothyroidism: treat with levothyroxine and titrate to TSH.

stem: A 36-year-old woman sees her GP with 3 months of weight loss despite a good appetite, sweating, a fine tremor and palpitations. Her eyes feel gritty and her partner says they look more prominent. She has a smooth, diffusely enlarged, non-tender thyroid with a soft bruit over it. TSH is suppressed and free T4 is raised. Her youngest child is 4 years old. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Hyperthyroidism with a smooth, diffuse goitre, a thyroid bruit and eye signs is typical of Graves' disease. Thyroid eye disease is specific to Graves' disease, caused by antibodies that stimulate the TSH receptor. TSH receptor antibody testing confirms the diagnosis.
why_wrong: A. Toxic multinodular goitre has an irregular, nodular gland and occurs in older people without eye disease. C. Subacute thyroiditis causes a painful, tender thyroid after a viral illness. D. A toxic adenoma is a single palpable nodule. E. Factitious thyrotoxicosis causes a small or impalpable thyroid.
pearl: Smoking increases the risk and severity of thyroid eye disease; advising patients to stop is part of management.
thinking: Weight loss, tremor, palpitations ↓ Suppressed TSH, high free T4 ↓ Smooth goitre with bruit ↓ Eye signs ↓ Graves' disease
exam_trap: A, toxic multinodular goitre — it is a common cause of hyperthyroidism, but the gland is nodular, patients are older, and there is no eye disease.
takeaway: Hyperthyroidism with diffuse goitre and eye disease is Graves' disease.

stem: A 47-year-old man is reviewed in the endocrine clinic with easy bruising, thin skin, difficulty climbing stairs, newly diagnosed diabetes and hypertension. He takes no steroid medicines in any form. An overnight dexamethasone suppression test shows failure of cortisol suppression, and a late-night salivary cortisol is raised, confirming hypercortisolism. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
why_correct: Once Cushing's syndrome has been confirmed biochemically, the next step is to find the cause. Plasma ACTH separates ACTH-independent disease (low ACTH, usually an adrenal tumour) from ACTH-dependent disease (normal or high ACTH, from a pituitary or ectopic source). This result decides which imaging and further tests are needed.
why_wrong: A. Adrenal imaging is appropriate only once ACTH is shown to be suppressed. B. Pituitary MRI follows confirmation of ACTH-dependent disease, and small incidental pituitary lesions are common. C. Hypercortisolism is already confirmed, so further screening tests add nothing. D. Petrosal sinus sampling is a specialised test used later to distinguish pituitary from ectopic ACTH.
pearl: Order in Cushing's: exclude steroid use, confirm excess cortisol, measure ACTH, then image the right place.
thinking: Features of cortisol excess ↓ No exogenous steroids ↓ Hypercortisolism confirmed ↓ Next, localise: ACTH-dependent or not ↓ Plasma ACTH
exam_trap: B, pituitary MRI — Cushing's disease is the commonest endogenous cause, but imaging before measuring ACTH risks chasing an incidental finding.
takeaway: Confirmed Cushing's syndrome: measure plasma ACTH before any imaging.

presentation: Primary adrenal insufficiency — confirming the diagnosis
stem: A 28-year-old man with vitiligo sees his GP with 3 months of tiredness, weight loss, dizziness on standing and a craving for salty food. His palmar creases and gums look darker than usual. His blood pressure falls on standing. Blood tests show a low sodium and a raised potassium. He is not acutely unwell. Which investigation is most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis?
why_correct: Fatigue, weight loss, postural hypotension, salt craving and pigmentation with low sodium and high potassium, in someone with another autoimmune condition, suggest primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease). The short Synacthen test confirms it: cortisol fails to rise adequately after synthetic ACTH. A high plasma ACTH shows the cause is in the adrenal glands.
why_wrong: A. A single random cortisol is unreliable for confirming or excluding adrenal insufficiency. C. Dexamethasone suppression tests look for cortisol excess, not deficiency. D. The aldosterone to renin ratio screens for primary hyperaldosteronism. E. Imaging is not used to make the diagnosis, and autoimmune adrenalitis is the commonest UK cause.
pearl: If adrenal crisis is suspected, give IV or IM hydrocortisone straight away after taking blood; do not delay treatment for a Synacthen test.
thinking: Fatigue, weight loss, pigmentation ↓ Low sodium, high potassium, postural drop ↓ Suspected Addison's disease ↓ Needs dynamic test of adrenal reserve ↓ Short Synacthen test
exam_trap: A, random cortisol — it is quick and often done first, but a single value cannot confirm adrenal insufficiency; a stimulation test is needed.
takeaway: Suspected Addison's disease is confirmed with a short Synacthen test.

stem: A 58-year-old woman is diagnosed with type 2 diabetes after two raised HbA1c results. She has a BMI of 31 kg/m2 and has started making changes to her diet and activity. She has no history of cardiovascular disease or heart failure, and her renal function and urine albumin to creatinine ratio are normal. She has no contraindications to any diabetes medicines. According to current NICE guidance, what is the most appropriate initial drug treatment?

options.A: Metformin alone, adding a second drug later if HbA1c rises
options.C: Modified-release metformin with an SGLT2 inhibitor

correct_answer: C. Modified-release metformin with an SGLT2 inhibitor
why_correct: NICE now recommends offering modified-release metformin together with an SGLT2 inhibitor as initial treatment for adults with type 2 diabetes, including those without cardiovascular disease, heart failure or chronic kidney disease. The combination improves glucose control and weight and reduces cardiovascular events compared with metformin alone. If metformin is not tolerated or is contraindicated, an SGLT2 inhibitor is offered alone.
why_wrong: A. Metformin alone with later step-up was the previous pathway and has been replaced. B. Sulfonylureas cause hypoglycaemia and weight gain and are not first-line. D. GLP-1 receptor agonists are not recommended as initial treatment for this group. E. Insulin is not first-line for a well patient with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes.
pearl: Before starting an SGLT2 inhibitor, warn about genital fungal infections, dehydration and the rare risk of ketoacidosis, including during acute illness, when the drug should be paused.
thinking: New type 2 diabetes ↓ No cardiovascular, heart failure or kidney disease ↓ Not early-onset ↓ Current NICE initial treatment ↓ MR metformin plus SGLT2 inhibitor
exam_trap: A, metformin alone — this was standard practice for years and appears in many older resources, but NICE now offers an SGLT2 inhibitor with metformin from the start.
takeaway: Type 2 diabetes initial drug treatment: modified-release metformin with an SGLT2 inhibitor.

stem: A 58-year-old woman with a history of two kidney stones has routine blood tests at her GP surgery. Adjusted calcium is raised at 2.85 mmol/L. Parathyroid hormone is 5.9 pmol/L (reference range 1.6 to 6.9). Renal function and vitamin D are normal. She takes no regular medicines. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: When calcium is high, PTH should be suppressed. A PTH in the upper half of the reference range is therefore inappropriately normal and indicates primary hyperparathyroidism, usually from a single parathyroid adenoma. Kidney stones are a typical complication.
why_wrong: B. Malignancy raises calcium through PTH-related peptide or bone metastases, with suppressed PTH. C. Sarcoidosis raises calcium through excess activated vitamin D, which suppresses PTH. D. Vitamin D toxicity also suppresses PTH, and her vitamin D is normal. E. She takes no diuretics; thiazides cause only mild hypercalcaemia and often unmask underlying primary hyperparathyroidism rather than explaining it.
pearl: A high calcium with a normal PTH is not reassuring. Any PTH that is not suppressed in hypercalcaemia points to the parathyroid glands.
thinking: Raised calcium ↓ PTH should be suppressed ↓ PTH in normal range, so inappropriately normal ↓ History of kidney stones ↓ Primary hyperparathyroidism
exam_trap: B, malignancy — it is a common and serious cause of hypercalcaemia, but it suppresses PTH; an unsuppressed PTH points to the parathyroid glands.
takeaway: Hypercalcaemia with an unsuppressed PTH means primary hyperparathyroidism.

stem: A 44-year-old man sees his GP with several months of sudden episodes of pounding headache, palpitations, drenching sweats and pallor, each lasting 10 to 20 minutes. A pharmacist measured his blood pressure during one attack at 210/120 mmHg, but readings in the surgery between attacks are normal. Recent bloods showed impaired fasting glucose. Thyroid function is normal. What is the most appropriate investigation?

options.D: Start propranolol and review in 4 weeks

why_correct: Episodes of headache, palpitations and sweating with paroxysmal severe hypertension and normal readings in between suggest a phaeochromocytoma. The first step is biochemical confirmation, with plasma free metanephrines or 24-hour urinary metanephrines. Imaging is arranged only after the biochemistry is positive.
why_wrong: B. Imaging comes after biochemical confirmation, as incidental adrenal lesions are common. C. Urinary 5-HIAA is for carcinoid syndrome, which typically causes flushing and diarrhoea rather than hypertensive episodes. D. A beta-blocker without prior alpha-blockade can cause a dangerous rise in blood pressure in phaeochromocytoma. E. Ambulatory monitoring confirms hypertension but cannot diagnose the cause.
pearl: In phaeochromocytoma, alpha-blockade (for example phenoxybenzamine) is always started before any beta-blocker, both medically and before surgery.
thinking: Episodes of headache, palpitations and sweating ↓ Paroxysmal severe hypertension ↓ Suspect catecholamine excess ↓ Confirm biochemically first ↓ Plasma free metanephrines
exam_trap: D, propranolol — palpitations and anxiety-like attacks make a beta-blocker tempting, but unopposed beta-blockade in phaeochromocytoma can cause a hypertensive crisis.
takeaway: Suspected phaeochromocytoma: plasma free metanephrines first, imaging second.

stem: A 71-year-old woman on the medical ward is being treated for community-acquired pneumonia. Her sodium has fallen to 122 mmol/L. She takes no diuretics and has not been vomiting. She has moist mucous membranes, no postural drop in blood pressure, a normal JVP and no oedema. Serum osmolality is low, urine osmolality is inappropriately high and urine sodium is raised. Thyroid function and a morning cortisol are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
correct_answer: B. Syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion
why_correct: Hyponatraemia with low serum osmolality, inappropriately concentrated urine and a raised urine sodium in a euvolaemic patient, with thyroid and adrenal disease excluded and no diuretics, meets the criteria for SIADH. Pneumonia is a recognised cause. Fluid restriction and treatment of the pneumonia are the usual first steps.
why_wrong: A. She is clinically euvolaemic, with no history of fluid loss. C. Primary polydipsia produces very dilute urine, not concentrated urine. D. A normal morning cortisol makes adrenal insufficiency unlikely. E. She is not taking a diuretic.
pearl: SIADH is a diagnosis of exclusion: check volume status, exclude diuretics, hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency before making it.
thinking: Low sodium and low serum osmolality ↓ Concentrated urine with high urine sodium ↓ Clinically euvolaemic ↓ Thyroid, adrenal and diuretics excluded ↓ SIADH due to pneumonia
exam_trap: D, adrenal insufficiency — it can produce an identical biochemical picture, but a normal morning cortisol makes it unlikely here.
takeaway: Euvolaemic hyponatraemia with concentrated urine, after exclusions, is SIADH.

stem: A 41-year-old woman with Graves' disease, who stopped taking carbimazole 2 months ago, is brought to the emergency department with a chest infection. She is agitated and confused, with a temperature of 40.1 degrees C, vomiting and diarrhoea. ECG shows atrial fibrillation at 156 beats per minute. TSH is suppressed and free T4 is very high. Which treatment approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Lugol's iodine first, then propylthiouracil an hour later, with propranolol and hydrocortisone
options.B: Propylthiouracil first, then Lugol's iodine at least an hour later, with propranolol and hydrocortisone
options.C: Radioactive iodine once the infection has been treated

correct_answer: B. Propylthiouracil first, then Lugol's iodine at least an hour later, with propranolol and hydrocortisone
why_correct: Fever, confusion, gastrointestinal upset and fast atrial fibrillation in a patient with untreated Graves' disease and an infection indicate thyroid storm. Treatment is a thionamide such as propylthiouracil to block hormone synthesis, then iodine at least an hour later to block release, plus a beta-blocker, hydrocortisone, and supportive care in a high-dependency setting. The precipitating infection must also be treated.
why_wrong: A. Giving iodine before a thionamide can provide extra substrate for hormone production. C. Radioactive iodine is not used in thyroid storm and can worsen it. D. Surgery is not done during storm; the patient must first be stabilised medically. E. Beta-blockade and cooling help symptoms but do not stop hormone production or release.
pearl: Use paracetamol, not aspirin, for fever in thyroid storm; aspirin displaces thyroid hormone from binding proteins and raises free hormone levels.
thinking: Known Graves', stopped treatment, infection ↓ Fever, confusion, fast AF ↓ Thyroid storm ↓ Block synthesis first, then release ↓ Thionamide, then iodine, with propranolol and hydrocortisone
exam_trap: A, iodine first — it contains the same drugs as the correct answer, but giving iodine before the thionamide can fuel more hormone production.
takeaway: Thyroid storm: thionamide first, iodine an hour later, plus beta-blocker and hydrocortisone.

stem: A 39-year-old man who does not have diabetes has had several episodes of confusion, odd behaviour and sweating in the early morning, which settle when he eats breakfast. He has gained weight recently because he eats frequently to prevent the episodes. During a supervised fast, he develops symptoms with a plasma glucose of 2.1 mmol/L. At that time, insulin and C-peptide are both inappropriately high, and a sulfonylurea screen is negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Symptoms of hypoglycaemia with a documented low glucose that resolve with food (Whipple's triad) confirm true hypoglycaemia. High insulin with high C-peptide shows the insulin is being made by the body, and a negative sulfonylurea screen excludes drug-induced release. This points to an insulin-secreting pancreatic tumour, an insulinoma.
why_wrong: A. Injected insulin gives a high insulin with a suppressed C-peptide. B. Sulfonylureas also raise both insulin and C-peptide, but the drug screen is negative. C. Adrenal insufficiency can cause hypoglycaemia but with low, appropriately suppressed insulin. E. Dumping syndrome causes symptoms after meals following gastric surgery, not fasting hypoglycaemia.
pearl: High insulin with low C-peptide = injected insulin. High insulin and high C-peptide = insulinoma or sulfonylurea, so always check a sulfonylurea screen.
thinking: Fasting symptoms relieved by eating ↓ Documented hypoglycaemia ↓ High insulin and high C-peptide ↓ Sulfonylurea screen negative ↓ Insulinoma
exam_trap: B, covert sulfonylurea use — it produces exactly the same insulin and C-peptide pattern as an insulinoma, so the negative drug screen is the deciding clue.
takeaway: Fasting hypoglycaemia with high insulin, high C-peptide and negative drug screen is insulinoma.

stem: A 46-year-old man sees his GP because he has felt persistently low for over two months. He no longer enjoys watching football with his son, wakes at 4 a.m. unable to get back to sleep, has lost his appetite, feels guilty and worthless, and is struggling to concentrate at work. His symptoms are severe and are significantly affecting his functioning. He has no thoughts of self-harm, no psychotic symptoms and no history of elevated mood. He would like to try both medication and talking therapy. What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.C: Zopiclone for sleep with review in 4 weeks
options.E: Urgent referral to the crisis team for admission

correct_answer: B. Sertraline combined with individual CBT
why_correct: For a more severe depressive episode, NICE lists a combination of individual CBT and an antidepressant as the most effective first option, chosen together with the patient. An SSRI such as sertraline is preferred because of its safety and tolerability. He should be reviewed within a few weeks of starting, with advice on side effects and safety-netting.
why_wrong: A. Tricyclics are more toxic in overdose and less well tolerated, so they are not first choice. C. A hypnotic treats only insomnia and does not treat depression. D. Low-intensity self-help alone is suitable for less severe depression, not for severe symptoms with marked impairment. E. Admission is not needed without high risk, psychosis or inability to care for himself.
pearl: Ask about suicidal thoughts in every depressed patient. Review people starting antidepressants early, and sooner for those under 25 because of a possible increase in suicidal thinking at the start.
thinking: Low mood, anhedonia, early waking, guilt and poor concentration ↓ Severe symptoms with marked impairment, no risk or psychosis ↓ More severe depression in a patient wanting both treatments ↓ SSRI plus individual CBT
exam_trap: D, guided self-help — tempting because low-intensity interventions are often the first step for depression, but they are for less severe episodes and are insufficient for severe symptoms.
takeaway: More severe depression: offer combined individual CBT and an SSRI such as sertraline.

stem: A 19-year-old woman is assessed by the early intervention in psychosis team after her mother noticed seven months of increasing withdrawal and self-neglect. She describes voices discussing her actions and believes neighbours are inserting thoughts into her head. Her mood is not elevated or depressed, and a urine drug screen is negative. A diagnosis of first-episode schizophrenia is made and she agrees to start treatment. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.C: Oral second-generation antipsychotic (e.g. aripiprazole) with psychological interventions

correct_answer: C. Oral second-generation antipsychotic (e.g. aripiprazole) with psychological interventions
why_correct: For first-episode psychosis NICE recommends an oral antipsychotic, chosen with the patient after discussing likely benefits and side effects, together with psychological interventions such as CBT for psychosis and family intervention. A second-generation drug like aripiprazole is a common choice, partly because of a lower risk of metabolic and hormonal side effects. Baseline physical health checks (weight, glucose, lipids, prolactin, ECG where indicated) should be done before starting.
why_wrong: A. Lithium is a mood stabiliser for bipolar disorder, not schizophrenia. B. Clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia after at least two adequate trials of other antipsychotics. D. An SSRI does not treat psychotic symptoms. E. Depot preparations are usually reserved for those who prefer them or have adherence difficulties, not routine first-line use.
pearl: Treatment-resistant schizophrenia means failure of two different antipsychotics at adequate dose and duration, at least one second-generation; only then offer clozapine, with mandatory blood monitoring.
thinking: Hallucinations, thought insertion and withdrawal for months ↓ No mood disorder or substance cause ↓ First-episode schizophrenia ↓ Oral antipsychotic plus psychological interventions
exam_trap: B, clozapine — tempting because it is the most effective antipsychotic, but its risk of agranulocytosis restricts it to treatment-resistant illness after two other antipsychotics have failed.
takeaway: First-episode schizophrenia: oral antipsychotic chosen with the patient, plus CBT for psychosis and family intervention.

stem: A 61-year-old man with bipolar disorder, stable on lithium for many years, is brought to the emergency department by his wife. Over three days he has developed vomiting, loose stools, a coarse tremor, unsteady walking and muddled speech. Two weeks ago his GP added bendroflumethiazide for hypertension. His serum lithium level is well above the therapeutic range and his creatinine has risen from baseline. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Reduce the lithium dose and recheck the level in 1 week
options.B: Continue lithium and start propranolol for the tremor
options.C: Stop lithium and bendroflumethiazide, give IV fluids and seek specialist advice about haemodialysis
options.D: Give activated charcoal and repeat the lithium level
options.E: Give haloperidol for the confusion and continue lithium

correct_answer: C. Stop lithium and bendroflumethiazide, give IV fluids and seek specialist advice about haemodialysis
why_correct: Coarse tremor, ataxia, slurred speech and confusion with a high lithium level indicate toxicity, precipitated here by a thiazide that reduces renal lithium clearance and by gastrointestinal fluid loss. Lithium and the precipitant should be stopped, and IV fluids given to restore volume and promote renal excretion. Advice should be sought from TOXBASE or the National Poisons Information Service and the renal team, as haemodialysis is indicated in severe toxicity, especially with neurological features or impaired kidney function.
why_wrong: A. Symptomatic toxicity is an emergency, and continuing any lithium delays recovery. B. Continuing lithium is dangerous and propranolol does not treat toxicity. D. Activated charcoal does not bind lithium. E. Antipsychotics do not treat lithium toxicity and can worsen neurotoxicity.
pearl: Drugs that raise lithium levels include thiazides, ACE inhibitors, ARBs and NSAIDs. Dehydration and intercurrent illness also precipitate toxicity; coarse tremor replaces the fine tremor of therapeutic use.
thinking: Long-term lithium with new thiazide and diarrhoea ↓ Coarse tremor, ataxia, dysarthria and confusion ↓ High lithium level with renal impairment means symptomatic toxicity ↓ Stop lithium and thiazide, IV fluids, discuss dialysis
exam_trap: D, activated charcoal — tempting because charcoal is a standard decontamination step in poisoning, but lithium is not adsorbed by charcoal, so it offers no benefit.
takeaway: Lithium toxicity: stop lithium and the precipitant, give IV fluids and discuss haemodialysis with specialists.

stem: A 22-year-old man with anorexia nervosa is admitted to a medical ward for nutritional stabilisation. His BMI is very low and he has eaten almost nothing for the past two weeks. He is alert and orientated. Blood tests before feeding show low phosphate, low magnesium and low potassium. A dietitian is about to start nasogastric feeding. What is the most significant medical risk to plan for over the next few days?
why_correct: When nutrition is reintroduced after prolonged starvation, insulin release drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells, causing a sharp fall in serum levels that can lead to arrhythmias, heart failure, respiratory failure, seizures and death. Low electrolytes before feeding, very low BMI and minimal recent intake place him at high risk. Feeding should start cautiously and increase gradually, with thiamine and B vitamins, electrolyte replacement and daily blood monitoring.
why_wrong: B. Starvation and refeeding cause low, not high, electrolyte levels; hypercalcaemia is not a feature. C. DKA requires insulin deficiency with hyperglycaemia and ketosis, which is not described. D. Hypernatraemia is not the characteristic danger of refeeding; fluid retention is more typical. E. Pancreatitis is not a recognised major risk of starting nasogastric feeding here.
pearl: Hypophosphataemia is the biochemical hallmark of refeeding syndrome. Start feeding cautiously in high-risk patients, give thiamine before and during feeding, and check phosphate, potassium and magnesium daily.
thinking: Severe malnutrition with little recent intake ↓ Low phosphate, potassium and magnesium before feeding ↓ Feeding will drive electrolytes into cells ↓ Refeeding syndrome is the major risk
exam_trap: E, pancreatitis from tube feeding — tempting because enteral feeding has gastrointestinal complications, but the life-threatening risk in this setting is electrolyte shift causing refeeding syndrome.
takeaway: Severely malnourished patient with low phosphate before feeding: high risk of refeeding syndrome — feed slowly and monitor.

stem: A 26-year-old nursery worker tells her GP that she cannot stop worrying that she will pass germs to the children. She washes her hands dozens of times a day until they crack and bleed, and her routines take over two hours daily. She recognises the fears are excessive and wishes she could stop. There are no psychotic symptoms and her mood is otherwise good. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.B: CBT including exposure and response prevention

correct_answer: B. CBT including exposure and response prevention
why_correct: This is obsessive-compulsive disorder: intrusive, unwanted contamination obsessions recognised as excessive, with time-consuming washing compulsions. CBT including exposure and response prevention (ERP) is the most effective psychological treatment, with intensity matched to the degree of impairment. An SSRI is an alternative or addition for moderate to severe impairment, often needing higher doses than for depression.
why_wrong: A. Benzodiazepines do not treat OCD and carry a risk of dependence. C. Antipsychotics are only used as specialist augmentation in resistant OCD, not first-line. D. Psychodynamic therapy lacks evidence for OCD. E. Treating the skin damage alone ignores the underlying disorder.
pearl: In OCD the thoughts are ego-dystonic and recognised as one's own; this distinguishes them from psychotic thought insertion. Intrusive harm thoughts in OCD are not associated with acting on them.
thinking: Intrusive contamination fears recognised as excessive ↓ Repetitive washing taking hours a day ↓ Obsessive-compulsive disorder ↓ CBT with exposure and response prevention
exam_trap: E, emollients and dermatology referral — tempting because the hand dermatitis is the visible problem, but it is a consequence of compulsive washing and the OCD itself needs treatment.
takeaway: OCD: first-line treatment is CBT including exposure and response prevention, with an SSRI if impairment is greater.

stem: A 34-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his partner. For ten days he has barely slept, talks rapidly and cannot be interrupted, has started planning several new businesses and has spent most of their savings. He is irritable when challenged. He has no previous psychiatric history and takes no regular medicines; physical examination and a urine drug screen are unremarkable. He is diagnosed with a manic episode. What is the most appropriate initial medication?
why_correct: For an adult with acute mania who is not already taking an antimanic drug, NICE recommends an antipsychotic such as haloperidol, olanzapine, quetiapine or risperidone as first choice, because they act quickly and are effective. Lithium can be added if the response is inadequate, and longer-term prophylaxis is considered once the episode settles. Any antidepressant should be stopped in mania.
why_wrong: A. Lithium is effective but slower in onset and is not the first-choice drug for acute mania in someone not already on treatment. B. Antidepressants can worsen or prolong mania. C. Valproate is not the first-line choice and carries serious risks, including in people who could father or bear children. E. A benzodiazepine may be used briefly for agitation but is not the main antimanic treatment.
pearl: In mania: stop antidepressants, start an antipsychotic, and plan long-term mood stabilisation once settled. Valproate must be avoided in anyone of childbearing potential unless strict criteria are met.
thinking: Reduced sleep, pressured speech, grandiose plans and reckless spending ↓ Manic episode, not on any antimanic drug ↓ Needs rapid control ↓ Start an antipsychotic such as olanzapine
exam_trap: A, lithium monotherapy — tempting because lithium is the classic bipolar drug, but its slower onset makes an antipsychotic the first choice for an acute manic episode.
takeaway: Acute mania in someone not on treatment: start an antipsychotic (haloperidol, olanzapine, quetiapine or risperidone).

stem: An 84-year-old man was admitted two days ago with community-acquired pneumonia. Tonight the nurses report that he is restless, pulling at his cannula, drowsy at times and unable to follow conversations, though he was lucid on admission. He has not opened his bowels for five days and his bladder is palpable. He is not hypoxic and is not a danger to others. What is the most appropriate management?

options.B: Raise the bed rails and use physical restraint
options.C: Identify and treat the causes, with reorientation and supportive care
options.D: Prescribe regular haloperidol for the rest of the admission

correct_answer: C. Identify and treat the causes, with reorientation and supportive care
why_correct: Acute fluctuating confusion with inattention in an older inpatient is delirium. Management centres on finding and treating precipitants (here infection, constipation and urinary retention), reviewing medicines, and providing non-drug measures such as reorientation, familiar people, glasses and hearing aids, good lighting, hydration, sleep hygiene and mobilisation. Short-term antipsychotic use is reserved for distress or risk that does not respond to these measures.
why_wrong: A. Benzodiazepines can worsen delirium and are reserved for specific situations such as alcohol withdrawal. B. Restraint and bed rails increase agitation and injury risk. D. Regular antipsychotics are not appropriate; if needed, the lowest dose is used for the shortest time. E. Neuroimaging is not routine without head injury, focal signs or another specific indication.
pearl: Delirium has multiple causes: remember PINCH ME — Pain, Infection, Nutrition, Constipation, Hydration, Medication, Environment, plus urinary retention.
thinking: Acute onset, fluctuating attention and drowsiness ↓ Delirium in an older inpatient ↓ Infection, constipation and retention are precipitants ↓ Treat the causes with non-drug supportive care
exam_trap: E, CT head — tempting because new confusion raises fear of intracranial pathology, but with clear reversible precipitants and no head injury or focal signs, imaging is not the first step.
takeaway: Delirium: treat the underlying causes and use non-drug measures; sedation is a last resort.

stem: A 52-year-old woman is on the surgical ward two days after admission with acute cholecystitis. She has become anxious, sweaty and tremulous, with a pulse of 112 bpm and nausea. Her partner reveals that she drinks over a bottle of wine and some spirits every day. She is orientated, with no ataxia or eye movement abnormality, and her liver function is not significantly impaired. A withdrawal assessment scale shows significant withdrawal. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: IM haloperidol to control her agitation
options.E: IV glucose infusion now, with thiamine once she is eating

why_correct: Significant alcohol withdrawal needs a benzodiazepine to control symptoms and prevent seizures and delirium tremens; chlordiazepoxide is the usual choice in the UK, given in a fixed reducing or symptom-triggered regimen. Inpatients with harmful drinking should receive parenteral thiamine (Pabrinex) to prevent Wernicke's encephalopathy, given before any glucose. Lorazepam or oxazepam is preferred if there is significant liver impairment.
why_wrong: A. Haloperidol does not treat withdrawal, lowers the seizure threshold and is not first-line. C. Thiamine is essential but does not treat withdrawal, and oral absorption is unreliable in heavy drinkers. D. Withholding treatment risks seizures and delirium tremens. E. Glucose before thiamine can precipitate Wernicke's encephalopathy.
pearl: Alcohol withdrawal often appears 6 to 24 hours after the last drink, with seizures and delirium tremens later. Hidden withdrawal is common in surgical patients who stop drinking on admission.
thinking: Tremor, sweating, anxiety and tachycardia after admission ↓ Heavy daily alcohol intake ↓ Significant alcohol withdrawal with risk of seizures and Wernicke's ↓ Chlordiazepoxide plus parenteral thiamine
exam_trap: C, oral thiamine alone — tempting because thiamine prevents Wernicke's, but it does nothing for withdrawal itself and oral absorption is poor; a benzodiazepine and parenteral thiamine are both needed.
takeaway: Significant alcohol withdrawal: chlordiazepoxide plus parenteral thiamine, and never give glucose before thiamine.

presentation: ECT under the Mental Health Act
stem: A 70-year-old man with severe depression and nihilistic delusions has stopped eating and drinking and is becoming physically compromised. Several antidepressant trials have failed. He is detained under section 3 of the Mental Health Act. The team believes ECT may be life-saving. He refuses ECT, but assessment shows he lacks capacity to make this decision. There is no advance decision refusing ECT and no attorney or deputy. His wife supports treatment. What is the most appropriate course of action?

options.A: Give ECT on the basis of his wife's consent
options.B: Give ECT under the Mental Capacity Act in his best interests
options.C: Apply to the Court of Protection before any treatment
options.D: Start a further antidepressant and review in six weeks
options.E: Give ECT once a Second Opinion Appointed Doctor certifies it is appropriate, using urgent treatment provisions if immediately necessary

correct_answer: E. Give ECT once a Second Opinion Appointed Doctor certifies it is appropriate, using urgent treatment provisions if immediately necessary
why_correct: ECT is highly effective in severe, life-threatening or psychotic depression. For a detained patient who lacks capacity to consent, the Mental Health Act allows ECT only if a Second Opinion Appointed Doctor (SOAD) certifies it is appropriate and it does not conflict with a valid advance decision or a decision by an attorney or deputy. Where treatment is immediately necessary to save life, it can be started under the urgent treatment provisions while awaiting the SOAD.
why_wrong: A. Relatives cannot consent to treatment on behalf of an adult in England and Wales. B. ECT for a detained patient is governed by the Mental Health Act safeguards, not the Mental Capacity Act. C. A court application is unnecessary because the Mental Health Act provides the framework. D. Delaying effective treatment while he deteriorates physically is unsafe.
pearl: ECT is the treatment of choice for life-threatening depression with refusal of food and fluids, catatonia or severe psychotic depression. A patient with capacity who refuses ECT cannot be given it, except under urgent treatment provisions.
thinking: Severe psychotic depression with refusal of food and fluid ↓ ECT is likely life-saving ↓ Detained and lacks capacity, no advance refusal ↓ ECT under the Mental Health Act with SOAD certification
exam_trap: B, Mental Capacity Act best interests — tempting because he lacks capacity, but for a detained patient ECT is regulated by the Mental Health Act and requires SOAD approval.
takeaway: ECT for a detained patient lacking capacity requires SOAD certification, unless urgently needed to save life.

stem: A 29-year-old woman sees her GP four months after being violently assaulted on her way home from work. She has vivid intrusive memories and nightmares of the attack, avoids the area and anything that reminds her of it, startles easily and sleeps poorly. She has been unable to return to work. She has no thoughts of self-harm and would like help. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
why_correct: Re-experiencing, avoidance and hyperarousal persisting beyond a month after trauma, with functional impairment, indicate post-traumatic stress disorder. NICE recommends trauma-focused psychological therapy, such as trauma-focused CBT or EMDR, as first-line treatment for adults. Drug treatment is considered if the person prefers it or declines psychological therapy.
why_wrong: A. Sertraline is an option only if the person prefers medication or declines psychological therapy. B. Propranolol is not recommended for treating PTSD. C. Single-session debriefing is not recommended and may be harmful. D. A hypnotic treats only the insomnia and carries dependence risk.
pearl: PTSD triad: re-experiencing, avoidance and hyperarousal. Active monitoring is reasonable only for mild symptoms within the first month after trauma.
thinking: Assault four months ago ↓ Flashbacks, nightmares, avoidance and hypervigilance ↓ Functional impairment means PTSD ↓ Trauma-focused CBT (or EMDR)
exam_trap: A, sertraline — tempting because SSRIs are licensed for PTSD, but psychological therapy is first-line and drugs are reserved for those who prefer them or decline therapy.
takeaway: PTSD in adults: offer trauma-focused CBT or EMDR first; avoid single-session debriefing.

stem: A 38-year-old woman with fair skin and a history of sunburn shows her GP a mole on her calf. Her partner thinks it has changed over the last two months. Which feature of the lesion would most strongly suggest a melanoma?

options.A: Uniform light brown colour with a symmetrical round outline
options.B: Soft, raised, skin-coloured lesion unchanged for many years
options.D: Asymmetrical shape with several shades of brown and black
options.E: Diameter of 3 mm with fine surface scale

correct_answer: D. Asymmetrical shape with several shades of brown and black
why_correct: Asymmetry, irregular border, colour variation, increasing size and evolution are the key warning signs of melanoma, and change in shape, size or colour are major features of the weighted 7-point checklist used in UK primary care. A changing lesion that is asymmetrical with multiple colours needs referral on a suspected cancer pathway. Dermoscopy, if available and the clinician is trained, can support the assessment but should not delay referral.
why_wrong: A. A symmetrical lesion with uniform colour is typical of a benign naevus. B. A soft, stable, skin-coloured lesion suggests a benign intradermal naevus. C. A stuck-on warty appearance suggests seborrhoeic keratosis. E. Small size and mild scale are not features that strongly suggest melanoma.
pearl: Major 7-point checklist features: change in size, shape or colour. Minor features: diameter 7 mm or more, inflammation, oozing and change in sensation. Any change in a mole deserves careful assessment.
thinking: Changing pigmented lesion in a fair-skinned adult ↓ Look for asymmetry, irregular border and colour variation ↓ Multiple colours with asymmetry are high-risk features ↓ Most suggestive of melanoma
exam_trap: C, waxy stuck-on surface — tempting because seborrhoeic keratoses can be dark and change, but the stuck-on warty appearance is characteristic of a benign lesion.
takeaway: Asymmetry and colour variation in a changing mole strongly suggest melanoma: refer on a suspected cancer pathway.

stem: A 45-year-old woman sees her GP with several well-defined pink plaques covered with silvery scale on both knees and her lower back. Her nails show some pitting. She has no joint pain or swelling. The plaques are itchy and embarrassing but cover only a small area of her body. She has never had treatment. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.B: Emollient plus a potent topical corticosteroid and a topical vitamin D analogue
options.C: A reducing course of oral prednisolone

correct_answer: B. Emollient plus a potent topical corticosteroid and a topical vitamin D analogue
why_correct: Limited chronic plaque psoriasis on the trunk and limbs is treated topically first. NICE recommends a potent topical corticosteroid applied once daily plus a topical vitamin D analogue applied once daily at a different time, for up to 4 weeks, with emollients throughout. If this is not effective, a vitamin D analogue alone or a combined preparation can follow.
why_wrong: A. Ciclosporin is a systemic treatment for extensive or severe disease not controlled topically. C. Systemic corticosteroids can provoke severe or pustular flares when withdrawn and are avoided in psoriasis. D. Biologics are reserved for severe disease after failure of standard systemic treatment. E. Antifungal cream does not treat psoriasis.
pearl: Nail pitting and onycholysis are clues to psoriasis. Ask about joint symptoms at each review, as psoriatic arthritis can develop and needs rheumatology referral.
thinking: Well-defined plaques with silvery scale on extensor surfaces ↓ Nail pitting supports psoriasis ↓ Limited disease with no previous treatment ↓ Emollient plus potent steroid and vitamin D analogue
exam_trap: C, oral prednisolone — tempting as a quick way to settle inflammation, but systemic steroids can cause a severe rebound or pustular flare in psoriasis.
takeaway: Limited plaque psoriasis: emollient plus potent topical steroid and vitamin D analogue first-line.

stem: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the GP by his father because of itchy skin that keeps him awake. He has had dry skin since infancy and has asthma. There are dry, red, thickened patches in the creases behind his knees and inside his elbows with scratch marks. There is no weeping, crusting or punched-out erosions, and he is otherwise well. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Regular emollients plus a topical corticosteroid for the flare
options.E: A short course of oral prednisolone

correct_answer: A. Regular emollients plus a topical corticosteroid for the flare
why_correct: Atopic eczema in children is managed with liberal, regular emollients used for washing and moisturising, even when the skin is clear. Flares are treated with a topical corticosteroid of potency matched to severity and site, applied to inflamed areas until settled. Triggers should be identified and parents given clear written guidance.
why_wrong: B. There are no signs of bacterial infection such as weeping or crusting, so antibiotics are not needed. C. Topical calcineurin inhibitors are second-line, usually for sites such as the face or when steroids are unsuitable. D. Antihistamines are not recommended routinely; a sedating one may be used briefly for sleep disturbance. E. Systemic steroids are not used for routine childhood eczema flares.
pearl: Punched-out erosions, painful rapidly worsening eczema and fever suggest eczema herpeticum, which needs urgent same-day aciclovir and referral.
thinking: Itchy, dry, thickened flexural skin in an atopic child ↓ Atopic eczema with a current flare ↓ No infection or eczema herpeticum ↓ Regular emollients plus topical steroid
exam_trap: C, topical tacrolimus — tempting as a steroid-sparing option, but calcineurin inhibitors are second-line and reserved for specific sites or steroid problems.
takeaway: Childhood eczema: regular emollients always, with a topical corticosteroid for flares.

stem: A 47-year-old man attends the emergency department with two days of spreading redness, heat and swelling of his left forearm that began after a scratch while gardening. He has had rigors. His temperature is 38.6 degrees C, pulse 108 bpm and blood pressure 128/76 mmHg; he is alert. There is no crepitus, blistering, skin necrosis or pain out of proportion to the signs. He has no allergies. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Oral flucloxacillin with review in 48 hours
options.C: IV flucloxacillin, with admission or ambulatory IV care

correct_answer: C. IV flucloxacillin, with admission or ambulatory IV care
why_correct: This is cellulitis with systemic features such as fever, rigors and tachycardia, but without signs of sepsis with organ dysfunction or necrotising infection. Flucloxacillin is the first-choice antibiotic, and IV treatment is appropriate when the patient is systemically unwell. Care can be delivered on the ward or through an ambulatory IV service, switching to oral treatment as he improves; the edge of the erythema should be marked to monitor progress.
why_wrong: A. Oral treatment suits patients who are systemically well; this man has fever, rigors and tachycardia. B. Topical antibiotics do not treat cellulitis, a deeper dermal infection. D. There are no features of necrotising fasciitis to justify surgery. E. Doxycycline is reserved for penicillin allergy and is not the first choice here.
pearl: Pain out of proportion, rapid spread, crepitus, bullae, skin necrosis or severe systemic upset suggest necrotising fasciitis, which needs emergency surgical referral.
thinking: Spreading erythema and swelling after a skin break ↓ Fever, rigors and tachycardia mean systemic illness ↓ No necrotising features or organ dysfunction ↓ IV flucloxacillin with inpatient or ambulatory care
exam_trap: A, oral flucloxacillin — tempting because it is the right antibiotic for most cellulitis, but systemic illness with fever and tachycardia calls for IV treatment.
takeaway: Cellulitis with systemic illness: IV flucloxacillin, as an inpatient or via ambulatory IV care.

stem: A 16-year-old boy sees his GP about spots on his face and upper back. There are many inflamed papules and pustules with some comedones, but no nodules, cysts or scarring. He has used an over-the-counter benzoyl peroxide wash every day for three months with little change. He is otherwise well and keen to try something more effective. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Topical fixed combination of a retinoid and an antibiotic (e.g. tretinoin with clindamycin)
options.B: Oral isotretinoin prescribed by the GP

correct_answer: A. Topical fixed combination of a retinoid and an antibiotic (e.g. tretinoin with clindamycin)
why_correct: For moderate acne, NICE recommends a 12-week course of a fixed topical combination, such as tretinoin with clindamycin or adapalene with benzoyl peroxide, or a topical treatment combined with an oral tetracycline. A combination of a retinoid with an antibiotic is more effective than either alone and reduces antibiotic resistance. Response should be reviewed at the end of the course.
why_wrong: B. Isotretinoin is prescribed only under specialist supervision and is reserved for severe or resistant acne. C. Minocycline is not recommended, and antibiotics should not be used as monotherapy for acne. D. Topical antibiotic monotherapy promotes resistance and is not recommended. E. Topical steroids do not treat acne and can worsen it.
pearl: Never use antibiotics alone for acne: always combine with a topical retinoid or benzoyl peroxide. Refer for isotretinoin if acne is severe, scarring, or fails two courses of appropriate treatment.
thinking: Papules and pustules without nodules or scarring ↓ Moderate acne not responding to benzoyl peroxide alone ↓ Combination topical therapy is first-line for moderate acne ↓ Topical retinoid plus antibiotic
exam_trap: C, oral minocycline — tempting because oral antibiotics are familiar acne treatments, but minocycline is not recommended and antibiotic monotherapy drives resistance.
takeaway: Moderate acne: use a fixed topical combination; never use antibiotics alone.

stem: A 40-year-old office worker sees her GP with three weeks of intense itching that is worst at night. There are small red papules and short, wavy grey lines on her wrists, between her fingers and around her waist. Her husband has recently started itching too. There is no crusting or thickened skin, and she is not pregnant. What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.A: Permethrin 5% cream to the affected areas only
options.D: Permethrin 5% cream to the whole body, repeated after 7 days, with all close contacts treated at the same time

correct_answer: D. Permethrin 5% cream to the whole body, repeated after 7 days, with all close contacts treated at the same time
why_correct: Nocturnal itch, burrows in the finger webs and wrists and an itchy household contact indicate scabies. Permethrin 5% cream is applied to the whole body, including the scalp, neck, face and ears in adults where indicated, and under the nails, left on for 8 to 12 hours, then washed off and repeated after 7 days. All household and close contacts must be treated at the same time, and bedding and clothing washed at a high temperature.
why_wrong: A. Mites live beyond visible lesions, so treating only affected areas leads to failure. B. Antihistamines relieve itch but do not kill the mite. C. Topical steroids can mask and worsen scabies. E. Oral ivermectin is reserved for crusted scabies or treatment failure under specialist advice.
pearl: Itch can persist for up to 4 weeks after successful treatment, so it does not mean treatment has failed. Crusted scabies is highly contagious and needs specialist management.
thinking: Nocturnal itch with burrows on hands and wrists ↓ Partner also itching ↓ Scabies ↓ Whole-body permethrin, repeated after a week, with contacts treated
exam_trap: A, permethrin to affected areas only — tempting because it uses the correct drug, but scabies requires whole-body application and treatment of all contacts to prevent reinfestation.
takeaway: Scabies: whole-body permethrin repeated after 7 days, treating all close contacts at the same time.

presentation: Basal cell carcinoma at a high-risk site
stem: A 71-year-old retired farmer sees his GP about a lesion at the inner corner of his left lower eyelid. It has grown slowly over a year into a pearly nodule with a rolled edge and fine surface vessels, and it now extends onto the eyelid margin close to the tear duct. The GP is concerned that waiting for a routine appointment could allow it to involve the tear drainage system and make surgery considerably more complex. There is no palpable lymphadenopathy. What is the most appropriate management?

options.E: Reassure him that this is a seborrhoeic keratosis

why_correct: A pearly nodule with a rolled edge and telangiectasia is typical of a nodular basal cell carcinoma. NICE advises a routine referral for most suspected BCCs, but a suspected cancer pathway referral should be considered where there is particular concern that delay could have a significant impact, for example because of the lesion's site or size. A periocular lesion extending onto the eyelid margin near the tear duct, with a specific concern about more complex surgery if delayed, meets that threshold; surgical excision is usually the definitive treatment.
why_wrong: A. Routine referral suits most BCCs, but this lesion's site and progression mean delay could significantly affect outcome. C. Cryotherapy is unsuitable for a nodular BCC at a high-risk periocular site. D. Topical treatments are for superficial BCC, not a nodular lesion near the eye. E. The pearly rolled edge and telangiectasia are features of BCC, not seborrhoeic keratosis.
pearl: Most BCCs are slow-growing and rarely metastasise, so routine referral is usual. Site, size and the impact of delay on surgery are what justify a faster referral.
thinking: Pearly nodule with rolled edge and telangiectasia ↓ Nodular BCC ↓ Periocular site involving the eyelid margin with concern that delay worsens surgery ↓ Suspected cancer pathway referral
exam_trap: A, non-urgent referral — tempting because it is the correct route for most BCCs, but particular concern that delay will significantly affect treatment at a critical site justifies a faster pathway.
takeaway: Most BCCs need routine referral; use a suspected cancer pathway when site or size makes delay significant.

stem: A 66-year-old man sees his GP with a painful rash on the left side of his lower back and flank. Two days before it appeared he felt burning and tingling in the same area. The rash appeared yesterday and consists of clusters of vesicles on a red base in a band that stops at the midline. His face and eyes are not affected, he is otherwise well and he is not immunosuppressed. What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.D: Oral antiviral (aciclovir or valaciclovir) for 7 days

correct_answer: D. Oral antiviral (aciclovir or valaciclovir) for 7 days
why_correct: A painful unilateral dermatomal vesicular rash preceded by tingling is herpes zoster. In a person over 50 presenting within 72 hours of rash onset, an oral antiviral for 7 days is recommended to reduce pain, duration and the risk of post-herpetic neuralgia; valaciclovir or famciclovir can be used if adherence to five-times-daily aciclovir is a concern. Analgesia and advice to avoid contact with pregnant women without immunity, neonates and immunosuppressed people should be given.
why_wrong: A. Antiviral treatment is indicated in a person of this age presenting early. B. Topical aciclovir is not effective for shingles. C. IV treatment is for immunosuppressed patients or severe or disseminated disease. E. Steroids alone are not recommended and do not treat the viral infection.
pearl: Shingles involving the tip of the nose (Hutchinson's sign) or with eye symptoms needs same-day ophthalmology assessment. Immunosuppressed patients need antivirals whatever the timing.
thinking: Prodromal tingling then painful dermatomal vesicles ↓ Herpes zoster ↓ Over 50 and presenting within 72 hours ↓ Oral antiviral for 7 days
exam_trap: A, analgesia only — tempting because shingles is self-limiting, but in older patients presenting early, antivirals reduce acute pain and the risk of post-herpetic neuralgia.
takeaway: Shingles in someone over 50 within 72 hours of rash: give an oral antiviral for 7 days.

stem: A 70-year-old long-sighted man attends an urgent treatment centre late in the evening. Since leaving a dimly lit cinema an hour earlier he has had a severely painful red left eye, haloes around lights and reduced vision, and he has vomited twice. The left cornea looks cloudy and the pupil is semi-dilated and unreactive to light. The eye feels hard on gentle palpation through the lid. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Chloramphenicol eye drops and GP review in 48 hours
options.B: Start pressure-lowering treatment such as acetazolamide and pilocarpine, and refer to ophthalmology immediately
options.C: Dilate the pupil with tropicamide to examine the fundus
options.D: CT head for suspected subarachnoid haemorrhage
options.E: Topical steroid drops and next-day eye clinic review

correct_answer: B. Start pressure-lowering treatment such as acetazolamide and pilocarpine, and refer to ophthalmology immediately
why_correct: A painful red eye with haloes, vomiting, a hazy cornea, a fixed mid-dilated pupil and a hard globe after time in dim light is acute angle-closure glaucoma, a sight-threatening emergency. Treatment to lower intraocular pressure (acetazolamide, pilocarpine to constrict the pupil, often with a topical beta-blocker) should be started while arranging immediate same-day ophthalmology review for definitive laser iridotomy.
why_wrong: A. This is not conjunctivitis; delay risks permanent optic nerve damage. C. Dilating the pupil can worsen angle closure. D. Headache and vomiting can mimic a neurological cause, but the red eye, hazy cornea and hard globe localise the problem to the eye. E. Steroids treat anterior uveitis, which causes a small pupil and does not raise pressure this acutely.
pearl: Dim light, reading or dilating drops can trigger angle closure in long-sighted older people because the pupil dilates and blocks drainage in an already narrow angle.
thinking: Painful red eye with haloes and vomiting ↓ Hazy cornea, fixed mid-dilated pupil, hard eye ↓ Raised intraocular pressure from angle closure ↓ Lower pressure now and get specialist help ↓ Acetazolamide, pilocarpine and immediate ophthalmology referral
exam_trap: D, CT head — tempting because severe headache with vomiting suggests an intracranial cause, but the red eye with a cloudy cornea and fixed pupil points to angle-closure glaucoma.
takeaway: Painful red eye, haloes, fixed mid-dilated pupil: lower the pressure and refer immediately.

stem: A 45-year-old woman who wears strong glasses for short sight phones her GP surgery. Since yesterday evening she has noticed a shower of dark specks and brief flashes in her left eye. This morning a dark shadow began to spread across the upper part of her vision in that eye. The eye is not painful or red. What is the most appropriate action?

options.B: Reassure her that this is a harmless vitreous detachment
options.C: Urgent referral to the TIA clinic
options.D: Start aspirin and arrange carotid Doppler scans
options.E: Same-day assessment by the eye emergency service

correct_answer: E. Same-day assessment by the eye emergency service
why_correct: New floaters and flashes followed by a spreading shadow in the field of vision in a short-sighted patient is a retinal detachment until proven otherwise. She needs same-day ophthalmology assessment, because prompt surgical repair, especially before the macula detaches, gives the best chance of preserving central vision.
why_wrong: A. A two-week wait risks progression to macula-off detachment and permanent visual loss. B. Flashes and floaters alone may be a vitreous detachment, but a field defect indicates retinal detachment. C. A spreading curtain with flashes and floaters is a retinal, not a vascular, problem. D. Aspirin and carotid imaging are for amaurosis fugax, which is transient and not preceded by floaters.
pearl: Flashes and floaters alone need urgent assessment for a retinal tear; add a curtain or shadow and it becomes a same-day retinal detachment emergency. Myopia is a major risk factor.
thinking: Myopic patient with new floaters and flashes ↓ Now a spreading shadow in the field ↓ Retina is separating ↓ Sight-threatening, time-critical ↓ Same-day eye emergency assessment
exam_trap: B, Reassure as vitreous detachment — tempting because vitreous detachment is common and causes flashes and floaters, but a shadow in the visual field means the retina itself is involved.
takeaway: Flashes, floaters and a field shadow mean retinal detachment: same-day ophthalmology.

stem: A 62-year-old woman with long-standing type 2 diabetes is referred by the diabetic eye screening service. Her reading vision in the right eye has worsened over two months. Optical coherence tomography shows marked thickening of the retina at the centre of the macula with intraretinal fluid. There are no new vessels. What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.E: Improved glucose control alone with screening review in 12 months

why_correct: Centre-involving diabetic macular oedema with reduced vision is treated with intravitreal anti-VEGF agents (such as aflibercept, ranibizumab or faricimab), which NICE recommends and which give better visual outcomes than laser for this pattern. Systemic control of glucose, blood pressure and lipids should be optimised alongside, but is not enough on its own.
why_wrong: A. Panretinal laser treats proliferative retinopathy with new vessels, which is absent here. C. Topical NSAIDs are not a treatment for diabetic macular oedema. D. Vitrectomy is reserved for complications such as non-clearing vitreous haemorrhage or traction. E. Vision is already falling from centre-involving oedema, so delay risks permanent loss.
pearl: Diabetic eye disease: centre-involving macular oedema with visual loss is treated with anti-VEGF; proliferative retinopathy is treated with panretinal laser.
thinking: Diabetic patient with falling central vision ↓ OCT shows centre-involving macular oedema ↓ No new vessels, so not proliferative ↓ Treatment of choice for centre-involving oedema ↓ Intravitreal anti-VEGF
exam_trap: A, Panretinal laser — tempting because laser is the classic diabetic eye treatment, but it is used for proliferative disease, not centre-involving macular oedema.
takeaway: Centre-involving diabetic macular oedema with visual loss: intravitreal anti-VEGF.

stem: A 67-year-old retired taxi driver is seen in the GP surgery after his optometrist noticed changes in his eyes. Over 18 months his vision has become misty in both eyes and colours look faded. He has stopped driving at night because oncoming headlights dazzle him, and he is keen to drive again. Visual acuity is reduced in both eyes, the red reflex is dull and lens opacities are visible. The fundi look normal where they can be seen. What is the most appropriate management?

options.D: New glasses and review once the cataracts are mature

why_correct: Gradual bilateral blurring, faded colours, glare from headlights and lens opacities with a dull red reflex indicate cataracts. NICE advises referral for cataract surgery when the cataract affects quality of life, such as driving, and there is no requirement to wait for the cataract to become mature. Phacoemulsification with lens implant is the only effective treatment.
why_wrong: A. No supplement reverses or treats cataract. B. Lubricants relieve dry eyes but do not improve lens opacity. D. Waiting for maturity is outdated advice; surgery is offered when symptoms affect daily life. E. Steroid drops do not treat cataract and long-term steroid use can cause it.
pearl: Refer for cataract surgery based on the impact on the patient's life, not on visual acuity alone or the maturity of the cataract. Posterior subcapsular cataracts cause particular glare problems.
thinking: Gradual bilateral blur with glare and faded colours ↓ Dull red reflex with lens opacities ↓ Cataract ↓ Symptoms affect driving and quality of life ↓ Refer for cataract surgery
exam_trap: D, Wait until mature — tempting because older teaching delayed surgery, but current practice offers surgery as soon as the cataract affects daily life.
takeaway: Refer for cataract surgery when it affects daily life; waiting for maturity is not required.

stem: An 80-year-old man tells his optician that over the past two weeks the edges of door frames look wavy through his right eye and there is a grey smudge in the middle of the page when he reads. Examination shows a raised grey-green lesion with a small haemorrhage at the right macula. What is the most likely diagnosis and the most appropriate treatment?

options.A: Neovascular (wet) age-related macular degeneration — intravitreal anti-VEGF injections
options.B: Dry age-related macular degeneration — vitamin supplements and low-vision aids
options.C: Central retinal vein occlusion — aspirin and observation
options.D: Neovascular (wet) age-related macular degeneration — panretinal laser photocoagulation

correct_answer: A. Neovascular (wet) age-related macular degeneration — intravitreal anti-VEGF injections
why_correct: Rapid onset of distortion of straight lines (metamorphopsia) and a central scotoma with a raised lesion and haemorrhage at the macula indicates choroidal neovascularisation, that is wet AMD. It needs rapid referral to a macular service, and intravitreal anti-VEGF injections are first-line treatment, stabilising and often improving vision.
why_wrong: B. Dry AMD causes slow, gradual loss without haemorrhage or sudden distortion. C. Retinal vein occlusion causes widespread retinal haemorrhages, and aspirin is not a treatment for it. D. Panretinal laser is for proliferative diabetic retinopathy, not wet AMD. E. Macular hole causes a central defect but not a raised neovascular lesion with haemorrhage.
pearl: Sudden distortion of straight lines in an older person means wet AMD until proven otherwise: refer urgently, as anti-VEGF works best when started early.
thinking: Older patient with new distortion and central blur ↓ Raised macular lesion with haemorrhage ↓ Choroidal neovascularisation ↓ Wet AMD ↓ Intravitreal anti-VEGF
exam_trap: B, Dry AMD — tempting because dry AMD is far more common, but the speed of onset, distortion and haemorrhage point to the wet, treatable form.
takeaway: Sudden wavy lines in an older patient suggest wet AMD: urgent referral for anti-VEGF.

stem: A 31-year-old woman attends the early pregnancy unit with seven weeks of amenorrhoea and a day of light brown vaginal bleeding.
