stem: A 23-year-old woman is admitted to the acute medical unit having taken an overdose the previous evening. She has vomited repeatedly, is sweaty, and describes a constant buzzing in her ears with muffled hearing. A venous blood gas shows a metabolic acidosis with a raised anion gap. Which drug did she most likely take?
why_correct: Vomiting, sweating, tinnitus with reduced hearing and a raised anion gap metabolic acidosis after an overdose point to aspirin. Salicylates disrupt cellular metabolism, producing acid, and directly affect the inner ear. A salicylate level guides treatment such as urinary alkalinisation or haemodialysis in severe cases.
why_wrong: A. Amitriptyline causes drowsiness, anticholinergic signs, seizures and arrhythmias rather than tinnitus. B. Paracetamol causes delayed liver injury and does not cause tinnitus. C. Iron causes vomiting and acidosis but not tinnitus or hearing change. D. Lithium toxicity causes tremor, ataxia and confusion rather than tinnitus with acidosis.
pearl: Tinnitus or deafness after an overdose should prompt a salicylate level, even when the patient does not name the drug taken.
thinking: Overdose with repeated vomiting ↓ tinnitus and muffled hearing ↓ raised anion gap metabolic acidosis ↓ combination fits salicylate toxicity ↓ Aspirin
exam_trap: C, Iron sulfate — iron overdose also causes vomiting and a metabolic acidosis, but it does not affect hearing, which is the discriminating clue.
takeaway: Overdose with vomiting, acidosis and ear symptoms suggests aspirin: check a salicylate level.

stem: A 29-year-old man on an acute psychiatric ward received intramuscular haloperidol for severe agitation two days ago. He is now sweating heavily, has a high temperature and is drowsy. His limbs show uniform lead-pipe stiffness, and his blood pressure and heart rate fluctuate widely. Creatine kinase is markedly raised. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Hyperthermia, lead-pipe rigidity, altered consciousness, autonomic instability and a raised creatine kinase after a dopamine antagonist are the hallmarks of neuroleptic malignant syndrome. It typically develops over days after starting or increasing an antipsychotic. Management is to stop the antipsychotic, give supportive care with cooling and fluids, and seek urgent senior and critical care input.
why_wrong: A. An acute dystonic reaction causes sudden muscle spasms such as oculogyric crisis, without fever or autonomic instability. B. Serotonin syndrome follows serotonergic drugs and causes clonus and hyperreflexia rather than lead-pipe rigidity. C. Malignant hyperthermia is triggered by volatile anaesthetics or suxamethonium. D. Meningoencephalitis can cause fever and drowsiness but does not explain the rigidity and timing after haloperidol.
pearl: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome evolves over days with lead-pipe rigidity and slow reflexes. Serotonin syndrome evolves over hours with clonus and hyperreflexia.
thinking: Recent haloperidol ↓ fever, drowsiness and autonomic instability ↓ lead-pipe rigidity with high CK ↓ dopamine blockade syndrome ↓ Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
exam_trap: B, Serotonin syndrome — it shares fever, confusion and autonomic instability, but the trigger is serotonergic and the neuromuscular sign is clonus, not lead-pipe rigidity.
takeaway: Fever, lead-pipe rigidity and a high CK after an antipsychotic means neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

stem: A 30-year-old man attends the GP surgery with three days of sore throat, runny nose and a dry cough. He is afebrile with no tonsillar exudate or enlarged neck glands. He asks for antibiotics because he is going on holiday next week. The GP explains that this is most likely viral, so antibiotics would not shorten it, advises on self-care, and explains when to seek help. No prescription is issued. Which principle is the GP demonstrating?
why_correct: Antimicrobial stewardship means using antimicrobials only when they are likely to benefit the patient, to reduce resistance and avoid unnecessary adverse effects. Explaining that a self-limiting viral illness will not respond to antibiotics, giving self-care advice and safety-netting is a core stewardship approach in primary care. NICE guidance supports a no-antibiotic or back-up strategy for most respiratory tract infections.
why_wrong: A. Delayed prescribing involves issuing a back-up prescription to use if symptoms worsen, which did not happen here. C. Therapeutic duplication is prescribing overlapping drugs. D. Defensive practice is acting mainly to protect the clinician rather than to benefit the patient. E. Polypharmacy refers to the use of multiple medicines.
pearl: Most upper respiratory tract infections are viral and self-limiting. Explaining the expected course and safety-netting is as important as the decision not to prescribe.
thinking: Viral-sounding upper respiratory illness ↓ patient requests antibiotics ↓ GP explains no benefit and offers self-care with safety-netting ↓ responsible use of antimicrobials ↓ Antimicrobial stewardship
exam_trap: A, Delayed antibiotic prescribing — it is a stewardship tool and sounds similar, but it involves issuing a back-up prescription, and none was given here.
takeaway: Withholding antibiotics for viral illness, with explanation and safety-netting, is antimicrobial stewardship.

stem: A 41-year-old man attends the GP surgery with a tender swelling on the back of his shoulder that has enlarged over four days. There is a warm, red, fluctuant lump about the size of a plum, with a yellow point at its centre and a small rim of surrounding redness. He is afebrile and otherwise well. Which management is most appropriate?

options.E: Review in one month if it persists

why_correct: A fluctuant, pointing swelling is a collection of pus, and the definitive treatment of a skin abscess is incision and drainage. Antibiotics penetrate a walled-off collection poorly and are reserved for extensive surrounding cellulitis, systemic illness or higher-risk patients. Pus can be sent for culture at the time of drainage.
why_wrong: A. Topical antibiotics do not treat a deep collection. B. Antibiotics alone rarely resolve an established abscess. D. Excision biopsy is for suspected tumours, not infection. E. Delaying treatment allows the infection to extend and cause systemic illness.
pearl: Fluctuance means pus. If pus is present, it needs to be drained; antibiotics are an adjunct, not the main treatment.
thinking: Enlarging painful lump ↓ warm, red, fluctuant and pointing ↓ established abscess ↓ pus needs a route out ↓ Incision and drainage
exam_trap: B, Oral flucloxacillin alone — it covers the likely staphylococcal cause, but an antibiotic cannot reliably penetrate an established abscess, which needs drainage.
takeaway: A fluctuant skin abscess is treated by incision and drainage, not antibiotics alone.

stem: A 52-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes attends the emergency department with three days of throbbing pain beside her anus. The pain is constant, not just on opening her bowels, and she can no longer sit down. Her temperature is 38.4°C. There is a hot, red, tender, indurated swelling at the anal margin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A constant throbbing pain with a hot, red, tender swelling at the anal margin and fever indicates a perianal abscess, usually arising from infection of an anal gland. Diabetes increases the risk. Treatment is prompt surgical incision and drainage, with antibiotics in addition if there is systemic illness or significant surrounding cellulitis.
why_wrong: A. A thrombosed external haemorrhoid is a painful bluish lump but does not cause fever or a hot, indurated swelling. B. A pilonidal abscess arises in the natal cleft, not at the anal margin. C. A fissure causes pain on defecation and a visible split, not fever with a swelling. E. Rectal prolapse causes a mass protruding through the anus, usually without fever.
pearl: Fever with a hot, tender perianal swelling is an abscess until proved otherwise. Diabetes and Crohn's disease increase the risk.
thinking: Constant perianal pain, unable to sit ↓ fever ↓ hot, red, indurated swelling at the anal margin ↓ infected collection near the anus ↓ Perianal abscess
exam_trap: A, Thrombosed external haemorrhoid — it causes a painful perianal lump, but not fever, induration or spreading redness.
takeaway: A hot, tender perianal swelling with fever is a perianal abscess needing drainage.

stem: A 55-year-old taxi driver attends the GP surgery for review two weeks after a flare of gout in his right ankle, which has now settled. It is his third flare this year. He is overweight and asks what changes he can make himself to reduce further attacks. Which advice is most appropriate?

options.A: Replace water with fruit juice to stay hydrated
options.B: Reduce his alcohol intake, particularly beer
options.C: Lose weight quickly with a very low-calorie fasting diet
options.D: Increase his intake of offal and shellfish for protein
options.E: Avoid all physical activity to protect his joints

correct_answer: B. Reduce his alcohol intake, particularly beer
why_correct: Alcohol, particularly beer, raises serum urate and is a common trigger for gout flares, so reducing intake is recommended. Other helpful measures include gradual weight loss, regular exercise and staying well hydrated with water. With recurrent flares he should also be offered urate-lowering therapy.
why_wrong: A. Fructose-sweetened drinks, including some fruit juices, raise urate. C. Rapid weight loss or fasting can raise urate and provoke flares, whereas gradual loss is beneficial. D. Offal and shellfish are purine-rich and increase urate. E. Regular activity is encouraged and does not worsen gout.
pearl: Lifestyle advice in gout: limit alcohol (especially beer), avoid sugary drinks, lose weight gradually and keep active. Recurrent flares warrant urate-lowering therapy.
thinking: Recurrent gout flares ↓ asking about self-help ↓ identify factors that lower urate ↓ alcohol is a key modifiable trigger ↓ Reduce alcohol, particularly beer
exam_trap: C, Lose weight quickly with a very low-calorie fasting diet — weight loss helps gout, so it tempts, but rapid weight loss and fasting can raise urate and trigger attacks.
takeaway: Reducing alcohol, especially beer, is a key self-help measure to reduce gout flares.

stem: A 46-year-old man is seen in the rheumatology clinic with three months of painful, swollen hands. Squeezing across his knuckles is painful on both sides, and several finger joints are swollen. He feels stiff for well over an hour each morning. Hand X-rays are normal. Which antibody test is most specific for rheumatoid arthritis?
why_correct: Anti-CCP antibodies are highly specific for rheumatoid arthritis and support the diagnosis in a patient with symmetrical small-joint synovitis. A positive result also predicts a more erosive course. NICE recommends testing rheumatoid factor first in suspected rheumatoid arthritis and anti-CCP if rheumatoid factor is negative, but anti-CCP is the more specific test.
why_wrong: A. Rheumatoid factor is common in RA but is also found in other conditions and healthy older people, so it is less specific. B. ANA is sensitive for lupus but not specific for RA. D. HLA-B27 is a genetic marker associated with spondyloarthritis, not an antibody test for RA. E. Anti-dsDNA is specific for systemic lupus erythematosus.
pearl: Rheumatoid factor is more widely used but less specific; anti-CCP is highly specific and predicts erosive disease. Normal early X-rays do not exclude RA.
thinking: Symmetrical small-joint swelling ↓ prolonged morning stiffness ↓ suspected rheumatoid arthritis ↓ choose the most specific antibody ↓ Anti-CCP antibody
exam_trap: A, Rheumatoid factor — it is the best known and is tested first in practice, but it is less specific than anti-CCP.
takeaway: Anti-CCP is the most specific antibody test for rheumatoid arthritis.

stem: A 71-year-old man with long-standing seropositive rheumatoid arthritis is seen in pre-assessment before an elective hip replacement. He mentions a few months of pain at the back of his head and upper neck, tingling in both hands and increasing clumsiness with buttons. Examination shows brisk reflexes in all four limbs and upgoing plantar responses. Which complication needs to be considered?
why_correct: Long-standing rheumatoid arthritis can weaken the ligaments stabilising the atlantoaxial joint, allowing subluxation that compresses the upper cervical cord. Occipital and neck pain with upper motor neurone signs in all four limbs suggests cervical myelopathy from this cause. It needs urgent imaging and specialist review, and is particularly important before anaesthesia because neck manipulation during intubation can cause cord injury.
why_wrong: A. Nerve root compression causes lower motor neurone signs in one dermatome, not brisk reflexes in all limbs. C. Carpal tunnel syndrome causes median nerve sensory symptoms without upper motor neurone signs or neck pain. D. Mononeuritis multiplex causes patchy lower motor neurone deficits. E. Peripheral neuropathy reduces reflexes rather than making them brisk.
pearl: Neck pain with upper motor neurone signs in rheumatoid arthritis suggests atlantoaxial subluxation. Flag it before any general anaesthetic.
thinking: Long-standing rheumatoid arthritis ↓ occipital and neck pain ↓ hand clumsiness with brisk reflexes and upgoing plantars ↓ high cervical cord compression ↓ Atlantoaxial subluxation
exam_trap: C, Bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome — it is common in RA and causes tingling hands, but it cannot produce brisk reflexes or extensor plantars.
takeaway: Rheumatoid arthritis with neck pain and upper motor neurone signs suggests atlantoaxial subluxation.

stem: A 39-year-old man attends the GP surgery with two months of pain in the small joints of his hands and feet. The GP wants to judge whether this is more likely to be inflammatory or mechanical. Which additional feature of the history would most suggest an inflammatory arthritis?

options.A: Pain that is worse at the end of a working day
options.B: Stiffness on waking that lasts more than an hour and eases with activity
options.C: Brief stiffness after sitting that resolves within minutes
options.D: Pain that is relieved by resting the joints
options.E: Episodes of the joints locking or giving way

correct_answer: B. Stiffness on waking that lasts more than an hour and eases with activity
why_correct: Prolonged early morning stiffness that improves with use is a hallmark of inflammatory joint disease, reflecting synovitis that eases as the joints are moved. Along with joint swelling and symmetrical small-joint involvement, it should prompt urgent rheumatology referral. Mechanical problems tend to worsen with use and improve with rest.
why_wrong: A. Pain building up through the day with use suggests a mechanical or degenerative process. C. Short-lived stiffness after inactivity is typical of osteoarthritis. D. Inflammatory pain typically improves with movement, whereas rest relieves mechanical pain. E. Locking and giving way suggest a mechanical internal joint problem.
pearl: Inflammatory: prolonged morning stiffness, better with activity. Mechanical: brief stiffness, worse with use, better with rest.
thinking: Small-joint pain in hands and feet ↓ need to separate inflammatory from mechanical ↓ inflammatory pain eases with movement ↓ long morning stiffness is characteristic ↓ Prolonged morning stiffness easing with activity
exam_trap: D, Pain relieved by resting the joints — rest sounds like a sensible response to inflammation, but inflammatory symptoms worsen with immobility and improve with movement.
takeaway: Morning stiffness lasting over an hour and easing with activity suggests inflammatory arthritis.

stem: A 58-year-old woman who takes naproxen daily for osteoarthritis develops abrupt, severe upper abdominal pain an hour before arriving in the emergency department. She is lying completely still, and any movement worsens the pain. Her abdomen is board-like with guarding throughout and absent bowel sounds. She is tachycardic. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Sudden severe abdominal pain with a board-like abdomen, generalised guarding and a patient lying still are signs of generalised peritonitis. In a patient taking an NSAID, a perforated peptic ulcer is the likely cause. She needs resuscitation, an erect chest X-ray or CT, and urgent surgical review.
why_wrong: A. Pancreatitis causes severe epigastric pain but rarely a truly board-like abdomen with such a sudden onset. B. Biliary colic causes colicky pain without peritonism. C. Gastritis causes epigastric discomfort without peritonitis. D. An inferior MI can cause epigastric pain but not a rigid abdomen.
pearl: Board-like rigidity with a patient lying still means peritonitis. NSAIDs and steroids increase the risk of peptic ulcer perforation.
thinking: Sudden severe abdominal pain ↓ lying still, rigid abdomen ↓ generalised peritonitis ↓ NSAID use suggests ulcer perforation ↓ Perforated abdominal viscus
exam_trap: A, Acute pancreatitis — it also causes severe upper abdominal pain with tenderness, but sudden onset and board-like rigidity point to perforation.
takeaway: Sudden pain with a rigid abdomen means peritonitis: suspect perforation and get urgent surgical review.

stem: An 80-year-old woman is sent from her care home to the emergency department with three days of colicky abdominal pain. Her abdomen has become swollen and tense, she has vomited several times, and staff report she has not passed wind for two days. On auscultation the bowel sounds are high-pitched and tinkling. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Colicky pain, abdominal distension, vomiting and absolute constipation are the cardinal features of intestinal obstruction. High-pitched, tinkling bowel sounds indicate a mechanical obstruction. She needs fluid resuscitation, nasogastric decompression, imaging to find the level and cause, and surgical review.
why_wrong: B. Paralytic ileus causes distension and absent flatus, but bowel sounds are absent and pain is not usually colicky. C. Diverticulitis causes left iliac fossa pain and fever rather than this picture. D. Gastroenteritis causes vomiting and diarrhoea rather than failure to pass flatus. E. Urinary retention causes suprapubic swelling and discomfort but not vomiting with absolute constipation.
pearl: Colicky pain, distension, vomiting and absolute constipation suggest obstruction. Tinkling bowel sounds suggest mechanical obstruction; silence suggests ileus or late obstruction.
thinking: Colicky abdominal pain ↓ distension and vomiting ↓ no flatus for two days ↓ tinkling bowel sounds ↓ Intestinal obstruction
exam_trap: B, Paralytic ileus — it also causes distension and absent flatus, but bowel sounds are absent rather than tinkling, and colicky pain is unusual.
takeaway: Colicky pain, distension, vomiting and absolute constipation indicate intestinal obstruction.

stem: A 44-year-old man attends the emergency department with a day of colicky central abdominal pain and repeated bilious vomiting. He has not opened his bowels or passed wind since yesterday. He had a laparotomy after a road traffic collision ten years ago and has a healed midline scar. His hernial orifices are normal. An abdominal X-ray shows dilated central loops of small bowel. What is the most likely cause?
why_correct: Colicky central pain, early bilious vomiting, absolute constipation and dilated small bowel loops indicate small bowel obstruction. In a patient with previous abdominal surgery and normal hernial orifices, adhesions are by far the most likely cause. Many cases settle with conservative management (nil by mouth, nasogastric decompression and fluids), but signs of strangulation need urgent surgery.
why_wrong: A. Hernias are a common cause of small bowel obstruction, but his hernial orifices are normal. C. Sigmoid volvulus causes large bowel obstruction, usually in older adults with chronic constipation. D. Colorectal cancer causes large bowel obstruction and is less likely at his age. E. Gallstone ileus is rare and occurs mainly in older women.
pearl: In small bowel obstruction, look for a scar and examine the hernial orifices: adhesions after previous surgery and hernias are the commonest causes.
thinking: Colicky central pain with bilious vomiting ↓ absolute constipation ↓ dilated small bowel loops ↓ previous laparotomy, hernial orifices normal ↓ Adhesional small bowel obstruction
exam_trap: A, Obstructed inguinal hernia — hernias are a leading cause of small bowel obstruction, but his hernial orifices are normal and he has had previous surgery.
takeaway: Small bowel obstruction after previous abdominal surgery is most likely due to adhesions.

stem: An 82-year-old man with Parkinson's disease and long-standing constipation is brought in from his care home with marked abdominal distension and a day of not passing wind. An abdominal X-ray shows a large, inverted U-shaped loop of dilated colon arising from the pelvis, consistent with sigmoid volvulus. Which complication is the main reason urgent decompression is needed?

options.E: Malignant change in the bowel wall

correct_answer: C. Ischaemia of the twisted bowel
why_correct: In volvulus the bowel twists around its mesentery, creating a closed loop and compromising its blood supply. Without prompt decompression this can progress to ischaemia, gangrene and perforation. Sigmoid volvulus is usually decompressed endoscopically with a flatus tube, with surgery if there are signs of ischaemia or recurrence.
why_wrong: A. Aspiration is a risk with vomiting but is not the main danger of the twist itself. B. Urinary retention can occur with distension but is not the critical complication. D. Electrolyte disturbance may occur but is not the reason for urgent decompression. E. Volvulus does not cause malignant change.
pearl: Volvulus creates a closed loop with mesenteric twisting. Pain out of proportion, peritonism or a raised lactate suggests ischaemia and needs surgery.
thinking: Older man with chronic constipation ↓ distension and absolute constipation ↓ X-ray shows sigmoid volvulus ↓ mesenteric twist threatens blood supply ↓ Ischaemia of the twisted bowel
exam_trap: A, Aspiration pneumonia — it is a genuine risk in a frail patient with distension and vomiting, but the danger that makes this an emergency is loss of blood supply to the bowel.
takeaway: Volvulus threatens the bowel's blood supply, so it needs urgent decompression.

stem: A 78-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation stopped her apixaban two weeks ago because of nosebleeds. She now attends the emergency department with sudden, severe central abdominal pain. She is writhing and distressed, yet her abdomen is soft with only mild tenderness and no guarding. Her lactate is raised. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Severe abdominal pain out of proportion to examination findings in a patient with atrial fibrillation, particularly one who has stopped anticoagulation, strongly suggests embolic occlusion of the superior mesenteric artery. A raised lactate supports bowel ischaemia, although a normal lactate does not exclude it. Urgent CT angiography and surgical or vascular intervention are needed.
why_wrong: A. Pancreatitis causes epigastric pain radiating to the back with marked epigastric tenderness. B. Biliary colic causes right upper quadrant pain without a raised lactate. D. Renal colic causes writhing pain but in the loin radiating to the groin, without a raised lactate. E. Diverticulitis causes localised left iliac fossa tenderness and fever.
pearl: Pain out of proportion to the examination is the key early sign of mesenteric ischaemia. Signs of peritonitis appear late, once the bowel is infarcting.
thinking: Atrial fibrillation, anticoagulation stopped ↓ sudden severe abdominal pain ↓ soft abdomen with minimal signs ↓ raised lactate ↓ Acute mesenteric ischaemia
exam_trap: D, Renal colic — writhing with a soft abdomen is typical of colic, but the pain is central, the lactate is raised and she has a clear embolic source.
takeaway: Severe pain with minimal signs in atrial fibrillation suggests mesenteric ischaemia.

stem: A 49-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a night of heavy drinking during which he retched violently many times. He then developed sudden, severe pain behind his breastbone radiating to his back, and is now breathless. He is pale, sweaty, tachycardic and hypotensive. There is a crackling sensation when the skin at the base of his neck is pressed. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Severe chest pain after forceful retching, with shock and surgical emphysema in the neck, indicates full-thickness oesophageal rupture (Boerhaave syndrome). Leakage of gastric contents into the mediastinum causes mediastinitis and rapid deterioration. It needs resuscitation, CT with oral contrast, broad-spectrum antibiotics, nil by mouth and urgent specialist surgical input.
why_wrong: A. A Mallory-Weiss tear is a mucosal tear causing haematemesis, usually without shock or surgical emphysema. B. Pancreatitis can follow alcohol but does not cause surgical emphysema. C. Aortic dissection causes tearing pain to the back but is not linked to retching or surgical emphysema. E. Pneumothorax can cause surgical emphysema but does not follow retching with shock in this way.
pearl: Vomiting followed by chest pain and surgical emphysema is Boerhaave syndrome until proved otherwise. Mallory-Weiss causes bleeding, Boerhaave causes perforation.
thinking: Repeated forceful retching ↓ sudden severe chest pain to the back ↓ shock ↓ surgical emphysema in the neck ↓ Oesophageal rupture
exam_trap: A, Mallory-Weiss tear — it also follows retching after alcohol, but it is a partial mucosal tear causing haematemesis, not shock with surgical emphysema.
takeaway: Chest pain, shock and surgical emphysema after violent retching means oesophageal rupture.

stem: A 29-year-old man who has been constipated since starting a new desk job sees his GP about bright red blood on the toilet paper and dripping into the pan after straining. Opening his bowels is not painful. He has no change in stool frequency, weight loss or abdominal pain, and abdominal and rectal examinations are otherwise normal. What is the most likely cause?
why_correct: Painless bright red blood on the paper or dripping into the pan after straining, in a young adult with constipation, is typical of haemorrhoids. Internal haemorrhoids are not usually palpable on rectal examination and are best seen on proctoscopy. Management starts with increasing fibre and fluids to soften stools and reduce straining.
why_wrong: A. A fissure causes sharp pain on defecation. B. Colorectal cancer is unlikely in a young man without weight loss, change in bowel habit or other red flags. C. Ulcerative colitis causes bloody diarrhoea with urgency rather than blood after straining. D. Angiodysplasia is a cause of bleeding mainly in older adults.
pearl: Bright red, painless bleeding on the paper or in the pan after straining suggests haemorrhoids. Pain suggests a fissure. Older age or red flags need further assessment.
thinking: Young adult with constipation ↓ bright red blood after straining ↓ painless defecation ↓ no red flags ↓ Haemorrhoids
exam_trap: A, Anal fissure — it also causes bright red blood on the paper in constipated patients, but it is typically very painful on defecation.
takeaway: Painless bright red bleeding after straining in a young adult is most often due to haemorrhoids.

stem: A 26-year-old woman who had her first baby six weeks ago has become constipated. She describes a sharp, tearing pain each time she opens her bowels, followed by a burning ache that lasts about an hour, and a streak of bright red blood on the toilet paper. Gently parting the buttocks reveals a small longitudinal split at the posterior anal margin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Severe tearing pain during defecation, a prolonged ache afterwards, a little bright red blood and a visible posterior midline split are characteristic of an anal fissure. Constipation and hard stools are the usual cause, and the postnatal period is a common time. Treatment is stool softening with fibre, fluids and laxatives, with topical glyceryl trinitrate or diltiazem if it does not heal.
why_wrong: B. A thrombosed external haemorrhoid causes a tender bluish lump rather than a split. C. A perianal abscess causes a constant throbbing pain and a hot swelling. D. Crohn's-related fissures tend to be off the midline, multiple or painless. E. Pruritus ani causes itching rather than defecation pain.
pearl: Most fissures lie in the posterior midline. Lateral or multiple fissures should prompt consideration of Crohn's disease, infection or malignancy.
thinking: Postnatal constipation ↓ sharp pain on defecation lasting afterwards ↓ streak of bright red blood ↓ posterior midline split seen ↓ Anal fissure
exam_trap: B, Thrombosed external haemorrhoid — it causes acute anal pain after childbirth or straining, but it presents as a tender lump, not a split with defecation pain.
takeaway: Sharp pain on defecation with a posterior midline split is an anal fissure.

stem: A 64-year-old woman attends her GP because she now has to stop for breath halfway up the hill to the shops. She has had a morning cough with small amounts of clear sputum for several winters and needed antibiotics twice last year for chest infections. She smoked 20 cigarettes a day for 40 years and stopped last year. There is no history of childhood wheeze or hay fever. Post-bronchodilator spirometry shows an obstructive pattern with only a small change after salbutamol. Which condition best accounts for her symptoms?
why_correct: Progressive exertional breathlessness and a chronic productive cough in a long-term smoker, with airflow obstruction that persists after a bronchodilator, is COPD. The minimal bronchodilator response and lack of atopic history point away from asthma. Management includes smoking cessation support, pulmonary rehabilitation where appropriate, vaccinations and inhaled therapy.
why_wrong: A. Asthma usually shows variable symptoms and marked bronchodilator reversibility, often with an atopic history. B. Bronchiectasis causes daily copious purulent sputum and is confirmed on CT, not suggested by small amounts of clear sputum. C. Heart failure causes breathlessness with orthopnoea and oedema, not fixed airflow obstruction on spirometry. E. Pulmonary fibrosis causes a restrictive pattern with fine inspiratory crackles, not obstruction.
pearl: COPD is diagnosed clinically in a person with risk factors and confirmed by post-bronchodilator spirometry showing airflow obstruction; a large bronchodilator response should make you reconsider asthma.
thinking: Long-term smoker in middle age ↓ chronic morning cough, recurrent winter infections and progressive exertional breathlessness ↓ obstructive spirometry with little bronchodilator response ↓ no atopic or childhood history ↓ COPD
exam_trap: A, Asthma — obstructive spirometry and wheezy chest infections tempt towards asthma, but the persistent obstruction after salbutamol, heavy smoking history and lack of atopy fit COPD.
takeaway: Persistent post-bronchodilator airflow obstruction in a long-term smoker with chronic cough and breathlessness is COPD.

stem: A 69-year-old man with known COPD is brought to the emergency department by ambulance with an exacerbation. The crew gave high-flow oxygen through a non-rebreathe mask throughout the journey. On arrival he is increasingly drowsy and difficult to rouse. Pulse oximetry reads 99%, his hands are warm with a bounding pulse, and he has a coarse flapping tremor. His temperature is 37.3°C, capillary glucose is normal, he has not received any sedating medicines and he has no known liver disease. What is the most likely cause of his reduced consciousness?

options.B: Carbon dioxide retention worsened by uncontrolled oxygen

correct_answer: B. Carbon dioxide retention worsened by uncontrolled oxygen
why_correct: Drowsiness, warm peripheries, a bounding pulse and a flapping tremor after high-concentration oxygen in COPD indicate hypercapnia. In susceptible patients, excess oxygen worsens ventilation-perfusion mismatch and reduces respiratory drive, so carbon dioxide rises. Oxygen should not be stopped abruptly; it should be controlled, usually via a Venturi mask, titrated to a lower target saturation and guided by arterial blood gases.
why_wrong: A. He is afebrile with no source of sepsis described, and the signs are those of carbon dioxide retention. C. A normal capillary glucose excludes hypoglycaemia. D. His saturation is high, so hypoxia is not the cause. E. Hepatic encephalopathy can cause a flap, but he has no liver disease and the timing follows high-flow oxygen.
pearl: In patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, give controlled oxygen through a Venturi mask aiming for 88–92% and check a blood gas; never simply remove oxygen from a hypoxaemic patient.
thinking: COPD exacerbation given high-flow oxygen ↓ now drowsy with saturation at the top of the range ↓ warm peripheries, bounding pulse and flapping tremor ↓ signs of carbon dioxide retention, not hypoxia ↓ Carbon dioxide retention worsened by uncontrolled oxygen
exam_trap: D, Hypoxic brain injury — reduced consciousness in a breathless patient tempts towards hypoxia, but his saturation is high; the danger here is too much oxygen, not too little.
takeaway: In COPD, uncontrolled oxygen can drive carbon dioxide retention; titrate oxygen to a controlled target.

stem: A tall, thin 19-year-old man calls an ambulance after a sudden sharp pain on the left side of his chest while sitting at his desk revising for exams. The pain catches when he breathes in and he feels short of breath. He smokes cannabis. In the emergency department he is alert, his oxygen saturation is mildly reduced and his blood pressure is normal. The left side of his chest is hyper-resonant to percussion with quiet breath sounds. What is the leading diagnosis?
why_correct: Sudden one-sided pleuritic pain and breathlessness in a tall, thin young man, with hyper-resonance and reduced breath sounds on that side, indicates air in the pleural space. He is haemodynamically stable, so this is a primary spontaneous pneumothorax rather than a tension pneumothorax. A chest X-ray confirms it, and management depends on symptoms and size in line with British Thoracic Society guidance.
why_wrong: B. Pulmonary embolism can cause sudden pleuritic pain but does not produce one-sided hyper-resonance with reduced air entry. C. Pericarditis causes central pain eased by sitting forward, with a rub rather than unilateral chest signs. D. Chest wall pain does not cause breathlessness, reduced saturation or altered percussion. E. Pneumonia causes fever, productive cough and dullness rather than hyper-resonance.
pearl: Hyper-resonance with reduced breath sounds points to air; dullness points to fluid or consolidation. Tracheal deviation with hypotension signals tension pneumothorax and needs immediate decompression.
thinking: Tall, thin young male smoker ↓ sudden unilateral pleuritic pain and breathlessness at rest ↓ hyper-resonant percussion with reduced breath sounds on the same side ↓ air in the pleural space, haemodynamically stable ↓ Pneumothorax
exam_trap: B, Pulmonary embolism — sudden pleuritic pain with breathlessness and low saturation tempt towards a clot, but PE usually leaves the chest examination normal, whereas hyper-resonance localises air to the pleural space.
takeaway: Sudden pleuritic pain with one-sided hyper-resonance and quiet breath sounds is pneumothorax.

stem: A 71-year-old woman is seen on a GP home visit. For three days she has had shivering attacks, a cough bringing up rust-coloured sputum and a sharp pain in her right side when she breathes in. Her temperature is 38.6°C and she is mildly tachypnoeic but fully oriented. There is dullness to percussion at the right base with bronchial breathing and coarse crackles over the same area. Which diagnosis best fits?
why_correct: Fever, rigors, productive cough and pleuritic pain with focal signs of consolidation (dullness, bronchial breathing and crackles over one zone) indicate community-acquired pneumonia. Rust-coloured sputum is classically associated with pneumococcal infection. Severity should then be assessed with a validated score such as CRB-65 to help decide between home and hospital management.
why_wrong: A. Pulmonary embolism can cause pleuritic pain and low-grade fever but not focal consolidation with purulent sputum. B. An effusion gives stony dullness with reduced, not bronchial, breath sounds. D. Lung cancer is a slower illness with weight loss and does not present as a three-day febrile illness. E. Acute bronchitis causes cough without focal chest signs.
pearl: Bronchial breathing over an area of dullness means consolidated lung; dullness with absent breath sounds suggests fluid instead.
thinking: Three days of fever, rigors and productive cough ↓ pleuritic right-sided pain ↓ dullness, bronchial breathing and crackles in one zone indicate consolidation ↓ acute infective picture in the community ↓ Community-acquired pneumonia
exam_trap: B, Pleural effusion — dullness at the base tempts towards fluid, but an effusion quietens breath sounds, whereas bronchial breathing over the dull area signals consolidation.
takeaway: Acute fever and productive cough with focal consolidation signs is community-acquired pneumonia.

stem: A 24-year-old woman with asthma is brought to the emergency department by her partner after two days of worsening wheeze despite frequent use of her blue inhaler. She is now drowsy and responds only to voice, her lips look blue and she is too breathless to attempt a peak flow reading. On auscultation there is very little air entry and almost no audible wheeze. How should this attack be classified?
why_correct: A silent chest, cyanosis and altered consciousness during an asthma attack are features of life-threatening asthma, indicating exhaustion and impending respiratory failure. Reduced wheeze here reflects very poor airflow, not improvement. She needs immediate senior and critical care involvement alongside oxygen, nebulised bronchodilators and systemic steroids.
why_wrong: A. Acute severe asthma describes marked distress, such as being unable to complete sentences, but without cyanosis, a silent chest or drowsiness. B. A moderate exacerbation involves worsening symptoms with no severe or life-threatening features. C. Anaphylaxis follows an allergen exposure, often with urticaria, angioedema or hypotension. E. A panic attack would not cause cyanosis, a silent chest or drowsiness.
pearl: A quiet chest in a breathless asthmatic is an alarm sign, not reassurance: falling wheeze with rising exhaustion means airflow is critically reduced.
thinking: Known asthmatic with an attack unresponsive to her reliever ↓ drowsy and cyanosed with minimal air entry ↓ silent chest and altered consciousness are life-threatening features ↓ risk of respiratory arrest, escalate immediately ↓ Life-threatening asthma
exam_trap: A, Acute severe asthma — being unable to perform a peak flow tempts towards a severe attack, but cyanosis, drowsiness and a silent chest move this into the life-threatening category.
takeaway: Silent chest, cyanosis or drowsiness in an asthma attack means life-threatening asthma; escalate at once.

stem: A 74-year-old man with type 2 diabetes tells his GP that oncoming headlights now dazzle him so much that he has stopped driving after dark. Over the past year reading print has become hazy and colours seem duller. His eyes are not painful or red. On ophthalmoscopy the red reflex in both eyes is dimmed and patchy, making the fundus difficult to see. Which condition best explains his symptoms?
why_correct: Gradual painless blurring with glare from bright lights and faded colours, together with a dimmed red reflex, indicates opacity of the lens: cataract. Age and diabetes are both risk factors. Referral for surgery is considered when symptoms affect daily life, such as driving.
why_wrong: B. Open-angle glaucoma causes painless peripheral field loss, often unnoticed, with optic disc cupping rather than glare. C. Macular degeneration causes central distortion or a central blind spot, with a normal red reflex. D. Diabetic retinopathy is often asymptomatic until maculopathy or haemorrhage and does not dim the red reflex in this way. E. Retinitis pigmentosa causes night blindness and tunnel vision beginning earlier in life.
pearl: An abnormal red reflex in an older adult with gradual glare and blurred vision is cataract until proven otherwise; in an infant it may signal congenital cataract or retinoblastoma.
thinking: Older man with gradual painless visual blurring ↓ glare from headlights and faded colours ↓ dimmed red reflex obscuring the fundus ↓ opacity in the lens ↓ Cataract
exam_trap: D, Diabetic retinopathy — his diabetes tempts towards retinopathy, but glare, faded colours and a dimmed red reflex localise the problem to the lens, not the retina.
takeaway: Gradual painless blurring with glare and a dimmed red reflex in an older adult is cataract.

stem: A 63-year-old man speaks to his GP by telephone. For a week, every time he looks up to reach a high shelf or lies back on his pillow, the room spins violently for less than a minute and then settles. Between attacks he feels completely normal. He has no hearing loss, tinnitus, headache, weakness or difficulty speaking. At a face-to-face review the following day, the Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre to the right reproduces his vertigo with a burst of torsional nystagmus after a short delay. Which condition is responsible?
why_correct: Short episodes of rotatory vertigo triggered by specific head positions, with normal hearing and a positive Dix-Hallpike test showing delayed torsional nystagmus, is benign paroxysmal positional vertigo. It is caused by displaced otoconia in a semicircular canal, most often the posterior canal. It is treated with a particle repositioning manoeuvre such as the Epley manoeuvre rather than vestibular sedatives.
why_wrong: A. Vestibular neuritis causes continuous vertigo lasting days after a viral illness, not brief positional spells. C. Ménière disease causes attacks lasting hours with fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus and aural fullness. D. A posterior circulation TIA is not reproducibly triggered by head position and usually has other neurological symptoms. E. Labyrinthitis causes prolonged vertigo with hearing loss.
pearl: Timing is the key to vertigo: seconds with position change suggests BPPV, hours with hearing symptoms suggests Ménière disease, and days of constant vertigo suggests vestibular neuritis.
thinking: Brief rotatory vertigo lasting under a minute ↓ triggered by looking up and lying back ↓ no hearing or neurological symptoms ↓ positive Dix-Hallpike with delayed torsional nystagmus ↓ Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
exam_trap: D, Vertebrobasilar transient ischaemic attack — vertigo on looking up tempts towards posterior circulation ischaemia in an older man, but reproducible positional triggering, a typical Dix-Hallpike response and no neurological deficit fit BPPV.
takeaway: Seconds-long vertigo on head position change with a positive Dix-Hallpike test is BPPV.

stem: A 52-year-old woman tells her GP that for over a year she has been unable to stop worrying: about her job security, her adult children's safety, the household bills and even small things such as being late for appointments. She cannot switch off, feels on edge and irritable, tires easily and struggles to concentrate at work. She does not have sudden attacks of fear, avoid particular places or carry out repeated rituals, and her mood is not persistently low. Thyroid function is normal. What is the best explanation for her symptoms?
why_correct: Excessive, hard-to-control worry about many everyday matters for months, with restlessness, irritability, fatigue and poor concentration, is generalised anxiety disorder. Excluding physical causes such as thyroid disease is appropriate. NICE recommends a stepped-care approach, starting with education and active monitoring, then low-intensity psychological interventions such as guided self-help, and then CBT or drug treatment.
why_wrong: B. Panic disorder involves recurrent, unexpected episodes of intense fear with physical symptoms. C. A depressive episode requires persistent low mood or loss of interest, which she does not have. D. OCD involves intrusive obsessions with compulsions, not broad everyday worry. E. Health anxiety is focused on fear of having a serious illness, not on many areas of life.
pearl: The defining feature of generalised anxiety disorder is worry that is excessive, spread across many areas of life and difficult to control, with physical tension, rather than episodic panic or a single feared focus.
thinking: Persistent worry for over a year ↓ spread across work, family, money and minor matters ↓ restlessness, irritability, fatigue and poor concentration ↓ no panic attacks, rituals, avoidance or low mood, and thyroid normal ↓ Generalised anxiety disorder
exam_trap: C, Depressive episode — tiredness, poor concentration and irritability overlap with depression, but her mood is not persistently low and worry is the dominant feature.
takeaway: Excessive, uncontrollable worry about many everyday things with physical tension is generalised anxiety disorder.

stem: A 41-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her husband. For the past week she has slept only two hours a night yet says she has never felt better. She talks rapidly, jumps from topic to topic and is planning to open three businesses at once. She has spent the family's savings on designer goods and was sent home from work for inappropriate behaviour. She was treated for depression twice in the past. A urine drug screen is negative and she is fully oriented. Which diagnosis best explains her presentation?
why_correct: A week of elevated mood, greatly reduced need for sleep, pressured speech, flight of ideas, grandiose plans and reckless spending, with marked impairment at work, is a manic episode. With previous depressive episodes this indicates bipolar affective disorder. She needs urgent psychiatric assessment, including risk assessment, and treatment usually starts with an antipsychotic.
why_wrong: A. Schizophrenia is characterised by delusions, hallucinations and thought disorder without a primary disturbance of mood. C. Agitated depression involves low mood with restlessness, not euphoria and grandiosity. D. Delirium causes fluctuating attention and disorientation, and she is fully oriented. E. Emotionally unstable personality disorder causes long-standing rapid mood shifts and impulsivity, not a distinct episode with reduced need for sleep.
pearl: Ask about previous depressive episodes in anyone presenting with mania: the combination indicates bipolar disorder, and an antidepressant given alone can trigger a switch into mania.
thinking: Week-long change in behaviour ↓ elevated mood with little need for sleep ↓ pressured speech, flight of ideas, grandiosity and reckless spending ↓ marked impairment, oriented, drug screen negative ↓ Manic episode
exam_trap: A, Schizophrenia — grandiose plans and disorganised speech tempt towards a primary psychosis, but the core disturbance here is elevated mood with reduced need for sleep, which defines mania.
takeaway: Elevated mood with reduced need for sleep, pressured speech and reckless behaviour is a manic episode.

stem: A 58-year-old man who took early retirement three months ago is persuaded by his wife to see the GP. For the past two months he has felt flat most of the day, has given up golf because it no longer gives him any pleasure, and wakes at 4 am unable to get back to sleep. He has lost weight without trying, feels exhausted and blames himself for letting his family down. He denies any thoughts of harming himself. Thyroid function and full blood count are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Two months of persistent low mood and loss of pleasure with early-morning waking, weight loss, fatigue and excessive guilt is the picture of a depressive episode. Although retirement was a trigger, the severity and biological features go beyond an adjustment reaction. Management includes a risk assessment and treatment matched to severity, such as psychological therapy, an antidepressant or both.
why_wrong: B. Adjustment disorder causes distress in response to a stressor without the full depressive syndrome of biological symptoms and guilt. C. Dysthymia is a milder, chronic low mood lasting years. D. Alzheimer disease presents with progressive memory loss rather than low mood with guilt and anhedonia. E. Generalised anxiety disorder is dominated by excessive worry rather than low mood and anhedonia.
pearl: A clear trigger does not rule out a depressive episode: if core and biological symptoms are present, diagnose and treat depression rather than calling it an understandable reaction.
thinking: Two months of low mood and anhedonia ↓ early-morning waking, weight loss and fatigue ↓ excessive guilt ↓ physical causes excluded, full depressive syndrome despite a trigger ↓ Depressive episode
exam_trap: B, Adjustment disorder — the recent retirement tempts towards an adjustment reaction, but anhedonia, early-morning waking, weight loss and guilt indicate a full depressive episode.
takeaway: Low mood and anhedonia with biological symptoms over weeks is a depressive episode, even after a clear trigger.

stem: A 74-year-old woman sees her GP with a two-week history of a new headache over her left temple. Her scalp feels sore when she brushes her hair, and her jaw starts to ache after a few minutes of chewing meat. She has felt stiff around her shoulders in the mornings, and yesterday the vision in her left eye went blurred for several minutes. Which diagnosis must be urgently considered?
why_correct: A new temporal headache in an older adult with scalp tenderness, jaw claudication and transient visual disturbance is giant cell arteritis until proven otherwise. With visual symptoms she needs immediate high-dose glucocorticoids and same-day specialist assessment, as delay risks permanent blindness. Inflammatory markers and temporal artery ultrasound or biopsy should not delay treatment.
why_wrong: A. Polymyalgia rheumatica explains the shoulder stiffness but not the headache, jaw claudication or visual disturbance, which indicate arteritis. C. TMJ dysfunction causes jaw pain on movement but not scalp tenderness or visual symptoms. D. Tension-type headache is a bilateral, band-like headache without jaw or visual symptoms. E. Acute angle-closure glaucoma causes a red, painful eye with haloes, not jaw claudication.
pearl: Jaw claudication is one of the most specific features of giant cell arteritis; with any visual symptoms, start steroids the same day and do not wait for test results.
thinking: Older woman with a new temporal headache ↓ scalp tenderness and jaw claudication ↓ shoulder girdle stiffness suggests associated polymyalgia ↓ transient visual blurring signals risk of permanent loss ↓ Giant cell arteritis
exam_trap: A, Polymyalgia rheumatica alone — morning shoulder stiffness tempts towards PMR, but the cranial symptoms and visual disturbance mean arteritis, which needs urgent higher-dose treatment.
takeaway: New headache with jaw claudication and visual symptoms in an older adult is giant cell arteritis; treat urgently.

stem: A 28-year-old woman at 16 weeks of pregnancy is telephoned by her midwife. The urine sample sent at her booking appointment has shown a significant pure growth of Escherichia coli, sensitive to nitrofurantoin, amoxicillin and cefalexin. She has no dysuria, frequency, loin pain or fever and feels well. How should this result be managed?

options.A: No action because she has no symptoms
options.B: Repeat the urine culture at her next routine appointment
options.C: Prescribe an antibiotic guided by the sensitivities
options.D: Arrange a renal tract ultrasound first
options.E: Advise increased fluid intake and cranberry products

correct_answer: C. Prescribe an antibiotic guided by the sensitivities
why_correct: Bacteriuria found on screening in pregnancy should be treated even without symptoms, because it increases the risk of pyelonephritis and has been linked with preterm birth. The antibiotic is chosen according to sensitivities and safety in pregnancy, and a repeat culture is sent afterwards to confirm clearance. Trimethoprim is avoided in the first trimester and nitrofurantoin at term.
why_wrong: A. Unlike in non-pregnant adults, asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy should not be left untreated. B. Waiting until the next visit leaves her at risk of pyelonephritis. D. A renal ultrasound is not needed before treating uncomplicated bacteriuria. E. Fluids and cranberry products are not a treatment for confirmed bacteriuria.
pearl: Asymptomatic bacteriuria is screened for at booking and treated in pregnancy, followed by a test-of-cure culture; outside pregnancy it is generally not treated in otherwise healthy adults.
thinking: Pregnant woman at booking ↓ significant growth of E. coli on urine culture ↓ no urinary symptoms ↓ pregnancy raises the risk of progression to pyelonephritis ↓ Prescribe an antibiotic guided by the sensitivities
exam_trap: A, No action because she has no symptoms — this is right for most non-pregnant adults and so tempts, but pregnancy is a key exception where screening-detected bacteriuria is treated.
takeaway: Treat asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy with a sensitivity-guided antibiotic and check clearance.

stem: A 45-year-old woman attends her GP with thick, red, sharply bordered patches covered in silvery scale on her scalp, extending just beyond the hairline and behind her ears. She has similar patches in her natal cleft. Several of her fingernails have small pits and the tips are lifting from the nail bed. Her father had a similar rash. Which condition best explains these findings?
why_correct: Well-demarcated red plaques with silvery scale at the scalp margin, behind the ears and in the natal cleft, together with nail pitting, onycholysis and a family history, are typical of psoriasis. Nail involvement also signals a higher risk of psoriatic arthritis, so she should be asked about joint symptoms. Scalp disease is usually treated first with a potent topical corticosteroid.
why_wrong: A. Seborrhoeic dermatitis causes greasy yellowish scale with poorly defined edges and no nail pitting. B. Tinea capitis mainly affects children and causes patchy hair loss with scaling. D. Discoid eczema causes itchy coin-shaped patches on the limbs without nail pitting. E. Lichen planus causes itchy, flat-topped violaceous papules and can cause nail ridging, not silvery plaques.
pearl: Look for psoriasis in hidden sites such as the scalp margin, behind the ears, umbilicus and natal cleft, and examine the nails for pitting and onycholysis.
thinking: Sharply bordered red plaques with silvery scale ↓ scalp margin, behind the ears and natal cleft ↓ nail pitting and onycholysis ↓ positive family history ↓ Psoriasis
exam_trap: A, Seborrhoeic dermatitis — scaling on the scalp and behind the ears tempts towards seborrhoeic dermatitis, but its scale is greasy and poorly defined, and it does not pit the nails.
takeaway: Sharply demarcated silvery plaques with nail pitting point to psoriasis, even in hidden sites.

stem: An 11-year-old girl with asthma and hay fever is brought to the GP because of itching that keeps her awake. Her skin is dry and rough, with thickened, scratched patches in the creases in front of her elbows and behind her knees, and around her neck and wrists. The rash has come and gone since she was a toddler and is worse in winter. Nobody else at home is itchy. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Chronic relapsing itchy, dry skin with lichenified patches in the flexures, in a child with asthma and hay fever, is atopic eczema. Treatment is based on regular, generous emollients with topical corticosteroids of appropriate potency for flares. Itch that disturbs sleep is an important marker of severity and impact on quality of life.
why_wrong: A. Psoriasis causes well-demarcated plaques with silvery scale, usually on extensor surfaces. B. Allergic contact dermatitis is confined to areas of contact with an allergen. C. Scabies usually causes itch in household contacts too, with burrows in the finger webs. E. Tinea corporis causes an annular scaly lesion with central clearing.
pearl: Lichenification, thickened skin with exaggerated markings, is a sign of chronic scratching and is typical of long-standing flexural atopic eczema.
thinking: Child with personal atopy (asthma, hay fever) ↓ chronic relapsing itchy, dry skin since early childhood ↓ lichenified patches in the flexures, neck and wrists ↓ no household itch or annular lesions ↓ Atopic eczema
exam_trap: C, Scabies — intense night-time itch and wrist involvement tempt towards scabies, but years of relapsing flexural rash with atopy and no affected household members fit eczema.
takeaway: Chronic itchy, dry, lichenified flexural skin in an atopic child is atopic eczema.

stem: A 34-year-old man who works on a dairy farm notices a pink patch on the side of his neck that has slowly enlarged over three weeks. It itches, and the centre has faded while the raised, scaly rim keeps spreading outwards. A pharmacist sold him hydrocortisone cream, after which it grew faster. He does not recall any tick bite. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: An itchy, slowly expanding annular lesion with a scaly advancing edge and central clearing is a dermatophyte infection, tinea corporis; contact with cattle is a recognised source. Topical steroids suppress inflammation while allowing the fungus to spread, sometimes called tinea incognito. Skin scrapings can confirm the diagnosis, and a topical antifungal such as terbinafine is usually effective.
why_wrong: B. Discoid eczema forms uniformly inflamed coin-shaped patches without central clearing. C. Granuloma annulare forms a smooth ring of skin-coloured papules without scale. D. Pityriasis rosea starts with a herald patch followed by many smaller oval patches on the trunk. E. Erythema migrans is an expanding, non-scaly red ring after a tick bite in Lyme disease.
pearl: If a scaly rash worsens after a topical steroid, think fungal infection and take skin scrapings before prescribing further treatment.
thinking: Itchy patch enlarging over weeks ↓ annular with central clearing and a scaly raised edge ↓ worsened by a topical steroid ↓ animal contact as a source of dermatophytes ↓ Tinea corporis
exam_trap: E, Erythema migrans — an expanding ring in a farm worker tempts towards Lyme disease, but erythema migrans is not scaly and there is no tick bite, while the scaly advancing edge indicates fungal infection.
takeaway: An itchy annular lesion with central clearing and a scaly edge, worsened by steroids, is tinea corporis.

stem: A 31-year-old woman at 32 weeks of pregnancy rings her community midwife because she has been scratching her hands and the soles of her feet all night for a week. Apart from scratch marks, her skin looks normal and there is no rash elsewhere. She feels otherwise well, with no headache, visual disturbance or abdominal pain, and her blood pressure at a check yesterday was normal. Which test will most help confirm the likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Itching of the palms and soles, worse at night, without a rash in the third trimester suggests intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy. Raised serum bile acids confirm the diagnosis, and liver function tests are usually checked at the same time. Higher bile acid levels are linked with a greater risk of stillbirth, so results guide monitoring and timing of birth under obstetric care.
why_wrong: A. A full blood count does not diagnose cholestasis. B. Thyroid disease can cause generalised itch but does not explain the classic palmar and plantar pattern in late pregnancy. C. Iron deficiency is common in pregnancy but is not the key test for this presentation. D. A protein:creatinine ratio assesses pre-eclampsia, which presents with hypertension and proteinuria rather than isolated itch.
pearl: Itch without a rash in late pregnancy, especially of the palms and soles and worse at night, should prompt bile acid and liver function testing; the itch resolves after birth.
thinking: Third trimester ↓ intense itching of the palms and soles, worse at night ↓ no primary rash, only scratch marks ↓ suspect obstetric cholestasis ↓ Serum bile acids
exam_trap: D, Urine protein:creatinine ratio — liver involvement in late pregnancy tempts towards checking for pre-eclampsia, but her blood pressure is normal and isolated palmar and plantar itch points to cholestasis.
takeaway: Itch of the palms and soles without a rash in late pregnancy needs serum bile acids.

stem: A 33-year-old woman is in labour at term, attempting a vaginal birth after one earlier caesarean birth. Her labour has been augmented with oxytocin. She suddenly develops a constant, tearing lower abdominal pain between contractions, the contractions stop, and she becomes tachycardic. On vaginal examination the presenting part is higher than it was an hour earlier. The CTG shows a prolonged fetal bradycardia. Which complication is most likely?
why_correct: Sudden severe constant pain, loss of contractions, maternal tachycardia, recession of the presenting part and acute fetal bradycardia in a woman with a previous caesarean scar indicate uterine rupture. Oxytocin augmentation increases the risk. This is an obstetric emergency requiring immediate senior help, maternal resuscitation and a category 1 caesarean section.
why_wrong: A. Abruption causes pain and fetal distress with a tense, woody uterus, but contractions continue and the presenting part does not recede. C. Amniotic fluid embolism presents with sudden collapse, breathlessness and coagulopathy rather than localised tearing pain. D. Cord prolapse causes fetal bradycardia with cord felt or seen below the presenting part, without maternal pain. E. Hyperstimulation causes excessively frequent contractions, not cessation of contractions.
pearl: Key signs of uterine rupture are a scarred uterus, sudden pain, cessation of contractions, loss of station and an abnormal CTG; fetal heart changes are often the earliest sign.
thinking: Labour after a previous caesarean with oxytocin augmentation ↓ sudden tearing pain and contractions stopping ↓ maternal tachycardia and presenting part rising ↓ acute fetal bradycardia ↓ Uterine rupture
exam_trap: A, Placental abruption — sudden pain with fetal bradycardia tempts towards abruption, but cessation of contractions and loss of station in a scarred uterus point to rupture.
takeaway: Sudden pain, stopped contractions and loss of station with fetal bradycardia after a caesarean means uterine rupture.

stem: A 29-year-old woman who conceived by IVF is at 39 weeks on the labour ward. Her 20-week scan reported a low-lying placenta, but a later scan showed it had moved clear of the cervix. Shortly after the midwife performs an amniotomy, there is a gush of bright red blood. Within a minute the CTG shows a sudden, profound fetal bradycardia. She has no abdominal pain, her uterus is soft and she is haemodynamically stable. What is the most likely cause of the bleeding?

options.E: Cervical trauma from the amniotomy hook

why_correct: Painless bleeding at the moment of membrane rupture followed immediately by profound fetal bradycardia, with a stable mother, indicates tearing of unprotected fetal vessels running through the membranes: vasa praevia. The blood lost is fetal, so the baby can exsanguinate rapidly. A history of a low-lying placenta and IVF conception are risk factors, and an immediate category 1 caesarean with neonatal resuscitation is needed.
why_wrong: A. Abruption usually causes pain and a tender, tense uterus. B. Placenta praevia was excluded on the later scan and causes maternal bleeding without such immediate fetal compromise. C. Uterine rupture causes severe pain and maternal instability, usually with a uterine scar. E. Minor cervical trauma would not cause sudden profound fetal bradycardia.
pearl: In vasa praevia the bleeding is fetal, so even a small loss is catastrophic for the baby while the mother remains well; risk factors include a low-lying placenta, IVF and placental variants.
thinking: Bleeding immediately after membrane rupture ↓ sudden profound fetal bradycardia ↓ mother stable, painless, soft uterus ↓ fetal vessels torn within the membranes ↓ Vasa praevia
exam_trap: B, Placenta praevia — painless bright red bleeding with a history of a low-lying placenta tempts towards praevia, but the placenta moved clear and the bleeding coincided with membrane rupture and immediate fetal compromise.
takeaway: Painless bleeding at membrane rupture with immediate fetal bradycardia means vasa praevia.

stem: A 26-year-old woman is reviewed on the postnatal ward four days after an emergency caesarean section for a prolonged labour. She has a temperature of 38.4°C with pain low in her abdomen, and her lochia has become offensive. The uterus is bulky and tender on palpation. Her wound is clean and dry, her breasts are soft and non-tender, and her calves are normal. Which diagnosis best fits?
why_correct: Fever, lower abdominal pain, offensive lochia and a tender uterus after delivery are typical of postpartum endometritis. Caesarean section, especially after prolonged labour, is the main risk factor. She should be assessed for sepsis and started on broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics, with an ultrasound if retained products are suspected.
why_wrong: A. Mastitis causes a painful, red, firm area of breast, and her breasts are normal. B. The wound is clean and dry, so a wound infection does not explain her signs. C. Pyelonephritis causes loin pain and urinary symptoms rather than uterine tenderness and offensive lochia. D. DVT causes leg swelling and pain, and her calves are normal.
pearl: Postpartum fever has a short list of sources: uterus, wound, breasts, urinary tract, chest and legs; offensive lochia with a tender uterus localises it to the endometrium.
thinking: Postnatal fever after caesarean section ↓ lower abdominal pain with offensive lochia ↓ bulky, tender uterus ↓ wound, breasts and legs normal ↓ Endometritis
exam_trap: B, Surgical wound infection — fever after a caesarean tempts towards the wound, but it is clean and dry, while offensive lochia and uterine tenderness point to the endometrium.
takeaway: Postnatal fever with offensive lochia and a tender uterus is endometritis.

stem: An 83-year-old man is admitted from his care home to the orthopaedic ward with a fractured neck of femur. He arrives with a bag of medicine boxes, some dispensed via his GP and some via a hospital cardiology clinic. The care home's medicines chart lists a different dose of one of his heart tablets from that printed on the box. You are the foundation doctor writing his inpatient drug chart. What should you do first to reduce the risk of a medication error?

options.A: Prescribe each medicine exactly as printed on the boxes he brought
options.B: Carry out medicines reconciliation using more than one reliable source
options.C: Withhold all his regular medicines until after surgery
options.D: Copy the care home chart onto the drug chart
options.E: Ask the patient to recall each medicine and dose

correct_answer: B. Carry out medicines reconciliation using more than one reliable source
why_correct: Medicines reconciliation means compiling an accurate list of what the patient is actually taking by comparing several sources, such as the GP record, care home chart, medicine labels and specialist letters, and resolving any discrepancies. It identifies omissions, duplications and dose errors at transfer of care, when errors are most common. Pharmacy teams should be involved soon after admission.
why_wrong: A. Labels may be out of date and already conflict with another source, so they cannot be used alone. C. Stopping all medicines can cause harm, for example from omitting cardiac drugs or anticoagulants. D. The care home chart is only one source and already conflicts with another. E. Recall by a frail, injured older patient is unreliable as the only source.
pearl: Transfers of care are high-risk points for medication errors; reconcile using at least two sources and document what was checked and any changes made.
thinking: Admission from a care home after a fall ↓ medicines from several prescribers with a dose discrepancy ↓ transfer of care is a high-risk point for errors ↓ compare several reliable sources and resolve differences ↓ Carry out medicines reconciliation using more than one reliable source
exam_trap: D, Copy the care home chart onto the drug chart — the care home chart looks authoritative, but it already conflicts with the boxes, so relying on it alone could carry an error forward.
takeaway: On admission, reconcile medicines from more than one reliable source before prescribing.

stem: A 37-year-old woman was started on lamotrigine for epilepsy by her neurologist three weeks ago. She now has a widespread blistering rash with painful mouth ulcers and sore eyes, and she is admitted to hospital. Once she is receiving appropriate treatment, the ward doctor wants to report the suspected drug reaction. Which route should be used?

options.A: The local incident reporting system only
options.B: Notification to the UK Health Security Agency
options.C: A letter to the drug manufacturer only
options.D: Referral to the General Medical Council

why_correct: Suspected adverse drug reactions in the UK are reported to the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency through the Yellow Card scheme. Serious reactions, such as suspected Stevens-Johnson syndrome, should always be reported, even if causality is uncertain. Any health professional, and patients themselves, can submit a report.
why_wrong: A. Local incident systems record safety events within a trust but do not replace national adverse reaction reporting. B. UKHSA receives notifications of specified infectious diseases, not drug reactions. C. Contacting the manufacturer alone does not feed into the national monitoring system. D. The GMC regulates doctors and is not involved in reporting drug reactions.
pearl: Report any suspected serious adverse reaction to any medicine through the Yellow Card scheme, and all suspected reactions to products under additional monitoring (black triangle).
thinking: New antiepileptic started weeks ago ↓ blistering rash with mucosal involvement, a serious reaction ↓ suspected adverse drug reaction ↓ national reporting system run by the MHRA ↓ The Yellow Card scheme
exam_trap: A, The local incident reporting system only — hospital doctors are used to filing incident reports, but a suspected adverse drug reaction must be reported nationally through the Yellow Card scheme.
takeaway: Report suspected adverse drug reactions in the UK through the MHRA Yellow Card scheme.

stem: A 66-year-old man at a GP review asks about a new drug to prevent hip fracture. The leaflet he has read states that, in a large trial, the relative risk of hip fracture with the drug compared with placebo was 0.5. He asks you what this means. Which explanation is correct?

options.A: His own risk of fracture will fall by 50 percentage points
options.B: Half of all patients who take the drug will be protected from fracture
options.C: The number needed to treat to prevent one fracture is 2
options.D: The drug doubles the risk of fracture compared with placebo
options.E: People taking the drug had half the risk of hip fracture of those taking placebo

correct_answer: E. People taking the drug had half the risk of hip fracture of those taking placebo
why_correct: Relative risk is the risk of the outcome in the treated group divided by the risk in the control group. A value of 0.5 means the risk among people taking the drug was half that of those taking placebo, a 50% relative risk reduction. On its own it does not tell you the absolute benefit, which depends on the patient's baseline risk.
why_wrong: A. A fall in percentage points describes absolute risk reduction, which cannot be derived from the relative risk alone. B. The relative risk does not mean that half of patients are protected. C. The number needed to treat depends on the absolute risk reduction, not the relative risk. D. A relative risk below 1 indicates reduced, not increased, risk.
pearl: When explaining benefit to patients, pair relative risk with absolute figures: halving a small risk gives a much smaller absolute benefit than halving a large one.
thinking: Relative risk is risk in the treated group divided by risk in the control group ↓ a value below 1 means reduced risk ↓ 0.5 means the treated group's risk is half the control group's ↓ absolute benefit needs the baseline risk ↓ People taking the drug had half the risk of hip fracture of those taking placebo
exam_trap: A, His own risk of fracture will fall by 50 percentage points — it confuses a relative reduction with an absolute one; a baseline risk of 4% would fall to 2%, not by 50 points.
takeaway: A relative risk of 0.5 means the outcome risk is halved relative to control, not an absolute 50% fall.

stem: A journal club discusses a study that recruited 400 people with bladder cancer and 400 matched people without it, then compared how often each group had previously worked in the dye industry. For this exposure, the paper quotes 3.0 as the odds ratio. A trainee is asked to interpret this figure. Which statement is correct?

options.A: The odds of previous dye-industry work were three times higher among people with bladder cancer than among controls
options.B: The study measured the incidence of bladder cancer in dye workers as three times that in other workers
options.C: 3% of dye workers will develop bladder cancer
options.D: Dye-industry work causes a third of all bladder cancers
options.E: Dye-industry work reduces the odds of bladder cancer by a third

correct_answer: A. The odds of previous dye-industry work were three times higher among people with bladder cancer than among controls
why_correct: A case-control study starts with people who have the disease (cases) and people without it (controls) and looks back at their exposures. The odds ratio compares the odds of exposure in cases with the odds in controls, so a value of 3 means cases had three times the odds of past dye-industry work. When a disease is rare the odds ratio approximates the relative risk, but a case-control design cannot measure incidence directly.
why_wrong: B. Case-control studies select participants by disease status, so they cannot measure incidence. C. An odds ratio is a ratio, not the percentage of people affected. D. The proportion of cases due to an exposure is the attributable fraction, not the odds ratio. E. An odds ratio above 1 indicates a positive association, not a reduction.
pearl: Match the measure to the design: case-control studies give odds ratios, while cohort studies and trials can measure incidence and give relative risks.
thinking: Case-control design selects by disease status ↓ exposure history compared between cases and controls ↓ odds ratio is the odds of exposure in cases divided by the odds in controls ↓ a value of 3 indicates a positive association ↓ The odds of previous dye-industry work were three times higher among people with bladder cancer than among controls
exam_trap: B, The study measured the incidence of bladder cancer in dye workers as three times that in other workers — this reads the odds ratio as a cohort relative risk, but a case-control study cannot measure incidence.
takeaway: In a case-control study, the odds ratio compares exposure odds between cases and controls; it does not measure incidence.

presentation: Interpreting A Confidence Interval Crossing The Null
stem: A randomised trial compares a new antihypertensive drug with standard treatment. For stroke, it reports a risk ratio of 0.85 and a 95% CI of 0.70 to 1.04. A GP reading the paper wonders what conclusion can be drawn about stroke. Which interpretation is correct?

options.A: The new drug significantly reduces stroke risk
options.B: The trial proves the two drugs are equally effective
options.C: The result is compatible with no difference in stroke risk between treatments
options.D: The new drug increases stroke risk
options.E: The p-value for this result is below 0.05

correct_answer: C. The result is compatible with no difference in stroke risk between treatments
why_correct: For a ratio measure, the value representing no difference is 1. Because the 95% confidence interval runs from below 1 to above 1, the data are compatible with a reduction, no effect or a small increase, so the result is not statistically significant at the 5% level. This does not prove the drugs are equivalent; the trial may simply lack the precision to detect a difference.
why_wrong: A. Statistical significance would require the whole interval to lie below 1. B. Failing to show a difference is not proof of equivalence. D. The point estimate suggests a reduction, and the interval includes both benefit and harm. E. An interval that crosses 1 corresponds to a p-value above 0.05.
pearl: For ratios (relative risk, odds ratio, hazard ratio) the null value is 1; for differences (mean difference, risk difference) it is 0. Check whether the interval crosses the right line.
thinking: Ratio measure, so the null value is 1 ↓ the 95% interval runs from 0.70 to 1.04 ↓ it includes 1 ↓ not statistically significant, but not proof of equivalence ↓ The result is compatible with no difference in stroke risk between treatments
exam_trap: A, The new drug significantly reduces stroke risk — the point estimate below 1 tempts towards benefit, but the interval crosses 1, so a true reduction has not been demonstrated.
takeaway: A confidence interval crossing the null value means the result is compatible with no difference, not proof of none.

stem: A 47-year-old woman who has worn strong glasses for short-sightedness since childhood attends eye casualty. Yesterday she noticed a shower of black specks and brief flickering lights in her left eye. This morning a shadow has appeared in the lower part of her vision in that eye and is creeping upwards. The eye is white and painless. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Photopsia and a sudden shower of floaters followed by an advancing shadow or field defect are the warning features of rhegmatogenous retinal detachment. High myopia is a recognised risk factor. This is a sight-threatening emergency needing same-day ophthalmology assessment, particularly before the macula becomes involved.
why_wrong: A. Posterior vitreous detachment causes flashes and floaters but does not produce a progressive field defect. B. Vitreous haemorrhage causes floaters or hazy vision but not the preceding flashes with a spreading shadow from one edge. C. Migraine aura is usually bilateral, lasts minutes and resolves fully. D. Central retinal artery occlusion causes abrupt, profound painless loss of vision without preceding flashes or floaters.
pearl: Flashes and floaters alone may be posterior vitreous detachment; once a shadow or curtain appears, assume retinal detachment and refer the same day.
