thinking: Myopic patient with new flashes and floaters ↓ followed by a spreading shadow in one eye ↓ peripheral retina has lifted away ↓ painless, white eye ↓ Retinal detachment
exam_trap: A, Posterior vitreous detachment — it tempts because it also causes new flashes and floaters, but it does not cause a field defect; the advancing shadow means the retina itself has detached.
takeaway: Flashes plus floaters plus an advancing shadow equals retinal detachment until proven otherwise.

stem: A 46-year-old accountant visits his optometrist because over the past year he has struggled to read his phone and restaurant menus, especially in dim light, and now finds himself stretching his arm out to bring text into focus. His distance vision while driving is unchanged and he has no eye pain or glare. Which explanation is most likely?
why_correct: Presbyopia is the gradual, age-related loss of the lens's ability to accommodate for near objects, usually becoming noticeable in the mid-forties. Patients hold reading material further away and need better lighting, while distance vision is preserved. It is corrected with reading glasses or varifocal lenses.
why_wrong: A. Cataract usually causes glare and blurring at all distances rather than a selective near-focus problem. B. Myopia causes blurred distance vision with good near vision, the opposite of this pattern. C. Open-angle glaucoma is asymptomatic early and affects peripheral fields, not reading focus. E. Macular degeneration distorts central vision at all distances and typically affects older patients.
pearl: Near vision worsening in the mid-forties with normal distance vision is presbyopia. Holding text at arm's length is the classic clue.
thinking: Mid-forties ↓ difficulty only with near tasks ↓ holds text further away, distance vision normal ↓ reduced lens accommodation ↓ Presbyopia
exam_trap: A, Cataract — it tempts because it is a common age-related cause of reduced vision, but it blurs vision at all distances and causes glare rather than a pure loss of near focusing.
takeaway: Gradual near-vision difficulty with normal distance vision in middle age is presbyopia.

stem: A 64-year-old man is reviewed at the practice nurse leg clinic with a shallow, sloughy wound just above the inner ankle that has been present for four months. He has prominent varicose veins, the skin around the ankle is hard, eczematous and stained brown, and his legs ache by the end of the day. Both foot pulses are easily felt. Which type of ulcer is this?
why_correct: Venous ulcers occur in the gaiter area, often over the medial malleolus, and are shallow with sloping edges. Surrounding haemosiderin staining, venous eczema, lipodermatosclerosis and varicose veins reflect chronic venous hypertension. An ankle-brachial pressure index should be checked before starting compression therapy.
why_wrong: A. Arterial ulcers are painful, punched-out, on the foot or toes, with absent pulses. C. Neuropathic ulcers occur on pressure points of the sole in a numb foot. D. Malignant change is possible in a long-standing ulcer but is not the likeliest cause given these classic venous features. E. Pyoderma gangrenosum produces a rapidly enlarging, painful ulcer with a violaceous undermined edge.
pearl: Gaiter area, sloping edge, brown staining and varicose veins indicate a venous ulcer. Always check arterial supply before compression.
thinking: Chronic shallow ulcer above the medial malleolus ↓ haemosiderin staining, eczema and hardened skin ↓ varicose veins with palpable pulses ↓ chronic venous hypertension ↓ Venous ulcer
exam_trap: A, Arterial ulcer — it tempts because it is the other main cause of chronic leg ulcers, but arterial ulcers are painful, punched-out, on the foot and occur with absent pulses.
takeaway: A shallow gaiter-area ulcer with brown staining and varicose veins is venous: check ABPI, then compress.

stem: A 57-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes attends her annual diabetic review. The nurse finds a painless, round ulcer surrounded by thick callus on the sole beneath the ball of her right big toe. She was unaware of it. She cannot feel the monofilament at several sites on either foot, but her feet are warm and the foot pulses are bounding. Which mechanism best explains the ulcer?

options.A: Loss of protective sensation from peripheral neuropathy
options.B: Critical ischaemia from peripheral arterial disease

correct_answer: A. Loss of protective sensation from peripheral neuropathy
why_correct: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy removes protective sensation, so repeated pressure over a bony prominence such as the first metatarsal head goes unnoticed and causes callus and then ulceration. The ulcer is painless and the foot is warm with good pulses. She needs same-day referral to the diabetic foot protection or multidisciplinary foot service.
why_wrong: B. Ischaemic ulcers are usually painful, on the toes or heel, with a cool foot and weak or absent pulses. C. Venous ulcers occur around the ankle, not under the forefoot. D. Gouty tophi lie over joints and are rarely the cause of a plantar pressure ulcer. E. Vasculitic ulcers are usually painful, multiple and accompanied by purpura.
pearl: A painless plantar ulcer with callus in a warm, numb foot with good pulses is neuropathic. Diabetic foot ulcers need urgent specialist foot team referral.
thinking: Diabetes with loss of monofilament sensation ↓ painless ulcer with callus under a pressure point ↓ warm foot with bounding pulses, so circulation intact ↓ unnoticed repetitive pressure ↓ Loss of protective sensation from peripheral neuropathy
exam_trap: B, Critical ischaemia from peripheral arterial disease — it tempts because arterial disease is common in diabetes, but the warm foot with bounding pulses and a painless callused ulcer point to neuropathy.
takeaway: Painless, callused plantar ulcer in a warm, numb diabetic foot is neuropathic.

stem: A 34-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department three weeks after a caesarean section. This morning she developed a sharp pain in the right side of her chest that catches when she breathes in, together with sudden breathlessness. Her pulse is 112/min and oxygen saturation is lower than expected on air. Breath sounds are normal and equal on both sides, and she has no cough or fever. Which condition is the leading concern?
why_correct: The postpartum period, especially after caesarean section, carries a high risk of venous thromboembolism. Sudden pleuritic pain, breathlessness, tachycardia and hypoxia with a clear chest are typical of pulmonary embolism. She should be assessed promptly, with anticoagulation started while awaiting imaging unless contraindicated.
why_wrong: A. A pneumothorax would usually reduce breath sounds on the affected side. B. Pericarditis causes central pain eased by sitting forward, usually without hypoxia. D. Pneumonia would usually cause fever, cough and focal chest signs. E. Costochondritis causes reproducible chest wall tenderness without tachycardia or hypoxia.
pearl: In a postpartum woman, sudden pleuritic pain with breathlessness, tachycardia and hypoxia but a clear chest is pulmonary embolism until proven otherwise.
thinking: Recent caesarean section, a strong thrombotic risk ↓ sudden pleuritic pain and breathlessness ↓ tachycardia and hypoxia ↓ clear chest with equal breath sounds ↓ Pulmonary embolism
exam_trap: A, Spontaneous pneumothorax — it tempts because of sudden pleuritic pain and breathlessness, but breath sounds are equal and normal, and the postpartum state points to thromboembolism.
takeaway: Postpartum sudden pleuritic pain, breathlessness and hypoxia with a clear chest suggests pulmonary embolism.

stem: A 66-year-old woman telephones her GP surgery. An hour ago, while watching television, the vision in her right eye went dark as if a light had been switched off. Her left eye is unaffected. She has no eye pain, redness or headache, and she has never had anything similar. How should the GP handle this call?

options.A: Book a routine optometrist appointment this week
options.B: Arrange immediate same-day emergency eye assessment
options.C: Offer a routine GP appointment next week
options.E: Advise rest and to call back if not better in two days

correct_answer: B. Arrange immediate same-day emergency eye assessment
why_correct: Sudden painless loss of vision in one eye may be due to central retinal artery occlusion, giant cell arteritis, vitreous haemorrhage or retinal detachment, all of which threaten sight. She needs immediate assessment by emergency eye services, and an arterial occlusion should also be treated as a stroke-equivalent event needing vascular work-up.
why_wrong: A. A routine optometry review delays assessment of a potentially sight-threatening emergency. C. Waiting a week risks permanent visual loss and misses a possible vascular event. D. Antibiotic drops treat conjunctivitis, which does not cause visual loss. E. Watching and waiting is unsafe for sudden visual loss.
pearl: Sudden painless monocular visual loss is an emergency. Think retinal artery occlusion, giant cell arteritis, retinal detachment and vitreous haemorrhage, and refer the same day.
thinking: Sudden loss of vision in one eye ↓ painless, white eye ↓ possible retinal vascular occlusion or other sight-threatening cause ↓ time-critical ↓ Arrange immediate same-day emergency eye assessment
exam_trap: A, Book a routine optometrist appointment this week — it tempts because optometrists see many eye problems, but sudden visual loss needs emergency specialist assessment, not a routine check.
takeaway: Sudden painless loss of vision in one eye always needs same-day emergency assessment.

stem: A 79-year-old man is brought to the GP by his daughter, who says the television is always too loud and he struggles to follow family conversations at restaurants. He feels his hearing has slowly declined over several years in both ears equally. He has no ear pain, discharge or dizziness. Otoscopy shows clear canals and normal eardrums, Rinne testing is positive on both sides and the Weber test is central. Which diagnosis fits best?
why_correct: Presbycusis is age-related, bilateral, symmetrical sensorineural hearing loss that usually affects high frequencies first. Patients struggle most with speech against background noise. Tuning fork tests are consistent with sensorineural loss, and management is referral for audiology assessment and hearing aids.
why_wrong: A. Otosclerosis causes conductive loss, usually in younger adults, with a negative Rinne test. B. Earwax would be seen on otoscopy and causes conductive loss. D. A vestibular schwannoma typically causes unilateral or asymmetrical hearing loss with tinnitus. E. Ménière disease causes episodic vertigo, tinnitus and fluctuating hearing loss.
pearl: Gradual, symmetrical hearing loss in an older adult, worst in background noise, with normal otoscopy is presbycusis. Asymmetrical loss needs further investigation.
thinking: Older adult with gradual hearing loss ↓ bilateral and symmetrical ↓ normal otoscopy, tuning fork tests suggest sensorineural loss ↓ no vertigo or unilateral features ↓ Presbycusis
exam_trap: B, Impacted earwax — it tempts because it is a common, treatable cause of hearing loss in older people, but the canals are clear on otoscopy and the tuning fork findings indicate sensorineural loss.
takeaway: Slowly progressive, symmetrical hearing loss in older age with normal ears is presbycusis.

stem: A 58-year-old publican, who has smoked 20 cigarettes a day for forty years, sees his GP because his voice has been croaky and rough for over a month. He had no cold beforehand, has no sore throat and the hoarseness has not improved. Examination of the neck is normal. What should the GP do next?

options.A: A course of oral amoxicillin and review
options.B: A trial of a proton pump inhibitor for reflux
options.C: Referral on the suspected cancer pathway to ENT
options.E: Voice rest and review in three months

correct_answer: C. Referral on the suspected cancer pathway to ENT
why_correct: Persistent, unexplained hoarseness in an older adult, especially a smoker, is a red-flag symptom for laryngeal cancer. NICE suspected cancer guidance supports urgent referral to ENT so that the larynx can be examined directly. Early diagnosis greatly improves outcomes and the chance of preserving the voice.
why_wrong: A. There is no evidence of infection, and antibiotics would delay diagnosis. B. Treating presumed reflux would delay investigation of a red-flag symptom. D. A routine referral is too slow for possible cancer. E. Prolonged voice rest delays the diagnosis of a possible laryngeal tumour.
pearl: Hoarseness that persists without explanation in an older smoker needs urgent ENT assessment to visualise the larynx.
thinking: Older heavy smoker ↓ persistent hoarseness with no preceding infection ↓ red flag for laryngeal malignancy ↓ needs direct laryngeal examination quickly ↓ Referral on the suspected cancer pathway to ENT
exam_trap: B, A trial of a proton pump inhibitor for reflux — it tempts because reflux is a common cause of hoarseness, but in an older smoker with persistent symptoms an empirical trial delays urgent exclusion of cancer.
takeaway: Persistent unexplained hoarseness in an older smoker needs an urgent suspected cancer referral.

stem: A 45-year-old man attends his GP with a painless swelling of the left side of his scrotum which has slowly enlarged over several months. The swelling is smooth and fluctuant, the examiner can get above it, and no separate testis is palpable within it. It glows brightly when a pen torch is held against it. Which diagnosis fits best?
why_correct: A hydrocele is fluid within the tunica vaginalis surrounding the testis, so the testis cannot be felt separately and the swelling transilluminates. Being able to get above it shows it is confined to the scrotum. Ultrasound is advised in adults to exclude an underlying testicular cause.
why_wrong: A. An epididymal cyst also transilluminates, but it lies separate from and usually above the testis, which can be felt distinctly. B. An inguinal hernia extends from the groin, so the examiner cannot get above it, and it does not usually transilluminate. C. A varicocele feels like a bag of worms and does not transilluminate. D. A testicular tumour is a firm, solid mass that does not transilluminate.
pearl: Transilluminates and testis not separately palpable indicates hydrocele; transilluminates and testis separate suggests epididymal cyst. Scan new hydroceles in adults.
thinking: Painless scrotal swelling ↓ can get above it, so confined to scrotum ↓ transilluminates, so fluid-filled ↓ testis not separately palpable ↓ Hydrocele
exam_trap: A, Epididymal cyst — it tempts because it also transilluminates, but an epididymal cyst lies separate from the testis, which can be felt distinctly.
takeaway: A transilluminating scrotal swelling surrounding an impalpable testis is a hydrocele.

stem: A 42-year-old woman with three children is seen in the gynaecology clinic with periods that have become progressively heavier and more painful over two years. Bimanual examination finds a symmetrically bulky, soft and tender uterus. Transvaginal ultrasound shows diffuse thickening of the myometrium with a heterogeneous texture, but no discrete masses. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Adenomyosis is the presence of endometrial tissue within the myometrium, typically in parous women in their late thirties and forties. It causes heavy, painful periods and a diffusely enlarged, boggy, tender uterus. Ultrasound shows diffuse, heterogeneous myometrial thickening rather than well-defined fibroids.
why_wrong: A. Fibroids cause an irregularly enlarged, firm uterus and appear as discrete, well-defined masses on ultrasound. B. Endometrial cancer typically presents with postmenopausal or intermenstrual bleeding, not progressive painful periods with a uniformly bulky uterus. C. Endometriosis causes cyclical pain and dyspareunia, usually with a normal-sized uterus. E. A polyp causes intermenstrual bleeding and is seen within the cavity, not as diffuse myometrial change.
pearl: Bulky, boggy, tender, symmetrically enlarged uterus in a parous woman with heavy painful periods suggests adenomyosis; discrete masses suggest fibroids.
thinking: Parous woman in her forties ↓ progressive heavy, painful periods ↓ uniformly bulky, tender uterus ↓ diffuse myometrial thickening without discrete masses ↓ Adenomyosis
exam_trap: A, Uterine fibroids — it tempts because fibroids are the commonest cause of heavy bleeding with an enlarged uterus, but they appear as discrete masses and make the uterus irregular rather than diffusely bulky and tender.
takeaway: Heavy painful periods with a diffusely bulky, tender uterus is adenomyosis.

stem: A 62-year-old woman attends the emergency department with swelling of her lower lip and the left side of her tongue that developed over a few hours this morning. It is not itchy and there is no rash or wheeze. Her voice is normal and oxygen saturation is normal on air. She has hypertension treated with ramipril, which she has taken for 18 months, and has never had swelling before. Which is the most likely cause?

options.A: Angioedema due to her ACE inhibitor
options.D: Allergic contact dermatitis from a lip product

correct_answer: A. Angioedema due to her ACE inhibitor
why_correct: ACE inhibitors reduce the breakdown of bradykinin, which can cause non-itchy angioedema of the lips, tongue and face without urticaria. It can appear at any time, even after months or years of treatment. The ACE inhibitor must be stopped permanently, the airway monitored closely and the reaction recorded, as antihistamines and adrenaline often work less well than in allergic angioedema.
why_wrong: B. Anaphylaxis usually has a trigger exposure with rapid onset and features such as urticaria, wheeze or hypotension. C. Hereditary angioedema usually presents in childhood or adolescence with a family history. D. Contact dermatitis causes an itchy, eczematous rash rather than deep tongue swelling. E. Ludwig angina is a floor-of-mouth infection with fever, pain and dental sepsis.
pearl: ACE inhibitor angioedema is bradykinin-mediated, without itch or wheals, and can start years into treatment. Stop the drug permanently and watch the airway.
thinking: Lip and tongue swelling ↓ no itch, urticaria or wheeze ↓ bradykinin rather than histamine mechanism ↓ long-term ACE inhibitor use ↓ Angioedema due to her ACE inhibitor
exam_trap: B, Anaphylaxis — it tempts because facial and tongue swelling suggests an allergic emergency, but there is no urticaria, wheeze or haemodynamic compromise, and the non-itchy swelling in a patient on ramipril indicates bradykinin-mediated angioedema.
takeaway: Non-itchy lip or tongue swelling in a patient on an ACE inhibitor suggests drug angioedema.

stem: A 36-year-old man started carbamazepine for trigeminal neuralgia three weeks ago. He telephones his GP surgery and is seen at home: for two days he has had a high temperature and sore, red eyes, then painful ulcers on his lips and inside his mouth. Today dusky red patches have spread across his chest and back, and some areas are blistering, with skin peeling when touched. What should the GP do now?

options.A: Continue carbamazepine and start oral prednisolone
options.B: Apply a potent topical steroid and review in one week
options.C: Switch to phenytoin and review in a few days
options.D: Start oral aciclovir for herpetic stomatitis
options.E: Stop carbamazepine and arrange emergency hospital admission

correct_answer: E. Stop carbamazepine and arrange emergency hospital admission
why_correct: Fever, conjunctivitis, painful mucosal ulceration and spreading dusky lesions with blistering and skin detachment soon after starting carbamazepine indicate Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis. Prompt withdrawal of the culprit drug is the single most important step, followed by urgent admission for specialist dermatology, ophthalmology and supportive care, often in a burns or intensive care setting. The reaction should be reported through the Yellow Card scheme.
why_wrong: A. Continuing the culprit drug allows the reaction to progress, and oral steroids are not a substitute for admission. B. This is a life-threatening skin failure that cannot be managed with topical treatment in the community. C. Phenytoin is another aromatic anticonvulsant that can cross-react and cause the same reaction. D. Herpes does not explain the widespread blistering rash with skin detachment, and delaying admission is dangerous.
pearl: Fever, mucosal erosions and blistering skin with peeling after a new drug indicates SJS or TEN. Stop the drug and admit urgently; aromatic anticonvulsants are common culprits.
thinking: Recently started carbamazepine ↓ fever and sore eyes, then mouth ulcers ↓ spreading dusky lesions with blistering and skin detachment ↓ severe cutaneous drug reaction ↓ Stop carbamazepine and arrange emergency hospital admission
exam_trap: D, Start oral aciclovir for herpetic stomatitis — it tempts because painful mouth ulcers suggest herpes, but the conjunctivitis, widespread blistering and skin peeling after a new drug indicate SJS or TEN.
takeaway: Suspected SJS or TEN: stop the culprit drug at once and admit as an emergency.

stem: A 22-year-old woman with newly diagnosed focal epilepsy is started on carbamazepine by the neurology team. She has used the combined pill for several years and is in a stable relationship. She asks her GP whether she needs to think about anything regarding her pill. What is the key issue to discuss?

options.A: Her pill will raise carbamazepine to toxic levels
options.B: Carbamazepine will cause her periods to stop permanently
options.C: Her pill will be less effective at preventing pregnancy
options.D: Her pill will lower carbamazepine levels and worsen seizure control
options.E: There is no clinically relevant interaction

correct_answer: C. Her pill will be less effective at preventing pregnancy
why_correct: Carbamazepine induces liver enzymes, which speed up the metabolism of oestrogen and progestogen and reduce the contraceptive effectiveness of the combined pill. She should be advised to use a method unaffected by enzyme inducers, such as a copper or levonorgestrel intrauterine device or the progestogen-only injection, in line with FSRH guidance. Pre-pregnancy counselling about antiseizure medicines is also important.
why_wrong: A. The pill does not significantly increase carbamazepine levels. B. Carbamazepine does not cause permanent amenorrhoea. D. Combined pills reduce lamotrigine levels, not carbamazepine levels. E. The interaction is clinically important and can lead to unplanned pregnancy.
pearl: Enzyme-inducing antiseizure drugs reduce the effectiveness of hormonal contraception. Intrauterine methods or the progestogen-only injection remain reliable.
thinking: Combined pill user ↓ starts carbamazepine ↓ hepatic enzyme induction ↓ faster metabolism of contraceptive hormones ↓ Her pill will be less effective at preventing pregnancy
exam_trap: D, Her pill will lower carbamazepine levels and worsen seizure control — it tempts because combined pills do lower lamotrigine levels, but with carbamazepine the problem is the other way round: the antiseizure drug weakens the pill.
takeaway: Enzyme-inducing antiseizure drugs make the combined pill unreliable; switch to an unaffected method.

stem: An 18-year-old woman visits her practice nurse before moving into university halls of residence. Her records show she was absent from school on the day of the Year 9 meningococcal immunisation and has never had it since. She is otherwise fully immunised. She asks which vaccine will protect her against the meningococcal groups covered by the routine teenage programme. Which vaccine should be offered?
why_correct: The routine UK adolescent programme includes the MenACWY conjugate vaccine, which protects against meningococcal groups A, C, W and Y and reduces carriage in teenagers. Those who missed it remain eligible for a catch-up dose up to their 25th birthday, and first-time university entrants are specifically encouraged to have it. She should be offered MenACWY now.
why_wrong: A. MenB vaccine is given in the infant programme and does not protect against groups A, C, W or Y. B. Hib/MenC covers only group C, and is not the adolescent vaccine. C. HPV vaccine protects against human papillomavirus, not meningococcal disease. E. Pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine protects against pneumococcus and is used mainly for older and at-risk groups.
pearl: MenACWY is the routine teenage meningococcal vaccine, and people who missed it can catch up until their 25th birthday. Encourage it before university.
thinking: Teenager who missed the school meningococcal dose ↓ moving into shared university accommodation ↓ adolescent vaccine covers groups A, C, W and Y ↓ catch-up eligibility applies ↓ MenACWY conjugate vaccine
exam_trap: A, MenB vaccine — it tempts because group B is an important cause of meningococcal disease, but MenB is part of the infant schedule and does not cover the groups in the adolescent programme.
takeaway: Missed the teenage meningococcal dose? Offer MenACWY catch-up, especially before university.

stem: A GP is part of a regional working group preparing comments for the UK National Screening Committee on a proposal to introduce population screening for a cancer. The proposal lists several features of the cancer and of the suggested test. Which feature would most strongly support introducing a screening programme?

options.A: The cancer is very rare in the target population
options.B: Treatment is equally effective whenever it is started
options.C: The only available test is invasive, painful and costly
options.D: The cancer causes rapid death before any symptom-free stage
options.E: It has a detectable symptom-free stage at which treatment improves outcome

correct_answer: E. It has a detectable symptom-free stage at which treatment improves outcome
why_correct: Screening is only worthwhile if a condition has a recognisable latent or early symptomless stage, and if treating it at that stage leads to better outcomes than treating it once symptoms appear. This is central to the Wilson and Jungner principles used by the UK National Screening Committee. Other requirements include an important health problem, an acceptable and accurate test, and benefits outweighing harms.
why_wrong: A. A very rare condition generally gives too few true positives to justify population screening. B. If early treatment is no better than later treatment, early detection gives no benefit. C. A screening test must be acceptable to the population, so an invasive, painful test is unsuitable. D. With no detectable symptomless phase, there is nothing for screening to find early.
pearl: Screening works only if there is a detectable early phase and early treatment changes the outcome. Otherwise it just adds anxiety, cost and overdiagnosis.
thinking: Purpose of screening is earlier detection ↓ needs a detectable symptomless stage ↓ early treatment must improve outcome ↓ otherwise no benefit ↓ It has a detectable symptom-free stage at which treatment improves outcome
exam_trap: B, Treatment is equally effective whenever it is started — it tempts because effective treatment sounds desirable, but if timing makes no difference, detecting the disease early gives no benefit.
takeaway: Screening needs a detectable early stage where earlier treatment improves outcome.

stem: A GP practice audits a rapid throat swab test for group A streptococcus in patients with sore throats. Of those tested, 50 had a positive rapid test, and throat culture confirmed streptococcal infection in 45 of these 50. What does the figure of 45 out of 50 (90%) represent?
why_correct: The positive predictive value is the proportion of people with a positive test result who truly have the condition: true positives divided by all positive results. Here 45 of the 50 positive tests were confirmed, giving a positive predictive value of 90%. It answers the patient's question: given a positive result, how likely is it that I have the disease?
why_wrong: A. Sensitivity is the proportion of all people with the disease who test positive, so its denominator is everyone with the disease. B. Specificity is the proportion of people without the disease who test negative. D. Negative predictive value is the proportion of negative results that are truly disease-free. E. A likelihood ratio combines sensitivity and specificity and is not a simple proportion of positives.
pearl: Predictive values start from the test result; sensitivity and specificity start from disease status. Predictive values also change with how common the disease is.
thinking: Denominator is all positive test results ↓ numerator is those confirmed to have disease ↓ true positives divided by all positives ↓ probability of disease given a positive test ↓ Positive predictive value
exam_trap: A, Sensitivity — it tempts because both measures involve true positives, but sensitivity divides by everyone with the disease, whereas here the denominator is everyone who tested positive.
takeaway: PPV is true positives divided by all positive results: the chance a positive is correct.

stem: A 16-year-old boy sees his GP about a dragging ache in the left side of his scrotum that is worse after football and towards the end of the day. Standing, there is a soft, irregular swelling above the left testis that feels like a collection of worm-like strands; it becomes much less obvious when he lies flat. It does not transilluminate, and both testes feel normal. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: A varicocele is a dilatation of the pampiniform venous plexus. It is much more common on the left because the left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein at a right angle. It feels like a bag of worms above the testis, is more prominent on standing and empties when lying down, and causes a dragging ache. Most need only reassurance, but referral is considered for pain, testicular growth concerns or subfertility.
why_wrong: B. A hydrocele is a smooth swelling surrounding the testis that transilluminates. C. An epididymal cyst is a smooth, discrete, transilluminating lump separate from the testis. D. A hernia extends from the groin, so the examiner cannot get above it, and it often has a cough impulse. E. Torsion causes sudden severe pain with a tender, high-riding testis, not a chronic dull ache.
pearl: Left-sided bag of worms that empties lying down is a varicocele. A new right-sided varicocele, or one that does not empty, needs imaging to exclude a retroperitoneal or renal mass.
thinking: Dull dragging scrotal ache ↓ soft worm-like swelling above the left testis ↓ prominent standing, reduces lying flat ↓ does not transilluminate ↓ Varicocele
exam_trap: D, Indirect inguinal hernia — it tempts because it can also reduce on lying down, but a hernia extends from the groin, so the examiner cannot get above it, whereas this soft swelling of worm-like strands lies above the testis within the scrotum.
takeaway: A left-sided bag of worms above the testis that empties on lying down is a varicocele.

stem: A 34-year-old man sees his GP because his partner noticed that his left testicle feels harder and slightly bigger than the right. He has no pain, fever or urinary symptoms. On examination there is a hard, non-tender irregularity arising from the body of the left testis. The epididymis feels normal and the swelling does not transilluminate. How should he be managed?

options.A: Reassure and review in six weeks
options.D: Refer on a suspected cancer pathway to urology
options.E: Advise scrotal support and simple analgesia

correct_answer: D. Refer on a suspected cancer pathway to urology
why_correct: A hard, painless swelling arising from the body of the testis is testicular cancer until proven otherwise. NICE suspected cancer guidance supports a suspected cancer pathway referral for a non-painful enlargement or change in shape or texture of the testis. Scrotal ultrasound and tumour markers follow, and outcomes are excellent when it is caught early.
why_wrong: A. Watchful waiting delays the diagnosis of a likely malignancy. B. There is no pain, fever or urinary symptom to suggest infection, and antibiotics would only delay assessment. C. Semen analysis has no role in assessing a testicular mass. E. Supportive measures treat inflammation, not a suspicious solid lump.
pearl: Location is the key: a lump you cannot separate from the testis is suspicious, whereas a lump separate from it (epididymal cyst) or one that transilluminates (hydrocele) is usually benign.
thinking: Young man with a new testicular change ↓ Painless, hard, arising from the testis itself ↓ No transillumination, epididymis normal ↓ Treat as testicular cancer until proven otherwise ↓ Suspected cancer pathway referral to urology
exam_trap: B, doxycycline for epididymo-orchitis — it tempts because it is the commonest cause of scrotal swelling in young men, but there is no pain, fever or urinary symptom, and treating a tumour with antibiotics wastes valuable weeks.
takeaway: A painless, hard lump within the testis needs urgent urology referral, not antibiotics or reassurance.

stem: A 24-year-old man is brought to his GP by his mother. For two months he has stayed in his bedroom, convinced that newsreaders on television are sending coded instructions meant only for him. He describes a man's voice that talks about him in the third person, narrating what he is doing. A urine drug screen is negative and he has no medical history. Which term best describes this group of symptoms?
why_correct: A fixed false belief that broadcasts carry personal messages (delusions of reference) and a voice giving a running commentary in the third person (an auditory hallucination) are psychotic symptoms. Third-person running commentary is a first-rank symptom that is particularly characteristic of schizophrenia. A first presentation of psychosis should be referred urgently to an early intervention in psychosis service.
why_wrong: A. Obsessional thoughts are recognised by the person as their own and resisted, unlike delusions. B. Depersonalisation is a feeling of being detached from oneself, without false beliefs or voices. C. Overvalued ideas are strongly held but understandable beliefs, not bizarre and fixed. D. Confabulation is filling memory gaps with false memories, as in Korsakoff syndrome.
pearl: Hallucinations and delusions together define psychosis; voices discussing the patient in the third person or giving a running commentary are first-rank symptoms of schizophrenia.
thinking: Young man, social withdrawal ↓ Belief that television sends messages to him ↓ Voice describing his actions in the third person ↓ Delusions plus hallucinations, drug screen negative ↓ Psychotic symptoms
exam_trap: C, overvalued ideas — they are also strongly held beliefs, but they are understandable within the person's culture and background; a belief that newsreaders send personal coded messages is a delusion.
takeaway: Delusions plus hallucinations, such as third-person running commentary, are psychotic symptoms.

stem: A 59-year-old publican who has smoked since his teens and drinks heavily tells his GP that his voice has been rough and croaky for the past two months. He had no cold beforehand, and voice rest has not helped. He has no stridor and no difficulty swallowing. Which action is most appropriate?

options.B: Trial of a proton pump inhibitor and review in three months
options.C: Refer on a suspected cancer pathway to ENT
options.D: Refer to speech and language therapy
options.E: Arrange a chest radiograph and reassure if normal

correct_answer: C. Refer on a suspected cancer pathway to ENT
why_correct: Persistent, unexplained hoarseness in a middle-aged smoker who drinks heavily is a red flag for laryngeal cancer. NICE suspected cancer guidance supports a suspected cancer pathway referral to ENT so that the larynx can be examined directly with laryngoscopy. Early laryngeal cancer is highly treatable.
why_wrong: A. There is no infection, and antibiotics do not treat persistent hoarseness. B. Reflux laryngitis is a diagnosis of exclusion and a three-month trial would delay a cancer diagnosis. D. Voice therapy may follow ENT assessment but must not replace it. E. A chest radiograph may look for lung cancer affecting the recurrent laryngeal nerve, but a normal film does not exclude laryngeal cancer.
pearl: Smoking and alcohol multiply the risk of head and neck cancer. Hoarseness lasting weeks without an infection needs the larynx visualised.
thinking: Smoker and heavy drinker ↓ Hoarse for weeks, not after a cold ↓ No improvement with voice rest ↓ Red flag for laryngeal cancer ↓ Suspected cancer referral to ENT
exam_trap: B, PPI trial — reflux is a common cause of hoarseness, but in a high-risk patient a long empirical trial delays laryngoscopy and possible cancer diagnosis.
takeaway: Persistent unexplained hoarseness in a smoker needs urgent ENT referral, not trial treatments.

stem: A 26-year-old competitive swimmer attends her GP with a three-day history of a painful, itchy left ear and a small amount of discharge. Pressing on the tragus makes her wince. Otoscopy shows a red, swollen ear canal containing debris; the eardrum, where visible, looks normal. She is not diabetic and is otherwise well. What is the likeliest diagnosis?
why_correct: Ear pain and itch with tragal tenderness, a red swollen canal and debris, in someone whose ears are often wet, is otitis externa. It is an infection or inflammation of the external ear canal and is usually treated with topical acidic, antibiotic or steroid drops after cleaning. In people with diabetes or immunosuppression, severe pain should raise concern for necrotising otitis externa.
why_wrong: A. A perforated drum would be seen, and pain typically eases once the drum perforates; tragal tenderness is not a feature. B. Cholesteatoma causes painless, foul-smelling discharge and hearing loss over months. C. Mastoiditis causes swelling and tenderness behind the ear with fever. D. Ramsay Hunt syndrome causes ear pain with vesicles and facial nerve palsy.
pearl: Pain on moving the pinna or pressing the tragus localises the problem to the ear canal; swimming, eczema and cotton bud use are common triggers.
thinking: Swimmer with an itchy, painful ear ↓ Pain on pressing the tragus ↓ Red, swollen canal with debris ↓ Normal-looking drum ↓ Otitis externa
exam_trap: A, acute otitis media with perforation — discharge suggests a burst drum, but the drum looks normal and tragal tenderness places the problem in the canal.
takeaway: Tragal tenderness and a swollen, red ear canal mean otitis externa, not middle ear infection.

stem: A 30-year-old man who works in a residential care home attends his GP with three weeks of itching that keeps him awake at night. There are small papules and short, wavy greyish tracks on the sides of his fingers and the front of his wrists, and some itchy papules on his penis. Several residents he looks after have also been scratching. What is the likeliest diagnosis?
why_correct: Intense itch worse at night, burrows on the fingers and wrists, genital papules and itching in close contacts are classic features of scabies, an infestation with Sarcoptes scabiei. It spreads through prolonged skin contact and outbreaks are common in care homes. Treatment is permethrin cream applied to the whole body and repeated after a week, with all close contacts treated at the same time.
why_wrong: A. Contact dermatitis follows exposure to an irritant or allergen and does not spread between people. B. Lichen planus causes purple, flat-topped papules on the wrists but no burrows and is not contagious. D. Dermatitis herpetiformis causes grouped vesicles on the elbows, knees and buttocks, linked with coeliac disease. E. Pompholyx causes deep-seated blisters on the palms and fingers, without burrows or spread to contacts.
pearl: Burrows are the diagnostic sign of scabies. Treat every close contact at the same time, even without symptoms, and warn that itch can persist for weeks after successful treatment.
thinking: Night-time itch for weeks ↓ Burrows on fingers and wrists, genital papules ↓ Close contacts also itching ↓ Contagious infestation ↓ Scabies
exam_trap: A, contact dermatitis — a care worker's hands are often exposed to gloves and soaps, but burrows, genital lesions and itching residents point to an infestation spreading between people.
takeaway: Night itch, finger web burrows and itchy contacts mean scabies: treat everyone at once.

stem: A 17-year-old boy attends his GP surgery with an itchy rash that started this morning. He shows photographs on his phone of raised, pale-centred pink swellings on his thigh that disappeared within a few hours, while new ones appeared on his back and arms. Today's lesions blanch and fade without leaving bruising or marks. He has no lip swelling or breathing difficulty and is otherwise well. What is the likeliest diagnosis?
why_correct: Itchy wheals that each last less than a day, appear in new places as old ones fade and leave no mark are typical of urticaria. It results from mast cell release of histamine and is often triggered by infection, food or drugs, though frequently no cause is found. A non-sedating antihistamine is first-line treatment.
why_wrong: B. Erythema multiforme causes fixed target lesions lasting days, mainly on the hands and feet. C. Urticarial vasculitis causes lesions lasting more than a day that are often painful and leave bruising. D. Erythema nodosum causes tender, red nodules on the shins. E. Pityriasis rosea causes a herald patch followed by a scaly rash on the trunk that lasts weeks.
pearl: Individual urticarial wheals fade within 24 hours without trace; lesions that last longer, burn or leave bruising suggest urticarial vasculitis and need further assessment.
thinking: Itchy raised wheals ↓ Each fades within hours as new ones appear ↓ No marks or bruising left ↓ No angioedema or airway features ↓ Urticaria
exam_trap: B, erythema multiforme — pale-centred lesions can look target-like, but erythema multiforme lesions are fixed for days, whereas these move and fade within hours.
takeaway: Itchy wheals that come and go within hours and leave no mark are urticaria.

stem: A 69-year-old woman attends her GP with burning pain under her left breast and around to her back that began three days ago. Yesterday a band of clustered blisters on a red base appeared in the same area. The rash stops sharply at the front of her chest in the middle. She had chickenpox as a child. What is the likeliest diagnosis?
why_correct: Pain in a band around one side of the chest followed by clustered vesicles in the same dermatome, stopping at the midline, is shingles. It is caused by reactivation of varicella-zoster virus that has stayed dormant in a sensory ganglion since chickenpox. Oral antivirals are most useful when started early, particularly in older people, and analgesia is important.
why_wrong: A. Contact dermatitis follows the area of contact with an allergen and is itchy rather than painful in a dermatomal band. B. Bullous pemphigoid causes large, tense, itchy blisters spread widely, often on the limbs. C. Impetigo causes honey-crusted lesions, usually on the face, without preceding nerve pain. E. Dermatitis herpetiformis causes symmetrical itchy vesicles on extensor surfaces.
pearl: Pain often comes before the rash in shingles and can be mistaken for cardiac, pleural or abdominal disease; involvement of the tip of the nose suggests ophthalmic zoster needing urgent eye assessment.
thinking: Older woman with unilateral burning chest pain ↓ Vesicles appear in the same band ↓ Rash stops at the midline ↓ Dermatomal varicella-zoster reactivation ↓ Herpes zoster
exam_trap: B, bullous pemphigoid — it is a common blistering disease in older people, but its blisters are large, tense and widespread, not a painful band that respects the midline.
takeaway: Painful vesicles in a single dermatome that stop at the midline are shingles.

stem: A 19-year-old man attends a walk-in centre with a rash on the backs of his hands and on his palms that appeared over 48 hours. The lesions are round, with a dusky centre, a paler ring and an outer red rim. A week ago he had a crop of cold sores on his upper lip. His mouth, eyes and genitals are unaffected and he feels well. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Target lesions with three zones on the hands, appearing about a week after herpes simplex, are classic erythema multiforme. It is an immune reaction, most often triggered by herpes simplex virus, and is usually self-limiting. Treatment is supportive, with antiviral prophylaxis considered for frequent recurrences.
why_wrong: B. Stevens-Johnson syndrome is usually drug-induced and causes widespread blistering with mucosal involvement and systemic illness. C. Urticarial wheals fade within hours and do not form fixed three-zone targets. D. Hand, foot and mouth disease causes small oval vesicles with mouth ulcers, mainly in young children. E. Secondary syphilis causes non-itchy copper-coloured macules on the palms and soles, not target lesions.
pearl: Herpes simplex is the commonest trigger for erythema multiforme; drugs are the commonest trigger for Stevens-Johnson syndrome, which always involves the mucosae.
thinking: Young man with lesions on the hands ↓ Fixed target lesions with three zones ↓ Cold sores a week earlier ↓ No mucosal involvement, systemically well ↓ Erythema multiforme
exam_trap: B, Stevens-Johnson syndrome — targets raise fear of SJS, but there is no mucosal involvement, no blistering or skin pain, and the trigger was herpes simplex rather than a drug.
takeaway: Target lesions on the hands a week after a cold sore, with no mucosal disease, mean erythema multiforme.

stem: A 47-year-old landscape gardener asks his GP to look at several marks on his skin because his wife says one of them looks different from the others. The GP examines each of the lesions carefully. Which finding would most strongly suggest melanoma?

options.A: A round, evenly brown mole that has been unchanged for 20 years
options.B: A brown lesion with a ragged, notched edge that has recently changed shape
options.C: A soft, raised, flesh-coloured mole with hairs growing from it
options.D: A waxy, brown plaque with a greasy, stuck-on surface
options.E: A firm pink-brown papule on the leg that dimples when pinched

correct_answer: B. A brown lesion with a ragged, notched edge that has recently changed shape
why_correct: An irregular, notched border and a recent change in shape are major warning features of melanoma in both the ABCDE approach and the weighted seven-point checklist used in UK primary care. A lesion with these features should be referred on a suspected cancer pathway to dermatology. Change in an existing lesion is particularly important.
why_wrong: A. A symmetrical, evenly coloured mole that has not changed for years is reassuring. C. A soft, flesh-coloured hairy lesion is typical of a benign intradermal naevus. D. A waxy, stuck-on lesion is a seborrhoeic keratosis, which is benign. E. A firm papule that dimples on pinching is a dermatofibroma, which is benign.
pearl: Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Colour variation, Diameter and Evolution are the warning features; change in size, shape or colour carries the greatest weight in the UK seven-point checklist.
thinking: Patient worried about a mole that looks different ↓ Compare features against melanoma warning signs ↓ Irregular, notched border ↓ Recent change in shape ↓ Most suspicious for melanoma
exam_trap: D, the waxy, stuck-on plaque — seborrhoeic keratoses can be dark and alarming, but their greasy, stuck-on surface is characteristic of a benign lesion.
takeaway: An irregular border and a recent change in shape are the features that most raise concern for melanoma.

stem: A 58-year-old man with hereditary haemochromatosis, managed with regular venesection, presents to the emergency department with a hot, swollen right knee that came on overnight. There has been no injury. He is apyrexial and otherwise well. A knee radiograph shows fine linear calcification within the joint cartilage. Which condition is most likely?
correct_answer: E. Acute calcium pyrophosphate crystal arthritis (pseudogout)
why_correct: Haemochromatosis is a recognised cause of calcium pyrophosphate deposition, and cartilage calcification (chondrocalcinosis) on the radiograph supports it. An acute hot knee in this setting is most likely pseudogout. The knee should still be aspirated to exclude infection; the fluid shows weakly positively birefringent, rhomboid crystals.
why_wrong: A. Gout more often affects the first toe joint and does not cause chondrocalcinosis. B. Septic arthritis must always be excluded by aspiration, but he is apyrexial and the radiograph and history favour crystal arthritis. C. Reactive arthritis follows a gut or genital infection, which is not described. D. Haemarthrosis is usually caused by trauma or anticoagulation, neither of which is present.
pearl: Think of metabolic causes when pseudogout presents in a younger patient: haemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism and hypomagnesaemia are the classic associations.
thinking: Acute hot, swollen knee ↓ History of haemochromatosis ↓ Chondrocalcinosis on radiograph ↓ No fever, trauma or infection history ↓ Pseudogout, still aspirate to exclude sepsis
exam_trap: A, gout — it is the commonest crystal arthritis, but haemochromatosis and cartilage calcification point specifically to calcium pyrophosphate disease.
takeaway: Haemochromatosis with an acute hot knee and chondrocalcinosis points to pseudogout; still aspirate.

stem: A 27-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her flatmate. For the past week she has slept two or three hours a night yet says she has never felt better. She talks rapidly, jumping between topics, and has spent all her savings on designer clothes and a business plan that she says will make her a millionaire. She has lost her job after arguing with her manager. A urine drug screen is negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Elevated mood with little need for sleep, pressured speech with flight of ideas, grandiose plans and reckless spending, causing severe disruption such as job loss, define a manic episode. A negative drug screen makes a substance-induced cause less likely. Mania usually indicates bipolar affective disorder and needs urgent psychiatric assessment.
why_wrong: A. Generalised anxiety causes persistent worry and tension, not elevated mood or grandiosity. C. Delirium causes fluctuating confusion and inattention, usually with a medical cause. D. Emotionally unstable personality disorder causes long-standing, rapidly shifting emotions rather than a distinct episode of elation. E. ADHD is a lifelong pattern of inattention and impulsivity, not a new episode with reduced need for sleep.
pearl: A reduced need for sleep without tiredness is one of the most useful signs of mania; ask about it whenever someone presents with unusual energy or spending.
thinking: Week of very little sleep without fatigue ↓ Elevated mood, rapid speech, flight of ideas ↓ Grandiose plans and reckless spending ↓ Marked social and work disruption, drug screen negative ↓ Manic episode
exam_trap: D, emotionally unstable personality disorder — impulsive spending and conflict tempt this answer, but personality disorders are long-standing patterns, whereas this is a distinct episode with elevated mood and reduced sleep.
takeaway: Elevated mood, little need for sleep, grandiosity and reckless spending causing disruption mean mania.

stem: A 70-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes, who smoked for 40 years, tells her GP that a cramping ache in her right calf forces her to stop each time she walks to the post office. Standing still for a minute or two eases it, and she can then carry on. She has no pain at rest and her skin is intact. Her right foot pulses are weak. What is the likeliest diagnosis?
why_correct: Cramping calf pain that comes on with walking a consistent distance and eases quickly on standing still, with weak foot pulses, is intermittent claudication. It is caused by peripheral arterial disease, for which diabetes and smoking are major risk factors. The ankle-brachial pressure index confirms the diagnosis, and management starts with smoking cessation, supervised exercise and cardiovascular risk reduction.
why_wrong: B. Spinal stenosis pain is relieved by sitting or bending forwards, not simply by standing still, and pulses are normal. C. Chronic limb-threatening ischaemia causes rest pain, ulceration or gangrene. D. Venous insufficiency causes aching, swelling and skin changes that are worse after standing, not pain on walking. E. A ruptured Baker cyst causes sudden calf pain and swelling resembling a DVT.
pearl: Claudication eases with standing still; neurogenic claudication from spinal stenosis needs sitting or leaning forwards and is often worse walking downhill.
thinking: Smoker with diabetes ↓ Calf cramp on walking a set distance ↓ Relief within minutes on standing still ↓ Weak foot pulses, no rest pain ↓ Intermittent claudication
exam_trap: B, lumbar spinal stenosis — it also causes leg pain on walking in older people, but it needs sitting or bending forward to ease and the pulses are normal.
takeaway: Calf pain on walking eased by standing still, with weak pulses, is intermittent claudication.

stem: A 63-year-old man who has smoked about a packet a day since his teens sees the practice nurse because he gets breathless walking up hills. He has coughed up white sputum most winter mornings for several years. He never had childhood wheeze or hay fever, and his symptoms change little from day to day. Post-bronchodilator spirometry shows an obstructive pattern that does not reverse. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A long smoking history, exertional breathlessness, chronic productive cough and persistent airflow obstruction after bronchodilator are the features of COPD. The lack of atopy and of day-to-day variation makes asthma less likely. Stopping smoking is the single most effective intervention to slow disease progression.
why_wrong: A. Asthma typically starts earlier, varies over time, is linked with atopy and shows reversible obstruction. B. Bronchiectasis causes daily large volumes of purulent sputum and recurrent infections. D. Pulmonary fibrosis causes a dry cough, fine crackles and a restrictive pattern on spirometry. E. Heart failure causes orthopnoea and oedema, not chronic sputum with fixed obstruction.
pearl: Spirometry confirms COPD by showing obstruction that persists after bronchodilator; marked reversibility or variability should make you reconsider asthma.
thinking: Long-term heavy smoker ↓ Breathless on exertion, chronic morning sputum ↓ No atopy or variability ↓ Fixed obstruction after bronchodilator ↓ COPD
exam_trap: A, asthma — wheeze and breathlessness overlap, but asthma shows variability and reversibility, whereas fixed obstruction in a heavy smoker with no atopy points to COPD.
takeaway: A heavy smoker with chronic sputum, breathlessness and fixed obstruction on spirometry has COPD.

stem: A 16-year-old girl with known asthma develops wheeze and chest tightness during a cross-country run on a cold morning. When the school nurse assesses her, she can talk normally in full sentences, her breathing rate is only slightly raised and she is alert and pink. What should she be given first for quick relief?
correct_answer: E. Inhaled salbutamol via a spacer
why_correct: Wheeze and chest tightness triggered by exercise and cold air, without features of severe or life-threatening asthma, need rapid bronchodilation with an inhaled reliever. A short-acting beta-2 agonist such as salbutamol, taken through a spacer, works within minutes. If she uses an inhaled corticosteroid–formoterol inhaler as her reliever, that is the inhaler she should use instead.
why_wrong: A. Oral steroids reduce airway inflammation over hours and are used for moderate or worse attacks, not for immediate relief. B. An antihistamine does not relieve bronchospasm. C. Montelukast is a preventer and does not act quickly enough for relief. D. Adrenaline is for anaphylaxis, not a mild asthma attack.
pearl: Exercise-induced symptoms often mean asthma control is poor; after the episode, review her preventer, inhaler technique and whether she is using her reliever often.
thinking: Known asthma ↓ Wheeze triggered by exercise and cold air ↓ Speaks in full sentences, alert, only mildly tachypnoeic ↓ Mild attack needs fast bronchodilation ↓ Inhaled salbutamol via spacer
exam_trap: A, oral prednisolone — steroids are central to treating attacks, but they take hours to work and are not needed for a mild episode that responds to a reliever.
takeaway: A mild asthma attack is treated first with an inhaled reliever such as salbutamol via a spacer.

stem: A 74-year-old woman with severe COPD, who uses nebulisers at home, is brought to the emergency department with increased breathlessness and green sputum. The paramedics have been giving her 15 L/min oxygen via a reservoir mask, and she has become drowsy. Her oxygen saturation is 99%. Which oxygen strategy is most appropriate?

options.A: Continue high-flow oxygen as her saturation is satisfactory
options.C: Change to controlled oxygen via a Venturi mask, aiming for 88-92%, and check an arterial blood gas
options.D: Give oxygen only if her saturation falls below 80%
options.E: Change to humidified high-flow oxygen without blood gas monitoring

correct_answer: C. Change to controlled oxygen via a Venturi mask, aiming for 88-92%, and check an arterial blood gas
why_correct: In patients with COPD at risk of carbon dioxide retention, uncontrolled high-concentration oxygen can worsen hypercapnia and cause drowsiness and respiratory acidosis. British Thoracic Society guidance advises controlled oxygen through a Venturi mask with a target saturation of 88-92%. An arterial blood gas is needed to assess carbon dioxide and pH and to decide whether non-invasive ventilation is required.
why_wrong: A. A high saturation does not exclude rising carbon dioxide, and her drowsiness suggests it is already happening. B. Stopping oxygen suddenly can cause dangerous rebound hypoxaemia. D. Allowing saturation to fall that low risks harmful hypoxaemia. E. Uncontrolled oxygen without blood gas monitoring repeats the original error.
pearl: Never withhold oxygen from a hypoxic patient with COPD; titrate it. Drowsiness on high-flow oxygen in COPD should make you suspect hypercapnia and check a blood gas.
thinking: Severe COPD exacerbation ↓ High-flow oxygen given, now drowsy ↓ Saturation high, carbon dioxide likely rising ↓ Need controlled oxygen with a target range ↓ Venturi mask, 88-92% target, arterial blood gas
exam_trap: B, stop all oxygen — recognising the danger of high-flow oxygen tempts candidates to remove it entirely, but this causes rebound hypoxaemia; the answer is to control it, not stop it.
takeaway: In COPD at risk of hypercapnia, give controlled oxygen to a target range and check a blood gas.

stem: A 68-year-old woman with heart failure and chronic kidney disease, who already takes ramipril, had spironolactone added at the cardiology clinic a fortnight ago. She attends the emergency department feeling generally weak and noticing palpitations. Her ECG shows tall, tented T waves. Which drug-related abnormality is most likely?
why_correct: Spironolactone is an aldosterone antagonist that reduces potassium excretion in the distal nephron. The risk of hyperkalaemia is greater when it is combined with an ACE inhibitor and when kidney function is impaired. Tall, tented T waves with weakness and palpitations suggest significant hyperkalaemia needing urgent treatment and review of these drugs.
why_wrong: A. Spironolactone retains potassium rather than causing its loss. C. Hypercalcaemia is not caused by spironolactone and shortens the QT interval rather than peaking T waves. D. Spironolactone does not cause hypoglycaemia. E. Hypermagnesaemia is unusual and not linked to spironolactone.
pearl: Potassium-sparing diuretic plus ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker plus CKD is a common route to dangerous hyperkalaemia; check renal function and potassium soon after starting or changing doses.
thinking: Spironolactone added to ramipril ↓ Background chronic kidney disease ↓ Weakness and palpitations ↓ Tall, tented T waves ↓ Hyperkalaemia
exam_trap: A, hypokalaemia — many diuretics lower potassium, but spironolactone is potassium-sparing, and peaked T waves indicate high, not low, potassium.
takeaway: Spironolactone with an ACE inhibitor in CKD readily causes hyperkalaemia: monitor potassium.

stem: A 57-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes started lisinopril for hypertension eight weeks ago. She now has an irritating, tickly cough without sputum that keeps her awake at night. She is afebrile, her chest is clear on examination and a chest radiograph is normal. Which mechanism best explains her cough?

options.B: Blockade of beta-2 receptors in the airways

why_correct: ACE also breaks down bradykinin, so inhibiting it allows bradykinin to accumulate in the airways, irritating sensory nerves and causing a dry cough. This is a common class effect and can begin weeks or months after starting treatment. Switching to an angiotensin II receptor blocker, which does not affect bradykinin, usually resolves it.
why_wrong: B. Beta-2 blockade causes bronchospasm with non-selective beta blockers, not ACE inhibitors. C. ACE inhibitors reduce, rather than increase, angiotensin II. D. Mast cell histamine release is the mechanism in allergic reactions, not ACE inhibitor cough. E. There are no reflux symptoms, and the timing fits the new drug.
pearl: ACE inhibitor cough can take weeks to settle after stopping the drug; angiotensin receptor blockers are the usual substitute because they do not raise bradykinin.
thinking: New ACE inhibitor ↓ Dry, tickly cough ↓ Normal examination and chest radiograph ↓ Drug class effect ↓ Bradykinin accumulation
exam_trap: C, increased angiotensin II activity — angiotensin is the familiar part of the pathway, but ACE inhibitors lower angiotensin II; the cough comes from the bradykinin that ACE normally breaks down.
takeaway: ACE inhibitor dry cough is caused by bradykinin build-up; switch to an angiotensin receptor blocker.

stem: A 74-year-old man with atrial fibrillation who takes warfarin is prescribed a seven-day course of clarithromycin for a chest infection. Five days later he notices large bruises on his arms, and his gums bleed when he brushes his teeth. His INR is well above his target range. Which explanation is most likely?

options.A: Clarithromycin has induced liver enzymes, reducing warfarin's effect
options.B: His diet has contained more vitamin K than usual
options.C: Clarithromycin has inhibited warfarin metabolism, increasing its effect
options.D: Clarithromycin has reduced the absorption of warfarin
options.E: The infection has caused a rise in his platelet count

correct_answer: C. Clarithromycin has inhibited warfarin metabolism, increasing its effect
why_correct: Clarithromycin inhibits the liver cytochrome P450 enzymes that metabolise warfarin, so warfarin levels and its anticoagulant effect rise, increasing the INR and bleeding risk. Antibiotics can also reduce vitamin K production by gut bacteria. INR should be checked more often whenever an interacting drug is started or stopped in someone on warfarin.
why_wrong: A. Enzyme induction would lower the INR, not raise it. B. Extra vitamin K reduces warfarin's effect and lowers the INR. D. Reduced absorption would weaken warfarin's effect. E. A higher platelet count would not cause bruising and bleeding.
pearl: Enzyme inhibitors such as macrolides, fluconazole and amiodarone increase warfarin's effect; enzyme inducers such as rifampicin and carbamazepine reduce it.
thinking: Stable on warfarin ↓ New clarithromycin course ↓ Bruising, gum bleeding, raised INR ↓ Enzyme inhibition raises warfarin levels ↓ Increased anticoagulant effect
exam_trap: A, enzyme induction — candidates recall that antibiotics interact with warfarin but confuse direction; induction lowers the INR, whereas clarithromycin is an inhibitor and raises it.
takeaway: Enzyme inhibitors like clarithromycin increase warfarin's effect: check the INR when starting them.

stem: A 52-year-old man started high-intensity atorvastatin after a myocardial infarction six weeks ago. He presents to the emergency department with aching, weak thighs and shoulders and says his urine has become the colour of cola. Which investigation best confirms the suspected diagnosis?
why_correct: Muscle pain and weakness with dark urine after starting a statin suggest rhabdomyolysis, with myoglobin from damaged muscle colouring the urine. A markedly raised creatine kinase confirms muscle breakdown. The statin should be stopped, and renal function and potassium checked because myoglobin can cause acute kidney injury.
why_wrong: A. Troponin assesses cardiac muscle injury, and his symptoms are in skeletal muscle. B. Urate relates to gout, not muscle breakdown. C. ESR is a non-specific marker of inflammation and does not confirm muscle damage. E. Statins can raise liver enzymes, but these do not confirm rhabdomyolysis.
pearl: Statin myopathy is more likely with high doses, older age, hypothyroidism, renal impairment and interacting drugs such as macrolides and fibrates.
thinking: Recently started high-intensity statin ↓ Proximal muscle aches and weakness ↓ Cola-coloured urine from myoglobin ↓ Suspected rhabdomyolysis ↓ Creatine kinase
exam_trap: A, troponin — after a recent myocardial infarction it is tempting to test the heart, but his symptoms are skeletal muscle pain and dark urine, which point to rhabdomyolysis.
takeaway: Muscle pain and dark urine on a statin suggest rhabdomyolysis: check creatine kinase and renal function.

stem: An 82-year-old woman, who lives alone, was started on indapamide for hypertension a month ago. Her daughter brings her to the GP because she has become muddled, unsteady on her feet and has fallen twice this week. She is not dehydrated and has no focal neurological signs. Which drug-related electrolyte disturbance best explains her presentation?
why_correct: Thiazide and thiazide-like diuretics such as indapamide impair the kidney's ability to dilute urine, causing hyponatraemia, particularly in older women. Low sodium causes confusion, unsteadiness and falls, and can progress to seizures. Sodium should be checked urgently and the diuretic reviewed.
why_wrong: B. Thiazides cause potassium loss, not retention. C. Thiazides can raise calcium slightly, but this rarely causes confusion; hyponatraemia is far more common. D. Thiazides lower rather than raise sodium. E. Thiazides cause magnesium loss, not excess.
pearl: Older age, female sex and low body weight increase the risk of thiazide hyponatraemia; check sodium within a few weeks of starting a thiazide-like diuretic.
thinking: Older woman recently started on indapamide ↓ New confusion, unsteadiness and falls ↓ Thiazide-like diuretics impair urine dilution ↓ Sodium falls ↓ Hyponatraemia
exam_trap: C, hypercalcaemia — thiazides do reduce calcium excretion and high calcium can cause confusion, but the rise is usually mild; hyponatraemia is the classic thiazide cause of confusion and falls.
takeaway: New confusion and falls in an older woman on a thiazide-like diuretic suggest hyponatraemia.

stem: A 66-year-old man of African-Caribbean family origin was started on amlodipine for hypertension by his GP a month ago. He now notices puffy ankles, worse in the evenings. He is not breathless, his jugular venous pressure is not raised, his chest is clear and a urine dipstick shows no protein. What is the most likely cause of his ankle swelling?
why_correct: Dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers such as amlodipine dilate arterioles more than venules, raising capillary pressure and causing fluid to leak into the tissues of the ankles. It is a common, dose-related side effect and is not due to fluid overload, so diuretics help little. Reducing the dose or switching to another class usually resolves it.
why_wrong: A. Heart failure would usually cause breathlessness, a raised JVP or chest signs. B. Nephrotic syndrome causes heavy proteinuria, which the dipstick excludes. C. DVT is usually unilateral and tender, not bilateral, evening-predominant swelling. D. Hypothyroidism causes non-pitting myxoedema with other features, not swelling soon after a new drug.
pearl: Calcium-channel blocker oedema reflects capillary pressure rather than salt and water retention, so loop diuretics are ineffective; consider a lower dose or an alternative drug.
thinking: New amlodipine ↓ Bilateral ankle swelling, worse in evenings ↓ No signs of heart failure ↓ No proteinuria, not unilateral ↓ Adverse effect of amlodipine
exam_trap: A, heart failure — bilateral ankle swelling in an older man suggests it, but there is no breathlessness, raised JVP or chest signs, and the timing fits the new drug.
takeaway: Bilateral ankle swelling soon after starting amlodipine is a common side effect, not fluid overload.

stem: A 74-year-old woman with angina had bisoprolol started at the cardiology clinic last week. She attends her GP feeling light-headed and tired, especially when she stands up from a chair. Her pulse is regular at 42 bpm and her blood pressure is low-normal. Her thyroid function was normal last month. What is the most likely explanation?
why_correct: Beta blockers slow the heart by blocking sympathetic stimulation of the sinoatrial node and atrioventricular conduction. A new, marked bradycardia with light-headedness soon after starting bisoprolol is a recognised adverse effect. The dose should be reduced or stopped, and an ECG checked for heart block.
why_wrong: A. Dehydration usually causes a fast pulse, not a slow one. C. Hypothyroidism can slow the pulse, but her thyroid function was recently normal. D. Vasovagal syncope causes brief episodes with a trigger, not persistent bradycardia. E. Anaemia causes tiredness with a normal or fast pulse.
pearl: When a patient feels dizzy after starting a rate-limiting drug, check the pulse and an ECG; beta blockers can unmask conduction disease such as heart block.
thinking: Bisoprolol recently started ↓ Light-headed and tired ↓ Regular pulse of 42 bpm ↓ Other causes of a slow pulse excluded ↓ Beta-blocker bradycardia
exam_trap: A, postural hypotension from dehydration — dizziness on standing fits postural hypotension, but dehydration causes a compensatory tachycardia, not a pulse in the 40s.
takeaway: New dizziness with a very slow pulse after starting a beta blocker suggests drug-induced bradycardia.

stem: A 34-year-old man started sertraline for depression five days ago. He telephones the practice saying that he feels queasy after each dose and has had slightly loose stools. He has no fever, tremor, agitation, muscle twitching or thoughts of self-harm. He asks whether he should stop the tablets. What is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: Stop sertraline as these symptoms indicate serotonin syndrome
options.B: Record a sertraline allergy and do not restart it
options.D: Explain that these are common early side effects that often settle, and continue with review
options.E: Arrange an urgent upper gastrointestinal endoscopy

correct_answer: D. Explain that these are common early side effects that often settle, and continue with review
why_correct: Nausea and loose stools are common, usually short-lived side effects in the first weeks of SSRI treatment. They often improve if the medicine is continued, sometimes taken with food. He should be reviewed soon after starting, as is standard with antidepressants, and advised to seek help if he develops worrying symptoms such as suicidal thoughts or signs of serotonin syndrome.
why_wrong: A. Serotonin syndrome causes fever, agitation, tremor and muscle twitching, none of which he has. B. Mild gastrointestinal upset is a side effect, not an allergy. C. Switching is premature for mild, expected symptoms that often settle. E. There is nothing to suggest peptic ulcer disease needing endoscopy.
pearl: Warn patients about early SSRI side effects before they start; knowing that nausea is expected and usually transient improves adherence.
thinking: SSRI started five days ago ↓ Mild nausea and loose stools ↓ No features of serotonin syndrome ↓ Common, transient early side effects ↓ Reassure, continue and review
exam_trap: A, serotonin syndrome — gastrointestinal symptoms occur in serotonin syndrome, but it also needs neuromuscular and autonomic features such as tremor, clonus, fever and agitation.
takeaway: Mild nausea in the first weeks of an SSRI is common and usually settles: continue and review.

stem: A 23-year-old woman is reviewed at her GP surgery five days after starting trimethoprim for a urinary infection. She has developed a widespread, itchy, blotchy pink rash of flat and slightly raised spots on her trunk and limbs. Her mouth, eyes and genitals are unaffected, there are no blisters, the skin is not painful and she is afebrile and well. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.C: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms

why_correct: An itchy, widespread maculopapular rash a few days after starting a new drug, with no mucosal involvement, blistering, skin pain or systemic illness, is a simple drug eruption. It is the most common type of drug reaction. The drug should be stopped and recorded as the cause, with emollients and antihistamines for symptoms.
why_wrong: A. Stevens-Johnson syndrome involves mucous membranes, painful skin and blistering with systemic illness. B. Toxic epidermal necrolysis causes extensive skin detachment and severe illness. C. DRESS causes fever, facial swelling, lymphadenopathy and organ involvement, usually weeks after starting the drug. E. Erythema nodosum causes tender red nodules on the shins, not a widespread itchy rash.
pearl: Red flags that turn a drug rash into an emergency: mucosal involvement, blistering, skin pain, fever, facial swelling or organ dysfunction.
thinking: New antibiotic five days ago ↓ Widespread itchy maculopapular rash ↓ No mucosal involvement, blisters or skin pain ↓ Systemically well ↓ Uncomplicated drug eruption
exam_trap: A, Stevens-Johnson syndrome — antibiotics such as trimethoprim are recognised triggers, but SJS needs mucosal involvement, painful skin and blistering, all absent here.
takeaway: An itchy drug rash without mucosal involvement, blisters, skin pain or fever is a simple drug eruption.

stem: A 38-year-old man sees his GP. His father, now 58, was recently diagnosed with Huntington disease after developing involuntary jerky movements and personality change. The man has two young children and wants to understand how the condition is passed on in families. Which statement about its inheritance is accurate?

options.A: It is autosomal recessive, so his children are affected only if both parents carry the gene
options.B: It is autosomal dominant, so a child of an affected parent has a 1 in 2 chance of inheriting it
options.C: It is X-linked recessive, so only sons can be affected
options.D: It is mitochondrial, so it is passed on only by mothers
options.E: It is X-linked dominant, so all daughters of an affected man are affected

correct_answer: B. It is autosomal dominant, so a child of an affected parent has a 1 in 2 chance of inheriting it
why_correct: Huntington disease is caused by an expanded CAG trinucleotide repeat in the HTT gene and is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. Each child of an affected parent has a 50% chance of inheriting the expansion, regardless of sex. This man therefore has a 1 in 2 risk himself, and his children's risk depends on whether he carries it.
why_wrong: A. One abnormal copy is enough to cause Huntington disease, so it is not recessive. C. Men and women are affected equally, so it is not X-linked recessive. D. It is a nuclear gene disorder and can be passed on by either parent. E. It is not X-linked; sons and daughters of an affected father are equally at risk.
pearl: Huntington disease shows anticipation: the CAG repeat can expand between generations, particularly through paternal transmission, giving earlier onset in children.
thinking: Affected father with chorea and personality change ↓ Huntington disease ↓ CAG repeat in HTT, one copy sufficient ↓ either sex affected and either sex transmits ↓ autosomal dominant, 1 in 2 risk per child
exam_trap: A, autosomal recessive — many inherited neurological disorders are recessive, but Huntington disease needs only one expanded allele, so it is dominant.
takeaway: Huntington disease is autosomal dominant: each child of an affected parent has a 50% risk.

stem: A 26-year-old woman in her first pregnancy attends the antenatal clinic. Her booking blood results show she is RhD negative with no red cell antibodies detected. The midwife recommends routine antenatal anti-D immunoglobulin, and she asks what it is designed to prevent. Which condition does it aim to prevent?

options.B: Haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn
options.D: ABO incompatibility jaundice in the newborn
options.E: A transfusion reaction if she bleeds at delivery

correct_answer: B. Haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn
why_correct: If an RhD-negative woman carries an RhD-positive baby, fetal red cells crossing into her circulation can sensitise her to make anti-D antibodies. In this or a later pregnancy, these IgG antibodies cross the placenta and destroy fetal red cells, causing haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn. Anti-D immunoglobulin clears fetal cells before she becomes sensitised.
why_wrong: A. Neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia involves platelet antigens, not RhD, and is not prevented by anti-D. C. Anti-D has no effect on pre-eclampsia. D. ABO incompatibility is a separate cause of neonatal haemolysis that anti-D does not prevent. E. Transfusion reactions are prevented by cross-matching, not by anti-D prophylaxis.
pearl: Anti-D only works before sensitisation; once a woman has formed her own anti-D antibodies, prophylaxis is of no benefit and the pregnancy needs specialist monitoring.
thinking: RhD-negative mother, possible RhD-positive fetus ↓ fetomaternal haemorrhage can sensitise her ↓ maternal anti-D IgG crosses placenta ↓ fetal red cell destruction ↓ anti-D prophylaxis prevents haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn
exam_trap: D, ABO incompatibility jaundice in the newborn — it is also an antibody-mediated neonatal haemolysis, but it involves ABO antigens and is not prevented by anti-D.
takeaway: Anti-D prevents RhD sensitisation and so prevents haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn.

stem: A 58-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer phones the palliative care nurse. She started modified-release morphine for bone pain last week, and her pain is now well controlled. She has only opened her bowels once in five days, passing hard pellets with straining. She is not vomiting, is passing wind, and her abdomen is soft. What is the most appropriate management?

options.B: Stop morphine and switch to paracetamol alone
options.D: Start a regular laxative, such as a macrogol with senna

correct_answer: D. Start a regular laxative, such as a macrogol with senna
