why_correct: Constipation is an expected adverse effect of regular opioids because they reduce gut motility, and it does not lessen with time. It should be treated with a regular laxative, typically an osmotic laxative and a stimulant laxative together, titrated to effect. Ideally a laxative is prescribed at the same time as a regular opioid is started.
why_wrong: A. Bulk-forming laxatives are avoided in opioid-induced constipation because they can worsen symptoms when gut motility is reduced. B. Stopping effective analgesia would leave her in pain when the constipation can be treated. C. Loperamide is an antidiarrhoeal and would worsen constipation. E. She has no features of obstruction, so imaging is not needed.
pearl: Opioid-induced constipation does not develop tolerance, unlike nausea and drowsiness; whenever a regular opioid is prescribed, a regular laxative should be prescribed with it.
thinking: Recently started regular morphine ↓ hard, infrequent stools ↓ no vomiting, passing wind, soft abdomen, so not obstruction ↓ predictable opioid side effect, slowed transit ↓ regular osmotic plus stimulant laxative
exam_trap: A, ispaghula husk — fibre seems a natural first step for constipation, but bulk-forming laxatives are unhelpful and can worsen opioid-induced constipation.
takeaway: Treat opioid constipation with a regular osmotic plus stimulant laxative, not bulk-forming agents.

presentation: Unilateral Nasal Obstruction With Epistaxis (Red Flag)
stem: A 64-year-old retired carpenter sees his GP with three months of a blocked left nostril. He has had several episodes of blood-stained discharge from the same side, without fever, facial pain or symptoms on the right. Anterior rhinoscopy shows no obvious bleeding point. Which is the best next step?

options.A: Intranasal corticosteroid spray and review in three months
options.B: A course of oral antibiotics for sinusitis
options.C: Silver nitrate cautery in the surgery

why_correct: Persistent one-sided nasal blockage with blood-stained discharge in an older adult is a red flag for a sinonasal tumour, particularly with occupational wood dust exposure. Symmetrical conditions such as rhinitis rarely cause strictly unilateral symptoms. He needs urgent ENT assessment with endoscopic examination and imaging.
why_wrong: A. A steroid trial would delay diagnosis of a possible tumour. B. There are no features of acute bacterial sinusitis. C. Cautery treats a visible anterior bleeding point, which is absent, and does not address the obstruction. E. Reassurance is inappropriate with unexplained unilateral red-flag symptoms.
pearl: Unilateral symptoms are the warning sign in the nose: persistent one-sided blockage, bloody discharge or facial swelling needs ENT examination, especially with wood dust exposure.
thinking: Older man with persistent unilateral nasal blockage ↓ recurrent blood-stained discharge from same side ↓ no infection, no visible anterior bleeding point ↓ wood dust exposure ↓ possible sinonasal tumour, urgent ENT referral
exam_trap: A, intranasal corticosteroid spray — it is the right first step for rhinitis, but unilateral blockage with bleeding is not rhinitis and needs examination, not a trial of treatment.
takeaway: Persistent unilateral nasal blockage with bleeding needs urgent ENT assessment to exclude a tumour.

stem: A 66-year-old woman who drinks heavily and smokes visits her GP about a sore in the floor of her mouth. It has not healed in six weeks despite her dentist adjusting her denture. On examination there is a firm ulcer with raised edges, and a hard, non-tender lump is felt in the left side of her neck. Which is the best next step?

options.A: Urgent referral on the suspected head and neck cancer pathway
options.B: Benzydamine mouthwash and review in one month
options.D: Routine dental referral for further denture adjustment
options.E: Reassure her that this is an aphthous ulcer

correct_answer: A. Urgent referral on the suspected head and neck cancer pathway
why_correct: A non-healing oral ulcer with rolled edges in a smoker and heavy drinker, together with a hard neck lump, strongly suggests oral squamous cell carcinoma with nodal spread. Unexplained oral ulceration that persists, or a persistent unexplained neck lump, warrants a suspected cancer pathway referral. Biopsy and staging are carried out by the head and neck team.
why_wrong: B. Symptomatic treatment and a month's wait would delay a probable cancer diagnosis. C. Antifungal treatment is for candida, which causes white plaques, not an indurated ulcer. D. The ulcer has already failed to heal after denture adjustment. E. Aphthous ulcers are shallow, painful and heal within a couple of weeks; they do not cause hard neck nodes.
pearl: Persistence after removing an obvious cause is the key warning sign: a mouth ulcer that does not heal once trauma is corrected needs urgent specialist assessment.
thinking: Smoker and heavy drinker ↓ oral ulcer not healing after cause removed ↓ firm with raised edges ↓ hard neck node ↓ suspected oral cancer, urgent cancer pathway referral
exam_trap: D, routine dental referral for further denture adjustment — trauma is a common cause of mouth ulcers, but this one has already failed to heal after adjustment and there is a hard neck node.
takeaway: A non-healing oral ulcer in a smoker or drinker, especially with a neck lump, needs urgent cancer referral.

stem: An 84-year-old care home resident with type 2 diabetes takes gliclazide and metformin. He has had diarrhoea and vomiting for three days and has barely eaten, but staff have continued his usual tablets. At 6 am he is found sweaty and drowsy with slurred speech. A fingerprick glucose reading is 2.6 mmol/L. What best explains his presentation?
why_correct: Sulfonylureas such as gliclazide stimulate insulin release regardless of the blood glucose, so continuing them while not eating causes hypoglycaemia. Older people and those with dehydration or reduced kidney function are at higher risk. He needs immediate glucose treatment appropriate to his conscious level, followed by observation because sulfonylurea hypoglycaemia can recur over many hours.
why_wrong: A. Slurred speech and drowsiness can mimic stroke, but the low glucose explains them and must be corrected first. B. Infection may contribute, but the low glucose is the direct cause of his symptoms. C. Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state causes very high glucose, not low. E. Diabetic ketoacidosis causes high glucose and is unusual in type 2 diabetes on these drugs.
pearl: Always check capillary glucose in any patient with confusion, drowsiness or focal neurology; sick day advice includes reviewing sulfonylureas when a patient is not eating.
thinking: Older man on gliclazide ↓ not eating due to vomiting, tablets continued ↓ sweating, drowsiness, slurred speech ↓ low capillary glucose ↓ sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycaemia
exam_trap: A, acute stroke — slurred speech and drowsiness suggest a stroke, but hypoglycaemia is a classic stroke mimic and the low glucose explains the picture.
takeaway: Gliclazide continued while not eating causes hypoglycaemia, which can be prolonged and mimic stroke.

stem: A 22-year-old woman attends the GP surgery for a repeat prescription of her combined pill. She mentions that over the last few months she has had episodes where shimmering zigzag lines spread across her vision for about 20 minutes and then fade, followed by a throbbing one-sided headache. Her blood pressure is normal and she does not smoke. What is the most appropriate advice about her contraception?

options.A: Continue the combined pill and add a triptan for the headaches
options.B: Stop the combined pill and offer a progestogen-only or non-hormonal method
options.C: Switch to a combined pill with a lower oestrogen dose
options.D: Continue the combined pill but take it continuously without a break
options.E: Continue the combined pill and refer urgently for brain imaging

correct_answer: B. Stop the combined pill and offer a progestogen-only or non-hormonal method
why_correct: Her visual symptoms are a typical aura, so she has migraine with aura. In women with migraine with aura, combined hormonal contraception carries an unacceptable increase in the risk of ischaemic stroke and is contraindicated. She should stop the combined pill and be offered an effective alternative, such as a progestogen-only method or a copper intrauterine device, with interim contraceptive advice.
why_wrong: A. Treating the headache does not remove the stroke risk of combined hormonal contraception. C. Any dose of oestrogen remains contraindicated in migraine with aura. D. Continuous use still exposes her to oestrogen and the same stroke risk. E. A typical aura with full resolution and normal examination does not need urgent imaging, and the pill should not be continued.
pearl: Ask every woman starting or continuing combined hormonal contraception about headache with aura; progestogen-only methods and the copper coil are suitable alternatives.
thinking: Combined pill user ↓ spreading zigzag visual disturbance that resolves, then headache ↓ migraine with aura ↓ oestrogen increases ischaemic stroke risk ↓ stop combined pill and switch method
exam_trap: C, switch to a combined pill with a lower oestrogen dose — it sounds like a safer compromise, but migraine with aura contraindicates all combined hormonal methods.
takeaway: Migraine with aura contraindicates combined hormonal contraception; switch to a progestogen-only or non-hormonal method.

stem: A 74-year-old woman develops sudden severe mid-back pain while bending to lift a bag of shopping. She has had no fall or other injury. A spinal X-ray shows a wedge compression fracture of the T12 vertebra. She has no weight loss or night sweats, and her full blood count, calcium, ESR and serum protein electrophoresis are all normal. Which underlying condition is most likely?
why_correct: A vertebral compression fracture from minimal stress, such as bending or lifting, in an older woman is a fragility fracture, and osteoporosis is the most likely cause. Normal blood count, calcium, ESR and protein electrophoresis make malignancy unlikely. She should have a fracture risk assessment with DXA scanning and be considered for bone-protective treatment, calcium and vitamin D.
why_wrong: A. Myeloma can cause vertebral collapse, but normal blood count, calcium, ESR and electrophoresis make it unlikely. B. Osteomalacia causes bone pain, muscle weakness and abnormal calcium, phosphate or vitamin D. C. Metastases are unlikely with no cancer history, no systemic features and normal bloods. D. Paget disease causes bone pain and deformity with a raised alkaline phosphatase, not typical wedge fractures.
pearl: Many vertebral fragility fractures are found incidentally or dismissed as back strain; a vertebral fracture strongly predicts future hip and wrist fractures.
thinking: Older woman with minimal-trauma vertebral fracture ↓ fragility fracture ↓ normal FBC, calcium, ESR, electrophoresis ↓ malignancy unlikely ↓ osteoporosis, arrange DXA and bone protection
exam_trap: A, multiple myeloma — it is a classic cause of vertebral collapse in older people, but the normal blood count, calcium, ESR and electrophoresis argue strongly against it.
takeaway: A low-trauma fracture in an older adult is a fragility fracture; assess for osteoporosis.

stem: A 69-year-old man sees his GP because his hats have become tight and he has recently been fitted with a hearing aid. He also has an aching right shin, which looks bowed and feels warmer than the left. Blood tests show a raised alkaline phosphatase, with normal calcium, phosphate, albumin, bilirubin and transaminases. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Skull enlargement, deafness, bowing and warmth of a long bone with an isolated raised alkaline phosphatase are classic features of Paget disease of bone. Disordered, excessive bone turnover produces enlarged, weak and vascular bone. Calcium and phosphate are usually normal. Diagnosis is supported by X-ray and isotope bone scan, and bisphosphonates are used for bone pain.
why_wrong: B. Osteomalacia typically causes low calcium or phosphate, proximal muscle weakness and diffuse bone pain. C. Prostate metastases can raise alkaline phosphatase but do not cause skull enlargement, bowing and warmth of a limb. D. Primary hyperparathyroidism causes raised calcium. E. Multiple myeloma usually causes a normal alkaline phosphatase, raised calcium and anaemia.
pearl: Deafness in Paget disease comes from skull involvement compressing the auditory nerve or affecting the ossicles; increasing hat size is a classic history clue.
thinking: Older man with enlarging skull and deafness ↓ bowed, warm tibia ↓ isolated raised alkaline phosphatase ↓ normal calcium, phosphate and liver tests ↓ Paget disease of bone
exam_trap: C, bone metastases from prostate cancer — sclerotic metastases also raise alkaline phosphatase in older men, but they do not cause skull enlargement, deafness and a warm bowed tibia.
takeaway: Isolated raised ALP with bone pain, bowing or skull enlargement in an older adult suggests Paget disease.

stem: A 9-year-old boy is brought to the GP by his mother. For the past year he has had a dry cough at night and episodes of wheeze, which happen even without colds. They are worse in spring and after visits to his grandmother's house, where there is a dog. He had eczema as a baby and his father has hay fever. A salbutamol inhaler from the out-of-hours service helped quickly. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Recurrent wheeze and nocturnal cough that occur between viral infections, triggered by allergens such as pollen and animal dander, and relieved by a bronchodilator, indicate asthma. A personal history of eczema and family history of atopy add weight. The diagnosis should be supported with objective tests where possible, such as spirometry with bronchodilator reversibility or FeNO.
why_wrong: A. Viral-induced wheeze occurs only with colds and the child is well between episodes. C. Cystic fibrosis causes chronic productive cough, recurrent chest infections and poor growth. D. A foreign body causes sudden-onset symptoms, often one-sided, not recurrent allergen-triggered episodes. E. Allergic rhinitis causes nasal symptoms and does not explain wheeze.
pearl: Symptoms between colds, at night and with allergen triggers, plus personal or family atopy, move a wheezy child from viral-induced wheeze towards asthma.
thinking: Recurrent wheeze and night cough ↓ occurs without colds ↓ triggered by pollen and dog exposure ↓ atopic history and bronchodilator response ↓ asthma
exam_trap: A, viral-induced wheeze — it is very common in children, but his symptoms occur without colds and are triggered by allergens, which points to asthma.
takeaway: Recurrent wheeze between colds with allergen triggers and atopy suggests asthma; confirm objectively.

stem: A 23-year-old woman with known acute intermittent porphyria attends the emergency department with severe abdominal pain, repeated vomiting and a fast heart rate. She is anxious and her urine is dark. Her serum sodium is low. Her medicines are paracetamol as needed, folic acid, a salbutamol inhaler, an emollient cream, and carbamazepine, which her neurologist started three weeks ago for focal seizures. Which of her medicines is most likely to have precipitated this attack?
why_correct: Acute porphyria attacks are triggered by factors that increase demand for haem synthesis, including enzyme-inducing drugs. Carbamazepine induces hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes and is a recognised precipitant of acute porphyria. The attack causes abdominal pain, vomiting, tachycardia, hyponatraemia and psychiatric features. The drug should be stopped under specialist advice and treatment includes analgesia, carbohydrate and intravenous haem arginate.
why_wrong: A. Paracetamol at normal doses is considered safe in acute porphyria. B. Folic acid does not induce haem synthesis and is safe. C. A topical emollient has no meaningful systemic effect. D. Salbutamol is not a recognised precipitant.
pearl: Other precipitants of acute porphyria include alcohol, fasting, infection and some hormonal drugs; always check a drug's safety in a specialist porphyria drug database before prescribing.
thinking: Known acute intermittent porphyria ↓ abdominal pain, vomiting, tachycardia, hyponatraemia, anxiety ↓ acute attack ↓ enzyme-inducing drug recently started ↓ carbamazepine
exam_trap: A, paracetamol — it is the most frequently used drug on her list and might seem a likely culprit, but it is safe in porphyria; enzyme inducers such as carbamazepine are the problem.
takeaway: Enzyme-inducing drugs such as carbamazepine can precipitate acute porphyria attacks.

stem: A 27-year-old man attends the medical admissions unit with a week of fever and painful, swollen ankles. On both shins there are several raised, tender, bruise-like red-purple lumps a few centimetres across, which are warm to touch. There are no blisters, ulcers or target lesions. His chest X-ray shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. What are the skin lesions?
why_correct: Tender, warm, red-purple nodules on both shins are erythema nodosum, an inflammation of the subcutaneous fat. Together with ankle arthritis, fever and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, this is Löfgren syndrome, an acute form of sarcoidosis that usually resolves spontaneously. Other causes of erythema nodosum include streptococcal infection, tuberculosis, inflammatory bowel disease, pregnancy and some drugs.
why_wrong: A. Erythema multiforme causes target lesions, often on the hands and feet. B. Pretibial myxoedema causes non-tender, waxy plaques in Graves disease. D. Cellulitis is usually unilateral and spreading, not multiple discrete nodules on both shins. E. Pyoderma gangrenosum causes rapidly enlarging painful ulcers with a purple edge.
pearl: Erythema nodosum fades like a bruise over weeks without scarring or ulceration; always look for an underlying cause, including a chest X-ray.
thinking: Tender red-purple nodules on both shins ↓ inflammation of subcutaneous fat ↓ erythema nodosum ↓ with ankle arthritis and bilateral hilar nodes ↓ Löfgren syndrome of sarcoidosis
exam_trap: D, cellulitis — red, warm, tender skin on the leg suggests infection, but cellulitis is usually one-sided and spreading, not multiple bilateral nodules.
takeaway: Tender red nodules on both shins are erythema nodosum; look for sarcoidosis, infection, IBD or drugs.

stem: A 33-year-old woman sees her GP six weeks after giving birth. The delivery was complicated by a massive postpartum haemorrhage requiring several units of blood. Her breast milk never came in despite repeated attempts to feed. She feels exhausted, cold all the time and lightheaded when she stands up. She has not had a period since the birth. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Massive postpartum haemorrhage can cause ischaemic necrosis of the pituitary, which enlarges in pregnancy and is vulnerable to hypotension. Failure of lactation is often the first sign, from prolactin deficiency, followed by amenorrhoea, fatigue, cold intolerance and postural dizziness from deficiencies of gonadotrophins, TSH and ACTH. She needs pituitary hormone testing and, if cortisol is deficient, steroid replacement before thyroxine.
why_wrong: A. Postnatal depression causes low mood and fatigue but does not prevent lactation or cause postural hypotension. B. Postpartum thyroiditis does not explain failure of lactation and amenorrhoea. C. Asherman syndrome causes amenorrhoea from uterine scarring but no lactation failure or systemic symptoms. D. Primary adrenal failure would not explain absent lactation and cold intolerance, and is not linked to haemorrhage.
pearl: In hypopituitarism, always replace glucocorticoid before thyroxine, because starting thyroxine first can precipitate an adrenal crisis.
thinking: Massive postpartum haemorrhage ↓ pituitary infarction ↓ failure of lactation (prolactin) ↓ amenorrhoea, cold intolerance, postural dizziness (gonadotrophins, TSH, ACTH) ↓ Sheehan syndrome
exam_trap: A, postnatal depression — exhaustion after a difficult delivery fits, but it does not explain failure of lactation, cold intolerance and postural dizziness.
takeaway: Failure to lactate after major postpartum haemorrhage suggests Sheehan syndrome; test pituitary function.

stem: A 49-year-old woman attends the breast clinic for review. Two years ago she had a left mastectomy with axillary node clearance followed by radiotherapy. Over the past few months her left arm has gradually swollen and feels heavy, and her watch has become tight. The skin of the forearm is thickened, the swelling pits only slightly, and the arm is not red, hot or painful. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Gradual, painless swelling of the arm with heaviness and skin thickening after axillary node clearance and radiotherapy is secondary lymphoedema caused by impaired lymphatic drainage. Swelling becomes less pitting as tissue fibrosis develops. Management is through a specialist lymphoedema service with compression garments, skin care, exercise and manual lymphatic drainage; recurrence should be excluded if it develops suddenly.
why_wrong: A. A DVT usually causes more sudden swelling, often with pain and venous distension. B. Cellulitis causes a red, hot, painful limb, often with fever. C. Superior vena cava obstruction causes swelling of the face and both arms with distended neck veins. E. Lipoedema is symmetrical fat deposition in the legs, mainly in women, and does not follow lymph node surgery.
pearl: Patients with lymphoedema are prone to recurrent cellulitis; good skin care and early antibiotics for infection are important parts of management.
thinking: Previous axillary node clearance and radiotherapy ↓ gradual painless arm swelling and heaviness ↓ skin thickening, minimal pitting ↓ impaired lymphatic drainage ↓ secondary lymphoedema
exam_trap: A, upper limb deep vein thrombosis — cancer increases clot risk, but the slow, painless onset with skin thickening over months is typical of lymphoedema.
takeaway: Gradual painless limb swelling after lymph node surgery or radiotherapy is secondary lymphoedema.

stem: A 35-year-old man sees his GP with several months of cough at night, wheeze and chest tightness that come and go, with good weeks and bad weeks. He has never smoked. The GP plans objective testing to confirm the suspected diagnosis. Which result would most strongly support asthma?

options.A: A restrictive pattern with a normal FEV1/FVC ratio
options.B: Fixed airflow obstruction unchanged after a bronchodilator
options.C: Airflow obstruction that improves substantially after a bronchodilator
options.D: Reduced gas transfer with hyperinflated lungs
options.E: Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy on chest X-ray

correct_answer: C. Airflow obstruction that improves substantially after a bronchodilator
why_correct: Asthma is characterised by variable and reversible airflow obstruction caused by airway inflammation and bronchial hyperresponsiveness. Obstructive spirometry that improves significantly after a bronchodilator demonstrates this reversibility. Other supportive tests include a raised FeNO, blood eosinophils and peak flow variability over time.
why_wrong: A. A restrictive pattern suggests interstitial lung disease or chest wall disease. B. Fixed obstruction without reversibility is typical of COPD. D. Reduced gas transfer with hyperinflation suggests emphysema. E. Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy suggests sarcoidosis, not asthma.
pearl: Spirometry can be normal between asthma attacks, so a normal result does not exclude asthma; tests are best done when symptomatic and supported by FeNO or peak flow monitoring.
thinking: Never-smoker with episodic wheeze, night cough, chest tightness ↓ symptoms vary over time ↓ suspected asthma ↓ asthma is defined by variable, reversible airflow obstruction ↓ obstruction improving after bronchodilator
exam_trap: B, fixed airflow obstruction unchanged after a bronchodilator — obstruction is present in both asthma and COPD, but it is the reversibility, not the obstruction itself, that points to asthma.
takeaway: Asthma is variable, reversible airflow obstruction; bronchodilator reversibility supports the diagnosis.

stem: A 74-year-old woman with severe COPD, who has had previous admissions needing non-invasive ventilation, is brought to the emergency department breathless with an exacerbation. The paramedics have given 15 L/min of oxygen via a non-rebreather mask throughout the journey. On arrival her oxygen saturation is 98%, but she has become increasingly drowsy and has a bounding pulse and warm hands. An arterial blood gas shows a raised PaCO2 and acidosis. Which is the most likely explanation for her deterioration?
why_correct: In some patients with severe COPD, high-concentration oxygen worsens carbon dioxide retention, mainly by worsening ventilation-perfusion mismatch and by the Haldane effect, with reduced respiratory drive contributing. The result is hypercapnic acidosis with drowsiness, bounding pulse and warm peripheries. Oxygen should be reduced to a controlled device targeting saturations of 88 to 92%, and non-invasive ventilation considered if acidosis persists.
why_wrong: A. Pulmonary embolism causes hypoxaemia, which is not present, and does not typically cause drowsiness with hypercapnia. B. A tension pneumothorax causes hypoxia and haemodynamic collapse, not high saturations with drowsiness. C. Hypoglycaemia does not explain a raised PaCO2. E. There is no history of opioid use.
pearl: Patients known to retain carbon dioxide should carry an oxygen alert card; titrate oxygen to the target range rather than stopping it abruptly, which can cause dangerous hypoxia.
thinking: Severe COPD with previous ventilation ↓ high-flow oxygen with saturations of 98% ↓ drowsy, bounding pulse, warm hands ↓ raised PaCO2 with acidosis ↓ oxygen-induced carbon dioxide retention
exam_trap: A, pulmonary embolism — it is a cause of deterioration in COPD, but her saturations are high and the picture is hypercapnia, not hypoxaemia.
takeaway: Uncontrolled oxygen in CO2-retaining COPD causes hypercapnic acidosis; target saturations of 88 to 92%.

stem: A 26-year-old woman with schizophrenia is visited at home by her community psychiatric nurse. She has missed her last two depot antipsychotic injections. Her family says that for three weeks she has been sleeping poorly and staying in her room, and she is convinced that her neighbours are watching her through the television. She is fully orientated, her attention is normal, and a urine drug screen is negative. Which is the most likely explanation?
why_correct: The return of persecutory delusions, social withdrawal and sleep disturbance after missing antipsychotic treatment in a person with known schizophrenia is a relapse of psychosis. Stopping antipsychotics is the most common cause of relapse. She needs early review by the mental health team, assessment of risk and support to restart treatment.
why_wrong: A. Delirium causes fluctuating attention and disorientation, both of which are normal here. B. The urine drug screen is negative and there is a clear alternative explanation. C. There is no prominent low mood, and the delusions are not mood-congruent. D. Akathisia is a restless side effect of antipsychotics, not a cause of delusions after stopping them.
pearl: Early warning signs of relapse, such as poor sleep and withdrawal, often appear weeks before overt psychotic symptoms; relapse plans help patients and families spot them.
thinking: Known schizophrenia ↓ missed depot injections ↓ poor sleep, withdrawal, persecutory delusions ↓ orientated, normal attention, negative drug screen ↓ relapse of schizophrenia
exam_trap: A, delirium — new psychotic symptoms can be part of delirium, but her normal orientation and attention, together with stopping treatment, make relapse far more likely.
takeaway: Returning psychotic symptoms after stopping antipsychotics in schizophrenia indicate relapse.

stem: An FY1 doctor covering a haematology ward overnight is requested to write up an antifungal drug she has never used before for a 39-year-old man receiving chemotherapy. The nurse says the previous doctor usually wrote a particular dose and suggests she use that. Which course of action is safest?

options.A: Prescribe the dose the nurse suggests, as it has been used before
options.B: Check the BNF or local guidance and seek advice from a senior or pharmacist before prescribing
options.C: Prescribe the lowest dose she can recall seeing to minimise toxicity
options.D: Ask the patient what dose he took during a previous admission
options.E: Copy the dose from another patient's chart on the same ward

correct_answer: B. Check the BNF or local guidance and seek advice from a senior or pharmacist before prescribing
why_correct: Doctors must prescribe only within their competence and must have adequate knowledge of the drug, its dose, interactions and monitoring. When a medicine is unfamiliar, the safe course is to consult a reliable reference such as the BNF or local guidelines and to seek advice from a senior colleague or pharmacist. The prescriber remains personally responsible for the prescription she signs.
why_wrong: A. Hearsay from a colleague is not a reliable dosing source and the prescriber remains accountable. C. An arbitrary low dose may be ineffective, which is dangerous in an immunocompromised patient. D. A patient's recollection may be wrong and his circumstances, such as renal function, may have changed. E. Another patient's dose may reflect a different indication, weight or organ function.
pearl: Never prescribe a drug you do not know: check the BNF or local guidance, and ask a senior or pharmacist. You are accountable for every prescription you sign.
thinking: Unfamiliar drug and uncertain dose ↓ Prescriber accountable for the prescription ↓ Informal sources are unreliable ↓ Use a validated reference and expert advice ↓ Check the BNF or local guidance and seek advice
exam_trap: A, using the nurse's suggested dose — it feels collaborative and efficient, but it is unverified and the FY1 bears responsibility for any error.
takeaway: Unfamiliar drug: check a reliable reference and seek senior or pharmacist advice before you prescribe.

stem: A 79-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation is seen at home by her GP after three days of diarrhoea. She now has nausea, poor appetite and says objects look yellow-tinged. Her regular medicines include digoxin, which she has taken at the same dose for years. Blood tests show an acute kidney injury. Which property of digoxin best explains why she is now at risk of toxicity?

options.A: The difference between an effective and a toxic level is small
options.B: There is a wide margin between effective and toxic doses
options.C: It is cleared entirely by the liver, so kidney function is irrelevant
options.D: Toxicity generally needs many times the usual daily dose
options.E: Its effects are unaffected by changes in potassium concentration

correct_answer: A. The difference between an effective and a toxic level is small
why_correct: Digoxin has a narrow therapeutic index, so a modest rise in plasma concentration can tip a patient from benefit into toxicity. It is mainly renally excreted, so dehydration and acute kidney injury reduce clearance and raise levels even when the dose is unchanged. Nausea, anorexia and visual disturbance such as yellow-tinged vision are typical of toxicity.
why_wrong: B. This describes a wide therapeutic index, the opposite of digoxin. C. Digoxin is largely renally cleared, which is why her kidney injury matters. D. Toxicity can occur with levels only slightly above the therapeutic range. E. Hypokalaemia increases susceptibility to digoxin toxicity.
pearl: Narrow therapeutic index drugs such as digoxin, lithium, phenytoin and theophylline become toxic with small changes in level, often triggered by illness, renal impairment or interacting drugs.
thinking: Long-term stable digoxin dose ↓ New dehydration and acute kidney injury ↓ Reduced renal clearance raises the level ↓ Small rise is enough to cause toxicity ↓ Narrow gap between effective and toxic levels
exam_trap: C, liver clearance — candidates may not recall how digoxin is eliminated, but it is mainly renal, which is precisely why her kidney injury precipitated toxicity.
takeaway: Narrow therapeutic index: small changes in level, often from illness or renal impairment, cause toxicity.

presentation: Warfarin and a newly prescribed drug
stem: A 67-year-old man taking warfarin for atrial fibrillation telephones his GP surgery. An urgent treatment centre has just given him a course of clarithromycin for a chest infection, and he asks if it will interfere with his blood thinner. What is the most appropriate step before advising him?

options.A: Advise him to omit warfarin until the antibiotic course has finished
options.B: Tell him that short antibiotic courses do not affect warfarin
options.C: Check a drug-interaction reference such as the BNF
options.D: Ask him for his most recent cholesterol result
options.E: Request his blood group from the hospital laboratory

correct_answer: C. Check a drug-interaction reference such as the BNF
why_correct: Warfarin has many clinically important interactions, and several antibiotics, including macrolides, can enhance its anticoagulant effect and raise the INR. The appropriate first step is to check a reliable interaction source such as the BNF, then advise the patient and arrange earlier INR monitoring or anticoagulant clinic input as indicated. Advice should be based on the specific interaction rather than a blanket rule.
why_wrong: A. Stopping anticoagulation without a reason exposes him to stroke risk. B. Short antibiotic courses can significantly alter the INR. D. A cholesterol result has no bearing on warfarin interactions. E. Blood group does not predict drug interactions.
pearl: Any new drug in a patient on warfarin, including antibiotics and over-the-counter or herbal products, should prompt an interaction check and usually closer INR monitoring.
thinking: Patient on warfarin ↓ New antibiotic started ↓ Warfarin has many significant interactions ↓ Advice must be specific and evidence-based ↓ Check a drug-interaction reference
exam_trap: A, omitting warfarin — it seems a safe way to avoid bleeding, but stopping anticoagulation creates stroke risk and is not how interactions are managed.
takeaway: New medicine with warfarin: check an interaction reference, then advise and arrange INR monitoring as needed.

stem: A 45-year-old woman with bipolar disorder, stable on lithium for several years, attends the emergency department after four days of vomiting and watery diarrhoea. She now has a coarse tremor, slurred speech and an unsteady gait. Which mechanism best explains her current presentation?

options.A: Diarrhoea has increased the rate of lithium absorption from the gut
options.B: Gastroenteritis has induced the liver enzymes that metabolise lithium
options.C: Missed doses during vomiting have caused lithium withdrawal
options.D: Fluid and sodium loss have reduced renal lithium clearance, raising the level
options.E: Lithium has caused hypoglycaemia during the illness

correct_answer: D. Fluid and sodium loss have reduced renal lithium clearance, raising the level
why_correct: Lithium is handled by the kidneys in a similar way to sodium, so dehydration and sodium depletion increase its reabsorption and reduce clearance. The serum level rises and toxicity develops, causing coarse tremor, ataxia, dysarthria and confusion. Patients on lithium should be advised to seek review promptly during vomiting or diarrhoea, and a level and renal function should be checked.
why_wrong: A. Diarrhoea does not increase lithium absorption; if anything, absorption falls. B. Lithium is not metabolised by the liver; it is excreted unchanged by the kidneys. C. Missing doses would lower the level and would not cause this neurological picture. E. Lithium does not characteristically cause hypoglycaemia.
pearl: Lithium toxicity is often precipitated by dehydration, renal impairment or interacting drugs such as NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors and diuretics. Coarse tremor and ataxia are warning signs.
thinking: Stable lithium dose ↓ Vomiting and diarrhoea cause fluid and sodium loss ↓ Kidneys retain lithium with sodium ↓ Serum level rises into toxic range ↓ Reduced renal clearance causing toxicity
exam_trap: C, missed doses — vomiting suggests doses were lost, but that would lower the level; the neurological signs point to accumulation, not withdrawal.
takeaway: Dehydration in a patient on lithium reduces renal clearance and can quickly cause toxicity.

stem: A 63-year-old man with psoriatic arthritis takes weekly methotrexate. He telephones his GP with mouth ulcers, shivering and a fever. A full blood count taken this morning for routine monitoring shows a very low neutrophil count. How should the GP manage this?

options.A: Continue methotrexate and repeat the blood count in one week
options.B: Withhold methotrexate and arrange same-day hospital assessment
options.C: Increase folic acid to daily and continue methotrexate
options.D: Prescribe oral amoxicillin and review in 48 hours
options.E: Halve the methotrexate dose and recheck bloods next month

correct_answer: B. Withhold methotrexate and arrange same-day hospital assessment
why_correct: Fever with severe neutropenia in a patient on methotrexate suggests bone marrow toxicity with possible neutropenic sepsis, which is a medical emergency. Methotrexate should be stopped and the patient assessed urgently in hospital for blood cultures and prompt intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics. Specialist management of the toxicity, which may include folinic acid, follows in hospital.
why_wrong: A. Continuing the drug and waiting a week risks overwhelming infection and further marrow suppression. C. Routine folic acid does not reverse established toxicity and continuing methotrexate is unsafe. D. Oral antibiotics in the community are inadequate for suspected neutropenic sepsis. E. Any continued methotrexate is inappropriate with severe neutropenia and fever.
pearl: Patients on methotrexate must report sore throat, mouth ulcers, fever or bruising at once; fever with neutropenia is treated as neutropenic sepsis.
thinking: Methotrexate with fever and mouth ulcers ↓ Very low neutrophil count ↓ Marrow toxicity with possible neutropenic sepsis ↓ Stop the drug and treat as emergency ↓ Withhold methotrexate and same-day hospital assessment
exam_trap: E, halving the dose — a dose reduction seems a measured response, but severe neutropenia with fever needs the drug stopped and emergency care.
takeaway: Methotrexate with fever and neutropenia: stop it and send the patient for urgent hospital assessment.

stem: A 70-year-old man with hypertension who smokes telephones his GP. Yesterday, a dark shadow came down over the vision of his left eye like a curtain, lasted around ten minutes and then cleared completely. His eye was not painful and his vision is now normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Brief, painless, one-eyed visual loss that resolves completely, often described as a curtain, is amaurosis fugax, caused by transient retinal ischaemia usually from carotid or cardiac emboli. It is a form of transient ischaemic attack and signals a high early stroke risk. He should be managed as a TIA with urgent specialist assessment, including carotid imaging.
why_wrong: A. Retinal detachment causes flashes, floaters and a persisting field defect rather than full recovery. B. Migraine aura is usually binocular with positive phenomena such as zigzag lights, typically in younger people. C. Angle-closure glaucoma causes a painful red eye with haloes and nausea. E. Retinal vein occlusion causes persisting visual loss with haemorrhages on fundoscopy.
pearl: Amaurosis fugax is a TIA of the eye: arrange urgent specialist TIA assessment and carotid imaging, as stroke may follow soon.
thinking: Older man with vascular risk factors ↓ Sudden painless monocular visual loss ↓ Complete recovery within minutes ↓ Transient retinal ischaemia ↓ Amaurosis fugax
exam_trap: A, retinal detachment — the curtain description is shared, but detachment does not resolve completely within minutes.
takeaway: Brief painless one-eyed visual loss that fully resolves is amaurosis fugax and is managed as a TIA.

presentation: Progressive memory loss in an older adult
stem: A 78-year-old woman is brought to her GP by her daughter. Over the past 18 months she has increasingly repeated the same questions, misplaced belongings and recently got lost driving to a shop she has used for years. She is alert, her symptoms do not fluctuate, and there are no hallucinations, falls or stroke history. Blood tests are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: An insidious, steadily progressive decline in short-term memory with later disorientation in familiar places is the typical pattern of Alzheimer disease, the commonest cause of dementia. The absence of fluctuation, hallucinations, parkinsonism or stepwise decline makes other types less likely. She should be referred to a memory assessment service after reversible causes have been excluded.
why_wrong: B. Lewy body dementia usually has fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations and parkinsonism. C. Vascular dementia typically shows stepwise decline with vascular events or focal signs. D. Delirium is acute, fluctuating and associated with impaired attention or consciousness. E. Getting lost in familiar places and functional decline go beyond normal ageing.
pearl: Gradual short-term memory loss progressing to disorientation suggests Alzheimer disease; fluctuation, hallucinations or stepwise decline point elsewhere.
thinking: Older woman with gradual onset ↓ Short-term memory loss then getting lost ↓ Alert, no fluctuation ↓ No hallucinations, parkinsonism or stepwise course ↓ Alzheimer disease
exam_trap: E, normal ageing — mild forgetfulness is common, but getting lost on a familiar route shows functional impairment that is not normal.
takeaway: Insidious, progressive short-term memory loss in an older adult points to Alzheimer disease.

stem: A practice is evaluating a rapid throat swab for streptococcal infection. In the evaluation, 200 adults were confirmed by culture not to have the infection, and 180 of them had a negative rapid test. Which measure of test performance does this result describe?
why_correct: Specificity is the proportion of people without the disease who correctly test negative. Here 180 of the 200 people without infection tested negative, giving a specificity of 90%. It depends only on people who truly do not have the condition.
why_wrong: A. Positive predictive value is the proportion of positive tests that are true positives. C. Sensitivity is the proportion of people with the disease who test positive. D. Negative predictive value is the proportion of negative tests that are true negatives, which needs people with the disease in the calculation. E. Accuracy uses all true results across the whole tested group.
pearl: Sensitivity and specificity start from true disease status; predictive values start from the test result and vary with prevalence.
thinking: Group defined by absence of disease ↓ Count how many test negative ↓ True negatives over all without disease ↓ That is the definition of specificity ↓ Specificity of 90%
exam_trap: D, negative predictive value — both involve negative results, but NPV starts from people who tested negative, not people known to be disease-free.
takeaway: Specificity is the proportion of people without the disease who test negative.

stem: A blood test for a cancer performs well in a specialist hospital clinic of symptomatic patients, where most positive results are confirmed. It is then offered to well adults in the general population, where the condition is rare. The test's sensitivity and specificity are unchanged, yet most positive results in this setting turn out to be false. What best explains this?

options.A: Selection bias in the original hospital evaluation
options.B: Higher specificity in the community producing more false positives
options.D: Lower prevalence reducing the positive predictive value
options.E: Higher negative predictive value producing false positives

correct_answer: D. Lower prevalence reducing the positive predictive value
why_correct: Positive predictive value depends on prevalence as well as on test characteristics. When a condition is rare, even a small false-positive rate applied to the large unaffected population produces more false positives than there are true positives. This is a key reason why population screening can generate many false alarms.
why_wrong: A. The stem states sensitivity and specificity are unchanged, so bias in the original study does not explain the finding. B. Higher specificity reduces false positives rather than increasing them. C. Lead-time bias affects apparent survival, not the proportion of positive tests that are correct. E. Negative predictive value concerns negative results and cannot produce false positives.
pearl: Same test, different population: as prevalence falls, PPV falls and NPV rises, even though sensitivity and specificity stay constant.
thinking: Test characteristics unchanged ↓ Moved from high to low prevalence setting ↓ False positives from large healthy group dominate ↓ Proportion of positives that are true falls ↓ Lower prevalence reduces PPV
exam_trap: A, selection bias — it is tempting to blame the original study, but the stem fixes sensitivity and specificity, leaving prevalence as the explanation.
takeaway: When prevalence is low, positive predictive value falls, even for an accurate test.

stem: A 70-year-old man has a PSA test after reading about it online. He is found to have a small, low-grade prostate cancer and is placed on active surveillance. He remains symptom-free from it and dies nine years later from a stroke. Which term best describes the detection of his prostate cancer?
why_correct: Overdiagnosis is the detection of a genuine disease that would never have caused symptoms or death during the person's lifetime. His cancer was real but indolent, and he died of an unrelated cause without it ever becoming clinically relevant. Overdiagnosis leads to anxiety, labelling and sometimes unnecessary treatment, which is a major consideration in screening decisions.
why_wrong: A. Lead-time bias is an apparent survival gain because diagnosis is made earlier, not detection of harmless disease. B. Length-time bias describes screening preferentially finding slower-growing disease, making screen-detected cases appear to do better; it is a related but different concept. D. A false positive means the disease is absent, whereas his cancer was real. E. Selection bias relates to how study participants are chosen.
pearl: Overdiagnosis is a true diagnosis that brings no benefit: the disease is real but would never have harmed the patient.
thinking: Cancer found by testing ↓ Disease confirmed as real ↓ Never caused symptoms ↓ Died of unrelated cause ↓ Overdiagnosis
exam_trap: B, length-time bias — it also involves slow-growing tumours being picked up, but it describes a distortion of survival statistics, not the individual detection of harmless disease.
takeaway: Overdiagnosis is detecting a real disease that would never have caused harm in the person's lifetime.

stem: Researchers want to know whether early introduction of cow's milk in infancy is linked to type 1 diabetes. They recruit 200 children who already have type 1 diabetes and 400 children of similar age who do not, and then review health visitor records to compare how each child was fed as a baby. Which study design has been used?
why_correct: Participants are selected according to whether they have the outcome (type 1 diabetes or not), and past exposure is then compared between the groups. Starting from the outcome and looking back at exposure defines a case-control study. This design is efficient for rare outcomes and produces an odds ratio.
why_wrong: B. A cohort study starts with exposure groups and follows them for outcomes. C. A cross-sectional study measures exposure and outcome at one point in time without selecting on outcome. D. No intervention was allocated by the investigators. E. Ecological studies compare populations, not individual children.
pearl: Case-control: select by outcome, look back at exposure, report an odds ratio. Useful for rare diseases but prone to recall bias.
thinking: Groups chosen by presence or absence of disease ↓ Past exposure compared ↓ Direction is outcome to exposure ↓ No intervention allocated ↓ Case-control study
exam_trap: B, cohort study — the records describe events that happened before diagnosis, but participants were selected by outcome, not by exposure.
takeaway: Selecting by outcome and looking back at exposure defines a case-control study.

stem: Investigators recruit 3,000 nurses who do not have breast cancer. At the start, they record whether each nurse regularly works night shifts. They then follow all of them for 15 years and compare the rate of new breast cancer between night-shift and day-shift workers. Which study design has been used?
why_correct: Participants free of the outcome are grouped by exposure (night-shift work) and followed forward in time to compare the incidence of disease. This is the defining structure of a prospective cohort study, which can calculate incidence and relative risk. The investigators did not assign the exposure, so it is observational.
why_wrong: A. A case-control study selects participants by outcome and looks back at exposure. B. A cross-sectional study measures exposure and outcome at a single time point. D. An ecological study uses population-level data rather than individuals. E. The investigators did not randomly allocate shift patterns.
pearl: Cohort studies start with exposure and follow people forward, allowing incidence and relative risk to be calculated; they suit common outcomes and rare exposures.
thinking: Participants free of disease at start ↓ Grouped by exposure ↓ Followed forward over years ↓ Incidence compared, no allocation ↓ Prospective cohort study
exam_trap: E, randomised controlled trial — two comparison groups followed over time can resemble a trial, but the nurses chose their shifts and were not randomised.
takeaway: Grouping by exposure and following forward for outcomes defines a cohort study.

stem: A trial compares a new oral anticoagulant with warfarin in adults with atrial fibrillation. A computer program allocates each participant to one of the two treatments, and the published baseline table shows the groups are very similar in age, kidney function and stroke risk. Why have the investigators used this allocation method?

options.A: To prevent participants knowing which drug they are taking
options.B: To balance known and unknown confounding factors between the groups
options.C: To increase the statistical power of the trial
options.D: To make the findings applicable to all patients with atrial fibrillation
options.E: To ensure every participant receives the new treatment

correct_answer: B. To balance known and unknown confounding factors between the groups
why_correct: Random allocation distributes both measured and unmeasured characteristics evenly between groups, so differences in outcome can be attributed to the treatment rather than to confounding. The similar baseline table is evidence that randomisation has worked. It is the main strength of a randomised controlled trial over observational designs.
why_wrong: A. Concealing treatment from participants is blinding, which is a separate process. C. Power depends mainly on sample size and event rate, not on randomisation. D. Generalisability depends on who is recruited, not how they are allocated. E. Half the participants receive the comparator, not the new drug.
pearl: Randomisation controls confounding; blinding reduces performance and detection bias; sample size determines power. Keep the three separate.
thinking: Computer-based random allocation ↓ Groups similar at baseline ↓ Balances measured and unmeasured factors ↓ Outcome differences attributable to treatment ↓ Controls confounding
exam_trap: A, preventing participants knowing their drug — this is blinding, which is often confused with randomisation but serves a different purpose.
takeaway: Randomisation balances known and unknown confounders between groups.

stem: A large cohort study investigates whether drinking coffee daily is linked to pancreatic cancer. After ten years, the researchers calculate that the relative risk is 1.0 when comparing daily coffee drinkers with people who do not drink coffee. How should this result be interpreted?

options.A: The risk of pancreatic cancer is the same in both groups
options.B: Daily coffee drinking doubles the risk of pancreatic cancer
options.C: Daily coffee drinking halves the risk of pancreatic cancer
options.D: Coffee has been shown to cause pancreatic cancer

correct_answer: A. The risk of pancreatic cancer is the same in both groups
why_correct: Relative risk is the risk in the exposed group divided by the risk in the unexposed group. A value of 1.0 means the two risks are equal, so the study shows no association between daily coffee drinking and pancreatic cancer. Whether any estimate is significant depends on its confidence interval.
why_wrong: B. A doubling of risk would be a relative risk of 2. C. Halving of risk would be a relative risk of 0.5. D. Observational studies alone cannot prove causation, and here no association was found. E. A point estimate of 1.0 indicates no effect and cannot by itself show significance.
pearl: RR above 1 means higher risk with exposure, below 1 lower risk, and exactly 1 no difference. A confidence interval crossing 1 means no significant association.
thinking: Relative risk equals risk exposed over risk unexposed ↓ Value of 1.0 ↓ Numerator equals denominator ↓ No difference between groups ↓ Same risk in both groups
exam_trap: E, statistically significant — a precise-looking number from a large study can seem significant, but a ratio of 1.0 means no effect.
takeaway: A relative risk of 1.0 means no difference in risk between exposed and unexposed groups.

stem: A 62-year-old man is being started on simvastatin by his GP after a cardiovascular risk assessment. During the consultation he mentions that he drinks a large glass of grapefruit juice every morning with breakfast. How should the GP respond?

options.A: Reassure him that fruit juice only affects drugs taken on an empty stomach
options.B: Check the interaction in the BNF and advise him accordingly
options.C: Advise him to take the statin and the juice 12 hours apart
options.D: Prescribe half the usual statin dose without discussing it
options.E: Decide not to offer a statin at all

correct_answer: B. Check the interaction in the BNF and advise him accordingly
why_correct: Grapefruit juice inhibits intestinal CYP3A4 and can markedly increase blood levels of some drugs, including simvastatin, raising the risk of myopathy. The appropriate response is to check the specific interaction in a reliable reference and give him clear advice, such as avoiding grapefruit juice or choosing a statin less affected by it. Interactions should be managed individually rather than by guesswork.
why_wrong: A. The interaction is metabolic and is not limited to drugs taken on an empty stomach. C. The enzyme inhibition lasts many hours, so spacing doses does not reliably avoid the interaction. D. Changing the dose without explanation is not evidence-based and excludes him from the decision. E. Withholding indicated treatment is unnecessary when the interaction can be managed.
pearl: Grapefruit juice inhibits CYP3A4 for a prolonged period, so separating doses does not help; check the specific drug and give clear advice.
thinking: Drug started that may interact with grapefruit ↓ Grapefruit inhibits CYP3A4 ↓ Levels may rise, increasing toxicity ↓ Advice must be specific to the drug ↓ Check the BNF and advise
exam_trap: C, separating the doses — spacing works for some absorption interactions, but grapefruit's enzyme inhibition lasts long enough to make timing ineffective.
takeaway: Food-drug interactions such as grapefruit should be checked in the BNF and explained to the patient.

stem: A 66-year-old woman has been taking high-dose prednisolone for four months for giant cell arteritis. While on holiday she ran out of tablets and has taken none for five days. She now attends the emergency department with profound fatigue, vomiting, dizziness on standing and low blood pressure. She has no headache or visual symptoms. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Months of high-dose glucocorticoid suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, so the adrenals cannot produce enough cortisol when steroids are stopped suddenly. This causes adrenal insufficiency, which can progress to adrenal crisis with vomiting, hypotension and collapse. She needs urgent parenteral hydrocortisone, and long-term steroids should always be weaned gradually.
why_wrong: A. A relapse of giant cell arteritis would usually cause headache, jaw claudication or visual symptoms. B. Gastroenteritis does not explain the context of abrupt steroid withdrawal and is a dangerous assumption here. C. Stopping steroids would lower, not raise, blood glucose. E. Hyperthyroidism does not follow steroid withdrawal and would not typically cause hypotension of this kind.
pearl: Patients on long-term steroids should carry a steroid emergency card and never stop abruptly; suspected adrenal crisis is treated with hydrocortisone without waiting for results.
thinking: Months of high-dose prednisolone ↓ Adrenal axis suppressed ↓ Abrupt cessation ↓ Vomiting, postural dizziness, hypotension ↓ Adrenal insufficiency
exam_trap: B, viral gastroenteritis — vomiting points to gut infection, but the abrupt steroid withdrawal and hypotension make adrenal insufficiency the dangerous and likely cause.
takeaway: Stopping long-term high-dose steroids abruptly can cause adrenal insufficiency; always wean them.

stem: A 33-year-old woman with cystic fibrosis has received several courses of intravenous tobramycin for chest exacerbations. At her clinic review she reports ringing in both ears, difficulty following conversations and feeling unsteady when walking in the dark. Which adverse effect is most likely?
why_correct: Tobramycin is an aminoglycoside, and this class can damage the cochlear and vestibular hair cells. This produces tinnitus, hearing loss and imbalance that is worse when visual cues are reduced, as in the dark. The damage may be permanent, so the drug should be reviewed and audiology assessment arranged.
why_wrong: A. Peripheral neuropathy causes numbness and tingling rather than tinnitus and hearing loss. B. Red man syndrome is an infusion reaction to vancomycin. C. BPPV causes brief vertigo with head movements and does not cause hearing loss or tinnitus. E. Hepatotoxicity is not a characteristic aminoglycoside effect and would not explain these symptoms.
pearl: Aminoglycosides affect both hearing and balance; vestibular damage shows as unsteadiness, especially in the dark when vision cannot compensate.
thinking: Repeated aminoglycoside courses ↓ Tinnitus and reduced hearing ↓ Unsteadiness worse in the dark ↓ Cochlear and vestibular damage ↓ Ototoxicity
exam_trap: C, BPPV — unsteadiness suggests a benign vestibular cause, but BPPV does not cause tinnitus or hearing loss and does not fit the drug history.
takeaway: Tinnitus, hearing loss or imbalance on an aminoglycoside suggests ototoxicity.

stem: A 71-year-old retired farmer who had a kidney transplant ten years ago and takes immunosuppressants attends his GP. Over the past six weeks a firm, crusted, tender lump has grown on the back of his left hand. It has a raised keratotic surface and bled after he caught it on a gate. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A rapidly growing, firm, tender, keratotic nodule that bleeds on sun-exposed skin is typical of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma. Chronic sun exposure and organ-transplant immunosuppression both greatly increase the risk. He should be referred on a suspected cancer pathway, because SCC can metastasise.
why_wrong: A. Basal cell carcinoma grows slowly over months to years and is typically pearly with surface telangiectasia. B. Seborrhoeic keratosis is a long-standing, stuck-on, waxy lesion that does not grow rapidly. C. Actinic keratosis is a flat, rough, scaly patch rather than a firm nodule. E. A new rapidly growing, bleeding nodule in an immunosuppressed older adult should not be assumed to be a wart.
pearl: Transplant recipients have a markedly increased risk of SCC; any rapidly enlarging, tender or bleeding keratotic lesion on sun-exposed skin needs urgent referral.
thinking: Older man with heavy sun exposure ↓ Immunosuppressed after transplant ↓ Rapidly growing, firm, keratotic, bleeding nodule ↓ Features of invasive keratinocyte cancer ↓ Squamous cell carcinoma
exam_trap: A, basal cell carcinoma — it is the commonest skin cancer, but it grows slowly and is pearly rather than keratotic and tender.
takeaway: A rapidly growing, firm, keratotic nodule on sun-damaged skin suggests squamous cell carcinoma.

presentation: Rough scaly lesions on sun-damaged skin
stem: A 74-year-old woman who has gardened all her life shows her GP several flat, pink patches on her forehead and the backs of her hands. They feel rough like sandpaper and are easier to feel than to see. None is raised, tender or bleeding. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Multiple flat, rough, scaly patches on chronically sun-exposed skin in an older person are typical of actinic keratoses. They are caused by cumulative ultraviolet damage and are premalignant, with a small risk of progressing to squamous cell carcinoma. Management includes sun protection and topical treatment or cryotherapy, with review of any lesion that becomes thickened, tender or bleeds.
why_wrong: B. Squamous cell carcinoma typically presents as a raised, growing, often tender nodule. C. Seborrhoeic keratoses are raised, waxy and stuck-on in appearance. D. Discoid eczema causes itchy, coin-shaped patches not confined to sun-exposed sites. E. Psoriasis causes well-demarcated plaques with silvery scale, usually on extensor surfaces and the scalp.
pearl: Actinic keratoses are often felt before they are seen; thickening, tenderness or bleeding suggests progression to SCC.
thinking: Older woman with lifelong sun exposure ↓ Flat, rough, scaly patches ↓ Confined to sun-exposed sites ↓ No nodule, tenderness or bleeding ↓ Actinic keratosis
exam_trap: B, squamous cell carcinoma — it shares the same sun-damage background, but the lesions here are flat and non-tender, without a nodule.
takeaway: Flat, rough, sandpaper-like patches on sun-damaged skin are actinic keratoses.

presentation: Dry mouth, dry eyes and parotid swelling
stem: A 52-year-old woman tells her GP that her eyes feel gritty all the time, she needs a drink of water to swallow dry food such as crackers, and she keeps a glass by her bed at night. Over the past year she has had several bouts of tender swelling in front of both ears. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Persistent dry eyes and dry mouth with recurrent parotid swelling in a middle-aged woman are characteristic of Sjögren syndrome, an autoimmune disease of the exocrine glands. Investigations include anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies and specialist rheumatology assessment. It also carries an increased risk of lymphoma, so persistent gland enlargement needs review.
why_wrong: A. Mumps causes an acute, self-limiting parotitis with fever rather than chronic dryness and recurrent episodes. B. Systemic sclerosis mainly causes skin thickening, Raynaud phenomenon and organ fibrosis. C. A salivary stone causes unilateral swelling with meals and does not cause dry eyes. E. Rheumatoid arthritis can be associated with secondary Sjögren syndrome but would present with inflammatory joint disease.
pearl: Dry eyes plus dry mouth with parotid swelling suggests Sjögren syndrome; check anti-Ro and anti-La and remember the increased lymphoma risk.
thinking: Middle-aged woman ↓ Gritty dry eyes and dry mouth ↓ Recurrent bilateral parotid swelling ↓ Autoimmune exocrine gland disease ↓ Sjögren syndrome
exam_trap: C, salivary gland calculus — gland swelling suggests obstruction, but a stone is usually unilateral, meal-related and does not cause dry eyes.
takeaway: Chronic dry eyes and dry mouth with parotid swelling point to Sjögren syndrome.

presentation: Inflammatory back pain in a young adult
stem: A 26-year-old man attends his GP with six months of pain in his lower back and buttocks. The pain wakes him in the second half of the night, and he is stiff for a long time in the morning, easing as he walks around. Ibuprofen helps considerably, but rest makes it worse. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Chronic back pain beginning in a young adult, with night waking, prolonged morning stiffness, improvement with activity and a good response to NSAIDs, is the inflammatory pattern typical of axial spondyloarthritis. Buttock pain reflects sacroiliac joint involvement. He should be referred to rheumatology for assessment, as delays in diagnosis are common.
why_wrong: A. Mechanical back pain usually worsens with activity and improves with rest. B. Disc prolapse typically causes acute pain with radicular leg symptoms. C. Fibromyalgia causes widespread pain and fatigue rather than localised inflammatory back pain. D. Spinal stenosis affects older adults and causes leg pain on walking that eases with sitting or bending forward.
pearl: Inflammatory back pain: onset under about 40, insidious, improves with exercise, worse with rest, night pain and good NSAID response. Refer to rheumatology.
thinking: Young man with chronic back pain ↓ Night waking and prolonged morning stiffness ↓ Better with movement, worse with rest ↓ Buttock pain and NSAID response ↓ Axial spondyloarthritis
exam_trap: A, mechanical back pain — it is by far the commonest cause, but it follows the opposite pattern, worsening with activity and easing with rest.
takeaway: Back pain that improves with exercise and worsens with rest in a young adult suggests axial spondyloarthritis.

presentation: Tender shin nodules in Crohn disease
stem: A 23-year-old woman with Crohn disease is reviewed in the gastroenterology clinic during a flare. She has developed several tender, warm, raised red lumps on both shins over the past week. They look like bruises and the overlying skin is intact. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Tender, red, bruise-like nodules on both shins with intact skin are typical of erythema nodosum, an inflammation of subcutaneous fat. It is a recognised extraintestinal manifestation of inflammatory bowel disease and often parallels disease activity, so it usually settles as the flare is treated. Other causes include streptococcal infection, sarcoidosis, pregnancy and some drugs.
why_wrong: A. Pyoderma gangrenosum starts as a pustule and progresses to a painful ulcer with a purple undermined edge. B. Cellulitis is usually unilateral, spreading and associated with systemic upset. D. Erythema multiforme causes target lesions, often on the hands and feet. E. HSP causes palpable purpura on the buttocks and legs, usually in children, rather than tender nodules.
pearl: Erythema nodosum tracks IBD activity, whereas pyoderma gangrenosum may not; nodules with intact skin suggest EN, ulceration suggests PG.
thinking: Crohn disease flare ↓ Tender red nodules on both shins ↓ Bruise-like, skin intact ↓ Recognised extraintestinal manifestation ↓ Erythema nodosum
exam_trap: A, pyoderma gangrenosum — it is the other classic IBD skin lesion, but it ulcerates, whereas these nodules have intact skin.
takeaway: Tender red nodules on the shins in IBD are erythema nodosum, often reflecting disease activity.

stem: A 66-year-old man sees his GP because he gets up three times each night to pass urine. He says it takes a while to get going, the flow stops and starts, and he dribbles after he has finished. He is afebrile and a urine dipstick is negative. Digital rectal examination reveals a smooth, symmetrically enlarged, non-tender prostate with a preserved median sulcus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Hesitancy, an intermittent stream, terminal dribbling and nocturia are typical lower urinary tract symptoms of bladder outlet obstruction in an older man. A smooth, symmetrical, non-tender gland with a preserved median sulcus on rectal examination supports benign prostatic enlargement. Assessment in primary care usually includes urinalysis, renal function and, after counselling, a PSA test.
why_wrong: A. Prostate cancer is usually suggested by a hard, irregular or nodular gland, although it can coexist and needs considering. B. Urethral stricture typically affects men with previous instrumentation, infection or trauma and the prostate is not enlarged. C. Chronic prostatitis causes pelvic or perineal pain and the gland is often tender. E. Overactive bladder causes urgency and frequency rather than predominantly voiding symptoms.
pearl: Separate storage symptoms (urgency, frequency, nocturia) from voiding symptoms (hesitancy, poor stream, dribbling); voiding symptoms point towards outlet obstruction such as prostatic enlargement.
thinking: Older man with hesitancy, intermittent flow and dribbling ↓ Voiding symptoms suggest outlet obstruction ↓ No infection, smooth symmetrical non-tender prostate ↓ Benign prostatic enlargement
exam_trap: A, Prostate cancer — it is the diagnosis everyone fears in an older man with urinary symptoms, but a smooth symmetrical gland with a preserved sulcus points to benign enlargement; cancer is suggested by a hard, irregular gland.
takeaway: Voiding symptoms with a smooth, symmetrically enlarged prostate suggest benign prostatic enlargement.

stem: A 26-year-old man attends his GP after noticing a firm swelling in his right testis while showering three weeks ago. It does not hurt. On examination there is a hard, irregular mass that cannot be separated from the body of the testis. It does not transilluminate, and the epididymis feels normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A painless, hard mass arising within the body of the testis in a young man is testicular cancer until proven otherwise, and germ cell tumours are the commonest type in this age group. NICE recommends referral on a suspected cancer pathway for a non-painful enlargement or change in the shape or texture of the testis, with urgent scrotal ultrasound. The mass being inseparable from the testis and not transilluminating distinguishes it from benign scrotal swellings.
why_wrong: A. An epididymal cyst lies separate from and above or behind the testis and usually transilluminates. B. A hydrocele surrounds the testis, transilluminates and the testis may be hard to feel through it. C. Chronic epididymitis affects the epididymis, which is normal here, and is usually tender. D. A varicocele feels like a bag of worms above the testis and is not a testicular mass.
pearl: Ask three questions of any scrotal swelling: can you get above it, is it separate from the testis, and does it transilluminate? A solid intratesticular mass needs urgent ultrasound.
thinking: Young man with painless scrotal lump ↓ Hard and inseparable from the testis ↓ Not transilluminable, epididymis normal ↓ Testicular germ cell tumour
exam_trap: A, Epididymal cyst — common, painless and benign, so it is tempting to reassure, but a cyst sits separate from the testis and transilluminates, whereas this mass is solid and within the testis.
takeaway: A painless, solid lump within the testis of a young man is cancer until proven otherwise.

stem: A 38-year-old woman tells her GP that for the past eight months her periods have been so heavy that she floods through pads, passes clots and has to change protection overnight. Her cycle is regular, and she has no bleeding between periods or after sex. Her cervical screening is up to date and abdominal examination is normal. Which investigation should be offered to her routinely?
why_correct: NICE advises that all women presenting with heavy menstrual bleeding should have a full blood count, because chronic blood loss commonly causes iron-deficiency anaemia that may need treatment in its own right. Further tests are guided by the history and examination rather than done routinely. With a regular cycle, no intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding and a normal examination, she may be offered treatment without further investigation.
why_wrong: A. Ultrasound is reserved for women with a suspected structural cause, such as an enlarged uterus or pelvic mass on examination. C. Ferritin is not routinely needed; the full blood count is the recommended first test. D. Thyroid tests are indicated only if there are other features of thyroid disease. E. Coagulation testing is for women with features suggesting a bleeding disorder, such as heavy periods since menarche or other bleeding problems.
pearl: Heavy menstrual bleeding is defined by its impact on a woman's quality of life rather than by measured blood loss; a full blood count is the one routine test.
thinking: Heavy, regular periods with clots and flooding ↓ No intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding, normal examination ↓ Main routine concern is anaemia from blood loss ↓ Full blood count
exam_trap: C, Serum ferritin — iron deficiency is the worry, so measuring iron stores seems logical, but guidance recommends a full blood count for everyone and does not advise routine ferritin testing.
takeaway: Every woman with heavy menstrual bleeding needs a full blood count; other tests depend on the history.

stem: A 61-year-old retired bus driver sees her GP with a cough that has not settled over six weeks. She has noticed a little blood in her sputum on one occasion and has lost a few kilograms without trying. She has smoked for most of her adult life. She has no fever or night sweats and no travel history or known contact with tuberculosis. A chest radiograph demonstrates an irregular opacity at the right hilum. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A persistent cough, haemoptysis and unintentional weight loss in a long-term smoker over the age of 40, with a unilateral hilar opacity on chest X-ray, strongly suggests lung cancer. NICE recommends referral on a suspected cancer pathway when a chest X-ray suggests lung cancer, or for anyone aged 40 and over with unexplained haemoptysis. Smoking history is the most important risk factor.
why_wrong: A. Tuberculosis can cause cough, haemoptysis and weight loss, but there are no fevers, night sweats or risk factors here. B. Bronchiectasis causes chronic daily purulent sputum over a long period rather than a new hilar mass. C. Sarcoidosis typically causes bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy in younger adults. E. Pneumonia is an acute febrile illness, which does not fit six weeks of symptoms without fever.
pearl: Any smoker or ex-smoker aged 40 or over with unexplained haemoptysis, or a chest X-ray suggestive of cancer, should be referred on a suspected lung cancer pathway.
thinking: Long-term smoker with persistent cough ↓ Haemoptysis and weight loss ↓ Unilateral irregular hilar opacity, no infective features ↓ Bronchial carcinoma
exam_trap: A, Pulmonary tuberculosis — haemoptysis with weight loss is a classic TB picture, but the absence of fever, night sweats and exposure, together with a heavy smoking history and a hilar mass, makes cancer far more likely.
takeaway: Smoker over 40 with persistent cough, haemoptysis and weight loss: think lung cancer and refer urgently.

stem: A 72-year-old retired man tells his GP that over the past year he has become increasingly short of breath walking up hills, and he has an irritating cough that produces no sputum. On examination he has finger clubbing and fine end-inspiratory crackles over both bases posteriorly. There is no wheeze, his jugular venous pressure is not raised and he has no ankle oedema. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Gradually worsening exertional breathlessness, a dry cough, finger clubbing and fine bibasal end-inspiratory crackles in an older man are the classic features of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. The normal jugular venous pressure and absence of oedema make heart failure less likely. High-resolution CT of the chest is the key investigation, alongside spirometry, which typically shows a restrictive pattern.
why_wrong: A. COPD causes wheeze and productive cough and does not cause clubbing. B. Bronchiectasis produces copious daily sputum with coarse crackles. C. Heart failure crackles are usually accompanied by a raised JVP, oedema or orthopnoea, none of which are present. E. Asthma causes variable wheeze and does not cause clubbing or fixed fine crackles.
pearl: Clubbing in a patient with chronic breathlessness should never be attributed to COPD; think of fibrosis, bronchiectasis or lung cancer.
thinking: Progressive exertional breathlessness with dry cough ↓ Clubbing and fine bibasal 'Velcro' crackles ↓ No signs of fluid overload or airflow obstruction ↓ Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
exam_trap: C, Congestive cardiac failure — bibasal crackles and breathlessness in an older man commonly mean heart failure, but these crackles are fine and dry with clubbing, and there is no raised JVP or oedema.
takeaway: Clubbing plus fine bibasal end-inspiratory crackles and a dry cough suggests pulmonary fibrosis.

stem: A 70-year-old man has a chest X-ray before elective hip surgery. He has no respiratory symptoms. The film shows bilateral, irregular calcified areas of pleural thickening along the diaphragms and lateral chest walls, with clear lung fields. He spent many years as a heating engineer fitting and stripping pipe insulation in old buildings. Which occupational exposure most likely explains these findings?
why_correct: Calcified pleural plaques, particularly along the diaphragm and lateral chest walls, are the commonest manifestation of past asbestos exposure and typically appear decades later. Work involving old pipe lagging and insulation is a classic source. Plaques are benign and usually asymptomatic, but they mark exposure that also carries risks of asbestosis, mesothelioma and lung cancer.
why_wrong: A. Coal dust causes coal workers' pneumoconiosis with lung nodules rather than pleural plaques. B. Silica causes upper lobe nodules and eggshell calcification of hilar nodes. D. Mouldy hay causes farmer's lung, a hypersensitivity pneumonitis. E. Bird droppings cause bird fancier's lung, also a hypersensitivity pneumonitis without pleural plaques.
pearl: Pleural plaques are a marker of asbestos exposure, not a premalignant lesion, but they should prompt advice on smoking cessation and awareness of mesothelioma symptoms.
thinking: Incidental calcified pleural thickening ↓ Diaphragmatic and lateral chest wall distribution ↓ Occupational history of old pipe insulation work ↓ Asbestos
exam_trap: B, Silica — calcification on a chest film brings silicosis to mind, but silica calcifies hilar lymph nodes in an eggshell pattern and affects the lung, not the pleura.
takeaway: Calcified pleural plaques indicate previous asbestos exposure, often decades earlier.
