There is a vesicle on the tip of his nose and his left eye is red and watering. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A painful vesicular rash preceded by burning pain and confined to one side of the forehead and upper eyelid follows the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve, which is herpes zoster ophthalmicus. A lesion on the tip of the nose (Hutchinson sign) indicates nasociliary branch involvement and a high risk of eye disease. He needs prompt oral antiviral treatment and same-day ophthalmology assessment because of the red eye.
why_wrong: A. Erysipelas causes a well-demarcated red, raised plaque without vesicles in a dermatome. B. Impetigo produces honey-crusted lesions, usually around the nose and mouth, without dermatomal pain. C. Contact dermatitis is itchy and follows the area of contact, not a nerve distribution. D. Herpes simplex causes grouped vesicles but not a full dermatomal rash with prodromal pain.
pearl: Hutchinson sign (vesicles on the nasal tip) indicates nasociliary involvement and a high risk of ocular zoster. Any eye involvement needs same-day ophthalmology review plus oral antivirals.
thinking: Prodromal burning pain over one side of the forehead ↓ Vesicles in one dermatome stopping at the midline ↓ Ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve, with a nasal tip lesion ↓ Herpes zoster ophthalmicus
exam_trap: D, Primary herpes simplex infection — both cause grouped vesicles, but a strict dermatomal distribution with prodromal pain in an older adult is zoster.
takeaway: Dermatomal forehead blisters with a nasal tip lesion: HZO, so refer to eye services same day.

stem: A 54-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes cut her thigh while gardening two days ago. She now has excruciating pain in the thigh, far worse than the patchy redness suggests, and the skin feels hard and woody with dusky purple areas. She is confused, her pulse is 124 beats per minute and her blood pressure is 88/50 mmHg. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Pain out of proportion to visible skin changes, woody induration, dusky discolouration and rapid systemic toxicity after a minor wound in a person with diabetes are red flags for necrotising fasciitis. It is a surgical emergency. She needs sepsis resuscitation, broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics and immediate senior surgical review for debridement, which should not be delayed for imaging.
why_wrong: B. Simple cellulitis causes tenderness that matches the redness and does not produce septic shock this quickly. C. A deep vein thrombosis causes swelling and aching without skin necrosis or septic shock. D. Erysipelas is a superficial, well-demarcated infection without woody induration. E. Superficial thrombophlebitis causes a tender cord along a vein with no systemic toxicity.
pearl: Pain out of proportion to the skin findings is the earliest clue to necrotising fasciitis. Woody skin, dusky patches, crepitus or bullae and rapid sepsis demand immediate surgery.
thinking: Minor wound in a person with diabetes ↓ Severe pain beyond the visible redness, woody skin, dusky areas ↓ Rapid septic shock and confusion ↓ Necrotising fasciitis
exam_trap: B, Simple cellulitis — redness after a cut looks like cellulitis, but disproportionate pain, woody skin and early shock signal deep necrotising infection.
takeaway: Pain out of proportion to redness with rapid sepsis: necrotising fasciitis, call surgeons.

stem: A 41-year-old woman shows her GP a mole on the back of her calf. Her partner says it has changed over three months: one side is now much darker than the other, the edge has become ragged, and it bled once after she shaved her legs. It occasionally itches. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A pigmented lesion that has changed in size, shape or colour, with an irregular border, variable pigmentation, itch and bleeding, scores highly on the weighted seven-point checklist and is suspicious for melanoma. She should be referred on the suspected cancer pathway for dermatology assessment, and the lesion should not be removed in primary care.
why_wrong: A. Seborrhoeic keratoses have a stuck-on, warty surface and are stable. B. A benign naevus is symmetrical with an even colour and does not change. C. Basal cell carcinoma is usually pearly with telangiectasia on sun-exposed skin of the head and neck. E. Dermatofibroma is a firm nodule that dimples when pinched and stays stable.
pearl: Change is the most important warning feature of a pigmented lesion. Major features: change in size, shape or colour; minor: diameter over 7 mm, inflammation, oozing or bleeding, altered sensation.
thinking: Pigmented lesion that has changed over months ↓ Asymmetrical colour and ragged border ↓ Bleeding and itch add further concern ↓ Melanoma
exam_trap: B, Benign compound naevus — most moles are benign, but a lesion that is evolving in colour and border must be treated as suspected melanoma.
takeaway: A changing pigmented lesion with irregular border and colour needs suspected cancer referral.

stem: A 52-year-old woman tells her GP that her eyes feel gritty and she is using lubricating drops many times a day. She cannot eat crackers without sipping water, her dentist has found several new cavities, and both cheeks in front of her ears have become swollen. She takes no regular medicines. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Dry, gritty eyes, a dry mouth causing difficulty with dry foods, dental caries and parotid swelling in a middle-aged woman are typical of Sjögren syndrome, an autoimmune condition targeting the lacrimal and salivary glands. Anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies support the diagnosis. Patients have an increased lifetime risk of lymphoma, so persistent gland swelling should be monitored.
why_wrong: A. Lupus causes rash, joint pain and multisystem features rather than predominant dryness. B. Sarcoidosis can enlarge the parotids but usually involves the lungs and lymph nodes. D. She takes no medicines, so a drug cause is unlikely. E. Rheumatoid arthritis presents with inflammatory joint disease, although secondary Sjögren syndrome can occur with it.
pearl: Dry eyes plus dry mouth plus parotid swelling suggest Sjögren syndrome. Check anti-Ro and anti-La, and remember the increased risk of lymphoma and of congenital heart block in pregnancy.
thinking: Gritty dry eyes needing frequent drops ↓ Dry mouth with dental caries ↓ Bilateral parotid swelling, no drug cause ↓ Sjögren syndrome
exam_trap: D, Medication-induced dry mouth — anticholinergic drugs are a common cause of dryness, but she takes no medicines and the parotid swelling suggests an autoimmune cause.
takeaway: Dry eyes, dry mouth and parotid swelling in a middle-aged woman: Sjögren syndrome.

stem: For several years, a 44-year-old teacher has noticed her fingers turning white then blue in the cold. Over the past year her finger skin has become thick and shiny and she can no longer make a full fist. There are small pitted scars on her fingertips, red spots on her face that blanch on pressure, and she has troublesome heartburn with food sticking on swallowing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Raynaud phenomenon with progressive thickening and tightening of the finger skin (sclerodactyly), digital pitting scars, telangiectasia and oesophageal dysmotility indicate systemic sclerosis. She needs rheumatology referral and screening for internal organ involvement, including the lungs, heart and kidneys.
why_wrong: A. Primary Raynaud phenomenon causes colour changes alone, without skin thickening or digital scars. C. Lupus causes rash, arthralgia and multisystem involvement but not sclerodactyly. D. Dermatomyositis causes proximal weakness with a heliotrope rash and Gottron papules. E. Rheumatoid arthritis causes inflammatory synovitis, not skin thickening.
pearl: Raynaud phenomenon plus skin tightening of the fingers, digital pits, telangiectasia and dysphagia suggest systemic sclerosis. Secondary Raynaud has digital ulcers or pits; primary does not.
thinking: Long-standing Raynaud phenomenon ↓ Thick, tight finger skin and digital pitting scars ↓ Telangiectasia and oesophageal symptoms ↓ Systemic sclerosis
exam_trap: A, Primary Raynaud phenomenon — the colour changes are the most obvious feature, but skin thickening and digital scars mean a secondary cause.
takeaway: Raynaud plus tight finger skin, digital pits and reflux suggests systemic sclerosis.

stem: A 71-year-old man with polymyalgia rheumatica has been taking oral prednisolone for four months and is expected to need it for at least a year. At a review, he asks why his GP has also prescribed weekly alendronic acid with daily calcium and vitamin D. Which complication of his steroid treatment are these medicines intended to prevent?
why_correct: Prolonged systemic glucocorticoid therapy reduces bone formation and increases bone loss, raising fracture risk early in treatment. Older people and those expected to take steroids for several months are offered bone protection, typically a bisphosphonate such as alendronic acid with adequate calcium and vitamin D. This reduces the risk of vertebral and other fragility fractures.
why_wrong: A. Peptic ulcer prevention uses a proton pump inhibitor, not a bisphosphonate. B. Adrenal suppression is managed by gradual tapering and sick-day guidance. C. Hyperglycaemia is managed by glucose monitoring and treatment. E. Steroid myopathy is not prevented by bisphosphonates.
pearl: Long-term oral steroids are a major cause of secondary osteoporosis. Consider bone protection early, particularly in older people or those with a previous fragility fracture.
thinking: Prolonged oral prednisolone ↓ Steroids reduce bone formation and increase bone loss ↓ Bisphosphonate plus calcium and vitamin D prescribed ↓ Prevention of osteoporosis and fragility fracture
exam_trap: A, Peptic ulceration — steroids are often co-prescribed with gastroprotection, but that is a proton pump inhibitor, whereas alendronic acid protects bone.
takeaway: Long-term steroids need bone protection to prevent osteoporotic fractures.

stem: A 68-year-old man attends his GP after noticing a painless hard lump behind his right nipple while showering. The nipple has become slightly pulled in over recent weeks. The lump is fixed and irregular, and the left breast feels normal. He takes no regular medicines and drinks little alcohol. What is the most important diagnosis to exclude?
why_correct: A hard, irregular, fixed unilateral subareolar lump with nipple retraction in an older man must be treated as possible breast cancer. NICE advises urgent suspected cancer referral for men aged 50 and over with a unilateral subareolar mass. Assessment in a breast clinic includes examination, imaging and biopsy.
why_wrong: B. Gynaecomastia is usually soft, rubbery, often tender and bilateral, without nipple retraction. C. A lipoma is soft and mobile. D. A sebaceous cyst lies within the skin and often has a punctum. E. An abscess is painful and inflamed, usually with fever.
pearl: In men, a firm, eccentric or fixed breast lump with nipple changes is cancer until proven otherwise. Gynaecomastia is typically central, soft, tender and often bilateral.
thinking: Older man with a unilateral subareolar lump ↓ Hard, fixed, irregular ↓ Nipple retraction ↓ Exclude male breast cancer with urgent referral
exam_trap: B, Gynaecomastia — the commonest male breast swelling, but it is soft, often tender and bilateral, whereas a hard fixed lump with nipple retraction suggests cancer.
takeaway: A hard unilateral subareolar lump in an older man needs urgent suspected cancer referral.

stem: A 44-year-old woman who moved to the UK from a country with a high incidence of tuberculosis 18 months ago sees her GP. She has had a cough for six weeks, feels feverish each evening, wakes soaked in sweat and has lost weight. Which is the most appropriate first investigation?
why_correct: When active pulmonary tuberculosis is suspected, a chest X-ray is the key first imaging test, looking for upper lobe consolidation, cavitation or lymphadenopathy. It should be accompanied by sputum samples for acid-fast bacilli microscopy, culture and molecular testing to confirm the diagnosis and check drug sensitivity.
why_wrong: B. A CT pulmonary angiogram looks for pulmonary embolism, which does not fit weeks of sweats and weight loss. C. Interferon-gamma release assays detect TB infection but cannot distinguish latent from active disease. D. Spirometry assesses airflow obstruction and does not diagnose infection. E. Bronchoscopy is reserved for when sputum cannot be obtained or is unhelpful.
pearl: Suspected active pulmonary TB: chest X-ray plus sputum samples for microscopy, culture and molecular testing. IGRA and Mantoux tests are for latent infection, not active disease.
thinking: Recent arrival from a high-incidence country ↓ Six weeks of cough, evening fevers, sweats and weight loss ↓ Suspected active pulmonary TB ↓ Chest X-ray first, with sputum samples
exam_trap: C, Interferon-gamma release assay alone — it is a TB blood test, but it detects infection rather than active disease and cannot replace imaging and sputum testing.
takeaway: Suspected active pulmonary TB: start with a chest X-ray and sputum samples.

stem: A 36-year-old woman was diagnosed with HIV last month and has a very low CD4 count; she has not yet started antiretroviral therapy. She now has three weeks of gradually worsening breathlessness on exertion and a dry cough. Her chest sounds almost clear, but her oxygen saturation falls markedly when she walks around the ward. Chest X-ray shows bilateral faint shadowing spreading out from the hila. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Subacute exertional breathlessness, a dry cough, marked desaturation on exercise despite few chest signs and bilateral perihilar interstitial shadowing in someone with advanced untreated HIV are typical of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia. It is an AIDS-defining opportunistic infection. First-line treatment is high-dose co-trimoxazole, with corticosteroids added when hypoxia is significant.
why_wrong: A. Pneumococcal pneumonia presents acutely with fever, productive cough and lobar consolidation. B. Pulmonary embolism causes sudden breathlessness and usually a clear chest X-ray. D. Kaposi sarcoma of the lung is less common and usually accompanies skin or mouth lesions. E. Mycoplasma pneumonia is not linked to severe immunosuppression and causes a milder, self-limiting illness.
pearl: In advanced HIV, gradual exertional breathlessness, dry cough and desaturation on walking with near-normal chest signs suggest PCP. Co-trimoxazole treats it and is also used as prophylaxis.
thinking: Advanced untreated HIV with low CD4 ↓ Subacute exertional breathlessness and dry cough ↓ Exercise desaturation with perihilar interstitial shadowing ↓ Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia
exam_trap: A, Pneumococcal pneumonia — bacterial pneumonia is common in HIV, but its acute onset, fever and lobar consolidation contrast with this subacute interstitial picture.
takeaway: Advanced HIV with exertional desaturation and perihilar shadowing: Pneumocystis pneumonia.

stem: A 27-year-old man attends an eye casualty clinic with a painful, red, blurred right eye. He has had crops of painful mouth ulcers several times a year since his teens and has scars on his scrotum from previous painful ulcers. A small pustule developed at the site of a blood test taken last week. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Recurrent painful oral ulcers, recurrent genital ulcers that scar, uveitis and pathergy (a pustule at a needle-puncture site) together form the classic picture of Behçet disease, a variable vessel vasculitis. Eye involvement can threaten sight, so he needs urgent ophthalmology management and rheumatology involvement.
why_wrong: A. Herpes simplex can cause recurrent oral or genital lesions but not uveitis with pathergy. B. Reactive arthritis causes arthritis, urethritis and conjunctivitis after infection, not recurrent oral and scarring genital ulcers. C. Crohn's disease can cause mouth ulcers and eye inflammation but genital ulcers and pathergy are not typical. E. Lupus can cause painless oral ulcers but not scarring genital ulcers or pathergy.
pearl: Recurrent oral ulcers plus genital ulcers, uveitis, skin lesions or pathergy suggest Behçet disease. It is more common in people from the Middle East and along the historic Silk Road.
thinking: Recurrent painful mouth ulcers ↓ Scarring genital ulcers ↓ Uveitis and pathergy reaction ↓ Behçet disease
exam_trap: C, Crohn's disease — oral ulcers and eye inflammation occur in Crohn's, but recurrent scarring genital ulcers and pathergy are characteristic of Behçet disease.
takeaway: Recurrent oral and genital ulcers with uveitis and pathergy suggest Behçet disease.

stem: A 41-year-old man has familial adenomatous polyposis, and genetic testing confirms he carries one pathogenic APC variant. His partner has no family history of the condition. Their first child, now 13, has tested negative on predictive genetic testing. The couple are expecting another baby and ask what the chance is that this baby has inherited the condition. What is the risk?

options.E: Less than 50%, because their first child was unaffected

why_correct: A heterozygous parent with an autosomal dominant condition passes either the affected or the unaffected allele to each child with equal probability, so every pregnancy carries a 50% chance of inheriting the condition. Each pregnancy is an independent event, so the outcome for their first child does not change the risk for the next.
why_wrong: A. A 25% risk applies to each child of two carrier parents with an autosomal recessive condition. C. A 75% chance of carrying at least one affected allele applies when both parents are heterozygous for a dominant condition. D. All children would inherit only if the affected parent were homozygous. E. Previous outcomes do not alter the probability for future pregnancies.
pearl: Autosomal dominant with one heterozygous parent gives a 50% risk for each child, regardless of sex or previous outcomes. Chance has no memory between pregnancies.
thinking: Father heterozygous for a dominant condition ↓ Partner unaffected ↓ Each child receives one of his two alleles at random ↓ 50% risk in every pregnancy
exam_trap: E, Less than 50% because their first child was unaffected — parents often feel previous outcomes change future odds, but each pregnancy is independent.
takeaway: One heterozygous parent with a dominant condition: 50% risk for each child, every time.

stem: A 28-year-old woman whose brother has haemophilia A has been confirmed as a carrier on genetic testing. Her husband has no bleeding disorder. They are planning a family and attend a genetics clinic. Which statement best describes the risk to their children?

options.A: Each son has a 50% chance of being affected
options.B: Each daughter has a 50% chance of being affected
options.D: Sons and daughters are at equal risk of being affected
options.E: No child can be affected because the father is unaffected

correct_answer: A. Each son has a 50% chance of being affected
why_correct: A carrier mother has one normal and one affected X chromosome. A son receives his single X from his mother, so each son has a 50% chance of inheriting the affected X and, having no second X to compensate, will be affected. Each daughter has a 50% chance of being a carrier but will usually not be affected because she also inherits a normal X from her father.
why_wrong: B. Daughters receive a normal X from their father, so they are usually carriers rather than affected. C. Sons inherit either maternal X at random, so only half are affected on average. D. In X-linked recessive conditions males are affected far more than females. E. The condition is passed through the carrier mother, regardless of the father.
pearl: X-linked recessive with a carrier mother and unaffected father: each son 50% affected, each daughter 50% carrier. An affected father passes it to all daughters (carriers) and no sons.
thinking: Mother is a carrier of an X-linked recessive condition ↓ Sons receive one X, from their mother ↓ Daughters also receive a normal X from their father ↓ Each son has a 50% chance of being affected
exam_trap: B, Each daughter has a 50% chance of being affected — daughters do have a 50% chance of inheriting the affected X, but this makes them carriers rather than affected.
takeaway: Carrier mother in X-linked recessive disease: half of sons affected, half of daughters carriers.

stem: A 29-year-old woman who works night shifts in a warehouse and rarely goes outside in daylight has had months of aching in her ribs and hips. She now struggles to climb stairs and to rise from a low chair without using her arms. Blood tests show a low-normal calcium, low phosphate, raised alkaline phosphatase and very low vitamin D. Which diagnosis fits best?
why_correct: Very low vitamin D impairs mineralisation of bone, causing diffuse bone pain and tenderness, proximal muscle weakness and a waddling gait. Biochemistry typically shows low or low-normal calcium, low phosphate, a raised alkaline phosphatase and secondary hyperparathyroidism. Limited sunlight exposure is a common UK cause, and treatment is vitamin D replacement with adequate calcium.
why_wrong: A. Osteoporosis is painless until a fracture occurs, and bone biochemistry is normal. B. Polymyositis causes proximal weakness with a raised creatine kinase, not bone pain and vitamin D deficiency. D. Paget disease typically affects older adults, with an isolated raised alkaline phosphatase and normal vitamin D. E. Primary hyperparathyroidism causes a raised calcium.
pearl: Osteomalacia: bone pain, proximal myopathy, low vitamin D, low or normal calcium, low phosphate and raised ALP. Osteoporosis: normal biochemistry and no pain until fracture.
thinking: Little sunlight exposure ↓ Diffuse bone pain and proximal muscle weakness ↓ Low vitamin D, low phosphate, raised ALP ↓ Osteomalacia
exam_trap: A, Osteoporosis — both weaken bone, but osteoporosis has normal biochemistry and no pain until fracture, whereas osteomalacia causes pain and abnormal bone chemistry.
takeaway: Bone pain, proximal weakness, low vitamin D and raised ALP point to osteomalacia.

stem: A 49-year-old woman with obesity and hypertension sees her GP about tiredness. She wakes with headaches, never feels refreshed and nods off while watching television in the evening. Her husband has moved to the spare room because she snores very loudly and he has heard her choke and gasp during the night. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Loud snoring with witnessed choking or gasping, unrefreshing sleep, morning headaches and excessive daytime sleepiness in a person with obesity and hypertension are typical of obstructive sleep apnoea, caused by repeated upper airway collapse during sleep. She should be assessed with a sleepiness score and referred for a sleep study. Weight loss helps, and CPAP is the main treatment for moderate to severe disease.
why_wrong: A. Narcolepsy causes sleep attacks and cataplexy, not loud snoring with choking. B. Hypothyroidism can cause tiredness and weight gain but does not explain witnessed choking episodes. D. Insomnia involves difficulty sleeping rather than excessive daytime sleepiness. E. Depression causes low mood and fatigue rather than snoring and nocturnal gasping.
pearl: Snoring, witnessed apnoeas or choking, and daytime sleepiness suggest OSA. Risk factors include obesity, a large neck and hypertension; ask about driving if sleepiness is excessive.
thinking: Obesity and hypertension ↓ Loud snoring with witnessed choking and gasping ↓ Unrefreshing sleep, morning headaches, daytime sleepiness ↓ Obstructive sleep apnoea
exam_trap: B, Hypothyroidism — it causes tiredness and weight gain and is worth checking, but it does not explain the witnessed choking and gasping during sleep.
takeaway: Snoring with witnessed choking and daytime sleepiness suggests obstructive sleep apnoea.

stem: A 62-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer has bone pain that is no longer controlled by regular paracetamol and naproxen. The palliative care team plans to start modified-release oral morphine. Which adverse effect should be anticipated and actively prevented from the start of treatment?
why_correct: Constipation occurs in most people taking regular opioids and, unlike nausea or drowsiness, it does not improve with tolerance. A laxative, typically a stimulant with or without a softener, should be prescribed alongside regular opioids from the outset, with the dose adjusted to maintain comfortable bowel movements.
why_wrong: B. Opioid-induced nausea is common at the start but usually settles within days. C. Opioids slow gut transit and cause constipation rather than diarrhoea. D. Opioids do not typically raise blood pressure and can cause hypotension. E. Opioids are more likely to cause urinary retention than frequency.
pearl: Always co-prescribe a laxative with regular opioids: constipation is common and does not settle with tolerance. Nausea and drowsiness usually improve within days.
thinking: Starting regular strong opioid ↓ Opioids reduce gut motility ↓ Tolerance does not develop to this effect ↓ Constipation should be anticipated and prevented with a laxative
exam_trap: B, Nausea that persists throughout treatment — nausea is a common early opioid effect, but it usually settles within days, whereas constipation persists.
takeaway: Prescribe a regular laxative whenever regular opioids are started.

stem: An 84-year-old woman is on the orthopaedic ward two days after a hip hemiarthroplasty. She has chronic kidney disease and was started on regular oral morphine for pain. The nurse calls because she is now difficult to rouse. Her respiratory rate is 7 breaths per minute, her pupils are pinpoint and her capillary blood glucose is normal. Which diagnosis best explains her deterioration?

options.C: Hypoactive delirium due to urinary infection

why_correct: Reduced consciousness, respiratory depression and pinpoint pupils in a patient recently started on morphine point to opioid toxicity. Morphine and its active metabolites are renally cleared, so chronic kidney disease allows them to accumulate even at standard doses. Management is airway support and oxygen with titrated naloxone, followed by review of the opioid prescription.
why_wrong: A. Fat embolism causes hypoxia, confusion and a petechial rash, typically with a raised respiratory rate. C. Delirium may cause drowsiness but would not explain pinpoint pupils and a very low respiratory rate. D. A stroke would usually produce focal neurology rather than symmetrical pinpoint pupils with bradypnoea. E. No history of COPD is given, and hypercapnic failure does not cause pinpoint pupils.
pearl: In older patients and those with renal impairment, morphine metabolites accumulate; choose lower doses or an alternative opioid and monitor sedation and respiratory rate closely.
thinking: Recently started morphine ↓ renal impairment reduces clearance ↓ drowsy, bradypnoeic, pinpoint pupils ↓ opioid toxicity
exam_trap: C, hypoactive delirium due to urinary infection — older postoperative patients often become drowsy with infection, but delirium does not explain pinpoint pupils with a very low respiratory rate.
takeaway: Pinpoint pupils, drowsiness and slow breathing after starting morphine mean opioid toxicity.

stem: A 61-year-old man asks his GP whether a cholesterol-lowering tablet is worth taking. The GP shows him a large trial in which 8% of people taking placebo had a heart attack over five years, compared with 5% of those taking the tablet. Which value represents the tablet's absolute risk reduction?
why_correct: Absolute risk reduction is the event rate in the control group minus the event rate in the treatment group: 8% minus 5% gives 3 percentage points. It tells the patient how much his own risk changes in real terms and is the most useful figure for shared decision-making.
why_wrong: B. 5% is the event rate with the tablet, not the reduction. C. 8% is the event rate with placebo. D. 33 is the number needed to treat (100 divided by 3), not the absolute risk reduction. E. 37.5% is the relative risk reduction (3 divided by 8).
pearl: Relative risk reductions sound impressive; absolute risk reductions and numbers needed to treat give a more honest picture for patients. The NNT is 1 divided by the ARR.
thinking: Control event rate 8% ↓ treatment event rate 5% ↓ ARR = control minus treatment ↓ 3%
exam_trap: E, 37.5% — this is the relative risk reduction, which candidates often confuse with the absolute figure because it is the number usually quoted in headlines.
takeaway: ARR = control event rate minus treatment event rate; NNT = 1 divided by ARR.

stem: At a journal club, a foundation doctor presents a placebo-controlled trial of a new osteoporosis drug. Over three years, the risk ratio for hip fracture in the drug group compared with the placebo group was 0.75. An older woman considering the drug asks what this means for her. Which explanation is correct?

options.A: Her risk of hip fracture would be 75% lower
options.B: Her risk of hip fracture would be 25% lower relative to placebo
options.C: Her risk of hip fracture would be 0.25% lower
options.D: Her risk of hip fracture would be 7.5% lower
options.E: The drug would make no difference to her risk

correct_answer: B. Her risk of hip fracture would be 25% lower relative to placebo
why_correct: Relative risk reduction equals 1 minus the relative risk, so 1 − 0.75 gives 0.25, a 25% relative reduction in hip fracture compared with placebo. This describes the proportional change in risk, not the absolute change, which depends on her baseline risk.
why_wrong: A. 75% is the risk remaining in the treated group relative to placebo, not the reduction. C. 0.25% wrongly treats the proportion as a percentage point change. D. 7.5% has no basis in the figures given. E. A risk ratio below 1 indicates reduced risk, so the drug does make a difference, subject to the confidence interval.
pearl: A relative risk of 1 means no difference; below 1 means reduced risk and above 1 increased risk. Check whether the confidence interval crosses 1 before calling a result significant.
thinking: Risk ratio 0.75 ↓ treated group keeps 75% of the placebo risk ↓ RRR = 1 − RR ↓ 25% lower relative risk
exam_trap: A, 75% lower — candidates read the risk ratio directly as the reduction, when 0.75 is the proportion of risk that remains.
takeaway: Relative risk reduction = 1 − relative risk; an RR of 0.75 means a 25% relative reduction.

stem: A cohort study finds that adults who regularly carry a cigarette lighter have a much higher rate of lung cancer than those who do not. When the researchers adjust their analysis for tobacco use, the link between carrying a lighter and lung cancer is no longer seen. Which concept best explains the original finding?
why_correct: Tobacco use is linked both to carrying a lighter and, independently, to lung cancer, so it created a false association between the two. Once it was adjusted for, the apparent effect disappeared, which is the defining feature of confounding.
why_wrong: A. Selection bias arises from how participants are recruited and would not be removed by adjusting for smoking. C. Reverse causation would mean lung cancer led to carrying a lighter, which is implausible. D. Observer bias relates to how outcomes are measured by assessors. E. A chance finding would not neatly disappear after adjustment for a known risk factor.
pearl: A confounder is associated with the exposure, independently causes the outcome and does not lie on the causal pathway. Randomisation is the best way to balance confounders, known and unknown.
thinking: Exposure (lighter) linked to outcome (lung cancer) ↓ third factor (smoking) linked to both ↓ association vanishes after adjustment ↓ confounding
exam_trap: A, selection bias — candidates label any distorted result as bias, but an effect that vanishes on statistical adjustment for a third variable is confounding.
takeaway: If an association disappears after adjusting for a third factor, that factor was a confounder.

stem: A 56-year-old woman tells her GP that she has noticed marked hair thinning since starting a recently licensed tablet for her diabetes. The medicine carries an inverted black triangle symbol in the BNF, and hair loss is not listed as a known side effect. How should the GP report this suspected reaction?

options.A: Through the practice's local incident log only
options.C: To UKHSA as a notifiable event
options.E: By writing to the manufacturer only

correct_answer: D. Through the Yellow Card scheme
why_correct: Suspected adverse drug reactions are reported to the MHRA through the Yellow Card scheme, which is open to healthcare professionals and patients. Medicines marked with the black triangle are under additional monitoring, so any suspected reaction should be reported, even if the link is uncertain.
why_wrong: A. A local incident log records safety incidents within the practice but does not feed national medicines surveillance. B. The GMC regulates doctors and does not collect drug safety reports. C. UKHSA receives notifications of certain infectious diseases, not adverse drug reactions. E. Informing the manufacturer alone bypasses the national regulator's surveillance system.
pearl: Report all suspected reactions to black triangle medicines, and serious suspected reactions to established medicines; certainty about causation is not required before reporting.
thinking: New symptom after starting a medicine ↓ suspected adverse drug reaction ↓ black triangle means additional monitoring ↓ report via Yellow Card
exam_trap: A, the practice's local incident log — useful for errors and near misses, but an adverse drug reaction without any error needs national reporting to the MHRA.
takeaway: Suspected adverse drug reactions are reported to the MHRA via the Yellow Card scheme.

stem: A 72-year-old man with COPD takes modified-release theophylline. He was prescribed ciprofloxacin by an out-of-hours GP for suspected acute prostatitis. Four days later he attends the emergency department with vomiting, palpitations, a fine tremor and a fast heart rate. Which statement best explains why this combination has caused harm?

options.A: Ciprofloxacin speeds up theophylline metabolism, causing withdrawal
options.B: Theophylline is excreted unchanged by the kidneys, so the infection has raised its level
options.C: He is having an allergic reaction to ciprofloxacin
options.D: Theophylline has a narrow therapeutic index, so a modest rise in its level from reduced metabolism causes toxicity
options.E: The two drugs have unrelated side effects that have occurred together by chance

correct_answer: D. Theophylline has a narrow therapeutic index, so a modest rise in its level from reduced metabolism causes toxicity
why_correct: Theophylline has a narrow therapeutic index, meaning the gap between effective and toxic concentrations is small. Ciprofloxacin inhibits the liver enzymes that metabolise theophylline, so its level rises, producing nausea, vomiting, tremor and tachyarrhythmias. When an interacting drug is needed in a patient on a narrow therapeutic index medicine, choose an alternative, adjust the dose or monitor levels.
why_wrong: A. Ciprofloxacin inhibits rather than induces theophylline metabolism, so levels rise rather than fall. B. Theophylline is mainly cleared by hepatic metabolism, not unchanged renal excretion. C. Allergy would cause rash, urticaria or anaphylaxis, not this toxic picture. E. The symptoms match theophylline toxicity and follow a recognised interaction, so chance is unlikely.
pearl: Common narrow therapeutic index drugs include warfarin, lithium, digoxin, phenytoin, theophylline, ciclosporin and aminoglycosides; check the BNF for interactions before adding any new medicine.
thinking: Narrow therapeutic index drug ↓ new enzyme-inhibiting antibiotic ↓ level rises a little ↓ toxicity because the safety margin is small
exam_trap: A, ciprofloxacin speeds up metabolism — candidates muddle enzyme inducers and inhibitors; an inducer lowers levels and causes treatment failure, whereas this picture is toxicity from inhibition.
takeaway: With narrow therapeutic index drugs, small interaction-driven level changes cause toxicity or treatment failure.

stem: A 79-year-old man is being discharged from the medical ward with a new prescription for furosemide. He lives alone and manages his own tablets. Before he leaves, he asks which details on the pharmacy label matter most for taking it safely at home. Which information is essential?

options.B: The cost of the medicine to the NHS
options.C: How much to take and how often to take it
options.D: The name of the consultant who started it

correct_answer: C. How much to take and how often to take it
why_correct: The dose and frequency tell the patient how much to take and when, and errors in either are a common, preventable cause of medication harm. For a diuretic, the label and verbal advice should also cover timing, such as taking it in the morning to avoid night-time diuresis.
why_wrong: A. The batch number supports recalls and traceability, not day-to-day safe use. B. The cost does not help the patient take the medicine correctly. D. The prescriber's name may be recorded but does not guide safe administration. E. Opening hours help with repeat supplies but not with safe dosing.
pearl: Check understanding at discharge with teach-back: ask the patient to explain how and when he will take each new medicine.
thinking: Patient self-manages a new medicine ↓ main risk is wrong amount or wrong timing ↓ label must state dose and frequency ↓ how much and how often
exam_trap: A, the manufacturer's batch number — it appears on packaging and seems safety-related, but it serves recalls rather than guiding the patient's own dosing.
takeaway: For safe self-administration, the label must clearly state the dose and how often to take it.

stem: A ward pharmacist reviewing a 45-year-old man's drug chart notices that co-amoxiclav has been prescribed for his cellulitis. His wristband and notes record anaphylaxis to penicillin. The pharmacist contacts the prescriber and the antibiotic is changed before any dose is given. How should this event be classified?
why_correct: Co-amoxiclav contains amoxicillin, a penicillin, so prescribing it to a patient with documented penicillin anaphylaxis was an error. Because it was intercepted before administration, the patient was never exposed, which makes this a near miss. It should still be reported locally so the system can learn from it.
why_wrong: B. An adverse drug reaction requires the drug to have been given and to have caused harm. C. A side effect is a known effect of a drug that has actually been taken. D. No second drug interacting with the antibiotic is involved. E. No harm occurred because the drug was never given.
pearl: Combination antibiotics such as co-amoxiclav and piperacillin with tazobactam contain penicillins; always check the full composition against the allergy record.
thinking: Penicillin-containing drug prescribed despite documented anaphylaxis ↓ error identified before any dose ↓ patient never exposed ↓ near miss
exam_trap: E, a harmful medication incident — the error had serious potential, but classification depends on outcome; nothing reached the patient, so it is a near miss.
takeaway: An error caught before it reaches the patient is a near miss and should still be reported.

stem: A 58-year-old woman sees her GP because her voice has sounded rough and croaky for two months. She drinks heavily, smoked for 30 years and has recently noticed a dull ache in her right ear. She has had no cold or sore throat, and otoscopy is normal. Which diagnosis must be excluded?
why_correct: Persistent unexplained hoarseness in a smoker who drinks heavily must be assessed for laryngeal cancer, and ear pain with a normal ear examination is a further red flag because it may be referred from a throat tumour. NICE recommends considering a suspected cancer pathway referral for persistent unexplained hoarseness in adults of her age.
why_wrong: A. Vocal cord nodules occur with voice overuse, usually in younger professional voice users, and are not the diagnosis to exclude first. B. Reflux can cause hoarseness but is a diagnosis of exclusion in someone with these risk factors. D. Hypothyroidism may coarsen the voice but would not explain ear pain and is not the dangerous diagnosis. E. Normal otoscopy makes a middle ear effusion unlikely as the cause of her ear pain.
pearl: Ear pain with a normal ear in a smoker or heavy drinker should prompt examination of the throat: referred otalgia via the vagus and glossopharyngeal nerves can be the first sign of head and neck cancer.
thinking: Persistent hoarseness without infection ↓ smoking and alcohol risk ↓ referred otalgia with a normal ear ↓ exclude laryngeal cancer
exam_trap: B, laryngopharyngeal reflux — a common cause of a croaky voice, but attributing persistent hoarseness to reflux in a high-risk smoker can delay a cancer diagnosis.
takeaway: Persistent unexplained hoarseness in a smoker needs urgent assessment for laryngeal cancer.

stem: A 22-year-old man telephones his GP surgery with three days of stinging when passing urine and a clear discharge from the tip of his penis. He started a new sexual relationship a fortnight ago and did not use condoms. He has no fever or loin pain. How should he be managed?

options.A: Prescribe trimethoprim for a urinary tract infection
options.D: Arrange testing for sexually transmitted infections, ideally via a sexual health clinic
options.E: Advise more fluids and review if not better in two weeks

correct_answer: D. Arrange testing for sexually transmitted infections, ideally via a sexual health clinic
why_correct: Dysuria with urethral discharge after unprotected sex suggests urethritis from a sexually transmitted infection, most commonly chlamydia or gonorrhoea. He should be assessed for STIs, ideally at a sexual health service, with nucleic acid amplification testing, treatment guided by the findings and partner notification. Urinary tract infection is uncommon in young men and should not be assumed.
why_wrong: A. Treating presumed UTI without STI testing may miss gonorrhoea or chlamydia and drives resistance. B. Urgent urology referral is not indicated for urethritis in a young man. C. Imaging does not diagnose urethritis. E. Delay risks complications such as epididymitis and onward transmission.
pearl: Urethral discharge in a man is an STI until proven otherwise; gonorrhoea treatment should be guided by culture and sensitivity because of rising resistance.
thinking: Dysuria and urethral discharge ↓ recent unprotected sex ↓ young man, so UTI unlikely ↓ STI assessment
exam_trap: A, trimethoprim for a urinary tract infection — dysuria triggers a UTI reflex, but discharge after unprotected sex makes an STI far more likely, and UTI antibiotics will not treat it reliably.
takeaway: Dysuria with discharge after unprotected sex needs STI testing, not presumed UTI treatment.

stem: A 9-year-old boy with asthma is reviewed by the practice nurse. His mother says his cough and wheeze flare every year from late spring into summer, at the same time as he has sneezing and itchy, watery eyes. His symptoms are worse on dry, windy days and settle by the autumn. Which category of trigger best explains his flares?
why_correct: Seasonal flares in late spring and summer, alongside hay fever symptoms, point to an inhaled allergen such as grass pollen acting on sensitised airways. Recognising this allows avoidance advice, treatment of the allergic rhinitis and stepping up preventer therapy ahead of the pollen season.
why_wrong: B. Viral infections cause flares mainly in autumn and winter and are not tied to hay fever symptoms. C. Exercise-induced symptoms occur during or after activity rather than seasonally. D. Cold air triggers symptoms mainly in winter. E. Irritants cause symptoms on exposure throughout the year rather than a seasonal pattern.
pearl: Treating co-existing allergic rhinitis, for example with an intranasal corticosteroid, can improve asthma control in children with pollen-triggered symptoms.
thinking: Asthma flares in late spring and summer ↓ with sneezing and itchy eyes ↓ worse on dry windy days (high pollen) ↓ inhaled allergen
exam_trap: B, viral respiratory infection — the commonest trigger of childhood asthma attacks overall, but its peak is in winter and it does not come with itchy eyes.
takeaway: Seasonal asthma flares with hay fever symptoms point to an inhaled allergen such as pollen.

stem: A 28-year-old woman who smokes and is overweight presents with recurrent painful lumps in both groins and beneath her breasts over several years. Some discharge foul-smelling pus, and the skin shows interconnected draining tracts, double-headed comedones and rope-like scars. Swabs have repeatedly grown no pathogen. Which diagnosis fits best?
why_correct: Recurrent painful nodules and abscesses in flexural skin such as the groins and inframammary folds, with sinus tracts, double comedones and scarring, are characteristic of hidradenitis suppurativa. It is a chronic inflammatory disease of the hair follicle, and smoking and obesity are recognised risk factors. Management includes smoking cessation, weight loss, long-term antibiotics and dermatology referral for more severe disease.
why_wrong: A. Furuncles are staphylococcal infections that heal without sinus tracts and are usually swab-positive. B. Candidal intertrigo causes a red, macerated rash with satellite lesions, not nodules and abscesses. D. Erythrasma causes brown, scaly patches in skin folds that fluoresce coral pink under Wood's light. E. Epidermoid cysts are discrete, often with a punctum, and do not form interconnecting tracts.
pearl: Sinus tracts and scarring in the axillae, groins or under the breasts signal hidradenitis suppurativa; repeated incision and drainage alone rarely controls it.
thinking: Recurrent painful nodules in skin folds ↓ sinus tracts, double comedones and scarring ↓ smoker with raised BMI, sterile swabs ↓ hidradenitis suppurativa
exam_trap: A, recurrent furunculosis — recurrent boils look similar early on, but the flexural distribution, sinus tracts and sterile swabs point to hidradenitis suppurativa.
takeaway: Recurrent flexural abscesses with sinus tracts and scarring suggest hidradenitis suppurativa.

stem: An 11-year-old girl is brought to the GP with a painful lesion on the sole of her foot that has been present for three months. It is flat with a rough surface. On close inspection, tiny black dots are visible within it, and the lesion interrupts the normal skin lines. She swims weekly at a public pool. Which diagnosis is most probable?
why_correct: A rough lesion on the sole that disrupts skin lines and shows tiny black dots (thrombosed capillaries) is a plantar wart, caused by human papillomavirus. Communal changing areas and pools are common sources of spread. Most warts resolve spontaneously, and treatment options include salicylic acid or cryotherapy.
why_wrong: A. A callus is diffuse thickening over a pressure area, with preserved skin lines and no black dots. B. A corn has a hard central core at a pressure point and lacks black dots. C. Acral melanoma is rare in children and presents as an irregular pigmented lesion, not a rough papule with pinpoint dots. D. Molluscum causes smooth, pearly, umbilicated papules, not hyperkeratotic plantar lesions.
pearl: Paring a plantar lesion helps: warts show pinpoint bleeding or black dots and interrupt skin lines, whereas corns and calluses preserve them.
thinking: Rough painful lesion on the sole ↓ skin lines interrupted ↓ black dots of thrombosed capillaries ↓ HPV plantar wart
exam_trap: B, corn — also painful on weight bearing, but corns preserve skin lines and lack the black dots of thrombosed capillaries.
takeaway: Rough plantar lesion with black dots and broken skin lines is a viral wart (verruca).

stem: A 72-year-old man is reviewed on a stroke rehabilitation ward three weeks after a left middle cerebral artery infarct. Nursing staff report that he coughs and splutters during meals and his voice sounds wet and gurgly after drinks. He has had two chest infections since admission. Which underlying problem best explains these findings?

options.E: Hospital-acquired infection from poor hand hygiene

correct_answer: A. Aspiration due to unsafe swallowing
why_correct: Coughing while eating and drinking, a wet voice after swallowing and recurrent chest infections indicate dysphagia with aspiration, a common complication after stroke. Oral intake should be reviewed and his swallow formally reassessed by a speech and language therapist, who can advise on safe food and fluid textures and positioning.
why_wrong: B. Reflux causes heartburn and regurgitation, not coughing during swallowing with a wet voice. C. Heart failure causes breathlessness and orthopnoea, not symptoms linked to eating. D. Bronchiectasis causes chronic daily productive cough and would not begin with a stroke. E. Hospital infection does not explain coughing specifically during meals.
pearl: Patients with acute stroke should have their swallow screened before receiving any food, fluid or oral medication, with specialist assessment if the screen is failed.
thinking: Recent stroke ↓ coughing during meals and wet voice after drinks ↓ recurrent chest infections ↓ aspiration from unsafe swallowing
exam_trap: E, hospital-acquired infection from poor hand hygiene — recurrent inpatient chest infections tempt this, but the link to eating and a wet voice points to aspiration.
takeaway: Coughing on eating, a wet voice and recurrent chest infections after stroke mean aspiration: get a swallow assessment.

stem: A 38-year-old woman sees her GP because both breasts feel lumpy and sore, mainly in the week before her period. The discomfort eases once menstruation starts. On examination there is diffuse, rope-like nodularity in the upper outer quadrants of both breasts, with no discrete mass, skin change or nipple abnormality. Which diagnosis best fits?
why_correct: Bilateral, cyclical breast tenderness with diffuse nodularity that improves after menstruation is typical of fibrocystic change, a benign hormonal response in women of reproductive age. With no discrete lump or other red flag, reassurance, a well-fitting bra and simple analgesia are appropriate, with review if a discrete lump develops.
why_wrong: A. A fibroadenoma is a single discrete, smooth, mobile lump that does not usually vary with the cycle. C. Cancer typically presents as a discrete, hard, often painless lump, sometimes with skin or nipple changes. D. Periductal mastitis causes periareolar inflammation, often in smokers, with possible discharge or abscess. E. Fat necrosis follows trauma and forms a firm, irregular lump.
pearl: Cyclical bilateral breast pain with diffuse nodularity is usually benign; a new discrete lump at any age needs triple assessment through the appropriate referral route.
thinking: Bilateral breast lumpiness and pain ↓ worse premenstrually, eases with menstruation ↓ diffuse nodularity, no discrete mass ↓ fibrocystic change
exam_trap: A, fibroadenoma — the commonest benign breast lump in younger women, but it is a single discrete mobile mass rather than diffuse cyclical nodularity.
takeaway: Cyclical bilateral tenderness with diffuse nodularity and no discrete lump suggests fibrocystic change.

stem: A 56-year-old woman tells her GP that over the past three weeks she has noticed spots of blood on her bra from her left nipple. Gentle pressure produces blood-stained fluid from a single duct. There is no palpable lump, and the right breast is normal. She is otherwise well. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Reassure her that this is duct ectasia
options.B: Take a swab and prescribe flucloxacillin
options.C: Check prolactin and review with the result
options.D: Refer urgently on a suspected breast cancer pathway
options.E: Review in six months if it persists

correct_answer: D. Refer urgently on a suspected breast cancer pathway
why_correct: New, unilateral, blood-stained nipple discharge from a single duct needs urgent assessment to exclude an underlying lesion such as an intraductal papilloma or carcinoma. NICE supports a suspected cancer pathway referral for unilateral nipple discharge in women of this age, even without a palpable lump. Assessment usually includes imaging and further investigation of the affected duct.
why_wrong: A. Duct ectasia typically causes multi-duct, often bilateral, green or cream discharge and cannot be assumed with unilateral bloody discharge. B. Without signs of infection, antibiotics are inappropriate and delay diagnosis. C. Prolactin is relevant to bilateral milky discharge, not single-duct bloody discharge. E. Delaying assessment risks missing a malignancy.
pearl: Nipple discharge that is unilateral, single-duct, spontaneous or blood-stained is suspicious; bilateral, multi-duct, milky discharge is usually benign or endocrine.
thinking: Unilateral nipple discharge ↓ single duct and blood-stained ↓ woman in her fifties ↓ urgent suspected cancer referral
exam_trap: C, check prolactin — candidates link nipple discharge with hyperprolactinaemia, but that causes bilateral milky discharge, not single-duct bleeding.
takeaway: New unilateral blood-stained nipple discharge needs urgent breast referral.

presentation: Giant cell arteritis with visual symptoms
stem: A 71-year-old man presents to his GP with three weeks of a new headache over his right temple, scalp tenderness when combing his hair and aching in his jaw when he chews. This morning, the vision in his right eye went grey for a few minutes before recovering. Which complication is the most urgent concern?
why_correct: New temporal headache, scalp tenderness and jaw claudication in an older adult suggest giant cell arteritis. Transient monocular visual loss is a warning that the arteries supplying the optic nerve are affected, and without immediate high-dose corticosteroids this can progress to irreversible blindness, sometimes in both eyes. He needs same-day steroids and urgent specialist assessment, without waiting for biopsy or imaging.
why_wrong: A. Aortic aneurysm is a recognised late complication that develops over years, not the immediate threat. B. Stroke can occur but is much less common than visual loss, and his symptom specifically affected one eye. D. Scalp necrosis is a rare complication. E. Steroid-induced diabetes is a treatment side effect to monitor, not a reason to delay treatment.
pearl: In suspected giant cell arteritis, visual symptoms raise the urgency: start high-dose steroids immediately and arrange same-day ophthalmology or rheumatology review.
thinking: Older adult with temporal headache, scalp tenderness and jaw claudication ↓ giant cell arteritis ↓ transient monocular visual loss ↓ imminent risk of permanent blindness
exam_trap: A, thoracic aortic aneurysm — a true complication of giant cell arteritis, but it develops late; the urgent threat after transient visual loss is permanent blindness.
takeaway: Visual symptoms in giant cell arteritis threaten permanent blindness: give steroids immediately.

stem: A 66-year-old man describes several weeks of sudden spinning lasting under a minute whenever he lies back in bed or tilts his head up to reach a high shelf. He feels nauseated during attacks but is well between them. His hearing is normal and neurological examination is unremarkable. Which bedside test should be used to confirm the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Brief episodes of rotatory vertigo triggered by changes in head position, with normal hearing and neurology, are typical of benign paroxysmal positional vertigo. The Dix–Hallpike manoeuvre is the diagnostic test: it reproduces the vertigo and a torsional nystagmus when the affected ear is lowered. Once confirmed, it is treated with a repositioning manoeuvre such as the Epley manoeuvre.
why_wrong: A. The head impulse test is used in acute continuous vertigo to help separate peripheral from central causes. C. The Epley manoeuvre treats posterior canal BPPV once diagnosed rather than confirming it. D. Rinne and Weber tests assess hearing loss, which he does not have. E. Romberg's test assesses proprioception and balance, not positional vertigo.
pearl: BPPV vertigo lasts seconds and is provoked by position; continuous vertigo lasting days suggests vestibular neuronitis or a central cause.
thinking: Short spinning episodes ↓ triggered by lying back or looking up ↓ normal hearing and neurology ↓ BPPV, confirmed with Dix–Hallpike
exam_trap: C, Epley manoeuvre — closely linked with BPPV, but it is the treatment; the diagnostic test is the Dix–Hallpike.
takeaway: Positional vertigo lasting seconds suggests BPPV: diagnose with Dix–Hallpike, treat with Epley.

stem: A 34-year-old woman tells her GP that when she takes food from the freezer or walks to work on a chilly morning, several fingers suddenly turn pale and numb. They then become dusky purple and, on rewarming, flush and throb. Between episodes her hands look normal, and there are no ulcers, rashes or joint symptoms. What is this called?
why_correct: Episodic, cold-triggered colour change of the fingers from white (vasospasm) to blue (deoxygenation) to red (reactive hyperaemia) is Raynaud phenomenon. Normal hands between attacks with no ulcers, rash or joint symptoms suggest the primary form. Management is keeping the whole body and hands warm and stopping smoking, with nifedipine if symptoms are troublesome.
why_wrong: A. Chilblains are itchy or painful red-purple swellings that persist for days after cold exposure. B. Acrocyanosis is persistent, painless blue discolouration rather than episodic colour change. D. Carpal tunnel syndrome causes tingling in the median nerve distribution without colour change. E. Frostbite follows prolonged freezing exposure and causes tissue injury, not brief reversible episodes.
pearl: Features suggesting secondary Raynaud include onset later in life, digital ulcers, asymmetry, abnormal nailfold capillaries and symptoms of connective tissue disease.
thinking: Episodic cold-triggered finger changes ↓ white then blue then red ↓ normal between attacks ↓ Raynaud phenomenon
exam_trap: A, chilblains — also cold-related and affecting the fingers, but they are persistent inflammatory swellings rather than brief colour changes.
takeaway: Cold-triggered white-blue-red colour change of the fingers is Raynaud phenomenon.

stem: A 52-year-old man has noticed over four months that he struggles to lift his arms to shave and to get up from a low sofa. His thigh and upper arm muscles ache slightly. There is no rash, double vision or drooping of the eyelids, and sensation and reflexes are normal. He takes no regular medicines. His creatine kinase is markedly raised. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Gradually progressive, symmetrical weakness of the shoulder and hip girdle muscles with a markedly raised creatine kinase and normal sensation suggests an inflammatory myopathy such as polymyositis. The absence of rash argues against dermatomyositis. Further assessment includes myositis antibodies, EMG, muscle MRI or biopsy, and screening for an underlying malignancy.
why_wrong: A. Polymyalgia rheumatica causes pain and stiffness rather than true weakness, with a normal creatine kinase. C. Myasthenia gravis causes fatigable weakness, often with ptosis and double vision, and a normal creatine kinase. D. Guillain–Barré syndrome causes rapidly ascending weakness with lost reflexes over days. E. Motor neurone disease causes mixed upper and lower motor neurone signs such as fasciculations and brisk reflexes, without a markedly raised creatine kinase.
pearl: True proximal weakness with a high creatine kinase points to myopathy; stiffness with normal strength and a normal creatine kinase points to polymyalgia rheumatica.
thinking: Progressive difficulty lifting arms and rising from a seat ↓ symmetrical proximal weakness ↓ markedly raised creatine kinase, normal sensation, no rash ↓ polymyositis
exam_trap: A, polymyalgia rheumatica — also affects the shoulders and hips in older adults, but it causes stiffness rather than true weakness and does not raise creatine kinase.
takeaway: Symmetrical proximal weakness with a raised creatine kinase suggests an inflammatory myopathy such as polymyositis.

stem: A 58-year-old man attends his GP because over two months he has struggled to lift his arms to hang out washing and to get up from a low car seat. There is no ptosis or double vision, and the weakness does not worsen with repeated effort. Tendon reflexes and sensation in all limbs are normal. His serum creatine kinase is many times the upper limit of normal. Where is the primary pathology most likely to lie?
why_correct: Symmetrical proximal weakness with intact sensation and reflexes points to a myopathic process, and a markedly raised creatine kinase confirms damage to the muscle fibres themselves. This pattern fits an inflammatory myopathy such as polymyositis, which needs further assessment including screening for an associated malignancy in older adults.
why_wrong: A. Neuromuscular junction disorders cause fatigable weakness, often with ptosis or diplopia, and a normal creatine kinase. B. Anterior horn cell disease produces wasting and fasciculations with only a modest creatine kinase rise. D. Sensory nerve disease causes numbness and reflex loss, which are absent here. E. Corticospinal tract lesions give upper motor neurone signs such as brisk reflexes and spasticity.
pearl: A markedly raised creatine kinase localises weakness to muscle; neurogenic and junctional causes leave it normal or only mildly raised. Proximal symmetrical weakness plus high CK means myopathy until proven otherwise.
thinking: Proximal symmetrical weakness ↓ no fatigability, normal sensation and reflexes ↓ markedly raised creatine kinase signals muscle breakdown ↓ Skeletal muscle fibres
exam_trap: A, Neuromuscular junction — proximal weakness is also typical of myasthenia gravis, so it tempts; but myasthenia is fatigable, often affects the eyes, and does not raise creatine kinase.
takeaway: Proximal weakness with intact sensation and a high creatine kinase localises to skeletal muscle.

stem: A 36-year-old man sees his GP with a two-year history of attacks in which his feet, and sometimes his hands, become intensely red, hot and burning. Attacks are brought on by exercise, warm rooms or a hot bath, and he gets relief only by standing on a cold tiled floor or soaking his feet in cold water. Between attacks the skin looks normal and foot pulses are easily felt. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Episodic burning pain with redness and warmth of the extremities, triggered by heat and relieved by cooling, is the classic picture of erythromelalgia. It may be primary or secondary to conditions such as myeloproliferative disorders, so a full blood count is a sensible first test.
why_wrong: A. Raynaud phenomenon is triggered by cold and causes pallor then cyanosis, the opposite of this picture. B. Complex regional pain syndrome usually follows injury and is persistent rather than heat-triggered and fully resolving. C. Acute gout affects a single joint with swelling and is not provoked by warmth in both feet. E. Chilblains develop after cold exposure and present as itchy purple lesions on the toes.
pearl: Think of erythromelalgia as reverse Raynaud: heat brings on red, hot, burning extremities and cold relieves them. Check a full blood count to look for an underlying myeloproliferative disorder.
thinking: Recurrent red, hot, burning feet ↓ triggered by warmth and exercise ↓ relieved by cooling, normal between attacks with good pulses ↓ Erythromelalgia
exam_trap: A, Raynaud phenomenon — an episodic colour change in the extremities brings Raynaud to mind, but Raynaud is cold-triggered with white and blue phases, whereas this is heat-triggered redness.
takeaway: Heat-triggered red, hot, burning extremities relieved by cooling indicate erythromelalgia.

stem: An 81-year-old man has had three episodes over the past year of a hot, swollen knee or wrist, each settling over about a week. He is now seen on the medical admissions unit with a swollen left knee. A knee radiograph shows a thin line of calcification running through the cartilage and menisci, parallel to the joint surface. Synovial fluid Gram stain shows no organisms. Which diagnosis fits best?
why_correct: Calcification within articular cartilage and menisci (chondrocalcinosis) is the radiographic hallmark of calcium pyrophosphate deposition, which causes recurrent acute attacks of large-joint inflammation known as pseudogout, typically in the knee or wrist of older adults. Polarised microscopy of the aspirate would show weakly positively birefringent rhomboid crystals.
why_wrong: B. Gout classically affects the first toe joint and causes punched-out erosions rather than cartilage calcification. C. Reactive arthritis affects younger adults after a gut or genital infection. D. Septic arthritis is a single acute infection, not recurrent self-limiting episodes, and a negative Gram stain with chondrocalcinosis favours crystals, although culture is still needed. E. Osteoarthritis causes chronic mechanical pain with joint-space narrowing and osteophytes, not acute hot joints with chondrocalcinosis.
pearl: Chondrocalcinosis on an X-ray of an older person with recurrent hot knees or wrists points to calcium pyrophosphate disease. Always send the aspirate for culture, as infection and crystals can coexist.
thinking: Recurrent self-limiting hot large joints in an older man ↓ knee and wrist involvement ↓ linear calcification within cartilage on X-ray ↓ Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease
exam_trap: B, Gout — recurrent acute monoarthritis suggests gout, but gout favours the first toe joint and does not cause linear cartilage calcification.
takeaway: Recurrent hot knees or wrists with chondrocalcinosis indicate calcium pyrophosphate deposition.

stem: A 76-year-old woman is admitted to the ward breathless with bibasal crackles and pitting oedema to her knees. Echocardiography shows a reduced ejection fraction. She is given intravenous furosemide, passes a large volume of urine over the next few hours and her breathing improves. How does furosemide produce this effect?

options.A: It inhibits carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule
options.B: It blocks the sodium-chloride cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule
options.C: It antagonises aldosterone in the collecting duct
options.D: It blocks sodium reabsorption in the thick ascending limb, increasing sodium and water excretion
options.E: It directly increases the force of myocardial contraction

correct_answer: D. It blocks sodium reabsorption in the thick ascending limb, increasing sodium and water excretion
why_correct: Furosemide inhibits the sodium-potassium-chloride cotransporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle. This causes a powerful loss of sodium and water in the urine, reducing circulating volume, pulmonary congestion and peripheral oedema in heart failure.
why_wrong: A. Carbonic anhydrase inhibition is the action of acetazolamide, a weak diuretic. B. Blocking the distal sodium-chloride cotransporter is the action of thiazides such as bendroflumethiazide. C. Aldosterone antagonism is the action of spironolactone and eplerenone. E. Loop diuretics relieve symptoms through fluid loss, not by increasing contractility.
pearl: Loop diuretics relieve congestion and symptoms in heart failure but do not improve survival on their own. Monitor urea, electrolytes and weight while giving them.
thinking: Fluid overload from heart failure ↓ furosemide produces a brisk diuresis ↓ acts on the thick ascending limb transporter ↓ Increased sodium and water excretion
exam_trap: B, Thiazide action in the distal tubule — both are sodium-wasting diuretics, so they are easy to confuse, but furosemide acts on the loop of Henle and is far more potent.
takeaway: Loop diuretics block sodium reabsorption in the thick ascending limb, offloading salt and water.

stem: A 32-year-old woman at 26 weeks of her second pregnancy attends the antenatal clinic. She was offered a glucose tolerance test because her body mass index is raised and her first baby was large. Her booking HbA1c was normal, she has no previous history of diabetes, and both the fasting and 2-hour glucose values on the test are now raised. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Hyperglycaemia first detected in the second or third trimester in a woman with a normal booking HbA1c and no prior diabetes is gestational diabetes. It results from pregnancy-related insulin resistance, is first managed with diet and exercise, and needs postnatal glucose testing because of a raised lifetime risk of type 2 diabetes.
why_wrong: A. A normal booking HbA1c makes pre-existing type 2 diabetes unlikely. C. Maturity-onset diabetes of the young is a monogenic diabetes with a strong family history, and is not suggested here. D. Although insulin resistance rises in pregnancy, an abnormal glucose tolerance test is not normal. E. Type 1 diabetes presents with weight loss, polyuria and ketosis rather than an abnormal screening test.
pearl: Risk factors for gestational diabetes include a raised BMI, a previous large baby, previous gestational diabetes, a family history of diabetes and certain ethnic backgrounds. Recheck glucose after delivery.
thinking: Glucose tolerance test offered for risk factors ↓ raised values at 26 weeks ↓ normal booking HbA1c and no previous diabetes ↓ Gestational diabetes mellitus
exam_trap: A, Pre-existing type 2 diabetes — her risk factors overlap with type 2 diabetes, but the normal booking HbA1c shows the hyperglycaemia arose during pregnancy.
takeaway: Hyperglycaemia first found in later pregnancy after a normal booking HbA1c is gestational diabetes.

stem: A 47-year-old woman has a telephone consultation with her GP. Over the past eight months her cycles have lengthened to every six to nine weeks, and she wakes drenched in sweat most nights. She feels irritable and tired. Her last bleed was five weeks ago. She is otherwise well. Which term best describes her situation?
why_correct: Changing cycle length with vasomotor symptoms such as night sweats, while periods are still occurring, describes the perimenopause. NICE advises that in women over 45 with typical symptoms this can be diagnosed clinically without measuring FSH.
why_wrong: A. Premature ovarian insufficiency refers to loss of ovarian function before the age of 40. B. Postmenopause is diagnosed only after 12 months without a period, and she bled five weeks ago. D. Hypothyroidism causes tiredness but not night sweats with lengthening cycles in this pattern. E. Polycystic ovary syndrome causes long-standing irregular cycles from early adulthood, often with hirsutism, not new vasomotor symptoms in the late forties.
pearl: Over 45 with irregular periods and vasomotor symptoms: perimenopause is a clinical diagnosis. Remind her that contraception is still needed until menopause is confirmed.
thinking: Woman in her late forties ↓ lengthening cycles but still bleeding ↓ night sweats and mood change ↓ Perimenopause
exam_trap: B, Postmenopause — vasomotor symptoms suggest menopause, but postmenopause requires a full year without periods.
takeaway: Irregular but continuing periods with vasomotor symptoms over 45 indicate perimenopause.

stem: A 66-year-old man sees his GP with two days of burning pain followed by clusters of blisters on the left side of his forehead and scalp. On examination there are also vesicles on the side of the tip of his nose. His visual acuity is currently normal. Which complication is this distribution particularly associated with?

options.D: Ocular involvement such as keratitis or uveitis

correct_answer: D. Ocular involvement such as keratitis or uveitis
why_correct: Shingles in the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve is herpes zoster ophthalmicus, and vesicles on the tip or side of the nose (Hutchinson sign) show involvement of the nasociliary branch, which also supplies the eye. This strongly predicts corneal and intraocular inflammation, so oral antivirals should be started promptly and the eye assessed urgently, with same-day ophthalmology referral if there are eye signs.
why_wrong: A. Facial palsy with ear vesicles is Ramsay Hunt syndrome, which involves the facial nerve rather than the ophthalmic division. B. Hearing loss also belongs to Ramsay Hunt syndrome. C. Trigeminal neuralgia causes brief electric-shock pains and is not a recognised result of this rash pattern. E. Bacterial meningitis is not a typical complication of shingles.
pearl: Vesicles on the tip or side of the nose in forehead shingles signal nasociliary involvement and a high risk of eye disease. Start antivirals and get the eye examined urgently, even if vision seems normal.
thinking: Shingles in the ophthalmic dermatome ↓ vesicles on the side of the nose tip ↓ nasociliary branch also supplies the eye ↓ Ocular involvement such as keratitis or uveitis
exam_trap: A, Lower motor neurone facial palsy — facial shingles brings Ramsay Hunt syndrome to mind, but that involves the ear and facial nerve, not the forehead and nose.
takeaway: Forehead shingles with nose-tip vesicles predicts eye involvement and needs urgent eye assessment.

stem: A 17-year-old is referred to the adolescent gynaecology clinic because she has never had a period. She is tall, with well-developed breasts, but has very scanty hair in the axillae and pubic area. There is a small, firm swelling in each groin. Pelvic ultrasound shows no uterus. Which diagnosis is most probable?
why_correct: In complete androgen insensitivity a 46,XY individual has testes, often in the groin or abdomen, that produce testosterone which the tissues cannot respond to. Testosterone is converted to oestrogen, giving breast development, while lack of androgen effect causes scanty body hair, and anti-Müllerian hormone from the testes prevents a uterus forming.
why_wrong: A. Müllerian agenesis also causes an absent uterus with normal breasts, but pubic and axillary hair are normal because androgen action is intact. B. Turner syndrome causes short stature and absent breast development from ovarian failure. C. Congenital adrenal hyperplasia causes androgen excess with virilisation, not scanty hair. E. Kallmann syndrome causes absent puberty with poor breast development and loss of smell.
pearl: Primary amenorrhoea with breasts but no uterus: check body hair. Scanty hair means androgen insensitivity; normal hair means Müllerian agenesis. Confirm with karyotype.
thinking: Primary amenorrhoea with good breast development ↓ absent uterus ↓ scanty pubic and axillary hair plus groin swellings that are likely testes ↓ Androgen insensitivity syndrome
exam_trap: A, Mayer–Rokitansky–Küster–Hauser syndrome — it shares primary amenorrhoea, normal breasts and an absent uterus, but body hair is normal because the patient is 46,XX with normal androgen response.
takeaway: Breasts, no uterus and scanty body hair point to androgen insensitivity syndrome.

stem: A 17-year-old attends her GP because she has not started her periods. She has no cyclical pelvic pain. She has normal height, normal breast development and normal pubic and axillary hair. Pelvic ultrasound shows two normal-looking ovaries, but no uterus can be seen. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Mayer–Rokitansky–Küster–Hauser syndrome (Müllerian agenesis) is failure of the uterus and upper vagina to develop in a 46,XX individual. Because the ovaries function normally, breast development and pubic and axillary hair are normal, but there is primary amenorrhoea with an absent uterus.
why_wrong: A. Androgen insensitivity also causes an absent uterus with breasts, but pubic and axillary hair are scanty and gonads are testes, not ovaries. B. Turner syndrome causes short stature and poor breast development from ovarian failure. C. An imperforate hymen causes cyclical pain with a normal uterus filled with blood. E. Constitutional delay produces delayed breast and hair development, not complete puberty with an absent uterus.
pearl: Normal secondary sexual characteristics with primary amenorrhoea suggest an anatomical cause. Absent uterus with normal hair and ovaries is Müllerian agenesis.
thinking: Primary amenorrhoea with normal breasts and normal body hair ↓ ovaries present, so ovarian and androgen function intact ↓ uterus absent ↓ Mayer–Rokitansky–Küster–Hauser syndrome
exam_trap: A, Androgen insensitivity syndrome — breasts with an absent uterus suggest it, but normal pubic and axillary hair and visible ovaries rule it out.
takeaway: Primary amenorrhoea with normal hair and ovaries but no uterus indicates Müllerian agenesis.

stem: A 72-year-old woman on warfarin for a previous pulmonary embolism has a routine INR test at the anticoagulation clinic. Her INR is 9.1, having been in range for months. She started a course of clarithromycin five days ago for a chest infection. On telephone review she has no bleeding or bruising and feels well. How should this be managed?

options.A: Admit for intravenous vitamin K and prothrombin complex concentrate
options.B: Continue warfarin unchanged and repeat the INR next week
options.C: Reduce the warfarin dose slightly and continue
options.D: Stop warfarin permanently and start aspirin
options.E: Withhold warfarin and give oral vitamin K (phytomenadione)

correct_answer: E. Withhold warfarin and give oral vitamin K (phytomenadione)
why_correct: A markedly raised INR without bleeding is managed by withholding warfarin and giving a small dose of oral vitamin K (phytomenadione), as set out in the BNF, then rechecking the INR and restarting warfarin once it has fallen back towards range. Clarithromycin inhibits warfarin metabolism and is the likely cause of the rise.
why_wrong: A. Intravenous vitamin K with prothrombin complex concentrate is for major bleeding. B. Continuing unchanged leaves her at high risk of bleeding. C. A small dose reduction without withholding warfarin does not lower a very high INR quickly enough. D. She still needs anticoagulation for her clot history, and aspirin is not an adequate substitute.
pearl: Match warfarin reversal to bleeding: no bleeding means withhold, plus oral vitamin K if the INR is very high; major bleeding means IV vitamin K and prothrombin complex concentrate. Check for interacting drugs such as macrolides.
thinking: Very high INR on warfarin ↓ no bleeding, so no emergency reversal needed ↓ withhold the drug and lower the INR safely ↓ Withhold warfarin and give oral vitamin K
exam_trap: A, Intravenous vitamin K and prothrombin complex concentrate — a very high INR feels like an emergency, but full reversal is reserved for major bleeding and would over-correct a well patient.
takeaway: Very high INR without bleeding: withhold warfarin and give oral vitamin K.

stem: A 29-year-old man with a known peanut allergy eats a cereal bar at work. Within minutes he develops swollen lips, widespread urticaria, a hoarse voice and wheeze, and he feels faint. His blood pressure is low. He is given intramuscular adrenaline by paramedics and improves. What underlies his reaction?

options.C: Antibodies against cell-surface antigens (type II) hypersensitivity
