She now feels dizzy and nauseated, is irritable, and describes brief electric jolts through her head when she moves her eyes. She has no fever, diarrhoea or muscle twitching, and her mood was good until she ran out. What best explains her symptoms?
why_correct: Abruptly stopping an SSRI, particularly one with a short half-life such as paroxetine, commonly causes dizziness, nausea, irritability and electric-shock sensations within a few days. These symptoms are distinctive for discontinuation syndrome. Restarting the drug usually resolves them, and any future stopping should be done by gradual tapering.
why_wrong: A. Serotonin syndrome results from excess serotonin, not stopping a drug, and causes fever, clonus and diarrhoea. B. Depressive relapse develops more slowly and does not cause dizziness or electric-shock sensations. C. Vestibular neuronitis causes severe vertigo but not irritability or electric jolts. E. Migraine aura causes visual or sensory symptoms followed by headache, not shock-like sensations on eye movement.
pearl: Paroxetine and venlafaxine have short half-lives and cause the most discontinuation symptoms; fluoxetine causes the fewest. Taper antidepressants rather than stopping abruptly.
thinking: Paroxetine stopped abruptly ↓ Symptoms within days ↓ Dizziness, nausea, irritability ↓ Electric-shock sensations ↓ SSRI discontinuation syndrome
exam_trap: B, relapse of depression — irritability after stopping an antidepressant suggests it, but relapse is slower and does not cause dizziness or electric jolts.
takeaway: Dizziness and electric-shock sensations after abruptly stopping an SSRI mean discontinuation syndrome.

stem: At her booking appointment, a 31-year-old woman in her first pregnancy is found to be blood group O RhD-negative with no red cell antibodies. Her partner is RhD-positive. The midwife explains that she will be offered routine anti-D immunoglobulin in the third trimester. What is the main purpose of this treatment?

options.B: To prevent maternal sensitisation to fetal RhD antigen
options.C: To prevent ABO incompatibility in the newborn
options.D: To reduce the risk of pre-eclampsia
options.E: To neutralise anti-D antibodies she already has

correct_answer: B. To prevent maternal sensitisation to fetal RhD antigen
why_correct: If an RhD-negative woman is exposed to RhD-positive fetal red cells, she may produce anti-D antibodies that cross the placenta and cause haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn, mainly in later pregnancies. Anti-D immunoglobulin clears fetal red cells from her circulation before her immune system responds. Routine antenatal prophylaxis, together with doses after sensitising events and after birth if the baby is RhD-positive, greatly reduces this risk.
why_wrong: A. Anti-D is preventive and does not treat fetal anaemia, which needs specialist fetal medicine care. C. Anti-D has no effect on ABO incompatibility. D. Anti-D does not affect the risk of pre-eclampsia. E. Anti-D cannot reverse sensitisation once a woman has formed her own antibodies.
pearl: Give anti-D after potentially sensitising events such as abdominal trauma, bleeding after 12 weeks, external cephalic version and amniocentesis, in addition to routine prophylaxis.
thinking: RhD-negative mother, RhD-positive partner ↓ Fetus may be RhD-positive ↓ Fetal cells entering maternal circulation ↓ Anti-D clears them before an immune response ↓ Prevents maternal sensitisation
exam_trap: A, treat existing fetal anaemia — anti-D is associated with haemolytic disease, but it is prophylactic and only works before the mother has been sensitised.
takeaway: Anti-D prevents RhD-negative mothers from becoming sensitised to fetal RhD-positive cells.

stem: A 5-year-old girl is brought to the GP because several children at her nursery have been unwell. She has had a mild fever for two days and very itchy spots that started on her scalp and chest. On examination there are red papules, clear fluid-filled blisters and crusted lesions side by side, mostly on the trunk, with a few shallow ulcers inside her mouth. Her palms and soles are spared. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Chickenpox causes intensely itchy crops of lesions that progress from papules to vesicles to crusts, so lesions at different stages are seen together. The rash is concentrated on the trunk, scalp and face and may involve the mouth. Management is usually supportive, with advice on keeping her away from nursery until all lesions have crusted.
why_wrong: A. Hand, foot and mouth disease causes mouth ulcers with vesicles on the hands and feet, which are spared here. B. Measles causes a maculopapular rash that starts behind the ears, with cough, conjunctivitis and coryza. C. Impetigo causes honey-crusted lesions, usually around the nose and mouth, not widespread vesicles. E. Scarlet fever causes a fine sandpaper-like rash with a strawberry tongue and sore throat.
pearl: Lesions at different stages concentrated on the trunk point to chickenpox. Avoid NSAIDs in chickenpox because of the association with severe skin infection.
thinking: Nursery outbreak, mild fever ↓ Very itchy rash starting on scalp and chest ↓ Papules, vesicles and crusts together ↓ Truncal distribution, palms spared ↓ Chickenpox
exam_trap: A, hand, foot and mouth disease — mouth ulcers with vesicles in a nursery child suggest it, but the truncal rash with crops at different stages and spared palms and soles fit chickenpox.
takeaway: Itchy truncal crops of papules, vesicles and crusts together indicate chickenpox.

stem: A 23-year-old woman attends a sexual health clinic asking to start 'the pill'. She gets headaches a few times a year that are preceded by about 20 minutes of zigzag lines spreading across her vision. She does not smoke and her blood pressure is normal. Which contraceptive method is contraindicated?
why_correct: Her headaches are preceded by a spreading visual disturbance, which is migraine with aura. Migraine with aura already increases the risk of ischaemic stroke, and oestrogen-containing contraception increases it further, so combined hormonal methods are contraindicated (UKMEC 4). Progestogen-only and non-hormonal methods are suitable alternatives.
why_wrong: A. The copper IUD contains no hormones and is safe in migraine with aura. B. The progestogen-only pill does not carry the stroke risk of oestrogen and can be used. C. The implant is progestogen-only and is suitable. D. The levonorgestrel IUS is progestogen-only and is suitable.
pearl: Ask about aura before prescribing combined contraception; if a woman on the combined pill develops new migraine with aura, stop it and switch to a progestogen-only or non-hormonal method.
thinking: Wants contraception ↓ Headache preceded by spreading visual disturbance ↓ Migraine with aura ↓ Oestrogen adds to stroke risk ↓ Combined pill contraindicated
exam_trap: B, progestogen-only pill — it is a hormonal pill and some assume all hormonal methods are unsafe in migraine, but the stroke risk relates to oestrogen.
takeaway: Migraine with aura contraindicates oestrogen-containing contraception; progestogen-only methods are fine.

stem: A 20-year-old woman phones her GP surgery for advice. She has norovirus and vomited about an hour after taking her combined contraceptive pill this morning. She has been taking the pill correctly for a year and had unprotected sex two days ago. What is the key issue with today's pill?

options.A: It may cause liver damage while she is unwell
options.B: Her risk of venous thromboembolism has greatly increased
options.C: She has received a hormone overdose
options.D: The pill may not have been absorbed, so contraceptive cover may be reduced
options.E: She will need to stop the pill permanently

correct_answer: D. The pill may not have been absorbed, so contraceptive cover may be reduced
why_correct: Vomiting soon after taking the combined pill, or severe persistent diarrhoea, can prevent the hormones being absorbed. The dose may therefore count as missed and contraceptive protection may be reduced. She should take another pill as soon as possible and follow missed-pill advice if the vomiting continues, including using extra precautions where advised.
why_wrong: A. A short gastrointestinal illness does not make the combined pill hepatotoxic. B. Dehydration may slightly increase thrombotic risk, but the main concern after early vomiting is loss of absorption. C. Vomiting reduces rather than increases the hormone absorbed. E. A brief illness does not mean she needs to stop the pill permanently.
pearl: If vomiting occurs within a few hours of taking an oral contraceptive, take another pill; if illness continues, treat each affected day as a missed pill.
thinking: Combined pill taken this morning ↓ Vomited shortly afterwards ↓ Hormone may not be absorbed ↓ Dose may count as missed ↓ Reduced contraceptive protection
exam_trap: B, venous thromboembolism — the combined pill is linked with VTE and dehydration may add to this, but the immediate issue after early vomiting is lost contraceptive cover.
takeaway: Vomiting soon after the combined pill can mean a missed dose and reduced protection.

stem: A 57-year-old woman with primary Sjögren's syndrome attends a rheumatology review. Her eyes feel gritty, and she needs a sip of water to swallow crackers or bread. She asks which problem in her mouth she is most at risk of as a result of her condition. Which complication is most likely?
why_correct: Saliva washes away food debris, buffers acids and has antibacterial properties that protect the teeth. When saliva is reduced, as in Sjögren's syndrome, dental decay develops rapidly, often at unusual sites such as the gum margins. Regular dental review, high-fluoride toothpaste and saliva substitutes or stimulants help reduce the risk.
why_wrong: A. Gingival hyperplasia is typically caused by drugs such as phenytoin, ciclosporin or calcium channel blockers. B. Oral lichen planus is a separate inflammatory condition and is not caused by dry mouth. C. Tonsillar enlargement is not a recognised consequence of reduced saliva. D. Macroglossia is associated with conditions such as amyloidosis or hypothyroidism, not dry mouth.
pearl: Dry mouth also predisposes to oral candidiasis. People with Sjögren's syndrome should have regular dental checks and be aware of their increased lymphoma risk.
thinking: Sjögren's syndrome ↓ Reduced saliva ↓ Loss of buffering and antibacterial protection ↓ Rapid tooth decay ↓ Dental caries
exam_trap: A, gingival hyperplasia — it is a familiar oral complication in exams, but it is drug-induced rather than caused by dry mouth.
takeaway: Chronic dry mouth removes saliva's protection and greatly increases the risk of dental caries.

stem: A 45-year-old woman with ulcerative colitis bumped her shin on a car door 10 days ago. A small pustule appeared and has broken down into a deep, extremely painful ulcer that is spreading quickly. The edge of the ulcer is ragged, purple and overhangs the base. A wound swab grew no significant organisms, and the ulcer enlarged after a nurse attempted debridement. Which diagnosis fits best?
why_correct: A rapidly enlarging, very painful ulcer with a violaceous undermined edge, starting from a pustule after minor trauma in a patient with inflammatory bowel disease, is pyoderma gangrenosum. Worsening after debridement (pathergy) and a sterile swab support the diagnosis. Treatment is with corticosteroids or other immunosuppressants under dermatology advice, and surgical debridement should be avoided.
why_wrong: A. Erythema nodosum causes tender nodules that do not ulcerate. C. Venous ulcers are shallow, slowly progressive and usually around the medial malleolus with venous skin changes. D. Necrotising fasciitis causes severe systemic illness with pain out of proportion to skin findings and rapid spread along fascial planes. E. Squamous cell carcinoma grows slowly over months and is not typically extremely painful after minor trauma.
pearl: Pathergy, where a lesion worsens after minor trauma or surgery, is a clue to pyoderma gangrenosum; avoid debridement and treat with immunosuppression.
thinking: Ulcerative colitis ↓ Pustule after minor trauma ↓ Rapid, very painful ulcer with purple undermined edge ↓ Sterile swab, worse after debridement ↓ Pyoderma gangrenosum
exam_trap: A, erythema nodosum — it is the commoner IBD-related skin lesion on the shins, but it causes nodules rather than ulcers.
takeaway: A painful ulcer with a purple undermined edge in IBD is pyoderma gangrenosum: avoid debridement.

stem: A 30-year-old woman developed aching in her right forearm after a heavy weight-training session two weeks ago. She now finds it hard to pick up coins. When asked to pinch a sheet of paper between her thumb and forefinger, the tips of these digits straighten so that the pads, rather than the tips, meet. Sensation in her hand is entirely normal. Which nerve lesion is most likely?

options.A: Median nerve at the carpal tunnel
options.E: Radial nerve at the spiral groove

why_correct: The anterior interosseous nerve is a purely motor branch of the median nerve in the forearm, supplying flexor pollicis longus, the lateral part of flexor digitorum profundus and pronator quadratus. Its injury weakens flexion of the thumb interphalangeal joint and the index finger distal interphalangeal joint, so she cannot form a tip-to-tip pinch. Because the nerve carries no skin sensation, sensation in the hand is normal.
why_wrong: A. Median nerve compression at the carpal tunnel causes sensory symptoms in the lateral fingers and thenar weakness rather than loss of long flexors. B. Ulnar nerve lesions weaken the intrinsic hand muscles and cause sensory loss in the little finger. D. The posterior interosseous nerve supplies finger and thumb extensors, causing finger drop without sensory loss. E. Radial nerve injury at the spiral groove causes wrist drop with sensory loss over the dorsum of the hand.
pearl: A pure motor deficit with loss of the tip-to-tip pinch (an inability to make an 'OK' sign) and normal sensation suggests an anterior interosseous nerve lesion.
thinking: Forearm pain after exertion ↓ Weak tip pinch, pads meet instead of tips ↓ Weak thumb IP and index DIP flexion ↓ No sensory loss ↓ Anterior interosseous nerve
exam_trap: A, median nerve at the carpal tunnel — the AIN is a median branch, but carpal tunnel syndrome causes sensory symptoms and thenar weakness, not loss of long flexors with normal sensation.
takeaway: Weak thumb and index tip flexion with normal sensation indicates anterior interosseous nerve palsy.

stem: A 44-year-old man attends the emergency department with two days of severe low back pain radiating down both legs. He has not passed urine since the morning but does not feel the urge to. Examination shows reduced pinprick sensation over the perineum, around the anus, over the buttocks and on the inner thighs. Which term best describes this sensory finding?
why_correct: Reduced sensation over the perineum, perianal region, buttocks and inner thighs, the areas that would contact a saddle, is saddle anaesthesia. It reflects compression of the sacral nerve roots and, with bilateral sciatica and painless urinary retention, strongly suggests cauda equina syndrome. He needs an emergency MRI of the lumbosacral spine and urgent spinal surgical referral.
why_wrong: A. L5 loss affects the lateral leg and dorsum of the foot, not the perineum. B. Stocking distribution loss is typical of peripheral neuropathy and affects the feet and lower legs. C. Dissociated sensory loss, as in syringomyelia, affects pain and temperature but spares other modalities in a cape distribution. D. Brown-Séquard syndrome causes ipsilateral weakness and loss of proprioception with contralateral loss of pain sensation.
pearl: Red flags for cauda equina syndrome include bilateral sciatica, saddle sensory change, new bladder or bowel dysfunction and sexual dysfunction; arrange emergency MRI.
thinking: Back pain with bilateral leg pain ↓ Painless urinary retention ↓ Reduced sensation over perineum, buttocks and inner thighs ↓ Sacral root compression ↓ Saddle anaesthesia
exam_trap: A, L5 dermatomal loss — sciatica brings single nerve root lesions to mind, but perineal and buttock sensory loss reflects sacral roots and the saddle pattern.
takeaway: Perineal and buttock numbness with back pain is saddle anaesthesia: suspect cauda equina syndrome.

stem: A 62-year-old woman with generalised myasthenia gravis is admitted with a chest infection. Over the next 24 hours her voice becomes nasal, she struggles to swallow her saliva, she cannot lift her head off the pillow and her breathing becomes shallow. Her pyridostigmine dose has not been changed, and she has no excess sweating, salivation, diarrhoea or small pupils. Which complication is most likely?
why_correct: Myasthenic crisis is a life-threatening exacerbation in which bulbar and respiratory muscle weakness threaten the airway and ventilation, and infection is the commonest trigger. Neck flexion weakness and bulbar failure are warning signs of impending respiratory failure. She needs urgent senior and critical care input, serial bedside measurement of respiratory function (forced vital capacity rather than oxygen saturations) and specialist neurology treatment such as intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange.
why_wrong: A. Cholinergic crisis follows excess anticholinesterase dosing and causes muscarinic features such as sweating, salivation, diarrhoea and miosis, which are absent. B. Guillain–Barré syndrome is an ascending neuropathy with areflexia, not an exacerbation in a patient with known myasthenia. C. Lambert–Eaton syndrome is a separate, usually paraneoplastic, condition in which weakness improves with repeated effort. E. A brainstem stroke would be abrupt in onset with long-tract or cranial nerve signs, not a gradual infection-related decline.
pearl: In myasthenia, oxygen saturations fall late. Monitor forced vital capacity, look for neck flexion weakness and bulbar failure, and avoid drugs that worsen neuromuscular transmission such as aminoglycosides.
thinking: Known myasthenia gravis ↓ Trigger present: intercurrent infection ↓ Bulbar weakness, neck flexion weakness and shallow breathing ↓ No muscarinic features and no dose increase, so not cholinergic ↓ Myasthenic crisis
exam_trap: A, Cholinergic crisis — it tempts because it also causes worsening weakness in treated myasthenia, but it needs a recent rise in anticholinesterase dose and produces muscarinic features such as salivation, sweating and miosis, none of which are present here.
takeaway: Myasthenia plus bulbar and respiratory weakness after an infection is myasthenic crisis until proven otherwise.

stem: The daughter of a 74-year-old man with Parkinson's disease telephones his GP. Ten days after ropinirole was added to his co-careldopa, he began seeing small children playing in the garden who are not there. He is otherwise alert and orientated, his memory has been stable, he has no fever or urinary symptoms, and his eyesight is unchanged. Which explanation best accounts for these symptoms?

options.C: Adverse effect of the dopamine agonist

correct_answer: C. Adverse effect of the dopamine agonist
why_correct: Dopamine agonists such as ropinirole commonly cause visual hallucinations and other psychotic features, particularly in older people, and the close link in time to starting the drug points to this. He is alert with stable cognition, making delirium or a primary dementia less likely. Management is to review the most recently added drug and reduce it gradually with specialist advice, rather than adding a typical antipsychotic.
why_wrong: A. Delirium causes fluctuating attention and confusion, and he is alert with no sign of infection. B. Charles Bonnet syndrome occurs with significant visual loss, and his vision is unchanged. D. Dementia with Lewy bodies involves cognitive decline and fluctuation, which are absent, and does not explain the timing after a new drug. E. Schizophrenia rarely begins at this age and would not be tied to a medication change.
pearl: Never stop Parkinson's medication abruptly because of the risk of a neuroleptic malignant-like syndrome, and avoid haloperidol and other typical antipsychotics, which can severely worsen parkinsonism.
thinking: Parkinson's disease on dopaminergic therapy ↓ New dopamine agonist started days before ↓ Well-formed visual hallucinations with clear consciousness and stable cognition ↓ No infection and no visual loss ↓ Adverse effect of the dopamine agonist
exam_trap: D, Dementia with Lewy bodies — it tempts because visual hallucinations and parkinsonism are both core features, but there is no cognitive decline or fluctuation, and onset straight after a new dopamine agonist points to a drug effect.
takeaway: New hallucinations soon after starting a dopamine agonist are drug-induced until proven otherwise.

stem: A 52-year-old man is on the orthopaedic ward 36 hours after fixation of an ankle fracture. Nurses note that he has become shaky, sweaty and agitated, and he then has a generalised tonic-clonic seizure. Before admission he drank spirits every day, and his gamma-GT is raised. His capillary glucose and serum sodium are normal. Which is the probable cause of his seizure?
why_correct: Abrupt cessation of regular heavy drinking on admission produces withdrawal, with tremor, sweating and agitation typically starting within hours and seizures most often in the first day or two. Normal glucose and sodium make metabolic causes unlikely. He should be managed with a benzodiazepine-based withdrawal regimen according to local protocol and given parenteral thiamine to prevent Wernicke's encephalopathy.
why_wrong: A. Hypoglycaemia is excluded by the normal capillary glucose. C. Fat embolism typically follows long-bone or pelvic fractures and presents with hypoxia, confusion and a petechial rash rather than tremor and sweating. D. Wernicke's encephalopathy causes confusion, ataxia and eye signs, not withdrawal features with seizures. E. Hepatic encephalopathy causes drowsiness and asterixis in advanced liver disease, and seizures are not typical.
pearl: Withdrawal seizures occur early; delirium tremens, with hallucinations, confusion and autonomic instability, usually appears a little later and is a medical emergency.
thinking: Daily heavy drinker admitted to hospital ↓ Alcohol stopped abruptly on admission ↓ Tremor, sweating and agitation within a day or two ↓ Glucose and sodium normal ↓ Alcohol withdrawal seizure
exam_trap: D, Wernicke's encephalopathy — the alcohol history makes thiamine deficiency tempting, but Wernicke's presents with confusion, ataxia and ophthalmoplegia, whereas tremor, sweating and an early seizure point to withdrawal.
takeaway: A seizure with tremor and sweating a day or two after admission in a heavy drinker is alcohol withdrawal.

stem: A 68-year-old woman attends her GP with tiredness and pins and needles in both feet for several months. She has taken omeprazole every day for many years for reflux. She eats a varied diet including meat and drinks little alcohol. Her tongue is smooth and red. Her full blood count shows a raised mean cell volume and her thyroid function is normal. What is the most likely cause?
why_correct: Gastric acid is needed to free vitamin B12 from dietary protein, so long-term proton pump inhibitor use can impair absorption and cause deficiency. Macrocytosis, glossitis and peripheral sensory symptoms fit B12 deficiency, and the neurological involvement makes folate deficiency less likely as the sole cause. B12 should be measured and replaced, with intramuscular hydroxocobalamin when there are neurological features, and the ongoing need for the PPI reviewed.
why_wrong: B. Folate deficiency causes macrocytosis but does not usually cause peripheral neuropathy, and her diet is varied. C. Hypomagnesaemia is a recognised PPI effect but causes cramps, tetany and arrhythmias, not macrocytosis or glossitis. D. Iron deficiency causes a low, not raised, mean cell volume. E. She drinks little alcohol, so an alcohol-related cause is unlikely.
pearl: Long-term PPIs are linked with B12 deficiency, hypomagnesaemia, fractures and C. difficile infection. Review the indication regularly and step down where possible.
thinking: Long-term PPI use ↓ Reduced gastric acid impairs release of B12 from food ↓ Macrocytosis and glossitis ↓ Peripheral paraesthesia suggests neurological involvement ↓ Vitamin B12 deficiency
exam_trap: C, Hypomagnesaemia — it is the PPI adverse effect most often highlighted in drug safety warnings, but it does not explain a raised MCV or glossitis.
takeaway: Long-term PPI use can cause vitamin B12 deficiency; check B12 in macrocytosis or neuropathy.

stem: A 31-year-old woman attends a preconception clinic. Two years ago she had an unprovoked deep vein thrombosis, and blood tests since then have repeatedly shown lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin antibodies. She is planning her first pregnancy and asks what problems she might face. Her condition is most characteristically linked with which complication of pregnancy?
why_correct: Her history fits antiphospholipid syndrome, in which antibody-mediated thrombosis in the placental circulation causes placental insufficiency. The classic obstetric associations are recurrent miscarriage and later fetal loss, with pre-eclampsia, fetal growth restriction and preterm birth also more common. She needs specialist preconception and antenatal care; pregnancy is usually managed with low-dose aspirin and low molecular weight heparin, and any warfarin must be switched early because it is teratogenic.
why_wrong: A. Gestational diabetes relates to insulin resistance and is not a feature of antiphospholipid syndrome. B. Obstetric cholestasis is a liver condition of pregnancy unrelated to antiphospholipid antibodies. D. Hyperemesis gravidarum is linked to high hCG states such as multiple or molar pregnancy, not thrombophilia. E. Placenta praevia relates to where the placenta implants and to previous uterine surgery, not antibody-mediated thrombosis.
pearl: Antiphospholipid syndrome is one of the few treatable causes of recurrent miscarriage, so women with recurrent losses should be tested for lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin antibodies.
thinking: Unprovoked thrombosis ↓ Persistently positive antiphospholipid antibodies ↓ Antiphospholipid syndrome ↓ Placental thrombosis and insufficiency ↓ Miscarriage and fetal loss
exam_trap: E, Placenta praevia — it is a placental complication, so it can seem linked, but it reflects where the placenta implants, not thrombosis within the placental circulation.
takeaway: Antiphospholipid syndrome characteristically causes recurrent miscarriage and fetal loss through placental thrombosis.

stem: A 38-year-old man attends the emergency department with sudden, severe colicky pain that radiates from his right loin to his groin, and he cannot keep still. Dipstick urinalysis shows blood only. He is afebrile with normal observations, and his pain settles after an NSAID. Which imaging should be arranged to confirm the cause?

options.D: Low-dose non-contrast CT of the kidneys, ureters and bladder

correct_answer: D. Low-dose non-contrast CT of the kidneys, ureters and bladder
why_correct: In non-pregnant adults with suspected renal colic, NICE advises urgent low-dose non-contrast CT KUB, ideally within 24 hours of presentation. It detects almost all stones regardless of composition, shows their size and position, and can identify alternative diagnoses. Contrast is not needed and could obscure stones within the urinary tract.
why_wrong: A. Ultrasound is first line in pregnancy and in children but is less sensitive for ureteric stones in adults. B. A plain X-ray misses radiolucent stones and is used mainly to follow up known radio-opaque stones. C. Contrast is unnecessary and can mask stones within the urinary tract. E. MRI is less sensitive for calculi and is not used as an urgent first test.
pearl: Fever with a ureteric stone suggests an obstructed, infected kidney, which needs emergency decompression with a nephrostomy or ureteric stent.
thinking: Loin-to-groin colicky pain in an adult ↓ Haematuria on dipstick ↓ Suspected ureteric stone ↓ Not pregnant, so CT is appropriate ↓ Low-dose non-contrast CT KUB
exam_trap: A, Renal tract ultrasound — it avoids radiation and is used in pregnancy and in children, but in non-pregnant adults it is less sensitive than non-contrast CT for ureteric stones.
takeaway: Suspected renal colic in a non-pregnant adult: urgent low-dose non-contrast CT KUB.

stem: A 22-year-old woman sees her GP for the third time in four months with burning on passing urine and frequency. Urine samples sent at her last two visits showed white cells but grew no organisms, and her symptoms did not settle with antibiotics for cystitis. She now also mentions a change in vaginal discharge and some bleeding after sex. She has had a new partner in the last six months and they do not use condoms. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Dysuria with sterile pyuria, abnormal discharge and post-coital bleeding in a young woman with a new partner suggests chlamydial urethritis and cervicitis. Chlamydia is the commonest bacterial sexually transmitted infection in the UK and is often missed when symptoms are labelled as a urinary infection. A vulvovaginal NAAT swab should be taken, and treatment is usually doxycycline, with partner notification and testing for other STIs.
why_wrong: A. Interstitial cystitis is a diagnosis of exclusion and does not explain discharge or post-coital bleeding. C. Bacterial vaginosis causes a thin, fishy-smelling discharge but not dysuria with pyuria or post-coital bleeding. D. Candidiasis causes itch and a thick white discharge rather than pyuria and cervical bleeding. E. True bacterial cystitis would grow organisms on culture and respond to antibiotics.
pearl: Sterile pyuria in a sexually active young adult should prompt testing for chlamydia and gonorrhoea; other causes include renal tuberculosis, stones and partially treated infection.
thinking: Recurrent dysuria not responding to cystitis treatment ↓ Pus cells but no growth: sterile pyuria ↓ Discharge and post-coital bleeding suggest cervicitis ↓ New partner without condoms ↓ Chlamydia trachomatis infection
exam_trap: E, Recurrent E. coli cystitis — urinary symptoms make it the default label, but repeated cultures with no growth, poor response to antibiotics and cervical symptoms point to a sexually transmitted cause.
takeaway: Dysuria with sterile pyuria and discharge in a sexually active young woman: test for chlamydia.

stem: A 61-year-old woman tells her GP that over the past two months her left nipple has started to pull inwards. It previously pointed outwards like the right one. She has no nipple discharge, pain or fever, and on examination no discrete lump is felt in either breast. Which diagnosis must be ruled out first?
why_correct: A recently acquired, one-sided nipple retraction can be caused by an underlying carcinoma tethering the ducts behind the nipple, even when no lump is palpable. She should be referred on a suspected cancer pathway for triple assessment: clinical examination, imaging and biopsy if needed. Benign causes are only accepted once cancer has been excluded.
why_wrong: A. Duct ectasia can cause nipple retraction, but it is often bilateral and slit-like and is a diagnosis made after cancer is excluded. C. Fat necrosis usually follows trauma and presents as a firm lump. D. Periductal mastitis typically affects younger smokers with pain, inflammation or discharge. E. A fibroadenoma is a mobile lump in younger women and does not cause nipple retraction.
pearl: Long-standing bilateral nipple inversion is usually congenital and benign; it is new, one-sided change that raises concern.
thinking: Woman in her sixties ↓ New nipple retraction ↓ One side only, previously normal ↓ Malignancy can tether ducts without a palpable lump ↓ Breast cancer must be excluded
exam_trap: A, Mammary duct ectasia — it genuinely causes nipple retraction in this age group, but it is a diagnosis reached after imaging, and new one-sided change must be treated as possible cancer first.
takeaway: New unilateral nipple retraction needs urgent breast referral to exclude cancer.

stem: A 30-year-old man presents to his GP with three weeks of an intensely itchy rash that keeps him awake. Examination shows short, wavy grey lines between his fingers, excoriated papules on the front of his wrists and around his waist, and several itchy nodules on the penis. His partner has started itching too. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Burrows in the finger webs, itchy papules at the wrists and waist, genital nodules, itch worse at night and an affected close contact are classic for scabies, caused by the Sarcoptes scabiei mite. First-line treatment is permethrin 5% cream applied to the whole body and repeated after a week, with all household and close contacts treated at the same time and bedding and clothing washed hot.
why_wrong: A. Contact dermatitis follows an exposure pattern and does not produce burrows or spread to contacts. C. Dermatitis herpetiformis gives grouped vesicles on extensor surfaces and is linked to coeliac disease. D. Lichen planus gives violaceous flat-topped papules and is not contagious. E. Pityriasis rosea starts with a herald patch, has a trunk-based rash and is only mildly itchy.
pearl: Itch can persist for several weeks after successful scabies treatment because of a hypersensitivity reaction, so this alone is not a sign of treatment failure.
thinking: Intense itch worse at night ↓ Burrows in the finger webs ↓ Papules at wrists and waist, genital nodules ↓ Close contact also itchy ↓ Scabies
exam_trap: A, Contact dermatitis — itchy hands are common with irritants, but contact dermatitis does not cause burrows or genital nodules or spread to a partner.
takeaway: Nocturnal itch, finger-web burrows and itchy contacts mean scabies: treat everyone at the same time.

stem: An 81-year-old woman is admitted from her care home with three days of cough productive of green sputum, and a chest X-ray shows right lower lobe consolidation. Staff say that until yesterday she was fully orientated, but she now does not know where she is or what day it is. She has bronchial breathing at the right base and a raised white cell count. Which feature most clearly indicates more severe pneumonia?
why_correct: New confusion is one of the components of the CURB-65 score used in the UK to assess the severity of community-acquired pneumonia, alongside urea, respiratory rate, blood pressure and age. It reflects systemic illness and predicts higher mortality, so it should prompt senior review, consideration of more intensive treatment and close monitoring. Sputum colour, fever, white cell count and focal chest signs support the diagnosis but are not part of the severity score.
why_wrong: A. Purulent sputum supports a bacterial infection but does not predict severity. B. Fever is common in pneumonia and is not a CURB-65 criterion. C. A raised white cell count supports infection but is not used to grade severity. E. Bronchial breathing indicates consolidation, not how ill the patient is.
pearl: In primary care, CRB-65 (without urea) helps decide whether a patient with pneumonia needs hospital assessment. Always compare current mental state with the patient's usual baseline.
thinking: Community-acquired pneumonia confirmed ↓ Severity is graded with CURB-65 ↓ Confusion is a core component ↓ The other findings are diagnostic, not prognostic ↓ New confusion
exam_trap: C, Raised white cell count — it looks like an objective marker of how unwell she is, but it is not part of the CURB-65 score and correlates poorly with mortality.
takeaway: New confusion in pneumonia is a CURB-65 feature indicating more severe disease.

stem: A 35-year-old woman attends the emergency department after her baby caught her right eye with a fingernail this morning. The eye is painful and gritty, keeps watering, and she finds bright light uncomfortable. Visual acuity is normal in both eyes, the pupil is round and reactive, and there is no history of a high-speed or metal fragment injury. Which test is most useful to confirm the likely diagnosis?

options.E: Fluorescein staining viewed under blue light

correct_answer: E. Fluorescein staining viewed under blue light
why_correct: This is a likely corneal abrasion. Fluorescein dye is taken up where the corneal epithelium is missing and fluoresces green under cobalt blue light, confirming the abrasion and showing its size. The upper lid should also be everted to look for a retained foreign body. Treatment is usually a topical antibiotic such as chloramphenicol with analgesia, and review if symptoms do not settle quickly.
why_wrong: A. Tonometry measures intraocular pressure and is used for glaucoma, not surface defects. B. Fundoscopy examines the retina and will not show an epithelial defect. C. Orbital X-ray is for suspected metallic intraocular foreign body after a high-velocity injury, which is absent. D. A swab is for suspected infective conjunctivitis or keratitis, not acute minor trauma.
pearl: Contact lens wearers with a painful red eye need same-day ophthalmology review to exclude microbial keratitis, and should not wear lenses until healed.
thinking: Minor trauma to the eye ↓ Pain, watering, photophobia and grittiness ↓ Normal acuity, no high-velocity injury ↓ Suspected epithelial defect ↓ Fluorescein staining under blue light
exam_trap: C, Plain X-ray of the orbits — imaging seems thorough after eye trauma, but it is only indicated for suspected high-velocity metallic foreign bodies, not a fingernail scratch.
takeaway: Suspected corneal abrasion is confirmed by fluorescein staining under blue light.

stem: A 64-year-old Black British woman is referred by her optometrist after a routine eye test. She has no symptoms and no eye pain. Intraocular pressures are raised in both eyes, the optic discs show enlarged cups with thinning of the neuroretinal rim, and visual field testing reveals defects in the periphery that she had not noticed. The anterior chambers are of normal depth. Which diagnosis best fits these findings?
why_correct: Primary open-angle glaucoma is a chronic, painless optic neuropathy with characteristic disc cupping and peripheral field loss, usually associated with raised intraocular pressure. It is often detected at routine optometry checks because central vision is preserved until late. Risk factors include older age, Black African or Caribbean heritage and a family history. She needs referral to ophthalmology, where treatment aims to lower the pressure; NICE now recommends selective laser trabeculoplasty as the first treatment for many patients, with pressure-lowering eye drops such as a prostaglandin analogue as the alternative.
why_wrong: B. Acute angle closure causes a painful red eye, blurred vision with haloes and a shallow anterior chamber. C. Ocular hypertension is raised pressure without optic disc damage or field loss, whereas she has both. D. Normal-tension glaucoma has disc and field changes with normal pressures. E. Macular degeneration affects central vision and does not cause disc cupping.
pearl: First-degree relatives of people with glaucoma aged 40 or over are at higher risk and are eligible for free NHS sight tests; encourage them to have regular checks.
thinking: Asymptomatic, detected at a routine eye test ↓ Raised intraocular pressure ↓ Optic disc cupping with peripheral field loss ↓ Painless, normal anterior chamber depth ↓ Primary open-angle glaucoma
exam_trap: C, Ocular hypertension — raised pressure is present, but ocular hypertension by definition has no disc damage or field loss, and she has both.
takeaway: Painless peripheral field loss with disc cupping and raised pressure is primary open-angle glaucoma.

stem: Nursery staff notice that a 4-year-old girl's left eye seems to drift outwards, especially when she is tired. At her GP appointment the reflection of a pen torch sits in the centre of the right pupil but towards the inner edge of the left pupil. When her right eye is covered, the left eye moves to take up fixation. Which diagnosis fits best?
why_correct: An asymmetric corneal light reflex and movement of the deviating eye on the cover test confirm a true ocular misalignment, which is strabismus (squint), here an outward-turning eye. Any child with a suspected squint should be referred to orthoptics or paediatric ophthalmology, as untreated strabismus can lead to amblyopia. A red reflex check is also needed to exclude serious underlying causes.
why_wrong: B. In pseudostrabismus the corneal reflexes are symmetrical and the cover test shows no movement. C. A refractive error can contribute to squint but does not by itself produce a displaced light reflex with a corrective movement. D. A sixth nerve palsy causes an inward-turning eye with failure of abduction, not an outward drift. E. Retinoblastoma may present with squint, but the key sign is an absent or white red reflex, which is not described.
pearl: A child with a squint and an abnormal or white red reflex needs urgent ophthalmology referral to exclude retinoblastoma.
thinking: Child with an eye that drifts ↓ Asymmetric corneal light reflex ↓ Deviated eye moves on cover test ↓ True ocular misalignment ↓ Strabismus
exam_trap: B, Pseudostrabismus due to epicanthic folds — common in young children and often reassured, but it has symmetrical light reflexes and a normal cover test, unlike this child.
takeaway: An asymmetric light reflex with movement on cover test confirms strabismus; refer to prevent amblyopia.

stem: A 24-year-old woman in her first pregnancy is on the labour ward at term. Her membranes ruptured more than a day ago and labour is being induced. She now has a high temperature and a fast pulse. Her uterus is tender between contractions and the draining liquor has become offensive-smelling. The CTG shows a rising fetal baseline heart rate. There is no vaginal bleeding. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Maternal fever and tachycardia, uterine tenderness, offensive liquor and fetal tachycardia after prolonged rupture of membranes indicate intrauterine infection (chorioamnionitis). It can lead to maternal sepsis and neonatal infection. Management follows the sepsis pathway with blood cultures and broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics, expediting delivery and informing the neonatal team.
why_wrong: A. Abruption causes pain, a tense uterus and often bleeding, but not fever or offensive liquor. B. Pyelonephritis causes fever with loin pain and urinary symptoms rather than uterine tenderness and offensive liquor. D. Epidural-related fever is usually low grade, does not cause uterine tenderness or offensive liquor, and no epidural is mentioned. E. Endometritis occurs after delivery, and she has not yet delivered.
pearl: Prolonged rupture of membranes, repeated vaginal examinations and group B streptococcus colonisation increase the risk of chorioamnionitis; the baby may need assessment and antibiotics after birth.
thinking: Prolonged rupture of membranes ↓ Maternal fever and tachycardia ↓ Uterine tenderness and offensive liquor ↓ Fetal tachycardia ↓ Chorioamnionitis
exam_trap: A, Placental abruption — uterine tenderness and fetal compromise are shared features, but abruption does not cause fever or offensive liquor.
takeaway: Fever, uterine tenderness and fetal tachycardia after prolonged membrane rupture mean chorioamnionitis.

stem: A 66-year-old Black man attends his GP with nocturia and a weaker stream over the past year. On rectal examination the prostate is asymmetrical, with a hard nodule in the right lobe, and the central groove cannot be felt. He has no fever and the gland is not tender. Which diagnosis needs to be considered?
why_correct: A hard, nodular, asymmetrical prostate with loss of the median sulcus on rectal examination is suspicious of prostate cancer. NICE advises referral on a suspected cancer pathway when the prostate feels malignant, whatever the PSA result, although PSA is usually checked as well. Black men have a higher risk of prostate cancer and tend to present younger.
why_wrong: A. Benign hyperplasia produces a smooth, symmetrically enlarged, rubbery gland with a preserved median sulcus. B. Chronic prostatitis causes pelvic pain and a boggy or tender gland rather than a hard nodule. C. A urethral stricture causes a poor stream but does not change the prostate on examination. E. A prostatic abscess causes fever, severe pain and a fluctuant, very tender gland.
pearl: Lower urinary tract symptoms do not distinguish cancer from benign enlargement; examination findings and PSA guide referral.
thinking: Older man with lower urinary tract symptoms ↓ Rectal examination performed ↓ Hard, asymmetric nodule with loss of the central groove ↓ Not tender, no fever ↓ Prostate cancer
exam_trap: A, Benign prostatic hyperplasia — it is the commonest cause of his urinary symptoms, but it produces a smooth, symmetrical gland, not a hard nodule with loss of the sulcus.
takeaway: A hard, irregular prostate on rectal examination needs suspected cancer referral.

stem: A 19-year-old woman who runs for her university athletics team has had no periods for eight months; her cycles were previously regular. She trains twice a day and has lost weight this season. Urine hCG is negative. Blood tests show low LH, FSH and oestradiol, with normal prolactin and thyroid function. She has no acne or excess hair growth. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Intense exercise, weight loss and low energy availability suppress hypothalamic GnRH release, causing low LH, FSH and oestrogen and secondary amenorrhoea. Normal prolactin and thyroid function exclude other common endocrine causes. The low-oestrogen state risks bone loss, so management focuses on restoring energy balance, often with dietetic and psychological support, and screening for disordered eating.
why_wrong: A. Polycystic ovary syndrome causes oligomenorrhoea with hyperandrogenism and normal or raised LH, not low gonadotrophins. B. Premature ovarian insufficiency causes high FSH with low oestrogen. D. A prolactinoma would cause raised prolactin. E. Asherman's syndrome follows uterine instrumentation and causes amenorrhoea with normal hormone levels.
pearl: Amenorrhoea in athletes may be part of relative energy deficiency in sport, which also affects bone health and performance; consider bone density assessment if amenorrhoea is prolonged.
thinking: Secondary amenorrhoea with a negative pregnancy test ↓ Heavy training and weight loss ↓ Low LH, FSH and oestradiol ↓ Prolactin and thyroid normal ↓ Functional hypothalamic amenorrhoea
exam_trap: B, Premature ovarian insufficiency — it also causes low oestrogen and amenorrhoea in a young woman, but FSH is high because the ovaries have failed, whereas here gonadotrophins are low.
takeaway: Amenorrhoea with low gonadotrophins after weight loss and heavy exercise is hypothalamic.

stem: A 31-year-old woman attends the emergency department with three days of increasing pain and swelling on the right side of her vulva, and she now finds it hard to sit or walk. She is afebrile. On examination there is a hot, very tender, fluctuant swelling in the lower part of the right labium majus, posterolateral to the vaginal entrance. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: The Bartholin's glands lie posterolaterally on either side of the vaginal entrance, and blockage of a duct causes a cyst that can become infected to form a painful, fluctuant abscess. Treatment is drainage, commonly with Word catheter insertion or marsupialisation, with antibiotics if there is surrounding cellulitis or systemic upset. A new Bartholin's swelling in an older woman should be biopsied to exclude malignancy.
why_wrong: A. Sebaceous cysts arise in hair-bearing skin, are usually small and are not specifically sited beside the introitus. B. Skene's glands lie beside the urethral opening anteriorly, not at the back of the vaginal entrance. C. Gartner's duct cysts lie within the anterolateral vaginal wall and are usually painless. E. An inguinal hernia extending into the labium arises from the groin and has a cough impulse.
pearl: Bartholin's abscesses often recur after simple incision, which is why Word catheter insertion or marsupialisation is preferred to keep the duct open.
thinking: Painful, enlarging vulval swelling ↓ Fluctuant and tender ↓ Lower labium, posterolateral to the introitus ↓ Site of the Bartholin's gland ↓ Bartholin's gland abscess
exam_trap: B, Skene's duct abscess — another paravaginal gland abscess, but Skene's glands sit beside the urethra at the front, not at the back of the vaginal entrance.
takeaway: A tender, fluctuant swelling posterolateral to the vaginal entrance is a Bartholin's abscess.

stem: A 66-year-old woman who has had four vaginal deliveries tells her GP she can feel something 'coming down' that is worse at the end of the day. She sometimes has to push the lump back to finish emptying her bladder, and has had two urinary infections this year. On examination with a Sims speculum, the front wall of the vagina bulges downwards when she strains, while the cervix stays high. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Descent of the anterior vaginal wall on straining is a cystocele, the bladder bulging into the vagina through weakened pelvic support. Incomplete emptying, needing to push the bulge back to void and recurrent urinary infections are typical. Vaginal birth, age, menopause and obesity are risk factors, and management ranges from pelvic floor muscle training and vaginal pessaries to surgical repair depending on symptoms and wishes.
why_wrong: A. A rectocele is a posterior wall bulge causing difficulty with bowel emptying. C. In uterine prolapse the cervix descends, but here it stays high. D. An enterocele is small bowel herniating through the upper posterior vaginal wall or vault, usually after hysterectomy. E. A urethral diverticulum gives a tender anterior mass with post-void dribbling and discharge, not a bulge on straining.
pearl: Use a Sims speculum with the patient in the left lateral position to examine the anterior and posterior walls separately, and ask her to strain to reveal prolapse.
thinking: Sensation of a vaginal lump ↓ Older woman after several vaginal births ↓ Bladder emptying problems and recurrent infections ↓ Anterior wall descends on straining, cervix high ↓ Cystocele
exam_trap: C, Uterine prolapse — the commonest image of prolapse, but the cervix remains high and the bulge comes from the anterior wall, so the bladder is the organ prolapsing.
takeaway: Anterior vaginal wall descent with bladder symptoms is a cystocele.

presentation: Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Lip
stem: A 72-year-old retired fisherman attends his GP with a sore that has slowly grown on the lower lip over four months. It has a hard, raised edge with a central ulcer, and it bleeds when he shaves or eats. He has smoked a pipe for most of his life. There is a small, firm lymph node under his chin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A slowly enlarging, indurated, ulcerated lesion on the lower lip of an older man with long-term sun exposure and pipe smoking is typical of squamous cell carcinoma. The lower lip receives the most sun, and lip SCC can spread to submental and submandibular nodes. He should be referred on a suspected cancer pathway for biopsy and treatment.
why_wrong: A. Actinic cheilitis is a premalignant dry, scaly change of the lip without a hard ulcerated lesion or lymphadenopathy. B. Basal cell carcinoma usually affects facial skin and the upper lip rather than the lower lip vermilion, and rarely spreads to nodes. C. A mucocele is a soft, bluish, fluid-filled swelling that does not ulcerate and bleed. D. Herpes labialis causes recurrent short-lived vesicles that heal within days.
pearl: Cutaneous SCC can metastasise, unlike most basal cell carcinomas, so always examine the regional lymph nodes when assessing a suspicious lesion on the lip or ear.
thinking: Older man with outdoor work and pipe smoking ↓ Lower lip lesion growing over months ↓ Indurated edge, ulceration and bleeding ↓ Regional lymph node enlargement ↓ Squamous cell carcinoma
exam_trap: A, Actinic cheilitis — it occurs on the same sun-damaged lip and can progress to SCC, but it is a flat scaly change, not an indurated ulcer with a palpable node.
takeaway: An enlarging, indurated ulcer on the lower lip of a sun-exposed older adult is SCC until proven otherwise.

stem: A 22-year-old woman is admitted from the emergency department with severe central abdominal pain, vomiting, dark urine and weakness of both arms. She also seems anxious and briefly hallucinated overnight. Acute intermittent porphyria is suspected and the ward team is writing her drug chart. Which of the following should be avoided?

options.D: A medicine listed as porphyrinogenic, such as certain anticonvulsants

correct_answer: D. A medicine listed as porphyrinogenic, such as certain anticonvulsants
why_correct: Porphyrinogenic medicines induce hepatic ALA synthase and can worsen or prolong an acute attack, so they must be avoided. Many anticonvulsants, some antibiotics and hormonal preparations fall into this group, and the UK porphyria drug database should be checked before prescribing. Opioids, paracetamol and intravenous glucose are generally regarded as safe.
why_wrong: A. Glucose suppresses ALA synthase and is part of supportive treatment. B. Morphine is considered safe and is commonly needed for the severe pain. C. Paracetamol is considered safe in acute porphyria. E. Sodium chloride is safe and may be needed because hyponatraemia is common in attacks.
pearl: Hyponatraemia from SIADH is common in acute porphyria attacks and can cause seizures; managing these is challenging because many anticonvulsants are themselves porphyrinogenic.
thinking: Abdominal pain, dark urine, motor neuropathy ↓ Psychiatric symptoms ↓ Suspected acute porphyria ↓ Drugs that induce ALA synthase worsen attacks ↓ Avoid porphyrinogenic medicines
exam_trap: B, Morphine for pain — opioids feel risky in someone with neuropsychiatric symptoms, but they are considered safe in porphyria and adequate analgesia is essential.
takeaway: In suspected acute porphyria, check every medicine against a porphyria-safe list and avoid porphyrinogenic drugs.
review_note: key option is near-tautological; needs rewriting as specific drugs and a check against the UK porphyria drug database (dropped from pack 04, 17 Oct 2026)

stem: A 61-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and protein in her urine calls the GP surgery because of a tickly, dry cough that has kept her awake for several weeks. It began shortly after a new tablet was added for her blood pressure and kidneys. She has no fever, breathlessness or sputum and her chest sounds clear. Which drug is most likely responsible?
why_correct: A persistent dry cough is a well-known adverse effect of ACE inhibitors such as lisinopril, caused by accumulation of bradykinin. An ACE inhibitor is the expected choice for hypertension in type 2 diabetes with albuminuria because it protects the kidneys. If the cough is troublesome, NICE suggests switching to an angiotensin II receptor blocker.
why_wrong: A. Amlodipine typically causes ankle swelling, flushing and headache. B. Indapamide causes electrolyte disturbance such as hyponatraemia and hypokalaemia. C. Bisoprolol may cause tiredness, cold peripheries or bronchospasm in asthma, not a dry cough. D. Doxazosin causes postural hypotension.
pearl: Angiotensin II receptor blockers do not inhibit bradykinin breakdown, so they rarely cause cough and are the usual alternative.
thinking: Dry cough without infection ↓ Started after a new antihypertensive ↓ Diabetes with albuminuria suggests ACE inhibitor was chosen ↓ Bradykinin accumulation ↓ Lisinopril
exam_trap: C, Bisoprolol — beta-blockers are linked with breathing problems, but they cause bronchospasm in asthma, not a persistent dry cough.
takeaway: A new dry cough after starting an antihypertensive suggests an ACE inhibitor.

stem: A 58-year-old man is on the surgical ward two days after a bowel resection. He has type 2 diabetes treated with metformin and dapagliflozin, which were continued around surgery. He is eating little, has vomited several times, has abdominal discomfort and is breathing deeply and rapidly. His blood pressure is normal, his abdomen is soft without peritonism, and his capillary glucose is only slightly raised. Which complication should be suspected?
why_correct: SGLT2 inhibitors such as dapagliflozin can cause diabetic ketoacidosis with near-normal or only modestly raised glucose. Surgery, fasting, vomiting and acute illness are typical triggers, which is why these drugs should be stopped before surgery and during acute illness. Deep, rapid breathing reflects a metabolic acidosis, and blood ketones and a blood gas should be checked.
why_wrong: A. Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state involves very high glucose and dehydration without significant ketoacidosis. B. Hypoglycaemia would show a low glucose and does not cause deep sighing breathing. C. An anastomotic leak should be considered after bowel surgery, but he is not shocked, the abdomen is soft, and the drug history with acidotic breathing and near-normal glucose points to ketoacidosis. D. Diabetes insipidus causes polyuria and thirst, not acidosis.
pearl: Always check blood ketones in an unwell patient on an SGLT2 inhibitor, even if the glucose is normal.
thinking: Taking an SGLT2 inhibitor ↓ Surgery, fasting and vomiting ↓ Deep, rapid breathing ↓ Only mildly raised glucose ↓ Euglycaemic DKA
exam_trap: A, Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state — it is the other diabetic emergency in type 2 diabetes, but it needs very high glucose and has no marked ketoacidosis.
takeaway: An unwell patient on an SGLT2 inhibitor can have DKA despite near-normal glucose.

stem: A 79-year-old woman in a care home takes warfarin for a previous deep vein thrombosis. She has been eating very little during a recent cold. The district nurse finds her INR is 6.4, well above her target range. She has no bruising, blood in the urine or stool, nosebleeds or other bleeding, and she feels well. What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Give prothrombin complex concentrate to correct the INR
options.B: Give intravenous vitamin K straight away
options.C: Continue the usual dose and recheck in a week
options.D: Withhold warfarin and manage according to the INR and bleeding risk

correct_answer: D. Withhold warfarin and manage according to the INR and bleeding risk
why_correct: A high INR without bleeding is managed by stopping warfarin temporarily, finding the cause, and restarting at a lower dose once the INR falls, guided by the level and the patient's bleeding risk. Poor food intake during illness reduces vitamin K and is a common trigger. Very high INRs may also need a small oral dose of vitamin K, as set out in the BNF.
why_wrong: A. Prothrombin complex concentrate is for major bleeding. B. Intravenous vitamin K is reserved for bleeding; without bleeding, oral vitamin K is used only at very high INRs, and unnecessary reversal makes re-anticoagulation harder. C. Continuing the same dose leaves her at significant risk of bleeding. E. Fresh frozen plasma is not used without bleeding and is less effective than prothrombin complex concentrate.
pearl: Reduced food intake, intercurrent illness, alcohol and new interacting drugs are the commonest causes of an unexpectedly high INR.
thinking: High INR on warfarin ↓ No bleeding ↓ Reduced oral intake during illness ↓ Withhold warfarin, find cause ↓ Restart at adjusted dose when INR falls
exam_trap: A, Give prothrombin complex concentrate to correct the INR — it rapidly normalises the INR, but it is reserved for major bleeding and carries a thrombosis risk.
takeaway: A high INR without bleeding is managed by withholding warfarin and acting according to the INR and bleeding risk.

stem: A 72-year-old man with atrial fibrillation has taken warfarin for years with stable INRs. He has had a painful dental abscess, and his dentist prescribed a five-day antibiotic course. At his anticoagulation clinic visit a week later his INR is far above his usual range. Which antibiotic is most likely to have caused this?
why_correct: Metronidazole inhibits the hepatic enzymes (CYP2C9) that metabolise warfarin, so it markedly raises the INR and bleeding risk. It is commonly prescribed for dental infections, which makes this a frequent real-world interaction. The BNF advises avoiding it in patients on warfarin where possible, or monitoring the INR closely and adjusting the dose.
why_wrong: A. Phenoxymethylpenicillin is not a classic cause of a marked INR rise. B. Topical fusidic acid has minimal systemic absorption. C. Nitrofurantoin is used for urinary infection and is not a major warfarin interaction. D. Flucloxacillin, if anything, may lower the INR.
pearl: Other drugs that raise the INR include clarithromycin, erythromycin, ciprofloxacin, fluconazole and amiodarone.
thinking: Stable INR on warfarin ↓ Dental abscess treated with antibiotic ↓ INR rises sharply ↓ Enzyme inhibition of warfarin metabolism ↓ Metronidazole
exam_trap: A, Phenoxymethylpenicillin — it is also used for dental infections, but it is not a major cause of INR rise.
takeaway: Metronidazole strongly increases the effect of warfarin; check the INR or avoid it.

stem: A 68-year-old woman has had Parkinson disease for nine years and takes co-careldopa. Her daughter brings her to the neurology clinic because she now has restless, twisting, flowing movements of her trunk and arms, which are worst about an hour after each dose. Her tremor and stiffness are well controlled at those times. She does not take any antipsychotic. What is the most likely explanation?
why_correct: After several years of levodopa, many patients develop dyskinesias, involuntary choreiform or writhing movements. They are typically peak-dose, occurring when plasma levodopa levels are highest, as in this case. Management includes adjusting the dose timing or size, or adding amantadine, guided by a specialist.
why_wrong: A. Essential tremor is an action tremor, not writhing movements linked to doses. B. Tardive dyskinesia follows long-term dopamine antagonists such as antipsychotics, which she does not take. C. A functional disorder should not be assumed when a known drug cause fits. D. Peripheral neuropathy causes sensory loss or weakness, not involuntary movements.
pearl: Motor complications of levodopa include wearing-off, on-off fluctuations and peak-dose dyskinesia; they are more likely with higher doses and younger age at onset.
thinking: Long-standing Parkinson disease ↓ Years of levodopa ↓ Writhing movements ↓ Peak about an hour after a dose ↓ Levodopa-induced dyskinesia
exam_trap: B, Tardive dyskinesia — it also causes involuntary writhing, but it follows dopamine-blocking drugs, not dopamine replacement.
takeaway: Involuntary writhing movements at peak levels after years of levodopa are levodopa-induced dyskinesia.

stem: On a day-surgery unit, a 17-year-old girl is given intravenous metoclopramide for vomiting after a laparoscopic appendicectomy. About forty minutes later her jaw clenches, her tongue keeps pushing forwards and her head is twisted to the left. She is fully alert and frightened, and her temperature, pulse and blood pressure are normal. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: Tetanus from a contaminated surgical wound
options.D: Acute dystonic reaction to the antiemetic

correct_answer: D. Acute dystonic reaction to the antiemetic
why_correct: Metoclopramide blocks dopamine D2 receptors in the basal ganglia and can provoke an acute dystonic reaction within hours of a dose, especially in young women and adolescents. Sustained twisting of the neck, trismus and tongue protrusion in an alert patient with normal observations is the classic picture. It usually settles promptly with an anticholinergic such as procyclidine.
why_wrong: A. Tetanus develops days after a contaminated wound, not within an hour of a clean operation, and is accompanied by spasms triggered by stimuli. B. Hypocalcaemic tetany causes carpopedal spasm and perioral tingling rather than torticollis and tongue protrusion. C. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome evolves over days with fever, generalised rigidity, autonomic instability and reduced consciousness. E. A focal seizure is brief and often alters awareness; it does not produce sustained posturing with preserved alertness after a new dopamine antagonist.
pearl: Under the MHRA advice, metoclopramide should be used only short term (up to 5 days) because of the risk of neurological adverse effects, and young patients are most susceptible to acute dystonia.
thinking: Recent intravenous dopamine antagonist ↓ Sustained involuntary muscle contraction of neck, jaw and tongue ↓ Alert, afebrile, normal observations ↓ Onset within an hour of the dose ↓ Acute dystonic reaction
exam_trap: C, Neuroleptic malignant syndrome — it is the dramatic dopamine-antagonist reaction everyone remembers, but it needs fever, rigidity and autonomic upset developing over days.
takeaway: Sudden twisting postures in an alert young person shortly after metoclopramide indicate an acute dystonic reaction.

stem: A 52-year-old man was started on levothyroxine after radioiodine treatment for Graves' disease. Over the past year his TSH has stayed above the reference range even though his GP has increased the dose twice. He says he never misses a tablet: he swallows it whole with a glass of water at the same time every morning, together with his breakfast of toast and coffee before driving to work. Which aspect of how he takes the tablet is most likely to explain his results?

options.A: Taking it alongside his breakfast and coffee
options.B: Taking it with a glass of water
options.C: Taking it at the same time each day
options.D: Swallowing it whole rather than chewing it
options.E: Taking it in the morning rather than at bedtime

correct_answer: A. Taking it alongside his breakfast and coffee
why_correct: Levothyroxine absorption from the small bowel is reduced by food and by coffee, so taking it with breakfast can leave the TSH persistently high despite good adherence and dose increases. It should be taken on an empty stomach, usually 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast or caffeine-containing drinks. Correcting the timing is preferable to repeatedly increasing the dose.
why_wrong: B. Water is the recommended drink to take levothyroxine with. C. A consistent time each day supports stable absorption. D. The tablet is designed to be swallowed whole. E. A morning dose before food is the standard advice; taking it in the morning is not the problem.
pearl: Other common causes of a raised TSH on stable levothyroxine include calcium, iron and antacids taken at the same time, coeliac disease and poor adherence.
thinking: TSH high despite dose increases ↓ Good adherence reported ↓ Ask exactly how the tablet is taken ↓ Taken with breakfast and coffee ↓ Food and caffeine reduce absorption ↓ Take on an empty stomach before breakfast
exam_trap: E, Taking it in the morning rather than at bedtime — some people do take it at night, which tempts, but morning dosing is perfectly correct as long as it is before food.
takeaway: Levothyroxine should be taken on an empty stomach, separated from food, coffee and mineral supplements.

stem: A carer at a residential home calls the GP about an 84-year-old woman whose thinking has become muddled over the last three days. She is drowsy in the mornings, agitated in the evenings and has been picking at her bedclothes. An out-of-hours doctor recently started promethazine at night for poor sleep. She has not passed urine since early morning and her mouth is very dry. Which property of the new medicine most likely explains this picture?
why_correct: Promethazine is a sedating antihistamine with strong antimuscarinic activity. In older people, blocking central muscarinic receptors readily causes fluctuating confusion (delirium), while peripheral effects give dry mouth and urinary retention. The new drug, the time course and the anticholinergic features point to this cause, and the medicine should be stopped.
why_wrong: A. Serotonergic excess causes agitation with clonus, sweating and hyperthermia, not dry mouth and urinary retention. C. Promethazine does not stimulate dopamine receptors; dopaminergic drugs cause hallucinations but not retention and a dry mouth. D. Enzyme induction alters the levels of other drugs and would not itself produce this syndrome. E. Promethazine has no mineralocorticoid effect, which would cause fluid retention and hypokalaemia rather than delirium.
pearl: Each additional anticholinergic medicine increases the cumulative anticholinergic burden, which is linked to delirium, falls and cognitive decline in older adults.
thinking: Acute fluctuating confusion in an older person ↓ New sedating antihistamine started ↓ Dry mouth and urinary retention ↓ Points to antimuscarinic toxicity ↓ Stop the drug and review the anticholinergic burden
exam_trap: A, Serotonergic activity — agitation and confusion after a new drug can suggest serotonin toxicity, but the dry mouth and urinary retention are antimuscarinic features.
takeaway: In older people with new delirium, look for medicines with anticholinergic activity.

presentation: ACE inhibitor and renal artery stenosis
stem: A 64-year-old woman had her left kidney removed for renal cell carcinoma several years ago. She now has hypertension that is difficult to control, and imaging shows a tight stenosis of the right renal artery. Ten days after her GP adds perindopril, her creatinine has risen sharply. How does the new drug cause this fall in kidney function?

options.A: Raised erythropoietin production increasing blood viscosity
options.B: Loss of angiotensin II-mediated efferent arteriolar constriction lowering glomerular pressure
options.C: Direct toxic injury to the tubular epithelium
options.D: Constriction of the afferent arteriole reducing renal blood flow
options.E: Obstruction of urine outflow at the bladder neck

correct_answer: B. Loss of angiotensin II-mediated efferent arteriolar constriction lowering glomerular pressure
why_correct: With a stenosed artery supplying her only kidney, glomerular filtration pressure is maintained by angiotensin II constricting the efferent arteriole. An ACE inhibitor removes this constriction, so intraglomerular pressure and GFR fall abruptly. The same applies to bilateral renal artery stenosis, and the drug should be stopped.
why_wrong: A. ACE inhibitors tend to lower, not raise, erythropoietin and do not cause hyperviscosity. C. The injury is haemodynamic, not a direct tubular toxicity. D. Afferent arteriolar constriction is the NSAID mechanism, not the effect of ACE inhibition. E. ACE inhibitors do not cause bladder outflow obstruction.
pearl: A rise in creatinine of more than about 30% after starting an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker should prompt review of the drug and a search for renovascular disease.
thinking: Solitary kidney with a stenosed renal artery ↓ GFR depends on efferent arteriolar tone ↓ Angiotensin II maintains that tone ↓ ACE inhibitor removes it ↓ Glomerular pressure and GFR fall
exam_trap: D, Afferent arteriolar constriction — it sounds logical when renal blood flow is reduced, but that is the NSAID story; ACE inhibitors act on the efferent side.
takeaway: In renal artery stenosis to a solitary kidney or both kidneys, ACE inhibitors drop GFR by removing efferent arteriolar constriction.

stem: At his annual diabetes review in general practice, a 63-year-old man who has taken metformin for eight years mentions tingling in both feet that has crept up to his ankles. His glycaemic control has been good. His full blood count shows a raised mean cell volume, and he drinks very little alcohol. Which deficiency should be checked for first?
why_correct: Long-term metformin reduces vitamin B12 absorption in the terminal ileum, and deficiency can cause a peripheral neuropathy and macrocytosis. In a man with good glycaemic control, new sensory symptoms with a raised MCV should not simply be attributed to diabetic neuropathy. B12 should be measured and replaced if low.
why_wrong: A. Thiamine deficiency causes neuropathy and Wernicke encephalopathy but not macrocytosis, and is not linked to metformin. B. Folate deficiency causes macrocytosis but not this neuropathy, and metformin is principally associated with B12 malabsorption. C. Vitamin D deficiency causes bone pain and myopathy, not macrocytosis. E. Pyridoxine deficiency is linked to isoniazid and causes neuropathy with a microcytic, not macrocytic, picture.
pearl: MHRA advice is to check vitamin B12 in people on metformin who develop neuropathy or anaemia, and to consider periodic monitoring in those at risk, as the deficiency can mimic or worsen diabetic neuropathy.
thinking: Long-term metformin ↓ Ascending sensory symptoms in the feet ↓ Raised MCV ↓ Metformin impairs ileal B12 absorption ↓ Check vitamin B12
exam_trap: B, Folate — it also causes macrocytosis, but it does not explain the neuropathy and is not the deficiency classically caused by metformin.
takeaway: Neuropathy or macrocytosis in a patient on long-term metformin should prompt a vitamin B12 level.

stem: A 45-year-old woman with obesity began weekly semaglutide injections through a specialist weight management service two weeks ago. She reports mild queasiness, feeling full after only a few mouthfuls and occasional loose stools. She has no abdominal pain, fever or vomiting, and her abdomen is soft and non-tender. What is the most likely explanation for her symptoms?

options.C: Expected gastrointestinal adverse effects of the new drug

correct_answer: C. Expected gastrointestinal adverse effects of the new drug
why_correct: GLP-1 receptor agonists slow gastric emptying and act centrally to reduce appetite, so nausea, early fullness and altered bowel habit are common, especially after starting or increasing the dose. Her symptoms are mild, began with the drug and come without pain or abnormal signs. They usually settle with time, smaller meals and slower dose escalation.
why_wrong: A. Pancreatitis is a rare adverse effect and presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back. B. Cholecystitis causes right upper quadrant pain, fever and tenderness. D. Gastric outlet obstruction causes persistent, often projectile vomiting of undigested food. E. Coeliac disease would not begin abruptly with a new medicine and the timing points to the drug.
pearl: Patients on GLP-1 receptor agonists should be told to seek urgent help for severe persistent abdominal pain, which may indicate pancreatitis.
thinking: New GLP-1 receptor agonist ↓ Mild nausea, early satiety, loose stools ↓ No pain, fever or abnormal signs ↓ Drug slows gastric emptying and suppresses appetite ↓ Expected gastrointestinal adverse effects
exam_trap: A, Acute pancreatitis — it is the serious warning attached to this drug class, but it causes severe abdominal pain, which she does not have.
takeaway: Mild nausea and early fullness after starting a GLP-1 receptor agonist are expected effects, while severe abdominal pain needs urgent assessment.

stem: A 60-year-old man with gastroparesis asks his GP whether he could try domperidone, which a friend found helpful. He has ischaemic heart disease and already takes citalopram. Which adverse effect is the most important to consider before prescribing it?
correct_answer: E. QT prolongation and ventricular arrhythmia
why_correct: Domperidone can prolong the QT interval and has been associated with serious ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death. The risk is greater in older people, those with heart disease and those taking other QT-prolonging drugs such as citalopram. In this man it is likely to be contraindicated, and any use should be at the lowest dose for the shortest time.
why_wrong: A. Agranulocytosis is linked to drugs such as carbimazole and clozapine, not domperidone. B. Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus is a lithium effect. C. Pulmonary fibrosis is associated with amiodarone, methotrexate and nitrofurantoin. D. Sensorineural deafness is a recognised toxicity of aminoglycosides and loop diuretics.
pearl: The MHRA restricts domperidone to relief of nausea and vomiting, at the lowest effective dose for a short course, and contraindicates it in people with cardiac disease or conduction problems and in those taking QT-prolonging drugs.
thinking: Request for domperidone ↓ Background ischaemic heart disease ↓ Already on another QT-prolonging drug ↓ Domperidone prolongs QT ↓ Risk of ventricular arrhythmia
exam_trap: A, Agranulocytosis — a rare but serious blood reaction that comes to mind with many drugs, but it is not the safety concern with domperidone.
takeaway: Domperidone carries a risk of QT prolongation and sudden cardiac death, so check cardiac history and interacting drugs first.

stem: During pre-operative assessment for a hernia repair, a 55-year-old man says he cannot take codeine. After a dental extraction last year it made him feel sick and he vomited twice; he had no rash, lip or tongue swelling, wheeze or faintness. How should this be recorded in his notes?

options.A: As an allergy to all opioids
options.B: Not recorded, as it was a minor reaction
options.C: As anaphylaxis to codeine, to be cautious
options.D: As an intolerance (non-allergic side effect) to codeine, describing the reaction
options.E: As a contraindication to every opioid analgesic

correct_answer: D. As an intolerance (non-allergic side effect) to codeine, describing the reaction
why_correct: Nausea and vomiting are predictable, dose-related side effects of codeine, not an immune-mediated allergy. Recording it accurately as an intolerance, with the nature of the reaction, keeps the information available to prescribers without wrongly excluding useful analgesics. Clear documentation of both drug and reaction type is part of safe prescribing.
why_wrong: A. Labelling this as an opioid allergy is inaccurate and could deny him effective post-operative pain relief. B. Even minor reactions should be documented so future prescribers can make informed choices. C. Vomiting alone is not anaphylaxis, and an overstated label is misleading. E. A side effect of one drug does not contraindicate a whole class.
pearl: When recording a drug reaction, document the drug, the reaction, its timing and severity, and whether it was allergic or a side effect, as recommended by NICE guidance on drug allergy.
thinking: Previous reaction to codeine ↓ Nausea and vomiting only ↓ No skin, airway or circulatory features ↓ Predictable side effect, not allergy ↓ Record as intolerance with details
exam_trap: C, As anaphylaxis to be cautious — over-labelling feels safe, but it is inaccurate and can block appropriate treatment later.
takeaway: Record side effects as intolerances, not allergies, and describe exactly what happened.

presentation: Yellow Card reporting of suspected adverse reactions
stem: A 30-year-old woman is admitted to the dermatology ward with widespread blistering, mucosal ulceration and skin peeling three weeks after starting lamotrigine for epilepsy.
