Waiting for toxicity means harm has already happened. E. New medicines are a common cause of toxicity or reduced effect in drugs of this kind.
pearl: Other drugs with a narrow therapeutic index include lithium, digoxin, warfarin, gentamicin, ciclosporin and theophylline.
thinking: Narrow therapeutic index drug ↓ Small gap between effective and toxic levels ↓ Interactions and dose changes shift levels ↓ Individualise dosing ↓ Monitor and check interactions
exam_trap: D, Checking levels only once toxicity appears — it may seem efficient, but the purpose of monitoring is to prevent toxicity, not confirm it.
takeaway: Narrow therapeutic index drugs need careful dosing, monitoring and vigilance for interactions.

presentation: Purpose of blood monitoring for a medicine
stem: A 30-year-old woman with schizophrenia that has not responded to two other antipsychotics is about to start clozapine in a community mental health clinic. She is told that she will need frequent blood tests and asks the doctor why. Which is the best explanation?

options.A: So that her prescription can be repeated without any review
options.B: Because blood tests are a legal requirement for all medicines
options.C: To detect harmful adverse effects early and make sure it remains safe to continue
options.D: To prevent side effects from developing in the first place
options.E: To confirm that the diagnosis of schizophrenia is correct

correct_answer: C. To detect harmful adverse effects early and make sure it remains safe to continue
why_correct: Some medicines can cause serious adverse effects that are silent at first. Clozapine can cause neutropenia and agranulocytosis, so regular full blood counts allow these to be detected before infection develops, and treatment stopped if needed. Monitoring therefore keeps treatment safe rather than preventing side effects altogether.
why_wrong: A. Monitoring is part of review, not a way of avoiding it. B. Most medicines do not need blood monitoring; it is required for specific drugs with particular risks. D. Monitoring detects side effects early but cannot stop them from occurring. E. Blood tests do not confirm a psychiatric diagnosis.
pearl: Clozapine needs full blood count monitoring weekly for the first 18 weeks, then less often, through a registered monitoring service.
thinking: Medicine with serious silent risks ↓ Blood tests can show harm before symptoms ↓ Early detection allows action ↓ Treatment continues only if safe ↓ Monitoring supports safety
exam_trap: D, Preventing side effects — it is tempting to think monitoring stops harm happening, but it only detects it early so action can be taken.
takeaway: Blood monitoring for a medicine detects adverse effects early so that treatment remains safe.

stem: A 55-year-old man on a cardiology ward is receiving his first dose of intravenous benzylpenicillin for suspected infective endocarditis. Within minutes he becomes breathless with an audible wheeze, flushed and clammy, and his blood pressure falls sharply. Which mechanism best explains this reaction?

options.A: Antibody-mediated destruction of cells (type II hypersensitivity)
options.D: Direct non-immune mast cell activation from a rapid infusion
options.E: IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation (type I hypersensitivity)

correct_answer: E. IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation (type I hypersensitivity)
why_correct: Wheeze, flushing and hypotension within minutes of penicillin are features of anaphylaxis. Previously formed IgE antibodies bound to mast cells and basophils are cross-linked by the drug, releasing histamine and other mediators that cause bronchospasm and vasodilatation. He needs immediate intramuscular adrenaline following Resuscitation Council UK guidance, and the allergy must be documented.
why_wrong: A. Type II reactions cause problems such as haemolytic anaemia, not immediate bronchospasm and shock. B. Type III reactions, such as serum sickness, occur days to weeks after exposure. C. Type IV reactions develop over days and usually cause rashes. D. Direct mast cell activation is typical of a rapid vancomycin infusion, whereas penicillin anaphylaxis is IgE-mediated.
pearl: Mast cell tryptase taken as soon as possible after anaphylaxis, with repeat samples, supports the diagnosis and referral to an allergy service.
thinking: IV penicillin given ↓ Wheeze and hypotension within minutes ↓ Anaphylaxis ↓ Drug cross-links IgE on mast cells ↓ Type I hypersensitivity
exam_trap: D, Direct mast cell activation — this is also rapid and causes flushing, but it is linked to fast vancomycin infusions, not penicillin, and is not IgE-mediated.
takeaway: Rapid anaphylaxis after penicillin is a type I, IgE-mediated hypersensitivity reaction.

presentation: Methotrexate toxicity with an interacting antibiotic
stem: A 49-year-old man with severe psoriasis takes weekly methotrexate. He phones the GP surgery one week after starting trimethoprim for a urinary infection, saying he has a temperature, painful ulcers inside his mouth and new bruises on his arms and legs. What is the most appropriate concern?

options.A: Possible methotrexate toxicity needing same-day assessment
options.B: Expected side effects that can wait for his next routine blood test
options.C: Folate deficiency needing a higher dose of folic acid
options.D: A viral illness that needs rest and paracetamol
options.E: Recurrent aphthous ulcers needing a steroid mouthwash

correct_answer: A. Possible methotrexate toxicity needing same-day assessment
why_correct: Fever, mouth ulcers and bruising in someone on methotrexate suggest bone marrow suppression and mucositis. Trimethoprim is an antifolate that increases methotrexate toxicity, which makes this more likely. He needs same-day assessment with an urgent full blood count, liver and renal function, methotrexate should be withheld, and the combination avoided in future.
why_wrong: B. These are warning signs of possible life-threatening toxicity, not side effects that can wait. C. Increasing folic acid alone would not address possible marrow failure. D. Fever on methotrexate must not be assumed to be viral until neutropenia is excluded. E. Isolated aphthous ulcers would not explain the fever and bruising.
pearl: Trimethoprim and co-trimoxazole should be avoided with methotrexate because their combined antifolate effect can cause severe bone marrow suppression.
thinking: Weekly methotrexate ↓ New trimethoprim ↓ Fever, mouth ulcers and bruising ↓ Suggests marrow suppression ↓ Withhold methotrexate and arrange urgent bloods
exam_trap: D, Viral illness — fever and mouth soreness can come with a virus, but on methotrexate they must prompt urgent exclusion of neutropenia.
takeaway: Fever, mouth ulcers or bruising on methotrexate need urgent assessment for toxicity.

stem: A 44-year-old man with schizophrenia is reviewed by his community psychiatric nurse six weeks after starting haloperidol. His partner says he has become slow to get going, his face looks expressionless and his hands shake when resting. He has no fever, confusion or muscle rigidity of sudden onset. Which category of adverse effect is most likely?
why_correct: Antipsychotics block dopamine D2 receptors in the nigrostriatal pathway, producing extrapyramidal side effects. Drug-induced parkinsonism, with bradykinesia, reduced facial expression and tremor, typically appears over weeks. It is more common with high-potency first-generation drugs such as haloperidol and is managed by reducing the dose or switching to an antipsychotic with lower risk.
why_wrong: A. Serotonin syndrome causes agitation, hyperthermia, clonus and autonomic instability after serotonergic drugs. B. Anticholinergic toxicity causes dry mouth, urinary retention, dilated pupils and confusion, not parkinsonism. C. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome causes fever, severe rigidity, altered consciousness and autonomic instability. D. Hyperprolactinaemia causes galactorrhoea and sexual dysfunction, not movement problems.
pearl: Extrapyramidal effects include acute dystonia (hours to days), akathisia and parkinsonism (weeks) and tardive dyskinesia (months to years).
thinking: Started haloperidol weeks ago ↓ Slowness, expressionless face, resting tremor ↓ No fever or confusion ↓ Dopamine blockade in the nigrostriatal pathway ↓ Extrapyramidal side effect
exam_trap: C, Neuroleptic malignant syndrome — it is the antipsychotic reaction people fear most, but without fever, severe rigidity or reduced consciousness it does not fit.
takeaway: Parkinsonian features on an antipsychotic are an extrapyramidal side effect.

stem: A 27-year-old woman used hyoscine hydrobromide patches for seasickness during a long ferry trip. The next day she attends a walk-in centre because her mouth is very dry, she cannot focus on her phone screen, she has not opened her bowels and she is struggling to pass urine. Which additional finding would be expected on examination?

options.A: Large pupils that react poorly to light

correct_answer: A. Large pupils that react poorly to light
why_correct: Hyoscine is an antimuscarinic drug, and blocking parasympathetic muscarinic receptors explains her dry mouth, blurred near vision, constipation and urinary retention. Loss of parasympathetic tone to the iris and ciliary muscle causes dilated, poorly reactive pupils and loss of accommodation. Tachycardia, warm dry skin and confusion may also occur.
why_wrong: B. Pinpoint pupils suggest opioid toxicity or cholinergic excess. C. Anticholinergic drugs typically cause tachycardia, not bradycardia. D. Salivation is reduced, not increased. E. Constipation, not diarrhoea, is expected.
pearl: A useful memory aid for anticholinergic toxicity is 'hot as a hare, dry as a bone, red as a beet, blind as a bat, mad as a hatter, full as a flask'.
thinking: Antimuscarinic drug used ↓ Dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, retention ↓ Parasympathetic blockade ↓ Iris sphincter relaxes ↓ Dilated pupils
exam_trap: B, Pinpoint pupils — pupil size is easy to mix up between toxidromes, but small pupils point to opioids or cholinergic excess, not anticholinergic effects.
takeaway: Anticholinergic effects include dilated pupils alongside dry mouth, constipation and urinary retention.

stem: An 81-year-old man with stage 3 chronic kidney disease lives in a care home and takes several regular medicines. A GP prescribes trimethoprim for a urinary tract infection. Trimethoprim reduces potassium excretion in the distal nephron in a similar way to amiloride. Which complication should be monitored for?
why_correct: Trimethoprim blocks epithelial sodium channels in the distal nephron, reducing potassium excretion in the same way as amiloride. In older people with chronic kidney disease, or those taking other potassium-raising medicines such as ACE inhibitors or spironolactone, this can cause clinically significant hyperkalaemia. Potassium and renal function should be checked, especially if the course is prolonged.
why_wrong: A. Trimethoprim does not raise calcium. B. Reduced potassium excretion raises, not lowers, potassium. C. Hypoglycaemia is not a typical effect of trimethoprim. E. Trimethoprim does not cause iron deficiency.
pearl: Common potassium-raising drugs include ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, spironolactone, amiloride, trimethoprim, NSAIDs and heparin.
thinking: Older man with CKD ↓ New drug that reduces renal potassium excretion ↓ Potassium accumulates ↓ Risk greater with other potassium-raising medicines ↓ Monitor for hyperkalaemia
exam_trap: B, Hypokalaemia — many diuretics cause potassium loss, but drugs acting like amiloride retain potassium instead.
takeaway: Drugs that reduce renal potassium excretion can cause hyperkalaemia, especially in chronic kidney disease.

presentation: Anticholinergic adverse effects in older people
stem: During a GP medication review, a 76-year-old woman who takes amitriptyline for neuropathic pain and recently started chlorphenamine for itching says her mouth feels like sandpaper, she has become constipated, her reading vision is blurred and she has to strain to pass urine. Which type of adverse drug effect best explains this combination?
why_correct: Amitriptyline and first-generation antihistamines such as chlorphenamine both block muscarinic receptors, and their effects add up. Dry mouth, constipation, blurred near vision and urinary hesitancy are classic antimuscarinic effects. Older people are especially sensitive and are also at risk of confusion and falls, so the total anticholinergic burden should be reviewed and reduced.
why_wrong: A. Serotonin syndrome causes agitation, sweating, tremor, clonus and hyperthermia. C. Excess cholinergic activity causes the opposite: salivation, diarrhoea, urinary frequency and small pupils. D. Opioid withdrawal causes diarrhoea, yawning, sweating and dilated pupils, and she is not taking an opioid. E. Lithium toxicity causes tremor, ataxia and gastrointestinal upset, and she is not taking lithium.
pearl: Tools such as the Anticholinergic Burden scale help identify older patients whose combined medicines put them at risk of confusion, falls and cognitive decline.
thinking: Older patient on several medicines ↓ Dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, urinary hesitancy ↓ Parasympathetic blockade ↓ Amitriptyline plus chlorphenamine add up ↓ Antimuscarinic effects
exam_trap: C, Excess cholinergic activity — the terms sound similar, but cholinergic excess causes wet, overactive features rather than dryness and retention.
takeaway: Dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision and urinary retention suggest antimuscarinic adverse effects, often from several drugs combined.

stem: A 63-year-old retired builder with severe hip osteoarthritis is awaiting joint replacement. Paracetamol alone has not controlled his pain, so his GP plans to keep him on naproxen. Over the past year he has had two bouts of heartburn and upper abdominal burning, both settling once the naproxen was paused. Which type of drug should be co-prescribed to protect his upper gut while he continues the anti-inflammatory?
why_correct: He needs to continue an NSAID despite previous NSAID-related dyspepsia, so gastroprotection is indicated. A proton pump inhibitor such as omeprazole or lansoprazole suppresses acid secretion by blocking the parietal cell H+/K+ ATPase and reduces the risk of NSAID-associated ulceration. NICE CKS advises offering a PPI to people at higher gastrointestinal risk who need ongoing NSAID treatment.
why_wrong: A. Calcium-channel blockers lower blood pressure and have no protective effect on the gastric mucosa. B. Oral bisphosphonates can themselves irritate the oesophagus and would add to his upper gut symptoms. C. Loop diuretics act on the kidney and do nothing to prevent acid-related injury. E. Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors increase cholinergic activity and can actually increase gastric acid secretion.
pearl: When an NSAID is unavoidable, use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time and co-prescribe a PPI, especially in older people or those with previous dyspepsia or ulcer.
thinking: Ongoing NSAID is needed for pain ↓ Previous NSAID-related dyspepsia means higher GI risk ↓ Gastroprotection is indicated ↓ Acid suppression is the protective strategy ↓ Co-prescribe a proton pump inhibitor
exam_trap: E, Oral acetylcholinesterase inhibitor — the name can be confused with drugs that reduce acid, but these cholinergic agents (such as donepezil) tend to increase acid secretion and offer no mucosal protection.
takeaway: A patient who must stay on an NSAID after NSAID-related dyspepsia should be co-prescribed a proton pump inhibitor.

stem: A 29-year-old woman with trigeminal neuralgia was started on carbamazepine by her neurologist six weeks ago. Her partner brings her to the emergency department because she has been vomiting, has a dull headache and seems muddled. She looks well hydrated, with no oedema, normal skin turgor and no postural drop. Blood tests show a sodium of 121 mmol/L with low plasma osmolality, while her urine is concentrated with a high urinary sodium. Thyroid function and a 9am cortisol are normal and she takes no other regular medicines. What is the most likely cause of her low sodium?

options.A: Excessive water drinking from primary polydipsia
options.C: Renal salt wasting from diuretic use
options.D: Inappropriate antidiuretic hormone effect caused by carbamazepine

correct_answer: D. Inappropriate antidiuretic hormone effect caused by carbamazepine
why_correct: She is euvolaemic with hypotonic hyponatraemia, inappropriately concentrated urine and a high urinary sodium, which is the pattern of SIADH. Thyroid and adrenal causes have been excluded and she takes no diuretic. Carbamazepine enhances ADH release and increases renal sensitivity to it, so the timing after starting the drug points to a drug-induced SIADH-like state.
why_wrong: A. Primary polydipsia produces maximally dilute urine, not concentrated urine. B. Hypothyroidism can impair water excretion but her thyroid function is normal. C. Diuretic-related sodium loss needs diuretic exposure and usually causes hypovolaemia, neither of which is present. E. Adrenal insufficiency is excluded by a normal morning cortisol and would not be caused by carbamazepine.
pearl: Carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine are classic drug causes of SIADH, alongside SSRIs, tricyclics, antipsychotics, opioids and some chemotherapy agents such as cyclophosphamide and vincristine.
thinking: New carbamazepine then vomiting and confusion ↓ Low sodium with low plasma osmolality ↓ Clinically euvolaemic with concentrated urine and high urinary sodium ↓ Thyroid, cortisol and diuretic causes excluded ↓ Drug-induced SIADH
exam_trap: A, Excessive water drinking from primary polydipsia — it also causes euvolaemic hyponatraemia, but the kidneys respond by producing very dilute urine, whereas here the urine is concentrated.
takeaway: Euvolaemic hyponatraemia with concentrated urine in someone recently started on carbamazepine is a drug-induced SIADH picture.

stem: Staff at a residential home call the out-of-hours GP because Margaret, aged 88, has become drowsy and disorientated over two days and fell in her room this morning. Three months ago her blood pressure tablets were changed by adding indapamide to her amlodipine; she also has a statin, four-times-daily paracetamol for back pain and a reliever inhaler for asthma. Hospital bloods after transfer reveal profound hyponatraemia. Which drug on her chart is the likeliest culprit?
why_correct: Indapamide is a thiazide-like diuretic, and thiazides are among the commonest drug causes of hyponatraemia. They act in the distal convoluted tubule, where they block sodium reabsorption and impair the kidney's ability to dilute urine. Older, low-weight women are especially susceptible, and confusion, drowsiness and falls are typical presentations.
why_wrong: A. Amlodipine typically causes ankle swelling and flushing rather than hyponatraemia. B. Paracetamol at normal doses does not lower sodium. C. Salbutamol can shift potassium into cells but does not cause marked hyponatraemia. E. Atorvastatin is linked with muscle aches and raised liver enzymes, not low sodium.
pearl: Thiazide-induced hyponatraemia can appear weeks to months after starting the drug, so a long-standing prescription does not exclude it; check sodium and potassium after starting and periodically thereafter.
thinking: Older woman with confusion and a fall ↓ Severe hyponatraemia on bloods ↓ Scan medication list for sodium-lowering drugs ↓ Indapamide is a thiazide-like diuretic ↓ Thiazides impair urinary dilution and cause hyponatraemia
exam_trap: A, Amlodipine — it is a common blood pressure drug in older people and causes side effects such as oedema, but it is not a recognised cause of significant hyponatraemia.
takeaway: In an older woman with hyponatraemia, a thiazide or thiazide-like diuretic such as indapamide is a prime suspect.

stem: A 55-year-old woman with long-standing reflux attends the practice nurse complaining of painful cramps in her calves and hands, and occasional tingling around her mouth. Routine bloods show a low magnesium and a borderline low calcium. She has taken the same regular tablets for several years: lansoprazole daily, ramipril, levothyroxine and vitamin D, plus a moisturising cream. Which medicine is the most likely cause of the magnesium result?
why_correct: Long-term proton pump inhibitor use can reduce intestinal magnesium absorption and cause hypomagnesaemia, which is highlighted by the MHRA and BNF. Low magnesium causes cramps, paraesthesia and tetany, and it also impairs parathyroid hormone release, which explains her low-normal calcium. Lansoprazole taken for several years is therefore the likeliest culprit.
why_wrong: A. Levothyroxine at replacement doses does not lower serum magnesium. C. Ramipril is more likely to raise potassium than to lower magnesium. D. A topical moisturiser has no systemic effect on electrolytes. E. Vitamin D does not cause hypomagnesaemia and would tend to raise calcium.
pearl: Hypomagnesaemia can cause refractory hypocalcaemia and hypokalaemia, which will not correct until the magnesium is replaced.
thinking: Cramps and perioral tingling ↓ Low magnesium with borderline low calcium ↓ Look for drugs that reduce magnesium ↓ Long-term proton pump inhibitor use ↓ Lansoprazole is the likely cause
exam_trap: C, Ramipril — ACE inhibitors are frequently linked with electrolyte disturbances, but their typical effect is a raised potassium, not a low magnesium.
takeaway: Long-term proton pump inhibitors are a recognised cause of hypomagnesaemia, which can present with cramps and tetany.

presentation: Acute hyperkalaemia on an ACE inhibitor
stem: A 76-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by ambulance with generalised weakness after a three-day bout of diarrhoea. She takes ramipril for hypertension. The point-of-care blood gas shows a potassium well above the normal range and her urine output has been low. What is the most appropriate approach at this stage?

options.A: Record a 12-lead ECG, assess severity and the cause, and review her medicines including ramipril
options.B: Give oral potassium chloride to stabilise the level
options.C: Double the ramipril dose to protect her kidney perfusion
options.E: Send her home and repeat bloods at her next routine GP check

correct_answer: A. Record a 12-lead ECG, assess severity and the cause, and review her medicines including ramipril
why_correct: Hyperkalaemia on an ACE inhibitor needs prompt assessment of severity, and an ECG is essential because cardiac toxicity determines urgency and the need for calcium to stabilise the myocardium. The cause must then be identified: dehydration from diarrhoea has probably caused acute kidney injury, compounded by the ACE inhibitor. Ramipril should be withheld while she is unwell, in line with NICE guidance on acute kidney injury and sick day rules.
why_wrong: B. Potassium supplements would make the hyperkalaemia worse. C. Increasing the ACE inhibitor would further reduce aldosterone and raise potassium. D. Spironolactone is a potassium-sparing aldosterone antagonist and would worsen it. E. Significant hyperkalaemia can cause fatal arrhythmias and needs immediate assessment, not routine follow-up.
pearl: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, diuretics, NSAIDs and metformin should be temporarily stopped during dehydrating illness such as vomiting or diarrhoea, then restarted once eating and drinking normally.
thinking: Weakness after diarrhoea in a patient on ramipril ↓ High potassium and low urine output ↓ Check the ECG to judge cardiac risk ↓ Identify cause: likely AKI plus ACE inhibitor ↓ Treat according to severity and withhold the ACE inhibitor
exam_trap: E, Repeat bloods at a routine GP check — this may seem proportionate if she looks stable, but hyperkalaemia can trigger arrhythmia without warning and needs same-day assessment.
takeaway: Hyperkalaemia on an ACE inhibitor needs an ECG, assessment of severity and cause, and a review of the drug.

stem: A 67-year-old man attends his hypertension follow-up six weeks after bendroflumethiazide was added to his treatment. He reports mild nausea and some trouble concentrating at work. His blood tests show a sodium that has fallen well below his previous normal result. His other medicines are colecalciferol, an emollient cream for eczema, an alginate antacid as needed and a salbutamol inhaler. Which of his medicines is most likely to explain the blood result?
why_correct: Thiazide diuretics such as bendroflumethiazide are a well recognised cause of hyponatraemia. By blocking sodium chloride reabsorption in the distal tubule they impair the kidney's diluting capacity, so water is retained relative to sodium. The timing after starting the drug and the symptoms of nausea and poor concentration fit this picture.
why_wrong: A. A topical emollient has no systemic effect on sodium. B. Colecalciferol in excess can raise calcium but does not cause hyponatraemia. C. Alginate antacids contain some sodium and do not lower serum sodium. D. Salbutamol may lower potassium but is not a cause of marked hyponatraemia.
pearl: Thiazides cause several metabolic effects: hyponatraemia, hypokalaemia, hypercalcaemia, hyperuricaemia with gout and impaired glucose tolerance.
thinking: New antihypertensive added recently ↓ Nausea and poor concentration ↓ Sodium has fallen ↓ Bendroflumethiazide is a thiazide ↓ Thiazides cause hyponatraemia
exam_trap: C, Alginate antacid — gut medicines can seem linked to electrolyte problems, but alginates contain sodium and do not cause hyponatraemia.
takeaway: Check sodium after starting a thiazide, as these drugs are a common cause of hyponatraemia.

stem: A 72-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has taken naproxen most days for years. She is referred for gastroscopy after weeks of gnawing upper abdominal pain, and a benign gastric ulcer is found. She asks the endoscopist why her tablets have caused this. Which mechanism best explains NSAID-related ulceration?

options.A: Loss of prostaglandin-dependent protection of the stomach lining
options.B: Increased secretion of protective gastric mucus
options.C: Reduced acid production as the main cause of injury
options.D: Greater bile output from the liver

correct_answer: A. Loss of prostaglandin-dependent protection of the stomach lining
why_correct: NSAIDs inhibit cyclo-oxygenase, especially COX-1, which reduces prostaglandin synthesis in the gastric mucosa. These prostaglandins normally maintain mucus and bicarbonate secretion and mucosal blood flow, so their loss leaves the lining vulnerable to acid and pepsin. Older age and long-term use, as here, add to the risk.
why_wrong: B. NSAIDs reduce, rather than increase, mucus and bicarbonate secretion. C. NSAIDs do not mainly act by reducing acid; prostaglandin loss tends to increase acid exposure. D. Bile output is not the mechanism of NSAID-induced gastric injury. E. Insulin release is irrelevant to ulcer formation.
pearl: Selective COX-2 inhibitors cause fewer ulcers than traditional NSAIDs but carry a higher cardiovascular risk, so they do not remove the need for careful risk assessment.
thinking: Long-term naproxen ↓ Benign gastric ulcer at endoscopy ↓ NSAIDs inhibit COX-1 ↓ Less mucosal prostaglandin ↓ Less mucus, bicarbonate and blood flow, so ulceration
exam_trap: C, Reduced acid production — it sounds pharmacological and plausible, but NSAIDs do not mainly change acid; they remove the prostaglandins that protect the mucosa.
takeaway: NSAIDs cause ulcers by blocking COX and removing prostaglandin-mediated mucosal protection.

stem: A 41-year-old woman training for a marathon has taken ibuprofen at the maximum over-the-counter dose for about two months for a sore Achilles tendon. She now sees her GP with a burning pain high in the abdomen, waking her at night and eased by eating. She has no weight loss or difficulty swallowing. Which complication of her analgesic use is the most likely explanation?
why_correct: Prolonged regular ibuprofen inhibits prostaglandin synthesis and weakens gastric and duodenal mucosal defences. Night-time burning epigastric pain relieved by food is typical of duodenal ulceration. Peptic ulcer disease is the classic gastrointestinal complication of NSAID use.
why_wrong: A. Gallstones cause right upper quadrant colicky pain, often after fatty meals, and are not caused by NSAIDs. C. Achalasia causes progressive difficulty swallowing and is unrelated to NSAIDs. D. MALT lymphoma is associated with H. pylori infection, not NSAIDs. E. Acute pancreatitis causes severe constant pain radiating to the back and is not a typical NSAID effect.
pearl: Test for H. pylori in NSAID users with ulcer disease: the two risk factors add together, and eradication reduces recurrence.
thinking: Regular high-dose ibuprofen for weeks ↓ Burning epigastric pain at night, eased by food ↓ No alarm features ↓ NSAIDs damage gastroduodenal mucosa ↓ Peptic ulcer disease
exam_trap: E, Acute pancreatitis — it also causes epigastric pain, but it is usually severe, constant and radiates to the back, and it is not a characteristic NSAID complication.
takeaway: Regular NSAID use is a leading cause of peptic ulcer disease.

stem: At a community pharmacy, a 66-year-old woman who takes low-dose aspirin after a minor stroke asks for something stronger for her painful knee. She has had indigestion in the past. The pharmacist considers which medicines would add most to her risk of stomach or duodenal ulceration if taken regularly. Which of the following carries that risk?

options.B: An oral NSAID such as naproxen

correct_answer: B. An oral NSAID such as naproxen
why_correct: Oral NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandin production and increase the risk of gastric and duodenal ulceration and bleeding. Combining them with aspirin, as she already takes, multiplies that risk, and her age and previous dyspepsia add to it. Paracetamol or a topical NSAID would be safer first choices for her knee pain.
why_wrong: A. Paracetamol does not damage the gastric mucosa at normal doses. C. Loratadine is a non-sedating antihistamine without ulcer risk. D. Amoxicillin can cause diarrhoea but not peptic ulceration. E. Salbutamol is a bronchodilator and does not cause ulcers.
pearl: Topical NSAIDs are recommended before oral NSAIDs for knee and hand osteoarthritis because systemic absorption, and therefore gastrointestinal risk, is much lower.
thinking: Older woman on aspirin ↓ Previous indigestion ↓ Wants stronger analgesia ↓ Oral NSAIDs reduce mucosal prostaglandins ↓ NSAID plus aspirin raises ulcer and bleeding risk
exam_trap: D, Amoxicillin — it is used in H. pylori eradication, which may make it seem linked to ulcers, but it treats rather than causes peptic ulceration.
takeaway: Adding an oral NSAID to aspirin in an older person markedly raises the risk of peptic ulceration.

stem: A 64-year-old woman on warfarin after a pulmonary embolism telephones the anticoagulation clinic. Over the past few days she has had several nosebleeds that take a long time to stop and her gums bleed when she brushes her teeth. Ten days ago her GP prescribed clarithromycin for a chest infection. Which medicine-related factor is most likely to explain her bleeding?

options.B: Excessive anticoagulation from an enhanced warfarin effect
options.E: Nasal dryness from the chest infection

correct_answer: B. Excessive anticoagulation from an enhanced warfarin effect
why_correct: Clarithromycin inhibits CYP3A4 and reduces warfarin metabolism, so the warfarin effect and INR rise. Over-anticoagulation causes mucosal bleeding such as prolonged nosebleeds and gum bleeding. Her INR should be checked promptly and the dose adjusted or reversed according to the result and severity of bleeding.
why_wrong: A. Clarithromycin is not a typical cause of thrombocytopenia; the key effect is a drug interaction with warfarin. C. Vitamin B12 deficiency does not increase anticoagulation. D. Hypothyroidism alone does not explain bleeding on warfarin and, if anything, reduces warfarin sensitivity. E. Local dryness might cause a single minor nosebleed but not repeated prolonged bleeding with gum bleeding.
pearl: Common enzyme inhibitors that raise the INR include macrolides, fluconazole, metronidazole, amiodarone and ciprofloxacin; always check the INR soon after starting or stopping an interacting drug.
thinking: On warfarin ↓ New antibiotic started ↓ Several sites of mucosal bleeding ↓ Clarithromycin inhibits warfarin metabolism ↓ Excessive anticoagulation
exam_trap: E, Nasal dryness from the infection — local causes are common for a single nosebleed, but repeated prolonged bleeding with gum bleeding in someone on warfarin points to a raised INR.
takeaway: New bleeding in a patient on warfarin should prompt a search for over-anticoagulation, often from a drug interaction.

stem: During a telephone review in a nurse-led hypertension clinic, a 61-year-old man mentions that since bendroflumethiazide was started two months ago he has had trouble getting and keeping an erection. He is embarrassed and wonders if the tablet could really be to blame. Which statement is most accurate to share with him?

options.A: A number of medicines, including some blood pressure tablets, can contribute to erectile problems
options.B: Tablets cannot affect erections, so the cause must lie elsewhere
options.D: Erectile problems at his age are always psychological
options.E: New erectile problems mean a cancer must be excluded first

correct_answer: A. A number of medicines, including some blood pressure tablets, can contribute to erectile problems
why_correct: Several drug classes can contribute to erectile dysfunction, including thiazide diuretics, beta-blockers, antidepressants, antipsychotics, 5-alpha reductase inhibitors and opioids. The timing after starting bendroflumethiazide makes the drug a plausible contributor, so a medication history is a key part of assessment. Other causes, especially cardiovascular risk and diabetes, should still be considered.
why_wrong: B. Medicines are a well recognised cause of erectile dysfunction. C. Hypogonadism is only one of many causes and is not confirmed by symptoms alone. D. Psychological factors can contribute, but organic and drug causes are common at his age. E. Erectile dysfunction on its own is not a sign of cancer.
pearl: Erectile dysfunction can be an early marker of cardiovascular disease, so assess blood pressure, lipids, glucose or HbA1c and overall cardiovascular risk.
thinking: New erectile dysfunction ↓ Started a thiazide two months earlier ↓ Thiazides are a recognised drug cause ↓ Medicines can contribute ↓ Explain this and review treatment options
exam_trap: D, Always psychological — embarrassment and stress may seem to fit, but organic and drug-related causes are common and must not be dismissed.
takeaway: Always take a medication history in erectile dysfunction, as several common drugs can contribute.

stem: A 34-year-old man attends a sexual health clinic worried about difficulty maintaining erections and delayed ejaculation. He has a regular partner, no new sexual contacts and no genital symptoms. His GP started sertraline for generalised anxiety eight weeks ago, and the problems began a few weeks later. What should be a central part of his assessment?

options.A: Urgent PSA test and suspected cancer referral
options.B: Scrotal ultrasound to look for a testicular tumour
options.C: Prescribe sildenafil and leave his other treatment unchanged
options.D: Refer for psychosexual therapy as the first step
options.E: Review his current medicines for adverse effects

correct_answer: E. Review his current medicines for adverse effects
why_correct: SSRIs such as sertraline commonly cause sexual dysfunction, including erectile difficulty, reduced libido and delayed ejaculation. The onset weeks after starting the drug makes it the likely cause, so a medication review is central. Options may include discussing a dose change or alternative with his GP rather than simply adding another drug.
why_wrong: A. Erectile dysfunction in a young man is not a feature of prostate cancer and does not need PSA testing. B. A testicular tumour is not suggested by these symptoms. C. Treating the symptom without addressing the probable cause is not the best first step. D. Psychological factors may play a part, but the new medicine should be reviewed before assuming a psychological cause.
pearl: SSRI-related sexual dysfunction is common and under-reported, so ask about it directly when reviewing antidepressants.
thinking: Young man with new erectile difficulty ↓ Also delayed ejaculation ↓ Sertraline started shortly before ↓ SSRIs commonly cause sexual side effects ↓ Review his medicines
exam_trap: D, Psychosexual therapy first — his anxiety makes a psychological cause tempting, but the new sertraline is a likely and reversible cause that should be reviewed first.
takeaway: In new erectile dysfunction, review current medicines for adverse effects before assuming another cause.

stem: An 80-year-old man who takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation is brought to the emergency department after tripping at home. A cut on his shin keeps oozing despite pressure, and his INR is far above his target range. He is alert, with stable observations. What should be done first?

options.A: Continue warfarin and recheck the INR next week
options.B: Dress the wound and leave the warfarin dose unchanged
options.C: Switch to a direct oral anticoagulant and discharge
options.D: Give tranexamic acid and continue warfarin as before
options.E: Assess the severity of bleeding and correct the over-anticoagulation

correct_answer: E. Assess the severity of bleeding and correct the over-anticoagulation
why_correct: Active bleeding with a markedly raised INR needs assessment of how severe the bleed is, followed by correction of anticoagulation. For minor bleeding this usually means withholding warfarin and giving intravenous vitamin K, while major bleeding requires prothrombin complex concentrate as well. The reason for the high INR, such as interacting drugs or illness, should also be sought.
why_wrong: A. Continuing warfarin with a very high INR and active bleeding risks further haemorrhage. B. Local treatment helps the wound but leaves the dangerous INR uncorrected. C. Switching drug does nothing about the current excess warfarin effect. D. Tranexamic acid does not reverse warfarin, and continuing the same dose is unsafe.
pearl: Vitamin K takes several hours to work; prothrombin complex concentrate gives immediate reversal and is used with vitamin K for major bleeding.
thinking: On warfarin with persistent bleeding ↓ INR well above target ↓ Judge whether the bleed is minor or major ↓ Withhold warfarin and reverse with vitamin K, adding PCC if major ↓ Find the cause of the high INR
exam_trap: B, Dress the wound and continue warfarin — local measures seem enough for a skin wound, but the underlying excessive anticoagulation is the real problem and must be corrected.
takeaway: Bleeding with a high INR means assess severity and reverse the anticoagulation accordingly.

stem: A 69-year-old man of Black African family background is brought to the emergency department by his daughter because his lips and tongue have swollen over the last hour and his voice sounds thick. There is no rash or itch. Two weeks ago his GP started ramipril for high blood pressure. Which drug adverse effect is most likely?
why_correct: ACE inhibitors reduce breakdown of bradykinin, which can cause non-itchy, non-urticarial swelling of the lips, tongue and upper airway. People of Black African or African-Caribbean origin have a higher risk. A change in voice suggests airway involvement, so the airway must be assessed urgently and the ACE inhibitor stopped permanently.
why_wrong: A. Acute dystonia causes involuntary muscle spasms, often after antiemetics or antipsychotics, not soft tissue swelling. C. Stevens-Johnson syndrome causes mucosal ulceration and a blistering rash over days. D. Serotonin toxicity causes agitation, clonus and autonomic instability. E. Hypocalcaemia causes perioral tingling and carpopedal spasm, not swelling.
pearl: ACE inhibitor angioedema is bradykinin-mediated, so it responds poorly to antihistamines and corticosteroids; airway protection is the priority.
thinking: Recently started ramipril ↓ Rapid lip and tongue swelling ↓ No urticaria or itch ↓ Higher risk in Black African family background ↓ ACE inhibitor angioedema
exam_trap: C, Stevens-Johnson syndrome — it involves the lips and mouth, but it causes mucosal erosions and skin blistering over days, not sudden swelling.
takeaway: Sudden lip and tongue swelling without urticaria in someone on an ACE inhibitor is angioedema until proven otherwise.

stem: A 45-year-old woman sees her GP with a fourth episode in six months of puffy swelling of her eyelids and cheek that lasts a day or two and then resolves. The swelling is not itchy and she has had no rash, fever or redness. She has taken lisinopril for three years without problems and has no personal or family history of similar swelling. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Recurrent, self-limiting, non-itchy facial swelling without urticaria is typical of bradykinin-mediated angioedema. ACE inhibitor angioedema can start months or years after the drug was begun, which often delays recognition. Lisinopril should be stopped and not replaced by another ACE inhibitor.
why_wrong: A. Cellulitis causes a red, warm, tender area with fever and does not come and go repeatedly. C. Contact dermatitis produces an itchy, eczematous rash at the site of contact. D. Rosacea causes persistent facial flushing, papules and pustules rather than episodic swelling. E. SVC obstruction causes persistent facial swelling with dilated chest veins and breathlessness, not resolving episodes.
pearl: Angioedema on an ACE inhibitor can occur for the first time after years of uneventful treatment, so a long history of use does not exclude the drug.
thinking: Recurrent episodic facial swelling ↓ No itch, rash or fever ↓ Long-term ACE inhibitor ↓ Angioedema can begin years after starting ↓ ACE inhibitor-induced angioedema
exam_trap: A, Facial cellulitis — facial swelling suggests infection, but there is no redness, heat or fever and the swelling resolves and recurs.
takeaway: Recurrent non-itchy facial swelling in someone on an ACE inhibitor suggests angioedema, even after years of use.

stem: A 77-year-old man with diabetes is seen on a GP home visit after falling twice in his kitchen. He describes feeling light-headed and unsteady over the past fortnight. Two weeks ago he started amitriptyline at night for painful neuropathy, in addition to his usual metformin, amlodipine, ramipril and atorvastatin. He has no injuries. What is the most appropriate initial approach?

options.A: Review all his medicines for adverse effects and interactions
options.B: Stop all his regular tablets permanently
options.C: Assume the falls were accidental and take no further action
options.D: Advise him to limit his fluid intake
options.E: Add betahistine to treat his dizziness

correct_answer: A. Review all his medicines for adverse effects and interactions
why_correct: Falls in an older person taking several medicines, especially just after a new drug, should prompt a structured medication review. Amitriptyline causes sedation and postural hypotension through alpha-blockade and anticholinergic effects, and these combine with his antihypertensives. The review should include lying and standing blood pressure and consider stopping or reducing the most likely culprits.
why_wrong: B. Stopping all medicines abruptly could cause harm from uncontrolled diabetes or blood pressure. C. Repeated falls with dizziness need assessment, not assumption. D. Restricting fluids would worsen postural hypotension. E. Adding betahistine treats a symptom without addressing the likely drug cause and increases polypharmacy.
pearl: Drugs commonly linked to falls include antihypertensives, sedatives, antidepressants, antipsychotics, opioids and anticholinergics; tools such as STOPP/START help identify them.
thinking: Older man with repeated falls ↓ Light-headedness after a new drug ↓ Amitriptyline causes sedation and postural hypotension ↓ Already on two antihypertensives ↓ Review the whole medication list
exam_trap: E, Add betahistine — it targets the dizziness directly, but it is a prescribing cascade that ignores the likely medication cause.
takeaway: Falls after a new medicine in an older person call for a full medication review.

stem: On an orthogeriatric ward, an 86-year-old woman is recovering from a hip fracture sustained in a fall at home. She had been feeling faint on getting out of bed for several weeks. Her regular medicines are ramipril, amlodipine, furosemide, doxazosin and zopiclone at night, and the nurses record a significant drop in blood pressure on standing. What is the most appropriate first step?

options.A: Review her medicines for adverse effects and interactions
options.B: Start fludrocortisone to raise her standing blood pressure
options.C: Refer her to the falls clinic and leave her medicines unchanged
options.D: Add a second hypnotic to improve her sleep
options.E: Stop every blood pressure tablet immediately

correct_answer: A. Review her medicines for adverse effects and interactions
why_correct: She has postural hypotension and is taking several drugs that lower blood pressure, plus a hypnotic that increases falls risk. A structured medication review, ideally with a pharmacist, can identify which drugs to reduce or stop. This is the first step in NICE falls guidance and is more appropriate than adding drugs or making abrupt changes.
why_wrong: B. Adding fludrocortisone to counter the effects of other drugs worsens polypharmacy and can cause fluid overload. C. Falls services are valuable but contributing medicines should be addressed now. D. Hypnotics increase falls risk and should be reduced, not added. E. Stopping all antihypertensives at once without assessment may cause rebound hypertension or heart failure.
pearl: Alpha-blockers such as doxazosin are a common and easily overlooked cause of postural hypotension in older people.
thinking: Fall with hip fracture ↓ Faintness on standing and postural drop ↓ Several blood pressure lowering drugs plus a hypnotic ↓ Medicines likely contributing ↓ Structured medication review
exam_trap: E, Stop every blood pressure tablet — it addresses the postural drop, but abrupt wholesale withdrawal without assessment can cause harm; review and rationalise instead.
takeaway: In recurrent falls with postural hypotension, review medicines for adverse effects and interactions before adding anything new.

stem: On a surgical ward at night, a foundation doctor is asked to prescribe 500 mL of compound sodium lactate to run over 4 hours for a woman who is nil by mouth before an operation in the morning. The volumetric pump needs a rate in millilitres per hour. What rate should be set?
why_correct: Infusion rate equals volume divided by time. Dividing 500 mL by 4 hours gives 125 mL/hour. Setting the pump to this rate delivers the full volume in the prescribed time.
why_wrong: B. 100 mL/hour would give only 400 mL in 4 hours. C. 83 mL/hour corresponds to 500 mL over 6 hours. D. 167 mL/hour corresponds to 500 mL over 3 hours. E. 250 mL/hour would finish the bag in 2 hours, twice the intended rate.
pearl: For gravity-fed giving sets, drops per minute equals volume in mL multiplied by the drop factor, divided by time in minutes.
thinking: Identify the volume: 500 mL ↓ Identify the time: 4 hours ↓ Rate equals volume divided by time ↓ 500 divided by 4 ↓ 125 mL/hour
exam_trap: E, 250 mL/hour — this comes from halving the volume instead of dividing it by the number of hours, and would run the fluid in at double speed.
takeaway: Infusion rate in mL/hour equals total volume divided by the time in hours.

stem: A 58-year-old man is admitted to the medical ward with pneumonia and is too drowsy and breathless to drink reliably. A junior doctor is asked to write up his intravenous fluids for the next 24 hours. He has known chronic kidney disease and is taking furosemide. Which approach to prescribing his fluids is most appropriate?

options.A: Give 3 litres of 0.9% sodium chloride a day as a standard regimen
options.B: Use Hartmann's solution regardless of his kidney function
options.C: Start intravenous fluids only once oral intake falls below 1 litre a day
options.D: Keep the same regimen running until he is discharged
options.E: Assess his fluid status, electrolytes and losses, then prescribe and reassess regularly

correct_answer: E. Assess his fluid status, electrolytes and losses, then prescribe and reassess regularly
why_correct: NICE guidance on intravenous fluids in adults sets out a cycle: assess fluid status and needs, decide whether fluids are for resuscitation, routine maintenance or replacement of losses, prescribe accordingly, and reassess at least daily. His chronic kidney disease and diuretic make individual assessment of volume status and electrolytes especially important. Fluids should be stopped once he can drink adequately.
why_wrong: A. A fixed volume of saline ignores individual needs and risks overload and hyperchloraemic acidosis. B. Fluid choice should take into account his electrolytes and renal function. C. Fluids are given according to clinical need and assessment, not a fixed intake trigger. D. Fluid prescriptions must be reviewed regularly and stopped when no longer needed.
pearl: Routine maintenance in adults starts at about 25 to 30 mL/kg/day of water with roughly 1 mmol/kg/day each of sodium, potassium and chloride, and 50 to 100 g/day of glucose, adjusted to the individual.
thinking: Unable to drink safely ↓ Comorbid kidney disease and diuretic use ↓ Assess volume status, electrolytes and losses ↓ Choose resuscitation, maintenance or replacement ↓ Prescribe and reassess regularly
exam_trap: A, 3 litres of saline a day — a standard regimen feels safe and simple, but it ignores individual needs and can cause overload and electrolyte problems.
takeaway: Intravenous fluids should follow assessment, a tailored prescription and regular reassessment.

stem: A 66-year-old man with stable angina returns to his GP two weeks after being given a glyceryl trinitrate spray. He says it relieves his chest tightness within minutes, but each time he uses it he gets a throbbing headache and feels flushed. He has no other neurological symptoms and is otherwise well. What is the most likely explanation for the headache?
correct_answer: C. Vasodilation caused by the nitrate
why_correct: Glyceryl trinitrate releases nitric oxide and causes vasodilation, including of the meningeal and cerebral vessels, which produces a throbbing headache and flushing. This is a common, predictable and usually benign adverse effect that often lessens with continued use. He can be advised to sit down when using the spray, as dizziness and postural hypotension can also occur.
why_wrong: A. Raised intracranial pressure causes persistent, worsening headache with vomiting or visual change, not brief headaches after each dose. B. Hypoglycaemia causes sweating, tremor and confusion, and has no link with nitrate use. D. Meningitis causes fever, neck stiffness and illness, not a headache timed with each spray. E. Iron deficiency causes tiredness and breathlessness, not headache immediately after a dose.
pearl: Nitrates must not be combined with phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors such as sildenafil because of the risk of profound hypotension.
thinking: Headache after each GTN dose ↓ Accompanied by flushing ↓ Nitrates release nitric oxide ↓ Vasodilation of cranial vessels ↓ Benign expected adverse effect
exam_trap: A, Raised intracranial pressure — a repeated throbbing headache can raise concern, but the clear timing with each dose and lack of other features point to simple vasodilation.
takeaway: Headache and flushing after GTN are expected effects of vasodilation, not a warning sign.

stem: A 24-year-old rugby player is brought to the emergency department after vomiting bright red blood. He injured his shoulder a month ago and has been taking high-dose ibuprofen bought from several shops, often on an empty stomach. For the last week he has had burning upper abdominal pain. Which drug effect best explains his bleeding?

options.B: Damage to the gastrointestinal mucosa associated with NSAIDs
options.E: Reduced gastric acid output as the main effect

correct_answer: B. Damage to the gastrointestinal mucosa associated with NSAIDs
why_correct: NSAIDs such as ibuprofen inhibit cyclo-oxygenase, reducing prostaglandins that protect the gastric and duodenal mucosa, and they also impair platelet function. High doses taken on an empty stomach increase the risk of erosions and ulceration, which can bleed. His preceding epigastric pain followed by haematemesis fits NSAID-associated mucosal injury.
why_wrong: A. NSAIDs reduce rather than increase protective mucus. C. NSAIDs impair platelet function and do not raise platelet numbers. D. Calcium absorption is unrelated to upper gastrointestinal bleeding. E. NSAIDs do not mainly act by reducing acid; mucosal defence is lost.
pearl: The Glasgow-Blatchford score helps identify patients with upper gastrointestinal bleeding who may be safely managed without admission.
thinking: High-dose ibuprofen for weeks ↓ Epigastric pain then haematemesis ↓ NSAIDs remove protective prostaglandins ↓ Mucosal erosion and ulceration ↓ NSAID-associated mucosal injury causing bleeding
exam_trap: E, Reduced gastric acid output — it sounds like a drug effect, but less acid would protect rather than injure the mucosa, and this is not how NSAIDs work.
takeaway: NSAIDs cause upper GI bleeding through loss of prostaglandin-mediated mucosal protection.

stem: A 64-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation is taken to resus after vomiting a large amount of blood. She is pale and tachycardic. Her husband says she takes apixaban and took her last dose this morning. Her first haemoglobin is within the normal range. Which statement about her anticoagulant is correct?

options.A: Protamine sulfate is the reversal agent of choice
options.B: Vitamin K will quickly reverse its effect
options.C: The INR reliably reflects how anticoagulated she is
options.D: Apixaban can be continued because her haemoglobin is normal
options.E: Apixaban must be withheld and reviewed urgently as part of managing the bleed

correct_answer: E. Apixaban must be withheld and reviewed urgently as part of managing the bleed
why_correct: Major bleeding in a patient on a direct oral anticoagulant requires resuscitation, withholding the drug and urgent review of anticoagulant exposure, including timing of the last dose and renal function. Specific reversal with andexanet alfa or, if unavailable, prothrombin complex concentrate may be considered for life-threatening bleeding. Her pallor and tachycardia indicate significant blood loss despite the normal initial haemoglobin.
why_wrong: A. Protamine reverses heparin and has no effect on apixaban. B. Apixaban is a factor Xa inhibitor and does not act through vitamin K. C. The INR is not a reliable measure of apixaban activity. D. Haemoglobin may be normal early in acute haemorrhage before haemodilution occurs.
pearl: Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran, while andexanet alfa reverses the factor Xa inhibitors apixaban and rivaroxaban.
thinking: Haematemesis with pallor and tachycardia ↓ Taking apixaban, last dose this morning ↓ Early haemoglobin can be falsely reassuring ↓ Withhold the drug and assess exposure ↓ Consider specific reversal if life-threatening
exam_trap: B, Vitamin K will quickly reverse its effect — it is the familiar antidote for warfarin, but apixaban inhibits factor Xa directly and is unaffected by vitamin K.
takeaway: Major bleeding on apixaban means resuscitate, withhold and urgently review the anticoagulant, considering specific reversal.

stem: An 81-year-old woman is admitted from home to the acute medical unit with coffee-ground vomiting and black stools. Her blood pressure is low and she is clammy. Her medicines include warfarin for a previous deep vein thrombosis, omeprazole, simvastatin and calcium with vitamin D. Which medication-related issue needs the most urgent assessment?

options.A: Whether she has taken her omeprazole
options.C: Her level of anticoagulation, including the INR
options.D: Her calcium and vitamin D intake
options.E: Whether she is up to date with her vaccinations

correct_answer: C. Her level of anticoagulation, including the INR
why_correct: Major gastrointestinal bleeding in a patient on warfarin requires urgent measurement of the INR and assessment of anticoagulant effect alongside resuscitation. If the bleed is major, warfarin should be stopped and reversed with intravenous vitamin K and prothrombin complex concentrate. Knowing the INR guides how rapidly and fully reversal is needed.
why_wrong: A. Omeprazole is relevant to ulcer prevention but does not determine her bleeding risk now. B. Statin adherence has no bearing on acute bleeding. D. Calcium and vitamin D do not affect clotting in a clinically important way here. E. Vaccination status is not a priority in an acute bleed.
pearl: In major bleeding on warfarin, give prothrombin complex concentrate with intravenous vitamin K rather than fresh frozen plasma, which is slower and less effective.
thinking: Upper GI bleed with shock ↓ Taking warfarin ↓ Anticoagulation worsens bleeding ↓ Check the INR urgently ↓ Stop and reverse warfarin if major bleeding
exam_trap: A, Whether she has taken her omeprazole — it relates to the stomach and seems relevant, but the immediate danger comes from her anticoagulation.
takeaway: In a patient on warfarin with GI bleeding, urgently assess anticoagulation and the INR.

stem: A 72-year-old man calls NHS 111. He has passed black, sticky stools twice today and feels faint when standing. He has been taking rivaroxaban since a deep vein thrombosis three months ago and asks whether he should take tonight's dose as usual. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Take tonight's dose as normal and see the GP next week
options.B: Stop all of his medicines permanently
options.C: Stay at home, drink plenty of fluids and see how he feels
options.D: Arrange urgent assessment of the bleed and his anticoagulant exposure
options.E: Reassure him that rivaroxaban does not cause bleeding

correct_answer: D. Arrange urgent assessment of the bleed and his anticoagulant exposure
why_correct: Black, sticky stools with faintness suggest a significant upper gastrointestinal bleed, which is made more dangerous by anticoagulation. He needs urgent face-to-face assessment of bleeding severity and of his anticoagulant exposure, including timing of the last dose and renal function. Decisions about withholding, reversing or later restarting rivaroxaban follow from that assessment.
why_wrong: A. Taking another dose without assessment could worsen bleeding. B. Permanent withdrawal of all medicines is not justified without review; his DVT still needs treatment. C. Possible significant bleeding with faintness needs hospital assessment, not home care. E. All anticoagulants, including rivaroxaban, increase bleeding risk.
pearl: Melaena with postural symptoms is a red flag for significant upper GI bleeding and needs same-day emergency assessment.
thinking: Melaena and faintness on standing ↓ Taking rivaroxaban ↓ Possible significant GI bleed made worse by anticoagulation ↓ Do not take further doses without assessment ↓ Urgent assessment of bleed and anticoagulant exposure
exam_trap: C, Stay at home and drink fluids — he is talking and may sound well, but melaena with faintness on an anticoagulant needs urgent hospital assessment.
takeaway: A suspected significant bleed on a DOAC needs urgent assessment of bleeding severity and anticoagulant exposure.

stem: At the pharmacy counter, a 70-year-old man collecting his repeat prescription notices that his atorvastatin tablets are now white and oval instead of the pink tablets he had before. He worries he has been given the wrong medicine or a weaker version. The pharmacist explains that this is a generic product. Which explanation is correct?

options.A: Generic tablets contain less of the active drug to keep costs down
options.B: Generic tablets are licensed only for milder disease
options.C: Generic tablets contain the same active ingredient and must meet the same quality standards
options.D: Generic tablets contain a related but chemically different drug
options.E: Generic tablets are new products still in clinical trials

correct_answer: C. Generic tablets contain the same active ingredient and must meet the same quality standards
why_correct: Generic medicines contain the same active ingredient at the same strength as the branded product and must show bioequivalence and meet MHRA quality standards. Their colour, shape and inactive ingredients may differ, which explains the change in appearance. He can be reassured that his treatment is unchanged.
why_wrong: A. Generics contain the same dose of active drug. B. Generics are not restricted to milder disease; they are licensed for the same conditions as the original product. D. The active ingredient is chemically identical, not a related analogue. E. Generics are established medicines, produced after the original patent expires.
pearl: For a few drugs, such as certain antiepileptics, ciclosporin and tacrolimus, prescribers keep patients on a consistent brand or manufacturer because small differences in bioavailability can matter.
thinking: Tablet looks different ↓ Patient worries it is weaker or wrong ↓ It is a generic product ↓ Same active ingredient and strength ↓ Must meet the same quality standards
exam_trap: A, Less active drug to keep costs down — the lower price makes this myth tempting, but generics are cheaper because development costs are not repeated, not because they contain less drug.
takeaway: Generic medicines look different but contain the same active ingredient and meet the same quality standards.

stem: A 48-year-old woman saw a private gastroenterologist, who recommended a branded version of omeprazole for her reflux. At her GP practice she is told the NHS prescription will be issued generically, and she asks whether the generic will work as well. What is the key principle to explain?

options.A: Branded medicines are safer than generic versions
options.B: The generic contains the same active ingredient as the branded product
options.C: Generic medicines usually work less well than brands
options.D: Generic prescribing needs specialist approval on the NHS
options.E: The generic is a similar but chemically different compound

correct_answer: B. The generic contains the same active ingredient as the branded product
why_correct: A generic medicine contains the same active ingredient as the branded version and is required to be bioequivalent, so it produces the same therapeutic effect. Prescribing by generic name is standard NHS practice and helps reduce cost without reducing effectiveness. She can expect the same benefit from generic omeprazole.
why_wrong: A. Branding does not make a medicine safer; both must meet the same standards. C. Generics are not inherently less effective, as bioequivalence must be shown. D. Generic prescribing is routine and needs no specialist approval. E. The active ingredient is identical, not a different compound.
pearl: Generic prescribing is encouraged across the NHS; brand prescribing is reserved for situations where formulations are not interchangeable.
thinking: Patient worried generic is inferior ↓ Generic contains the same active ingredient ↓ Must be bioequivalent ↓ Same expected therapeutic effect ↓ Generic prescribing is routine NHS practice
exam_trap: A, Branded medicines are safer — many patients assume a brand means higher quality, but generics must meet the same regulatory standards for quality and safety.
takeaway: A generic medicine has the same active ingredient as the brand and is expected to work the same way.

stem: A 37-year-old woman is admitted to the gynaecology ward with pelvic sepsis and started on intravenous gentamicin alongside other antibiotics. The ward pharmacist asks the team to ensure appropriate monitoring is in place while the aminoglycoside continues. Which adverse effect is particularly important to monitor for?
why_correct: Gentamicin is an aminoglycoside that accumulates in renal tubular cells and can cause acute kidney injury, as well as dose-related ototoxicity. Serum creatinine and gentamicin levels should be monitored, with dosing adjusted to levels and renal function according to local protocol. Courses are kept as short as possible to reduce toxicity.
why_wrong: B. Gingival overgrowth is linked to phenytoin, ciclosporin and calcium-channel blockers, not gentamicin. C. Constipation is not a characteristic gentamicin toxicity. D. Gentamicin does not affect thyroid function. E. Hypoglycaemia is not a recognised toxicity of gentamicin.
pearl: Gentamicin ototoxicity can be irreversible and affects both hearing and balance, so ask about tinnitus, hearing loss and unsteadiness during treatment.
thinking: Patient on intravenous gentamicin ↓ Aminoglycosides accumulate in the kidney and inner ear ↓ Main toxicities are nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity ↓ Monitor creatinine and drug levels ↓ Adjust dosing to levels and renal function
exam_trap: B, Gingival overgrowth — it is a well known drug side effect that appears in many lists, but it belongs to phenytoin and ciclosporin, not aminoglycosides.
takeaway: Gentamicin requires monitoring of renal function and drug levels because of nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity.

stem: A 34-year-old man with a learning disability who lives in supported accommodation is brought to his dentist by a support worker. His gums have gradually thickened over several years and now partly cover his teeth, bleeding when brushed. He has had focal seizures since childhood and has taken the same single antiepileptic drug for most of that time. He has also developed coarsening of his facial features and increased body hair. Which drug is he most likely taking?
why_correct: Slowly progressive gum overgrowth in someone on long-term antiepileptic treatment points strongly to phenytoin. The accompanying coarsening of facial features and hirsutism are other recognised long-term effects of phenytoin. Poor oral hygiene worsens the overgrowth, so dental care is an important part of management.
why_wrong: A. Valproate causes weight gain, tremor and hair thinning rather than gum overgrowth. B. Levetiracetam is mainly associated with irritability and mood change. D. Lamotrigine is best known for causing rash, including Stevens–Johnson syndrome. E. Carbamazepine typically causes hyponatraemia, rash and blood dyscrasias, not gingival hyperplasia.
pearl: Other drugs that cause gingival overgrowth include ciclosporin and calcium channel blockers such as nifedipine and amlodipine.
thinking: Gradual gum overgrowth ↓ Long-term single antiepileptic since childhood ↓ Coarse facies and hirsutism as extra clues ↓ Pattern matches chronic phenytoin effects ↓ Phenytoin is the likely drug
exam_trap: E, Carbamazepine — it is another older enzyme-inducing antiepileptic often used for focal seizures, but it does not cause gum overgrowth or coarse facial features.
takeaway: Gum overgrowth with coarse facies and hirsutism in a long-term antiepileptic user suggests phenytoin.

stem: A 66-year-old retired bricklayer phones NHS 111. For the past month he has been taking naproxen prescribed for hip osteoarthritis, topped up with ibuprofen bought from a supermarket. Over the last week he has had a burning pain high in his abdomen after meals, and this morning he brought up a cupful of dark brown material that looked like coffee grounds. Which adverse drug effect is most likely?

options.A: Bleeding from upper gastrointestinal mucosal ulceration

correct_answer: A. Bleeding from upper gastrointestinal mucosal ulceration
why_correct: Two NSAIDs taken together increase the risk of gastric and duodenal ulceration considerably. Epigastric burning followed by coffee-ground vomiting describes bleeding from the upper gastrointestinal tract. He needs urgent assessment in hospital, with the NSAIDs stopped and risk scoring with a view to endoscopy.
why_wrong: B. NSAIDs can harm the kidneys, but this would not explain dyspepsia and vomited blood. C. Hepatitis is an uncommon NSAID effect and would cause jaundice or abnormal liver tests rather than haematemesis. D. Candida oesophagitis causes painful swallowing, mainly in immunosuppressed people, and is not an NSAID effect. E. NSAID-sensitive asthma causes wheeze, not gastrointestinal symptoms.
pearl: Combining two NSAIDs, or adding an NSAID to an anticoagulant, antiplatelet, SSRI or corticosteroid, markedly increases gastrointestinal bleeding risk.
thinking: Two NSAIDs taken together ↓ New post-prandial epigastric burning ↓ Coffee-ground vomit means altered blood ↓ Mucosal ulceration with bleeding ↓ Stop NSAIDs and assess urgently
exam_trap: B, Drug-induced acute kidney injury — NSAID nephrotoxicity is well known and he is older, but it does not account for dyspepsia or vomiting blood.
takeaway: Dyspepsia then coffee-ground vomiting in an NSAID user means upper GI bleeding until proven otherwise.

stem: An 81-year-old woman in a residential home has atrial fibrillation and takes warfarin. Five days ago she started clarithromycin for a chest infection. Care staff notice her urine is now red and she has several new bruises on her forearms. A point-of-care INR is well above her target range. What is the most important immediate consideration?

options.C: Bleeding caused by excessive warfarin effect

correct_answer: C. Bleeding caused by excessive warfarin effect
why_correct: Clarithromycin inhibits warfarin metabolism and can push the INR up sharply. Red urine together with new bruising and a raised INR indicates bleeding from over-anticoagulation, which must be addressed first. Management follows the BNF guidance for a high INR with bleeding, including withholding warfarin and giving vitamin K, with urgent reversal if bleeding is major.
why_wrong: A. A stone causes colicky loin pain and would not explain the bruising or raised INR. B. Infection can cause haematuria but does not explain widespread bruising and a raised INR. D. Glomerulonephritis causes haematuria with oedema and hypertension, not bruising and a high INR. E. Rhabdomyolysis causes dark urine from myoglobin after muscle injury, with no link to the INR.
pearl: Once the INR has been corrected, haematuria in an anticoagulated patient still needs investigation, because anticoagulation can unmask an underlying urological cancer.
thinking: Warfarin plus a new macrolide ↓ Enzyme inhibition raises the INR ↓ Haematuria and new bruising ↓ INR above target ↓ Treat as anticoagulant-related bleeding
exam_trap: B, Simple lower urinary tract infection — she is elderly and has just had an infection, but a UTI would not cause new bruising or a high INR.
takeaway: Bleeding with a high INR on warfarin, especially after a new interacting drug, is over-anticoagulation until proven otherwise.

stem: A 77-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease has been eating very little for three days because of gastroenteritis. Her daughter finds her sweaty, muddled and drowsy at home, and the ambulance crew record a low capillary glucose. Her diabetes is treated with gliclazide. Which action of this drug best explains her presentation?

options.A: Reduced glucose production by the liver
options.B: Increased glucose loss in the urine
options.C: Stimulation of insulin release from pancreatic beta cells
options.D: Slowed gastric emptying and reduced appetite
options.E: Increased peripheral insulin sensitivity through PPAR-gamma activation

correct_answer: C. Stimulation of insulin release from pancreatic beta cells
why_correct: Gliclazide is a sulfonylurea: it closes ATP-sensitive potassium channels on beta cells and causes insulin release regardless of the blood glucose level. If she stops eating, insulin release continues and hypoglycaemia follows. Reduced renal function and older age increase the risk and can prolong the episode.
why_wrong: A. Reduced hepatic glucose output is the main action of metformin, which rarely causes hypoglycaemia on its own. B. Increased urinary glucose loss describes SGLT2 inhibitors. D. Slowed gastric emptying and reduced appetite describe GLP-1 receptor agonists. E. PPAR-gamma activation is the mechanism of pioglitazone, which does not cause hypoglycaemia alone.
pearl: Sick day advice for sulfonylureas includes more frequent glucose checks and possibly withholding the dose if not eating, since hypoglycaemia can be prolonged.
thinking: Older woman with CKD ↓ Poor intake from gastroenteritis ↓ Low glucose with sweating and confusion ↓ Gliclazide drives insulin release whatever the glucose ↓ Sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycaemia
exam_trap: A, Reduced glucose production by the liver — this is the best-known diabetes drug action, but it belongs to metformin and does not cause significant hypoglycaemia on its own.
takeaway: Sulfonylureas stimulate insulin secretion, so they cause hypoglycaemia when intake falls.

stem: A 66-year-old man was started on a new drug by his GP three weeks ago for stabbing, electric-shock pains in his cheek triggered by shaving. He now presents to the medical take with nausea, unsteadiness and new confusion noticed by his husband. Serum sodium is 122 mmol/L. He appears euvolaemic, his urine is inappropriately concentrated with a high urine sodium, and thyroid and adrenal tests are normal. Which drug is the most likely cause?
why_correct: His facial pain is typical of trigeminal neuralgia, for which carbamazepine is the first-line drug. Carbamazepine increases antidiuretic hormone effect and is a recognised cause of SIADH, giving euvolaemic hyponatraemia with concentrated urine. The timing after starting the drug fits, and symptomatic hyponatraemia like his needs careful correction and review of the drug.
why_wrong: A. Gabapentin can cause dizziness and sedation but is not a typical cause of SIADH. C. Paracetamol does not cause hyponatraemia. D. Amlodipine causes ankle swelling and flushing rather than SIADH. E. Atorvastatin is associated with myalgia and raised liver enzymes, not hyponatraemia.
pearl: Other common drug causes of SIADH include SSRIs, tricyclic antidepressants, oxcarbazepine, PPIs and some antipsychotics.
thinking: Shock-like facial pain triggered by shaving ↓ Trigeminal neuralgia treated with carbamazepine ↓ Confusion three weeks later ↓ Euvolaemic hyponatraemia with concentrated urine ↓ Carbamazepine-induced SIADH
exam_trap: A, Gabapentin — it is also used for neuropathic pain and causes unsteadiness, but it is not a recognised cause of SIADH.
takeaway: Carbamazepine, used for trigeminal neuralgia and epilepsy, is a classic cause of SIADH.

stem: An 8-year-old girl had amoxicillin for an ear infection last year without any problem. Today she is given the first dose of a new course of co-amoxiclav suspension at the GP surgery. Within twenty minutes she is scratching at raised itchy weals on her chest and her eyelids have become puffy. Her voice is normal, she has no wheeze or stridor, and her pulse and blood pressure are normal for her age. Which mechanism underlies this reaction?

options.A: Deposition of immune complexes in small blood vessels
options.B: Antibody-directed destruction of red blood cells
options.D: Direct dose-dependent toxicity of the drug
options.E: Cross-linking of IgE on mast cells causing release of histamine and other mediators

correct_answer: E. Cross-linking of IgE on mast cells causing release of histamine and other mediators
why_correct: Onset within minutes of a drug, with urticaria and swelling, is an immediate type I hypersensitivity reaction. The drug cross-links specific IgE bound to mast cells, which degranulate and release histamine and other mediators. There are no airway, breathing or circulation features, so this is not anaphylaxis, but penicillin allergy should be documented clearly.
why_wrong: A. Immune complex deposition is type III hypersensitivity, as in serum sickness, which develops days later. B. Antibody-directed red cell destruction is type II hypersensitivity and causes haemolysis. C. T-cell mediated reactions are type IV and appear hours to days later, such as many drug rashes. D. Dose-dependent toxicity would not cause rapid urticaria and swelling after a normal first dose.
pearl: IgE-mediated allergy needs prior sensitisation, so it typically appears on re-exposure to a drug; reactions within an hour suggest IgE, whereas rashes appearing after several days are usually T-cell mediated.
thinking: Previous penicillin exposure, new course ↓ Reaction within minutes ↓ Urticaria and eyelid swelling ↓ No airway, breathing or circulation compromise ↓ Type I reaction driven by mast-cell degranulation
exam_trap: C, Delayed T-cell mediated inflammation — drug rashes are often T-cell driven, but those appear days later, not within twenty minutes.
takeaway: Immediate drug allergy is type I: IgE on mast cells triggers histamine release.

stem: A 38-year-old man attends a GP appointment with a three-day history of a blocked nose, sneezing and a mild cough. He is otherwise well, with normal observations and a clear chest. He is flying abroad next week and insists that he must have antibiotics to clear it up before then, saying a previous doctor always gave him some. The GP believes antibiotics are unnecessary and could cause harm. What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Prescribe a short course as a compromise to keep him satisfied
options.B: Prescribe a broad-spectrum antibiotic to cover every possibility
options.C: Prescribe them and record a bacterial diagnosis to justify it
options.D: Explain why antibiotics are not appropriate, decline to prescribe, and give self-care and safety-netting advice
options.E: Tell him that doctors have to prescribe whatever patients request

correct_answer: D. Explain why antibiotics are not appropriate, decline to prescribe, and give self-care and safety-netting advice
why_correct: The GMC expects doctors to prescribe only when they are satisfied the medicine serves the patient's needs. A viral upper respiratory infection does not need antibiotics, which carry risks of side effects and resistance. The doctor should explain this honestly, decline, and offer symptom advice and clear safety-netting about when to return.
why_wrong: A. A short course still exposes him to risk without benefit and reinforces the expectation. B. Broad-spectrum antibiotics add more harm and drive resistance. C. Recording a false diagnosis is dishonest and a serious probity breach. E. Doctors are not obliged to provide treatment they believe is not clinically appropriate.
pearl: If a doctor decides not to provide a treatment a patient wants, they should explain why and tell the patient they have the right to seek a second opinion.
thinking: Self-limiting viral cold ↓ Patient demands antibiotics ↓ No clinical indication and potential harm ↓ Doctor must prescribe only in the patient's interest ↓ Explain, decline and safety-net
exam_trap: A, A short course as a compromise — it seems to preserve the relationship, but it is still inappropriate prescribing with no benefit and real risk.
