takeaway: Do not prescribe medicines that are not indicated; explain why and offer appropriate alternatives.

presentation: Insulin in type 1 diabetes during admission
stem: A 23-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes on a basal-bolus insulin regimen is admitted to the orthopaedic ward with an ankle fracture that needs fixation the next morning. She is made nil by mouth from midnight. The night nurse bleeps the junior doctor to ask whether all her insulin should be stopped until she is eating again. Which principle should guide the reply?

options.A: All insulin should be withheld while she is nil by mouth
options.B: Capillary glucose needs checking only once a day while she is an inpatient
options.C: Her long-acting insulin should be stopped and replaced with a subcutaneous sliding scale
options.D: All her insulin doses should be halved until she is discharged
options.E: Insulin must not be omitted; basal insulin continues, adjusted as per perioperative guidance, with frequent glucose and ketone monitoring

correct_answer: E. Insulin must not be omitted; basal insulin continues, adjusted as per perioperative guidance, with frequent glucose and ketone monitoring
why_correct: In type 1 diabetes the pancreas makes no insulin, so stopping insulin even for a few hours can lead to ketosis and diabetic ketoacidosis, whether or not she is eating. Joint British Diabetes Societies inpatient guidance states that basal insulin should be continued during fasting, usually with a modest dose adjustment, and insulin should never be omitted without a clear clinical reason. Glucose and ketones should be monitored regularly around surgery.
why_wrong: A. Withholding all insulin in type 1 diabetes risks diabetic ketoacidosis within hours. B. Once-daily checks are far too infrequent for a fasting inpatient on insulin. C. Subcutaneous sliding scales are unsafe, and basal insulin should continue even if an intravenous insulin infusion is used. D. Arbitrary halving of all doses risks hyperglycaemia and ketosis.
pearl: Insulin omission in hospital is a recognised patient safety incident that can cause diabetic ketoacidosis in people with type 1 diabetes.
thinking: Type 1 diabetes means absolute insulin deficiency ↓ Fasting does not remove the need for basal insulin ↓ Stopping insulin risks DKA ↓ Continue basal insulin with guideline adjustment ↓ Monitor glucose and ketones closely
exam_trap: A, Withholding all insulin while nil by mouth — it sounds logical to avoid hypoglycaemia without food, but in type 1 diabetes it leads quickly to ketoacidosis.
takeaway: Never omit insulin in type 1 diabetes, even when the patient is not eating.

stem: A 26-year-old woman who works as a hairdresser is seen in the dermatology clinic with painful cystic acne on her back and jawline that has left scarring despite two courses of oral antibiotics with topical treatment. She is in a relationship and is not currently using contraception. The consultant plans to start oral isotretinoin. Which risk is most important to address before the first prescription?

options.E: Severe harm to an unborn baby

correct_answer: E. Severe harm to an unborn baby
why_correct: Isotretinoin is highly teratogenic, causing serious birth defects even with short exposure. She could become pregnant and is not using contraception, so she must be enrolled in the Pregnancy Prevention Programme, with highly effective contraception and negative pregnancy tests before, during and after treatment. Mood changes should also be discussed and monitored.
why_wrong: A. Isotretinoin does not cause hypoglycaemia; it can raise lipids and liver enzymes. B. Hearing loss is associated with aminoglycosides, not isotretinoin. C. Iron deficiency is not a recognised adverse effect. D. Premature epiphyseal closure is a rare reported effect in adolescents and is irrelevant in a 26-year-old adult.
pearl: Pregnancy testing and highly effective contraception are required throughout isotretinoin treatment and for one month after it stops.
thinking: Severe scarring acne despite antibiotics ↓ Isotretinoin planned ↓ Woman of childbearing potential without contraception ↓ Isotretinoin is highly teratogenic ↓ Pregnancy Prevention Programme first
exam_trap: D, Premature closure of growth plates — retinoids can affect bone, but she is an adult and this is not the key safety issue.
takeaway: Before isotretinoin in anyone who could become pregnant, pregnancy prevention is the priority.

stem: A 58-year-old man on the surgical ward is on day two of intravenous antibiotics for diverticulitis. The nurse calls because he has developed intensely itchy, raised, pale-centred welts on his trunk and thighs. Individual lesions fade within a few hours while new ones appear elsewhere. His lips, mouth and eyes are normal, there is no blistering or skin peeling, and his breathing, pulse and blood pressure are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Itchy raised weals that each last less than 24 hours and move around the skin are characteristic of urticaria. A newly started antibiotic is a likely trigger. Normal mucosae, no blistering and normal observations exclude a severe reaction or anaphylaxis, so stopping the culprit and giving a non-sedating antihistamine is appropriate.
why_wrong: A. Stevens–Johnson syndrome causes painful blistering, skin detachment and mucosal involvement, with systemic upset. B. Scabies causes persistent itchy burrows in finger webs and wrists, not fleeting weals. C. Erythema multiforme gives fixed target lesions lasting days. D. Cellulitis is a single hot, red, tender spreading area, not migrating weals.
pearl: In urticaria each individual weal resolves within 24 hours; lesions lasting longer suggest urticarial vasculitis.
thinking: New antibiotic two days ago ↓ Itchy raised pale-centred weals ↓ Each lesion fades in hours and moves ↓ No mucosal involvement or blistering, stable observations ↓ Acute urticaria
exam_trap: A, Stevens–Johnson syndrome — a new rash on antibiotics prompts worry about severe reactions, but there is no blistering, skin loss or mucosal involvement.
takeaway: Transient, migrating itchy weals after a new drug, with normal mucosae and observations, are urticaria.

stem: A 41-year-old nurse who works permanent night shifts has primary hypothyroidism. Her TSH has stayed above the reference range at three checks despite two dose increases, and she says she never misses a tablet. On questioning, she takes her levothyroxine when she gets home in the morning, together with her main meal of the day, before going to sleep. What is the most likely reason for her results?

options.A: Increased clearance of thyroxine by the kidneys
options.B: Excess iodine in her diet blocking the drug
options.D: Faster breakdown of thyroxine by the liver
options.E: Reduced absorption because she takes it with a meal

correct_answer: E. Reduced absorption because she takes it with a meal
why_correct: Levothyroxine is absorbed less well when it is taken with food, so taking it with a large meal can leave her under-replaced even though she is adherent. It should be taken on an empty stomach, usually at least 30 minutes before food or caffeine, at a consistent time. Adjusting the timing to suit her shifts and rechecking TSH after a few weeks is more sensible than further dose increases.
why_wrong: A. Renal excretion of thyroxine is not a recognised cause of under-replacement. B. Dietary iodine does not block levothyroxine. C. Thyroid hormone resistance is a rare genetic condition and is unlikely when there is a clear reversible cause. D. Enzyme induction by drugs can increase thyroxine metabolism, but she takes no such drug and the timing with food is the obvious problem.
pearl: Calcium, iron, antacids and proton pump inhibitors also reduce levothyroxine absorption, so they should be separated by several hours.
thinking: Persistently high TSH despite dose increases ↓ Adherence appears good ↓ Tablet taken with her main meal ↓ Food reduces levothyroxine absorption ↓ Take on an empty stomach at a consistent time
exam_trap: C, Tissue resistance to thyroid hormone — it seems to explain a poor response to rising doses, but it is rare and a simple absorption problem is far more likely.
takeaway: Check how levothyroxine is taken before increasing the dose; food reduces absorption.

stem: A 57-year-old woman with diabetic kidney disease attends the emergency department because her tongue has swollen overnight. This is her third episode in four months; previous episodes settled over a day or two and did not improve with antihistamines. There is no itching or rash, and she has had no new foods or insect stings. She has taken perindopril for two years without problems. Her airway is currently patent. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: ACE inhibitors reduce breakdown of bradykinin, which can cause recurrent non-itchy swelling of the tongue, lips and face without urticaria. It can start years after the drug was started, and it responds poorly to antihistamines. Perindopril should be stopped permanently and an alternative agent chosen, with airway monitoring during attacks.
why_wrong: A. Allergic angioedema is usually itchy, accompanied by hives and responsive to antihistamines. B. Contact dermatitis causes an itchy eczematous rash, not deep tongue swelling. D. Ludwig's angina is a spreading infection of the floor of the mouth with fever, pain and dental infection. E. A salivary stone causes painful swelling of the gland at mealtimes, not recurrent tongue swelling.
pearl: ACE-inhibitor angioedema is bradykinin-mediated, so antihistamines and steroids are often ineffective; an ARB can be considered with caution after specialist advice.
thinking: Recurrent tongue swelling ↓ No itch, rash or allergic trigger ↓ No response to antihistamines ↓ Long-term ACE inhibitor use ↓ Bradykinin-mediated ACE-inhibitor angioedema
exam_trap: A, Acute allergic urticaria with angioedema — swelling makes allergy the first thought, but there is no itch or hives and antihistamines did not help.
takeaway: Recurrent non-itchy angioedema without hives on an ACE inhibitor is drug-induced, even after years of use.

stem: A 70-year-old man attends a cardiac rehabilitation clinic three weeks after a heart attack. He says he woke this morning with a swollen upper lip and a thick feeling in his tongue that is not itchy, and he has no rash. He is breathing comfortably. Since discharge he has been taking several new medicines. Which of the following is most likely to have caused this?
why_correct: Ramipril, an ACE inhibitor started after his heart attack, is a recognised cause of angioedema. The swelling is due to bradykinin build-up, so it is typically non-itchy and occurs without urticaria, and it can involve the tongue and airway. The drug should be stopped and he should be assessed urgently for airway safety.
why_wrong: B. Bisoprolol commonly causes tiredness, cold peripheries and bradycardia, not angioedema. C. Atorvastatin is associated with muscle aches and raised liver enzymes. D. Clopidogrel mainly causes bleeding and bruising. E. Glyceryl trinitrate causes headache, flushing and low blood pressure.
pearl: ACE-inhibitor angioedema is more common in people of Black African or African-Caribbean descent and in smokers.
thinking: New medicines after a heart attack ↓ Non-itchy lip and tongue swelling ↓ No urticaria ↓ Bradykinin-mediated mechanism ↓ The ACE inhibitor is the likely cause
exam_trap: D, Clopidogrel — new antiplatelet drugs are often blamed for unusual reactions, but its main adverse effect is bleeding, not facial swelling.
takeaway: Non-itchy lip or tongue swelling without hives in someone on an ACE inhibitor points to the ACE inhibitor.

stem: During a heatwave, the wife of a 52-year-old landscape gardener with bipolar disorder phones his community mental health nurse. He has been working outdoors all week and drinking little. For two days he has had loose stools and vomiting, his hands have developed a coarse tremor, and today he seems muddled and slow to answer. He takes lithium. What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.A: Increase his lithium dose to cover a possible relapse
options.B: Continue lithium and check the level at his next routine blood test
options.C: Halve the lithium dose and review him in a week
options.D: Add propranolol for the tremor and continue lithium
options.E: Withhold lithium and arrange urgent same-day medical assessment with lithium level and renal function

correct_answer: E. Withhold lithium and arrange urgent same-day medical assessment with lithium level and renal function
why_correct: Dehydration from heat and gastrointestinal losses reduces lithium excretion, and coarse tremor, vomiting, diarrhoea and confusion are features of lithium toxicity. Lithium should be stopped and he needs urgent assessment with a serum lithium level, urea and electrolytes and fluid replacement. Severe toxicity may need specialist treatment such as haemodialysis.
why_wrong: A. Increasing the dose would worsen toxicity. B. Waiting for routine monitoring delays care for a potentially fatal problem. C. A reduced dose still adds lithium and delaying review is unsafe. D. Propranolol treats the fine tremor seen at normal levels, but a coarse tremor with confusion signals toxicity.
pearl: A fine tremor is common at therapeutic lithium levels, whereas a coarse tremor, ataxia, vomiting and confusion suggest toxicity.
thinking: Lithium user in hot weather ↓ Poor fluid intake with vomiting and diarrhoea ↓ Dehydration reduces lithium clearance ↓ Coarse tremor and confusion ↓ Stop lithium and assess urgently
exam_trap: D, Adding propranolol for the tremor — propranolol is used for lithium tremor, but that applies to fine tremor at normal levels, not toxicity with confusion.
takeaway: Suspected lithium toxicity needs lithium withheld and same-day assessment with levels and renal function.

stem: A 69-year-old man was diagnosed with giant cell arteritis 14 months ago and is still taking oral prednisolone, though at a reduced dose. At a GP medication review he asks which long-term problems he should be most concerned about. He was not started on any bone protection when the prednisolone began. Which complication of his treatment should be specifically assessed and prevented now?
why_correct: Long-term systemic corticosteroids reduce bone formation and increase bone loss, raising the risk of osteoporosis and fragility fractures, especially in the first months and at higher doses. Anyone on prolonged oral steroids, particularly at his age, should have their fracture risk assessed and usually be offered bone protection, such as a bisphosphonate with adequate calcium and vitamin D. This was missed when his treatment started.
why_wrong: A. Corticosteroids do not cause hypothyroidism. B. Parkinsonism is associated with antipsychotics and metoclopramide, not steroids. C. Iron-deficiency anaemia is not a direct steroid effect. D. Pulmonary fibrosis is linked to drugs such as amiodarone and methotrexate, not prednisolone.
pearl: Other important long-term steroid effects include cataracts, diabetes, hypertension, myopathy, infection risk and adrenal suppression.
thinking: Over a year of oral prednisolone ↓ Older man ↓ Steroids accelerate bone loss ↓ High risk of fragility fracture ↓ Assess fracture risk and offer bone protection
exam_trap: C, Iron-deficiency anaemia — steroids can cause gastrointestinal problems, but iron deficiency is not a recognised direct complication and is not the priority here.
takeaway: Prolonged systemic corticosteroids cause osteoporosis; assess fracture risk and offer bone protection.

presentation: Giving oral bisphosphonates in a care home
stem: A senior carer at a nursing home phones the GP practice about an 83-year-old resident who has just been started on weekly alendronic acid after a vertebral fracture. The resident usually has all her morning tablets brought to her in bed on a tray with breakfast and a cup of tea, and spends most of the morning reclining. How should staff give this new tablet?

options.A: With a full glass of plain water on an empty stomach, keeping her sitting or standing upright afterwards
options.C: With her cup of tea while she is reclined in bed
options.D: At the same time as her calcium and vitamin D tablet
options.E: With breakfast to protect her stomach

correct_answer: A. With a full glass of plain water on an empty stomach, keeping her sitting or standing upright afterwards
why_correct: Alendronic acid can cause oesophagitis and ulceration if the tablet lodges in the oesophagus. It should be swallowed whole with plain water on an empty stomach, and she must stay upright for at least 30 minutes before eating or drinking anything else. Her usual routine of tablets in bed with breakfast needs changing for this dose.
why_wrong: B. Crushing increases the risk of oesophageal irritation and food stops absorption. C. Taking it reclined allows reflux into the oesophagus, and tea reduces absorption. D. Calcium binds bisphosphonates and prevents absorption, so it must be taken at a different time. E. Food markedly reduces absorption, which is already very low.
pearl: Oral bisphosphonates are poorly absorbed even under ideal conditions, so any food, drink other than water, or calcium taken at the same time can make them ineffective.
thinking: Frail resident started on alendronic acid ↓ Usually takes tablets reclined in bed with breakfast ↓ Risk of oesophageal injury and poor absorption ↓ Needs plain water, empty stomach, upright posture ↓ Change her routine for this tablet
exam_trap: D, With her calcium and vitamin D tablet — both treat bone health so giving them together seems sensible, but calcium binds the bisphosphonate and blocks its absorption.
takeaway: Give oral bisphosphonates with plain water on an empty stomach and keep the patient upright afterwards.

stem: A 58-year-old man with asthma who has needed repeated courses of oral steroids is seen in the fracture liaison clinic after a low-trauma wrist fracture. His bone density scan confirms osteoporosis and weekly risedronate is prescribed. He says he would prefer to take it at night with a glass of milk, as he does with his other tablets. What instruction should he be given?

options.A: Take it with an antacid to help absorption
options.B: Crush it and mix it with a spoonful of food
options.C: Take it at night with his other tablets before going to bed
options.D: Take it with a glass of milk to protect his stomach
options.E: Take it with plain water on an empty stomach and stay upright afterwards

correct_answer: E. Take it with plain water on an empty stomach and stay upright afterwards
why_correct: Oral bisphosphonates must be swallowed with plain water on an empty stomach, and the patient must remain upright afterwards to reduce oesophageal irritation. Milk, other drinks and food reduce absorption. His plan to take it at night with milk would both block absorption and increase the risk of oesophageal injury when he lies down.
why_wrong: A. Antacids contain calcium, magnesium or aluminium that bind the drug and reduce absorption. B. Crushing the tablet increases oesophageal irritation, and food blocks absorption. C. Lying down soon after the tablet increases the risk of oesophagitis. D. Calcium in milk binds the bisphosphonate and prevents absorption.
pearl: Men can develop osteoporosis too; repeated oral steroids are a common cause and should prompt fracture risk assessment.
thinking: Steroid-induced osteoporosis in a man ↓ New weekly bisphosphonate ↓ Plans to take it at bedtime with milk ↓ Milk blocks absorption and lying down risks oesophagitis ↓ Plain water, empty stomach, stay upright
exam_trap: D, Taking it with a glass of milk — milk seems a gentle way to protect the stomach, but its calcium binds the drug and stops it working.
takeaway: Bisphosphonates go down with plain water only, never milk, and the patient stays upright.

stem: A 76-year-old man on an orthogeriatric ward is ready to go home after surgery for a hip fracture. The team want him to begin weekly alendronic acid at home. He gets occasional heartburn and wonders whether to swallow the new tablet alongside one of his chalky indigestion tablets to protect his gullet. What advice best lowers his chance of gullet injury from this drug?

options.A: Crush the tablet into a warm drink at bedtime
options.B: Take it in the middle of a large meal
options.C: Swallow it with a full glass of plain water and stay sitting or standing afterwards
options.D: Take it just before lying down to sleep
options.E: Take it with an antacid tablet to coat the oesophagus

correct_answer: C. Swallow it with a full glass of plain water and stay sitting or standing afterwards
why_correct: Bisphosphonate oesophagitis happens when the tablet or its contents stay in contact with the oesophageal lining. A full glass of plain water helps the tablet reach the stomach, and staying upright prevents reflux back into the oesophagus. His heartburn history makes these steps more important, and new swallowing pain or heartburn should prompt him to stop and seek advice.
why_wrong: A. Crushing and lying down at bedtime both increase oesophageal exposure to the drug. B. Food greatly reduces absorption. D. Lying down soon after the dose allows reflux and oesophageal injury. E. Antacids bind the bisphosphonate and stop it being absorbed, without protecting the oesophagus.
pearl: Patients starting oral bisphosphonates should be told to stop and seek advice if they develop pain on swallowing, difficulty swallowing or new or worsening heartburn.
thinking: Starting an oral bisphosphonate after hip fracture ↓ History of heartburn ↓ Oesophagitis risk from prolonged mucosal contact ↓ Plain water clears the tablet and upright posture prevents reflux ↓ Antacids would block absorption
exam_trap: E, Taking it with an antacid — it sounds protective for someone with heartburn, but antacids bind the drug and stop it working.
takeaway: Plenty of plain water and staying upright is what protects the oesophagus from bisphosphonates.

stem: A 61-year-old man with stable angina has taken bisoprolol for several years. At his local pharmacy he says he has run out and was planning to simply stop it because he thinks it is affecting his sex life and he wants to try without it. The pharmacist advises him not to stop suddenly. What is the main reason for this advice?

options.A: Hypoglycaemia once the beta-blocker wears off
options.C: Acute kidney injury from renal vasodilatation
options.D: Rebound sympathetic overactivity causing tachycardia and worsening angina
options.E: Bronchospasm as the drug leaves the body

correct_answer: D. Rebound sympathetic overactivity causing tachycardia and worsening angina
why_correct: Long-term beta-blockade increases the number and sensitivity of beta-adrenoceptors. Stopping suddenly exposes these receptors to normal adrenaline levels, causing rebound tachycardia, hypertension and worsening angina, and occasionally myocardial infarction or arrhythmia. Beta-blockers should be reduced gradually, and his concern about side effects should be discussed with his GP.
why_wrong: A. Beta-blockers can mask hypoglycaemia symptoms, but stopping them does not cause it. B. Beta-blocker withdrawal does not cause hypothyroidism. C. Stopping does not cause renal vasodilatation or kidney injury. E. Bronchospasm is a risk of starting a beta-blocker in asthma, especially a non-selective one, not of stopping one.
pearl: Erectile dysfunction is a recognised side effect of beta-blockers, and patients may stop them without telling anyone, so ask about it directly.
thinking: Years of bisoprolol for angina ↓ Plans to stop abruptly ↓ Receptors upregulated during treatment ↓ Sudden exposure to normal catecholamines ↓ Rebound tachycardia and worsening angina
exam_trap: E, Bronchospasm — it is the best-known beta-blocker hazard, but it relates to starting a beta-blocker in asthma, not to stopping one.
takeaway: Do not stop beta-blockers suddenly in heart disease; rebound sympathetic activity can worsen angina.

stem: A district nurse visiting a housebound 79-year-old man with type 2 diabetes realises, after leaving his flat, that she has given him twice his prescribed dose of long-acting insulin because two different doses were recorded on his chart. She returns to his home. He says he feels fine and has not yet eaten lunch. What is the immediate priority?

options.A: Check his capillary glucose, assess him, give carbohydrate and arrange continued glucose monitoring for the duration of the insulin's action
options.B: Leave him to call if he feels unwell, without checking his glucose
options.C: Advise him to skip lunch to avoid high glucose later
options.D: Arrange for his glucose to be checked at the next routine visit tomorrow
options.E: Give glucagon straight away whatever his glucose reading

correct_answer: A. Check his capillary glucose, assess him, give carbohydrate and arrange continued glucose monitoring for the duration of the insulin's action
why_correct: An excess insulin dose can cause severe and prolonged hypoglycaemia, especially with long-acting insulin and an older patient who lives alone. The priority is to check his glucose now, assess him, make sure he eats carbohydrate, and arrange monitoring through the period the insulin is acting, which may mean hospital admission if this cannot be done safely at home. The error should also be escalated to the prescriber and reported through the incident reporting system, and he should be told about it openly.
why_wrong: B. Feeling fine now does not exclude later hypoglycaemia, and he may not recognise symptoms. C. Skipping a meal greatly increases the risk of hypoglycaemia. D. Waiting until tomorrow leaves him unmonitored during the period of greatest risk. E. Glucagon treats established hypoglycaemia; giving it without checking glucose is not appropriate.
pearl: Long-acting insulin overdoses can cause hypoglycaemia lasting a day or more, so monitoring must continue for the duration of the insulin's action.
thinking: Double dose of long-acting insulin ↓ Older man living alone ↓ High risk of prolonged hypoglycaemia ↓ Check glucose, assess and give carbohydrate ↓ Monitor for the duration of insulin action and report the error
exam_trap: E, Giving glucagon straight away — it seems a proactive response to an overdose, but it treats hypoglycaemia once present and is not given without a glucose check.
takeaway: After an insulin overdose, check glucose, assess, give carbohydrate and monitor throughout the insulin's action.

stem: A 58-year-old man with chronic plaque psoriasis attends an urgent treatment centre with a sore, ulcerated mouth, two nosebleeds and new purple spots on his shins. Last week his pharmacy supplied a different brand of methotrexate tablets, and he admits he has been taking his usual dose each morning since then, believing the new box said 'daily'. He has no fever, cough or sore throat. What is the most likely explanation for his symptoms?

options.A: Herpetic gingivostomatitis with coincidental immune thrombocytopenia
options.B: An expected minor adverse effect of correctly prescribed treatment
options.C: Vitamin C deficiency causing gum bleeding and bruising
options.D: Erythema multiforme triggered by a recent infection
options.E: Methotrexate toxicity caused by inadvertent daily dosing

correct_answer: E. Methotrexate toxicity caused by inadvertent daily dosing
why_correct: For psoriasis and inflammatory arthritis, methotrexate is taken once a week. Taking the weekly dose every day for several days produces a large cumulative overdose, causing mucositis and bone marrow suppression with thrombocytopenia, which explains his mouth ulcers, nosebleeds and purpura. He needs urgent blood tests, withholding of methotrexate and specialist advice about folinic acid rescue.
why_wrong: A. Two unrelated conditions arising together is far less likely than one drug error explaining every feature. B. Mucositis with bleeding is a sign of toxicity, not an acceptable side effect, and he was not taking the drug as prescribed. C. Scurvy causes gum bleeding and perifollicular haemorrhages but develops over months of poor diet, not within a week of a dosing change. D. Erythema multiforme causes target lesions and does not explain nosebleeds or purpura from low platelets.
pearl: Changes of tablet brand, packaging or supplier are a recognised trigger for methotrexate dosing errors, so every supply should reinforce the single weekly day.
thinking: Weekly drug taken every day ↓ Mouth ulcers suggest mucositis ↓ Nosebleeds and purpura suggest low platelets ↓ Mucositis plus marrow suppression after an overdose ↓ Methotrexate toxicity
exam_trap: B, An expected minor adverse effect — mouth ulcers can occur on methotrexate at normal doses, but ulceration with bleeding after a week of daily dosing indicates serious toxicity needing urgent action.
takeaway: Mouth ulcers and bleeding in someone taking weekly methotrexate every day indicate toxicity until proven otherwise.

stem: On a gastroenterology ward, the pharmacist reviewing the chart of a 39-year-old woman with Crohn's disease notices that her oral methotrexate was transcribed on admission as a once-daily medicine. She has received it on five consecutive mornings instead of on her usual single day each week. She currently feels well. Which serious complication should the team now monitor her for most closely?
why_correct: Five daily doses of a weekly drug is a significant methotrexate overdose. The major danger is myelosuppression, producing neutropenia, thrombocytopenia and anaemia, often with mucositis, and it may appear several days after the error even if she feels well now. She needs methotrexate stopped, urgent full blood count, renal and liver tests, specialist advice on folinic acid and an incident report.
why_wrong: A. Retroperitoneal fibrosis is linked to drugs such as methysergide, not methotrexate. B. Hearing loss is a feature of aminoglycoside or platinum toxicity. C. Angle-closure glaucoma is linked to anticholinergic drugs and topiramate. E. Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus is classically caused by lithium.
pearl: Methotrexate is on the list of high-risk medicines for which a once-weekly regimen should always state the day of the week on the prescription and chart.
thinking: Weekly methotrexate charted as daily ↓ Five doses given equals a cumulative overdose ↓ Toxicity may be delayed even if she feels well ↓ Main life-threatening effect is on the marrow ↓ Monitor full blood count closely
exam_trap: E, Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus — it is a well-known drug toxicity, but it belongs to lithium; methotrexate overdose threatens the bone marrow, mucosa, liver and kidneys.
takeaway: Excess methotrexate dosing most dangerously causes bone marrow suppression, which can appear days after the error.

stem: A 67-year-old woman is admitted to the medical ward with community-acquired pneumonia. Her Summary Care Record lists six regular medicines, but she tells the foundation doctor that a hospital cardiologist stopped one of them last month and that she buys another tablet herself from the chemist. She has brought no medicines with her. What is the most appropriate way to establish what she should be prescribed?

options.A: Rely on the Summary Care Record as the official list
options.B: Prescribe only the tablets she can remember taking
options.C: Reconcile her medicines by checking several sources and resolving each discrepancy
options.D: Withhold every regular medicine until her GP surgery can confirm the list
options.E: Prescribe everything from the record and her account so nothing is missed

correct_answer: C. Reconcile her medicines by checking several sources and resolving each discrepancy
why_correct: Medicines reconciliation on admission compares at least two sources, such as the patient's own account, the GP or Summary Care Record, recent clinic letters, the community pharmacy and the medicines themselves. Each discrepancy, such as the drug stopped by the cardiologist and the one she buys herself, must be checked and documented so the inpatient chart is accurate. NICE recommends this is completed promptly, ideally within 24 hours of admission.
why_wrong: A. GP-held records often lag behind changes made by hospital specialists and omit over-the-counter products. B. Recall alone is incomplete and may miss important medicines or doses. D. Blanket withholding risks omitting time-critical or essential treatment. E. Combining both lists could restart a drug deliberately stopped and cause duplication or interactions.
pearl: Over-the-counter and herbal products are among the most frequently missed items in a drug history, so ask about them specifically.
thinking: Admission is a high-risk transition ↓ Record and patient account disagree ↓ Neither source is reliable alone ↓ Cross-check with clinic letters, pharmacy and the patient ↓ Document an agreed reconciled list
exam_trap: A, Relying on the Summary Care Record — it looks authoritative, but it does not reflect recent specialist changes or purchased medicines.
takeaway: An accurate admission drug list comes from reconciling more than one source, not from trusting a single list.

stem: An 81-year-old man with Parkinson's disease is on the orthopaedic ward after surgery for a fractured neck of femur. He was nil by mouth before theatre, and through a handover error none of his co-careldopa doses were given for 24 hours. He is now awake, swallowing safely and eating breakfast. What is the most appropriate approach to his Parkinson's medication?

options.A: Start haloperidol to manage any restlessness while levodopa is held
options.B: Restart his usual regimen at the normal times now and prevent further missed doses
options.C: Keep his Parkinson's medicines on hold until he is mobilising with physiotherapy
options.D: Restart at half dose and titrate back up over two weeks
options.E: Leave his Parkinson's medicines until discharge and arrange neurology review

correct_answer: B. Restart his usual regimen at the normal times now and prevent further missed doses
why_correct: Levodopa and other dopaminergic drugs are time-critical: missed or delayed doses can quickly cause severe rigidity, immobility, swallowing problems, aspiration and, rarely, a neuroleptic malignant-like syndrome. As he can now swallow, his usual regimen should be restarted at once at his normal times, and the omission should be reported. If he could not swallow, a non-oral route such as a rotigotine patch or nasogastric levodopa should be arranged.
why_wrong: A. Haloperidol blocks dopamine receptors and can severely worsen Parkinson's disease. C. Further delay prolongs withdrawal and will hinder rather than help rehabilitation. D. After a short omission, his usual effective doses should be resumed; slow re-titration leaves him under-treated. E. Waiting until discharge risks serious deterioration while in hospital.
pearl: Where a patient with Parkinson's disease cannot swallow, seek urgent advice from a Parkinson's specialist or pharmacist about a non-oral alternative rather than simply omitting doses.
thinking: Parkinson's disease on levodopa ↓ Doses missed around surgery ↓ Dopaminergic drugs are time-critical ↓ He can now swallow ↓ Restart his usual regimen promptly at his normal times
exam_trap: D, Restarting at half dose — a cautious re-introduction sounds safe, but after a short omission it simply prolongs under-treatment and the risk of complications.
takeaway: Parkinson's medicines are time-critical; restart the usual regimen promptly and avoid any further omissions.

stem: A 54-year-old lorry driver with type 2 diabetes calls NHS 111 on the second day of a norovirus illness. He has been vomiting repeatedly, has frequent watery stools, feels dizzy when he stands and has passed very little urine today. He takes metformin and atorvastatin. What advice should be given about his metformin?

options.A: Take an extra dose of metformin to offset illness-related hyperglycaemia
options.B: Take metformin only at night until he feels better
options.C: Pause metformin until he is eating and drinking normally again
options.D: Keep taking metformin as usual and sip fluids
options.E: Stop metformin and start a sulfonylurea in its place

correct_answer: C. Pause metformin until he is eating and drinking normally again
why_correct: During dehydrating illness, metformin should be temporarily stopped because reduced kidney perfusion can cause acute kidney injury, leading to metformin accumulation and a risk of lactic acidosis. It can be restarted once he has been eating and drinking normally for 24 to 48 hours. His dizziness and reduced urine output mean he also needs a same-day clinical assessment.
why_wrong: A. Extra metformin increases the risk of accumulation and lactic acidosis when the kidneys are underperfused. B. Changing the timing does not remove the risk while he is dehydrated. D. Continuing the drug through significant dehydration is exactly what sick day guidance aims to avoid. E. Switching to a sulfonylurea while he is barely eating risks hypoglycaemia, and a temporary pause is all that is needed.
pearl: Sick day guidance commonly covers several drugs that can be paused during dehydrating illness, including metformin, ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, diuretics, NSAIDs and SGLT2 inhibitors.
thinking: Type 2 diabetes on metformin ↓ Vomiting, diarrhoea and low urine output ↓ Risk of acute kidney injury ↓ Metformin accumulates and lactic acidosis becomes possible ↓ Pause metformin until eating and drinking normally
exam_trap: D, Continuing as usual with fluids — keeping diabetes treatment going seems sensible, but significant dehydration makes metformin unsafe until he recovers.
takeaway: Temporarily stop metformin during dehydrating illness and restart once eating and drinking normally.

stem: During a summer heatwave, a 77-year-old man with stage 3 chronic kidney disease visits his community pharmacy feeling lightheaded and thirsty. He has been drinking little and has been taking over-the-counter ibuprofen several times a day for a painful knee. He also takes ramipril. Why is the ibuprofen a particular concern?

options.A: Ibuprofen dilates the afferent arteriole and causes fluid overload
options.B: Chronic kidney disease prevents ibuprofen being absorbed, so it is ineffective
options.C: Ibuprofen reduces kidney perfusion and can cause acute kidney injury, especially when he is dehydrated
options.D: Ibuprofen protects the kidneys by reducing renal inflammation
options.E: Dehydration lowers ibuprofen levels, so he should take more

correct_answer: C. Ibuprofen reduces kidney perfusion and can cause acute kidney injury, especially when he is dehydrated
why_correct: Prostaglandins dilate the afferent arteriole and help maintain glomerular filtration when kidney perfusion is low. NSAIDs block prostaglandin synthesis, so in someone with chronic kidney disease who is dehydrated and also taking an ACE inhibitor, filtration can fall sharply and cause acute kidney injury. He should stop the ibuprofen, rehydrate and have his kidney function checked.
why_wrong: A. NSAIDs constrict rather than dilate the afferent arteriole by removing prostaglandin effects. B. Absorption is not reduced by chronic kidney disease, and the drug remains harmful. D. NSAIDs are nephrotoxic, not renoprotective. E. Dehydration increases rather than reduces the risk, and a higher dose would worsen it.
pearl: The combination of an NSAID, a diuretic and an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker is sometimes called the triple whammy because of its strong association with acute kidney injury.
thinking: Chronic kidney disease and dehydration ↓ Kidney relies on prostaglandin-driven afferent dilatation ↓ NSAID blocks prostaglandins ↓ Glomerular filtration falls, worsened by the ACE inhibitor ↓ High risk of acute kidney injury
exam_trap: A, Dilating the afferent arteriole — it uses the right vessel, but gets the mechanism backwards; loss of prostaglandin-mediated dilatation is what reduces filtration.
takeaway: NSAIDs can precipitate acute kidney injury, particularly in dehydration, chronic kidney disease and with ACE inhibitors.

stem: At her annual medication review with the practice pharmacist, a 74-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation and heart failure says she has felt very well for months and would like to stop her bisoprolol, as she thinks she no longer needs it. She takes five regular medicines in total. How should the pharmacist respond?

options.A: Agree that she can stop it today because she is well
options.B: Suggest she halves the dose and judges how she feels
options.C: Tell her all her medicines must be continued for life
options.D: Review why bisoprolol was started and the benefits, risks and withdrawal effects of stopping before advising
options.E: Advise her to stop it and restart only if symptoms return

correct_answer: D. Review why bisoprolol was started and the benefits, risks and withdrawal effects of stopping before advising
why_correct: Any decision to stop a medicine should start with its indication and the balance of benefit and harm for this patient. Bisoprolol here controls her heart rate and improves outcomes in heart failure, so feeling well may reflect that it is working; abrupt withdrawal of a beta-blocker can also cause rebound tachycardia and worsening heart failure. A shared decision based on this review respects her wishes while keeping her safe.
why_wrong: A. Feeling well may be a result of the medicine, and stopping without review risks deterioration. B. Self-directed dose reduction without assessing the indication is unsafe. C. Medicines should be reviewed regularly and some can appropriately be stopped. E. Stopping and waiting for symptoms ignores the indication and risks rebound effects and harm.
pearl: Structured medication review supports deprescribing where appropriate, but each drug should be judged on its indication, ongoing benefit and any withdrawal risk.
thinking: Patient wants to stop a medicine because she feels well ↓ Feeling well may mean the drug is working ↓ Check why it was started ↓ Weigh benefit, harm and withdrawal effects ↓ Make a shared decision
exam_trap: E, Stopping and restarting if symptoms return — it sounds patient-centred, but for drugs that prevent future harm or cause rebound effects, symptoms may appear too late.
takeaway: Before stopping any medicine, review its indication, benefits, risks and withdrawal effects with the patient.

stem: A 23-year-old man with juvenile idiopathic arthritis is moving from the children's service to the adult rheumatology clinic. He has previously had methotrexate injections given by his mother, and he is now being switched to oral methotrexate tablets that he will manage himself. Which piece of advice is most important to give him?

options.A: Take the tablets every four hours while his joints are painful
options.B: Take the full dose once a week on the same day, never daily
options.C: Take a double dose next time if a dose is missed
options.D: Take the tablets only on days when his joints flare
options.E: Stop his blood monitoring once his symptoms settle

correct_answer: B. Take the full dose once a week on the same day, never daily
why_correct: For inflammatory arthritis, methotrexate is taken as a single dose once a week, and accidental daily dosing is a recognised cause of serious and sometimes fatal toxicity. As he is taking over his own treatment for the first time, he must clearly understand the weekly schedule, with the day agreed and written down. He also needs advice about folic acid on a different day, regular blood tests and reporting sore throat, mouth ulcers or bruising.
why_wrong: A. Frequent dosing would quickly cause toxicity and is not how methotrexate works. C. Doubling up risks overdose; a missed dose should be discussed with the team rather than doubled. D. Methotrexate is a regular disease-modifying drug, not a treatment taken when needed. E. Blood monitoring must continue for as long as he takes methotrexate.
pearl: Patients starting methotrexate should carry a patient-held monitoring record or booklet and be told to report sore throat, fever, mouth ulcers or unexplained bruising promptly.
thinking: Young man taking over his own treatment ↓ Switching from injections to tablets ↓ Methotrexate is a weekly drug ↓ Daily dosing causes serious toxicity ↓ Emphasise one dose on the same day each week
exam_trap: E, Stopping monitoring once symptoms settle — improvement can make tests feel pointless, but marrow and liver toxicity can occur at any stage of treatment.
takeaway: The most important methotrexate advice is to take it once a week on the same day, never daily.

stem: A 72-year-old man with heart failure had his ramipril dose increased at a cardiology clinic three weeks ago. His routine blood tests at the GP surgery now show a raised potassium, and his creatinine has risen slightly. His other medicines are furosemide, amlodipine, lansoprazole and inhaled salbutamol as needed. Which medicine is most likely to have caused the raised potassium?
why_correct: ACE inhibitors reduce angiotensin II and therefore aldosterone secretion, so less potassium is excreted by the kidney. The recent dose increase, together with a small rise in creatinine, makes ramipril the likely cause. The potassium level should be repeated and acted on, with the ramipril dose reviewed and other potassium-raising factors checked.
why_wrong: B. Loop diuretics such as furosemide cause potassium loss and tend to lower it. C. Amlodipine does not have a meaningful effect on potassium. D. Lansoprazole is associated with low magnesium rather than high potassium. E. Salbutamol drives potassium into cells and lowers the serum level.
pearl: Potassium-sparing diuretics, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, angiotensin receptor blockers, trimethoprim and potassium supplements all add to the risk of hyperkalaemia with an ACE inhibitor.
thinking: New hyperkalaemia on routine bloods ↓ Ramipril dose recently increased ↓ ACE inhibitors reduce aldosterone ↓ Less renal potassium excretion ↓ Ramipril is the likely cause
exam_trap: B, Furosemide — it is a common culprit in electrolyte problems, but loop diuretics cause low rather than high potassium.
takeaway: ACE inhibitors can cause hyperkalaemia by reducing aldosterone, especially after dose increases or with renal impairment.

stem: A 26-year-old woman with bipolar affective disorder who has been stable on lithium for three years attends a sexual health clinic because her period is late. A pregnancy test is positive, and she estimates she is about six weeks pregnant. She is worried because she remembers being told lithium can affect a baby. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Tell her to stop lithium today and wait for her booking appointment
options.B: Advise her to continue lithium unchanged until the dating scan
options.C: Arrange urgent review of the lithium by her psychiatric team, without stopping it abruptly
options.D: Recommend termination of pregnancy because of the drug exposure
options.E: Start high-dose folic acid and make no other changes

correct_answer: C. Arrange urgent review of the lithium by her psychiatric team, without stopping it abruptly
why_correct: When a woman taking a potentially harmful medicine becomes pregnant, the medicine needs prompt specialist review that weighs fetal risk against the danger of relapse. Abruptly stopping lithium carries a high risk of relapse of bipolar disorder, while continuing it needs a careful decision, closer monitoring of levels and enhanced fetal assessment. Her psychiatric and maternity teams should be involved urgently so that she can make an informed decision.
why_wrong: A. Abrupt withdrawal of lithium greatly increases the risk of relapse, and the booking visit may be weeks away. B. Continuing unchanged without review delays an important, time-sensitive decision. D. Exposure does not automatically mean termination; she needs balanced information and choice. E. Folic acid is reasonable but does not address the need to review the lithium itself.
pearl: Lithium levels change during pregnancy and immediately after delivery, so women who continue it need closer monitoring and specialist obstetric and psychiatric input.
thinking: Newly pregnant ↓ Taking a medicine with known fetal risk ↓ Abrupt stopping risks maternal relapse ↓ Needs a rapid risk-benefit review ↓ Urgent specialist involvement without sudden withdrawal
exam_trap: A, Stopping lithium today — removing the exposure feels protective, but sudden withdrawal can trigger a serious relapse and much of the early exposure has already occurred.
takeaway: A confirmed pregnancy on a potentially harmful medicine needs urgent specialist review rather than an unplanned abrupt stop.

stem: A 34-year-old amateur rugby player comes to the emergency department with three days of gnawing upper abdominal pain and, since this morning, black, foul-smelling, sticky stools. For a shoulder injury he has been taking high-dose naproxen bought online for the past month, often on an empty stomach. He drinks little alcohol and has no history of liver disease. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: NSAIDs such as naproxen inhibit cyclo-oxygenase and reduce protective prostaglandins in the stomach and duodenum, leading to ulceration that can erode a vessel. Epigastric pain followed by melaena is typical of a bleeding peptic ulcer. He needs assessment of haemodynamic status and bleeding risk, the NSAID stopping, and endoscopy.
why_wrong: A. A Mallory-Weiss tear follows forceful retching or vomiting, which he does not report. C. Pancreatitis causes severe pain radiating to the back and vomiting, not melaena. D. Biliary colic causes episodic right upper quadrant pain and does not cause bleeding. E. Variceal bleeding occurs with portal hypertension, usually from chronic liver disease, which he does not have.
pearl: Risk of NSAID-related ulcer bleeding rises with higher doses, older age, previous ulcer, and co-prescribed anticoagulants, antiplatelets, corticosteroids or SSRIs.
thinking: High-dose NSAID use ↓ Epigastric pain ↓ Melaena points to an upper GI source ↓ No retching or liver disease ↓ Bleeding peptic ulcer
exam_trap: E, Oesophageal variceal bleeding — it is a dramatic cause of melaena, but needs portal hypertension, and nothing here suggests liver disease.
takeaway: Epigastric pain with melaena in someone taking an NSAID suggests a bleeding peptic ulcer.

stem: Two months after a myocardial infarction, a 70-year-old woman taking aspirin and ticagrelor is seen in the cardiology day unit. She describes a burning pain below her breastbone that is worse when her stomach is empty, and for two days her stools have been black and tarry. She has never had liver disease or vomiting. Which adverse drug effect is most likely responsible?
why_correct: Aspirin inhibits cyclo-oxygenase in the gastric mucosa, reducing protective prostaglandins and allowing peptic ulceration, while its antiplatelet effect, here combined with ticagrelor, makes any ulcer more likely to bleed. Epigastric pain worse on an empty stomach followed by melaena points to an upper GI ulcer source. Her cardiology team must be involved before any antiplatelet is stopped, because of the risk of stent thrombosis.
why_wrong: A. Varices occur with portal hypertension, and she has no liver disease. B. Ischaemic colitis causes left-sided abdominal pain with fresh bloody diarrhoea rather than epigastric pain and melaena. C. Angiodysplasia can bleed painlessly, but it does not explain her ulcer-type epigastric pain. E. A Mallory-Weiss tear needs preceding vomiting or retching, which she has not had.
pearl: Patients needing dual antiplatelet therapy after an acute coronary syndrome are often prescribed a proton pump inhibitor to reduce the risk of upper GI bleeding.
thinking: Aspirin plus a second antiplatelet ↓ Epigastric pain worse when hungry ↓ Black tarry stools mean upper GI blood ↓ No vomiting or liver disease ↓ Peptic ulcer haemorrhage
exam_trap: C, Angiodysplasia unmasked by antiplatelets — antiplatelets can provoke such bleeding, but angiodysplasia is painless and does not explain her epigastric pain.
takeaway: Aspirin can cause peptic ulceration and bleeding, presenting with epigastric pain and melaena.

stem: An 81-year-old man with atrial fibrillation who takes apixaban is brought to the emergency department after collapsing in the bathroom at night. He is pale and clammy, with a fast pulse and low blood pressure. On rectal examination there is black, tarry stool on the glove, and he takes no iron supplements. What is the most likely cause of his collapse?

options.C: Postural hypotension from his antihypertensive medicines

why_correct: Black, tarry stool on rectal examination indicates melaena from an upper GI source, and pallor, tachycardia and hypotension show significant blood loss. Anticoagulation with apixaban increases both the likelihood and severity of bleeding. He needs resuscitation, urgent bloods including a crossmatch, risk scoring, withholding of apixaban and consideration of reversal if the bleed is life-threatening, followed by endoscopy.
why_wrong: A. Vasovagal syncope is brief and would not explain melaena or ongoing shock. B. An arrhythmia could cause collapse but does not explain the melaena. C. He is not described as taking antihypertensives, and although postural hypotension may contribute, but persistent tachycardia, pallor and melaena point to blood loss. E. Haemorrhoids cause fresh red blood on the paper, not black, tarry stool.
pearl: Andexanet alfa is licensed for reversal of apixaban or rivaroxaban in life-threatening bleeding, but local guidance may favour prothrombin complex concentrate.
thinking: Anticoagulated older man collapses ↓ Pale, clammy, tachycardic and hypotensive ↓ Black tarry stool on rectal examination ↓ No iron to explain dark stool ↓ Gastrointestinal haemorrhage
exam_trap: C, Postural hypotension from antihypertensives — collapse at night in an older man often has this cause, but it does not explain melaena and ongoing shock.
takeaway: In an anticoagulated patient who collapses with melaena, assume gastrointestinal haemorrhage.

stem: A GP visits an 82-year-old woman in her care home after staff report that her stools have become black and sticky and she has become unsteady on her feet. She has had oral diclofenac for knee osteoarthritis for six weeks and has mentioned mild indigestion. She takes no iron or bismuth preparations and has no change in bowel frequency. Where is the bleeding most likely to be coming from?
why_correct: Black, sticky stool is melaena, produced when blood is digested as it passes from an upper GI source, most often a peptic ulcer. Diclofenac reduces gastric mucosal prostaglandins and her indigestion supports an ulcer. Her new unsteadiness suggests significant blood loss, so she needs urgent hospital assessment and the NSAID stopping.
why_wrong: B. Diverticular bleeding usually causes painless fresh or maroon blood per rectum, not melaena. C. Haemorrhoids cause bright red blood on the paper or in the pan. D. A colorectal tumour more often causes altered bowel habit or dark red blood mixed with stool, and she has neither. E. Colitis causes bloody diarrhoea, which she does not have.
pearl: Older people taking NSAIDs should be offered gastroprotection with a proton pump inhibitor, and the lowest effective dose for the shortest time should be used.
thinking: Six weeks of diclofenac ↓ Mild indigestion ↓ Black sticky stools without iron or bismuth ↓ Melaena means digested blood from high in the GI tract ↓ Upper gastrointestinal bleeding
exam_trap: B, Diverticular bleeding — it is the commonest cause of major lower GI bleeding in older people, but it produces fresh or maroon blood rather than melaena.
takeaway: Melaena in a patient taking NSAIDs points to upper gastrointestinal bleeding.

stem: A 59-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and advanced chronic kidney disease is brought to the emergency department after two days of vomiting and abdominal pain. He is breathing deeply and rapidly, and a venous blood gas shows a severe metabolic acidosis with a very high lactate; ketones are only mildly raised. There is no evidence of sepsis or bowel ischaemia. His repeat prescription has not been reviewed for several years. Which of his regular medicines is most likely to be contributing?
why_correct: Metformin is excreted unchanged by the kidneys, so it accumulates when renal function is severely reduced, and acute illness with vomiting worsens this further. Accumulation impairs lactate clearance and can cause metformin-associated lactic acidosis, which matches his severe acidosis with high lactate. Metformin should be stopped, and he needs urgent supportive treatment, which may include haemodialysis.
why_wrong: A. Amlodipine does not cause lactic acidosis. B. Omeprazole is associated with low magnesium, not lactic acidosis. D. Atorvastatin can cause muscle toxicity but is not a cause of lactic acidosis. E. Levothyroxine does not cause metabolic acidosis.
pearl: Metformin doses should be reduced as kidney function declines and the drug stopped when it falls to a severely reduced level, so regular review of renal function is essential.
thinking: Diabetes and advanced kidney disease ↓ Vomiting worsens renal clearance ↓ High anion gap acidosis with very high lactate ↓ No sepsis or ischaemia to explain it ↓ Metformin accumulation
exam_trap: D, Atorvastatin — statins are a familiar cause of serious drug toxicity, but their danger is muscle injury, not lactic acidosis.
takeaway: Metformin can accumulate in severe renal impairment or acute illness and cause lactic acidosis.

stem: A 71-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes is booked for CT coronary angiography. On the pre-scan checklist, the radiographer sees that she takes metformin and that her latest kidney function shows moderate impairment. The radiology protocol says the decision to pause metformin around the scan depends on her renal function and the risk of contrast-related kidney injury. What is the underlying reason her kidney function matters here?

options.A: Metformin itself makes iodinated contrast more toxic to the kidney
options.B: Metformin is largely broken down by the liver, so the kidneys are irrelevant
options.C: Metformin is cleared by the kidneys, so if they are impaired it can accumulate and cause lactic acidosis
options.D: Metformin is directly toxic to renal tubules, like aminoglycosides
options.E: Metformin frequently causes acute kidney injury after contrast

correct_answer: C. Metformin is cleared by the kidneys, so if they are impaired it can accumulate and cause lactic acidosis
why_correct: Metformin is not metabolised but excreted unchanged in the urine. If iodinated contrast causes acute kidney injury in someone whose renal function is already reduced, metformin may accumulate and increase the risk of lactic acidosis. That is why her renal function and contrast risk determine whether metformin is withheld temporarily, typically restarting once renal function is confirmed stable.
why_wrong: A. Metformin does not increase the nephrotoxicity of contrast; the concern is its accumulation if kidney injury occurs. B. Metformin is renally excreted with negligible hepatic metabolism. D. Metformin is not directly nephrotoxic. E. Metformin does not itself cause acute kidney injury after contrast.
pearl: People with normal renal function having a standard dose of intravenous contrast usually do not need to stop metformin; the precaution targets those with significant renal impairment or other risk factors.
thinking: Metformin user needs iodinated contrast ↓ Existing renal impairment ↓ Contrast may worsen kidney function ↓ Metformin is renally excreted and can accumulate ↓ Risk of lactic acidosis guides withholding
exam_trap: A, Metformin making contrast more nephrotoxic — the two are linked in protocols, but the risk runs the other way: contrast harms the kidney and metformin then accumulates.
takeaway: Renal function matters with contrast because metformin is renally cleared and can accumulate, causing lactic acidosis.

stem: A community pharmacist receives a new handwritten private prescription for a 69-year-old man with psoriatic arthritis that reads 'methotrexate 15 mg once daily'. The man says he was told by the consultant that his tablets would be taken on a Friday. Before dispensing, the pharmacist checks the usual dosing for this indication. Which schedule is standard for methotrexate in inflammatory arthritis?

options.B: Once weekly, on the same day each week
options.E: Only when joint pain is troublesome

correct_answer: B. Once weekly, on the same day each week
why_correct: In inflammatory conditions such as psoriatic and rheumatoid arthritis, oral methotrexate is given as a single dose once a week, with the day of the week specified. A prescription for daily dosing is very likely an error and could cause serious toxicity, so the pharmacist should not dispense it until the prescriber has confirmed the weekly regimen.
why_wrong: A. Twice-daily dosing would rapidly cause life-threatening toxicity. C. Methotrexate is not given hourly in any rheumatological indication. D. Monthly dosing is not how methotrexate is used in arthritis. E. It is a disease-modifying drug taken regularly, not as needed for pain.
pearl: Only one strength of methotrexate tablet should normally be dispensed to a patient, to avoid confusion between strengths.
thinking: Prescription says methotrexate daily ↓ Indication is inflammatory arthritis ↓ Standard regimen is weekly ↓ Patient already expects a weekly day ↓ Contact the prescriber before dispensing
exam_trap: A, Twice daily with food — many oral drugs are given this way, but applying it to methotrexate would cause a fatal overdose.
takeaway: Methotrexate for inflammatory arthritis is given once weekly on a set day.

presentation: Missed monitoring for a high-risk medicine
stem: A 66-year-old man with bipolar disorder has taken lithium for many years. A repeat prescription request reaches his GP, who notices that he has not attended for blood tests to check his lithium level, kidney function and thyroid function for nine months despite reminders. He says he has been busy caring for his wife. What is the safest course of action?

options.A: Stop lithium permanently and inform him by letter
options.B: Arrange the overdue blood tests and a review before issuing more supplies
options.C: Increase the lithium dose because the level is probably low
options.D: Ask him to judge from his symptoms whether his kidneys are affected
options.E: Issue a further six months of supplies and check again at the annual review

correct_answer: B. Arrange the overdue blood tests and a review before issuing more supplies
why_correct: Lithium has a narrow therapeutic range and can cause kidney damage and hypothyroidism, so it should only be continued with regular monitoring. The safe step is to arrange the overdue tests and a review promptly, issuing only a short supply if needed to avoid an abrupt stop, and to explore what has made attending difficult. Prescribing further supplies without results risks undetected toxicity.
why_wrong: A. Stopping lithium abruptly without review risks relapse of bipolar disorder, and he has not been assessed. C. Changing the dose without a level could cause toxicity. D. Kidney damage and toxicity can be silent until advanced, so symptoms are not a safe guide. E. Continuing long-term supplies without monitoring defeats the purpose of the safety checks.
pearl: Lithium toxicity is precipitated by dehydration, intercurrent illness and interacting drugs such as NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors and diuretics.
thinking: High-risk medicine needing blood monitoring ↓ Monitoring overdue for months ↓ Toxicity may be silent ↓ Avoid abrupt withdrawal ↓ Arrange tests and review before issuing more supplies
exam_trap: A, Stopping lithium permanently — it seems to remove the risk, but abrupt withdrawal without review exposes him to relapse and is not a shared decision.
takeaway: Medicines that need monitoring should not be supplied long term without the monitoring being done; arrange review before further supplies.

stem: A 63-year-old woman who takes a direct oral anticoagulant for a deep vein thrombosis three months ago telephones her community pharmacy. She has just realised that she forgot to take this morning's dose and asks how to catch up. What is the most appropriate general advice?

options.A: Take two doses together at the next scheduled time
options.B: Stop the anticoagulant until she has seen her GP
options.C: Skip the next two doses to avoid bleeding
options.D: Take the missed dose whenever she remembers, even if it is time for the next one
options.E: Follow the missed-dose instructions specific to her anticoagulant and its dosing schedule

correct_answer: E. Follow the missed-dose instructions specific to her anticoagulant and its dosing schedule
why_correct: Missed-dose advice differs between DOACs because they have different half-lives and are taken once or twice daily. The correct approach is to use the instructions in the product information or patient leaflet for her particular drug, which will specify whether the dose can still be taken and when. Doubling up or stopping both expose her to avoidable harm.
why_wrong: A. Doubling the dose increases the risk of bleeding. B. Stopping anticoagulation after a recent thrombosis risks recurrence. C. Omitting further doses leaves her unprotected against clot extension. D. Taking a missed dose close to the next one effectively doubles the dose and increases bleeding risk.
pearl: Patients starting a DOAC should be given an anticoagulant alert card and specific written guidance on what to do about missed doses.
thinking: Anticoagulant dose forgotten ↓ DOACs differ in half-life and frequency ↓ Missed-dose rules vary by product ↓ Doubling increases bleeding, omitting increases clot risk ↓ Follow the product-specific instructions
exam_trap: D, Taking it whenever she remembers — this is often sensible for once-daily drugs early in the day, but applied rigidly it can lead to two doses close together and bleeding.
takeaway: For a missed DOAC dose, follow the specific product's instructions rather than a single generic rule.

presentation: Methotrexate toxicity with an interacting antibiotic
stem: A 52-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis, who takes methotrexate correctly once a week, attends the emergency department with a fever, painful mouth ulcers and widespread bruising. Ten days ago an out-of-hours GP prescribed trimethoprim for a urinary tract infection. Her joints are no worse than usual. What should be suspected?

options.A: A viral illness with coincidental aphthous ulcers
options.C: Ordinary minor mucosal side effects of methotrexate
options.D: Methotrexate toxicity with marrow suppression, needing urgent assessment
options.E: Immune thrombocytopenia unrelated to her medicines

correct_answer: D. Methotrexate toxicity with marrow suppression, needing urgent assessment
why_correct: Trimethoprim is also a folate antagonist and reduces methotrexate excretion, so the combination can cause methotrexate toxicity even at a correct weekly dose. Fever, mouth ulcers and bruising suggest bone marrow suppression with possible neutropenic sepsis. She needs an urgent full blood count, renal function, cultures, withholding of methotrexate, immediate empirical intravenous antibiotics for suspected neutropenic sepsis without waiting for the count, and specialist advice about folinic acid.
why_wrong: A. Attributing fever and bruising to a viral illness could miss life-threatening neutropenic sepsis. B. Her joints are no worse, and a flare does not cause mouth ulcers and bruising. C. Ulcers with fever and bruising indicate serious toxicity, not an ordinary side effect. E. Immune thrombocytopenia would not explain fever and mucositis, and the drug interaction is the obvious cause.
pearl: Trimethoprim and co-trimoxazole should be avoided in patients taking methotrexate because of the risk of severe marrow suppression.
thinking: Weekly methotrexate taken correctly ↓ Recent trimethoprim, also a folate antagonist ↓ Fever, mouth ulcers and bruising ↓ Suggests marrow suppression and possible neutropenic sepsis ↓ Urgent bloods and withhold methotrexate
exam_trap: A, A viral illness with aphthous ulcers — fever with mouth ulcers is common in viral infections, but on methotrexate it must be treated as toxicity until a blood count proves otherwise.
takeaway: Fever, mouth ulcers and bruising on methotrexate suggest marrow toxicity and need urgent assessment, especially after an interacting drug.

stem: A 63-year-old woman started atorvastatin after a transient ischaemic attack six weeks ago. She now describes aching in both thighs and calves, worse after climbing stairs, with no early morning stiffness and no shoulder involvement. Her inflammatory markers and thyroid function are normal. Which condition is most likely?
why_correct: Symmetrical muscle aches beginning within weeks of starting a statin are typical of statin-associated muscle symptoms, ranging from myalgia to myopathy. Normal inflammatory markers, no morning stiffness and no shoulder girdle involvement make polymyalgia rheumatica unlikely, and normal thyroid function excludes hypothyroid myopathy. Creatine kinase should be measured to grade severity and guide whether the statin is paused.
why_wrong: B. Polymyalgia rheumatica causes shoulder and hip girdle pain with prolonged morning stiffness and raised inflammatory markers. C. Fibromyalgia causes long-standing widespread pain with fatigue and poor sleep, not new symmetrical leg aches soon after starting a drug. D. Spinal stenosis causes leg pain on walking relieved by bending forward, often with back pain. E. Her thyroid function is normal.
pearl: Statin-associated muscle symptoms are more likely with higher doses, older age, hypothyroidism, renal impairment and interacting drugs.
thinking: Recently started statin ↓ Symmetrical thigh and calf aches ↓ No morning stiffness and normal inflammatory markers ↓ Normal thyroid function ↓ Statin-associated myopathy
exam_trap: B, Polymyalgia rheumatica — her age fits, but it affects the shoulders and hips with morning stiffness and raised inflammatory markers, which she lacks.
takeaway: New symmetrical muscle aches soon after starting a statin suggest statin-associated myopathy.

stem: A 66-year-old man with atrial fibrillation was started on diltiazem for rate control three weeks ago by the cardiology clinic. He has taken simvastatin 40 mg for years without problems. He now reports aching and weakness in his thighs and upper arms, making it hard to get out of a chair, and his creatine kinase is raised. He has no tingling or numbness. Which explanation is most likely?

options.D: Statin-associated myopathy from raised simvastatin levels due to diltiazem

correct_answer: D. Statin-associated myopathy from raised simvastatin levels due to diltiazem
why_correct: Diltiazem inhibits CYP3A4, the enzyme that metabolises simvastatin, so simvastatin levels rise and the risk of myopathy and rhabdomyolysis increases. The timing after starting diltiazem, proximal muscle pain and weakness and a raised creatine kinase all fit. The simvastatin should be stopped or the dose reduced in line with BNF interaction advice, or switched to a statin less affected by CYP3A4, with creatine kinase and renal function checked.
why_wrong: A. Guillain-Barré syndrome causes ascending weakness with sensory symptoms and areflexia, and creatine kinase is not usually raised. B. Polymyalgia rheumatica causes girdle pain and stiffness, not true weakness with a raised creatine kinase. C. Hypokalaemic periodic paralysis causes episodic weakness, typically in younger people, and has no link to this drug change. E. Thyrotoxic myopathy is not suggested by the history, and the new interacting drug is the obvious trigger.
pearl: Common CYP3A4 inhibitors that raise simvastatin levels include clarithromycin, erythromycin, azole antifungals, diltiazem, verapamil, amiodarone and grapefruit juice.
thinking: Long-term simvastatin ↓ Diltiazem recently added ↓ CYP3A4 inhibition raises statin levels ↓ Proximal muscle pain, weakness and raised creatine kinase ↓ Interaction-related statin myopathy
exam_trap: B, Polymyalgia rheumatica — proximal symptoms in an older adult suggest it, but true weakness with a raised creatine kinase after a new interacting drug points to the statin.
takeaway: Drugs that inhibit statin metabolism, such as diltiazem, can precipitate statin myopathy.

stem: Four weeks after his atorvastatin dose was increased to the maximum following a heart attack, a 52-year-old man presents to the medical take with severe generalised muscle pain, tender calves and thighs, weakness, and urine the colour of cola. His creatine kinase is many times the upper limit of normal and his creatinine has risen. Urine dipstick is strongly positive for blood, but microscopy shows few red cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A markedly raised creatine kinase with severe muscle pain, weakness and dark urine indicates rhabdomyolysis. A dipstick positive for blood with few red cells on microscopy reflects myoglobin in the urine, and the rising creatinine shows acute kidney injury from myoglobin toxicity. The statin should be stopped and he needs aggressive intravenous fluids and monitoring of potassium and renal function.
why_wrong: A. Glomerulonephritis causes haematuria with red cells and casts on microscopy, and does not raise creatine kinase. B. Acute intermittent porphyria causes abdominal pain, neuropathy and dark urine but not a hugely raised creatine kinase. D. Haemolysis can darken urine but would not cause severe muscle pain or a very high creatine kinase. E. Polymyalgia rheumatica causes stiffness with a normal creatine kinase.
pearl: Hyperkalaemia is an early danger in rhabdomyolysis because potassium is released from damaged muscle, so check it urgently and repeat it.
thinking: Statin dose recently increased ↓ Severe muscle pain and weakness ↓ Very high creatine kinase ↓ Dipstick blood without red cells indicates myoglobin ↓ Rhabdomyolysis with acute kidney injury
exam_trap: D, Intravascular haemolysis — it also gives dark urine with a positive dipstick, but it does not cause muscle pain or a very high creatine kinase.
takeaway: Severe muscle pain, dark urine and a very high creatine kinase on a statin indicate rhabdomyolysis.

presentation: Assessing muscle aches on a statin
stem: A 49-year-old woman of South Asian background with type 2 diabetes began atorvastatin for primary prevention two months ago. At a review with the practice pharmacist, she mentions vague, bilateral aching in her calves that started a few weeks after the statin. She has no weakness and her urine is normal in colour. What is the most appropriate initial step?

options.A: Stop all statins permanently and record her as intolerant
options.B: Reassure her that statins do not cause muscle pain
options.C: Increase the atorvastatin dose to the maximum
options.D: Assess her symptoms, consider other causes and measure creatine kinase
options.E: Start coenzyme Q10 and review in six months

correct_answer: D. Assess her symptoms, consider other causes and measure creatine kinase
why_correct: New muscle symptoms on a statin need clinical assessment of their pattern and severity, a search for other causes and contributing factors such as hypothyroidism or interacting drugs, and measurement of creatine kinase. The result guides whether to continue, pause or change the statin. Because statins give important cardiovascular benefit, she should not be labelled as intolerant without this assessment.
why_wrong: A. Labelling her intolerant without assessment may deny her an effective preventive treatment. B. Statins can cause muscle symptoms, so reassurance alone is incorrect. C. Increasing the dose before assessment could worsen any statin-related muscle problem. E. Coenzyme Q10 is not recommended by NICE for statin muscle symptoms, and delaying assessment is unsafe.
pearl: If creatine kinase is very high, the statin should be stopped; if symptoms are tolerable and creatine kinase is only mildly raised, the statin may be continued or reduced with review.
thinking: Recently started statin ↓ New bilateral muscle aches ↓ No weakness or dark urine ↓ Assess, look for other causes and check creatine kinase ↓ Decide whether to continue, pause or change
exam_trap: A, Stopping all statins permanently — it removes the side effect, but without assessment it may needlessly deprive her of important cardiovascular protection.
takeaway: New muscle aches on a statin warrant assessment and a creatine kinase measurement before deciding what to do with the statin.

stem: A 47-year-old man attends the emergency department with aching thighs and difficulty climbing stairs. He has taken simvastatin for years, and five days ago an out-of-hours GP gave him clarithromycin for a chest infection. Since yesterday his urine has looked like cola. Dipstick testing is strongly positive for blood, but microscopy shows no red cells. Which adverse drug effect is most likely?

options.A: Immune haemolysis triggered by the antibiotic
options.B: Cholestatic liver injury from the macrolide

why_correct: Clarithromycin inhibits CYP3A4, so simvastatin levels rise sharply and can cause muscle breakdown. Proximal muscle pain and weakness with dark urine that is dipstick positive for blood but has no red cells on microscopy indicates myoglobinuria. Creatine kinase should be checked urgently, the statin stopped and intravenous fluids given to protect the kidneys.
why_wrong: A. Haemolysis gives dark urine but not muscle pain and weakness. B. Cholestasis darkens urine through bilirubin and causes jaundice and itch, not proximal myalgia. C. Interstitial nephritis causes rising creatinine, often with rash and fever, without primary muscle symptoms. D. Demyelinating neuropathy causes ascending weakness and areflexia, without myalgia or pigmented urine.
pearl: Simvastatin and atorvastatin are metabolised by CYP3A4, so the BNF advises stopping simvastatin temporarily while clarithromycin or erythromycin is given.
thinking: Long-term simvastatin ↓ New CYP3A4 inhibitor (clarithromycin) ↓ Proximal myalgia and weakness ↓ Cola urine, dipstick blood but no red cells = myoglobin ↓ Statin-induced rhabdomyolysis
exam_trap: A, Immune haemolysis — dark urine after a new antibiotic suggests haemolysis, but haemolysis does not explain proximal muscle pain and weakness.
takeaway: Muscle pain with dipstick-positive urine but no red cells in a patient on a statin plus an interacting drug suggests rhabdomyolysis.

stem: At a community pharmacy, a 63-year-old woman asks to buy naproxen for a flare of lower back pain. On questioning she says she was treated for a bleeding duodenal ulcer two years ago. The pharmacist advises against it and suggests she speaks to her GP. What is the main reason for this advice?
correct_answer: C. Recurrent ulceration with gastrointestinal bleeding
why_correct: NSAIDs block cyclo-oxygenase and reduce the prostaglandins that protect the stomach and duodenal lining. A previous ulcer, especially one that bled, is one of the strongest risk factors for NSAID-related ulceration and bleeding.
