It can be life-threatening and, on the face, can involve the eye. It needs immediate oral or IV aciclovir and same-day specialist assessment, with urgent ophthalmology review if the area around the eye is affected.
why_wrong: B. Impetigo causes weeping lesions with golden crusts and usually no fever or uniform punched-out erosions. C. Contact dermatitis is itchy rather than painful and does not cause fever. D. A simple eczema flare is itchy and does not produce clustered punched-out erosions or systemic upset. E. Pompholyx causes itchy deep-seated vesicles on the palms and soles.
pearl: Monomorphic punched-out erosions on eczema are the signature of eczema herpeticum; do not wait for virology results before starting aciclovir.
thinking: Known atopic eczema ↓ Contact with a cold sore ↓ Painful clustered blisters and punched-out erosions ↓ Fever and malaise ↓ Eczema herpeticum: urgent aciclovir
exam_trap: B, Secondary impetigo of eczema — infected eczema is common, but crusted weeping skin without fever does not fit the painful punched-out erosions here.
takeaway: Painful punched-out erosions and fever in eczema mean eczema herpeticum until proven otherwise.

stem: A 47-year-old man asks his GP about a rash that has troubled him for a year. He has thick, salmon-pink plaques with well-defined edges and silvery-white scale over his lower back, in his natal cleft and behind his ears. Several fingernails show tiny pits and lifting of the nail from the nail bed. His father had a similar rash. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Well-demarcated pink plaques with silvery scale, involvement of the natal cleft and scalp margins, nail pitting with onycholysis and a family history together point to chronic plaque psoriasis. Nail changes are present in many people with psoriasis and are linked to a higher risk of psoriatic arthritis. First-line treatment is a potent topical corticosteroid combined with a vitamin D analogue.
why_wrong: A. Discoid eczema forms itchy coin-shaped, often weeping plaques on the limbs without nail pitting. B. Tinea gives annular lesions with a scaly active edge and central clearing, and does not pit the nails. D. Lichen planus causes flat-topped, purple, itchy papules on the wrists with white lacy oral lesions. E. Seborrhoeic dermatitis has greasy yellow scale in sebaceous sites and lacks thick plaques and nail pits.
pearl: Ask everyone with psoriasis about joint pain and stiffness, and screen annually with a tool such as PEST, because psoriatic arthritis can develop before it is noticed.
thinking: Thick well-demarcated plaques ↓ Silvery scale on back, natal cleft and behind ears ↓ Nail pitting and onycholysis ↓ Family history ↓ Psoriasis
exam_trap: E, Seborrhoeic dermatitis — the area behind the ears and the scalp margin are shared sites, but nail pitting and thick silvery plaques belong to psoriasis.
takeaway: Silvery well-demarcated plaques plus nail pitting mean psoriasis.

stem: A 7-year-old boy is brought to his GP by his father because of dry, itchy skin that keeps him awake. The skin in the creases of his elbows and behind his knees is red and thickened, with scratch marks. He takes a blue reliever inhaler for wheeze and has hay fever every summer. His mother has asthma. Which diagnosis best accounts for his skin problem?
why_correct: An itchy dermatitis in the flexures of a school-age child, with a personal history of asthma and hay fever and a family history of atopy, is atopic eczema. Chronic scratching causes the thickening (lichenification). Management is regular generous emollients, with topical corticosteroids of appropriate potency for flares.
why_wrong: A. Contact dermatitis follows exposure to a specific substance and is not tied to a personal and family history of atopy. B. Scabies causes nocturnal itch with burrows in finger webs and affected household contacts. C. Psoriasis mainly affects extensor surfaces with silvery plaques rather than itchy flexural eczema. E. Seborrhoeic dermatitis in children is mainly cradle cap in infants, with greasy scale on the scalp and face.
pearl: Atopic eczema, asthma, allergic rhinitis and food allergy often cluster in the same person and family, and filaggrin gene variants increase the risk.
thinking: Itchy, dry skin ↓ Flexural distribution in a school-age child ↓ Thickened skin from scratching ↓ Personal asthma and hay fever, family atopy ↓ Atopic eczema
exam_trap: B, Scabies — night-time itch in a child suggests scabies, but there are no burrows or affected contacts, and the flexural pattern with atopy fits eczema.
takeaway: Flexural itchy eczema with asthma and hay fever is atopic eczema.

stem: A 70-year-old man who enjoys gardening is reviewed in the cardiology clinic. Two months ago he was started on amiodarone for atrial fibrillation. Over the summer he has developed a burning, red rash on his face, the V of his neck and the backs of his hands. The skin under his watch strap, behind his ears and beneath his chin is unaffected. What is the most likely cause?
why_correct: A rash limited to sun-exposed skin, with sharp sparing of shaded areas such as under a watch strap, behind the ears and under the chin, starting after a new drug, points to drug-induced photosensitivity. Amiodarone is a classic cause and can also cause blue-grey skin pigmentation. Advice is strict sun protection with clothing and high-factor broad-spectrum sunscreen, and review of whether the drug is still needed.
why_wrong: B. Polymorphic light eruption usually begins in spring in younger adults as itchy papules hours after sun exposure, without a drug trigger. C. Rosacea affects the central face with flushing and papulopustules, not the hands and neck. D. Seborrhoeic dermatitis affects greasy sebaceous areas, not a light-exposed pattern on the hands. E. Pityriasis versicolor causes scaly hypo- or hyperpigmented patches on the trunk.
pearl: Common photosensitising drugs include amiodarone, tetracyclines such as doxycycline, thiazide diuretics, sulfonamides, NSAIDs and retinoids.
thinking: New drug started ↓ Rash on face, neck V and backs of hands ↓ Sharp sparing of shaded skin ↓ Amiodarone is a known photosensitiser ↓ Drug-induced photosensitivity
exam_trap: B, Polymorphic light eruption — it also appears on light-exposed skin, but it is a spring-time papular eruption in younger people without a new drug as trigger.
takeaway: A rash only on sun-exposed skin after starting a new drug suggests drug-induced photosensitivity.

stem: A 17-year-old girl attends the emergency department an hour after taking ibuprofen for period pain. She has raised, itchy, pale-centred red weals over her arms and back; individual weals fade within a few hours while new ones appear elsewhere. Her lips and tongue are not swollen, her chest is clear and her blood pressure is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Itchy raised weals that each last less than a day and move around, appearing soon after a drug, are acute urticaria. NSAIDs are a common trigger, often through a non-allergic mechanism. With no airway, breathing or circulatory compromise this is not anaphylaxis, so treatment is a non-sedating antihistamine, avoidance of NSAIDs and advice on when to seek urgent help.
why_wrong: B. Anaphylaxis requires airway, breathing or circulatory involvement, all absent here. C. A morbilliform eruption is a fixed maculopapular rash appearing days into treatment, not transient weals. D. Erythema multiforme gives fixed target lesions, typically on the hands and feet, lasting days. E. Contact dermatitis follows skin contact with an allergen and causes eczema rather than weals.
pearl: Each individual urticarial weal resolves within 24 hours; lesions lasting longer, leaving bruising or pain, suggest urticarial vasculitis.
thinking: Recent NSAID ↓ Itchy raised weals ↓ Individual lesions come and go within hours ↓ No airway, breathing or circulation compromise ↓ Acute drug-induced urticaria
exam_trap: B, Anaphylaxis to ibuprofen — hives after a drug feel alarming, but without airway, breathing or circulatory features this is urticaria, not anaphylaxis.
takeaway: Transient itchy weals after a drug with no ABC compromise are drug-induced urticaria.

stem: A 31-year-old woman tells her GP that a few times a year she feels tingling and burning at the edge of her upper lip, and within a day a small cluster of tense, painful blisters appears in the same place. They crust over and heal in about ten days. Episodes tend to follow skiing holidays and sometimes come before her period. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.E: Herpes zoster of the maxillary nerve

why_correct: A tingling prodrome followed by grouped painful vesicles at the same spot on the lip border, recurring with triggers such as strong sunlight, menstruation, stress or illness, is recurrent herpes labialis (cold sores). HSV-1 lies dormant in the trigeminal ganglion and reactivates. Most episodes need only simple measures, though topical aciclovir started in the prodrome may slightly shorten an attack.
why_wrong: A. Impetigo causes honey-coloured crusts after fragile blisters and does not recur at the same spot with a tingling prodrome. C. Aphthous ulcers occur inside the mouth on non-keratinised mucosa, not as blisters on the lip border. D. Angular cheilitis causes cracked, sore corners of the mouth rather than vesicles. E. Shingles occurs once in a dermatome with a band of vesicles, not repeated identical episodes on the lip.
pearl: Advise people with active cold sores to avoid kissing newborns and anyone with eczema, because HSV can cause severe neonatal herpes or eczema herpeticum.
thinking: Tingling prodrome ↓ Cluster of painful blisters on the lip border ↓ Recurs at the same site ↓ Triggered by sunlight and menstruation ↓ Recurrent herpes simplex labialis
exam_trap: E, Herpes zoster of the maxillary nerve — facial vesicles with pain suggest it, but repeated identical attacks on the lip are typical of herpes simplex, not zoster.
takeaway: Recurrent tingling then grouped painful blisters on the lip are cold sores from HSV.

stem: A 52-year-old man with type 2 diabetes attends the emergency department with a swollen, painful right lower leg that has developed over two days. The admitting doctor is trying to decide between cellulitis and a deep vein thrombosis. Which examination finding would most favour cellulitis?

options.A: Pitting oedema of the whole leg
options.B: Tenderness along the line of the deep veins
options.C: Calf circumference larger than the other side
options.D: Hot, red, tender overlying skin with erythema spreading up the shin

correct_answer: D. Hot, red, tender overlying skin with erythema spreading up the shin
why_correct: Cellulitis is an infection of the dermis and subcutaneous tissue, so the hallmark is obvious skin involvement: hot, tender, spreading erythema of the overlying skin, often with a portal of entry such as a toe-web crack. A deep vein thrombosis typically causes swelling and deep tenderness with little superficial redness. Both can coexist, so if DVT remains possible it should still be assessed using the Wells score and D-dimer or ultrasound.
why_wrong: A. Pitting oedema of the entire leg is a criterion in the Wells score for DVT. B. Localised tenderness along the deep venous system is a Wells criterion for DVT. C. Calf swelling compared with the other leg is a feature that supports DVT. E. Collateral superficial veins that are not varicose are a Wells criterion for DVT.
pearl: Marking the edge of the erythema with a pen lets you see whether cellulitis is advancing or responding to antibiotics.
thinking: Unilateral painful swollen leg ↓ Cellulitis versus DVT ↓ DVT features are deep: swelling, venous tenderness, collaterals ↓ Cellulitis features are superficial: hot spreading erythema ↓ Hot, spreading skin erythema favours cellulitis
exam_trap: C, Calf circumference larger than the other side — swelling is present in both conditions, but measurable calf asymmetry is a Wells criterion pointing towards DVT.
takeaway: Hot spreading skin erythema points to cellulitis, whereas swelling and deep venous tenderness point to DVT.

stem: An 80-year-old care home resident with a chronic venous ulcer on her left shin is reviewed by the out-of-hours doctor because she has become more confused and has a temperature. The skin around the ulcer and up to her knee is now hot, red, swollen and very tender to touch, with poorly defined margins. Her right leg is unchanged. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Acute, unilateral, hot, tender, spreading redness and swelling of the lower leg with fever is cellulitis, and the chronic ulcer provides a portal of entry for streptococci or staphylococci. In older people, new confusion may be the main sign of systemic infection. Her systemic features and frailty mean she needs an assessment for sepsis and is likely to need hospital admission for IV antibiotics.
why_wrong: A. Gout affects joints, classically the first metatarsophalangeal joint, rather than causing spreading shin erythema around an ulcer. C. Venous eczema is itchy, scaly and usually bilateral, without fever. D. Lipodermatosclerosis is a chronic, hard, brownish 'inverted champagne bottle' change, not acute and febrile. E. Superficial thrombophlebitis causes a tender, cord-like vein with linear redness rather than diffuse spreading erythema.
pearl: Bilateral red legs are rarely cellulitis; think of venous eczema, lipodermatosclerosis or heart failure first.
thinking: Older woman with chronic leg ulcer ↓ New fever and confusion ↓ Unilateral hot, red, swollen, tender leg ↓ Ulcer is the portal of entry ↓ Cellulitis, assess for sepsis
exam_trap: C, Varicose (venous) eczema — red skin around a venous ulcer is common, but fever, heat, marked tenderness and one-sided spread mean infection.
takeaway: Acute one-sided hot, tender, red leg swelling with fever is cellulitis.

stem: A 30-year-old mother sees her GP with a month of itching that is worst when she gets into bed. Her partner and toddler have now started scratching too. She has small red papules on the sides of her fingers and on her wrists, waistband and around her nipples. Close inspection of a finger web shows a short, wavy grey line. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Intense itch worse at night, involvement of several people in the same household, papules in typical sites such as the finger webs, wrists, waistband and nipples, and a visible burrow are diagnostic of scabies, an infestation with Sarcoptes scabiei. The itch is a delayed hypersensitivity reaction, so it begins weeks after infestation. She and all household contacts need treatment at the same time.
why_wrong: A. Atopic eczema does not suddenly spread through a household and has no burrows. B. Urticaria produces transient weals and is not passed between family members. D. Dermatitis herpetiformis gives symmetrical itchy vesicles on the elbows, knees and buttocks and is linked to coeliac disease, not contacts. E. Contact dermatitis follows exposure to a substance and is not transmissible.
pearl: Itch can continue for several weeks after successful scabies treatment; persistent burrows or new lesions, not itch alone, suggest treatment failure.
thinking: Itch worse at night ↓ Several household members affected ↓ Papules on finger webs, wrists, waistband and nipples ↓ Burrow seen ↓ Scabies
exam_trap: A, Atopic eczema — itchy papules and scratch marks look eczematous, but transmission through the household and a burrow point to scabies.
takeaway: Night-time itch shared with household contacts plus burrows means scabies.

stem: A 24-year-old man attending a sexual health clinic is diagnosed with scabies after burrows are found on his wrists and papules on his penis. He shares a flat with his girlfriend, who has a mild itch, and a flatmate who has no symptoms. He asks what needs to happen next. What advice is most appropriate?

options.A: Treat him now and treat others only if they develop symptoms
options.B: Give him a course of oral flucloxacillin
options.C: Treat him, his girlfriend and the flatmate on the same day, whether or not they itch
options.D: Use a potent topical corticosteroid alone to clear the mites
options.E: Avoid washing clothes and bedding until the itch settles

correct_answer: C. Treat him, his girlfriend and the flatmate on the same day, whether or not they itch
why_correct: Scabies spreads by prolonged close skin contact, and people may be infested for weeks before itch develops. To prevent reinfestation, the patient, his sexual partner and household contacts should all be treated at the same time, usually with permethrin 5% cream applied to the whole body and repeated after seven days. Clothes, towels and bedding used in the previous few days should be washed hot or sealed in a bag.
why_wrong: A. Contacts without symptoms may already be infested, and treating them later allows re-infestation. B. Antibiotics do not kill mites and are only needed for secondary bacterial infection. D. Steroids may ease itch but do not eradicate scabies and can mask it. E. Hot washing of recently used clothing and bedding is part of treatment.
pearl: Scabies in the genital area should prompt screening for other sexually transmitted infections.
thinking: Burrows and genital papules ↓ Scabies diagnosed ↓ Close contacts may be infested before itching ↓ Untreated contacts reinfect ↓ Treat everyone at the same time
exam_trap: A, Treat him now and treat others only if they develop symptoms — it seems proportionate, but contacts are often infested before they itch and will reinfect him.
takeaway: In scabies, treat the patient and all close contacts simultaneously, symptomatic or not.

stem: A 45-year-old woman shows her GP a lump on her upper chest that she first noticed about three years ago. It is a smooth, round, dome-shaped swelling within the skin, tethered to the skin surface but moving freely over the deeper tissues. There is a small dark pore at its top, and occasionally foul-smelling cheesy material has come out when she squeezed it. It is not painful. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A long-standing, slowly enlarging dermal swelling attached to the skin with a central punctum, from which keratin with a cheesy smell can be expressed, is an epidermoid cyst. They are benign, lined with epidermis and filled with keratin. Treatment is only needed for symptoms or cosmetic concern, by complete excision of the cyst wall, ideally when not inflamed.
why_wrong: B. A lipoma is soft, lobulated and lies beneath the skin, so it is not attached to the skin and has no punctum. C. A dermatofibroma is a small firm nodule, often on the legs, that dimples when squeezed and does not discharge. D. Nodular basal cell carcinoma is pearly with telangiectasia and may ulcerate, not a cyst with a punctum. E. An abscess is acute, hot, red and painful.
pearl: An inflamed epidermoid cyst is often sterile; incision and drainage may be needed, but definitive excision should wait until the inflammation has settled.
thinking: Slow-growing painless lump for years ↓ Within the skin and tethered to it ↓ Central punctum ↓ Cheesy keratin discharge ↓ Epidermoid cyst
exam_trap: B, Lipoma — both are slow, painless and mobile, but a lipoma is soft, beneath the skin and lacks a punctum or discharge.
takeaway: A skin-attached lump with a central punctum that discharges cheesy material is an epidermoid cyst.

stem: A 26-year-old man of Black African heritage is worried about patches of skin that have lost their colour over the past year. There are chalk-white, sharply outlined patches arranged fairly symmetrically around both eyes and over both knees. The skin is otherwise normal in texture, with no scale or itch, and a small tuft of hair on one eyebrow has turned white. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Completely depigmented, chalk-white, sharply demarcated, symmetrical patches without scale, often around body openings and over bony areas, with whitening of hair (leucotrichia), are typical of non-segmental vitiligo. It results from autoimmune destruction of melanocytes. Under Wood's light the patches show bright white enhancement, and treatment options include potent topical steroids, sun protection and camouflage, with attention to the psychological impact.
why_wrong: A. Pityriasis versicolor gives finely scaly, hypo- or hyperpigmented patches on the trunk rather than complete depigmentation around the eyes. B. Post-inflammatory hypopigmentation follows a previous rash, is partial rather than complete, and is not symmetrical. C. Tinea causes itchy scaly annular plaques. E. Pityriasis alba causes ill-defined pale, slightly scaly patches on children's faces, not sharply demarcated depigmentation.
pearl: Vitiligo patches burn easily, so advise high-factor sunscreen on depigmented skin.
thinking: Chalk-white patches ↓ Sharp edges and symmetrical ↓ No scale, no itch ↓ White hairs in the patch ↓ Vitiligo
exam_trap: B, Post-inflammatory hypopigmentation — in darker skin pale patches are often post-inflammatory, but those are partial, follow a rash and are not symmetrical chalk-white.
takeaway: Symmetrical, sharply defined, chalk-white patches without scale are vitiligo.

stem: A 59-year-old man is admitted to the acute medical unit with fever and widespread painful skin. He began allopurinol for gout two weeks ago. The skin over his trunk and limbs is dusky red and is peeling away in large sheets, affecting around half his body surface, and gentle sideways pressure shears off the top layer. He has erosions in his mouth, crusted lips and red eyes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Fever, painful dusky skin with extensive full-thickness epidermal detachment, a positive Nikolsky sign and mucosal involvement, starting weeks after a high-risk drug, is toxic epidermal necrolysis, the most severe end of the Stevens–Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis spectrum. Allopurinol is one of the commonest causes. It is a dermatological emergency: stop the drug and manage in a specialist burns or intensive care setting.
why_wrong: A. Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome mainly affects young children, splits the skin more superficially and spares the mucous membranes. C. Erythema multiforme major has typical target lesions on the limbs, limited detachment, and is usually triggered by herpes simplex. D. Bullous pemphigoid causes tense blisters in older people with a negative Nikolsky sign and little mucosal disease. E. Pemphigus vulgaris develops gradually with flaccid blisters and oral erosions, not acute sheet-like detachment after a new drug.
pearl: The SCORTEN score estimates mortality in toxic epidermal necrolysis and should be calculated soon after admission.
thinking: New high-risk drug two weeks earlier ↓ Fever and painful skin ↓ Large-area epidermal detachment with positive Nikolsky sign ↓ Mucosal erosions ↓ Toxic epidermal necrolysis
exam_trap: A, Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome — skin peeling in sheets is shared, but SSSS mainly affects children and spares the mucosa.
takeaway: Extensive painful skin detachment with mucosal erosions after a new drug is toxic epidermal necrolysis.

stem: During a routine medication review, a 52-year-old woman mentions that the white patches on her hands and around her mouth were diagnosed by a dermatologist many years ago as loss of pigment cells. She wonders whether this makes her more prone to developing further health problems. For which group of disorders should her doctor remain alert?
why_correct: Vitiligo is an autoimmune disease, and affected people have a higher rate of other autoimmune conditions, most commonly autoimmune thyroid disease, as well as type 1 diabetes, pernicious anaemia, Addison's disease and alopecia areata. Clinicians should ask about symptoms of these disorders, and checking thyroid function is reasonable, particularly if there are symptoms.
why_wrong: A. Vitiligo does not cause a prothrombotic state. B. There is no link between vitiligo and renal stone formation. C. Vitiligo does not impair immunity against bacteria. E. Gallstones are not associated with vitiligo.
pearl: Autoimmune thyroid disease is the condition most often found alongside vitiligo.
thinking: Vitiligo is autoimmune loss of melanocytes ↓ Autoimmune diseases tend to cluster ↓ Thyroid disease is the commonest association ↓ Also type 1 diabetes, pernicious anaemia, Addison's ↓ Increased risk of other autoimmune disease
exam_trap: C, Bacterial meningitis — any 'immune' disease can suggest infection risk, but vitiligo reflects autoimmunity, not immunodeficiency.
takeaway: Vitiligo is linked with other autoimmune diseases, especially thyroid disease.

stem: A 27-year-old man who has just returned from three months working in Thailand notices pale, coin-sized patches on his chest and upper back that stand out against his suntan. They are not itchy. When the GP gently scrapes one with a spatula, a fine powdery scale comes away. Several patches have merged together. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Multiple pale (or sometimes brown) finely scaly patches on the upper trunk that become more obvious when the surrounding skin tans, with fine scale on scraping and coalescence, are typical of pityriasis versicolor. It is caused by overgrowth of Malassezia yeast, encouraged by heat and humidity. Treatment is ketoconazole shampoo used as a body wash, and pigment may take months to return after the yeast is cleared.
why_wrong: A. Vitiligo is completely depigmented with no scale. C. Guttate psoriasis causes small drop-like scaly pink papules, often after a sore throat. D. Tinea corporis forms itchy annular lesions with an active raised scaly edge. E. Pityriasis rosea begins with a herald patch and then oval pink patches in a Christmas-tree pattern, and resolves in weeks.
pearl: Pityriasis versicolor often recurs, especially in hot climates, so intermittent prophylactic antifungal washes may be advised.
thinking: Pale patches on the upper trunk ↓ More noticeable after tanning ↓ Fine scale on scraping ↓ Hot, humid climate ↓ Pityriasis versicolor
exam_trap: A, Vitiligo — pale patches that show up against a tan suggest it, but vitiligo has no scale and is completely depigmented.
takeaway: Fine scaly pale patches on the trunk that stand out after tanning are pityriasis versicolor.

presentation: Squamous cell carcinoma arising in actinic keratosis
stem: A 67-year-old woman who spent many years working outdoors has had a rough, gritty patch on the back of her right hand diagnosed as an actinic keratosis. At review in the GP surgery, the patch has become a raised, firm, tender nodule over the past two months, with a thick keratin crust, and it bled after minor contact. Which diagnosis should now be considered?
why_correct: Actinic keratoses are premalignant, and a small proportion progress to invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Warning signs of transformation are induration, thickening, growth, tenderness, ulceration and bleeding. NICE advises considering a suspected cancer pathway referral for a skin lesion that raises suspicion of squamous cell carcinoma.
why_wrong: B. Seborrhoeic keratoses are benign 'stuck-on', waxy warty lesions that do not arise from actinic keratoses. C. Pyogenic granuloma is a rapidly growing, bright red, friable vascular nodule that bleeds easily but lacks thick keratin and an actinic keratosis background. D. A new viral wart is uncommon in an older adult and would not explain a known actinic keratosis becoming an indurated, tender nodule. E. Discoid eczema produces itchy coin-shaped plaques, often multiple, not a single indurated nodule.
pearl: Tenderness, induration and rapid thickening in an actinic keratosis are red flags for squamous cell carcinoma.
thinking: Known actinic keratosis on sun-damaged skin ↓ Now raised, firm and tender ↓ Thick keratin crust and bleeding ↓ Change suggests invasion ↓ Squamous cell carcinoma: suspected cancer referral
exam_trap: C, Pyogenic granuloma — bleeding nodules suggest it, but the keratin crust and evolution from an actinic keratosis point to squamous cell carcinoma.
takeaway: An actinic keratosis that thickens, becomes tender or bleeds may have become squamous cell carcinoma.

stem: A 39-year-old woman attends her GP because her partner has noticed a mole on her back. She reports that it has got noticeably bigger over the past few months. On examination it is a brown lesion about 8 mm across with a little redness at one edge; she says it itches now and again and once oozed slightly. Which of these features carries the most weight in raising suspicion of melanoma?
why_correct: In the weighted 7-point checklist recommended by NICE, the major features, each scoring two points, are change in size, irregular shape and irregular colour. Minor features, each scoring one point, are largest diameter of 7 mm or more, inflammation, oozing and change in sensation such as itch. Recent enlargement is therefore the most important of the features listed, and her total score means she should be referred on a suspected cancer pathway.
why_wrong: A. Change in sensation such as itch is a minor (one point) feature. B. Oozing is a minor feature. C. Inflammation is a minor feature. D. A diameter of 7 mm or more is a minor feature.
pearl: A weighted 7-point checklist score of 3 or more should prompt a suspected cancer pathway referral for melanoma.
thinking: Pigmented lesion with several worrying features ↓ Apply the weighted 7-point checklist ↓ Major features: change in size, shape or colour ↓ Minor features: size 7 mm or more, inflammation, oozing, itch ↓ Enlargement carries the most weight
exam_trap: D, Diameter greater than 7 mm — size feels important, but in the checklist a large diameter is only a minor feature, whereas change in size is major.
takeaway: Change in size, shape or colour of a pigmented lesion is the strongest warning sign of melanoma.

presentation: Squamous cell carcinoma in a transplant recipient
stem: A 61-year-old man who had a kidney transplant ten years ago and takes long-term immunosuppression sees his GP about a lump on the top of his right ear. It appeared about two months ago and has grown quickly into a firm, crusted nodule with a hard keratin surface that bleeds when he catches it. He has many rough, sun-damaged patches on his scalp. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A rapidly growing, keratotic, crusted nodule that bleeds, on chronically sun-damaged skin of the ear, is typical of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma. Organ transplant recipients on immunosuppression have a markedly increased risk of squamous cell carcinoma, which can behave aggressively. NICE advises considering a suspected cancer pathway referral.
why_wrong: A. Basal cell carcinoma grows slowly over months to years and is pearly with rolled edges and telangiectasia rather than heavily keratotic. C. Amelanotic melanoma is a pink nodule without a keratin crust and is far less common. D. Actinic keratosis is a flat or slightly raised rough patch, not a rapidly enlarging firm nodule. E. Seborrhoeic keratosis is a benign, stuck-on, warty lesion that does not grow quickly or become indurated.
pearl: Immunosuppressed transplant recipients need regular skin surveillance and strict sun protection because of their high risk of squamous cell carcinoma.
thinking: Long-term immunosuppression ↓ Sun-damaged skin of the ear and scalp ↓ Rapidly growing firm keratotic nodule ↓ Bleeds on contact ↓ Squamous cell carcinoma
exam_trap: A, Basal cell carcinoma — it is the commonest skin cancer, but it grows slowly and lacks the thick keratin crust; transplant recipients get far more squamous cell carcinomas.
takeaway: A fast-growing, crusted, keratotic nodule on sun-damaged skin is squamous cell carcinoma until proven otherwise.

stem: A 12-year-old boy who bites his nails is brought to the GP by his father because of a cauliflower-like, rough growth beside the nail of his right index finger. It has slowly enlarged over several months, is painless, and paring the surface reveals tiny black dots. Which organism is responsible?
why_correct: A slowly growing, rough, hyperkeratotic papule around the nail in a nail-biter is a periungual common wart. The black dots on paring are thrombosed capillaries, typical of a wart. Common warts are caused by human papillomavirus infecting keratinocytes, and nail biting spreads the virus into damaged skin.
why_wrong: A. Molluscum causes smooth, pearly, umbilicated papules rather than rough keratotic growths. C. Herpes simplex around the finger (herpetic whitlow) causes painful grouped vesicles. D. Staphylococcus aureus causes acute painful paronychia with pus, not a chronic keratotic growth. E. Trichophyton rubrum causes tinea and onychomycosis with scaling or nail thickening, not a warty papule.
pearl: Most common warts in children resolve spontaneously within about two years, so treatment is optional and usually reserved for painful or troublesome lesions.
thinking: Chronic, painless, rough growth beside the nail ↓ Black dots on paring are thrombosed capillaries ↓ Nail biting damages skin and spreads infection ↓ Clinical diagnosis is a periungual common wart ↓ Common warts are caused by human papillomavirus
exam_trap: C, Herpes simplex virus type 1 — finger infection in a nail-biter suggests herpetic whitlow, but that is acutely painful and vesicular, not a slow keratotic growth.
takeaway: A rough, keratotic papule with black dots on paring is a wart caused by human papillomavirus.

stem: A 63-year-old retired farmer mentions to the practice nurse during a blood pressure check that a mole on his left forearm looks different. His wife has noticed over the last few months that it has become larger, its outline is now uneven and it has developed a darker patch. It does not itch or bleed and he is otherwise well. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Freeze the lesion with liquid nitrogen at the surgery
options.B: Refer on a suspected cancer pathway for assessment of possible melanoma
options.C: Reassure him because the lesion is not itching or bleeding
options.D: Take a shave sample at the surgery and await histology
options.E: Photograph the lesion and review it in three months

correct_answer: B. Refer on a suspected cancer pathway for assessment of possible melanoma
why_correct: A pigmented lesion that has changed in size, shape and colour has three major features on the weighted 7-point checklist, which makes melanoma a real possibility. NICE NG12 advises a suspected cancer pathway referral for a pigmented lesion scoring 3 or more, and dermoscopy and excision should be done by the specialist team. His outdoor occupation adds to his risk.
why_wrong: A. Cryotherapy destroys the lesion and prevents histological diagnosis of a possible melanoma. C. Many melanomas never itch or bleed, so their absence gives no reassurance. D. Partial or shave sampling in primary care risks inaccurate staging; suspicious lesions should be excised by specialists. E. Watchful waiting is inappropriate when a lesion has already shown change in size, shape and colour.
pearl: Breslow thickness of the excised melanoma is the most important prognostic factor, which is why suspicious lesions should be removed whole with a narrow margin rather than shaved or biopsied partially.
thinking: Pigmented lesion with recent change ↓ Change in size, shape and colour are major checklist features ↓ Score well above the referral threshold ↓ Melanoma must be excluded ↓ Urgent suspected cancer referral, no destructive or partial treatment in primary care
exam_trap: C, Reassuring because it does not itch or bleed — these are only minor features and melanoma is frequently symptom-free, so their absence does not lower concern.
takeaway: A pigmented lesion that has changed in size, shape or colour needs suspected cancer pathway referral for possible melanoma.

stem: An 81-year-old care home resident has several raised lesions on her back that a carer spotted while helping her wash. The GP finds well-circumscribed, warty, greasy-looking tan to dark brown plaques that look as if they have been pressed onto the surface, some with small keratin plugs. The resident says she has had them for years and they occasionally catch on her clothes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Multiple long-standing, greasy, warty brown plaques with a stuck-on look and keratin plugs on the trunk of an older adult are classic seborrhoeic keratoses. They are benign proliferations of epidermal keratinocytes and increase in number with age. They need no treatment unless irritated, or unless the diagnosis is uncertain.
why_wrong: A. Nodular melanoma is usually a single, rapidly growing, firm dark nodule, often with bleeding, not multiple long-standing stuck-on plaques. C. Pigmented basal cell carcinoma tends to be pearly with rolled edges and telangiectasia. D. Actinic keratoses are rough, scaly, pink lesions on sun-exposed skin such as the scalp and face. E. A dermatofibroma is a firm, single dermal nodule on the limbs that dimples on pinching.
pearl: The sudden eruption of many seborrhoeic keratoses (Leser-Trélat sign) can rarely signal an internal malignancy, especially gastrointestinal adenocarcinoma.
thinking: Older adult with multiple long-standing lesions ↓ Greasy, warty, brown and stuck-on appearance ↓ Keratin plugs on the surface ↓ Benign epidermal growth ↓ Seborrhoeic keratosis
exam_trap: A, Nodular melanoma — dark raised lesions in an older person prompt worry, but these are multiple, long-standing and stuck-on rather than a single changing nodule.
takeaway: A greasy, warty, stuck-on brown plaque in an older adult is a seborrhoeic keratosis.

stem: A 47-year-old lorry driver with type 2 diabetes calls into the minor injuries unit with a throbbing lump on the back of his neck that appeared four days ago. There is a single tender, hot, red nodule centred on a hair, with a yellow point at its tip. He has no fever and the surrounding skin is not spreading red. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A single, tender, pus-pointing nodule centred on one hair follicle is a furuncle (boil), a deep staphylococcal infection of the follicle. Friction from clothing on the neck and diabetes are risk factors. Small boils usually settle with warm compresses and drain spontaneously or after incision.
why_wrong: A. An infected epidermoid cyst arises from a pre-existing cyst, often with a punctum and a long history, rather than starting acutely around a hair. B. A carbuncle is a larger, multi-headed collection of linked furuncles, often with systemic upset. C. Cellulitis is diffuse spreading erythema without a pointing follicular collection. D. Hidradenitis suppurativa causes recurrent nodules in flexures such as the axillae and groin, not a single neck boil.
pearl: Recurrent boils should prompt testing for diabetes and consideration of Panton-Valentine leukocidin producing Staphylococcus aureus, particularly if close contacts are also affected.
thinking: Acute, single, tender nodule ↓ Centred on a hair follicle with a pus point ↓ No spreading erythema or fever ↓ Deep follicular staphylococcal infection ↓ Furuncle
exam_trap: B, Carbuncle — the neck is a common site for carbuncles, but these are larger and have several draining heads, whereas this is a single follicular nodule.
takeaway: A single painful, pus-pointing nodule centred on a hair follicle is a furuncle.

stem: A 58-year-old man is seen in the pre-operative assessment clinic before a knee replacement. The nurse notices thick, salmon-pink plaques with silvery-white scale over both knees and a similar linear plaque running along an old appendicectomy scar. Several fingernails show small pits. He says the patches have come and gone for years. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Well-defined salmon-pink plaques with silvery scale on the extensor knees, nail pitting and a lesion appearing along a scar (the Koebner phenomenon) together indicate chronic plaque psoriasis. The relapsing course over years also fits. Plaques near a planned surgical site are relevant as active psoriasis can increase wound complications.
why_wrong: A. Discoid eczema produces coin-shaped, crusted, often weeping patches without silvery scale or nail pitting. B. Tinea corporis gives annular lesions with an active scaly edge and central clearing, not symmetrical extensor plaques. D. Lichen planus has violaceous, flat-topped, polygonal papules on the wrists, with Wickham striae, though it can also koebnerise. E. Seborrhoeic dermatitis affects the scalp, face and chest with greasy yellow scale.
pearl: Koebner phenomenon, new lesions at sites of skin trauma, occurs in psoriasis, lichen planus and vitiligo.
thinking: Symmetrical plaques on extensor knees ↓ Silvery scale on salmon-pink base ↓ Lesion along an old scar suggests Koebner phenomenon ↓ Nail pitting ↓ Chronic plaque psoriasis
exam_trap: D, Lichen planus — it also koebnerises into scars, but its lesions are violaceous flat-topped papules rather than thick plaques with silvery scale and nail pits.
takeaway: Silvery-scaled extensor plaques with nail pitting and Koebnerisation point to psoriasis.

stem: A 14-year-old girl comes to a community pharmacy asking for something for her skin. She has open and closed comedones across her forehead and chin with scattered small red papules and a few pustules. She says the spots flare in the week before her period. Her cheeks are not flushed and there are no crusts. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Comedones (blackheads and whiteheads) mixed with inflammatory papules and pustules on the forehead and chin in an adolescent are diagnostic of acne vulgaris. Hormonal fluctuation before menstruation commonly worsens acne. Comedones are the key lesion that separates acne from look-alike facial eruptions.
why_wrong: A. Rosacea occurs in adults with flushing, erythema and telangiectasia, and comedones are absent. B. Perioral dermatitis gives small papules around the mouth, often after topical steroid use, without comedones. D. Impetigo causes honey-coloured crusted erosions, not comedones. E. Keratosis pilaris causes rough follicular papules on the outer upper arms and thighs.
pearl: Comedones are the hallmark of acne; a pustular facial rash without comedones should make you think of rosacea, perioral dermatitis or folliculitis.
thinking: Adolescent with facial spots ↓ Open and closed comedones present ↓ Inflammatory papules and pustules ↓ Premenstrual flare supports hormonal influence ↓ Acne vulgaris
exam_trap: A, Rosacea — pustules on the face can look similar, but rosacea lacks comedones and occurs in older adults with flushing.
takeaway: Comedones plus inflammatory papules in a teenager means acne vulgaris.

stem: Three weeks after returning from a backpacking trip during which she had a week of bloody diarrhoea, a 26-year-old woman attends her GP with painful, bruise-like lumps on the front of both lower legs. The lumps are warm, tender, poorly defined and do not ulcerate. Her ankles ache. She takes no regular medicines and is not pregnant. Which skin condition is she most likely to have?
why_correct: Tender, warm, poorly defined red-purple nodules on both shins that heal like a bruise without ulceration are erythema nodosum, a septal panniculitis. Gastrointestinal infections such as Yersinia, Campylobacter and Salmonella are recognised triggers, and arthralgia is common. It usually settles over weeks with rest and simple analgesia once the cause is addressed.
why_wrong: A. Pyoderma gangrenosum starts as a pustule that rapidly ulcerates with a violaceous undermined edge. B. Cutaneous vasculitis usually gives palpable purpura rather than deep tender nodules. D. Erythema multiforme causes target lesions, typically on the hands and feet, often after herpes simplex. E. Superficial thrombophlebitis produces a tender cord along a vein, usually unilateral.
pearl: Common causes of erythema nodosum include streptococcal throat infection, sarcoidosis, inflammatory bowel disease, tuberculosis, pregnancy, the combined pill and drugs such as sulfonamides; a chest X-ray to look for hilar lymphadenopathy is a standard early test.
thinking: Bilateral tender nodules on the shins ↓ Bruise-like, no ulceration ↓ Preceding bloody diarrhoea after travel ↓ Gastrointestinal infection is a known trigger ↓ Erythema nodosum
exam_trap: A, Pyoderma gangrenosum — it also occurs on the legs and is linked to bowel disease, but it ulcerates rapidly rather than resolving like a bruise.
takeaway: Tender red nodules on both shins after an infection suggest erythema nodosum.

stem: A 70-year-old widow moves into a residential home, bringing creams prescribed by her dermatologist for a skin condition on her lower back that she has had for decades. A newly employed carer asks the visiting district nurse how to recognise a flare. Which appearance would the nurse describe for this woman's plaque psoriasis?

options.B: Grouped painful blisters along one dermatome
options.C: Sharply defined red plaques covered by silvery-white scale
options.D: Flat-topped violet papules with fine white lines on the wrists
options.E: Ring-shaped patches with a scaly edge and clearer centre

correct_answer: C. Sharply defined red plaques covered by silvery-white scale
why_correct: Plaque psoriasis produces sharply demarcated, raised erythematous plaques topped by silvery-white scale, typically on the extensor surfaces, scalp, lower back and umbilicus. Removing the scale may reveal pinpoint bleeding (Auspitz sign). Recognising this pattern allows carers to report flares or new areas early.
why_wrong: A. Coin-shaped, crusted and weeping patches describe discoid eczema. B. Grouped painful vesicles in one dermatome describe shingles. D. Flat-topped violaceous papules with Wickham striae on the wrists describe lichen planus. E. Annular lesions with a scaly active edge and central clearing describe tinea corporis.
pearl: Psoriasis affects up to half of patients' nails, with pitting, onycholysis and subungual hyperkeratosis, and nail disease is a marker of increased risk of psoriatic arthritis.
thinking: Long-standing psoriasis on the lower back ↓ Plaque psoriasis is the commonest form ↓ Sharp borders and erythema ↓ Thick silvery-white scale ↓ Well-defined red plaques with silvery scale
exam_trap: E, Ring-shaped patches with a scaly edge — psoriasis plaques can clear centrally as they resolve, but an annular scaly edge with central clearing is the classic description of tinea.
takeaway: Plaque psoriasis looks like sharply demarcated red plaques with silvery scale.

stem: A 39-year-old man with a high BMI who smokes asks his GP about painful boils that keep coming back under his arms and between his buttocks. Over the last three years the lumps have repeatedly drained foul-smelling fluid, and he now has rope-like scars and paired blackheads in these areas. Swabs have grown only skin flora and courses of flucloxacillin have not prevented recurrences. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Recurrent painful nodules and abscesses in several flexural sites, with sinus tracts, rope-like scarring and double-headed comedones, are typical of hidradenitis suppurativa. Smoking and obesity are strong risk factors. It is a chronic inflammatory disease of the hair follicle rather than a primary infection, explaining poor response to antibiotics given for boils.
why_wrong: A. A pilonidal sinus is confined to the natal cleft and would not explain axillary disease. B. Furunculosis produces discrete boils that heal without sinus tracts or bridging scars and should respond to treatment. C. Erythrasma is a flat, reddish-brown, non-tender patch in the folds that fluoresces coral-red under Wood's light. E. Cutaneous Crohn disease is rare and would usually be accompanied by gut symptoms.
pearl: Weight loss and stopping smoking are central to managing hidradenitis suppurativa, and prolonged courses of oral tetracyclines are first-line systemic treatment for persistent disease.
thinking: Recurrent painful nodules in axillae and natal cleft ↓ Draining sinus tracts and rope-like scars ↓ Double-headed comedones ↓ Smoking and obesity ↓ Hidradenitis suppurativa
exam_trap: B, Recurrent staphylococcal furunculosis — repeated boils are the obvious thought, but negative swabs, sinus tracts and multi-site flexural scarring point to hidradenitis.
takeaway: Recurrent flexural nodules with sinus tracts and scarring indicate hidradenitis suppurativa.

stem: A 20-year-old male apprentice chef attends a GP appointment because of spots on his chest and shoulders that make him self-conscious when changing at the gym. Examination shows numerous blackheads with tender red papules and pustules over the upper chest, shoulders and back. His face is relatively spared. There is no fever and the lesions are not crusted. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Comedones mixed with inflammatory papules and pustules on the chest, shoulders and back are acne vulgaris; the trunk is a sebaceous area and is often involved even when the face is mild. Comedones are the feature that distinguishes acne from other follicular eruptions. Truncal acne often needs systemic treatment because topical agents are hard to apply to the back.
why_wrong: A. Pityrosporum folliculitis causes itchy, uniform small papules and pustules on the upper trunk without comedones. C. Guttate psoriasis gives small, scaly, drop-shaped plaques after a streptococcal sore throat. D. Bullous impetigo causes flaccid blisters that leave crusted erosions. E. Miliaria rubra (prickly heat) gives tiny itchy papules in hot conditions but no comedones.
pearl: Truncal acne with scarring or failure to respond to topical treatment is an indication for an oral tetracycline combined with a topical retinoid or benzoyl peroxide.
thinking: Young man with truncal spots ↓ Blackheads present ↓ Inflammatory papules and pustules ↓ Sebaceous areas: chest, shoulders and back ↓ Acne vulgaris
exam_trap: A, Pityrosporum folliculitis — it also affects the upper trunk in young men who sweat, but it is itchy, monomorphic and has no comedones.
takeaway: Comedones with papules and pustules on the trunk are still acne vulgaris.

stem: A 19-year-old man sends his GP photographs through an online consultation. They show raised, sharply bordered red patches with thick silvery scale on the backs of both elbows and over both knees, and heavy scaling that extends just beyond his hairline at the back of his head. His father has a similar rash. The patches are only mildly itchy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Symmetrical, sharply demarcated red plaques with thick silvery scale on the extensor elbows and knees, together with scalp scale extending beyond the hairline, are typical of plaque psoriasis. A first-degree relative with similar lesions supports the diagnosis, as psoriasis has a strong genetic component. Itch is usually mild compared with eczema.
why_wrong: A. Seborrhoeic dermatitis has greasy yellowish scale on the scalp, face and chest and does not cause extensor plaques. C. Tinea corporis gives asymmetric annular lesions with central clearing. D. Atopic eczema in adults favours the flexures, is very itchy and has poorly defined borders. E. Pityriasis rosea starts with a herald patch followed by oval lesions in a Christmas-tree pattern on the trunk.
pearl: Psoriasis is associated with obesity, cardiovascular disease, depression and psoriatic arthritis, so NICE advises screening for arthritis annually using a validated tool such as PEST.
thinking: Symmetrical extensor plaques ↓ Sharp borders with thick silvery scale ↓ Scalp scale beyond the hairline ↓ Positive family history ↓ Psoriasis
exam_trap: A, Seborrhoeic dermatitis — scalp scaling suggests it, but psoriatic scalp plaques are thick and well defined and the extensor plaques cannot be explained by seborrhoeic dermatitis.
takeaway: Silvery-scaled extensor plaques with scalp involvement and a family history mean psoriasis.

stem: A 33-year-old woman is reviewed at a contraception clinic two months after stopping her combined pill. Since then she has developed tender inflamed papules and pustules along her jawline and lower cheeks, with several blackheads and whiteheads. She does not flush with alcohol or heat and has not used steroid creams. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Comedones with inflammatory papules and pustules along the jawline are acne vulgaris, which commonly persists or appears in adult women. Stopping a combined pill can unmask acne because its oestrogen component had been suppressing androgen-driven sebum production. Features of polycystic ovary syndrome, such as hirsutism or irregular periods, are worth asking about.
why_wrong: A. Rosacea has flushing, background erythema and telangiectasia, without comedones. C. Perioral dermatitis gives small papules around the mouth, often after topical steroids, without comedones. D. Bacterial folliculitis gives follicular pustules, often after shaving, but not comedones. E. Seborrhoeic dermatitis causes greasy scaling around the nose, eyebrows and scalp rather than pustules.
pearl: In women with acne, a combined oral contraceptive can be added to topical treatment and is a useful option when contraception is also wanted.
thinking: Adult woman with jawline spots ↓ Comedones present ↓ Inflammatory papules and pustules ↓ Onset after stopping the combined pill ↓ Acne vulgaris
exam_trap: A, Rosacea — papules and pustules in an adult woman suggest rosacea, but there is no flushing or telangiectasia and comedones are present.
takeaway: Comedones in an adult with facial papules and pustules mean acne vulgaris, not rosacea.

stem: A 36-year-old woman shows the practice nurse a pea-sized lump on her lower leg that she first noticed after shaving nicked the skin a year ago. It is firm, slightly raised, pinkish-brown and has not changed since. When the skin on either side is squeezed together the lesion sinks below the surface. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A small, firm, stable pinkish-brown papule on the leg that dimples inward when pinched (the dimple sign) is a dermatofibroma. These benign fibrohistiocytic lesions often follow minor trauma such as an insect bite or shaving cut. No treatment is needed unless the diagnosis is uncertain or the lesion is troublesome.
why_wrong: A. Nodular basal cell carcinoma is pearly with rolled edges and telangiectasia, usually on sun-exposed skin of the head and neck. B. Amelanotic melanoma would typically be growing or changing, and does not dimple. C. An epidermoid cyst is a mobile subcutaneous swelling, often with a punctum, and bulges rather than dimples. D. Pyogenic granuloma is a rapidly growing, friable red nodule that bleeds easily.
pearl: A dermatofibroma that is enlarging, irregular or unusually large should be referred, as dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans can mimic it.
thinking: Firm, small papule on the leg ↓ Followed minor trauma ↓ Stable for a year ↓ Positive dimple sign on pinching ↓ Dermatofibroma
exam_trap: C, Epidermoid cyst — it is also a firm, long-standing lump, but it lies deeper, may have a punctum and does not dimple on lateral compression.
takeaway: A firm leg papule that dimples when pinched is a dermatofibroma.

stem: A 27-year-old man returns from a summer working holiday in Spain and books a GP appointment because his tan looks patchy. On his chest, upper back and shoulders there are numerous oval, pale, coalescing macules with a fine branny scale that becomes more obvious when the skin is scraped lightly. They are not itchy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Multiple pale, slightly scaly, coalescing macules on the upper trunk of a young adult, made more obvious after a tan, are typical of pityriasis versicolor. It is caused by overgrowth of the Malassezia yeast, which interferes with melanin production and leaves hypopigmented patches. Heat and sweating favour the yeast, and gentle scraping accentuates the fine scale.
why_wrong: B. Pityriasis alba gives poorly defined pale patches on the face of children with atopy, not the trunk of an adult. C. Vitiligo causes completely depigmented, chalk-white patches without scale. D. Pityriasis rosea has a herald patch followed by pink oval lesions with collarette scale. E. Guttate psoriasis causes small red scaly papules, often after a streptococcal sore throat, not pale macules.
pearl: Pityriasis versicolor is treated with ketoconazole shampoo applied to the affected skin, and the pale patches can take months to repigment even after the yeast is cleared.
thinking: Young adult after hot weather ↓ Pale macules on the upper trunk ↓ Fine scale accentuated by scraping ↓ Malassezia overgrowth ↓ Pityriasis versicolor
exam_trap: C, Vitiligo — pale patches that become obvious after tanning suggest it, but vitiligo is fully depigmented and has no scale.
takeaway: Pale, finely scaly patches on the upper trunk that show up after a tan are pityriasis versicolor.

stem: A 34-year-old warehouse worker tells her GP that deep, red, painful and itchy swellings appear on her shoulders about four to six hours after carrying heavy boxes on a strap, and across her waist after wearing a tight belt. Each swelling lasts more than a day. Between episodes her skin is normal and she has had no breathing difficulty, abdominal attacks or family history of swelling. Which condition best explains these symptoms?
why_correct: Deep, painful swellings appearing several hours after sustained pressure, at sites such as strap and belt areas, and lasting more than 24 hours are characteristic of delayed pressure urticaria. It is a form of chronic inducible urticaria. Higher-dose non-sedating antihistamines help less than in other urticarias, so avoiding pressure is important.
why_wrong: A. Hereditary angioedema causes non-itchy swelling without redness or weals, usually with a family history and attacks involving the gut or airway. B. Dermatographism produces linear weals within minutes of stroking the skin that fade within an hour. C. Contact dermatitis is an itchy eczematous rash at sites of allergen or irritant exposure, not deep swelling. D. Cholinergic urticaria produces tiny itchy weals with heat, exercise or sweating.
pearl: Inducible urticarias are diagnosed by provocation tests that reproduce the trigger, such as stroking for dermatographism or a weighted strap for delayed pressure urticaria.
thinking: Swelling at sites of sustained pressure ↓ Delay of several hours after the trigger ↓ Lasts more than a day ↓ Normal skin between episodes ↓ Delayed pressure urticaria
exam_trap: B, Dermatographism — it is the commonest physical urticaria and is triggered by pressure, but its weals appear within minutes and resolve quickly.
takeaway: Painful swelling hours after sustained pressure suggests delayed pressure urticaria.

stem: A 69-year-old woman has been nursed in bed on an orthopaedic ward for two weeks after a complicated pelvic fracture. A ward nurse asks the junior doctor to look at a wound on her right heel. The full thickness of skin has been lost and yellow fatty tissue lies in the base, but there is no slough or eschar obscuring the depth and no muscle, tendon or bone can be seen. How should this wound be classified?
why_correct: Full-thickness skin loss with visible subcutaneous fat, but no exposed muscle, tendon or bone, defines a category 3 pressure ulcer. The base is fully visible, so it can be staged. Prolonged immobility after a fracture makes the heel a classic pressure site.
why_wrong: A. An unstageable ulcer is one whose base is hidden by slough or eschar, which is not the case here. C. A category 2 ulcer involves partial-thickness loss, such as a shallow open ulcer or intact blister, without visible fat. D. A category 4 ulcer exposes bone, tendon or muscle. E. Moisture-associated skin damage is superficial and caused by incontinence or sweat, not full-thickness loss over a bony heel.
pearl: Every pressure ulcer of category 2 or above should be reported through local incident reporting, and stable dry eschar on the heel should usually be left intact rather than debrided.
thinking: Immobile patient with heel wound ↓ Full-thickness skin loss ↓ Fat visible in the base ↓ No bone, tendon or muscle and base not obscured ↓ Category 3 pressure ulcer
exam_trap: D, Category 4 pressure ulcer — the wound is deep and full thickness, but category 4 requires exposed bone, tendon or muscle.
takeaway: Visible fat without exposed muscle, tendon or bone means a category 3 pressure ulcer.

stem: A 41-year-old man with gout was started on allopurinol by his GP two weeks ago. He now phones NHS 111 and is advised to attend the urgent treatment centre, where he is found to have a fever, sore red eyes, painful erosions inside his mouth and dusky purple patches on his trunk that are starting to blister and peel when rubbed. What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.A: Stop allopurinol and arrange urgent hospital admission under dermatology
options.B: Halve the dose of allopurinol and review in one week
options.C: Continue allopurinol and start a potent topical corticosteroid
options.D: Prescribe an oral antihistamine and review at the GP surgery
options.E: Switch allopurinol to febuxostat and give emollients

correct_answer: A. Stop allopurinol and arrange urgent hospital admission under dermatology
why_correct: Fever, mucosal erosions, conjunctivitis and dusky skin that blisters and shears with friction (positive Nikolsky sign) a few weeks after starting allopurinol indicate Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis. The culprit drug must be stopped at once, as early withdrawal improves survival. He needs urgent admission, ideally to a burns or dermatology unit with ophthalmology input.
why_wrong: B. Any further exposure to the culprit drug, even at a lower dose, worsens the reaction. C. Continuing the drug is dangerous, and topical steroids do not treat this life-threatening reaction. D. Antihistamines and outpatient review would delay urgent supportive care. E. Changing urate-lowering therapy is not the priority, and the patient needs hospital care rather than emollients alone.
pearl: Allopurinol, carbamazepine, lamotrigine, phenytoin, sulfonamides and nevirapine are among the commonest triggers of Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, usually within the first eight weeks of treatment.
thinking: New drug started within weeks ↓ Fever with mucosal erosions and sore eyes ↓ Dusky skin that blisters and peels ↓ Severe cutaneous adverse reaction ↓ Stop the drug and admit urgently
exam_trap: E, Switching allopurinol to febuxostat — removing the drug seems addressed, but this treats the gout rather than the emergency and leaves a patient with blistering skin and mucosal disease outside hospital.
takeaway: Mucosal erosions with blistering skin after a new drug mean stop the drug and admit urgently.

stem: A 72-year-old woman on a surgical ward is given her first dose of intravenous co-amoxiclav for a wound infection. Twenty minutes later she reports itching, and the nurse finds raised pale weals with red flare spreading over her trunk and arms. She speaks in full sentences, has no stridor, wheeze or lip swelling, and her blood pressure and pulse are unchanged from earlier observations. The antibiotic has been stopped. Which statement best guides the next step?

options.A: She meets the criteria for anaphylaxis and needs intramuscular adrenaline now
options.B: This is likely hereditary angioedema and needs C1-esterase inhibitor
options.C: Hives alone do not define anaphylaxis, but she needs an ABCDE assessment and observation for progression
options.D: The rash suggests sepsis, so broad-spectrum antibiotics should be escalated
options.E: She can be reassured and no further monitoring is needed now the drug is stopped

correct_answer: C. Hives alone do not define anaphylaxis, but she needs an ABCDE assessment and observation for progression
why_correct: Anaphylaxis requires life-threatening airway, breathing or circulation problems, usually with skin changes, so widespread urticaria with normal observations does not meet the Resuscitation Council UK definition. Skin features can be the first sign of an evolving reaction, so she should be assessed systematically and observed for progression, with a non-sedating antihistamine for symptoms. The reaction should be documented as a penicillin allergy.
why_wrong: A. Adrenaline is indicated when there are airway, breathing or circulation problems, which she does not have. B. Hereditary angioedema causes swelling without weals and is not triggered by a first antibiotic dose. D. Weals appearing minutes after a new antibiotic indicate an allergic reaction, not sepsis. E. Reactions can progress, so she still needs observation and allergy documentation.
pearl: Skin and mucosal changes are absent in up to a fifth of cases of anaphylaxis, so airway, breathing and circulation problems are what define it, not the rash.
thinking: New intravenous antibiotic followed by weals ↓ No airway, breathing or circulation compromise ↓ Does not meet the definition of anaphylaxis ↓ Reaction may still progress ↓ Assess fully and observe, treat symptoms
exam_trap: A, Intramuscular adrenaline now — an acute reaction to penicillin feels like anaphylaxis, but without airway, breathing or circulation problems adrenaline is not indicated.
takeaway: Urticaria alone is not anaphylaxis, but the patient must be assessed and watched for progression.

stem: A 38-year-old man calls NHS 111 an hour after eating a prawn curry at a restaurant. He describes raised, very itchy blotches that look like nettle stings, which keep appearing in new places on his chest and legs while earlier ones fade. He has no swelling of the lips or tongue, no difficulty breathing or swallowing and does not feel faint. What type of skin reaction is he describing?
why_correct: Itchy, raised weals like nettle stings that move around, with individual lesions fading within hours, describe urticaria. Shellfish is a common food trigger of acute IgE-mediated urticaria. The absence of airway, breathing or circulation features means this is not anaphylaxis, and a non-sedating antihistamine is the usual first-line treatment.
why_wrong: B. Contact dermatitis is an eczematous rash at the site of skin contact that lasts days, not migrating weals. C. Erythema multiforme causes fixed target lesions, often on the hands and feet, lasting a week or more. D. A morbilliform drug eruption is a fixed measles-like rash appearing days after a new drug. E. Cellulitis is a localised, tender, hot area of spreading erythema, usually on one limb.
pearl: Individual urticarial weals typically resolve within 24 hours; lesions that persist longer, leave bruising or burn rather than itch should raise suspicion of urticarial vasculitis.
thinking: Food trigger shortly before onset ↓ Itchy raised weals that come and go ↓ Individual lesions fade within hours ↓ No airway, breathing or circulation problems ↓ Acute urticaria, not anaphylaxis
exam_trap: C, Erythema multiforme — both cause raised red lesions after a trigger, but erythema multiforme lesions are fixed targets that last days rather than migrating weals.
takeaway: Itchy, transient, migrating weals after a food trigger are urticaria.

stem: A 29-year-old woman is reviewed on the neurosurgical ward two days after removal of a pituitary tumour. She is passing large volumes of pale urine and keeps asking for water. Her capillary glucose is normal, her serum sodium is rising and her urine osmolality is low. Deficiency of which hormone best explains this?
why_correct: Polyuria with dilute urine, thirst and a rising sodium after pituitary surgery, with normal glucose, indicate cranial diabetes insipidus. Antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin) from the posterior pituitary inserts aquaporin-2 channels in the collecting ducts to reabsorb free water, so its lack causes dilute polyuria. Treatment is desmopressin, with careful fluid and sodium monitoring.
why_wrong: B. Aldosterone controls sodium reabsorption and potassium excretion; deficiency causes hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia rather than dilute polyuria. C. Cortisol deficiency causes hypotension and hyponatraemia and can actually mask diabetes insipidus. D. Atrial natriuretic peptide promotes sodium and water loss, so a lack would not cause polyuria. E. Insulin deficiency causes osmotic polyuria with high glucose, which is excluded here.
pearl: Diabetes insipidus after pituitary surgery can follow a triphasic pattern: early diabetes insipidus, then a phase of inappropriate ADH release with hyponatraemia, then permanent diabetes insipidus.
thinking: Pituitary surgery ↓ Large volumes of dilute urine and thirst ↓ Normal glucose, rising sodium ↓ Loss of free-water reabsorption ↓ Antidiuretic hormone deficiency
exam_trap: C, Cortisol — hypopituitarism after surgery makes adrenal insufficiency a real risk, but it causes hypotension and low sodium, not dilute polyuria with rising sodium.
takeaway: Dilute polyuria with a rising sodium after pituitary surgery reflects lack of antidiuretic hormone.

stem: A 74-year-old woman with multiple myeloma is admitted to the haematology ward from her care home because she has become drowsy and complains of abdominal pain. Blood tests show a markedly raised adjusted calcium with worsening renal function. Which feature is most directly caused by this electrolyte disturbance?

options.A: Prolonged QT interval on the ECG

correct_answer: E. Passing large volumes of urine
why_correct: Hypercalcaemia impairs the ability of the renal collecting duct to respond to antidiuretic hormone, causing a nephrogenic diabetes insipidus picture with polyuria. The resulting water loss and dehydration then worsen renal function and calcium further. Myeloma causes hypercalcaemia through osteoclast-activating bone destruction.
why_wrong: A. A prolonged QT interval is a feature of hypocalcaemia; high calcium shortens the QT interval. B. Carpopedal spasm is a feature of low, not high, calcium. C. Hypoglycaemia is not a feature of hypercalcaemia. D. Laryngeal stridor from laryngospasm occurs with severe hypocalcaemia.
pearl: Initial treatment of symptomatic hypercalcaemia is generous intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride for rehydration, followed by an intravenous bisphosphonate once the patient is filled.
thinking: Myeloma with drowsiness and abdominal pain ↓ Markedly raised calcium ↓ Calcium blocks the renal response to antidiuretic hormone ↓ Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus picture ↓ Polyuria
exam_trap: B, Carpopedal spasm — calcium disorders bring neuromuscular signs to mind, but tetany and spasm reflect hypocalcaemia, whereas high calcium causes weakness and reduced reflexes.
takeaway: Hypercalcaemia causes polyuria by blunting the kidney's response to antidiuretic hormone.

stem: A 55-year-old man is told by his GP that routine blood tests arranged for his annual hypertension review show a raised adjusted calcium with a parathyroid hormone that is not suppressed. He had a kidney stone two years ago. The GP asks him about symptoms. Which of the following would be most consistent with this result?

options.B: Twitching of the face when the cheek is tapped

why_correct: A raised calcium with an unsuppressed parathyroid hormone and a past kidney stone suggests primary hyperparathyroidism. High calcium reduces smooth-muscle and neuromuscular excitability, leading to constipation, along with thirst, polyuria, abdominal pain, low mood and fatigue. The classic summary is stones, bones, abdominal groans and psychic moans.
why_wrong: A. Perioral tingling is a feature of hypocalcaemia. B. Facial twitching on tapping (Chvostek sign) indicates hypocalcaemia. C. Diarrhoea is not typical of hypercalcaemia, which slows gut motility. D. Hand spasm (carpopedal spasm) occurs with low calcium.
pearl: Primary hyperparathyroidism is the commonest cause of hypercalcaemia in the community, whereas malignancy is the commonest cause in hospital inpatients.
thinking: Raised calcium with unsuppressed parathyroid hormone ↓ Previous renal stone ↓ Likely primary hyperparathyroidism ↓ High calcium reduces gut motility ↓ Constipation
exam_trap: D, Cramping spasm of the hands — it is a well-known calcium-related symptom, but carpopedal spasm reflects hypocalcaemia rather than a high calcium.
takeaway: Constipation, thirst and polyuria are typical of hypercalcaemia; tingling and spasms point to low calcium.

stem: A 52-year-old man is referred from his dentist, who noticed widening gaps between his lower teeth and a protruding jaw. He says his wedding ring no longer fits and he sweats heavily. At the GP practice his HbA1c is found to be in the prediabetic range. Excess of which hormone is the underlying cause?
why_correct: Prognathism, spacing of the teeth, enlarging hands and excessive sweating are classic features of acromegaly, almost always caused by a growth hormone-secreting pituitary adenoma. Growth hormone antagonises insulin action, producing insulin resistance and impaired glucose tolerance or diabetes. Diagnosis is by a raised IGF-1 and failure of growth hormone to suppress during an oral glucose tolerance test.
why_wrong: A. Excess cortisol also causes glucose intolerance, but with central obesity, striae and proximal weakness rather than jaw and hand enlargement. B. Excess prolactin causes galactorrhoea and hypogonadism, not acral growth. C. Excess thyroxine causes weight loss and tremor, not soft-tissue overgrowth. D. Excess parathyroid hormone causes hypercalcaemia, not acromegalic features.
pearl: Acromegaly is associated with colonic polyps and carcinoma, hypertension, cardiomyopathy and obstructive sleep apnoea, so these should be screened for.
thinking: Jaw protrusion and teeth spacing ↓ Enlarging hands and sweating ↓ Prediabetic HbA1c ↓ Growth hormone causes insulin resistance ↓ Growth hormone excess (acromegaly)
exam_trap: A, Cortisol — it is the classic hormone linked with high glucose, but the coarse acral and facial changes point to growth hormone excess.
takeaway: Acromegaly results from growth hormone excess, which causes insulin resistance.

stem: A 34-year-old woman who has had type 1 diabetes since childhood attends her annual diabetes review at the GP surgery. Her blood pressure is slightly higher than last year and her eGFR is normal. An albumin-to-creatinine ratio has been raised on three early-morning samples over six months, with no blood in the urine and no symptoms of infection. What is the most likely explanation?
why_correct: Persistently raised urinary albumin excretion in someone with long-standing type 1 diabetes, before any fall in eGFR and without haematuria, is the earliest sign of diabetic nephropathy. Rising blood pressure often accompanies it. Treatment with an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker, plus tight glucose and blood pressure control, slows progression.
why_wrong: A. IgA nephropathy typically presents with visible or non-visible haematuria, often after an upper respiratory infection. B. Infection was excluded and would not cause persistent albuminuria over months. D. Orthostatic proteinuria is excluded because early-morning samples are taken after lying flat overnight. E. Renal artery stenosis causes resistant hypertension and declining renal function rather than isolated albuminuria.
pearl: The albumin-to-creatinine ratio should be measured on an early-morning sample because this avoids false positives from orthostatic proteinuria and exercise.
thinking: Long-standing type 1 diabetes ↓ Persistently raised albumin-to-creatinine ratio ↓ Normal eGFR, no haematuria ↓ Earliest sign of diabetic kidney disease ↓ Diabetic nephropathy
exam_trap: A, IgA nephropathy — it is the commonest glomerulonephritis in young adults, but it usually causes haematuria, which is absent here.
takeaway: Persistent albuminuria in long-standing diabetes is early diabetic nephropathy.

stem: Paramedics bring a 79-year-old man with type 2 diabetes treated with gliclazide into the emergency department after his daughter found him with left-sided weakness and slurred speech. He has been off his food with a chest infection. On arrival his capillary glucose is very low. Within ten minutes of intravenous glucose, his speech and arm strength return completely to normal. What is the most likely explanation?

options.D: Focal neurological deficit due to hypoglycaemia

correct_answer: D. Focal neurological deficit due to hypoglycaemia
why_correct: Hypoglycaemia can produce focal deficits such as hemiparesis and dysarthria that mimic a stroke, and these resolve promptly once glucose is corrected. A sulfonylurea combined with reduced oral intake during illness is a classic cause in older people. This is why capillary glucose must be checked in every patient with suspected stroke before thrombolysis is considered.
why_wrong: A. A lacunar stroke would not resolve completely within minutes of glucose. B. Todd paresis follows a seizure, which is not described, and does not respond to glucose. C. A TIA is a diagnosis of exclusion, and here a clear reversible metabolic cause has been found. E. Functional disorder should not be diagnosed when an organic cause explains the symptoms and responds to treatment.
pearl: Sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycaemia can recur for many hours, so these patients need admission and repeated glucose monitoring after the initial correction.
thinking: Acute focal weakness and slurred speech ↓ Sulfonylurea plus poor oral intake ↓ Very low capillary glucose ↓ Complete resolution after glucose ↓ Hypoglycaemia mimicking stroke
exam_trap: C, Transient ischaemic attack — rapid complete recovery suggests TIA, but the deficit resolved in direct response to glucose correction, giving a clear metabolic cause.
takeaway: Always check glucose in suspected stroke; hypoglycaemia can cause focal deficits that resolve with glucose.

stem: A 26-year-old woman is seen at a sexual health clinic six months after stopping her combined pill. Her periods have not returned, and she has noticed a white fluid leaking from both nipples that stains her bra. Two pregnancy tests have been negative. She takes no other medicines. Which hormonal disturbance best explains her symptoms?
why_correct: Absent periods with bilateral milky nipple discharge in a non-pregnant woman suggest hyperprolactinaemia. Prolactin suppresses hypothalamic gonadotrophin-releasing hormone, reducing LH and FSH and causing amenorrhoea, while directly stimulating milk production. Serum prolactin, thyroid function and a medication review are the next steps.
why_wrong: A. Raised parathyroid hormone causes hypercalcaemia with stones, bone pain and constipation. B. Raised aldosterone causes hypertension and hypokalaemia. C. Lack of antidiuretic hormone causes polyuria and thirst. D. Low calcium causes tingling and muscle spasm, not galactorrhoea.
pearl: Primary hypothyroidism can raise prolactin because high TRH stimulates lactotrophs, so thyroid function should be checked in anyone with hyperprolactinaemia.
thinking: Amenorrhoea after stopping the pill ↓ Bilateral milky nipple discharge ↓ Pregnancy excluded ↓ Prolactin suppresses GnRH and drives lactation ↓ Hyperprolactinaemia
exam_trap: C, Deficiency of antidiuretic hormone — both conditions involve the pituitary, but lack of antidiuretic hormone causes dilute polyuria, not menstrual change or galactorrhoea.
takeaway: Amenorrhoea with galactorrhoea in a non-pregnant woman points to hyperprolactinaemia.
