stem: A 32-year-old woman is referred to a fertility clinic after two years of trying to conceive. Her periods became infrequent and then stopped altogether, and on examination expressible milky fluid is produced from both breasts. A pregnancy test is negative, thyroid function is normal, she takes no regular medicines and her serum prolactin is several times the upper limit of normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Infertility, amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea with a markedly raised prolactin, after pregnancy, hypothyroidism and drug causes have been excluded, are most likely due to a prolactinoma. This is the commonest functioning pituitary adenoma. Pituitary MRI confirms it, and a dopamine agonist such as cabergoline usually restores fertility.
why_wrong: A. Polycystic ovary syndrome causes irregular periods and infertility, but with hyperandrogenism rather than galactorrhoea and a marked prolactin rise. C. Cushing syndrome causes central obesity, striae and proximal myopathy. D. Acromegaly causes acral enlargement and coarse facial features. E. Premature ovarian insufficiency causes amenorrhoea with raised FSH and menopausal symptoms, not galactorrhoea.
pearl: A very high prolactin usually indicates a prolactinoma, whereas a modest rise with a large pituitary mass suggests a non-functioning tumour compressing the stalk.
thinking: Infertility and amenorrhoea ↓ Galactorrhoea ↓ Markedly raised prolactin ↓ Pregnancy, thyroid and drug causes excluded ↓ Prolactinoma
exam_trap: A, Polycystic ovary syndrome — it is the commonest cause of anovulatory infertility, but it does not cause galactorrhoea or a marked prolactin rise.
takeaway: A markedly raised prolactin with amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea, once secondary causes are excluded, suggests a prolactinoma.

stem: A 37-year-old woman attends a walk-in centre with frontal headaches that have been worsening for several months. On direct questioning, her periods stopped about eight months ago and she has noticed milky fluid when she presses her nipples. She is not pregnant, takes no medication and finished breastfeeding her youngest child five years ago. Which type of pituitary tumour is most likely?
why_correct: Headache with secondary amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea in a non-pregnant, non-breastfeeding woman suggests a prolactin-secreting pituitary adenoma. Lactotroph adenomas are the most common functioning pituitary tumours, and larger ones can cause headache by mass effect. Serum prolactin and pituitary MRI with visual field testing are the next steps.
why_wrong: A. Gonadotroph adenomas are usually clinically non-functioning and present with mass effect, not galactorrhoea. C. Somatotroph adenomas cause acromegaly with acral and facial enlargement. D. Corticotroph adenomas cause Cushing disease with central obesity and striae. E. Thyrotroph adenomas are rare and cause hyperthyroidism with a non-suppressed TSH.
pearl: Dopamine agonists such as cabergoline are first-line even for large prolactinomas, often shrinking them enough to avoid surgery.
thinking: Headaches suggesting a pituitary mass ↓ Secondary amenorrhoea ↓ Galactorrhoea ↓ Pregnancy, lactation and drugs excluded ↓ Lactotroph adenoma (prolactinoma)
exam_trap: A, Gonadotroph adenoma — non-functioning pituitary tumours commonly cause headache and can modestly raise prolactin, but galactorrhoea and amenorrhoea most strongly suggest a prolactinoma.
takeaway: Amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea with headache point to a prolactin-secreting pituitary adenoma.

stem: A 44-year-old man attends his GP with a year of reduced libido and erectile difficulty. More recently he has had frontal headaches and has clipped his car wing mirror twice, saying he does not notice vehicles on either side. Examination confirms loss of the outer halves of both visual fields. His serum prolactin is very high and testosterone is low. Which lesion is the most likely cause?

options.D: Clear cell carcinoma of the kidney

why_correct: A very high prolactin with hypogonadism points to a prolactinoma, a lactotroph adenoma of the anterior pituitary. Bitemporal hemianopia and headache show a large tumour compressing the optic chiasm. Men usually present late with macroadenomas because the early symptoms of low libido and erectile dysfunction are often not reported.
why_wrong: A. Thyroid carcinoma presents as a neck lump and does not produce very high prolactin. B. A cortisol-secreting adrenal adenoma causes Cushing syndrome, not hyperprolactinaemia or visual field loss. D. Renal cell carcinoma may produce erythropoietin or PTH-related peptide, but not this pituitary picture. E. Pancreatic adenocarcinoma typically causes painless jaundice and weight loss.
pearl: Dopamine agonists such as cabergoline are first-line even for large prolactinomas with visual loss, and often shrink the tumour without surgery.
thinking: Low libido and erectile dysfunction ↓ Low testosterone with very high prolactin ↓ Bitemporal hemianopia and headache ↓ Mass compressing the optic chiasm ↓ Prolactin-secreting pituitary macroadenoma
exam_trap: B, Cortisol-secreting adrenal adenoma — the word adenoma and the endocrine picture make it tempting, but adrenal tumours cannot cause chiasmal field loss or a very high prolactin.
takeaway: Very high prolactin with bitemporal hemianopia in a man indicates a pituitary prolactin-secreting macroadenoma.

stem: A 23-year-old woman attends a sexual health clinic because her periods stopped seven months ago. She has noticed a milky discharge from both nipples when she showers, although she has never been pregnant or breastfed. A urine pregnancy test is negative and she takes no regular medicines. Which endocrine disorder should be investigated first?
why_correct: Secondary amenorrhoea with bilateral milky nipple discharge outside pregnancy and breastfeeding is galactorrhoea, the hallmark of raised prolactin. Prolactin suppresses hypothalamic GnRH release, lowering LH and FSH and stopping ovulation. A serum prolactin level is the key test once pregnancy has been excluded.
why_wrong: A. Primary hyperparathyroidism causes hypercalcaemia with stones, bone pain and abdominal symptoms, not galactorrhoea. B. Diabetes insipidus presents with polyuria and thirst. D. Adrenal insufficiency causes fatigue, weight loss, pigmentation and hypotension. E. Phaeochromocytoma causes episodic headache, sweating, palpitations and hypertension.
pearl: Always check for drug causes of raised prolactin, especially dopamine antagonists such as antipsychotics, metoclopramide and domperidone, and check thyroid function because primary hypothyroidism can raise prolactin.
thinking: Secondary amenorrhoea ↓ Bilateral milky discharge not linked to pregnancy ↓ Pregnancy test negative, no causative drugs ↓ Galactorrhoea with amenorrhoea suggests excess prolactin ↓ Investigate for hyperprolactinaemia
exam_trap: D, Primary adrenal insufficiency — it is a classic endocrine cause of menstrual upset in a young woman, but it does not cause milk production.
takeaway: Galactorrhoea with amenorrhoea outside pregnancy should prompt a serum prolactin.

stem: A health visitor refers a 20-month-old boy to the paediatric clinic because his legs are bowed and he was late to walk. He has been exclusively breastfed with little solid food, has dark skin and rarely goes outside, and his mother has not been taking any supplements. His wrists look broadened and there is beading along the costochondral junctions. Deficiency of which vitamin best explains these findings?
why_correct: Bowed legs, wrist widening and a rachitic rosary are features of rickets, the failure of mineralisation of growing bone. Vitamin D is needed for gut absorption of calcium and phosphate, so deficiency leaves too little mineral for new bone matrix. Dark skin, little sunlight exposure and prolonged breastfeeding without supplements are classic risk factors.
why_wrong: A. Thiamine deficiency causes beriberi and Wernicke encephalopathy, not a bone mineralisation defect. B. Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy with bleeding gums and bone pain from subperiosteal haemorrhage, not rickets. C. Vitamin B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia and neurological signs. D. Vitamin K is needed for clotting factor production and is not the main regulator of calcium absorption.
pearl: UK advice is that breastfed babies should receive a daily vitamin D supplement from birth, and formula-fed babies need one once they take less than about 500 mL of formula a day.
thinking: Bowed legs and delayed walking ↓ Wide wrists and rachitic rosary ↓ Poorly mineralised growing bone, so rickets ↓ Risk factors of dark skin, low sunlight and no supplements ↓ Vitamin D deficiency reducing calcium absorption
exam_trap: B, Ascorbic acid (vitamin C) — scurvy also causes bone pain and refusal to walk in toddlers, but it causes bleeding problems rather than the wide wrists and bowed legs of rickets.
takeaway: Vitamin D drives intestinal calcium absorption, and deficiency in childhood causes rickets.

stem: A 14-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department by her father after a week of thirst, weight loss and passing large amounts of urine, followed today by vomiting and tummy pain. She is drowsy, her breath smells of pear drops and she is taking deep, laboured, sighing breaths. Venous blood gas shows a severe metabolic acidosis with high ketones and glucose. What is the name of this respiratory pattern?
why_correct: Kussmaul respiration is deep, laboured breathing driven by severe metabolic acidosis, as in this new presentation of diabetic ketoacidosis. Increasing the depth of each breath blows off carbon dioxide and partly compensates for the low bicarbonate. Its presence signals significant acidosis and needs urgent treatment.
why_wrong: A. Cheyne-Stokes respiration is a cycle of gradually deepening then shallowing breaths with pauses, seen in heart failure and brainstem injury. C. Biot or ataxic breathing is irregular and chaotic, suggesting medullary damage. D. Paradoxical breathing is inward movement of the chest or abdomen on inspiration, seen in flail chest or diaphragm weakness. E. Apneustic breathing has prolonged inspiratory holds and suggests pontine damage.
pearl: In children with DKA, fluids are given more cautiously than in adults because of the risk of cerebral oedema, and insulin is usually started an hour or more after fluids begin.
thinking: Polyuria, polydipsia and weight loss ↓ Vomiting, abdominal pain and ketotic breath ↓ Severe metabolic acidosis on blood gas ↓ Deep sighing breaths compensate by blowing off carbon dioxide ↓ Kussmaul respiration
exam_trap: A, Cheyne-Stokes respiration — it is the best-known named breathing pattern, but it is cyclical with pauses and is not a compensation for acidosis.
takeaway: Deep, sighing Kussmaul breathing reflects respiratory compensation for severe metabolic acidosis such as DKA.

stem: A 45-year-old woman is referred by her dentist, who has noticed new gaps between her lower teeth and that her lower jaw now juts forward. She says her wedding ring no longer fits, she sweats heavily and she has tingling in both hands at night. Comparing her face with an old photograph shows thickened lips and a more prominent brow. Excess secretion of which hormone is most likely?
why_correct: Enlarging hands, coarse facial features, prognathism with widely spaced teeth, sweating and carpal tunnel symptoms are classic acromegaly. This results from excess growth hormone after the growth plates have fused, usually from a pituitary adenoma. Growth hormone acts mainly through IGF-1, which is the first-line screening test.
why_wrong: A. ACTH excess causes Cushing disease, with central weight gain, striae and proximal weakness, not soft tissue overgrowth of the hands and jaw. B. PTH excess causes hypercalcaemia with stones and bone disease. C. TSH excess is rare and causes thyrotoxicosis with a goitre. E. ADH excess causes hyponatraemia from water retention.
pearl: Serum IGF-1 is the screening test for acromegaly, and failure of growth hormone to suppress during an oral glucose tolerance test confirms it.
thinking: Change in appearance over years ↓ Enlarged hands, prognathism and spaced teeth ↓ Sweating and bilateral carpal tunnel symptoms ↓ Soft tissue and bone overgrowth in an adult ↓ Growth hormone excess, acromegaly
exam_trap: A, Adrenocorticotrophic hormone — Cushing also changes facial appearance, but it gives a round plethoric face and weight gain, not jaw growth and enlarged hands.
takeaway: Adult acromegaly from growth hormone excess causes coarse features, enlarged hands and feet, sweating and carpal tunnel syndrome.

stem: A 19-year-old man with congenital adrenal hyperplasia is brought to the emergency department by friends from a music festival. He has had a day of profuse diarrhoea and vomiting, has not kept any of his tablets down and is now cold, clammy and very weak, with abdominal cramps. His blood pressure is low and his capillary glucose is at the lower end of normal. He carries a steroid emergency card. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.A: Intravenous fluids alone, then steroids if a random cortisol is low
options.B: Intravenous or intramuscular hydrocortisone with intravenous fluid resuscitation
options.C: Double his usual oral steroid doses and observe in the department
options.D: Intravenous antiemetic and oral rehydration solution
options.E: Oral fludrocortisone and restriction of intravenous fluids

correct_answer: B. Intravenous or intramuscular hydrocortisone with intravenous fluid resuscitation
why_correct: He depends on replacement steroids and has lost them through vomiting while unwell, causing an adrenal crisis. The treatment is immediate parenteral hydrocortisone, 100 mg IV or IM in adults, together with rapid IV fluid resuscitation with sodium chloride 0.9%, monitoring glucose. Treatment must never wait for cortisol results in a patient with known adrenal insufficiency.
why_wrong: A. Waiting for a cortisol level delays life-saving treatment, and the diagnosis is already known. C. He is vomiting and shocked, so oral steroids will not be absorbed and are inadequate. D. An antiemetic does not correct the missing cortisol and oral fluids are unsuitable in shock. E. Fludrocortisone has no role in emergency treatment, and restricting fluids would worsen his hypotension.
pearl: Steroid emergency cards and NHS guidance advise that anyone on steroid replacement who is vomiting or has diarrhoea and cannot take oral doses needs an emergency hydrocortisone injection and hospital assessment.
thinking: Known steroid-dependent condition ↓ Vomiting and diarrhoea, tablets not absorbed ↓ Shocked with abdominal pain and weakness ↓ Adrenal crisis ↓ Parenteral hydrocortisone and IV fluids without delay
exam_trap: A, Intravenous fluids alone, then steroids if a random cortisol is low — testing first sounds thorough, but delay can be fatal and the diagnosis is already established.
takeaway: In adrenal crisis give parenteral hydrocortisone and IV fluids immediately; never wait for blood results.

stem: A 74-year-old man with polymyalgia rheumatica has taken prednisolone for three years. He is on the orthopaedic ward two days after fixation of a hip fracture and has been nil by mouth for much of that time, so his morning tablets have not been given. Overnight he becomes drowsy and clammy, vomits repeatedly and complains of diffuse abdominal pain. His blood pressure has fallen and does not respond well to a fluid bolus, and his sodium is low. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Years of prednisolone suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, so the adrenals cannot respond to stress. Missing his steroid doses during the physiological stress of a fracture and surgery has precipitated an adrenal crisis, with vomiting, abdominal pain, hypotension resistant to fluids and hyponatraemia. He needs immediate IV or IM hydrocortisone and fluids.
why_wrong: A. A polymyalgia flare causes shoulder and hip girdle pain and stiffness, not shock and vomiting. C. Reflux causes heartburn and does not cause hypotension or hyponatraemia. D. Ileus causes distension and vomiting but would not explain fluid-resistant hypotension in a steroid-dependent patient. E. Fat embolism typically causes breathlessness, confusion and a petechial rash within a few days of long bone fracture, not vomiting with hypotension and low sodium.
pearl: Patients on long-term steroids who are nil by mouth around surgery need their glucocorticoid given parenterally, and extra cover is needed for the stress of the operation.
thinking: Long-term prednisolone suppresses the adrenal axis ↓ Doses missed while nil by mouth ↓ Surgical stress increases cortisol needs ↓ Vomiting, abdominal pain, refractory hypotension, low sodium ↓ Adrenal crisis
exam_trap: D, Postoperative ileus — vomiting after surgery commonly suggests ileus, but it does not explain fluid-resistant hypotension in someone whose steroids have been stopped.
takeaway: Anyone on long-term steroids who misses doses during illness or surgery is at risk of adrenal crisis.

stem: A 31-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes is 11 weeks pregnant and has been tightening her glucose control on advice from the joint diabetes antenatal clinic. Her partner says she has had several episodes recently, mostly in the late morning. She wants to know which feature would most strongly suggest an episode is due to low blood glucose rather than something else. Which feature is most characteristic of hypoglycaemia?

options.A: Gradual loss of hearing in one ear
options.B: Dark urine with yellowing of the eyes

correct_answer: D. Sudden sweating with trembling hands
why_correct: Falling glucose triggers an adrenergic response, so sweating, tremor, palpitations and hunger are the typical early warning symptoms. Confusion and drowsiness follow as the brain is deprived of glucose. Tighter control in early pregnancy increases the risk of hypoglycaemia, so recognising early symptoms matters.
why_wrong: A. One-sided hearing loss suggests an ear or nerve problem, such as a vestibular schwannoma. B. Dark urine and jaundice point to liver or biliary disease. C. Constant unilateral facial pain suggests a dental, sinus or trigeminal cause. E. Painless haematuria suggests urinary tract pathology including bladder cancer.
pearl: Pregnant women with type 1 diabetes should be offered continuous glucose monitoring and given glucagon, and their partners taught how to use it, because hypoglycaemia is more common in early pregnancy.
thinking: Type 1 diabetes with tighter control in pregnancy ↓ Episodic symptoms ↓ Low glucose triggers adrenaline release ↓ Autonomic symptoms of sweating and tremor ↓ Most characteristic early feature of hypoglycaemia
exam_trap: C, Constant one-sided facial pain — headache and facial discomfort can occur with low glucose, but a constant one-sided pain points to a local cause rather than an episodic adrenergic reaction.
takeaway: Sweating and tremor are the classic autonomic warning symptoms of hypoglycaemia.

stem: A 70-year-old man with type 2 diabetes on twice-daily mixed insulin is midway through his session at the haemodialysis unit when he becomes clammy and muddled about the date. He gave his usual morning insulin but only had a cup of tea for breakfast. A finger-prick glucose is 2.9 mmol/L. He is sitting up, talking and swallows a sip of water without coughing. What is the most appropriate immediate step?

options.A: Withhold all food and fluid until the session ends
options.B: Offer plain water and recheck the glucose
options.C: Give a fast-acting oral carbohydrate such as glucose tablets or fruit juice
options.D: Give an extra dose of long-acting insulin
options.E: Send a venous sample and treat once the laboratory result is back

correct_answer: C. Give a fast-acting oral carbohydrate such as glucose tablets or fruit juice
why_correct: He is hypoglycaemic but conscious, cooperative and able to swallow safely, so the first step is 15 to 20 g of quick-acting oral carbohydrate. The glucose should be rechecked after 10 to 15 minutes and treatment repeated if still low, followed by a longer-acting carbohydrate snack. Insulin given without food, combined with reduced insulin clearance in kidney failure, explains the episode.
why_wrong: A. Withholding food would worsen the hypoglycaemia. B. Water contains no glucose and will not correct the low level. D. More insulin would drive the glucose lower and could be fatal. E. A capillary result is enough to act on; delaying for a laboratory value risks deterioration.
pearl: Insulin and sulfonylureas are cleared more slowly in advanced kidney disease, so people on dialysis are at increased risk of prolonged hypoglycaemia.
thinking: Confused and clammy on insulin ↓ Capillary glucose low ↓ Conscious and swallowing safely ↓ Quick-acting oral carbohydrate first ↓ Recheck in 10 to 15 minutes, then a starchy snack
exam_trap: E, Send a venous sample and treat once the laboratory result is back — confirming a result feels safe, but hypoglycaemia is treated on the capillary reading without delay.
takeaway: A conscious hypoglycaemic patient who can swallow safely should be given fast-acting oral carbohydrate straight away.

stem: A 22-year-old man with type 1 diabetes is found by his flatmate on the morning after a long night out drinking. He went to bed without eating and took his usual long-acting insulin. He is pale, drenched in sweat, trembling and talking nonsense, and his flatmate phones NHS 111 for advice. Which condition must be assumed first?
why_correct: Alcohol blocks hepatic gluconeogenesis, and with no food and his usual basal insulin the risk of hypoglycaemia overnight and the next morning is high. Pallor, sweating, tremor and confusion are classic features. Hypoglycaemia is quickly reversible and potentially fatal, so it must be assumed and treated while help is arranged.
why_wrong: B. DKA develops over hours to days with thirst, vomiting, abdominal pain and deep breathing, not sudden sweating and tremor. C. Withdrawal occurs after stopping prolonged heavy drinking, not the morning after a single night out. D. Hyponatraemia causes confusion but not this acute adrenergic picture. E. Thyroid storm causes fever, tachycardia and agitation in known or undiagnosed thyrotoxicosis.
pearl: After drinking alcohol, people with insulin-treated diabetes should eat carbohydrate before bed and the next morning, because the risk of hypoglycaemia persists for many hours.
thinking: Insulin-treated diabetes ↓ Heavy alcohol with no food ↓ Alcohol suppresses glucose production by the liver ↓ Sweaty, pale, trembling, confused ↓ Assume hypoglycaemia and treat
exam_trap: C, Acute alcohol withdrawal — the drinking history and tremor point there, but withdrawal follows sustained heavy use, and the insulin with no food makes low glucose far more likely and urgent.
takeaway: In anyone taking insulin who becomes sweaty, shaky and confused, assume hypoglycaemia first.

stem: A 58-year-old taxi driver with type 2 diabetes on gliclazide attends his GP practice for a medication review during Ramadan. He has been fasting from dawn and took his full usual dose this morning. While in the waiting room he becomes shaky, sweaty and slightly muddled, and a practice nurse finds a capillary glucose of 3.1 mmol/L. What should be done first?

options.B: Advise him not to drive and complete a DVLA form
options.C: Correct the low glucose and break the fast
options.D: Start basal insulin to improve control during the fast
options.E: Discuss reducing his carbohydrate intake after sunset

correct_answer: C. Correct the low glucose and break the fast
why_correct: The immediate priority is to treat the hypoglycaemia with quick-acting oral carbohydrate and recheck, which means breaking the fast; religious guidance permits this when health is at risk. Once he has recovered, his gliclazide dose and timing for the rest of the fast should be reviewed. Driving advice is important but comes after he is safe.
why_wrong: A. HbA1c reflects control over months and does nothing for the acute low. B. Driving advice matters, but he must be treated first, and the decision to notify the DVLA depends on the type and frequency of episodes. D. Insulin would lower the glucose further. E. Restricting carbohydrate is irrelevant to an acute low and increases risk.
pearl: For people fasting during Ramadan on a sulfonylurea, the dose is usually reduced and taken with the sunset meal rather than in the morning.
thinking: Sulfonylurea taken while fasting ↓ Sweaty, shaky and muddled ↓ Capillary glucose low ↓ Immediate priority is to treat hypoglycaemia ↓ Then review medication timing and driving safety
exam_trap: B, Advise him not to drive and complete a DVLA form — driving safety is a real issue for a taxi driver, but it is not the first action while he is still hypoglycaemic.
takeaway: Treat hypoglycaemia first; medication review and safety advice follow once the patient has recovered.

stem: A 71-year-old woman with breast cancer that has spread to her spine is reviewed by the hospice doctor because her daughter says she has become muddled and sleepy over a week. She is drinking a lot, passing large volumes of urine and has not opened her bowels for five days. Her adjusted calcium is markedly raised. What is the most likely explanation for her new symptoms?
why_correct: Confusion, drowsiness, thirst, polyuria and constipation in a patient with bone metastases and a high calcium is hypercalcaemia of malignancy. It results from bone destruction by metastases or tumour secretion of PTH-related peptide. Treatment is IV fluids followed by an IV bisphosphonate.
why_wrong: A. Brain metastases can cause confusion but would not explain thirst, polyuria and a high calcium. B. Opioids cause drowsiness and constipation but not polyuria and thirst. C. SIADH causes low sodium and confusion but not polyuria or a high calcium. E. Hypoglycaemia causes acute sweating and confusion, not a week of thirst and polyuria.
pearl: Hypercalcaemia is one of the most common oncological emergencies and is most often seen with breast, lung and myeloma.
thinking: Known cancer with bone metastases ↓ Confusion and drowsiness ↓ Thirst, polyuria and constipation ↓ Calcium markedly raised ↓ Hypercalcaemia of malignancy
exam_trap: B, Opioid toxicity — drowsiness and constipation are typical of opioids in palliative care, but they do not cause polyuria or a high calcium.
takeaway: In a patient with cancer, confusion with thirst, polyuria and constipation should prompt a check for hypercalcaemia.

stem: A 66-year-old man with type 1 diabetes is on a surgical ward on the second day after a bowel resection. He is nil by mouth on intravenous fluids. The nurse calls because within the last half hour he has become restless and confused and is pulling at his drip. Which bedside test should be performed first to look for a rapidly reversible cause?
why_correct: In anyone with diabetes, sudden confusion must be assumed to be hypoglycaemia until a capillary glucose has excluded it. The test takes seconds, and low glucose is common in insulin-treated patients who are nil by mouth. If low, it can be corrected immediately, preventing seizures or brain injury.
why_wrong: A. A urine dipstick is unreliable for diagnosing infection in older adults and is not the urgent priority. C. Peak flow assesses asthma and does not explain acute confusion. D. An ECG may be useful later, but it does not identify the most common rapidly reversible cause here. E. Retention can cause agitation, but hypoglycaemia is more dangerous and must be checked first.
pearl: People with type 1 diabetes must never have all insulin stopped while nil by mouth; they need a variable-rate insulin infusion with glucose-containing fluids to avoid both hypoglycaemia and DKA.
thinking: Diabetes and nil by mouth after surgery ↓ Sudden confusion and agitation ↓ Many possible causes, one is immediately reversible ↓ Capillary glucose takes seconds ↓ Exclude hypoglycaemia first
exam_trap: D, Twelve-lead ECG — it is a common early test in an unwell surgical patient, but it does not address the most likely and quickly reversible cause in a person with diabetes.
takeaway: Check a capillary glucose in every patient with diabetes who becomes acutely confused.

stem: A 68-year-old man with insulin-treated type 2 diabetes recently had his dose increased. His wife finds him slumped on the bathroom floor, unresponsive to her voice but breathing. A home glucose meter gives a very low reading. Before the ambulance arrives she says she wants to pour sugary cola into his mouth. Why should she not do this?

options.A: Liquid could enter his airway and cause choking or aspiration
options.B: Oral glucose is absorbed too fast and causes kidney damage
options.C: Glucose drinks should never be given to anyone with diabetes
options.D: Glucose taken by mouth cannot be absorbed in hypoglycaemia
options.E: Cola will cause an immediate dangerous rise in glucose

correct_answer: A. Liquid could enter his airway and cause choking or aspiration
why_correct: An unconscious person cannot protect their airway, so fluid or food in the mouth may be inhaled, causing choking or aspiration pneumonia. Unconscious hypoglycaemia is treated with IM glucagon in the community if available, or IV glucose by paramedics or in hospital. She should place him in the recovery position and wait for help.
why_wrong: B. Oral glucose does not damage the kidneys. C. Oral glucose is the correct treatment for hypoglycaemia in people with diabetes who can swallow. D. Glucose is absorbed well by mouth in hypoglycaemia. E. A rise in glucose is the aim, and the danger here is the airway, not the glucose level.
pearl: Families of people taking insulin should be taught how to use a glucagon kit and to put an unresponsive person in the recovery position.
thinking: Insulin dose recently increased ↓ Unresponsive with a low glucose ↓ Cannot protect his airway ↓ Oral fluids risk aspiration ↓ Recovery position, glucagon or IV glucose instead
exam_trap: C, Glucose drinks should never be given to anyone with diabetes — it sounds plausible to a carer, but oral glucose is the standard treatment if the patient can swallow.
takeaway: Never give anything by mouth to an unconscious hypoglycaemic patient; use glucagon or IV glucose.

stem: A 15-year-old boy is seen in the paediatric endocrine clinic because his voice has not broken and he is teased for looking younger than his classmates. He is otherwise well with a normal sense of smell. Examination shows prepubertal testicular volumes and no pubic or axillary hair. Which blood result would best support a diagnosis of hypogonadism?
why_correct: Hypogonadism in boys means the testes are not producing enough testosterone, either because of testicular failure or lack of pituitary drive. A low testosterone confirms the deficiency, and LH and FSH then show where the problem lies. The other results do not assess gonadal function.
why_wrong: A. Raised amylase points to pancreatic or salivary gland disease. B. Low sodium alone may occur with adrenal insufficiency or SIADH but does not show gonadal failure. C. High glucose suggests diabetes. D. Raised conjugated bilirubin suggests liver or biliary disease.
pearl: Delayed puberty in boys is defined as no testicular enlargement by age 14, and the most common cause is constitutional delay, which often runs in families.
thinking: No pubertal signs at 15 ↓ Small testes and no body hair ↓ Suspect lack of testosterone ↓ Low testosterone confirms hypogonadism ↓ LH and FSH then distinguish primary from secondary
exam_trap: C, High fasting glucose — diabetes can affect growth and puberty, but glucose does not measure testicular function.
takeaway: A low serum testosterone confirms hypogonadism in a boy with delayed puberty.

stem: A 17-year-old boy attends his GP with his mother, who is worried he has not started puberty. He mentions he has never been able to smell cooking or perfume. He has small testes and sparse body hair, and is of normal height for his family. Blood tests show a low testosterone with low LH and FSH. Which type of disorder is most likely?
why_correct: Low testosterone with low or inappropriately normal LH and FSH means the pituitary or hypothalamus is not stimulating the testes, which is hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism. Lifelong anosmia with absent puberty suggests Kallmann syndrome, a failure of GnRH-secreting neurones to migrate. Treatment is with testosterone, or gonadotrophins if fertility is wanted.
why_wrong: A. Primary testicular failure, as in Klinefelter syndrome, causes raised LH and FSH. B. Androgen insensitivity produces a female phenotype in a genetic male, with high testosterone. C. Congenital adrenal hyperplasia in boys usually causes early puberty signs or salt wasting, not absent puberty with anosmia. E. Hypothyroidism can delay puberty, but anosmia and low gonadotrophins with low testosterone point to a hypothalamic cause.
pearl: Kallmann syndrome combines hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism with anosmia, and the sense of smell should be asked about in every adolescent with delayed puberty.
thinking: Absent puberty at 17 ↓ Low testosterone ↓ Low LH and FSH show a central cause ↓ Lifelong anosmia suggests Kallmann syndrome ↓ Hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism
exam_trap: A, Primary testicular failure (hypergonadotrophic hypogonadism) — small testes suggest a testicular problem, but primary failure gives high gonadotrophins, not low.
takeaway: Low testosterone with low gonadotrophins indicates hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism; anosmia suggests Kallmann syndrome.

stem: A 61-year-old woman of Black Caribbean heritage has had type 2 diabetes and hypertension for twelve years. At her annual review in the practice nurse clinic, her urine albumin to creatinine ratio is raised, and repeat early-morning samples over three months confirm this. Urine culture is negative and she has no haematuria. Which complication of diabetes does this finding indicate?
why_correct: Persistently raised urinary albumin, confirmed on repeat samples without infection, is the earliest sign of diabetic kidney disease. It reflects damage to the glomerular filtration barrier and is also a marker of increased cardiovascular risk. She should be offered an ACE inhibitor or ARB and an SGLT2 inhibitor in line with NICE guidance.
why_wrong: A. Peripheral neuropathy is found by foot examination, not urine testing. B. Retinopathy is detected by retinal screening. C. Autonomic neuropathy causes postural hypotension, gastroparesis or erectile dysfunction. D. Albuminuria raises cardiovascular risk, but it is a direct sign of kidney damage, not coronary disease itself.
pearl: Urine ACR should be tested at least annually in everyone with diabetes, and a raised result confirmed on repeat early-morning samples.
thinking: Long-standing diabetes and hypertension ↓ Raised urine ACR ↓ Confirmed on repeat, infection excluded ↓ Glomerular damage ↓ Diabetic kidney disease
exam_trap: D, Coronary artery disease — albuminuria does predict cardiovascular events, which makes this tempting, but the finding itself shows kidney damage.
takeaway: Persistent albuminuria in diabetes indicates diabetic kidney disease and should prompt renal protective treatment.

stem: A 50-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes diagnosed last month attends the diabetes clinic. She is surprised that the nurse has asked about her blood pressure, kidney function, weight, smoking and family history of heart disease, as she thought the main aim was to bring her sugar level down. Which principle best describes current UK management of type 2 diabetes?

options.A: Select drugs by HbA1c and add heart and kidney protection once the target is reached
options.B: Concentrate on HbA1c, checking kidney function only if symptoms develop
options.C: Delay all drug treatment until weight loss is achieved
options.D: Add an SGLT2 inhibitor only when HbA1c is very high
options.E: Consider cardiovascular, kidney, weight and glucose factors together

correct_answer: E. Consider cardiovascular, kidney, weight and glucose factors together
why_correct: Current NICE guidance takes a whole-person approach: medicines are chosen to reduce cardiovascular and kidney risk and to help weight as well as to lower glucose. Blood pressure, lipids and smoking strongly influence outcomes. Glycaemic targets are individualised alongside these factors.
why_wrong: A. Heart and kidney protection is considered from the start, not only after a glucose target is met. B. Kidney function and albuminuria must be checked routinely because early disease is silent. C. Lifestyle change is important but should not delay indicated drug treatment. D. SGLT2 inhibitors are chosen for cardiorenal benefit, not only for very high HbA1c.
pearl: In type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death, so blood pressure, statins and smoking cessation matter as much as glucose control.
thinking: Newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes ↓ Outcomes depend on more than glucose ↓ Assess cardiovascular risk, kidney function and weight ↓ Choose drugs for organ protection as well as glucose lowering ↓ Integrated, individualised management
exam_trap: A, Select drugs by HbA1c and add heart and kidney protection once the target is reached — it reflects older glucose-first teaching, but organ protection is now considered from the outset.
takeaway: Type 2 diabetes management is about cardiovascular, renal and weight outcomes as well as glucose.

presentation: First-line drug treatment in type 2 diabetes
stem: A 46-year-old warehouse supervisor has type 2 diabetes confirmed on two raised HbA1c results. He has no history of heart disease, heart failure or kidney disease, his eGFR is normal and he has started changing his diet. He is keen to start medicine. In line with current NICE guidance, which initial drug treatment should be offered?

options.A: Basal insulin to achieve rapid control
options.B: Modified-release metformin together with an SGLT2 inhibitor
options.C: Lifestyle advice alone for three months, then metformin

correct_answer: B. Modified-release metformin together with an SGLT2 inhibitor
why_correct: The updated NICE type 2 diabetes guideline recommends offering most adults modified-release metformin with an SGLT2 inhibitor as first-line drug treatment, rather than metformin alone. SGLT2 inhibitors reduce cardiovascular events, heart failure admissions and progression of kidney disease, and help with weight. The guideline specifies modified-release metformin, which is better tolerated in the gut than the standard-release form.
why_wrong: A. Insulin is reserved for very high glucose with symptoms or when other drugs fail, not routine first-line treatment. C. Drug treatment should not be delayed when diabetes is confirmed and the patient wants it. D. Gliclazide causes weight gain and hypoglycaemia and is not first-line. E. Pioglitazone causes fluid retention and weight gain and is a later option.
pearl: Before starting an SGLT2 inhibitor, warn about genital fungal infection and the risk of DKA, which may occur with only modestly raised glucose, and advise pausing the drug during acute illness.
thinking: Newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes ↓ Wants drug treatment ↓ No contraindications ↓ Current NICE advice is dual first-line therapy ↓ Modified-release metformin plus an SGLT2 inhibitor
exam_trap: C, Lifestyle advice alone for three months, then metformin — this was once common practice, but delay is not recommended when drug treatment is indicated.
takeaway: Current NICE guidance offers most adults with type 2 diabetes modified-release metformin plus an SGLT2 inhibitor at the start of drug treatment.

stem: A 38-year-old man with prediabetes goes to his GP to discuss his results. He says his fasting glucose seemed fine on the day of the test, and asks which blood test shows his average glucose level over a longer period. Which test is used for this purpose?

options.A: Serum fructosamine over the past week

why_correct: HbA1c measures the proportion of haemoglobin with glucose attached, which builds up over the red cell lifespan. It reflects average glucose over roughly the previous two to three months, so it is used for diagnosis and monitoring. A single fasting or random glucose only gives a snapshot.
why_wrong: A. Fructosamine reflects glucose over about two to three weeks and is used when HbA1c is unreliable. C. A random glucose is a single snapshot. D. C-peptide assesses endogenous insulin production, not average glucose. E. Urine glucose depends on the renal threshold and is not a measure of average glucose.
pearl: HbA1c is unreliable when red cell lifespan is altered, such as in haemolysis, recent blood loss or transfusion, pregnancy and haemoglobinopathies.
thinking: Asks about average glucose ↓ Single glucose measures are snapshots ↓ Glucose binds haemoglobin over the red cell lifespan ↓ Reflects roughly two to three months ↓ HbA1c
exam_trap: A, Serum fructosamine over the past week — it also measures glycation, but it covers only a few weeks and is a niche test.
takeaway: HbA1c reflects average glycaemia over about two to three months.

stem: A 59-year-old woman was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes two months ago and has just had her treatment increased because her HbA1c remained above her agreed target. At her review with the practice pharmacist she asks how often she will now need the test. According to NICE guidance, how often should HbA1c be measured while treatment is being adjusted?

options.D: Once a year as soon as treatment starts
options.E: Every three to six months until stable

correct_answer: E. Every three to six months until stable
why_correct: NICE advises measuring HbA1c every three to six months until the level is stable on unchanging treatment, then every six months. Because HbA1c reflects about two to three months of glucose, repeating it more often does not show the full effect of a treatment change. Annual testing alone is too infrequent while treatment is being adjusted.
why_wrong: A. Two-weekly testing is too soon to reflect a change in treatment. B. Four weeks is still too short for HbA1c to reflect a new average. C. Yearly testing would delay needed changes. D. Annual testing is not enough during titration.
pearl: Once HbA1c and treatment are stable, NICE recommends checking it every six months.
thinking: Treatment recently changed ↓ HbA1c reflects about two to three months ↓ Testing more often adds little ↓ Testing yearly delays action ↓ Every three to six months until stable
exam_trap: B, Every four weeks — frequent checks seem sensible after a change, but HbA1c cannot reflect a new steady state that quickly.
takeaway: Measure HbA1c every three to six months until stable, then six-monthly.

stem: An 80-year-old man with type 2 diabetes lives with his daughter, has moderate frailty and has had two falls this year. He takes metformin and gliclazide. At his GP review his daughter asks what HbA1c level the family should be aiming for. What is the most appropriate principle for setting his target?

options.A: Aim for the lowest possible HbA1c to prevent complications
options.B: Use one fixed national target for everyone with type 2 diabetes
options.C: Base the target solely on his age
options.D: Apply the same target used for people on metformin alone
options.E: Agree an individual target, weighing benefits against risks such as hypoglycaemia

correct_answer: E. Agree an individual target, weighing benefits against risks such as hypoglycaemia
why_correct: NICE recommends agreeing an individualised HbA1c target with each person. In frailty, falls and a sulfonylurea, the risk of hypoglycaemia outweighs the long-term benefit of very tight control, so a relaxed target is usually appropriate. His medicines, including gliclazide, should also be reviewed.
why_wrong: A. Aggressive lowering increases hypoglycaemia and falls risk in frail older people. B. A single fixed target ignores individual risks and preferences. C. Age alone is not enough; frailty, comorbidity and life expectancy matter more. D. Targets depend on the whole clinical picture, not only on which drugs are used.
pearl: Hypoglycaemia in older people may present atypically with falls, confusion or behaviour change rather than sweating and tremor.
thinking: Older man with frailty and falls ↓ Takes a sulfonylurea ↓ Tight targets raise hypoglycaemia risk ↓ Benefits of tight control take years ↓ Agree an individual, relaxed target
exam_trap: C, Base the target solely on his age — age seems an obvious guide, but frailty, comorbidity and hypoglycaemia risk matter more than age alone.
takeaway: HbA1c targets should be individualised, balancing benefit against harms such as hypoglycaemia.
